inversion path. 86 → 93 unit tests passing.

fix(contracts): refuse auto-generate on non-draft progress claims

Auto-generate re-builds the claim line breakdown and rewrites
gross_amount / retention_amount / net_due. Running it against a claim
that has left draft (submitted / approved / certified / paid / rejected)
silently corrupts the audit trail and reconciliation against AR.

Gate the entry point on claim.status == 'draft' and return 409 with a
structured error otherwise. Regression net lives in
backend/tests/integration/test_contracts_deep_audit.py.

fix(contracts): refuse lien waivers on draft or rejected claims

A lien waiver legally releases lien rights tied to a specific payment
application. Attaching one to a draft claim (never submitted to the
owner) has no underlying lien to release, and attaching one to a
rejected claim ties the waiver to an amount the owner explicitly
refused — both create a bogus paper trail that downstream lien-rights
software treats as authoritative.

Gate attach_lien_waiver on claim.status not in {'draft', 'rejected'}
and return 409 with a structured error otherwise.

fix(contracts): dedupe retention-release events + validate custom schedule

Two-part hardening of release_retention which together close a silent
double-spend on construction retention:

1) Reject duplicate release events. The metadata audit log was
   append-only but never consulted to dedupe, so calling the endpoint
   twice for the same event (substantial_completion, etc.) would each
   time release the configured percentage of net_held — asymptotically
   draining retention to zero regardless of the schedule's stated
   intent. Now returns 409 retention_event_already_released.

2) Validate custom_schedule percentages up-front. Negative, > 100, or
   non-numeric values used to be silently clamped by
   plan_retention_release (or raise an unhandled InvalidOperation).
   Now returns 400 invalid_custom_schedule with which key was bad and
   what value was supplied.

Together with the duplicate-event gate, this also makes a
fully-released contract idempotent: any further release event returns
amount_released == 0 instead of re-basing on stale held.

fix(contracts): force new contracts to start in draft status

The lifecycle FSM (draft → active → suspended / completed /
terminated) is enforced by dedicated transition endpoints that stamp
signed_at and publish the contracts.contract.signed event finance and
dashboards subscribe to. POST /contracts/ accepted status from the
payload, letting a caller create a contract directly in 'active' or
'completed' — skipping the signed_at audit stamp and the event hook,
producing a commercially-live contract with no record of how it got
there.

Force status='draft' and signed_at=None on create, regardless of
payload. The sign / suspend / resume / terminate endpoints remain
the only path that may change status.

test(geo-hub): e2e smoke for BIM + PropDev "View on map" CTAs

Adds a Playwright spec that exercises the v4.4.0 cross-module CTAs by
clicking ``bim-view-on-map`` / ``propdev-view-on-map`` and asserting
each one lands on the matching per-project / per-development Geo Hub
route. Also covers the new Safety / Punch List / Daily Diary CTAs
shipped in the follow-up commits so future regressions get caught in
one place. Gated on PLAYWRIGHT_GEO=1 because the destination mounts
Cesium, mirroring geo-hub.spec.ts.

feat(safety,geo-hub): WGS84 geo binding for HSE incidents

Adds nullable ``geo_lat`` / ``geo_lon`` columns to ``oe_safety_incident``
so incidents can be pinned on the project map. Surfaces them through
``IncidentCreate`` / ``IncidentUpdate`` / ``IncidentResponse`` and the
service layer, and adds the ``SafetyPage`` toolbar "View on map" CTA
that jumps to ``/projects/:id/geo``.

Migration strategy: a single inspector-guarded migration
``v3107_cross_module_geo_binding`` adds both ``oe_safety_incident``
and ``oe_punchlist_item`` columns (the punchlist binding rides on the
same migration so we don't fan out into two near-empty heads). Columns
are nullable with NO server_default — keeping them out of the
NOT-NULL-on-snapshot-replay class that bit us in #154. Fresh installs
get the columns via ``Base.metadata.create_all`` from the updated
models; existing installs run the migration as a strictly additive
batch_alter_table.

Daily Diary photos already carry ``lat`` / ``lng`` (predating this
work) so they need no schema change.

feat(punchlist,geo-hub): WGS84 geo binding for punch list items

Adds nullable ``geo_lat`` / ``geo_lon`` columns to ``oe_punchlist_item``
so items can be pinned in world space (companion to the sheet-pinned
``location_x`` / ``location_y``). Wires the fields through Create /
Update / Response schemas and the service constructor, and adds a
toolbar "View on map" CTA to ``PunchListPage`` that jumps to
``/projects/:id/geo``.

The DB column add ships in ``v3107_cross_module_geo_binding`` (the
combined HSE+Punchlist additive migration introduced in the preceding
commit) — same nullable + no-server_default discipline.

feat(geo-hub,daily-diary): cross-module pin layer endpoints

Exposes the project-scoped geo pins from HSE, Punchlist, and Daily
Diary through three new IDOR-gated read endpoints:

  GET /api/v1/geo-hub/projects/{id}/hse-pins
  GET /api/v1/geo-hub/projects/{id}/punchlist-pins
  GET /api/v1/geo-hub/projects/{id}/diary-photo-pins

Each returns rows that have lat/lon set; un-pinned rows and archived
diary photos are excluded so "no pin" never leaks to the map. Cross-
tenant access funnels through ``GeoHubService._verify_project_owner``
and returns 404 — never 403 — to avoid UUID existence oracles.

Adds the matching ``DailyDiaryPage`` "View on map" CTA (the photo lat/
lng columns already existed, so no schema change is needed for diary).

Tests: ``test_geo_hub_cross_module_pins.py`` covers the round-trip for
each layer, the un-pinned exclusion, the archived-photo exclusion, and
the cross-tenant 404 path. 7 new tests, all green; the existing
``test_geo_hub_api.py`` suite (36 tests) still passes unchanged.

fix(resources): preserve explicit zero cost_rate in proposed assignments

`propose_assignment` collapsed `data.cost_rate or resource.default_cost_rate
or Decimal('0')` to pick a value, treating an explicit `Decimal('0')` from
the caller as falsy and silently substituting the resource catalogue
default. That broke the rate-history snapshot for legitimately zero-cost
assignments (donated equipment, internally-loaned staff, pro-bono crews)
and inflated downstream cost rollups whenever a non-zero default was set
on the resource.

The same coalesce was applied to `currency`, which is a string field where
the bug never bit (empty string is the genuine "unspecified" sentinel),
but the equivalent rewrite is included for symmetry and clarity.

The fix branches on `is None` (the unambiguous "field not supplied"
sentinel) rather than truthiness, so the assignment freezes exactly what
the caller sent — including a real zero.

Adds `test_propose_assignment_explicit_zero_cost_rate_is_preserved` which
fails on the old `or`-coalesce and passes after the rewrite.

fix(resources): close cross-tenant IDOR on project-scoped endpoints

The resources router exposed nine project-scoped endpoints that trusted
the caller-supplied `project_id` (either as a query parameter or in the
request body) without ever verifying that the user owned that project.
That let one tenant:

* enumerate another tenant's pending resource requests via
  `GET /resources/requests/?project_id=X`
* read an arbitrary request by id via `GET /resources/requests/{id}`
* patch / delete / fulfill another tenant's resource requests
* file new resource requests against another tenant's project (the
  `resources.request` permission is granted to VIEWER on registration,
  so this is exploitable by any freshly-registered account)
* create or propose assignments against another tenant's project
* view another tenant's dispatcher board via
  `GET /resources/board/?project_id=X`

All nine endpoints now route through `verify_project_access`, which
returns 404 (not 403) on both "missing project" and "access denied" so
the endpoint cannot be used as a UUID-existence oracle. The unscoped
dispatcher board (`project_id=None`) is preserved — it remains the
org-wide view gated by `resources.read` only.

Adds `test_resources_idor.py` with one test per attack vector. Every
test was red against the pre-fix router and is green after the patch:

  9 passed in 225.24s

fix(changeorders): roll up summary money totals as Decimal not float

The /summary endpoint accumulated cost_impact via float() and rounded
the running total with round(x, 2). On a project with many small
deltas (0.10 + 0.20 + 0.05 …), repeated binary-float widening drifted
the KPI by sub-cent amounts that no manual reconciliation could
explain.

Replace the float chain with Decimal end-to-end, quantising once at
the persist/expose boundary (HALF_UP, 2dp) to match finance and
procurement conventions. Pydantic response schemas already accept
both Decimal and string forms via the existing _decimal_to_str
coercer, so the wire format stays identical.

fix(changeorders): turn approval-chain start TOCTOU into clean 409

start_approval_chain probed _has_approval_chain and then inserted the
chain rows in a separate flush. Under concurrency two callers could
both pass the probe; the unique index on (change_order_id, step_order)
caught the second writer at the database, but the raw IntegrityError
bubbled up to the API as a 500 with a leaked partial chain on
session state.

Wrap the post-add flush in a try/except IntegrityError. On collision
roll the session back and raise the same 409 the existing
already-exists branch returns, so the second caller sees a clean
'use /advance-approval' message and the database stays consistent.

fix(changeorders): race-safe advance_approval via conditional UPDATE

Two approvers clicking 'approve' on the same active step at the same
moment both passed the python-side active_row.decision == 'pending'
check, both stamped the row, both bumped the cursor. The CO ended up
advancing two steps in one click and the row's decided_at / comments
reflected only the slower writer.

Replace the in-memory mutation with UPDATE oe_changeorder_approval
SET … WHERE id = :id AND decision = 'pending'. The DB enforces
single-winner semantics: rowcount==0 means the row was already
decided, and the loser sees a clean 409 with 'concurrently decided by
another approver — refresh and retry'. Works the same on SQLite (dev)
and Postgres (prod) without a SELECT … FOR UPDATE round trip.

feat(changeorders): write ActivityLog row on every status transition

Submit / approve / reject / chain-reject paths previously logged
only to the Python logger and the event bus — both are ephemeral and
neither survives audit. A contractor disputing whose CO approval
landed at 16:43:02 had no first-class trace; the BUG-351 rejected_by
column gives the actor but no transition history.

Add a _safe_audit() wrapper around app.core.audit_log.log_activity
and call it from submit_order, reject_order, approve_order, and the
advance_approval reject branch. Rows live on oe_activity_log
alongside boq / invoice / ncr lifecycle records so dispute timelines
(FIDIC contemporary records, ISO 9001 traceability, SCL Protocol)
can be reproduced byte-for-byte. The wrapper swallows ActivityLog
failures so a missing table on a partial migration never rolls back
the business write.

fix(changeorders): block submitter from their own approval chain

start_approval_chain accepted any user-id list, including the
submitter's own id. The single-step approve_order / reject_order
paths enforce four-eyes via _assert_not_self_approval, but the
chain bypassed the same rule — a scope author could discreetly slot
themselves in as step 2 of 3 and rubber-stamp their own CO,
defeating the multi-approver requirement that the chain exists to
encode (closes the four-eyes loophole opened by BUG-353).

Reject (403) any chain start where submitter_id appears in
approver_user_ids, with a message that steers the caller to remove
themselves.

fix(inspections): close cross-tenant IDOR on complete/defect/NCR endpoints

Three mutating ``/api/v1/inspections/{id}/...`` endpoints fetched the
inspection by primary key and acted on it (state mutation, defect /
NCR creation in the inspection's parent project) without ever calling
``verify_project_access``. Any authenticated editor could:

* ``POST /{id}/complete/``       — flip another tenant's inspection to
  completed/pass|fail (write IDOR).
* ``POST /{id}/create-defect/``  — inject a punchlist item into another
  tenant's project.
* ``POST /{id}/create-ncr/``     — inject an NCR into another tenant's
  project.

Fix: resolve the inspection first, then run the standard project
ownership check before any state mutation. ``verify_project_access``
returns 404 on both "missing" and "not yours" so the endpoints can
no longer be used as an inspection-UUID enumeration oracle.

New integration suite ``test_inspections_idor.py`` covers the three
write-IDOR vectors plus three regression guards (read /, GET /{id},
GET /export/) and an owner-flow happy path. Suite fails on this
commit's parent and passes here.

fix(inspections): reject complete() from failed/illegal states (FSM gap)

``complete_inspection`` only checked two explicit "no-go" statuses
(``completed`` and ``cancelled``) and silently accepted anything
else as a launchpad — including the ``failed`` terminal-ish state.
That broke the documented re-inspection contract in
``_INSPECTION_STATUS_TRANSITIONS`` which says ``failed`` can only
transition to ``scheduled`` (re-schedule first, then re-inspect).

Tighten the gate to accept only ``scheduled`` (one-step shortcut)
and ``in_progress`` (canonical path). Anything else is a 400 with
a status-specific message.

New unit suite ``test_inspections_fsm.py`` pins the three FSM
endpoints: failed → 400, scheduled → 200, in_progress → 200.

fix(costmodel): make generate-budget-from-boq idempotent

R5 audit found that POST /5d/generate-budget/ silently doubled the
project BAC on re-run — each call appended a fresh BudgetLine per BOQ
position with no dedupe, so two clicks of the dashboard button (or a
retry from the frontend) created duplicate rows that aggregated into a
2x BAC and poisoned every downstream EVM rollup.

The service now skips positions already wired to a budget line for the
project. Migration v3107 adds a partial unique index
(project_id, boq_position_id) WHERE boq_position_id IS NOT NULL as a
belt-and-braces DB-level guard; manual budget lines without a position
link remain freely duplicable.

Migration includes a one-time dedupe pass (keep the oldest row per
project/position) so existing installs polluted by the bug can upgrade
cleanly.

fix(costmodel): reject duplicate (project_id, period) snapshots

R5 audit found CostSnapshot had no uniqueness on (project_id, period).
Two POST /5d/snapshots/ calls for the same month silently produced two
rows; get_latest_for_project then picked one arbitrarily, so EVM
rollups, dashboard SPI/CPI, and the S-curve flapped between competing
values whenever an estimator re-saved a month.

The service now 409s on duplicate periods and migration v3108 adds the
backing unique index.

What-if scenarios used to store their snapshot row with the current
YYYY-MM period, which would now collide with the real monthly
snapshot. Scenarios now key on 'wif:<short-id>:YYYY-MM' instead;
get_latest_for_project filters out the wif: prefix so a stray
scenario never masquerades as the canonical snapshot. The period
column widens from VARCHAR(10) to VARCHAR(40) to fit the new format.

fix(costmodel): surface tcpi=null when BAC <= AC instead of false zero

R5 audit caught a divide-by-zero path in calculate_evm: when a project
is exactly on-budget (BAC == AC) or already over-budget (BAC < AC),
TCPI = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) is mathematically undefined. The
legacy code routed this through _safe_divide and returned 0.0, which
the EVM dashboard happily rendered as "perfect efficiency required" —
the misleading opposite of the actual project state.

The endpoint now returns tcpi=null in that branch; EVMResponse.tcpi is
Optional[float] so OpenAPI clients see the change explicitly. The
existing on-track / at-risk classification path doesn't read TCPI so
no status downgrade is needed.

fix(costmodel): convert per-line currencies to project base in rollups

R5 audit caught the highest-impact correctness bug in the cost model
module: every rollup happily summed across budget-line currencies as
if they were the same unit. The SQL aggregate did
SUM(CAST(planned_amount AS Float)) with no regard for the per-row
``currency`` column, so a project running EUR base with a USD
subcontract line for 1000 would report 1000 EUR equivalent — not the
real 900 EUR (at 0.9 EUR/USD). The error cascaded into the dashboard
KPIs, the budget category breakdown, the EVM BAC, and the generated
cash flow S-curve.

Post-audit:

- ``BudgetLineRepository.aggregate_by_project`` and
  ``aggregate_by_category`` pull rows in Python and convert each via
  the project's ``fx_rates`` map (same convention as the BOQ resource
  rollup: stored_total * rate -> base units).
- ``generate_cash_flow_from_schedule`` does the same per-line FX
  conversion before bucketing outflows by period.
- A new module-level ``_amount_in_base`` helper carries Decimal
  end-to-end so a million-line BAC no longer drifts on floating-point
  accumulation, and missing FX rates degrade visibly (kept in their
  own units) instead of silently zeroing.

The Pydantic API contract is unchanged; only the numeric correctness
flips. Single-currency projects round-trip identically.
alembic(merge): unite v3107 cross-module-geo + v3108 costmodel-snapshot branches

fix(geo_hub): scope tileset reuse lookup by project to close cross-tenant URI leak (P0 IDOR)

POST /api/v1/geo-hub/tilesets/generate/ short-circuits to a "completed"
job when find_for_source(source_kind, source_id) returns a ready
tileset. The lookup was unscoped, so a tenant who guessed (or learned)
another tenant's source_id could enqueue against their OWN project
and receive a completed job whose output_uri pointed at the foreign
storage prefix.

Added project_id to find_for_source (optional for internal subscribers
that operate on trusted payloads), and pass data.project_id from
enqueue_tile_generation so reuse is bounded to the caller's tenant.

Regression test asserts that tenant B never gets back tenant A's
tileset_json_uri or tileset_id when they share the same source_id.

fix(geo_hub): rotate canonical elements around footprint centroid, not local origin (P1)

POST /api/v1/geo-hub/from-canonical/{id} with heading_deg != 0 used to
rotate every element AABB around (0, 0, 0). That works only when the
canonical export happens to be project-centred. Real-world converters
emit site coordinates with the origin at the surveyor's benchmark,
which can be hundreds of metres from the building footprint — rotating
around (0, 0) then translates the whole project away from its anchor,
producing a tileset that renders far from where the user dropped the
pin.

Fix: compute combined AABB once before rotating, then rotate each
element around the centroid of that combined AABB. Heading still loses
per-element orientation (the AABB is rebuilt from the rotated corners)
but the building stays anchored.

Regression tests cover the canonical 180-rotation-is-identity case
(building must overlap its original footprint), the failure mode of
the old origin-pivot path (remote box gets flung), and the
zero-heading noop.

fix(geo_hub): reject canonical-to-tileset with zero usable geometry (P1)

POST /api/v1/geo-hub/from-canonical/{id} used to persist a tileset
even when every canonical element lacked a usable spatial hint
(_element_geometry_aabb returned None for all of them). The resulting
tileset had feature_count=0, a region collapsed to the anchor point,
and a b3dm body whose mesh array was empty. Cesium silently renders
nothing, and the row would poison the (source_kind, source_id) reuse
short-circuit on the next generate call — subsequent valid imports
would short-circuit to the degenerate row.

Now raises 422 canonical_elements_have_no_geometry instead. Caller
fixes the upstream converter output and retries.

Regression test inserts a BIMModel whose elements have empty
bounding_box / quantities and asserts 422 + correct detail string.

fix(geo_hub): stabilise CesiumViewer effect to survive React Query refetches (P1)

CesiumViewer's mount effect depended on the entire mapConfig object
reference. React Query returns a brand-new object on every refetch
(every 30 s on stale revalidation) even when the body bytes are
identical, so the effect re-ran, called viewer.destroy(), rebuilt the
viewer from scratch and re-fetched the 3 MB Cesium runtime — wiping
the user's camera state and pan/zoom history.

Replace the object dependency with a memoised string signature that
keys on (mode, project_id, anchor lat/lon/alt, ready-tileset id+uri).
A refetch with identical content now produces the same signature and
the effect is skipped.

Regression test rerenders the viewer with a fresh-reference but
identical-content mapConfig and asserts the Viewer constructor was
called exactly once.

fix(fieldreports): close IDOR on workforce/equipment log endpoints

The ``/api/v1/fieldreports/`` router exposes four endpoints keyed off
an unscoped ``entry_id`` (``PATCH``/``DELETE /workforce/{entry_id}``
and ``PATCH``/``DELETE /equipment/{entry_id}``) plus two more keyed
off the parent ``report_id`` (``POST``/``GET
/reports/{report_id}/workforce/`` and the equipment twin). None of
them ran ``verify_project_access`` against the owning project, so any
authenticated user holding the ``fieldreports.*`` permission for one
project could:

* list / inject workforce + equipment rows on any other project's
  field report by guessing the parent ``report_id``;
* update or destructively delete any workforce / equipment row by
  guessing the row id directly.

Add two reusable IDOR guards (``_verify_report_access`` and the
``_verify_*_entry_access`` pair) that load the row, resolve the parent
report's project, and gate on ``verify_project_access``. Cross-tenant
calls now return 404 — matching the convention on every sibling
endpoint so the IDs cannot be turned into a UUID-existence oracle.

Regression suite at ``backend/tests/integration/test_fieldreports_idor.py``
covers all six vectors plus the owner-still-works happy path.

fix(fieldreports): bound and content-validate signature_data uploads

``signature_data`` accepted any ``str | None`` payload — a Text column
on the row and an unbounded string in the create / update schemas.
That meant an authenticated caller could:

* dump megabytes of arbitrary text into the column (the row is later
  embedded verbatim in the PDF export, so this also amplified into a
  multi-MB report download per call);
* store inline scripts / HTML in a field that the frontend renders
  back when the report opens for signature review.

Tighten the schema with an ``AfterValidator``: reject anything that
isn't a ``data:image/...`` URI, restrict the MIME subtype to the set
that real signature pads emit (png / jpeg / webp / svg+xml), and cap
the payload at 2 MB. Applied to both ``FieldReportCreate`` and
``FieldReportUpdate`` so the update path can't be used to launder an
oversize blob into an existing row.

Response schema stays permissive so historical rows still serialise
correctly. No DB migration needed.

Unit tests at ``tests/unit/test_fieldreports_signature_validation.py``
cover the happy path (png / jpeg / webp / none / empty) and every
rejection branch (plain text, script payload, ``data:text/html``,
unsupported MIME, oversize).

fix(fieldreports): bound and finite-check weather lat/lon query params

``GET /api/v1/fieldreports/weather/`` accepted unbounded ``lat`` /
``lon`` float query params and forwarded them straight to the
OpenWeatherMap call. The schema already constrained ``lat`` / ``lon``
on the ``FieldReportCreate`` payload, but the dedicated weather lookup
route — used by the field-report form to auto-fill weather on demand
— skipped both the WGS-84 range check and the finite-number check.

Practical consequence: a caller could send ``lat=999`` / ``lon=-1e9``
and force an outbound HTTP call with nonsense coordinates, or pass the
literal ``nan`` / ``inf`` and watch FastAPI happily coerce those into
the URL params despite ``ge`` / ``le`` not catching NaN.

Tighten the route with ``ge=-90`` / ``le=90`` (lat) and ``ge=-180`` /
``le=180`` (lon), plus an explicit ``math.isfinite`` guard that 422s
on NaN / Inf before any upstream call is made.

Integration tests at
``tests/integration/test_fieldreports_weather_coords.py`` cover six
out-of-range pairs and four non-finite pairs (parametrised) plus a
happy-path smoke check that proves valid coords still get past the
validator.

fix(fieldreports): magic-byte + size gate on import-file uploads

``POST /api/v1/fieldreports/reports/import/file/`` used to route purely
off the uploader-supplied filename: a ``.exe`` renamed to ``foo.xlsx``
would sail past the extension check straight into openpyxl, which then
either crashed the worker or chewed through memory. The body was also
read into RAM with no upper bound — the existing zip-bomb guard only
caught attacker-tractable .xlsx archives, not raw oversized .csv.

Add two gates before any parser allocates:

* 25 MB hard cap on the request body — well above any legitimate
  field-report sheet (a 10K-row import is ~2 MB).
* Magic-byte verification on Excel uploads using the shared stdlib
  ``app.core.file_signature.detect``: ``.xlsx`` must produce a ZIP
  signature (``PK\x03\x04``); legacy ``.xls`` must produce either OLE
  compound or ZIP. CSV stays best-effort (no magic bytes) but is
  still bounded by the size cap.

Integration suite at
``tests/integration/test_fieldreports_import_magic_byte.py`` covers
the renamed-exe rejection, random-blob rejection, oversize-upload
rejection, and the real-xlsx + plain-csv happy paths end to end.

fix(property_dev): close snag + warranty IDOR holes (task #156)

Every /api/v1/property-dev/snags/* and /api/v1/property-dev/warranty-claims/*
route accepted any authenticated CurrentUserPayload without walking the
snag/claim -> handover -> plot -> development -> project -> owner chain.

A logged-in user in tenant B could enumerate UUIDs and read, modify,
delete, fix, accept, reject or close any tenant's snags + warranty
claims. Listing endpoints also leaked existence via handover_id,
buyer_id and plot_id filters.

Adds four new ownership verifiers in router.py:
  _verify_owner_via_handover  (handover -> plot -> dev -> project)
  _verify_owner_via_snag      (snag -> handover -> ...)
  _verify_owner_via_warranty  (claim -> plot -> ...)
  _verify_owner_via_buyer     (buyer -> dev -> project)

Mirrors the existing _verify_owner_via_plot / _verify_owner_via_lead
closure pattern (forbidden-but-exists collapses to 404, admin bypass).
Wires every snag + warranty route to call the matching verifier.

Test: tests/integration/test_snag_warranty_idor.py (18 tests, all
failing before the fix on the snag/warranty routes -- now passing).
Tenant A creates snag + claim; tenant B (manager in their own org so
permission gates are not what stops them) cannot GET/PATCH/DELETE/fix/
wont-fix/accept/reject/close any of them and cannot list them by
buyer_id, plot_id or handover_id.

feat(property_dev): snag buyer_id + cost_impact + photos + category (task #156)

Extends the Snag entity for proper buyer-facing post-handover defect
tracking:

  buyer_id              GUID nullable, SET NULL on Buyer delete.
                        Lets buyer-portal-raised snags carry the raiser
                        (NULL when surveyor/contractor raises during
                        the handover ceremony).
  category              str(40), default 'general', validated against
                        cosmetic/functional/structural/mechanical/
                        electrical/plumbing/finishing/exterior/general/
                        safety. Mirrors punchlist categories so the
                        downstream snag -> punchlist auto-bridge can
                        copy it verbatim.
  cost_impact           Numeric(18,2), default 0. Pydantic enforces
                        ge=0 so negative repair costs are 422. Decimal
                        in/out -- no binary float drift on rollups.
  photos                JSON list of relative paths. Populated via the
                        new POST /snags/{id}/photos/ endpoint.
  linked_punch_item_id  GUID nullable. Reserved for the snag ->
                        punchlist auto-bridge (next commit).

POST /api/v1/property-dev/snags/{id}/photos/ accepts multipart photo
uploads, magic-byte validates against ALLOWED_PHOTO_TYPES (jpeg/png/
gif/webp/heic/heif/tiff), rejects SVG + everything else with 415, and
IDOR-gates via _verify_owner_via_snag.

create_snag also publishes property_dev.snag.created on the event bus
(payload: snag_id, handover_id, buyer_id, category, severity,

fix(dwg_takeoff): gate every endpoint by project to close IDOR sweep

Round-6 audit found every endpoint in `backend/app/modules/dwg_takeoff/
router.py` trusted the path / query `drawing_id` / `annotation_id` /
`group_id` without verifying the caller owns the underlying project.
Any user with the basic `dwg_takeoff.read` permission could enumerate
UUIDs and exfiltrate foreign tenants' drawings, layers, entities, SVG
thumbnails, annotations (which carry `measurement_value` fields that
feed BOQ totals via link-to-boq), and saved entity groups. Manager-
level callers could also delete or rescale foreign drawings — a 1:50
plan flipped to 1:5 inflates every derived measurement 100x before
it lands in the estimate.

Add three resolver helpers — `_gate_by_drawing`, `_gate_by_annotation`,
`_gate_by_group` — that each load the resource, walk to the owning
project, and delegate to the canonical `verify_project_access` (404
on both missing and forbidden, no UUID-existence probe). Wire every
read/write/delete endpoint through one of them. The annotation create
path additionally cross-checks that the body's `project_id` and the
drawing's actual `project_id` match, so a user can't plant a foreign-
drawing annotation inside their own project record.

Tests: `backend/tests/integration/test_takeoff_dwg_idor.py` (16 new
cross-tenant 404 assertions, one per endpoint) — fails on the
pre-fix code, passes after. `backend/tests/unit/test_idor_router_guards.py`
adds dwg_takeoff to the AST guard so future refactors that drop the
gate get caught statically.

fix(takeoff): switch measurement quantity columns to Numeric(18, 6)

`oe_takeoff_measurement.measurement_value` / `depth` / `volume` /
`perimeter` were stored as `Float` even though every one of them
flows into BOQ totals via `link-to-boq`. Binary float drift
accumulated across (points x scale -> measurement -> unit_rate x
measurement) leaked into the money column on multi-position
takeoffs — invisible per row, visible on roll-up.

The sibling `dwg_takeoff.DwgAnnotation.measurement_value` already
moved to `Numeric(18, 6)` in v3097_dwg_takeoff_decimal_quantities
back in Round 3. This brings the PDF takeoff surface up to the same
precision regime. `scale_pixels_per_unit` stays `Float` — it's a
UI calibration ratio used as a divisor and never persisted into a
money column, so migrating it would force every in-flight PDF
takeoff session to be re-calibrated for zero gain.

Migration: `v3107_takeoff_measurement_numeric` (idempotent — checks
the live column type before altering; no-op on Postgres rows already
on Numeric, batch-rewrite on SQLite). Single linear chain off
`v3106_geo_hub_init`.

Test: `tests/integration/test_takeoff_measurement_decimal.py` pins
each column's SQLAlchemy type so future Float regressions get
caught at unit-test time (no DB round-trip needed).

fix(takeoff): clamp polygon coordinates so payload can't inflate BOQ

`PointSchema.x` / `y` were unbounded floats. A malicious client could
ship `{"x": 1e30, "y": 1e30}` and the server-side shoelace recompute
produced absurd polygon areas that fed straight into BOQ totals via
`link-to-boq`. NaN / infinity slipped through with the same effect
because `Pydantic.ge` accepts NaN on some versions.

Tighten `PointSchema` two ways:

* Each axis is clamped to `+- 1_000_000` (PostScript-point ISO A0 at
  72 dpi tops out around 250 000, so a 4x safety margin still catches
  the gigayear payloads).
* An explicit field-validator rejects NaN / +-Inf so the downstream
  Decimal cast can't materialise a `Decimal('NaN')`.

Also cap `points` per measurement at 5000 entries on both create and
update — well above the densest real-world tracing (longest highway
centerline in the seed data is ~1200 vertices) but small enough that
no payload can peg the shoelace loop.

Test: `tests/integration/test_takeoff_coordinate_validation.py` —
9 cases covering each rejection (out-of-range, NaN, Inf, polygon
with a bad vertex, oversized point list) plus the happy path.

perf(takeoff): drop duplicate measurement lookup on PATCH/DELETE/link

`TakeoffService.update_measurement` / `delete_measurement` /
`link_measurement_to_boq` each called `self.get_measurement(...)` even
though the router had already loaded the row for the IDOR check via
`verify_project_access`. Every measurement mutation therefore ran two
identical `SELECT ... WHERE id=?` round-trips back-to-back — visible
as a sustained 2x SQL load when an estimator bulk-edits measurements
on a large takeoff.

Add an `existing: TakeoffMeasurement | None = None` kwarg to each of
the three service methods. The router now hands the pre-fetched row
through, so the service skips the redundant lookup. The legacy id-only
path is preserved for callers (CLI scripts, tests) that don't have
the row handy.

Test: `tests/integration/test_takeoff_measurement_no_duplicate_query.py`
patches `MeasurementRepository.get_by_id` and asserts `await_count == 0`
when `existing=` is supplied — a future refactor that re-introduces
the inner `get_measurement` call will fail this pin at unit-test time.

fix(meetings): close import-summary cross-tenant IDOR

The POST /api/v1/meetings/import-summary/ endpoint accepted a
project_id query parameter and went straight to transcript parsing
and meeting create with no verify_project_access gate. Any user
holding the meetings.create role could craft a fake transcript
and silently inject a fully-populated meeting (attendees, action
items, minutes) plus a Document into a foreign tenant's project.

Add the project-ownership check up-front so cross-tenant writes
fail with 404 — matching the convention used by every sibling
endpoint in the router. Regression suite at
backend/tests/integration/test_meetings_idor.py pins the boundary
and includes a regression guard so the legitimate owner path still
returns 200.

fix(meetings): coerce non-ISO due-date hints to None on import-summary

The transcript heuristic at _DUE_DATE_PATTERN happily captures
weekday and relative phrases (Friday, next week, end of month)
and stuffs them straight into ActionItemEntry.due_date — which
pydantic guards with a strict ^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$ regex. The
resulting ValidationError escaped as a 500, after the heuristic
step had already cross-linked the transcript file into the
Documents hub — leaving a half-imported orphan attachment on
the project.

Scrub any extracted due_date that isn't ISO YYYY-MM-DD to None
via the new _coerce_iso_due_date helper, and fold the raw hint
into the action-item description so reviewers can still see what
the speaker actually said. Integration test
test_import_summary_handles_nonstandard_due_date_hints in
backend/tests/integration/test_meetings_idor.py pins the
behaviour with a transcript that contains three offending phrases.

fix(meetings): reject document_ids that belong to a different project

A meeting's document_ids JSON array is a cross-module reference
into oe_documents_document. Pre-fix the field was persisted
verbatim, so a caller could attach a UUID resolving to a document
inside a sibling project — leaking the *existence* of foreign
documents into the meeting payload and parking a dangling FK
that survives deletion of the source project.

Add a per-project integrity gate in MeetingService that fans the
incoming document_ids through a single SELECT on Document.id /
project_id and raises 422 if any reference is missing or owned
by a different project. The check runs on both create_meeting
and update_meeting; series occurrences propagate the master's
already-validated set so the check is a no-op for them.

Missing documents return the same 422 (not 404) so the endpoint
can't be turned into a UUID-existence oracle. Integration test
test_create_meeting_rejects_foreign_document_ids pins the
behaviour at the HTTP boundary.

feat(meetings): stamp meeting.action_items_created event with stable event_key

complete_meeting publishes meeting.action_items_created via
event_bus.publish_detached as a fire-and-forget task. Although
the service is already guarded against re-completion (status
check raises 400 on a completed meeting), the bus itself is
detached — a transient retry inside the bus would re-fire the
notification handler in events.py and double-notify every task
owner.

Hand subscribers a stable event_key = meeting:complete:<id> so
they can dedupe defensively without any cross-module knowledge
of meetings internals. The key is derived from the immutable
meeting UUID, so two publishes for the same meeting always
collide. No behaviour change for current subscribers; new field
sits alongside the existing payload.

intercepts publish_detached via monkeypatch and asserts the
event_key shape.

fix(error-logger): filter network errors from auto-bug-report picker (#155)

Issue #155 (Mourdi59): the in-app 'Report bug' menu captured a benign

errorLogger.ts:

  (Firefox), 'Load failed' (Safari), all AbortError variants, 'The
  operation was aborted'

- New predicates: isNetworkErrorMessage, isTransientHttpStatus,
  isNetworkBlip, isLastErrorNetworkOnly

  error, (2) most recent error of any kind, (3) most recent entry.
  Real defects (ReferenceError, undefined-property TypeError, JSON
  parse, 4xx/422/500) always beat transport noise; backend-down
  sessions still get a payload via the override path.

  keeps them — only the picker filters them out.

Header.tsx (BugReportMenu):
- On open, calls isLastErrorNetworkOnly().
- Amber banner when true: 'Looks like a network issue, not a bug —
  check your connection and reload. If the problem persists, you can

fix(contracts): R7 audit — IDOR + clone safety + Decimal money + RBAC

The triage flagged the contracts module as "IDOR on all 59 endpoints"
and "Float money", but inspection confirmed the prior R5 sweep had
already landed comprehensive _verify_contract_access / _verify_claim_access
on every project-scoped endpoint, and every money column was already
Numeric(18, 4) / Pydantic Decimal. The remaining gap was clone safety
— there was no clone endpoint at all, so any future addition would
re-open both cross-tenant exfiltration (read source) and cross-tenant
injection (write into foreign destination) vectors.

This commit adds the clone endpoint with R7-grade safety from day one,
plus a regression net for the existing IDOR + Decimal + RBAC + FSM
guarantees so the next refactor cannot quietly re-open the holes.

Changes:

* New POST /contracts/{id}/clone endpoint with three-layer safety:
  - _verify_contract_access on the source contract (404 leak-safe)
  - verify_project_access on the destination when target_project_id
    differs from the source's project (blocks cross-tenant injection)
  - RequirePermission("contracts.clone") elevated to MANAGER

* ContractCloneRequest schema requires new_code (unique constraint),
  defaults include_lines and copy_subconfigs to True, defaults
  target_project_id to None (same-project clone).

* ContractsService.clone_contract():
  - Deep-copies SoV lines with two-pass parent_line_id remapping
  - Copies retention schedule / fee structure / gainshare config / LD
    clauses
  - Always lands the clone as status="draft" with signed_at=None — a
    cloned instrument must be re-signed
  - Copies terms by value (defensive against later clone-side mutation
    bleeding back into the source)
  - Strips retention_releases + lien_waivers from cloned metadata —
    those legal artefacts belong to the source's payment history
  - Records cloned_from_contract_id in metadata for lineage audit
  - Surfaces a 409 (not raw IntegrityError) on duplicate code
  - Emits contracts.contract.cloned event

* permissions.py registers contracts.clone at Role.MANAGER.

* New tests/modules/test_contracts_security.py — 17 tests pinning:
  - IDOR on GET (cross-tenant 404, not 403; happy path still passes)
  - IDOR on clone source (cross-tenant exfil blocked)
  - IDOR on clone destination (cross-tenant injection blocked)
  - Same-project clone happy path (no false-positive over-locking)
  - Duplicate code → 409 (not 500)
  - Decimal-string money serialization (JSON mode → str, py mode →
    Decimal) + ORM-level "no Float column" defensive guard
  - RBAC: VIEWER cannot update, EDITOR cannot clone, MANAGER+ can clone
  - Clone schema requires new_code (no silent UNIQUE violation)
  - FSM rejects completed→active / terminated→active; happy
    draft→active path still works; service surfaces 400 on invalid

No alembic migration — all money columns were already Numeric(18, 4)
and the clone endpoint adds no new tables.

registry and enforce it server-side in the SSE dispatch loop:

fix(costs): R7 audit — IDOR + Decimal money + magic-byte uploads + RBAC

Round-7 deep audit closes three trip-wires on the costs module:

1. IDOR — `GET /vector/v3-status/` now verifies project ownership
   before exposing the `language_mismatch` diagnostic block. Anonymous
   or cross-tenant callers still get the engine-status payload (it
   gates the catalogue-readiness banner) but the per-project
   diagnostics collapse to a sentinel — no leakage of bound_catalogue
   id, region, or language. 404-equivalent semantics for both
   "project missing" and "access denied" (no UUID-existence oracle).

2. Money is Decimal — every money/rate/factor field in the schemas
   now serialises as a Decimal-coercible string via Pydantic v2
   PlainSerializer. Covers CostItemResponse.rate, CostItemCreate.rate,
   CostItemUpdate.rate, CostAutocompleteItem.rate +
   cost_breakdown[*], CostSuggestion.unit_rate,
   RegionalIndexResponse.factor, RegionalAdjustResponse.{base_rate,
   factor_applied, adjusted_rate}, RecordUsageRequest.unit_rate_at_use,
   CostSearchQuery.min_rate/max_rate. RegionalIndexService.adjust now
   does Decimal × Decimal end-to-end with .quantize() instead of the
   old float * round() (no float drift on rollups). CostItem.rate
   stays String(50) at the column level for SQLite Decimal compat
   (long-standing decision in models.py); no migration needed.

3. Upload safety — `POST /import/file/` now does magic-byte sniffing
   against the first 16 bytes of every upload. `.xlsx`/`.xls` must
   match the ZIP or OLE container signature; `.csv` must decode as
   text without NUL bytes and must not sniff as a known container.
   Mismatches return 415, not 400. Adds a 25 MB upload cap (413 on
   overflow) so a renamed binary can't exhaust the parser.

4. RBAC — existing `RequirePermission("costs.update")` gate on
   PATCH/DELETE preserved; new regression test pins that a viewer
   role cannot mutate cost items.

- 199.99 rate round-trips as exact Decimal string
- Create accepts sub-cent Decimal-string body
- regional-adjust returns Decimal strings for all 3 money fields
- xlsx with PDF body returns 415
- csv with NUL bytes returns 415

perf(projects): replace in-memory code scan with SQL MAX aggregate

ProjectRepository.max_project_code_seq previously SELECT'd every row
matching the prefix and walked the rows in Python to find the highest
numeric suffix. With multi-tenant deployments now carrying hundreds of
projects per year-prefix, this became measurable wall time on every
create_project call (since each one calls _generate_project_code →
max_project_code_seq inside the _PROJECT_CODE_LOCK critical section).

Rewrite as a single
  SELECT MAX(CAST(SUBSTR(project_code, prefix_len+1) AS INTEGER))
  WHERE project_code LIKE prefix || '%'
aggregate so the scan runs database-side with constant rows transferred.

Postgres raises on a non-numeric CAST; a DBAPIError fallback to the old
Python-side scan preserves semantics for any legacy malformed codes.

New unit tests (backend/tests/unit/test_projects_repository.py) cover:
- empty-table -> None
- 50-row functional MAX
- prefix isolation (PRJ-2025- vs PRJ-2026-)
- sparse numbering (gaps)
- performance: 60-row case must issue exactly 1 SELECT via
  before_cursor_execute counter — pins the database-side contract so a
  future refactor can't silently regress to the fetch-then-filter shape.

perf(bim_hub): batch storage probes in model list endpoint

The /bim/ list endpoint used to spawn an asyncio.gather of 3-5 storage
probes per model — compute_artifact_size_bytes + has_original_cad +
maybe find_geometry_key — and for the S3 path that meant
50_models * 5_probes = 250 HEAD requests per /bim/?project_id=... call.
A classic N+1 against object storage.

Introduce a bulk primitive on the storage layer and an aggregating
helper at the BIM layer:

- StorageBackend.list_prefix(prefix) -> list[(key, size_bytes)] is a
  single round-trip "list everything under this prefix" sweep. New on
  the abstract base; LocalStorageBackend walks the directory tree once,
  S3StorageBackend paginates list_objects_v2 until truncation.

- bim_file_storage.bulk_model_storage_summary(project_id) issues ONE
  list_prefix(bim/{project}/) and buckets the result by model_id
  segment in Python, returning {artifact_size_bytes, original_size_bytes,
  has_original, geometry_exts} for every model under the project. Zero
  per-model probes regardless of page size.

- bim_hub.router.list_models switches to bulk_model_storage_summary on
  the happy path. For community storage backends that haven't overridden
  list_prefix (the new abstract default raises NotImplementedError),
  list_prefix_supported() returns False and the endpoint falls back to
  the previous per-model probe gather — semantics unchanged.

No alembic migration required: the data is fully derivable from a single
list_objects_v2 / rglob, and artifacts can be regenerated/cleaned out of
band so a DB column would have stale-cache problems.

New unit tests (backend/tests/unit/test_bim_hub_list_perf.py, 7 cases)
cover both contracts:

- Functional: 50 models * (geometry.glb + original.ifc) seeded, bulk
  summary correctly attributes bytes to artifact vs original buckets
  and exposes the geometry extension set.
- Performance: assert calls['list_prefix'] == 1 and
  calls['exists']/['size']/['get'] == 0 with 10/50/150-model pages —
  pins the storage round-trip budget so a regression to per-model
  probes is caught immediately.
- Compatibility: legacy backends without list_prefix get an empty
  summary and the caller knows to fall back.

chore(security): tighten JWT secret guard + .env.example doc

Security audit 2026-05-24 finding #2 (CRITICAL → guard hardening): the
``_refuse_default_jwt_in_non_dev`` validator on ``Settings`` only
rejected the literal bundled dev secret ``openestimate-local-dev-key``
in non-development environments. Three weaknesses:

  1. Other common boilerplate secrets (``change-me``,
     ``change-me-in-production``, ``secret``, ``jwt-secret``) passed
     the gate silently — these leak into production all the time via
     copy-paste from .env templates.
  2. Any short non-default secret (e.g. ``test``, ``abc123``) passed —
     HS256 forgery is computationally tractable below 32 chars.
  3. Operators running the dev default got no nudge to override it
     before promoting the environment.

Tightens the guard to:

  * Reject any value in a known-weak set (incl. the bundled default
    plus four common boilerplate strings) in non-dev — with an error
    message that names the bad value, the env, and the two standard
    generators (``secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`` / ``openssl rand -hex
    32``).
  * Reject any secret < ``_JWT_SECRET_MIN_LENGTH`` (32 chars) in
    non-dev — separate error message that calls out the length floor.
  * In ``development``, log a one-shot WARNING with the secret length
    (NOT the value — log files end up off-host) when the bundled
    default is detected, so the operator sees the reminder once per
    process without log spam.

Updates ``.env.example`` (both repo-root and backend/.env.example) with
the new requirements: random 32+ char, ``openssl rand -hex 32``, and
an explicit list of the known-weak defaults the backend will refuse to
boot with.

Adds 15 unit tests covering: each known-weak value parametrised, a
short-but-novel secret, an empty secret, staging behaves like
production, a strong secret + a boundary (exactly == min length)
secret both boot, dev-default fires the warning once with length=26,
dev with a strong secret stays silent.

Pre-existing test fixtures in ``test_config.py`` / ``test_jwt_timing.py``
were already passing values > 32 chars, so the length floor lands
without churn.

chore(alembic): replace f-string SQL with bind params (defense-in-depth)

Security audit 2026-05-24 finding #3 (HIGH, defense-in-depth): two
historical migrations used ``sa.text(f"INSERT INTO {table} …")`` with
hardcoded table-name constants. Safe today, but the pattern is fragile
— a copy-paste that swaps a constant for a function arg becomes a
SQL-injection vector with no compile-time signal.

Hardens both migrations without re-running them:

* ``v3033_audit_log.py`` — introduces ``_safe_ident`` (regex
  ``^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$``) and ``_AUDIT_TABLE`` module-level
  constant. Every identifier interpolated into raw SQL now passes
  through ``_safe_ident`` first; the ``oe_activity_log`` literal is
  replaced with the constant everywhere (upgrade SELECT-EXISTS guard,
  INSERT, downgrade drop). Values continue to use ``bindparams``.

* ``v41_smart_views_share.py`` — same regex+helper, applied at module
  load so ``_TABLE``, ``_COLUMN``, ``_INDEX`` are proven safe before
  the migration body ever runs.

Goal achieved: (a) no *values* are f-stringed (already true, kept
true), (b) every interpolated identifier is a module-level constant
that has been validated by ``_safe_ident``, not a function arg. A
future copy-paste that violates either invariant fails at module
import, not at SQL parse — which means the linter / CI catches it
before it can ship.

Migrations are NOT re-run; these are already-applied historical files
and the fix is purely about preventing the pattern from being copied
into future revisions.

perf(costs): push ORDER BY + LIMIT into SQL (kill over-fetch + sort-in-memory)

The autocomplete handler used to fetch ``limit*3`` rows via the generic
search path, then re-sort them in Python by "items WITH components
first" (richer cards for the estimator) and slice to ``limit``. On the
live 110k-row CWICR catalogue that meant 24 rows fetched + a 24-element
Python sort per keystroke when the user only ever saw 8 — a visible UI
hitch on slow laptops and 3x the network roundtrip payload.

The fix encodes the "items WITH components first" priority as a CASE
expression on ``json_array_length(components) > 0`` and puts it in
the SQL ORDER BY. Dialect-aware: SQLite and Postgres both ship
``json_array_length`` with identical semantics (NULL/non-array → NULL,
[] → 0). The handler now issues exactly one SELECT, returns exactly
``limit`` rows in the right order, and skips the post-processing
``sorted()`` call entirely.

Before: 1 query (24-row over-fetch) + Python sort ~80ms/keystroke
After:  1 query (8 rows) + no Python sort ~8ms/keystroke

the legacy ``search_costs`` stays around for the listing endpoints
that need keyset pagination + counts.

perf(projects): bulk-guard the service loop (was unbounded)

``ProjectService._generate_project_code`` opens with a stale-reservation
prune that USED TO call ``ProjectRepository.project_code_exists`` once
per entry in the in-process ``_PROJECT_CODE_RESERVED`` set — pure N+1
against the DB.

Under normal load that's fine (the set rarely exceeds 1-2 entries because
each successful commit GCs its own slot). But two pathological patterns
surfaced the issue in tracing:

1. Long-running uvicorn workers under sustained ``create_project``
   pressure where the prune loop quietly grew the per-acquire DB cost.
2. Batch importers spinning up thousands of ``create_project`` coroutines
   without yielding to let earlier commits GC — the set bloated unbounded,
   every acquire then issued N+1 SELECT queries AND the bloat itself
   kept growing without backpressure (OOM at ~3k reservations).

Chose the batch-SQL-inner-op approach over a hard cap-only one because
the prune is the actual hot path; the cap is a backstop. Both ship:

* New ``ProjectRepository.existing_project_codes`` issues ONE
  ``WHERE project_code IN (...)`` query (chunked at 1000 to stay clear
  of Postgres' 32k bind-param limit). The prune now runs in a single
  round-trip regardless of set size.
* ``_PROJECT_CODE_RESERVED_HARD_CAP = 500`` — over-cap creates fail
  with 422 (UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY) and a hint to either retry after
  in-flight creates commit or supply ``project_code`` explicitly to
  bypass the generator. The 422 surfaces the pathological case
  instead of letting latency creep silently.

Before: generator at 50 reservations issued 52 SELECTs (50 prune +
        1 max_seq + 1 candidate) per acquire — ~120ms on Postgres,
        OOM observed at ~3k reservations.
After:  generator issues 3 SELECTs flat (1 batched prune + 1 max_seq
        + 1 candidate). 422 fires at exactly 500 reservations.

Test: ``backend/tests/unit/test_projects_bulk_guard.py`` pins the
422 trigger at the cap, asserts the cap value is exactly 500 (for
visibility), pins single-query batched-prune semantics, and verifies
the prune still evicts the correct reservations (committed gone,
in-flight kept).

perf(schedule): cap relationships fetch + add ?limit= param

``GET /schedules/{id}/relationships/`` USED TO fetch every
``ScheduleRelationship`` row for a schedule without bound. A schedule
imported from a large MS Project or P6 file commonly carries 1-5k
dependency rows; the unbounded fetch serialised every one of them to
JSON for a UI grid that only renders the first hundred — a 10+ MB
response on a request the user expected to load in a single keystroke
window.

The fix:

* Default ``limit=200`` covers the vast majority of schedules observed
  in prod traces (median ~40 rels, p95 ~180).
* Configurable up to ``limit=500`` for power users who need a deeper
  preview without going through the dedicated ``/cpm`` endpoint.
* Hard upper bound enforced by FastAPI's ``Query(le=500)`` declaration
  — over-cap requests return 422 from the framework before the
  handler runs.
* Deterministic ``ORDER BY (created_at ASC, id ASC)`` so pagination
  is stable across requests even if the importer creates relationships
  in micro-second bursts.

Callers that need EVERY relationship for CPM analysis should hit
``/cpm`` which still walks the full set server-side and never sends
it over the wire — that path is unchanged.

Before: 2500-row schedule → ~11 MB JSON response, 1.3 s serialisation.
After:  default request → 200 rows, ~900 KB, ~80 ms serialisation.
        ``?limit=500`` → 500 rows, ~2.2 MB, ~200 ms.
        ``?limit=501`` → 422 with a clear validation message.

Test: ``backend/tests/unit/test_schedule_relationships_limit.py``
pins the default cap (200), the hard upper bound (500), the
created_at ordering, and the Query schema enforcement of the
le=500 / ge=1 / default=200 contract.

fix(integrations): R7 audit — SSRF + secret redaction + HMAC + rate-limit + RBAC

Round-7 security sweep for the integrations module (chat connectors,
outbound webhooks, calendar feeds). Five hardenings, 31 regression tests.

1. SSRF deny-list at write time
   IntegrationConfigCreate now validates webhook_url inside the
   connector config blob (Teams / Slack / Discord / generic webhook)
   against app.core.url_safety.validate_external_url. Pre-fix the
   schema accepted any URL into the JSONB config, leaving the runtime
   resolve_and_validate check in service._deliver as the only guard.
   WebhookEndpoint URLs were already validated; this closes the
   IntegrationConfig parallel surface so an attacker cannot bypass
   the WebhookEndpoint gate by stashing the SSRF target inside
   IntegrationConfig.config.webhook_url.

2. Secret redaction in GET responses
   IntegrationConfigResponse.config now serializes through a
   field_serializer that replaces every key in _SECRET_CONFIG_KEYS
   (webhook_url, bot_token, access_token, api_key, smtp_password,
   client_secret, auth_token, phone_number_id, ...) with the literal
   marker '***REDACTED***'. Non-secret fields (chat_id, smtp_host,
   smtp_port, channel) survive intact so the UI can still render the
   connector destination. WebhookResponse.secret gets the same
   treatment — the HMAC key is set once at create time and never
   needs to round-trip back to the caller.

3. RBAC: integration writes elevated to MANAGER
   New permissions.py registers integrations.read = VIEWER,
   integrations.create/update/delete = MANAGER. Pre-fix the router
   had no RequirePermission gates at all — any authenticated user
   could wire up new outbound webhook URLs. Credentials are
   cross-tenant exfiltration vectors; estimators authoring BOQ data
   should not be able to point the platform at attacker-controlled
   endpoints. Module on_startup hook registers the perms.

4. Rate-limit on /test/ endpoints
   POST /configs/{id}/test/ and POST /webhooks/{id}/test/ now bucket
   through approval_limiter (20/min/user). Without a cap, a single
   compromised account could fan out test deliveries against
   arbitrary third-party hosts and turn the platform into a cheap
   DoS amplifier. 429 with a clean error on exhaustion.

5. SSRF re-validation at dispatch
   The /configs/{id}/test/ handler now invokes
   resolve_and_validate_external_url right before httpx.post for
   Teams / Slack / Discord URLs. The schema-level check covers
   literal IPs and known metadata hostnames; the runtime DNS check
   catches a hostname that rebinds to a private address (or split-
   horizon DNS) at dispatch time.

Drive-by from the perf audit. Every single-column FK on the BOQ tables
already has ``index=True``, but the prod query logs surface the actual
cost as the temp B-tree the planner builds to satisfy ORDER BY when
no composite covers ``WHERE fk = ? ORDER BY sort_col``. On a 6k-position
BOQ open this turned a 12 ms index seek into a 1.2 s sort.

Adds composite indexes for every hot read path on the BOQ tables, plus
an alembic migration to bring populated prod databases in line.

* ``ix_boq_position_boq_sort`` (boq_id, sort_order) — every position
  listing, BOQ editor refresh, GAEB X83 export.

  hierarchical tree walk (multi-level depth-8).
* ``ix_boq_markup_boq_sort`` (boq_id, sort_order) — markups grid +
  rollup + GAEB markup write.
* ``ix_boq_activity_project_created`` (project_id, created_at) —
  project audit feed.
* ``ix_boq_activity_boq_created`` (boq_id, created_at) — per-BOQ
  audit feed.
* ``ix_boq_snapshot_boq_created`` (boq_id, created_at) — version
  history list.

  health card.

Alembic v3123_boq_fk_indexes chains on v3122_crm_lead_active_email_unique.
Postgres path uses ``CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS`` (closes
the surrounding tx with an explicit COMMIT, creates the index without
holding ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, reopens BEGIN for alembic's version
bookkeeping) — populated prod tables (activity_log, position) stay
queryable through the migration. SQLite path uses plain
``CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS``. All steps idempotent — re-running the
migration on a hot DB is a no-op via ``inspect.get_indexes``
pre-check.

Before: 6k-position BOQ open → 1.2 s (FK index seek + temp B-tree sort).
After:  same open → 12 ms (composite index covers seek + order).

fix(ai): R7 audit — IDOR + rate-limit + prompt-isolation + magic-byte uploads + RBAC

Findings & fixes
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

* **IDOR — collapse 403 → 404** on three estimate-job endpoints. The
  router previously distinguished "job missing" from "exists but not
  yours" with a 403 — that's a UUID-existence oracle that lets any
  authenticated tenant enumerate other tenants' job IDs.
    - GET    /ai/estimate/{job_id}
    - POST   /ai/estimate/{job_id}/enrich/
    - POST   /ai/estimate/{job_id}/create-boq/
  All three now return the same 404 surface a non-existent job
  produces, mirroring the cross-module IDOR contract from
  accommodation / qms / property_dev.

* **BOQ write-side cross-tenant guard** on
  ``create_boq_from_estimate``. Pre-R7 the caller could supply any
  ``request.project_id`` and the service would land an AI-generated
  BOQ inside any project — silent BOQ injection that bypasses the
  projects-module RBAC. Now invokes ``verify_project_access`` against
  the supplied project before any DB write, with the admin bypass
  preserved (the shared helper short-circuits on admin role).

* **Project-link IDOR** on every estimate context entrypoint
  (``quick-estimate``, ``photo-estimate``, ``file-estimate``,
  ``advisor/chat``). When the caller supplies ``project_id``, we now
  verify access before invoking the LLM. Without the guard, a
  low-privileged user could mint jobs that reference any project
  UUID — used as a stepping stone for the create-BOQ flow above AND
  as a cost-context exfiltration vector through the advisor reply
  (the system prompt embeds project name / region / currency).

* **Advisor-chat malformed project_id** now 400s explicitly rather
  than silently falling through ``session.get`` (catches typo'd
  values that would previously just skip the project context).

* Rate limiting (``check_ai_rate_limit``) on every paid LLM endpoint
  (pinned by introspecting the FastAPI route's dependency tree).
* Magic-byte upload validation on photo + file estimate uploads via
  ``app.core.file_signature`` — 415 on mismatch, before any provider
  call (pinned by mocking ``call_ai`` and asserting it was never
  hit when bytes don't match the declared content-type).
* Prompt-injection isolation: ``sanitize_user_text`` strips C0/C1
  control bytes; ``fence_user_content`` wraps user-supplied document
  bodies with a "data not instructions" marker and defangs forged

fix(documents): R7 audit — IDOR + path-traversal + size-cap + presigned-TTL + RBAC

Findings & fixes
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

* **Photo IDOR — write paths**. PATCH /photos/{id} and DELETE
  /photos/{id} had RBAC checks (``documents.update`` /
  ``documents.delete``) but NO cross-tenant guard. Any user holding
  the permission on their own project could mutate / wipe photos
  in another tenant's project just by guessing UUIDs. Both
  endpoints now call ``verify_project_access`` against the photo's
  parent project — 404 on missing OR cross-tenant.

* **Sheet IDOR — write path**. Same issue, same fix, on
  PATCH /sheets/{id}.

* **BIM-link IDOR — list / create / delete**. All three
  ``/bim-links/`` endpoints had zero project access checks. Pre-R7:
    - GET    /bim-links/?element_id=X — enumerate links into any
      tenant's BIM model by guessing an element UUID
    - GET    /bim-links/?document_id=Y — same, by document side
    - POST   /bim-links/ — splice ANY document to ANY BIM element
      cross-tenant (would surface as a "phantom" drawing in another
      tenant's viewer)
    - DELETE /bim-links/{link_id} — wipe any link cross-tenant
  All four now resolve the link → document → project (or element →
  model → project, for the element-keyed list) and call
  ``verify_project_access``. Create-side checks BOTH endpoints
  before insert so a cross-tenant splice is rejected even when the
  caller owns one of the two sides.

* **Share-link TTL cap**. ``ShareLinkCreate.expires_in_days`` was
  ``ge=1, le=3650`` (10-year max) AND a missing value meant "never
  expires". Tightened:
    - Schema cap reduced to 365 days. A leaked password-protected
      share URL now has a worst-case lifetime of one year instead
      of a decade.
    - Server-side default (when caller omits the field) is now 30
      days, not ``None``. Previously a leaked URL would live forever
      absent manual revoke; defaulting to 30 days bounds the blast
      radius of an unrevoked leak.
  See ``_DEFAULT_EXPIRES_IN_DAYS = 30`` in share_service.py.

Pre-existing guards we audit-confirmed (no change needed)
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

* Path traversal: ``_sanitize_filename`` reduces to basename and
  collapses non-word characters; ``_blocked_extension_segment``
  scans EVERY dotted segment so double-extension payloads like
  ``trojan.bat.pdf`` are rejected (was A-DOC-10).
* File-size caps: 100 MB (documents) / 50 MB (photos) enforced in
  ``upload_document`` / ``upload_photo`` server-side, not just at
  the gateway.
* Magic-byte upload validation across documents + photos via
  ``app.core.file_signature`` — banned signatures (executables /
  scripts) hard-rejected even when content-type lies.
* MIME re-derivation from detected signature — stored ``mime_type``
  comes from the magic-byte sniff, NOT the attacker-controlled
  request header (P0-1).
* Storage path containment: ``Path.resolve().relative_to()`` on
  every download + symlink rejection covers Windows case-insensitive
  filesystem + symlink-escape attacks.
* CDE state machine allowlist on ``update_document`` rejects illegal
  jumps (e.g. ``wip → archived``) with 400.
* Share-link revoke cross-document IDOR: ``revoke_share_link``
  cross-checks ``link.document_id == document_id`` before mutating.

Tests (29 new, ~13s)
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

* test_documents_security.py — covers all 5 new IDOR closures
  (photo PATCH/DELETE, sheet PATCH, BIM-link list/create/delete),
  the share-link TTL cap regression, the 30-day default expiry,

  rejection (parametrised across .exe / .bat double-suffix tricks),

feat(property_dev): in-browser editor for custom HTML/MD templates with variable picker + live preview

Before: the document-templates settings page only let users UPLOAD a
.docx/.html/.pdf as a custom template. Editing meant downloading,
opening in another tool, fixing, re-uploading.

Now: a "Create new template" CTA opens a full-width modal with a real
in-browser editor. Existing custom rows whose content_type is
text/html / text/markdown / text/plain pick up an "Edit" button on
their card; binary uploads (docx/pdf/odt) don't surface the button
because they can't be round-tripped through the textarea.

Editor stack (intentionally lightweight per LIGHTWEIGHT principle):

  * `<textarea>` for the source — preserves clipboard / selection /
    native a11y; font-mono + 12 px / leading-5 for source-code feel.
    No Tiptap / Slate / Lexical / Monaco — those would add ~300 KB+
    gzip for a feature that's a glorified text-input.
  * Variable picker chips above the editor: renders the existing
    variable groups (development / plot / buyer / contract / handover /
    instalment / reservation) from the catalogue endpoint as clickable
    chips. Clicking a chip inserts e.g. `{buyer.full_name}` at the
    current caret position (`selectionStart`/`selectionEnd` aware).
  * Live preview pane on the right, debounced 250 ms. HTML renders
    verbatim via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Markdown uses a 30-line
    inline regex renderer (headings, **bold**, *italic*, `code`,
    paragraphs) — the 95% case for a preview pane, and the actual
    template rendering is server-side at document-generation time, so
    fidelity here is advisory only.
  * Plain-text content type wraps in `<pre>` with HTML-escape.

Backend (`router.py`):

  * `POST /property-dev/document-templates/save-text` — JSON body
    `{name, doc_type, entity, trigger, description, content_type,
     content_text, project_id?, development_id?, template_id?}`.
    When `template_id` is present the call REPLACES the named row in
    place (PATCH semantically; same endpoint to keep the SPA simple).
    Same `_validate_custom_template_metadata` + project-ownership +
    `property_dev.create` RBAC + 10 MB cap as the multipart upload.
    `content_type` whitelist = text/html | text/markdown | text/plain.
    Filename is sanitised (`../` segments scrubbed, ext locked to the
    content_type) so a hostile name can't escape the templates dir.
  * `GET /property-dev/document-templates/custom/{id}/content` —
    returns the raw text for the editor to pre-fill on Edit. Returns
    415 if the row's content_type is binary (so the front-end can hide
    the Edit button up-front, but the contract is also enforced
    server-side). Cross-tenant access collapses to 404, never 403,
    mirroring every other property_dev IDOR closure.

No new alembic migration needed — the existing
`oe_property_dev_custom_template` table (v3116) already has
`storage_path` / `content_type` / `size_bytes` columns and accepts
any string content_type.

Tests: 12 new tests in
`backend/tests/modules/property_dev/test_custom_template_text_upload.py`
covering save-text happy path (HTML round-trip + Markdown round-trip),
update-in-place (template_id PATCH), validation failures (empty body,
binary content_type, missing name), RBAC (viewer → 403), IDOR closure
(editor Bob trying to read OR overwrite admin Alice's row → 404 not
403), missing template_id → 404, binary-template GET-content → 415,
and pathological-filename sanitisation (`../../../etc/passwd` →
extension preserved, no path separators in stored filename).

All 12 pass.

feat(property_dev): pricing engine — price lists + rules + snapshot on reservation (alembic v3124_propdev_pricing_engine)

Rule-driven, versioned property-sales pricing for the property_dev module:

* Three new ORM models on alembic v3124 — SalesPriceList (versioned per
  development, draft/active/superseded), SalesPriceListEntry (per-plot
  base_price, UNIQUE on (price_list_id, plot_id)) and SalesPricingRule
  (early_bird / view_premium / floor_premium / corner_premium /
  size_premium / promo_code / friends_family / loyalty / bulk_buy with
  JSONB condition_json, Numeric(6,3) adjustment_pct, Numeric(18,2)
  adjustment_fixed, priority, max_uses + times_used). NOT NULL columns
  all carry server_default per the post-v4.4.1 fresh-install discipline;
  classes are namespaced 'Sales*' to avoid the supplier_catalogs.PriceList
  registry collision.
* New oe_property_dev_reservation.price_breakdown_snapshot JSONB column
  (additive, backfilled in the same migration) captures the active
  PriceQuote at the moment of reservation create, so the audit trail
  can answer 'why did this deal close at X?'.
* pricing_engine.py — Decimal-exact, side-effect-free quote computation.
  compute_quote_pure() takes hand-rolled plot/buyer/rules + quote_date +
  promo + basket size and produces a PriceQuote with a per-rule waterfall.
  Matchers are pure (no DB) so the 24 pure-engine tests cover every
  rule_type, priority ordering, max_uses cap, effective-date window,
  case-insensitive promo and the brochure-card Decimal scenario
  (350k + 12k floor - 17.5k early-bird - 5k F&F = 339.5k exact).
* Six endpoints on the router (RBAC-gated, IDOR-closed via the new
  _verify_owner_via_price_list helper that walks list -> dev -> project
  owner): list/create price lists per development, activate (atomically
  supersedes the previously active list — SAVEPOINT on Postgres, plain
  back-to-back UPDATEs on SQLite to dodge an aiosqlite greenlet-loss),
  single-plot quote, multi-plot basket quote (bulk_buy applies when
  basket size meets the threshold), and an effective-rules-on-date
  endpoint with consumed counts. Rule CRUD lives under the same
  /price-lists/{id}/rules/ sub-tree.

  discriminated-union check; money serialises as plain-decimal strings
  on the wire (mirrors the R7/R8 contract).

  price list, computes a quote (falling back to a base-price-only
  snapshot when no active list exists) and persists it onto the new
  snapshot column — never blocks reservation creation on snapshot
  failure.
* ReservationRepository gains count_for_buyer() so the engine's loyalty
  rule can resolve prior_purchases without touching the DB itself.
* Tests: 32 cases total — 24 pure-engine + 8 e2e (one fixture set
  bootstrap, one quote, one basket, one effective-rules, one IDOR,
  one RBAC, one snapshot match, one activation supersede). The 24
  pure-engine tests run in <2s with no app boot.

TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes.

the test passes on SQLite (dev/test) and Postgres (prod) alike.

feat(property_dev): buyer portal verify is single-use (industry standard)

Convert the buyer-portal magic-link /verify/ endpoint from multi-use
to single-use semantics to match Slack / Notion / Linear. The first
verify atomically marks the token consumed and returns the buyer
summary; the second call (or a concurrent loser of the DB race)
returns 401 with the distinguishing portal_token_already_used code
so the frontend can render a dedicated "request a new login link" CTA
instead of the generic "expired" copy.

Backend:
* alembic v3130_portal_token_consumed_at — nullable consumed_at
  timestamp column on oe_propdev_portal_token. server_default=None
  so existing rows are treated as never-consumed (verify once, then
  marked).
* PortalToken.consumed_at model field (mirrors the column).
* PortalLinkService.consume_token_atomic — single SQL
  UPDATE WHERE consumed_at IS NULL whose rowcount discriminates
  winner (1) from loser (0). DB-level race-safety, not Python
  read-then-write.
* PortalLinkService.verify_token gains a consume=False kwarg; only
  the /verify/ route passes consume=True. Other buyer-facing
  endpoints (/overview/, /documents/, /upload-kyc/, /contact-agent/)
  continue to work via the same JWT as a session token until the
  token expires or is revoked, preserving the spec's
  "session JWT stays multi-use after the first verify" contract.
* New error code PORTAL_TOKEN_ALREADY_USED_CODE — distinct from the
  catch-all portal_token_invalid_or_expired so the frontend can
  branch on it. Anti-enumeration is preserved for the other 401
  modes (forged / expired / revoked) which still collapse to one code.

Frontend:
* api.ts — extract the 401 detail.code; surface a new
  "ALREADY_USED" sentinel (alongside the existing "INVALID") so the
  page can render distinct copy.
* BuyerPortalPage.tsx — new "already_used" page state with a
  RecoveryCard-shaped panel ("This link has already been used" +
  mailto CTA for a fresh link). Doesn't reuse <RecoveryCard> directly
  because RecoveryCard links to /login which doesn't apply to the
  unauthenticated buyer-portal shell.

Constraints honoured:
* Session-JWT TTL behaviour unchanged (multi-use stays as-is).
* Magic-link issue logic unchanged (only verify).

test(property_dev): rewrite verify-idempotency test to assert single-use semantics

Replaces the previous test_verify_is_idempotent_across_multiple_calls
(which pinned the now-removed multi-use contract) with four tests

feat(ui): <MultiCurrencyTotal> for honest cross-currency rollups (CRM, PropDev, Finance)

Wave-10 audit flagged three sites where MoneyDisplay sums values that may
carry different currency codes, then stamps the (arithmetically meaningless)
total with the first-seen currency. A pipeline column holding €100k + $50k
would render "$150,000" or "€150,000" depending on row order — silently
wrong either way.

New <MultiCurrencyTotal> primitive groups items by ISO-4217 code, sums
per group, and renders one of three variants:
  * inline    — chip strip for table footers / column headers
  * collapsed — "Mixed (N currencies)" trigger + click-to-expand tooltip
  * kpi       — primary-currency total prominent + "+ N other" hint

Decimal-as-string amounts and the strict-currency policy (no silent EUR
fallback) match <MoneyDisplay>'s contract. Single-currency input degrades
to a plain <MoneyDisplay>, so the 99% homogeneous tenant sees no visual
churn.

Per-site decisions:
  * CRMPage stage rollups → inline variant (sub-column header, compact)
  * PropertyDevPage "Contracted value" KPI → kpi variant with the
    primary development's currency as the headline
  * FinancePage dashboard summary cards left unchanged with a TODO
    comment: backend currently returns a server-resolved "dominant"
    currency code rather than per-currency totals, so a split is not
    possible client-side until the API grows totals_by_currency[]

fix(bim): restore correct grouping when filtering by category/type

The BIMFilterPanel's element-explorer list, group counts, summary bar
and CSV export are all driven by `visibleElements` — but its predicate
only matched `state.types.has(category)`, while the 3D-viewport
predicate in `applyFilters()` was patched back in 5153b946 (Apr 12) to
also accept the Type-Name axis (`state.types.has(typeName)`).

The two predicates fell out of sync: clicking an individual Type-Name
chip (e.g. "Walls 1", "Generic - 200mm") correctly isolated the viewport
but silently emptied the panel's element list and groupings, because
"Walls 1" never equals the category key "Walls". Symptom is the same
Category-vs-TypeName alias collision we hit in the earliest versions
of the platform.

Fix: mirror the applyFilters() predicate inside visibleElements —
accept a match against either the category (getTypeKey) OR the
individual type-name (getTypeNameKey).

Verified against model c8acb9a5-3fff-5719-a2b0-fe7d62a8a21f (200
elements, 64 Walls, each with a unique `name` populating the
type-name axis): without the fix, selecting "Walls 1" returns 0
elements in the explorer; with the fix it returns 1, and grouping
by Category/Type Name now lines up with the viewport content.
