ci: raise frontend build heap to 8 GB so the release artifacts build

The Vite/Rollup frontend build crossed Node's 6 GB old-space ceiling and died
with exit 134 (JavaScript heap out of memory) in the PyPI wheel build, the
unified Docker image build and the desktop installer build, so v11.2.0 did not
publish. Give the build an 8 GB ceiling in all three paths; the GitHub-hosted
runners have 16 GB so this stays safe.

feat(bim): stream large models as cached geometry tiles

The 3D viewer downloaded one GLB for the whole model and parsed it on the
main thread, with no-store caching, so a large model meant a slow transfer
and a UI freeze on every open. This adds a server-side tiler that bakes a
model's GLB into spatially partitioned, content-addressed sub-GLBs once, plus
endpoints that serve the tile manifest and the immutable tiles.

The tiler runs an adaptive octree over per-mesh centres and preserves the glTF
node names, so the viewer's existing mesh-to-element matching keeps working on
a streamed tile. Baking is idempotent and self-healing: a cached tileset is
reused only while the tiler version and a cheap source-geometry fingerprint
still match, so a re-converted model re-bakes on its own. The old monolithic
GLB path is untouched and stays the fallback for small or untiled models.

feat(bim): stream baked geometry tiles into the viewer with an offline cache

When a model has a baked tileset the viewer now loads it instead of the
single monolithic GLB. Content-addressed tiles are pulled cache-first from
IndexedDB, parsed in small chunks that yield to the event loop between them,
and merged into one group that feeds the existing scene matching unchanged.

Because the tiles are the same trimesh GLB format and preserve their glTF
node names, the downstream mesh-to-element matching needs no changes. Any
model without a tileset, a missing tile, or a parse error falls straight
through to the monolithic path, so this can only make loading faster. Tiles
are immutable, so a revisit or a site tablet that went offline reads the
geometry straight from disk rather than re-downloading the whole building.

feat(bim): add Model Review surface with in-viewer issue capture

Model Review is a focused, site-facing page for walking a 3D model and
raising coordination issues against it. It reuses the shared viewer, so it
inherits the fast streaming tile loader, and the issue register, and wires
the two with a live capture bridge: pick an element, hit "Raise issue here",
and the issue records the exact camera, the selected elements and a snapshot
of what is on screen.

The viewer gains an optional onSceneReady hook so a parent can drive it
directly. The bridge reads the camera and forces a synchronous render for the
snapshot, because the renderer runs without a preserved drawing buffer and a
plain canvas read would capture a blank frame. Reachable from the Model
Coordination menu at /model-review.

Also normalises the new streaming tile files to the house single-quote style.

feat(bim): add install-status colour mode to the model viewer

Model viewers get a new "Install status" colouring that answers the first
question on site: what is built, what is going up now, and what is still to
come. Each element is bucketed green (installed), amber (in progress) or grey
(pending).

The schedule decides when an element is 4D-linked, so a scheduled-as-complete
element reads green even if its measured percentage lags behind; otherwise the
latest BOQ progress percentage decides. Elements with neither stay in their
neutral colour. The bucket logic is a small pure function with unit tests; the
viewer reuses the existing colour pipeline and adds a three-swatch legend, and
the BIM page adds the mode to the "By schedule" group.

feat(bim): locate me in the model from device GPS

Adds a "locate me" control to the 3D model viewer. On a project that has a geo
anchor, it reads the device GPS, projects the fix against the anchor and drops a
pin in the model with a ground ring sized to the reported GPS accuracy. It is
honest about its limits: it refuses when the fix lands well outside the model
footprint, sizes the ring to the accuracy, and never claims survey-grade
precision. Clicking the control again hides the pin.

The projection math is a small pure module with unit tests. The pin is a
self-contained marker that owns and disposes its own meshes. Wired into both the
full BIM workspace and the Model Review surface.

feat(bim): full ERP context for a clicked model element

Clicking an element in the 3D viewer now shows everything the platform knows
about it in one panel: the linked BOQ position with its cost, plus linked
documents, tasks, schedule activities, requirements and validation. The model
still opens in skeleton mode for speed, and the context is fetched on demand
per click, so the fast load is untouched.

Backend adds GET /bim_hub/elements/{id}/context and an element_id filter on the
existing link composer, with the per-element response assembly shared between
the model-wide list and the single-element path. Frontend fetches the context
on selection and merges the link arrays into the selected element, and the BOQ
link rows now show quantity, rate and total. Covered by integration tests.

feat(bim): ask the AI assistant about a clicked model element

Adds an "Ask AI" action to the selected-element panel in the 3D viewer. It
takes everything the platform knows about that element (its identity and
quantities, the linked BOQ position with cost, linked documents, tasks,
schedule activities, requirements and validation) and pre-seeds the shared
assistant with a short, readable brief plus a question. The user reviews and
sends it, so nothing is asked on their behalf without a click, and they stay
in the viewer because the assistant is the global panel.

The prompt is built by a small pure helper (buildElementQuestion) that is
defensive about missing fields and coerces the Decimal-string money values,
covered by unit tests. The chat store gains a one-shot pendingPrompt that the
panel consumes once to prefill the composer. The button is wired on both the
BIM page and the Model Review page, and is hidden in portal mode where the
internal assistant is not reachable.

feat(bim): on-screen walk joystick for touch site mode

Walking the model on a phone or tablet was half working: you could drag to
look around, but moving needed a keyboard, so there was no way to actually
walk on a touch device. This adds a thumb-stick that appears in the bottom
corner while walk mode is on and the device is touch, and drives the camera
the same way WASD does.

WalkMode gains a small analog axis (setMoveAxis) that is combined with the
keyboard state, clamped so key plus stick can never exceed full speed, and
reset when walk mode ends. The stick math is a pure helper with unit tests,
and there is a new shared useIsTouch hook (pointer: coarse) that gates the
overlay so it never shows on a plain desktop. Keyboard walking is unchanged,
covered by the existing and new WalkMode tests.

feat(bim): adaptive render resolution for touch site mode

Walking a big model on a phone or a low-spec laptop could drop the frame rate
to a crawl. While walk mode is on and the device is touch, the viewer now
watches its own frame time and quietly trims the render resolution when frames
run slow, then eases it back up when there is headroom, so navigation stays
smooth and the picture is as sharp as the device can hold. On a desktop, or
outside walk mode, nothing changes and the manual quality presets are
untouched.

The controller is a pure state machine (frame time in, target pixel ratio
out) with a warm-up window, hysteresis and a cooldown so the resolution does
not flicker, covered by unit tests. The scene samples it from the render loop
and only resizes when the target actually moves. It never sharpens past the
quality ceiling in force when it turned on, and restores that ratio exactly
when walk mode ends.

feat(bim): save a model for offline use on site

Signal drops on a construction site. This adds a "Save for offline" button to
the Model Review header that downloads the model's streaming geometry tiles into
the device cache ahead of time, so the model then opens fully with no network:
prep it in the office, walk it on site.

It writes to the same content-addressed cache the streaming loader already
reads, so a saved model is served entirely from cache on the next open, with no
new storage layer. The button only shows for models that have a tileset, tells
you how much it will save, streams live progress and can be cancelled by
clicking again. A flaky connection still saves as much as it can and a second
run only fills the gaps, since already-cached tiles are skipped.

The download-and-cache path (prefetchModelTiles) parses no geometry and is
covered by unit tests over a mocked cache and fetch.

feat(bim): stream the model progressively so it builds up as it loads

Reorder the streamed tiles so the ones carrying the most geometry arrive
first, and reveal each tile the moment it parses instead of downloading
every tile and then popping the whole building in at the end. The bulk of
the structure shows up early and fills in from the ground up while the
small trailing tiles are still coming.

Scoped to the initial open, so a model switch keeps its atomic swap and
the two models never briefly overlap. It stays a pure optimization: any
missing tileset, bad tile or parse error drops the partial preview and
falls back to the monolithic load, and the final batched result is
byte-identical to before.

feat(takeoff): extend the ortho lock to vertex edits, moves and calibration

The 0/45/90 ortho lock used to constrain only a segment being drawn. Now the
same trigger, the toolbar toggle or a held Shift, also constrains the three
edits that were freehand. Dragging a vertex of an existing measurement squares
it against its neighbour edges, with closed area, volume and cloud shapes
wrapping around and open runs and arrows anchoring on the adjacent vertex.
Moving a whole measurement snaps the translation vector so the shape slides
along an axis instead of drifting off it. The second point of the two-click
scale calibration squares against the first, with a live rubber-band line so
the pick is what you see. While calibrating, the draw-path snap is suppressed
so an in-progress measurement can no longer hijack the scale click. Count
points and the rectangle and highlight boxes have no vertex chain to square,
so they stay freehand. The pure geometry helper was already in place and
tested; this wires it into the viewer. Closes #343.

Also fix the "needs OCR" banner, which remembered a dismissal only for the
current viewer mount and so came back on every reopen of the same scanned
drawing. The dismissal now persists per document in localStorage, keyed by the
stable document id like the group colours already are, so a banner closed once
stays closed. Local-only files with no document id keep the session-only
behaviour. Closes #346.

feat(cases): show the case hero illustration on a clean white tile at full block height

On wide screens the hero illustration now stretches to the full height of the case header block and sits on a plain white surface instead of a gradient tile with a ring, so the art reads as content and shows noticeably larger. The tile column is a bit wider too. Narrow screens keep the compact 4:3 thumbnail.

fix(bim): recover element quantities when a DDC export omits the named quantity columns

The two BIM XLSX ingest paths filled an element's quantities only by matching a
fixed list of column names, so a DDC export that labelled its quantity columns
differently (Qto_WallBaseQuantities.NetVolume, "Volume (m3)", localized or
bare-unit headers) landed with an empty quantities map. The honesty gate then
reported a geometrically fine model as having no quantities at all, and BOQ
export and the geometry views came back empty.

Both ingest paths now fall back, only when the named pass finds nothing, to a
shared recovery helper. First it reuses the BOQ column normaliser to pull the
quantity out of whatever column actually carries it, preferring a net value
over a gross one. Only if there is still no numeric quantity does it derive a
coarse figure from the element's bounding box, tagged quantities_source as
geometry_bbox so it reads as estimated rather than measured and never
overwrites a real value.

Adds unit tests for the recovery helper; the existing ingest integration tests
still pass.

fix(bim): quick takeoff links exactly the elements you isolated

The Link to BOQ button in the model filter panel rebuilt its set from the
active filter predicate, so it ignored element isolation and could link more
elements than the button counted. It now links the same isolation-aware
visible set the button shows, the one that Save as group and CSV export
already use, so the count, the export and the linked positions all agree.

fix(boq): stop silently dropping bad cells when pasting into a BOQ

Pasting from Excel or Google Sheets used to read anything that was not a
number as zero and skip rows that had no description, both without a word to
the user. The paste modal now counts the description-less rows it skips and
the number cells it cannot read, and shows them as a warning under the
preview. The in-grid paste tells you when it applied some cells but had to
skip others, instead of a plain pasted toast.

Adds a unit test for the paste parser diagnostics.

perf(bim): throttle viewer hover raycast to one per frame, skip during camera drag

The 3D viewer resolved element hover by raycasting the whole scene on every mousemove. On a large model a high-rate mouse fires many move events per frame, so this was the main cost of just moving the cursor over the model. Hover now coalesces to at most one raycast per animation frame and is skipped while a pointer button is held (the user is orbiting or panning, not hovering). Adds a SelectionManager test for the coalescing, the drag skip and clean teardown.

perf(bim): stream tiles viewport-first when the camera is already aimed

Tile streaming ordered tiles once by geometry mass and never by where the user was looking. When a deep-link (clash review or element focus) aims the camera at a spot before the geometry finishes, the viewer now streams the tiles nearest that spot first, so the region on screen fills in before the far side of the building. Plain cold opens, where the view only fits after geometry arrives, keep the geometry-mass order, so models authored at real-world coordinates are unaffected. Ordering only: the same tiles and geometry are built, just in a better sequence. Unit tests cover the viewport comparator, the viewer-space transform and the streamer wiring.

fix(bim): reuse the live scene on a fast remount instead of rebuilding it

The 3D viewer and the federated viewer disposed their WebGL scene right in the effect cleanup and rebuilt it on the next mount. Under React's development double-mount, an unmount followed by an immediate re-mount, that force-lost the GL context and then rebuilt on top of it, which read as a black canvas or a WebGL-unavailable notice. It also left a fresh, empty element manager holding a model id the loader still treated as loaded, so a bounding-box-only model rendered nothing.

Defer the teardown by one task. If the effect re-runs before it fires, the remount cancels the pending dispose and reuses the live scene and managers. A genuine unmount has no matching re-mount, so the timer fires and disposes for real. The shared DeferredTeardown primitive carries this and is unit tested, and SceneManager.dispose is now idempotent as a guard against a stray second dispose in the wider async window.

fix(boq): resolve BIM quantity links against their own model, not the first one

In a project with more than one BIM model the BOQ "pick quantity from BIM"
picker and the mini 3D preview resolved every position's linked elements
against a single project-level "first ready" model. A position whose elements
belong to another model then resolved to nothing (DB-UUID ids came back "not
found", so the quantity was silently unavailable) or to the wrong element
(stable ids are unique only per model, so the number was silently wrong).

Positions now record the model that owns their linked elements in a new
nullable cad_model_id column. It is stamped on the dominant link path when the
link is created (from the element's own model), on the match-apply path from
the match session's model, and carried through the duplicate and create
revision copies. The grid resolves each row against that model and falls back
to the project-level model only for legacy or single-model rows, so nothing
changes for existing single-model projects. A migration adds the column and
best-effort backfills it from the canonical link table.

perf(bim): yield with scheduler.yield between tile parses to shorten streaming

The streaming loader yielded to the event loop between tile parses with setTimeout(0). The browser clamps nested timeouts to about 4ms, and on a many-tile model that dead time between parses adds up and stretches the stream for no benefit. Where the engine exposes the Scheduler API (current Chromium, our site target) prefer scheduler.yield(), which hands control back for input and paint and then resumes the streaming task at a raised priority, keeping the same responsiveness without the clamp. Engines without the API fall back to setTimeout(0), byte-for-byte the old behaviour, so nothing regresses. Nothing the user sees changes. Covered by a unit test for the pick-and-fallback selection; the existing streaming contract tests still pass.

feat(schedule): edit task dependencies (FS/SS/FF/SF + lag) and reschedule the Gantt

Adds a predecessor editor to the schedule. Click a Gantt bar to open the
activity, pick another task as a predecessor, choose the link type
(FS/SS/FF/SF) and a lag in days (negatives are leads), and add, retype,
relag or remove each link. Every change writes through the relationship
store and then reschedules so the bars and dependency arrows move at once.

Backend adds PATCH /relationships/{id} to change an edge's type or lag and
POST /schedules/{id}/reschedule/, which runs the CPM engine over the
canonical edges, projects the early-date offsets onto calendar dates and
writes the moved start and end dates plus the critical-path flag and float.
Activities with a predecessor follow CPM; root activities keep their manual
start. Calendar resolution falls back to a Monday to Friday work week for
now; the calendar editor and the editable data grid come later.

perf(bim): render BIM elements opaque by default instead of translucent

The default element material was alpha-blended at 0.85 opacity, so the renderer sorted every element back-to-front each frame and lost early-z rejection - the biggest per-frame cost on a heavy model for a marginal see-through look. Make the default surface opaque. The see-through tools are untouched: per-category opacity, the isolation ghost and glass panes each set their own transparency at the moment they are used, so only the resting appearance changes. Selection highlight is a separate emissive pass, unaffected. Tests assert the default is opaque and that the per-category see-through toggle still yields transparency over it.

perf(bim): cap pixel ratio at 2 and trim resolution during desktop orbit

Two render-resolution changes. The renderer now uses min(devicePixelRatio, 2) through one named MAX_PIXEL_RATIO constant: retina and 2x panels stay fully sharp, only 3x phones and 4K panels are trimmed so a heavy model's fragment cost stays bounded. And desktop gets a conservative adaptive profile that only bites while the camera is actually moving on a slow model - it trims no lower than 0.75x and snaps straight back to full the instant the camera settles, so a still frame is always crisp and a fast model never triggers it. It reuses the touch controller, with the floor clamped to the current ceiling so a low-res quality preset makes it a no-op instead of fighting the preset. Covered by pixel-ratio clamp tests and adaptive-controller tests for the 0.75 floor and the clamped no-op.

feat(boq): per-element quantity formulas for BIM links

Closes the last part of #347. A quantity link can now project a
position's quantity out of its bound BIM elements with a per-element
arithmetic formula (area_m2 * 0.5, length_m * height_m and so on),
not only by reading a single quantity field. Each element's formula is
evaluated against its own variables and the results are combined with
the existing aggregation (sum, max, min, count, first).

The link gains two columns, projection_mode ('field' by default, or
'formula') and formula. Both are additive and nullable, existing rows
read as 'field' with no backfill, so the migration is safe to run on
production rather than stamped.

Formulas run through a small self-contained evaluator over Decimal with
an allow-listed grammar: add, subtract, multiply, divide, parentheses,
unary sign, numeric literals and bare variables only. No function calls,
no attribute access, no names beyond the element's own variables, all
rejected at parse time by walking the syntax tree. An unknown variable
or a division by zero is an explicit error, never a silent zero, and an
element that trips one is reported as missing so the review surface
stays honest.

The grid reuses the existing formula engine instead of shipping a second
evaluator, by teaching it to resolve bare identifiers from an element's
variables. The name normaliser, the numeric test and the variable
builder are mirrored on both sides and locked by a shared vectors
fixture that the frontend and backend tests both replay, so a formula
typed in the grid resolves to the same number the backend writes at
apply time.

feat(bim): bake GLB, tiles and property Parquet for every BIM import

Only the CAD-conversion path produced the fast-viewer artifacts before, so DAE,
CSV and demo models loaded as a multi-MB COLLADA on the main thread and their
"all properties" panel came up empty because there was no elements Parquet.

This adds one idempotent ensure_artifacts step to every import path. It makes
sure a plain uncompressed GLB exists (converting from the DAE once, keeping the
per-mesh node names by bbox rematching so element identity survives), bakes the
octree streaming tileset, and synthesises the elements Parquet from the
oe_bim_element rows keyed by id equal to mesh_ref (falling back to stable_id) so
the per-element property lookup and the filter panels return data for non-CAD
models too. Element identity travels as node name equal to mesh_ref equal to
stable_id equal to the Parquet id column; a test asserts that match survives the
DAE to GLB to tile chain.

It is wired into the CSV/DAE upload, the two demo seed attachers and the CAD
background worker, and kept as a lazy step inside ensure_tileset as
defense-in-depth for already-seeded models. Baking runs off the event loop and
every step is best-effort, so an artifact failure never breaks an import. No new
dependency and no migration; meshopt compression is left as a later separate
layer with a seam marked in _ensure_glb.

perf(bim): accelerate viewer picking with a per-mesh BVH

Click and hover in the BIM viewer raycast the whole scene, and without an
acceleration structure every ray scanned every triangle of every mesh. On a
real model that is the dominant cost of selecting or hovering an element.

Add three-mesh-bvh and build a bounds tree per individually-rendered mesh once
geometry finishes loading, so a ray descends a small tree instead. The patch
is behaviour-preserving: the accelerated raycast consults the tree only when a
geometry has one and otherwise runs the stock raycast, and we patch only Mesh,
never BatchedMesh, so the big-model batched path and its batchHandle to
element-id resolution stay untouched. Batched-away meshes are skipped and the
eager build is capped so a pathological model cannot stall the load. Element
identity is unchanged: the tree only changes which triangles a ray tests, so
the node-name to element-id match still resolves the same id.

Tests cover that a pick with the BVH active resolves to the correct element
id, that BVH and stock raycasts agree, and the no-tree fallback.

perf(bim): parse streamed tiles off the main thread with a fallback

Streaming a model parsed each tile's GLB with GLTFLoader.parse on the main
thread, in small yielding chunks. Move that parse into a module Worker: the
worker runs GLTFLoader.parse and replies with the scene serialized by three's
own Object3D.toJSON(), and the main thread rebuilds it with ObjectLoader. Going
through three's own round-trip means hierarchy, node names and materials are
reconstructed by three, not hand-rebuilt, so the viewer's node-name to
element-id match is unchanged.

It sits behind a robust fallback so it can never regress: if a Worker is
unavailable, or a worker parse errors or times out, the tile parses on the main
thread exactly as before. StreamOptions.parseOffThread forces the main-thread
path (kill switch and test seam), and the buffer is cloned to the worker rather
than transferred so the caller keeps its copy for that fallback.

Correctness is tested: the message protocol, the name and hierarchy round-trip,
and every fallback (worker error, timeout, unconstructable worker, crash). The
existing streaming tests run entirely through the main-thread fallback under
jsdom. A perf trace on a real large tiled model to size the actual win is still
owed and lands with the tiled-model ingest pipeline.

fix(documents): cap photo pixels and offload thumbnailing to stop OOM

A photo upload decoded the full image in-request to build a thumbnail,
with no limit on pixel count. A legitimate ~150 MP photo is only a few
MB on disk, so it passed the byte-size cap, but it decodes to roughly
600 MB of uncompressed RGB, which OOM-killed the single-worker container
on the 2 GB target box and blocked the event loop while it ran.

Add a MAX_PHOTO_PIXELS cap (64 MP, the same limit geo_hub uses for
rasters) and check it against the image header before any full decode.
Image.open is lazy, so reading the dimensions never allocates the pixel
buffer, and an over-limit image is now rejected with a clean 413 instead
of a crash. Pillow's own decompression-bomb guard is pinned to the same
cap as a second line of defence, so a hostile file that slips past the
header check still fails safely rather than exhausting memory.

The pixel check and the thumbnail decode both run in a worker thread now
via asyncio.to_thread, so a large image can no longer freeze the server
for other requests. A normal photo still thumbnails exactly as before.

feat(schedule): editable activity grid in the table view

The schedule Table view now renders a real editable grid instead of a
second Gantt. Each row edits the activity name, type, start and end
inline. Moving the start shifts the end by the same number of days so the
span is kept; editing the end changes the span. Duration stays read-only
because it is working days that the backend recomputes from the dates on
every save, so it cannot be derived honestly from a calendar span on the
client.

The predecessors cell opens the existing dependency editor, and a
Reschedule button recomputes dates from the dependency network so a bulk
edit does not silently overwrite typed dates: activities with a
predecessor move, roots keep their manual start.

Pure frontend, no schema change. Cell edits go through the existing
activity update endpoint (which recomputes the working-day duration) and
the reschedule endpoint that shipped with the dependency editor.

fix(routing): correct file-manager, widget and coordination API prefixes and quiet the takeoff console

The File Manager upload dialog posted CAD files to /api/v1/bim/ and
/api/v1/dwg/, which are not mounted - the modules live at /api/v1/bim_hub
and /api/v1/dwg_takeoff - so dragging an RVT, IFC or DWG into Project Files
failed silently. The Coordination Hub page called /api/v1/coordination
instead of /api/v1/coordination_hub, so every KPI, matrix and timeline
request 404'd and the page was dead. The project-detail NCR and HSE widgets
called /api/v1/qms/ncrs/ with a stray trailing slash (a hard 404 with
redirect_slashes off) and /api/v1/hse/investigations/ when the module is
hse_advanced. All corrected to the real mounts.

Also guarded the takeoff PDF render loop. getPage was unguarded and a
non-cancellation render error was rethrown out of a fire-and-forget async
block, so a rapid zoom or page flip surfaced as repeated Uncaught (in
promise) errors in the console. The whole render now sits in one try/catch
that silently drops superseded or cancelled renders and dev-warns the rest,
matching the other PDF viewers.

fix(deploy): resolve alembic script_location against the ini file

The unified container runs uvicorn with --app-dir /app/backend but keeps its
working directory at /app, so a bare script_location = alembic resolved to
/app/alembic, which does not exist. The /api/health head check raised on that
every 30 seconds (the Docker healthcheck interval), flooding the log with
Alembic head check failed: Path doesn't exist: alembic and leaving
alembic_head_matches perpetually null. Pointing script_location at
%(here)s/alembic resolves it against the ini file's own directory, so it works
whatever the working directory is. Schema creation was never affected,
create_all plus the column auto-migrate build it, this only restores the
health signal and stops the noise.

fix(ui): cap the case hero image to the text column and even up dashboard rows

On a case page the hero illustration could grow taller than the text next to
it, leaving its bottom edge well below the Case progress row. The image now
fills a column positioned against the text side, so its height tracks the copy
and the bottom edges line up. On the dashboard, cards sharing a row now stretch
to equal height, the latest site photos card spans two thirds so it reaches the
grid edge, and the RFI turnaround card widens to a half so it no longer leaves
a gap.

perf(bim): verify worker-parsed tiles keep the node-name match, else fall back

The off-thread tile parse round-trips through three's toJSON/ObjectLoader, which
should preserve node names exactly. Add a runtime self-check so a silent
round-trip loss can never degrade the mesh to element match: the worker now
reports the node-name set its parse produced, and the main thread, after
ObjectLoader rebuilds the scene, verifies the reconstruction carries the exact
same set. Those names are the keys the viewer's match walks, and a main-thread
parse of the same buffer is deterministic and yields the same set, so an
identical set means the match ratio cannot be worse than the main-thread parse.
If any name is dropped or altered, the worker scene is discarded and parse
resolves null, so the streamer falls back to the main-thread parse for that
tile. The silent-break risk becomes an automatic safe fallback.

Covered by a new test: a worker reply whose reported names the reconstruction
cannot satisfy resolves null.

test(bim): verify the real GLB tile round-trip preserves node names

The worker tile-parse tests run through the main-thread fallback under jsdom
(no real Worker), so the toJSON/ObjectLoader round-trip the off-thread path
relies on was only exercised indirectly. Add a test that runs a real GLB
through GLTFExporter, then GLTFLoader.parse, then toJSON, then ObjectLoader and
asserts the node names, the nested outer-ElementId hierarchy the mesh to
element match walks, and the mesh geometry all survive. This proves the happy
path: for a real GLB the names are preserved, so the fidelity self-check passes
and the worker scene is actually used rather than always discarded to the
fallback.

fix(takeoff): isolate and cap PDF parsing so an upload can't OOM the container

Uploading a PDF on the takeoff screen could take the whole container down with no log line. The upload endpoint parsed the PDF in the same process that serves every request, with no size cap, so a large or vector-dense drawing drove pdfplumber's table extraction past available RAM and the kernel OOM-killed the single uvicorn worker. A malformed PDF that segfaulted the native parser was the same kind of silent kill. Because it was one process, every user dropped at once.

The parse now runs in a separate, short-lived child process launched per upload. The child caps its own address space with RLIMIT_AS on POSIX and the parent enforces a wall-clock timeout, so a runaway or crashing parse dies cleanly and only takes the child with it while the API worker keeps serving. On a dense CAD sheet the child also skips the most memory-hungry table-finder pass and falls back to plain text, which is what actually triggered the out-of-memory in the field.

Uploads are now capped at a real 200 MB by default (still overridable with OE_TAKEOFF_MAX_UPLOAD_MB) instead of the old unlimited default, and the route reads at most the cap plus one byte so an oversized upload is rejected with 413 before the whole body is pulled into memory. The bytes are written to disk before parsing, so the document is never lost. If the child times out or crashes the upload still persists with no extracted pages plus a flag so it can be reprocessed, and only a clean run that genuinely cannot read a single page is rejected.

The in-process count and extract helpers now delegate to the same worker so there is a single parser, and the recognize and scale-detect paths are left as they are since they run on the already-capped stored file.

fix(match_elements): bound excel and pdf uploads to stop OOM

The from-excel and from-pdf session-creation handlers read the whole
request body into memory with file.read() and had no spreadsheet-bomb
guard or PDF page cap. A single oversized upload could push the
single-worker container into swap and OOM-kill it on the 2 GB target
box, the same class of failure already fixed for the documents and
takeoff uploads.

Both handlers now stream the upload to a temp file in 1 MB chunks and
abort past a byte cap, so an oversized body never lands fully in RAM and
the caller gets a clean 413 instead of a crash. The excel path then runs
the shared xlsx decompression-bomb guard before openpyxl touches the
bytes, and the pdf path counts pages with pymupdf (which never decodes
page content) and rejects a document with more pages than the cap before
the per-page table extraction that took down the takeoff container on
vector-dense sheets.

Normal files are unchanged: a real BoQ spreadsheet or tender PDF parses
to the same rows and flows into the same session-creation pipeline. The
caps are generous (100 MB xlsx, 200 MB pdf, 500 pages) so only abusive
or accidental oversized uploads are turned away.
style(takeoff): ruff-format the takeoff hardening test files

fix(reporting): cap export size so a huge report can't OOM the worker

The report export entry point builds the whole CSV, XLSX or PDF in
memory before streaming it back, and the XLSX writer holds a cell
object per value. A report whose snapshot carries a runaway row count,
for example a project with a very large bill of quantities or a long
incident log, could push the single worker into swap while assembling
the download, the same class of failure already fixed on the document
and match_elements upload paths.

export_report now counts the rows a snapshot would materialise and
turns away anything past a generous limit with a clear message that
tells the user to narrow the scope, before any writer runs. The count
is a cheap upper bound over the section payloads and never builds a
cell. The service layer already maps that error to a 400, so the caller
gets a clean response instead of a crash. Normal reports export exactly
as before and the html path is left ungated.

fix: cap file_search OCR raster and point-cloud inline decode against OOM

The file_search reindex OCR path rendered every PDF page with get_pixmap at
full resolution with no ceiling, so a large-format sheet or a maliciously
oversized page could allocate hundreds of MB and OOM the 2 GB core. Every page
render is now clamped so its pixmap never exceeds a pixel cap, the render DPI is
bounded, and one document is OCR'd through at most a fixed page count. Each page
pixmap is released before the next so peak memory stays a single page rather
than the whole document's rasters.

The point-cloud viewer decode read the whole scan into RAM before decimating and
ran the native laspy/pye57 decoder with no size ceiling. On a non-local backend
the object is now streamed to a temp file under a hard byte cap, refused with
HTTP 413 the moment it exceeds the cap instead of pulling the whole 5-200 GB
blob into memory, and the decoder refuses a source whose header declares more
points than the inline ceiling, so neither a multi-GB blob nor a LAZ or E57
decompression bomb can exhaust the core. The points response now carries the
total and returned counts so a decimated preview is never mistaken for the whole
scan.

Behaviour is unchanged for normal-sized inputs. These are front-door guards
only, with DB-free unit tests covering the render-scale clamp, the point-count
ceiling and the capped streamed spill.

fix(bim_hub): stream and cap the model upload so a big drop cannot OOM the box

The upload read both the element table and the geometry blob fully into memory and passed the xlsx to openpyxl with no decompression-bomb guard, so a single large drop could push the worker into swap and get it killed for everyone. The element table now streams to a bounded temp file (100 MB cap) before it is read back for the parser, the xlsx is checked for a decompression bomb before openpyxl opens it, and the geometry blob streams to disk (500 MB cap) and is handed to storage by path instead of sitting in RAM. Oversized uploads get a clean 413, an oversized geometry no longer leaves an orphan model, and normal uploads convert exactly as before.

fix(takeoff): open Project-Files PDFs against a real takeoff document

Opening a PDF from Project Files in the takeoff screen fired a flood of 404s and filed measurements under the wrong id. The deep-link carried the documents-table id, but the viewer's own calls (get document, detect-scale, page-scales, measurements) only resolve against takeoff_documents, so every one of them missed. The PDF still rendered because its bytes stream from the documents download route, but scale detection, page scales and measurements all failed.

The reason is that takeoff needs its own row. It persists page_scales, extracted_text and analysis, and every measurement has a foreign key to a takeoff document, none of which a documents row can hold. So opening a Project-Files document now finds or creates a real takeoff_document for it and the viewer uses that id everywhere.

A new endpoint, POST /documents/from-source/{id}, verifies the caller's access to the source document's project, and if a takeoff document already exists for that source in the project it returns it unchanged. Otherwise it reads the source PDF and runs it through the same hardened, isolated, size and page capped parse the direct upload uses, stamping the new row with the source id so the next open reuses it. Opening the same file twice never duplicates the row or re-parses, and an oversized or malformed source degrades the same way an upload does instead of taking the server down.

A new nullable source_document_id column on oe_takeoff_document is the idempotency key, with a matching index and an additive migration chained on the current head. The takeoff page now calls the endpoint when a file is opened from Project Files and drives the viewer off the returned takeoff id.

fix: add alembic migration for takeoff page_scales column

The oe_takeoff_document.page_scales column lives on the model but was only ever
created at runtime by create_all plus postgres_auto_migrate, so a DDL-restricted
external database never got the column and any read of page_scales failed there.
This adds the missing migration.

v3239 chains after v3238_takeoff_source_document_id, keeping a single linear
head. The column is additive and nullable JSON, so every existing row reads
unchanged and no backfill is needed. Upgrade and downgrade are inspector-guarded
so a re-run on a database that already picked the column up via create_all is a
no-op, matching the sibling takeoff migrations.

fix(packaging): ship backend locale files in the wheel

A pip install of openconstructionerp dropped six interface languages:
Bulgarian, Croatian, Indonesian, Romanian, Thai and Vietnamese. The
backend loads its UI translations at runtime from a locales directory
that sits next to the installed app package, but that folder lives
outside the packaged app tree and was never listed for inclusion, so
the built wheel carried none of the 26 locale JSON files.

At startup the loader found the directory missing and regenerated only
the 20 languages hard-coded in the fallback, which is why exactly those
six, the ones that exist solely as JSON, disappeared on a clean install
while a source checkout still showed all of them.

The wheel target now force-includes the locales folder at the same
top-level path the runtime looks up, so an installed package carries all
26 languages. The folder is outside the app package, so it does not
collide with the existing package walk or the double-add guard. Verified
against the rebuilt wheel: the archive now contains locales/bg.json, hr,
id, ro, th, vi and the rest, where before it held no locales directory
at all.

harden the published container for production by default

The unified image shipped with APP_ENV=development, so a bare docker run
exposed the interactive API docs, kept a wildcard CORS origin and ran in a
debug posture. It now defaults to production. The docs are hidden and the
wildcard origin is stripped (both were already wired to is_production), while
the quickstart compose still opts into development for a friendly first run.

Booting production used to require a JWT_SECRET or the app refused to start.
The image now auto-provisions one: when no real secret is set, get_settings
generates a strong random value, persists it under the data dir at
/data/.jwt-secret (chmod 600) and reuses it across restarts, so the container
comes up with zero configuration and still signs tokens with a secret that is
not the public repo default. Because /data is a mounted volume the secret
survives redeploys. An explicitly weak or too-short secret is left untouched
so the strict Settings validator still rejects it, and development stays a
no-op as before.

Also adds a coarse global request-body-size backstop above the per-endpoint
upload caps, so a single absurdly large body can no longer reach an endpoint
that reads it unbounded and OOM the one worker. Default ceiling 4 GiB, tunable
via OE_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES.
docs(takeoff): correct the page_scales column note now that its migration exists

chore(hygiene): stop internal working notes shipping in the wheel

Four underscore-prefixed working notes had been committed next to source
(a Brazil tier-2 followup plan that quotes a user by name and email, a
property-dev security audit describing IDOR fixes, and two AI-feature a11y
notes). The wheel packages the whole app tree, so these were on track to
ship inside a pip install. Remove them from tracking (they stay on disk as
local notes), ignore that whole class going forward, exclude it from the
wheel package walk, and widen the repo-hygiene denylist so the guard and the
built-wheel scan both catch it next time.

fix(takeoff): parse PDFs in-process on the desktop build

The isolated parser is spawned as sys.executable -m
app.modules.takeoff.pdf_extract_worker. In the packaged desktop app the
backend runs as a frozen one-file binary, so sys.executable is that binary
and -m is not honoured: the child exits non-zero and every takeoff upload
degrades to zero pages with no text or tables. Detect the frozen / desktop
case and run the exact same parser (same vector-density guard) in-process
instead, which is how the desktop build behaved before the subprocess
isolation landed. Server and container deployments keep the child-process
memory isolation unchanged.

fix(documents): stream uploads to disk so a large file cannot OOM the worker

Every upload path in the documents module read the whole request body into
memory with a bare await file.read() and only then checked the size cap. On
the single-worker 2 GB container a multi-GB upload OOM-killed the process
before the check could run, taking every connected user down with no log -
the exact symptom behind the report of the Documents '+' upload crashing the
container. Stream each upload to a temp file in 1 MB chunks that aborts past
the cap, then read the now-bounded bytes back, matching the pattern already
used by the element-matching and BIM upload paths. Covers the document
upload, revision, PDF-split and photo handlers. The test UploadFile builders
now use a real BytesIO-backed UploadFile so the streaming read terminates,
plus new tests assert the oversized path returns 413.

fix(schedule): anchor rescheduled successors at their root's real start

reschedule fed the CPM engine only id, duration and name, so the forward
pass floored every root at the project origin and rewrote each successor from
there. On a schedule with more than one independent chain, a chain whose root
starts later than the project origin had its successors scheduled at the
origin, i.e. weeks before their own predecessor even starts. The dependency
editor calls reschedule after every edge change, so a normal multi-chain edit
could produce that. Give the engine an optional per-activity start_offset that
acts as a start-no-earlier-than floor (default 0, so existing callers are
unchanged), and have reschedule pass each root its own manual start as that
floor while successors stay driven purely by the network. Adds pure-engine
tests reproducing the two-chain case.

fix(config): never let JWT secret persistence abort boot

_jwt_secret_persist_dir resolved the fallback path via Path.home() outside
any guard. Path.home() raises RuntimeError when no home directory can be
resolved (a minimal container with HOME unset and no passwd entry), which
would abort startup in a non-development deployment that sets no data-dir env
var. Catch it and fall back to a relative directory; a failed persist already
degrades to a per-process secret rather than crashing.

test(frontend): refresh the dashboard skeleton snapshot

The DashboardPage loading-state snapshot pinned the What's New chips, which
are release-coupled content. They changed over this release (the point-cloud
slice and onboarding chips replaced the older cost-base and design-options
ones), so the snapshot no longer matched. The page renders correctly; only
the captured chip set was stale. Regenerate it.

fix(schedule): keep a weekend-anchored root off the critical path

A root's manual start seeds its early_start as a calendar-day offset, but the
backward pass derives late_start on working days. When that start fell on a
weekend or holiday the two passes disagreed, giving the root a negative
total_float and a false critical flag that reschedule then persisted. The
engine now snaps a nonzero start floor forward to the next working day so
early_start lands on a working day. The zero floor is left untouched, so a
schedule with no manual root start reschedules exactly as before.

fix(schedule): snap the CPM origin too when the schedule starts off a working day

A schedule whose own start date falls on a weekend or holiday put its first
root at offset 0, where the previous guard skipped the working-day snap, so that
root still got a negative float and a false critical flag. Snap every start
floor, not just the nonzero ones. An offset already on a working day is returned
unchanged, so a normal working-day origin reschedules exactly as before. The
snap also guards against a calendar with no working weekday so it can never
loop.
chore(release): v11.3.0

feat(schedule): honor per-activity work calendars in reschedule

An activity can point at a named work calendar so its duration is measured on
its own work week - a six-day trade, or a crew with its own holidays - while the
rest of the schedule uses the default. The CPM engine now takes an optional
per-activity calendar and derives that activity's early and late dates on it, so
the two stay symmetric and the float is correct. reschedule batch-loads each
activity's calendar and threads it through, and the activity response carries
its calendar_id so the grid can show and pick it. Activities without one
reschedule exactly as before.

feat(schedule): work calendar editor and per-activity calendar picker

A planner can define named work weeks for a project - a five-day, six-day or
custom set of working days, each with its own hours per day and its own list of
public holidays - and assign one to any activity from the schedule table. The
per-row picker sets the activity's calendar and reschedules through the CPM
engine, so a six-day trade finishes sooner than a five-day one. It follows the
dependency editor's set-reschedule-refetch pattern, and calendar deletion uses
an inline confirm rather than a modal. Every string is translated.

fix(schedule): harden per-activity work calendars in CPM

Four fixes on top of the per-activity calendar work.

An activity calendar whose work_days carry no valid weekday (for example a
caller that stored ISO [7] for Sunday, where the engine counts Mon=0..Sun=6)
left the CPM engine with a week that has no working day, so the working-day
walk stepped forever and overflowed a single worker. The parse now drops
out-of-range entries and falls back to Monday-Friday, so a bad calendar can no
longer stall the process.

A six-day predecessor that finishes on a Saturday used to push a five-day
successor onto that Saturday without snapping it to the successor's own week,
which left the forward and backward passes asymmetric and produced negative
float and a false critical flag. The working-day snap now runs after the
predecessor maximum, so each successor starts on its own working day.

The Gantt activity payload now carries calendar_id, so the grid calendar
picker shows the activity's real calendar and clearing it back to the project
default takes effect.

Reschedule now resolves the schedule-wide calendar from the project's default
named calendar when one is set, and creating or updating a default calendar
demotes any previous default so a project keeps a single default.

fix(schedule): scope activity calendars to the project and fix the grid picker

A multi-agent review of the per-activity calendar work turned up two real
defects, both fixed here.

Reschedule resolved each activity's named work calendar by id with no project
filter, so an activity that carried a calendar id from another project (for
example one copied in through a schedule import) was silently scheduled on the
other project's work week instead of falling back to the schedule default. The
lookup is now scoped to the schedule's project, matching the write path that
already rejects a cross-project calendar, so a foreign or dangling id resolves
to nothing and the activity uses the schedule-wide calendar. Added an
integration test that assigns a foreign-project calendar and checks the
successor does not move.

The per-row calendar picker in the activity grid was an uncontrolled select
whose option list loads asynchronously, so an activity that already had a
calendar assigned showed Default until the row was touched, and a failed save
did not revert the shown value. The select is now controlled off the stored
calendar with an optimistic layer, so it shows the real calendar once the list
loads, the picked calendar immediately while the change is in flight, and the
stored value again if the save fails.

Also populate calendar_id on the activity list and detail responses, which
carried the field in the schema but never filled it.

chore(release): v11.4.0

Scheduling gains work calendars. Define named work weeks for a project, each
with its own hours per day and public holidays, assign one to any activity
from the schedule table, and rescheduling measures each activity's duration on
its own calendar while dates, float and the critical path stay consistent.
Activities left on the project default reschedule exactly as before.

test(schedule): teach the calendar repo stub the single-default reconcile

The create/update calendar paths now call clear_defaults_except to keep one
default per project, but the in-memory calendar repo stub in the unit tests
did not implement it, so test_calendar_crud_basics raised AttributeError. Give
the stub a faithful in-memory version so the unit suite exercises the same
single-default behaviour as the real repository. Test-only, no change to
shipped behaviour.

docs: credit Mourdi59 for the formula and schedule ideas

Mourtadha Diop raised the ideas behind the BOQ per-element quantity formulas
and multi-model BIM fixes (#347) and the schedule dependency editor, editable
activity grid and per-activity work calendar (#348). Both landed as our own
implementation. Extend his CONTRIBUTORS entry and add the two acknowledgment
rows so the report that led to the work is on record.

fix(backup): restore correctly when moving data to another machine

A backup carries the exporter's own users row with the password hash stripped
and an email that is usually already taken on the target install. Restore
re-inserted that row, so it hit the NOT NULL password and the unique email and
rolled the whole transaction back with a 500. That is exactly why a backup made
on one PC would export fine but fail to restore on another.

Restore now never re-creates the users table. The account doing the restore
already exists on the target machine with its own id, email and password, so
instead of cloning the exporter we repoint every ownership column on the
imported rows (owner_id, created_by, user_id and the like) to the restoring
user. The data then lands under that account and is actually visible there,
since the two machines mint different user ids.

Embedded files are written back too, so drawings, documents and photos move with
the data rather than leaving dangling references. File writes run outside the DB
transaction and are best-effort: a file that fails to write is a warning, not a
reason to undo the committed data restore. The response gains a files_restored
count.

The restore body moves into a testable service function, restore_backup_data,
which was the untested gap that let this ship broken. Adds a cross-machine
round-trip integration test plus unit tests for the ownership remap and the file
restore. Export and the per-user delete scope are unchanged.

fix(backup): keep AI settings out of restore and strip keys from exports

Ownership remap turned ai_settings into a footgun: the table has one row per
user with a unique user_id, so repointing the exporter's row to the restoring
user collided with that user's own settings and failed a merge restore, which is
the default mode. AI settings are per-account config, not project work data, so
restore now skips the table the same way it skips users, and the restoring
account keeps its own provider keys, which are the right ones for its
environment.

Exports now also strip every AI provider key (any *_api_key column), so a backup
file that gets copied between machines never carries a secret in plain text.
Adds unit coverage for the strip and a merge-mode ai_settings regression test.

fix(backup): make restore resilient and keep it inside the restoring account

Following the cross-machine restore fix, this hardens the restore itself.

A single record that cannot be inserted, most often an assembly whose globally
unique code already exists on the target, used to fail the whole-table write and
roll the entire restore back, so a transfer between two machines could land
nothing at all. Each row now imports in its own savepoint, with a fast bulk path
and a per-row fallback, so an offending row is skipped with a warning and
everything else still comes across.

Ownership is pinned to the account doing the restore rather than trusted from the
archive. That fixes a real case, a teammate-authored row in a shared export, and
also stops a crafted backup from inserting rows under someone else's login. File
restore only writes the blobs backing rows actually imported and never overwrites
a file already in storage, so a restore cannot clobber another account's data.
Oversized or malformed archive entries are rejected before they are read, and the
export secret filter now covers more credential-shaped column names.

fix(backup): default restore to merge and refuse a destructive replace

Replace mode cleared the account's own rows before importing, and in the
database a project delete cascades across dozens of project-scoped modules
the backup does not carry, so restoring with replace onto an account that
already held data destroyed diaries, takeoff, inspections and much more the
restore could never rebuild.

Merge is now the default. It adds the records a backup holds that are not
already there and removes nothing, which is the safe way to bring a backup
onto another machine or into an account that already has data. Replace is
allowed only into an empty account and is otherwise refused with a 409 that
points the user to merge.

Restore is also steadier: rows import per savepoint with a multi-pass
fallback, so one row that trips a constraint is skipped with a note instead
of sinking the whole transfer, and a self-referential row lands once its
parent is in. The restore screen surfaces the server's reason on failure and
states plainly which data a backup carries and which site records it does
not yet.
chore(release): v11.5.0

chore: remove retired OpenEstimator.io design artifacts

Drop the old logo-showcase pages and login-variant mockups that still carried the retired OpenEstimator.io brand, plus two dated .bak/.backup leftovers. None of them are wired into the app, the build or the e2e tests. Also switch the leftover brand names in the catalog import readme to OpenConstructionERP.
fix: match dashboard drop-zone height to the inbox card and enlarge the case stepper icon and arrows

chore: keep third-party product names off user-facing surfaces

Genericize commercial cost-database brand names (RSMeans, BKI, ENR, Sirados, Spon's, Batiprix) in the marketing site and all locale files, the AI cost-source prompt, the DWG import error messages and the docs. Open standards and public statistical sources such as BCIS and Destatis stay. No stored source values, enum values or file-format tokens were changed.

fix: make the Windows in-app updater work on the first try

The one-click update ran pip inside the running process, but on Windows the launcher keeps its own openconstructionerp.exe open, so pip could not overwrite it and failed with WinError 32 (file in use). It only went through on a second attempt after a restart. Now, on Windows, the locked launcher exes are renamed aside before pip runs (Windows allows renaming a running exe), pip writes fresh ones, and the originals are restored if pip did not regenerate them. Stale renamed stubs are swept on the next upgrade.

fix(photos): re-home photo blobs so previously uploaded photos keep showing

Photos record an absolute file_path at upload time. When the data dir
later changes - a fresh --data-dir per release, a restored backup, or
OE_DATA_DIR introduced after the fact - that absolute path goes stale, so
the serve endpoints 404 even though the same file sits under the current
base. That is why previously uploaded photos went blank while freshly
uploaded ones kept working.

The file and thumbnail routes now resolve through a re-home helper that
mirrors LocalStorageBackend._existing_path_for: try the stored path
first, then rebuild the key from the tail after the photos/thumbs segment
and probe the active base plus every platform-owned data root. Safe-root
containment and the symlink rejection are preserved, so nothing loosens.

feat(backup): derive the full user-owned backup scope from the schema

Personal backups covered a curated set of 19 tables. Every user-owned
table added since (equipment logs, CRM rows, portal data, HSE records and
more) fell outside the backup, so a restore on a fresh machine quietly
dropped that data.

This adds graph_scope, a pure fixpoint over the foreign-key and naming
graph rooted at users and projects: a table is in scope when it carries an
owner-ish user column, a project_id, or a real FK into an already in-scope
table. Reference and catalog tables stay out. Predicates are OR'd so every
ownership path a table exposes is kept.

Validated against the real schema: 474 tables now in scope versus 19, all
19 hand-written scopes reproduced, no orphan predicates, and no excluded
table carrying project_id or a user column. The service still uses the
hand map for now; wiring the derived scope in is the next step.

feat(dwg): carry the drawing's text font and support uploading a new revision

Two things site users hit on DWG/DXF takeoff.

Text font. The parsers dropped the text style, so the viewer had nothing
to render with and fell back to a generic font that did not match the
drawing. Both the DXF path (reads the STYLE table) and the DDC DWG path
(reads the text-style records) now capture each TEXT/MTEXT entity's style
name and the font it references, and the service carries those two fields
through to the viewer. Everything is defensive: a missing or malformed
style resolves to an empty font, never a failed parse.

Upload a new revision. Uploading a second drawing used to create a
separate drawing, so there was no revision history to compare. The new
upload_revision reuses the existing drawing row, writes the new file to a
fresh path so the previous blob is kept, and re-runs the same parse, which
stores it as the next version. Exposed as POST /drawings/{id}/revisions/,
gated on the drawing's project and the create permission.

chore(marketing): refresh the stat numbers to the current platform figures

The marketing site still carried old counts. Across index.html and all 20
locale files the module total is now 161, the language count is 27, and
the CAD list adds DXF and GLB (six formats: DWG, RVT, IFC, DGN, DXF, GLB),
matching the README and the app. The role-subset "17 of 161" wording is
kept, and the JSON-LD availableLanguage list stays at 20 because that
honestly describes how many languages the marketing pages themselves exist
in, not the product's language coverage.

perf(dashboard): code-split the widget cards so the page streams top to bottom

The dashboard blocked on one large chunk before anything showed. The 15
widget cards are now lazy-loaded, each inside its own grid-cell Suspense
boundary, so the shell and skeletons paint immediately and every widget's
JS and data arrive independently. Self-hiding widgets keep a null fallback
so an empty card never flashes a skeleton before removing itself; the
skeleton carries no text, so there is no locale-loading race.

chore(ui): refresh the login and about stat tiles to current figures

The login screen and About page still showed old counts. Languages now
read 27 and modules 161, matching the marketing site and the README, and
two locales that carried a stale "30 regional" are corrected to 48.

refactor(costs): describe cost benchmarks by function, not by product name

Replaces the third-party benchmark product names shown in the cost
benchmark data and the custom-module dialog with plain descriptions of
what they are (national building-cost benchmark, construction cost index,
unit-price reference), so no external brand appears in the UI.

docs(readme): reflect the current cost-base coverage and module count

The cost databases section still described the old footprint. It now names
the 8 national bases added on top of the CWICR global base (China, Turkey,
Brazil, Spain, Italy, Greece, Vietnam, Indonesia) and states the 30
regional markets the CWICR base is repriced into, instead of the stale
"11 regions". The role-onboarding line also moves from 46 to 161 modules.

feat(dwg): render the drawing font and wire the new-revision upload in the UI

Frontend side of the two DWG takeoff fixes. The viewer now resolves each
text entity's captured style/font to a CSS family (defaulting unknown or
empty to a sans stack instead of monospace, which is what fixed the common
wrong-font look), so text renders close to the drawing. The compare drawer
gains a clear "Upload new revision" action distinct from "compare a
different file", and the drawing viewer toolbar gets a "New revision"
button, so adding a version to the same drawing is discoverable and the
version diff runs on it automatically.

feat(backup): cover every user-owned table in a personal backup

The personal backup carried a fixed 19-table core and silently dropped
every other table a user owns, so a restore on a fresh machine quietly
lost contacts, site diaries, takeoff, inspections and safety records,
labor rates, custom catalogs, templates and notifications. The scope is
now derived from the whole mapped schema, rooted at the users and
projects tables and walking the ownership and foreign-key graph, so a
backup holds all of a user's own data across every module.

The derived tables come out parents before children, a topological sort
over the scope predicates, so a restore inserts a parent before any row
that references it and clears in reverse, keeping a cross-machine
transfer consistent across the hundreds of tables now covered. Shared

to the restoring account, embedded files restored, secrets stripped, and
one bad row skipped rather than sinking the transfer.

docs: simplify the cryptographic and export notice

Rewrote the crypto and export note in NOTICE and README in plain language. The app uses only standard published cryptography for sign-in (bcrypt and signed JWT), which as open source needs no special export licence, so the heavy regulation citations were more than an open project needs. Also dropped Syria from the sanctioned list, since the comprehensive Syria program was revoked in 2025, and made clear the note is information, not legal advice.

fix(desktop): stop the backend before install so Windows reinstall works, rename the sidecar

On Windows the backend ran as a separate process, openestimate-server.exe,
that could keep running after the app was closed or uninstalled. Windows locks
a running executable on disk, so the next install could not overwrite it and
failed with a file-in-use error until the process was ended by hand in Task
Manager.

The NSIS installer and uninstaller now stop that process first, through a tauri
installer hook at desktop/src-tauri/windows/hooks.nsh that runs taskkill before
files are written or removed. It stops both the new and the former process
name, so upgrading from an older install is not blocked either.

The sidecar binary is renamed from openestimate-server to
openconstructionerp-server across the pyinstaller spec, the tauri externalBin,
the sidecar lookup in main.rs, the build script and the release workflow, so
the app carries one name. The desktop crate and its stale 7.1.0 version are
brought in line with the release version too.

The ~/.openestimate data folder, the OE_ settings prefix and the pip
openestimate command are left as they are, so existing installs keep their
data and their commands keep working.

Bumped to 11.7.1.

docs: cite the accurate export-control basis in the crypto notice

The cryptographic notice reached the right conclusion but leaned on the
publicly-available-encryption source code provision (15 CFR 742.15(b)),
which is the wrong basis. bcrypt and JWT are authentication and digital
signature cryptography, and that function falls outside the Category 5
Part 2 encryption controls of the US EAR and the equivalent EU dual-use
list in the first place, so no export licence is required. Reworded to
rest on that basis and kept the open-source point as a secondary one.

The sanctions list is unchanged and stays verified against primary
sources: Cuba, Iran, North Korea and the Crimea, Donetsk and Luhansk
regions of Ukraine, with Syria correctly left out since its comprehensive
program was revoked in 2025.

encryption so no export licence is needed, refers to comprehensively
sanctioned destinations in general, and leaves the specifics to NOTICE.

fix(site): keep the by-the-numbers stat values on one line in every language

The stat cards let the big value wrap, so a wide figure like the 120,000+
cost-item count dropped its plus sign onto a second line in German and other
longer locales. The value now stays on one line and its font scales to fit the
card, so the number and its plus or percent sign always sit together at every
width. The live homepage is already updated; this brings the repo copies in
line.

fix(takeoff): clear the measurement hover card when a reshape starts

Hovering a measurement with the Select tool shows a small info card. Once
you pressed a vertex and started dragging it, the card froze at the spot
it held on mousedown, right next to the vertex, and sat on top of the area
being reshaped for the whole drag. The move handler returns early while a
drag is in flight, so it never got to refresh the card's position.

Drop the hover card where the drag is armed, in the mousedown handler, so
it disappears for the reshape and comes back on the next ordinary hover.
Clearing it there rather than in the move branch also covers a press that
is held, or pressed and released, without moving, which never reaches the
move handler at all.

Closes #353

fix(takeoff): offset distance and polyline value labels off the line

The value labels on a completed distance or polyline were pushed a fixed
number of pixels straight up from the geometry. That fails in two ways.
It ignores how wide the line is painted, so a measurement carrying a
real-world width renders as a band that swallows the small offset and the
label lands inside it, filled in the band's own colour. And straight up
only clears a horizontal line: on a near-vertical run it slides the label
along the line instead of away from it.

Offset each label perpendicular to its own segment now. Compute the
segment's up-facing unit normal, guard a zero-length segment by falling
back to straight up, and push the anchor out by half the painted band
plus the gap the code already used. Set the text alignment and baseline
from that normal so the text runs away from the line, then restore them
right away since canvas text state is global. The polyline total takes
the first segment's normal, and the name badge stays stacked above the
value in screen space but anchors to its far edge so a long name does not
grow back over the band.

Closes #355

feat(takeoff): per-measurement visibility toggle

The eye control only hid whole groups, so to hide a single measurement you
had to move it into its own group or hide the group it lived in. Add a
per-measurement eye button on each measurement row backed by a
hiddenMeasurements set keyed by measurement id, parallel to hiddenGroups.

A hidden measurement is honoured everywhere group visibility is: it leaves
the canvas render, drops out of the vertex snap pool, stops intercepting
clicks in the hit-test, is excluded from the legend count and total, and is
left out of the annotated PDF (the baked pages, the page selection and the
summary rows). It stays listed in the panel, dimmed with an eye-off icon,
so it can be restored, and hiding the selected measurement clears the
selection and the edit overlay.

The legend needed two corrections that also fix live bugs. Its rows now
derive the hidden flag from hiddenGroups directly instead of from a group's
absence in the summaries, so a group whose measurements are all hidden one
by one reads as present with nothing visible rather than as a hidden group;
and the legend is gated on the page having measurements at all, so hiding
the last visible thing no longer unmounts the rows that bring it back.

Per-measurement hiding is a view concern only. Like group hiding, it does
not touch the CSV, XLSX or BOQ exports or the quantity totals.

Closes #359

fix(takeoff): do not leak a vertex drag into a tool switched mid-press

Dragging a vertex with the Select tool and then pressing a drawing-tool
shortcut before releasing the mouse left the edit drag running. On release
the edit committed at the dragged position even though the canvas had
reverted to the pre-drag geometry the moment the tool changed, and the same
press was also consumed as a click by the tool just selected, starting a
stray measurement.

Track the primary press with two refs. pressActive is set on a primary
mousedown and cleared on a primary mouseup, in the canvas handler and in the
window mouseup listener that catches a release off-canvas. When selectTool
actually changes the tool, abandon any in-flight drag with finishDrag(false)
and, if a press is live, arm suppressNextClick. handleCanvasClick consumes
that click at the top and returns, the same way the pan guard does. The
suppression is keyed on the press rather than on dragRef, because Escape can
null dragRef mid-press while the click is still coming.

The window blur handler now also tears down every in-flight gesture, so a
button released in another application no longer strands a drag or a pan, and
touchstart clears the suppression flag so a press that ended off-canvas
cannot swallow the next tap.

Closes #356

feat(takeoff): show a wide line's width band while dragging it

A distance or polyline can carry a real-world line width, so it renders as a
wide band, but during an edit drag only a thin dashed outline followed the
cursor while the band stayed at the pre-drag position until release. For a
wide line the two band edges are exactly what the user is placing, so not
seeing them made precise placement hard.

Render the measurement being dragged from its live geometry in the pass that
already knows how to draw it. The completed-measurements loop now repoints the
dragged measurement to the preview points, so the band, the area and volume
fills, the value and per-segment labels, the vertex dots and the annotation
all follow the cursor, and there is still only one band on screen. The drag
overlay keeps drawing its dashed outline and handles on top.

dragPreview now carries the recompute patch that handleEditDragMove already
computed and used to discard. The repointed measurement projects value, unit
and area/width/height from it field by field, the way the mouseup commit does,
so the drag paints exactly what the release will store. The value label and
the overlay readout both go through measurementLabel now, so an imperial user
sees feet during the drag instead of the raw metric string.

Closes #357

fix(takeoff): pin the canvas chrome so it stops scrolling with the drawing

The legend, the tool hints, the calibration banner, the AI-suggestion pill
and the draw readout were absolutely positioned children of the scroll
container, so their corner offsets were measured against the scrolled
content rather than the viewport. Zoom in and pan, which is how anyone
works on a real drawing, and they left the view entirely or ended up parked
in the middle of the sheet on top of the work.

Wrap the scroll container in a non-scrolling positioning context that spans
the visible canvas, and move those six overlays out of the container into
that wrapper with their corner classes unchanged. The wrapper takes the
container's slot in the canvas column, flex-1 plus the fixed min-h-[320px]
floor, and passes it through, so the container keeps its own classes and the
definite-height chain fit-to-page depends on stays intact.

The hover card and the text-annotation input stay inside the scroll
container on purpose: both are positioned in canvas coordinates and are
meant to track the drawing.

Closes #354

feat(takeoff): let the group legend be dragged by its header

The legend had no position control, so once it was pinned to the corner of
the viewport it sat over the same corner of the drawing permanently, right
where a user often needs to place the next vertex, with no way to move it.

Grab it by its header and drop it anywhere. The position is held in state in
pixels from the pinned wrapper's top-left, with null meaning the default
bottom-left corner, and it is saved to localStorage as a workspace
preference so it is not written into the document. The drag runs off window
listeners so it survives the cursor leaving the small legend rectangle, and
it is torn down on mouseup, on window blur, and when the legend unmounts
mid-drag through a stable ref callback. The position is clamped into the
viewport on both bounds, on attach and through a ResizeObserver on the
viewport and the legend, so a sidebar toggle or a group coming and going can
never strand it off-screen. Double-clicking the header resets it.

The legend also gets a height cap now, a flex column with the header pinned
and the rows scrolling inside, so a page with many groups can no longer grow
the box and carry its own header off the top of the view. Pointer events
stay off the rows while a tool is armed, as before, but the header re-enables
them so the drag handle is grabbable under any tool without abandoning a
measurement in progress.

Closes #358

fix(notifications): add portal templates so Telegram shows real text

Portal notifications (user invited, message received) carried i18n keys
that had no server-side template, so channels without frontend i18n such
as the Telegram bridge printed the raw key string as the title and body
instead of readable text. The in-app bell looked right only because the
frontend locale ships its own copy. Added the missing portal entries to
the server template registry, with a regression test.

Closes #361

feat: rework the case page and add case-to-case flow

Rebuild the case detail page so the whole scenario reads on one screen. The
process is now a row of step cards at the top with the case summary and

New users used to wait on the wizard while a regional cost base imported

jobs, moves the user straight on to the next step, and shows a live

feat: build out Model Review with issue navigation, coordination mode, dashboard and report

Model Review had the viewer and the BCF issue register side by side but no

expect from a dedicated tool.

Zoom to issue flies the 3D view back to where an issue was raised and selects
the elements it was raised against, from the issue list or the detail drawer.

flying to each, with inline status changes and quick notes, paged with the

All of it reads the existing BCF endpoints, so there is no migration and no

feat: make the onboarding size choice show what each team size gets

The size step asked how big your team is but only showed a module count. Now

fix(desktop): open external links in the system browser

In the desktop shell every outbound link was dead. openExternalUrl tried to
import @tauri-apps/plugin-shell at runtime, but that package is not in the
bundle, so the import threw and nothing opened. Plain target=_blank anchors
never reached the browser either, since the webview just swallows them.
