chore: release 12.5.0

fix(auth): honor next after login so demo deep links land on the module

The case-study pages deep link into the running demo, for example
/schedule or /bim/federations. A signed-out visitor is bounced to
/login?next=/schedule and after sign-in should land there. But the
/login route guard rendered a hard-coded redirect to / the moment the
token was set, and that redirect won the race against the login form's
own navigate(next), so every deep link quietly ended up on the dashboard
instead of the module the visitor asked for.

Pull the next validation into one shared helper, safeNextPath, and route
both the login form and the authenticated-route guards (/login,
/login-next, /register, /forgot-password) through a small AuthedHome
component that uses it. Whichever redirect fires first now resolves to
the same validated destination. The helper keeps the open-redirect guard:
internal absolute paths only, never protocol-relative, never an auth
route that would loop.

Adds unit tests for safeNextPath and an integration test that renders the
guard in a router and confirms an authenticated visitor at
/login?next=/schedule lands on the schedule route.
chore: release 12.6.0

fix(auth): resolve the optional user on websocket handshakes, not just http

The app-level RLS dependency resolves the caller's tenant through the
optional-user chain, which read the bearer token via HTTPBearer. On a
websocket route fastapi calls HTTPBearer with no request and raises, so both
realtime sockets (live notifications and collaboration presence) rejected
their handshake with a 500. Read the token via HTTPConnection instead, the
shared base of Request and WebSocket, so the optional-user resolver and the
tenant and RLS context built on it also resolve on websocket routes. The
strict http auth path is unchanged.

test(realtime): guard the websocket handshake in the postgres gate

The RLS handshake break lived through four releases because nothing that
gates a release ever opened a websocket. The plain CI job that runs the
integration suite is chronically red from a frontend memory limit, so a
failure there tells nobody anything, and the presence test that did exist
accepted any exception at all, so a 500 read the same as a policy refusal.

Add a handshake test to tests/pg, the lane the PostgreSQL gate runs. It
mounts the real app-wide RLS dependency on a throwaway websocket route, so
it needs no cluster and no database: an anonymous handshake resolves to no
tenant and never reaches a query. It also pins the token resolver against a
websocket scope, which is the exact thing HTTPBearer cannot do. Tighten the
presence test to assert the 1008 close code instead of catching Exception.
chore: release 12.6.1

feat(site): explain what the desktop download actually gives you

The download section answered "how do I install it" three times over and
never answered what people ask next. Add a short explainer row under the
platform cards covering the three real questions: everything ships in the
download and nothing sits behind a paid tier, it runs on your own machine
with no account and no cloud in the middle, and there is nothing to keep
running because the database and the server are part of the same program.
Under that, two plain facts, the system requirements and what the first
minute looks like, so nobody has to guess whether their laptop will cope.

The section lede and the pip/Docker lede now say a bit more as well, in
particular when you would pick the server install over the desktop app.

Two fixes carried in the same file. The pip/Docker eyebrow was inline-flex
and packed onto the same line as its heading whenever both fitted the
centred wrapper, so it now takes its own line. The district panel drops its
backdrop wash: the WebGL canvas is transparent and the tint read as a faint
background box in both themes.

test(realtime): make the presence websocket tests reach a real entity

Two of the three presence tests connected with a random uuid for the entity
id. Once the tenant gate landed, that uuid resolved to no project, the socket
closed with 1008 before a frame was sent, and both tests had been failing ever
since inside a CI job that is red for unrelated reasons and that nobody reads.
The channel had no working coverage at all.

Seed a real project, BOQ, section and position and use that position as the
entity, and put the second user on the project's default team so they can
reach it: open registration creates viewers, not admins, so membership is the
only route in. All three tests pass now, including the two-user join fan-out.

chore: take the public website out of the product repository

The site is built and deployed on its own and the live host is the source of
truth for it, so carrying a second copy here only produced a tree that drifted
from what visitors actually see. The homepage in this repo and the one being
served had grown 6542 lines apart, which made every deploy a merge problem
rather than a copy.

marketing-site and the archived website-marketing tree are untracked, ignored
and added to the hygiene denylist so they cannot come back by accident. The
files stay in place locally, nothing is deleted from disk. Two documentation
build helpers go the same way: they are internal tooling, not something a
reader of the project is meant to run.

fix(ui): stop blank-currency money formatting from taking the page down

formatCurrency keeps a minimum of two fraction digits when it has no usable
currency code, and Intl throws a RangeError when the minimum exceeds the
maximum. A caller asking for whole money passes maximumFractionDigits alone,
which is what the finance summary card and the ROM estimate page do, so a blank
currency threw out of a branch that has no try/catch around it and took the
screen with it. Clamp the minimum to the maximum in both branches. The existing
test passed both ends at once, which is exactly why it never caught this.

Also mark the two point cloud capability cards that have no backend behind them.
The page promised measuring what was built and cut and fill volumes in the
present tense while neither has a control anywhere, which is the kind of surface
that costs more trust than it wins. The label is a separate key with a default,
so it reads honestly in every language before the translations land, and the
card order is untouched because those titles are keyed by index in 29 locales.

feat(i18n): fill the untranslated screens across all 28 locales

Every locale carried roughly 900 English strings that were rendering through
the defaultValue fallback, so whole panels stayed in English no matter which
language was picked. Kyrgyz was the worst case, it only had about half the
dictionary. This adds the missing strings to all of them, about 37 700 in
total, with placeholders verified to survive the round trip and terse labels
sent through a second pass with their key as context so that things like
"overdue by" do not come back reversed.

These are machine translations and they are a baseline, not a final pass. A
native review per locale is still worth doing, but an approximate translation
beats a silent English fallback and the diff is easy to revise later.

Also sizes the sidebar news card title to the nav labels instead of above
them, so it reads as part of the menu.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(i18n): close the last gap where every locale fell back to English

A second class of missing strings turned up after the first pass. These 814
keys live in en.ts but were never in any translation file, so they rendered
English in all 28 languages regardless of the user's choice. They escaped the
earlier sweep because that one walked the call sites looking for defaultValue
fallbacks, and these keys have a proper English entry instead. Found them by
diffing en.ts against the union of every other locale.

Kyrgyz is now at parity with the rest. It had looked far short of German, but
that turned out to be roughly 3 800 legacy keys German still carries which no
longer exist in en.ts, so there was nothing real to close there.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(i18n): translate the case playbooks and stop two surfaces from faking success

The /cases pages read their text from the app locale files, but the English
side comes from the page itself, so en.ts never carried the cases keys and
nothing flagged that a locale was missing them. Kyrgyz was missing 3369 of
them and quietly rendered English, and seven case long descriptions were
missing from every locale for the same reason. The English source for that
whole surface is the Key/Default pairs in the case playbooks, not en.ts, and
measuring locale coverage against en.ts will keep hiding gaps like this.

Also brings 182 newly keyed case strings into all 28 locales, adds the 242
English strings whose call sites carried an inline default but had no entry in
en.ts, and closes the seven per-locale strings that were genuinely absent
everywhere.

Two places were presenting a failure as a normal result. The BOQ templates page
caught every error from the templates endpoint and substituted its built-in
list, so a 500 or a dropped connection looked exactly like a working server
with a small catalogue. Only a 404 means the endpoint is absent, and only that
falls back now. The forecast panel linked to /costmodel, which is an API prefix
with no route behind it, so the link landed on the not-found page. It points at
/5d and goes through Link rather than a full page reload.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(takeoff): compare whole documents instead of the newest 500 rows each

Document comparison read each side with a limit of 500, and that query orders
by created_at descending before applying the limit, so the two sides were not
the same slice of the drawing set. A measurement inside one window and outside
the other came out as added or removed although nothing about it had changed,
and where it was linked to a BOQ position the invented delta went into
net_cost_impact, which create_variation_from_documents then puts into a draft
variation as an estimated cost impact. So a large comparison did not just hide
changes, it made some up. Keeping the cap and labelling the result as partial
was not an option, because the rows are not the first 500 in any consistent
sense and the label would have been false too.

Both sides are now read in full, paged in chunks with a ceiling that is
reported when it is reached, and the paging orders by created_at and id so
ties cannot reshuffle between pages and drop or duplicate rows.

The dashboard KPI probes and the coordination hub sub-aggregators caught every
exception and logged at debug, so a module that was installed but failed to
import reported zero and looked like a real answer. An expected absence on a
smaller install still logs at debug and still reports empty; anything else is
logged with its traceback.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(reporter): record the page an error happened on, not just the page it is filed from

A bug filed through the in-app reporter carries the component and route the
user is looking at when they open the form, and the stack of the last captured
error. Those are not always the same page: the user hits an error, navigates,
then files. Triage had no way to see the difference, so issue 391 was read as a
defect on the page named in its title when the captured crash belonged
somewhere else entirely.

The captured error now keeps the url it happened on and the report includes it.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(dashboards): let an unrelated debug line through, but never a silent failure

The regression guard on probe logging asserted that no record at all sat at
debug level. That is stricter than the thing it protects: adding an ordinary
debug trace to the same path would have failed it, and the failure would have
read as the swallowing bug coming back. It now asserts what actually matters,
that the failure is reported above debug and that nothing carrying an exception
is reported at debug and nowhere else.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(i18n): finish the kyrgyz locale so the module guides stop rendering in english

Kyrgyz was reported as complete because it had every case key the other locales
had. Counting keys hid two separate things. Three dwg takeoff strings had been
merged back as their own english source, which a key count cannot see, and 215
live keys were missing outright, 189 of them the module guide texts. A kyrgyz
user opening any module guide read english.

The guide english comes from the Key/Default pairs in the guide files, the same
shape the case playbooks use, so it was recoverable without touching en.ts. Ten
keys stay absent on purpose: each was renamed and has a live successor, so the
other locales are carrying the dead copy, not this one.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

chore: switch code comments and internal docs to English

Bug reports quoted verbatim in Russian had accumulated across frontend and
backend comments, three RFC documents and two changelog entries, and several of
them named a person directly. Our users are worldwide and the working language
of this repository is English, so those quotes are now paraphrased in English
and the personal attributions are gone. No described behaviour changed, and the
frontend build passes unchanged.

Translation payloads, locale files, Russian test fixtures, cost base values,
standard names such as GESN and FER, and unit tokens were deliberately left in
place. Those are data the product actually serves, not instructions to a reader.

Also closes a hole in .gitignore. The scratchpad directory at the repository
root was not ignored, so translation drafts kept there were one command away
from being published. Nothing had ever been committed from it.

fix(portfolio): mount the portfolio API, it was invisible to the module loader

The portfolio package shipped a full router, service, models and Alembic
revisions but no manifest.py. ModuleLoader.discover() skips any package without
one, so the router never mounted and all ten /api/v1/portfolio/ endpoints
answered 404 while the frontend page kept calling them. Nothing failed loudly
along the way: the tables were still created, because schema provisioning scans
the package directory instead of reading the manifest list, so the only symptom
anyone saw was a page that stayed empty.

Adding the manifest is the whole fix. Dependencies are taken from the imports
the code already makes, on users, projects and schedule_advanced, the last one
because cpm_logic builds on its portfolio CPM.

The new test pins the class of failure rather than this one module: a package
that declares routes must be discoverable. It stays narrow deliberately, since a
package with no router is a shared helper and correctly has no manifest, which
is the case for einvoice, measurement and price_breakdown. Verified by removing
the manifest again and watching the guard fail, then restoring it.

fix(ui): stop reporting a failed request as an empty project

Four pages defaulted a query result to an empty array and then read that
emptiness as fact. A request that failed is indistinguishable from an account
that genuinely has nothing, so an unreachable backend was rendered as settled
data rather than as a problem.

On the project detail page this reached money. The per-BOQ detail fetch uses
allSettled and kept only the fulfilled results, so when some of those requests
failed the budget, the position count and the validation score were summed over
the survivors and presented as the project total. A total failure at least
showed zeros; a partial one was invisible. Failures are now counted instead of
dropped. Nothing trustworthy renders an em dash, a short result labels the tile
as a failed load, cost per square metre is withheld while the total is not
whole, and the green validation badge is never awarded off a partial sample. The
BOQ count now follows the project rather than shrinking with each failed detail.

The DWG takeoff, point cloud and cost explorer pages had the milder form of the
same thing, and their empty states now require the query to have succeeded. This
matters more than it sounds: those pages told a user with an unreachable backend
to create a project first, and the natural response to that advice is to create
one that already exists.

The correct pattern was already in the repository at costs/CostsPage.tsx, which
distinguishes resolving successfully to empty from failing. Also replaced a
hardcoded BOQs label with its existing translation key.

fix(pipelines): compute totals over the whole BOQ, not over a preview

Two node paths in the Pipeline Builder read a bounded subset and reported the
answer as the whole.

The worse one: transform.filter read the envelope's rows key, which is a
preview capped at 25 and exists for the run UI rather than for arithmetic. A
source into filter into rollup graph therefore summed quantity times unit rate
over at most 25 positions and presented that as the project total, and a budget
gate downstream of it could pass on a project whose real total was far past the
limit. The filter now resolves the full row set the same way every other
aggregate and gate in the module already did.

The second: the envelope's id list is capped at 5000 so the node-state JSON
stays small, and the resolver re-read positions by that capped list, which
capped every total with it. The source now carries its BOQ scope, a handful of
ids, and the resolver goes back to that scope when the source says it had to cut
the list. The memory guard the cap exists for is unaffected, since the source
already loads those positions to build the envelope.

Tests pin both, and were checked by putting each defect back and watching them
fail. A third pins the behaviour that must not change, that a mutated what-if
envelope is never re-read, because re-reading would discard the values the
transform just wrote.

fix(cost-recovery): close the back-charge status field to its real states

The create and update schemas both declared status as a plain string, and the
update applies a blind setattr loop over whatever the payload carries, so any
value at all was written onto the row. Two things then failed quietly. The
record sat in a state that no filter and no analytics bucket matches, so it
vanished from the recovery reporting rather than showing up wrong. And the
agreed and recovered timestamps are stamped by comparing the incoming value
against the module constants, so a near miss such as a capitalised Proposed
left the record with no timestamp at all and nothing said so.

The wire type is now a closed enumeration living next to the constants it has to
agree with, and the read model stays a plain string on purpose so rows written
before this still serialise instead of failing to load.

Tests cover the accepted values, the near misses that used to slip through, and
that a partial update can still omit the field. One of them exists only to make
the two definitions fail loudly if someone adds a status to one and not the
other, which is how this kind of hole reopens.

fix(ui): read the whole list before summing it

Three pages called a list route once and treated the first page as the data set.
Those routes cap limit at 100, so a single request is a page, and the numbers
built on top of it were short on any project past that mark with nothing on
screen saying so.

The risk register fed that page into the Insights panel, whose total exposure
tile sums probability times impact cost. The safety dashboard counted pending
inspections and open NCRs from it, and because the filtering happens after the
cut rather than before it, the shortfall did not even scale predictably.

The risk register report was the worst of the three. It stated total risks and
total exposure in the header of a CSV that people keep and send on, computed
from the same first page, and it swallowed a failed fetch into an empty list, so
an unreachable backend produced a clean-looking report asserting there were no
risks and no exposure at all. The failure now reaches the caller, which already
turns it into a toast, and a register past the export ceiling refuses to
generate rather than quietly leaving rows out.

Adds the paging helper the three of them share. It returns whether the ceiling
stopped the read, so a partial result can never be presented as a complete one.

fix(tests): make the whole suite runnable again

test_dockerignore.py imports pathspec, which was never declared anywhere. The
module therefore failed to import, and an uncollectable module aborts the entire
pytest run rather than costing one file, so the full suite could not be run at
all. Every attempt ended in one collection error and 21692 deselected tests.

Two changes, because either alone leaves a hole. pathspec is now declared in the
dev extra so environments actually install it, and the import degrades to a
reported skip if something still lacks it, so one absent test dependency can
never take the suite down again.

Worth stating what this was hiding: these 77 tests assert that a docker build
context cannot pick up .env files, the local database or customer uploads. They
had never run. They pass.

fix(commercial): stop one call from deleting a live job's record

Deleting a contract had no lifecycle check whatsoever. The delete cascades, so a
signed contract that was actually running could be removed together with its
variations, progress claims, payment certificates and retention, on a single
call, with nothing asking whether that was meant. Only a draft can be deleted
now; a contract past that point is closed through its status, which is how change
orders already behave and where this guard comes from.

Deleting a subcontractor was the same shape with a different blast radius. It
took the firm's subcontract agreements with it, and behind those the payment
applications, retention ledger and ratings: the record of work somebody
performed and was paid for. It is refused now while any agreement exists, and
the message says how many are in the way. A firm you have stopped using is
marked through its prequalification status instead, and a record created in
error still deletes cleanly.

Creating a contract with a code that already exists raised an unhandled
IntegrityError against the unique constraint, which reaches the caller as a 500.
That is an error nobody can act on, for a mistake that is theirs to fix and
takes one word to describe. It answers 409 naming the duplicate code, and any
other integrity failure still propagates rather than being flattened into the
same message.

Tests were checked by removing each guard and watching them fail. Doing that
caught a mistake in the check itself: the first attempt matched an identical
condition earlier in the file and edited the wrong method, so the contract tests
passed while nothing was actually being verified.

fix(finance): refuse an invoice number that is already in use

There is no unique constraint behind invoice_number, and a caller-supplied
number was written straight through, so posting the same number twice gave you
two invoices carrying it. That number is what reconciliation, payment matching
and every accounting export key on, so the result is not a display quirk, it is
two documents nobody can tell apart.

create_invoice now checks a supplied number and answers 409 naming it, and only
generates when the caller leaves it empty. The generator's docstring also
claimed that using MAX rather than COUNT avoids race conditions. It does not.
MAX is what makes numbering survive a deletion, it does nothing about
concurrency, because nothing between the read and the insert holds a lock. That
claim is corrected. Closing the window properly needs a unique constraint on the
column, which has to wait until existing data is swept for duplicates.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(forms): save only the fields the user actually edited

A create/edit modal seeds itself from a record and then PATCHes every field on
the form back, touched or not. Correct a spec section on a submittal and the
description you never opened goes back with it, exactly as it stood when your
copy was loaded, undoing an edit somebody else made in between. There is no
error and no warning, because from the server's side it is an ordinary write.

Every update route dumps with exclude_unset=True, so a field left out of the
body is left alone in the database. Sending only what changed is therefore both
correct and sufficient, and it narrows the exposure from every field on the form
to the one field two people edited at once, which nothing on the client can fix
without a version token.

Fixed in variations across all five sub-entities, in submittals and in equipment
work orders. The baseline each save compares against is now built by the same
function that seeds the form, so the two cannot drift and a field nobody touched
cannot read as changed.

A second bug travelled with the first. Mapping a cleared field to undefined
means JSON.stringify drops the key, so emptying it did nothing at all and the
old value was still there on the next read. Submittals had this on the
description and on the required date. The date is the sharper case, because that
field sits behind a date pattern on the backend, so an empty string would have
been rejected too. Only null clears it, and the payload type now says so.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(ui): stop showing a failed project list as an account with no projects

Both pages loaded their project list through a helper that swallowed any error
into an empty array. The page then saw no projects, could not resolve a project
id, and told the user that variations are project scoped and they should go and
create or open a project. For anyone whose request had simply failed on a 401 or
a 500 that advice is confident and wrong, and it sends them off to fix a problem
they do not have.

The helper now lets the failure through. The no-project screen is only reached
once the list has actually come back, and a failed load gets the recovery card
with a retry that both pages already use for their other queries.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(takeoff): make detector proposals durable and reviewable

The offline detectors handed their candidates straight to the canvas and
kept nothing. A rejection was a local drop the server never learned about,
so a reload brought back everything the estimator had already dismissed,
and a colleague opening the same sheet saw none of the work. Confirming a
proposal was a rendering behaviour rather than a record.

row carrying every hit, which matches how the vision path stores a symbol
class and puts both in the same queue. GET on a document's proposals

review accepts or rejects one proposal.

auditable, and it is what a later suppression pass needs so the same wrong

feat(takeoff): wire proposal review to the server

Recognize, count by example and plan read all store what they propose as a
proposed row before they answer, but the viewer still treated a decision as a
local flag. Accepting one cleared a boolean and rejecting one filtered it off
the canvas, so neither decision ever reached the database. The row sat proposed
forever, a reload brought a rejection back, and a colleague opening the same
sheet saw every suggestion again.

back from the server response instead of keeping the detector's claim, because
the server re-derives the quantity from the geometry it stored and those two
numbers differ exactly when a detector over-claims. Geometry is deliberately
not sent on a plain accept, so geometry_edited stays honest about whether
somebody corrected the shape or just agreed with it.

Two holes in hydration would have made the round trip pointless. A rejected row
came back on the next reload, and a stored proposal came back looking like
agreed work, with no flag and no confidence. Both states are carried across now,
covered by tests.

Bulk accept and reject send their decisions in parallel and judge each one on
its own, so a single conflict from a colleague who got there first does not
strand the rest. The buttons latch while a round is in flight, and a suggestion
that was never persisted is handled explicitly rather than riding the success
path of a call that was never made.

average, matching what the server stores. A seeded count is only as trustworthy
as its worst hit, and an average lets one bad match hide behind good ones.

"greater than zero" check on it, and that ratio is squared into every room the
plan reader proposes. A scale entered a thousand times off produced quantities
a million times too large that still read like ordinary numbers. A scale the
model derives has been through plan_read.scale_is_plausible since the feature

and read as though their own calibration had been honoured. Empty areas send
them back to the calibration tool instead, which is already the ordinary
outcome on a sheet with no scale at all. So a user whose calibration was wrong
now gets empty areas and an explanation where they used to get confident
nonsense.

already performs before a proposal is ever written, each kept its own copy of

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(ui): say something when a query comes back with nothing

A screen that reads `data ?? []` rendered the same empty table whether the
list was genuinely empty or the request never came back at all. Mutations
have had a global error handler from the start, queries had none, so a
backend that was down read as a project with no data in it and the user
acted on an answer nobody gave them.

The new handler is deliberately narrow. It reports the one case nobody else
reports, the server failing to answer while the screen has nothing on it,
and stays quiet everywhere there is already a surface for the failure: a
query that opts out through meta, a background refetch over data already on
screen, timeouts and aborts that api.ts has toasted itself, and any 4xx,
since 401 and 403 redirect, 404 is drawn as a not-found state by the
features that ask for things which may be absent, 422 belongs to the form
that submitted it and 429 is toasted in api.ts. One message per twelve
seconds, the same window api.ts uses for timeouts, so a page firing ten
queries against a dead backend says one thing rather than ten.

The offline path is unaffected. A GET that misses the network while the
browser is offline returns the IndexedDB copy instead of rejecting, so a
page served from cache never reaches this handler.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(match): stop probing a local Qdrant through an HTTP proxy

The health probe went out through urllib's default opener, which installs a
proxy handler seeded from the environment. On POSIX the bypass check reads
no_proxy and nothing else, so loopback is not exempt unless the operator
listed it there. A machine with http_proxy set had its probe of a Qdrant
running on that same machine answered by the proxy instead, and the vector
database card then told the user Qdrant was not installed and offered to
download it, with Qdrant running the whole time.

A probe of a process on this host now goes direct. The exemption is scoped
to addresses that name this machine, literal loopback in either family plus
the name localhost, because a deployment pointing at a Qdrant elsewhere may
genuinely need the proxy and skipping it there would be the same mistake
pointing the other way. Only the name localhost is trusted without a lookup,
so a 1.5 second health check does not turn into a DNS round trip. The
binary download in install_qdrant_native keeps the default opener, since
GitHub Releases really is remote.

The retry against the root endpoint, which is the path a cold Qdrant takes
while collections mount, uses the same opener as the first attempt.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(takeoff): record where each measurement's scale came from

A takeoff stores the ratio a measurement was captured at but never its
origin, so when a sheet turns out to be mis-scaled there is no way to tell
which rows inherited the bad calibration and which were set from the
drawing's own scale note. The whole document goes back for a manual
re-check, and a wrong scale is the one error that multiplies through every
quantity on the page.

The new scale_source column is a closed set of six values: page_text,
recovered_text, vision_read, manual_calibration, preset and inherited. It is
nullable with no backfill, because NULL honestly means "not recorded" and
inventing a source for historical rows would defeat the point of a
provenance field. Detector proposals inherit whatever calibration the sheet
already carries. The plan-read builder separates a user calibration that
survived the plausibility check from a ratio the model read off the page,
since the same "1:100" carries different weight when it was inferred from
pixels rather than parsed from the text layer. A patch that moves the ratio
without stating a new source clears the old label instead of leaving a claim
that has quietly become false, and it reads presence rather than truthiness
so that explicitly clearing the ratio clears the source too.

Server side only for now. The client half, which states the source on create
and renders it in the properties panel and the export, follows next.

feat(takeoff): turn the proposal confidence number into a band the estimator can act on

A proposal showed its confidence as a bare percentage. Nothing on the screen
said what counted as good, so 71% meant one thing to the person who had used
the detector all week and something else to everyone else, and the review bar
gave no hint of how much of a batch deserved a closer look before accepting
it. The server has had the answer all along: it publishes its own cut points
at /plan-read/meta and applies them itself when it labels a proposal, but the
viewer never read them.

The badge now carries the band, not just the number, and the review bar shows
how many proposals fall in the low band so a batch that needs attention is
visible before "Accept all" is pressed. Thresholds come from the server
response rather than from a constant in the bundle, because they are
configurable per deployment and a hardcoded copy would drift silently and
then disagree with the label the server itself applied. The fallback pair is
used only when the endpoint says nothing.

A confidence that is missing, not a number, or outside the range reads as
"Not scored" rather than as low. The offline Recognize path produces
proposals with no score at all, and showing those in red would push people to
reject work the detector never claimed anything about.

test(takeoff): repair the scale auto-detect tests left behind by the banner removal

Four of these have been failing since issue #387 removed both the detecting
and the detected banner from the viewer. They still looked for the testids of
the elements that removal deleted, so they were asserting against a UI that no
longer exists and had stopped protecting anything.

Rewritten against what the component actually promises now: it renders nothing
and drives the detection through its callback. The docblock records why the
banners went, so the next person does not read the absent markup as a
regression and put it back.

feat(takeoff): state where a measurement's scale came from, or admit we do not know

Completes the client half of the scale provenance the server started storing in
the previous commit. The viewer now names the source when it creates or
reshapes a measurement, the properties panel shows it, and the exported
workbook carries it as a column so a reviewer can sort a sheet by how
trustworthy the ratio behind each quantity is.

The interesting part is where it declines to name one. Per-page calibration is
restored from stored rows, and rows written before the calibration flag existed
carry no flag, so the restore falls back to treating any ratio off the factory
default as a real calibration. That heuristic is good enough to bring a usable
scale back but not good enough to record as something a person did, so
measurements drawn on those pages are stamped with no source at all. Attributing
them would launder a guess into the one field a re-scale trusts when it decides
which rows to recompute, and a wrong provenance excludes exactly the rows that
needed recomputing most. Pages restored from the document's own page_scales
column are never uncertain, so nothing is lost where the answer is known.

The source is written together with the ratio it describes and never apart. A
reshape re-captures the geometry at whatever the page reads now, so its
provenance is re-attributed at the same time; sending the ratio alone would
leave a label describing a capture that no longer happened, which is the case
the server-side guard exists to clear.

Missing sources read as "Unknown" in the panel and in the export rather than as
a blank cell, because a blank looks like a column that failed to populate while
"Unknown" is a statement about the measurement.

fix(db): widen alembic's version column on the installs that actually needed it

Alembic creates its own version table with version_num as VARCHAR(32). Thirty
of this project's revision ids are longer than that, the longest being 51
characters, so on PostgreSQL any alembic run that records one of them aborts
with "value too long for type character varying(32)" before a single schema
change lands. SQLite ignores a declared length, which is why this stayed
invisible for so long.

A widening hook already existed in alembic/env.py, but it only helped
databases created by running migrations. The application's own boot-time stamp
configures a bare migration context and never loads env.py, so every database
created the canonical way, by booting the app first, got the stock
32-character column. The head id is short, so the stamp itself succeeded and
nothing looked wrong at boot. The narrow column then survived for the life of
the database, because alembic creates that table exactly once. The widening
was protecting the installs that did not need it and missing the ones that
did.

The implementation now lives in one module that both entry points call, since
two copies of this rule is how the paths came to disagree in the first place.
Covering it properly takes two halves: a creation hook for version tables that
do not exist yet, and an ALTER for the ones already in the field, which no
creation hook can ever reach. The repair runs on every boot because widening a
varchar in PostgreSQL is a catalog-only change on a single-row table, and it
sits in a savepoint so a database whose version table belongs to the ops role
rather than the app role fails without poisoning the caller's transaction. On
anything other than PostgreSQL the whole thing is inert.

This also retires a constraint a couple of earlier revisions carried in their
docstrings, that an id had to be kept under 32 characters to survive the boot
stamp. A test now holds the line instead, so a future long slug fails in the
gate rather than in somebody's upgrade.

feat(i18n): add the takeoff colour and file picker strings to every locale

Two pieces of work landed strings this week and both are read by code in the
commits that follow, so the keys go in first. A bisect between them then never
lands on a build where a string is referenced but not defined.

One key covers the colour grouping toggle in the takeoff viewer. Fourteen
cover the new picker that opens a drawing straight from the project file
register: its title and search box, the two different empty states, the labels
for a format that needs conversion first and one that another module handles,
and the failure toast.

Every locale gets the English source for now. An untranslated locale falls
back to English at runtime, which is the honest state until the translation
sweep runs and is better than a raw key showing on screen.

fix(format): stop number formatting throwing on an out of range digit pair

Both formatters passed a minimum and a maximum fraction digit count straight
to Intl, each with its own default. A caller that overrode only one end could
therefore produce a minimum above the maximum, which Intl answers with an
uncaught RangeError. In the chart path that meant a blank panel rather than a
misformatted number, and the engine's own clamping does not rescue a formatter
that passes both ends explicitly.

The pair now goes through one shared resolver that reconciles the two before
they reach Intl. When a maximum is given it is the hard constraint and the
minimum bends down to meet it. Non-finite and out of range values are clamped
instead of forwarded, so a bad caller degrades the output rather than losing
the render.

Currency digits are read from the running engine rather than from the static
minor-units table. The two disagree on sixteen codes where CLDR says zero
decimals, so reusing the table would have quietly changed what those
currencies render as today.

feat(ui): lighten the module info panels and fold explainers into the cases row

The information panel that sits above the content in every module read as a
coloured alert rather than as background reading. Its wash is now about half
as saturated in both themes. The border and the left accent bar are left
alone, so the panel still reads as one block and still carries its module
colour.

The longer explainer sections behave differently now. Collapsing one used to
leave an empty header sitting in the page, which is a strange reward for
asking for more room. The section now removes itself and registers with the
module info store, so it comes back from the button next to Cases, the same
place every other module explainer is reached from. The choice is remembered
per section.

Cost Data moves above Estimating in the sidebar. Cost data is the input to an
estimate, so the menu now runs in the order the work actually happens.

fix(takeoff): end the group colour feedback loop and export in screen order

A group's custom colour lives both in a map keyed by group name and mirrored
onto every measurement, so the scheme round-trips to the server inside the
existing metadata blob without a schema change. Two standing effects kept the
copies in step, one writing in each direction, each reading a snapshot the
other had already invalidated. When they disagreed there was no fixed point.
Each write republished the value it had read a render earlier, the pair
alternated indefinitely, every affected row stayed permanently dirty and so
blocked the debounced save, and the inconsistent map went back to local
storage, so a reload resumed the loop rather than ending it.

The direction is now one way by construction. The map is authoritative for
every group it knows about and the mirrored copy is a cache of it, never an
input, with one exception at hydration, which is how the map learns a group
exists. Hydration runs once per opened document, there is a single standing
writer, and the decision between them lives in a plain function rather than
inside an effect, so it can be tested directly.

Clearing an override that happens to equal the default colour now sends the
clear instead of folding it into "no override" and dropping it.

The exports follow the same on-screen order the sidebar and the annotated PDF
already use. A takeoff the user had deliberately arranged came out of the
workbook in the order the shapes were drawn, with nothing saying the
arrangement had been dropped.

Scale source is typed as the closed set the backend defines rather than as a
bare string, and the label table is keyed by that set, so adding a source
without giving it a label is a build error instead of a row reading "Unknown".

Covered by a test that loads a document written by an older build and asserts
no corrective write of any kind. Its control uses the same harness and sees
forty writes, so the zero means no write was made rather than that the test
cannot see one.

test(takeoff): pin the contract for opening a stored file in the viewer

The viewer resolves a project file to a takeoff document through a find or
create endpoint. Nothing pinned the parts of that behaviour the caller relies
on, so these tests state them against a real PostgreSQL.

Reopening the same file returns the same document with its measurements
intact rather than a second copy. A duplicate link is rejected by the unique
index. Direct uploads that have no source never collide with each other.
Deleting the source leaves the takeoff document and its measurements alone,
and a later attempt to reopen the deleted source is a clean 404 rather than a
half-resolved document. The link does not widen access to a project the user
cannot already reach.

feat(files): open a drawing straight from the project file register

Every viewer asked the user to find a file on their own disk, including files
they had already filed in the project. The takeoff, DWG takeoff, BIM, CAD
explorer and point cloud pages now offer the project's own files, filtered to
the formats that module can actually open, so nobody is offered a file that
would fail to load.

Formats that need the conversion step first, and formats another module
handles, are labelled as such rather than presented as an instant open. That
is more honest than a bare row that appears to promise a 3D view of a drawing.

Picking a file does not re-upload it. The takeoff page asks the backend to
find or create the takeoff document for that stored file, the same path the
existing deep link takes, and drives the viewer off the returned id. Two
reasons. Pushing the bytes back through the upload path would leave another
copy of the same drawing under a new id on every pick. And the page rasters,
annotations and recognition state belong to a takeoff document, so handing
the viewer a file register id would render the sheet and then fail every
recognition call made on it. The endpoint is idempotent, so picking the same
file twice reopens the same document.

The two empty states are kept apart on purpose. A project holding no
compatible file is told to add one, with a link to the register. A search that
matches nothing is told to clear the search. Telling someone there is no match
for a search they never typed is nonsense.

feat(cases): add ten cases for work the platform can now close

Ten playbooks covering ground the modules shipped over the last few weeks
made reachable: reviewing AI takeoff proposals, seeing every field mark on one
sheet, turning a document into a tracked action, reconciling a drawing issue
against the index, chasing overdue dates across a project, dry running an
approval route before committing it, building a parametric assembly,
automating a recurring check with a pipeline, and exporting a bill of
quantities to FIEBDC-3 or a facility handover to COBie.

Two guards come with them. Step icons are runtime strings resolved through a
map that falls back to a generic glyph, so a name nobody added was neither a
build error nor a runtime error, just the wrong picture rendered quietly.
Twenty five such names had accumulated. They are all mapped now and a test
fails on the next one.

The second guard checks that every step points at a route the app declares.
Reading App.tsx alone is not enough, because module routes are declared in
their manifests and mounted separately, so a manifest-only route looks dead to
a naive scan while a genuinely dead one passes a loose one. The test reads
both and compares on a normalised form, and asserts it found a plausible
number of routes so it cannot pass by having found none.

fix(progress): roll the project percentage up by quantity instead of taking the maximum

The headline percentage for a project was the maximum percent complete across
every entry recorded against it. One line item reported at ninety per cent
therefore presented itself as the whole project at ninety per cent, and
pooling project level readings with position level ones in the same aggregate
is what let it.

The percentage is now the quantity weighted rollup of the latest reading per
position as of the end of each period. A position nobody has measured counts
as zero and keeps its weight in the denominator, so unmeasured work drags the
number down rather than vanishing from it. A parent quantity is not counted on
top of its children. Where the bill of quantities carries no quantities at all
the result degrades to the unweighted mean over the same set, and where no
line was measured it falls back to the project level entries, which is what
those entries are for.

This changes numbers that appear in client reports. A project that read high
because one line ran ahead will now read lower and more truthfully.

Periods also carry the real count of observations recorded in them rather than
a placeholder.

test: fail loudly when the PostgreSQL cluster is missing

The fixture skipped when DATABASE_SYNC_URL was absent. A skip lets the gate
report green on a run where the tests that need a cluster never executed,
which is the one outcome this file exists to prevent. It now indexes the
variable, matching how the shared PostgreSQL helper reads it.

fix(takeoff): stop AI actions reading the previously opened drawing

The viewer recovered a document id by running a regular expression over the
PDF url it had been handed. That is fine while the two agree, and they stop
agreeing the moment somebody uses the toolbar's Load new PDF control on an
already open drawing. Loading a local file clears the document id, but the url
is a prop and keeps pointing at the server document that was open before, and
the page does not remount because its key did not change.

Recognize, Count similar and Read with AI then sent the previous drawing's id
to the server, which read that other drawing's stored PDF and returned
candidates from it, dropped onto the canvas of the file the user is actually
looking at. The scale-detect banner had the same shape: the previous drawing's
banner stayed up over the local file, and dismissing it wrote the dismissal
under the previous document's storage key.

All six sites now read the document id the viewer already holds in state,
which is null for a local file, so those actions decline with the "needs an
uploaded drawing" message instead of answering about the wrong drawing. After
this there is no id derived from a url anywhere in the viewer; the url survives
only where it belongs, as the thing the bytes are fetched from.

Verified by hand rather than by test, and the distinction matters here. Open a
server drawing, use Load new PDF in the toolbar to swap in a local file, then
press Recognize. The module suite passes 111 of 111 with Recognize replaced by
a hard null, so its green says nothing about this area; the honest position is
that these six sites have no automated coverage, and a one-line helper
extracted purely to have something to assert would stay green with every site
unconverted.

The module reported physical progress and offered no way to produce any. Every
empty panel told the user to record field entries while the only surface that
could actually record one was the 5D cost page, so the page read as a report
with no input and it was not obvious the numbers came from anywhere a person
could reach. That is what made it hard to tell what the module was for.

There is now a Record progress control in the header and in the empty states
that need it. It takes a percent, a period label, and either one BOQ position
or the project as a whole, and it says on screen why those two are different
readings rather than a convenience: position readings are what the project
percentage is rolled up from, weighted by design quantity, while a project
level reading is the fallback used only while no position has been measured.
Positions come from the quantity-variance payload the page already holds, so
opening the dialog costs no extra request.

The quantity variance panel deliberately does not offer it. With no positions
there is nothing to compare a reading against, so it points at the bill of
quantities instead of into a dead end that looks like help.

The explanatory copy is rewritten against how the rollup actually works now,
including that an unmeasured position counts as zero and keeps its share, so a
project with one finished line and three hundred untouched reads close to zero.

wording predates the weighted rollup and describes behaviour the page no longer
has. The page also had no How-it-works entry at all, which is its own reason

The takeoff module writes uploaded drawings to data/takeoff_documents,
next to a row of runtime directories that are all ignored already:

fix(takeoff): stop keeping a second copy of every drawing opened from project files

Opening a project file in takeoff used to write the bytes a second time,
so a document that lived in Project Files and had been opened for
measurement existed twice on disk under two unrelated names. Nothing
reconciled them. Now the takeoff row references the blob the documents
module already holds, and upload_document takes the resolved path so a
direct upload keeps writing its own bytes exactly as before.

The reason it copied in the first place was deletion. Removing the
project file would have pulled the ground out from under an open
takeoff. So deletion now hands takeoff its own copy immediately before
the unlink, and if that copy fails the original file is kept. That is
the trade delete_document already documents, an orphaned file is
recoverable and a row pointing at a deleted blob is not. The call is
direct rather than driven off the deleted event, because that event is
published detached and a subscriber would race the unlink and lose
nondeterministically, passing locally and failing under load.

Borrowing the path exposed something that had been harmless while every
row owned its bytes. Upload unlinks what it wrote when a parse fails or
when it loses a creation race, and with a borrowed path either one would
have deleted the user's project document off disk on an ordinary 400.
Both sites are now guarded on provenance and covered by tests.

The disk saving today is small, 4.3 MB measured on the production box,
because only two documents have ever been opened in takeoff. The ceiling
at full adoption is around 88 MB. This is worth doing to stop the leak
before adoption makes it expensive, not to recover space now.

perf(bim): make a model show something in the first moment instead of the last

Progressive streaming has not been doing anything on the models people
actually open. The octree returned the whole index list as a single leaf
whenever it held no more meshes than the per tile cap, and with a cap of
1200 against a floor of 400 that meant every model between those two
numbers baked into exactly one tile. The demo models are 719 meshes.
Streaming them fetched the same bytes in one request and fired its parsed
callback once, at the end. It was the old monolithic load with a manifest
round trip in front of it, which is why nobody has ever been able to
watch a model appear.

The cap is now 300, swept rather than guessed against the real 719 mesh
model: 400 gives 8 tiles and 86 KB before anything is drawn, 300 gives 19
tiles and 33 KB, 100 gives 25 tiles and 12 KB, and the payload overhead
runs between 4 and 7 percent. A ceiling of 256 tiles per model stops a
very large building shattering into thousands of requests, repartitioning
at a doubled threshold if the octree overshoots.

Ordering changed with it. Tiles were sorted by node count descending,
which optimises total progress and pessimises the thing a person on site
notices. Replayed against a real 80 tile, 204 MB model, the first six
concurrent downloads were 37.9 MB and the smallest of them 5.2 MB, so
nothing at all was drawn for roughly fifteen seconds on a 20 Mbit link.
Ranking by geometry density instead, node count over bytes, puts the most
building per byte first. The fixture holding that model's real statistics
is now in the tests, so the measurement is a regression gate rather than
something done once. Both ends are asserted: first paint improves and the
tail does not regress at any of the 75, 90 and 95 percent checkpoints.
The previous ordering stays exported and documented as the alternative
this is measured against.

End to end on the demo model with production defaults, bytes before the
first reveal go from 2641.6 KB to 5.2 KB, and the tiles expose the same
719 element names as the monolith with no duplicates, so selection,
properties and colour by property are unaffected.

Two consequences worth knowing. The tiler version bump re-bakes every
stored tileset, which invalidates saved offline packs; the button
correctly offers to save again, but nobody is told their copy expired.
And nothing in the code has ever evicted a cached tile, so that bump
would have stranded up to 204 MB per device forever. The cache database
now purges once on upgrade, which is safe because tiles are pure cache.

Re-baking removes the stale generation before building, so peak disk is
the larger of the two rather than their sum. Memory is the real
constraint: a bake holds every tile in RAM at once alongside the source
scene. A pre-flight check now requires room before the wipe, and fails
open so an unreadable volume can never stop a model loading. When only
the tiler version changed the old tiles still describe the same building
and are kept; when the source fingerprint changed they describe a
different one and are dropped in favour of the monolith.

fix(costs): stop national cost bases printing every description twice

Five of the seven published national bases render each work item as the
same sentence twice over. The description is built by concatenating the
two name columns whenever they differ, which was written for a base whose
columns hold two halves of one sentence. The translation pipeline then
translated both columns independently, so for the national bases the two
sides became two renderings of the same text and the join glued them
together. Spain in German reads "ABRISS DER KATALANISCHEN BOGENDECKE,
EINSCHLIESSLICH MANUELLE BELADUNG Abbruch des Gewoelbes zum Flachbogen,
einschliesslich manueller Beladung". Brazil joins untranslated Portuguese
onto German. Italy in Arabic joins one Arabic rendering to a second,
slightly different Arabic rendering, which nobody who does not read
Arabic would ever spot.

The obvious condition is the wrong one. The classic base diverges just as
completely, around a hundred percent, but there the two columns really
are complementary, a parent description plus a variant qualifier, both
already in the reader's language. So divergence cannot tell the two
situations apart and the join has to key on the kind of base instead,
which the registry already knows. The docstring said the columns were
native plus English, which describes neither case and is how this shipped
in the first place; it now states both real shapes and says outright why
divergence is not a usable signal.

Nothing is discarded. With the join off the description is the final
name, falling back to the original only where the final is empty, so both
translations stay in the data.

The predicate has to recognise three forms of region, not two: the home
region, the per language one, and the transient staging region the
language swap imports through. That third one is where the doubling was
actually being applied, so a predicate that knew only the first two would
have passed its tests and fixed nothing.

Verified by rendering the real strings for all seven bases through the
real code path rather than by reasoning about the columns. Brazil, Spain
and Vietnam now read in their own language, and the four that were
already clean are untouched. That also clears the way for a national base
to open in its own language, which is included here, because until now
three of those would have opened with an English sentence in front of
every description.

One trap is pinned by a test because it looks harmless: a base's parquet
file token is not its region id. Four of the eight ship as one and load
as the other, so a predicate built from file tokens passes a plausible
looking test and leaves half the fleet doubling.

fix(progress): report the reading the page actually has

The percentage on /progress was derived from the highest reading in a
window rather than the most recent one, and a parent's rollup counted only
the children somebody had already measured. Together that meant a foreman
who corrected 90 percent down to 30 saw 90, while /contracts billed the
same position at 30, and a parent with ten children reported 100 because
one of them was finished.

Progress entries are append-only, so a mistake is corrected by recording a
new entry and the reading that counts is the latest one. Making that true
needed an ordering key the table did not have. recorded_at defaults to
now(), which in PostgreSQL is the transaction timestamp and is therefore
identical for every row one transaction writes, and created_at is a Python
timestamp that ties on a coarse clock. With both tied the winner fell
through to a random uuid, so a bulk imported correction won only by luck.
Migration v3258 adds a monotonic seq, backfills existing rows in
recorded_at then created_at then id order, and restarts the sequence above
the highest backfilled value. ctid and xmin were considered and rejected
for reasons recorded in the migration itself.

seq is declared as a sequence with a server default rather than as an
identity column on purpose. The schema is built two ways here, and the
create_all path patches columns onto existing tables by reading
server_default alone. An identity column would have landed on an upgraded
database as a plain nullable bigint, null on every row, and the ordering
would have silently fallen back to the tied timestamps it exists to
replace.

The parent rollup now weights every leaf beneath the position, unmeasured
ones at zero, matching what the project headline already did. Leaves
rather than direct children, because an intermediate node carries a
quantity but never a reading of its own, so weighting it would charge its
full quantity against a zero and lose finished work underneath it.

Period deltas may now be negative. Flattening them made sense while the
series took the highest reading in a window, where a drop was an anomaly.
Under latest wins a correction downward is the point, and a delta of zero
next to a cumulative figure that visibly fell reads as a broken page.

Recorded percentages will not reproduce against reports generated before
this change. Nothing is recomputed or rewritten, but the same underlying
entries now yield a different and more conservative number.

The unit stub repository needed seq as well. It doubles the ranking
queries, so leaving it on the old ordering would have kept its tests green
while measuring a rule the production code no longer uses.

The MissingGreenlet failures in test_contracts_progress_bridge_db predate
this work and were verified identical against an unmodified checkout, so
they are not caused by the migration.

fix(auth): reject a backslash authority in the post-login redirect

The post-login redirect accepted any value starting with a single forward
slash and rejected only ones starting with two. A backslash in the authority
position defeats that pair. "/\host" starts with one slash, does not start
with two, and a browser still resolves it to http://host/, so a crafted sign-in
link could send a visitor off the site immediately after a successful login.
The login page in such a chain is genuinely ours, which is what makes the
pattern effective, so the fallback to the dashboard is the only thing that
should ever happen here.

The guard no longer tries to enumerate the separators a URL parser accepts. It
resolves the candidate against a sentinel origin and requires the result to
come back on that origin, which asks the same parser the browser will use. A
path that merely contains a backslash further along is still a valid internal
destination and still works.

Both front doors are covered. The second login route carried its own weaker
copy of the check, which also accepted auth routes and could bounce a signed-in
visitor back to the login screen, and it now shares the one helper so the two
cannot drift apart again.

fix(resources): keep leveling from emitting a plan that breaks its own links

Resource leveling walked activities in priority order, late start ascending,
then total float, then id. That key is precedence feasible only while lags are
non negative. With a negative lag, or a zero duration predecessor under one, a
predecessor can sort after its own successor. The placement loop then asks for
an earliest legal start the predecessor cannot supply because it has not been
placed yet, that branch is skipped, and the successor lands on its bare CPM
early start. The plan we hand back can violate the very link the CPM page draws.

The same order now runs through an eligibility gate. An activity becomes
available once every predecessor that leveling will actually place has been
handed out, and the original key still decides among the available ones. Two
inputs get deliberate treatment instead of an accidental one. A predecessor that
is in the network but absent from the CPM result is treated as satisfied, since
leveling never places it and waiting would starve the whole successor subtree. A
cycle, or any residue the gate cannot open, falls back to the plain key over
what is left, which is exactly today's behaviour for that step, so the loop
always drains and cannot deadlock on a network the CPM engine accepted.

For finish to start networks with non negative lags every predecessor already
sorts strictly ahead of its successors, so the returned order equals the old one
element for element and those plans come out byte identical.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(db): restore the constraints an upgraded install silently lost

The startup schema heal only ever added columns and indexes. Unique, check and
foreign key constraints were never restored, so an install upgraded through
create_all rather than alembic quietly lost any constraint that was added to a
table which already existed.

The unique constraints are the ones that carry weight. Six tables generate their
document number as the highest existing number plus one, write it, and rely on
catching the duplicate error to try again. NCR, safety incidents, safety
observations, quality inspections, requisitions and correspondence all work this
way. The constraint is not a safety net behind an application check, it is the
only check. Without it two people raising an NCR in the same moment both commit
NCR-001, with no error, no warning and no log line, on a document that gets
quoted by number in contractual claims.

The danger in fixing this is that the databases missing a constraint are exactly
the ones that may hold rows breaking it, and this code runs at startup. Adding a
unique constraint over duplicate rows fails, and a failure here does not degrade
a feature, it stops the application starting. So a unique is checked for
duplicates first and skipped with a loud log naming the table and columns if any
are found, leaving the rows for a person to reconcile. Check and foreign key
constraints go on as NOT VALID, which enforces them for every new row without
scanning what is already there, so an install with bad history keeps running.
Foreign keys are restored with their ON DELETE and ON UPDATE intact, because
healing one without them would swap one divergence for another. NOT NULL is
deliberately left alone, it needs a backfill decision per column and it is the
one that can lose data. Nothing raises to the caller and every statement keeps
its own savepoint.

The gating test is not "the constraint came back", which passes trivially. It
plants two rows with the same document number, drops the constraint, runs the
heal, and asserts the application still starts.

One trap is worth writing down because it cost a round. Constraint names cannot
be compared as strings. The naming convention re-wraps an already prefixed name,
so a couple of them resolve past the 63 character limit, and create_all did not
store those chopped at 63, it stored them hash mangled. Comparing the expression
instead does not work either, because the database rewrites what it stores. The
fix asks the same preparer create_all used for the name it would have produced.
Without that, the heal decided two healthy check constraints were missing and
added a duplicate of each on every boot.

fix(repositories): expire only the updated row after a single-row update

The update_fields template ran a Core UPDATE keyed on one primary key and
then called session.expire_all(). That invalidates every instance in the
session, not just the row that changed. On an async session the next read
of an expired attribute on any unrelated object has no greenlet to lazy-load
in, so it raises MissingGreenlet, and callers that legitimately held a
sibling object got an error that had nothing to do with what they wrote.

The replacement looks the updated instance up in the identity map and writes
the new values straight into its committed state, so the object stays loaded
and consistent with the database without a second round trip. Server-side
expressions are the one thing we cannot know the value of, so those columns
alone are expired and will be refetched on access. When the row is not in the
identity map there is nothing to reconcile and the function returns.

This is the same shape already proven in subcontractors and property_dev,
applied to the remaining 94 call sites across 49 files. An earlier estimate
put it at 86 sites in 39 files; that came from matching a fixed window above
each call, while the change here validates the whole coroutine body, which is
both stricter about what it rewrites and finds more of it. Sites where the
expire is not the last statement, or where it is not the single-row template,
were deliberately left alone and still need reading one by one.

It is now reference counted, and the count comes down in a finally so a failing
triage gives its entry back too. Registration happens before the acquire, so a
caller queued behind someone else is counted and cannot have the shared lock
swapped out from under it.

The obvious simpler fix, dropping the entry on every release, is wrong in a way
that two overlapping callers do not reveal: the second one looks the lock up
before the first releases and keeps its own reference, so it still serialises.
The break needs a third caller arriving after the first has released while the
second is still inside, and that one gets a brand new lock and runs straight
through alongside it. There is a test for exactly that, and it is the one that
fails against the naive version.

Red checked both ways. Against the old never-evict code four of the five tests
fail; against always-evict only the third-caller test fails, which is the point
of having it.

executed, and applied it to change orders and variation orders alike. Those

vocabulary here would otherwise contribute a silent zero, which is exactly the
failure being fixed.

stays pure, so there is now a test pinning the two copies to each other and to

fix(takeoff): give a group its own position instead of inheriting one

A group had no place of its own in the paint order. It rendered wherever its
earliest member happened to land in the flat stack, so restacking a single
measurement moved the whole group block with it, in the sidebar and on the
canvas. Someone bringing one shape to the front found the entire group had
jumped, which looks like the reorder did something other than what was asked.

Bands fix it. Each group gets a slot of its own, defaulting to first appearance
in the array, which is creation order and which no per-measurement reorder can
reach. The projection is band-major, so a group paints as one contiguous block
and a measurement can only move within its own group. Nothing is stored: two
clients looking at the same measurements derive the same bands.

Wired into every surface that reads the paint order, which is the part that
matters. The canvas pass, the click hit-test, the sidebar list, the annotated
PDF and the workbook all now project the same way, so none of them can drift
back out of agreement with the others. The exports derive their bands from the
whole measurement list rather than the page subset, since a per-page derivation
would give one group a different band on every sheet.

The sidebar's group buckets moved from a plain object to a Map. Iteration order
of that structure is the order the groups render, and an object enumerates
integer-like keys numerically ahead of everything else, so groups named for
levels or zones would have sorted themselves to the top regardless of band.
That is exactly how a takeoff names its groups.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(takeoff): let a measurement be dragged into another group

The sidebar drew a drop indicator over a row in another group and then refused
the move. Only an order key was written, and since the paint order became
band-major that key cannot reach outside the dragged row's own group, so the
gesture looked accepted and did nothing. Dragging a measurement onto a group is
also the obvious way to ask for it to be moved there, so the affordance was
promising something real.

The drop now writes the group as well as the key, and the key is computed
against the target group's rows rather than the flat list. Scoping matters: a
key picked against every row in the document is meaningless once the two groups
differ, because it would be compared against rows sitting in a different band
and could land the measurement anywhere inside its new group. With one group in
the document the scope is the whole list, so nothing changes there.

Most of this change is about the group order not moving underneath the user. A
band defaults to the group's first appearance in the array, which is stable
until a measurement changes group: move the first-appearing member of a group
out of it and the group is re-derived from whichever member is next, so two
group blocks trade places because one row was dragged. So a regrouping drop now
pins every group in the document where it is on screen before it moves
anything. A plain restack still pins nothing, or the derived default would be
dead code in every document after the first drag.

The pinned map rides the metadata blob mirrored onto each measurement, the way
the group colour scheme does, so it survives a reload with no schema change.
It is also built the way that pair was rebuilt after the colour feedback loop:
the map is authoritative, the copy on the row is a cache, the copy is read back
only while rehydrating a document, and the decision about which side to write
lives in a plain function rather than inside an effect. There is a test that
follows a pin through the mirror and back, because a pin that only lives in
component state passes everything except a reload.

Undo carries the group change alongside the key, flagged explicitly rather
than inferred from whether a group name is set: a name is legitimately empty,
and reading that as "no move" would leave the row where the redo put it.

fix(takeoff): let a measurement be dropped below a row, not only above it

Drag-to-reorder could put a measurement above any row in the sidebar and below
none of them. The slot after the last row of a group therefore had no gesture
that reached it, and getting a measurement there took two drags: drop it second
from bottom, then drag the row that used to be last up over it. The drop
indicator had the same hole, drawn only on the top edge of the hovered row, so
the interface had no way to say "put it below this one" either.

Every drop was computed as an insertion before the hovered row regardless of
where the pointer actually was. Now the half of the row the pointer is in
decides the side, and the indicator is drawn on the edge the measurement will
land against. The side is recomputed from the release point rather than read
from the hover state, since a drop can arrive without a final hover event on
the side it was released, and dropping somewhere other than where the line was
drawn is the whole complaint.

The row box is measured on every hover rather than cached, because the list
scrolls under the pointer while a drag is in progress.

There is a test for repeated drops into one gap. Each drop takes the midpoint
between its new neighbours, so the interval halves every time and float
precision is where two rows would start comparing equal and a reorder would
silently do nothing. Sixty drops in, the order still holds.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(takeoff): let a group block be dragged to a new position

A group had no gesture of its own. The only way to get one block above another
was to move its measurements across one at a time, and once a group stopped
inheriting its position from its members that stopped working at all, which is
correct but leaves the user with nothing. The group header now has its own grip
and its own drop target, with the same rule as the rows: the half of the header

made. For the same reason the renumbering covers every group in the document
and not the groups on the open sheet: the map is per document, and stamping
only what is on screen would drop the band of every group living on another
page and reshuffle sheets nobody was looking at. There is a test for that
specific case, since a single-page fixture cannot see it.

Reading the pinned map through a ref rather than a closure, so two drags in a
row compose instead of the second one computing from the map as it stood before
the first and quietly undoing it.

Undo carries the whole map both ways. An empty previous map is a real state,
the one where nothing had ever been pinned, and is written back as-is rather
than skipped as nothing to do.

fix(match): say why the vector service cannot start instead of a bare 500

setup under QDRANT_HOME raised an OSError that nothing caught, so it reached the

probing whether anything can be written, so the first real signal arrives later
and somewhere else.

error. Vector search keeps its data under QDRANT_HOME, which sits outside the
container's only declared volume, so operators add a bind mount there to keep it
across a container recreate, and Docker creates that mount root-owned while the
application runs as a non-root user.

fix(resumable-uploads): let a lost scratch chunk cost one chunk, not the upload

A chunk file that disappeared from the scratch directory could never be put
back. accept_chunk decided a chunk was a duplicate from the received_chunks
column alone and returned without writing, so the client was told its resend
had been accepted while the bytes stayed missing. chunk_store.has_chunk existed

rather than dead code, so it has one now.

answers with the same resumable 409, and keeps the parts it can still read. A
