fix(repositories): stop the shared update helper expiring the whole session

crm and webhook_leads each carry a module level _update_fields serving eight
repository classes between them, and both ended an update with
session.expire_all(). That reads as caution about staleness but under asyncio
it is a crash waiting for its caller. Expiring the session marks every loaded
object stale, so the next attribute read on any of them is a lazy load
attempted from async code, which raises MissingGreenlet instead of quietly
refetching. The object the caller just updated is affected too.

Both helpers now follow the form already used elsewhere in the tree: write the
values we already know straight onto the instance, and expire only the fields
whose new value was a SQL expression the database had to evaluate. Expiring
those still costs an await to read back, which is the point of separating them
rather than guessing a Python value for an expression.

Neither module had a single test in tests/pg, the only suite that can block a
merge, so a regression in a helper with this reach had nothing to stop it. The
new file pins the behaviour that matters: an unrelated loaded object stays
usable, the updated row reflects its new values, a computed field is expired
rather than guessed, and updating a row the session never loaded is not an
error. Three of those fail against the previous helper.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(collaboration): keep the pinned reply tree instead of expiring the session

The comment repository already knows why a lazy load hurts here. _pin_reply_tree
assigns replies with set_committed_value precisely so that serializing a nested
thread emits no SELECT, and its comment says plainly that a lazy one raises
MissingGreenlet on asyncpg. Then update_text and soft_delete ended with
session.expire_all(), which throws away those pins along with everything else
the session holds, so the next read of a thread pays the very cost the pinning
was there to avoid.

Both methods now write their new values onto the loaded comment. Every caller
passes plain Python values, so there is nothing the database needs to compute
and nothing to read back. edited_at was typed object and is now datetime, which
is what the only caller passes and what makes writing it directly provably
right.

feat(core): add apply_update so a bulk UPDATE stops expiring the whole session

Repositories that issue UPDATE ... WHERE id = :pk write past the ORM, so the
row changes while the instance the session holds keeps the old values. The
repair reached for across the tree was session.expire_all(), which is right for
that row and wrong for everything else loaded, and under asyncio it is not even
a refetch: expiring marks every object stale, so the next attribute read on any
of them is a lazy load attempted from async code and raises MissingGreenlet.
Reading back the row you just updated fails the same way.

apply_update does the narrow thing. Values the caller already has are written
onto the instance, and only fields whose new value was a SQL expression get
expired, because those have no Python value until the database evaluates them.
Expiring those still costs an await to read back, which is exactly why the two
kinds are separated rather than treated alike.

The gate is in tests/pg because the failure it guards against is asyncpg
behaviour. SQLite tolerated the lazy load that raises here, so a SQLite run
would pass on the very code this exists to reject.

fix(takeoff): stop reporting a broken PDF reader as a broken PDF

A user on 12.6.1 had every PDF upload fail while the built-in diagnostic
reported the PDF dependencies installed. Both halves of that were ours.

The diagnostic resolved pymupdf with find_spec, which locates a module
without executing it, so a wheel whose native extension will not load
passed the check and failed every upload. It also never looked at

now imports both, in a child of the same interpreter the upload path
parses in, so a reader that is broken only there is still caught and one

check a document that was fine. The worker now returns the reason with

Awarding a bid walks the sibling bids to refuse a second award. That read
only ever worked because the repository write called expire_all(), which
invalidated the RFQ and forced the next fetch to re-query. Once the write
stopped doing that, the guard read an empty list and a request for
quotation could be awarded twice.

Two things were wrong and both had to be fixed. The fetch used
session.get, which answers from the identity map without querying, so the
selectin loader on RFQ.bids never ran. Turning it into a query was not
enough either, because a plain query leaves an already loaded collection
alone, and an RFQ created in this session carries an empty bids list from
before any bid existed. It now queries with populate_existing so the
collection reflects the database.

Confirmed by removal. With session.get four of the eleven tests fail with
MissingGreenlet, with a plain query one fails because the guard no longer
refuses, and with both in place all eleven pass.

The docstring already claimed the bids were loaded here, which was true of
the intent and not of the code.

fix(deploy): stop a password with an at sign breaking the database URL

A quickstart install could fail with "Name or service not known" while the
PostgreSQL container beside it stayed healthy on the same password. The cause
was the URL. Compose interpolates the password straight into

  postgresql+asyncpg://oe:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@postgres:5432/openestimate

and a URL splits its user info at the first at sign, so a password of "pa@ss"
makes the host "ss@postgres", which resolves nowhere. PostgreSQL never noticed
because it receives the password as a plain environment variable, where the
character means nothing, and that asymmetry is what made the failure look like
a network problem.

Compose has no urlencode, so the assembly moves into Settings, which still has
the parts separate and can percent-encode them. Both compose files now pass
OE_DB_HOST, OE_DB_PORT, OE_DB_USER, OE_DB_NAME and OE_DB_PASSWORD instead of a
finished string. Setting DATABASE_URL directly still overrides everything, and
a URL that arrives already mangled is now refused by name rather than left to
fail later as a DNS error.

Doing it in Settings rather than in the container entrypoint is deliberate: the
backend-only image has no entrypoint script, so a shell fix would have covered
only half the deployments.

Money could be NaN. Decimal("NaN") and Decimal("Infinity") parse without

The last year's work week judged the whole range. work_day_numbers was
reassigned inside the per-year loop, so a country that moves its working week
at a year boundary had the new week applied retroactively.

An empty ECB time attribute produced undatable rows. The selector matches on
the attribute being present, not on it having a value, so rows went into the
NOT NULL rate_date column as the empty string, occupying the unique slot
forever without ever answering a lookup.

feat(retrieval): keep saved searches on the server instead of in the browser

A pinned search lived in localStorage, so it existed on one machine, in one
browser, until the profile was cleared. Someone who saved a set of facets at
the office did not have it at home, and nobody noticed the loss until they went
looking for a search that was no longer there.

Saved searches are now a table. One row per pinned set of facets, private to
the person who pinned it and scoped to the project the facets replay against,
because the search endpoint requires a project and a pin that cannot name one
is a row nobody can run.

The facets are separate columns rather than one JSON blob, which is what lets
the unique constraint on (user, project, signature) do its job: re-saving the
same facets updates the pin you already have instead of adding a second
identical entry. The signature is a hash of the canonical facet set, so two
searches that differ only in the order the filters were typed are one search.

Each row also carries how often it has been replayed and when it was last used,
so a list that has grown past a screenful can be ordered by what the person
actually runs rather than by when they happened to save it.

Writes are validated, and the outcome is stored on the row: a date range that
runs backwards, a record type that is not one of the three, a date that is not
a calendar date. Blocking failures answer 422 naming every reason at once
rather than the first one. Non-blocking findings are kept so the list can flag
a pin without re-running it.

A pin that belongs to somebody else answers 404 rather than 403, so the ids
cannot be walked to find out what exists.

fix(match-elements): report that the vector client is missing, not that the server is (#391)

The health card behind /match-elements probed the vector database server and
reported what it found. It never asked whether anything in the process could
talk to that server, and on the two channels users actually install from, that
is the thing that is missing.

The container image installs the base extra only, and the desktop lockfile is
compiled with no extras at all, so qdrant-client is absent from both. Matching
then stops at the import inside the cost adapter, which raises before a URL is
ever dialled. The ranker catches that and falls through to a metadata-only path
that needs the same client, so the request answers 200 with an empty candidate
list and nothing on screen says why. That is the report in #391: it does not
degrade to another way of matching, it returns nothing.

Meanwhile the card had two ways of being wrong about it. With the server up it
went green, above a matcher that could not return anything. With the server
down it offered to download and start one, and a user who took that offer got a
running server and the same empty results, because the missing piece was never
the server.

The report now carries whether the client can be imported, answered by actually
importing it rather than by locating it, since a package can be present and
still fail to import on a partial install, and those two answers differ exactly
when this matters. The offer to download the server is withheld when it would
change nothing. The frontend checks this before reachability and states the
situation instead of raising an alarm about the wrong component, and stops
polling, because a missing library cannot appear while the process runs.

What this does not do is put the client in the shipped builds. That is a
packaging decision with a real cost, and it is worth taking deliberately rather
than as a side effect of a bug fix.

into the service, which left the IDOR guard red. The guard is right to fail.
It pins that every single-resource mutation resolves its parent project at

thing standing between a caller and another tenant's data.

verify_project_access like the other registered guard wrappers, and
normalises its 404 so both cases still answer alike.

was measured, not assumed: with the route gate emptied out the cross-project
test still passes, because the service reaches the same verdict. The static
guard is the only instrument that can pin this, which is what its own header
says it is for.

documents as its convention for background jobs. No HTTP route can reach that
path, since the caller id is resolved from the token before the handler runs,

here rather than changed as a side effect of a routing fix.

fix(alembic): repair the second head that broke every self-hosted upgrade

The fx rate-set revision named v3234_cost_search_trgm as its parent. By the
time it was written v3234 was long closed: v3250_merge_open_heads had already
folded it into the mainline as one of four parents, and the tip had moved on
many revisions past it. The chain therefore had two heads, and alembic upgrade
head refused to run at all with "Multiple head revisions are present". Nobody
could upgrade in place until this was repaired.

It went unnoticed because our own production deploy is create_all plus alembic
stamp head and never walks the chain, so the break was invisible to us and
visible only to people self-hosting, which is the wrong way round.

The repair is a merge revision rather than a repointed parent. Rewriting the
fx revision's down_revision to the current tip would leave any database already
stamped at it treating every revision between the old parent and the new one as
an ancestor it had applied, and those migrations would then be skipped in
silence. A merge keeps both paths and is safe from either side. The head count
is back to one with all 305 revisions reachable.

The guard that should have caught this reads the revisions with ast instead of
importing them, so it needs no database and cannot be disabled by an unrelated
import error in any of the three hundred revision files. It also checks that
every named parent exists and that there is a single base. Removing the merge
makes it fail and name both heads.

fix(tests): stop hand-stepping application event subscribers into asyncpg

A test that reloads an events module and re-registers its handlers on the
process-global bus has to put the bus back. test_boq_events did not, so
_on_position_created stayed subscribed to boq.position.created for the rest of
the run. It now snapshots both registries per test and restores them verbatim,
which also undoes the wider half of that leak: the reload helper clears the bus
first, dropping every other module subscription along with it.

The harness then chose its publish regime from a hand-kept set of three handler
names. That set covered the three wildcard subscribers and none of the 150-odd
per-event ones, so the leaked subscriber looked pure, was stepped by hand,
suspended inside a live asyncpg read and left the session-scoped loop corrupted.
Every later test in the process died in selectors.py with WinError 10038 without
reaching application code, and the pair test_boq_events plus any later BOQ test
that writes a position reproduced it three times out of three.

The classification is structural now and derived from the module a handler was
defined in, so a new event_bus.subscribe anywhere under app/ is covered the day
it lands and no test has to know it exists. A plain non-async subscriber counts
too, since the bus dispatches it through asyncio.to_thread. Leaked subscribers
stay on the bus and are excluded at the publish boundary instead of being
deleted from it: deleting made every test that asserts on the wiring pass alone
and fail in a chunk, which is the same order-dependent shape as the bug.

The unsound recovery is gone with it. Closing a half-stepped coroutine throws
GeneratorExit into something that may be suspended in asyncpg, and re-publishing
afterwards fires every handler that already completed a second time. That branch
is now unreachable by construction and raises with the handler names if
construction ever slips.

test_event_publish_regime is rewritten against real application subscribers from
both registries, since its previous stand-in was classified by name and the name
no longer decides anything. It also pins that the rule covers each of the three
names the old list kept plus two per-event subscribers it had no way to know
about.

tests/unit test_b*.py went from 11 failed, 1431 passed, 1 skipped, 13 errors to
1453 passed, 1 skipped.

fix(deploy): make quickstart-image work with the image that is published

The database moved from a finished URL to its parts so a password containing
an at sign would stop breaking the host. Reading those parts is a property of
the image, and no published image has it: latest is whatever we released last,
and every release so far predates the change. So a fresh clone running
make quickstart-image gets a compose file that passes OE_DB_HOST and friends to
an image that looks only for DATABASE_URL, finds nothing, and exits before it
reaches Python. That is the route we tell people to take when the frontend
build fails, and it has been broken since the parts landed.

The image overlay now passes the finished URL as well. An image that predates
the parts uses it and starts, which is the behaviour it always had. An image
that understands the parts ignores it, so nothing changes for a source build.

Passing both would ordinarily undo the fix for anyone on the image route, since
a URL wins over the parts. It does not win when it is visibly the damage the
parts exist to prevent. A host containing an at sign is not a host, it is the
tail of a password that the URL split in the wrong place, so when the parts are
present they are used instead. Without them nothing is guessed and the
container still refuses to start naming the reason, because inventing a host
there would take away the only message that says what is wrong.

The entrypoint made the same call and made it fatal. It now says which source
it is using and carries on when the parts can rescue it, and keeps the hard
error for the case where they cannot.

fix(dwg-takeoff): stop a conversion holding the drawing row while it runs

A 22 MB drawing failed to convert, and then the application stopped answering
for that drawing. Setting the scale timed out after 45 seconds, the failed
upload could not be deleted, and a restart was the only way to clear it. Those
read as three problems and are one.

The background conversion marks the drawing processing and then runs for
minutes, but its session did not commit until the conversion had finished. The
row lock taken by that update was therefore held for the whole conversion, so
every other write to the same drawing queued behind it and the browser gave up
at its own 45 second limit. The larger the drawing, the longer the application
looks dead, which is why this arrives as a report about a big file.

The transition is now committed when it happens. That releases the row before
the slow part begins, and it also makes the status true: a transition inside an
open transaction is visible to nobody, so the page polling the drawing had been
reading uploaded for the entire conversion while the code above it was written
to report progress.

The timeout message now names the limit and the variable that raises it. The
old wording read as a verdict on the file, so the reporter tried the same
upload several times and rebooted the machine, when a large drawing on a slow
box may simply need longer than the default five minutes.

Tests are in the PostgreSQL lane because a lock is only observable between two
real connections. One of the four holds the others honest: it makes the same
write by hand without committing and shows the competing statement really is
refused, so the three that assert success cannot pass against a database that
never locked anything.

fix(startup): create the sequence a column defaults from before adding the column

On a database whose oe_progress_entry predates the seq column, the boot-time
heal emitted ADD COLUMN seq BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT nextval(...) against a
sequence that was not there, and PostgreSQL rejected the statement. The two
indexes over that column and its duplicate check failed after it, all four at
warning level, so the boot carried on and every read of the progress module
failed against a column the ORM selects and the table does not have.

It was not a first-boot problem that a restart clears. create_all builds its
standalone sequence list from the sequences whose column is None, and this one
is attached to a column, so it is filtered out; its only other route is CREATE
TABLE, which does not run for a table that already exists. Nothing in the
app-managed upgrade path was ever going to create it. Only alembic upgrade head
would have, and the embedded and quickstart runtimes are stamped rather than
run. A fresh install was fine throughout, which is why this went unnoticed:
the breakage was visible only to people who already had the product.

The heal now creates any sequence a model column defaults from, before the
column pass. Across all 598 tables exactly one column is affected, checked
three ways, so the fix is generic on purpose rather than because more are
known. On a healthy database it adds nothing.

actually does they disagree, and a database built by walking the chain

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(alembic): freeze the schema divergence and put the guards in a lane that runs

create_all is the source of truth for our schema and alembic records which
revisions count as applied. That is the arrangement in practice, so env.py now
says it in its docstring rather than leaving the next reader to infer it. It
also names what follows: a fresh install is short-circuited before the chain
is walked, the chain does not walk from base because the root revision has an
empty body, and a database that has our tables but no alembic_version row is
the one population this does not serve. Stamp it, do not run upgrade head
expecting self repair.

The divergence is frozen rather than repaired. create_all emits varchar(36)
for every identity column and always will, because GUID is a type decorator
over String(36) with no load_dialect_impl. Fifty three revisions declare a
native UUID instead, and reconciling them is a multi-day job whose value goes
to a narrow population. The new guard does the affordable half and stops the
gap growing, with the offending files frozen in a closed list derived by
scanning rather than by hand.

The guard is deliberately coarse. A precise version was written first and
missed a revision that returns the type from a helper and takes it as a
parameter, so it now matches the type reference itself. Every indirection a
detector has to resolve is another way to fall through it, and a site it
cannot resolve counts as clean, which is how a guard ends up enforcing
nothing.

Both alembic guards move into tests/pg. This is the point of the change. The

fix(finance): fill the budget currencies that were written blank, and stop stamping EUR

Four write paths ignored the contract that a budget line must carry the
currency of its project, so the rows they wrote landed empty and the finance
table rendered a column of em-dashes. The write paths were fixed earlier; this
repairs the rows they already wrote.

Only empty rows are touched, never rewritten, so an imported line that already
carries a real currency is left alone. When the parent project has no currency
of its own the budget row stays blank, because a blank is honest and a guessed
currency is not. Verified on a real database rather than by reading: a line
already carrying USD under a EUR project came through the same run untouched,
the reverse case did too, and a EUR project and a USD project produced
different answers in one pass, which is what shows it reads the parent rather
than a constant. Second run updates nothing.

The length guard earns its place. A project currency is ten characters wide
and a budget currency is three, so copying a longer value across would abort
the whole migration. Rows that do not fit stay blank rather than being cut in
half.

Separately, the revision that introduced the column added it with a server
default of EUR while the model declares an empty string, and the model says in
a comment on that very column why: no database default, because service code
has to supply the currency from the project or per-project rollups quietly
bias toward one currency. Adding a column with a default writes that default
into every row already in the table, so an install that walked that revision
had every budget line it held stamped EUR regardless of what it actually was.
That is now an empty string. It only helps installs that have not run the
revision yet, which is the population still exposed; one that already ran it
keeps those rows, and they cannot be told apart from a currency someone chose
on purpose.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(dwg-takeoff): give a running conversion somewhere to report itself alive

The orphan detector has to answer whether the task owning a conversion died,
and it has been approximating that with elapsed time. The approximation cannot
work, because the work it is compared against has no upper bound. The DDC
subprocess is capped by OE_DWG_CONVERT_TIMEOUT_S, but the xlsx parse that
follows it has no timeout at all and its cost tracks the size of the drawing.
Measured on a 200,000 row export, that parse alone took 86 seconds.

So this column carries a liveness signal instead, refreshed on an interval we
choose. The cutoff stops being a guess about how long a customer's drawing
takes and becomes a fact about how often we write, which is the only one of
the two we control.

Nullable with no default, and the absence of a default is the point. A default
would stamp every existing row with a timestamp, and a timestamp reads as "a
conversion was alive at that moment", which for those rows would be an
invention. NULL means no conversion has run for this row since the column
shipped, which is not the same as a stale one and must not be read as death.

The downgrade drops the column rather than being left empty, unlike v3269. The
difference is what is held: v3269 backfilled a user-meaningful value that could
not be told apart from one a user typed, so undoing it would have destroyed
real data. This holds an ephemeral signal from a background task and is worth
nothing once the task is gone.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(dwg-takeoff): stop the orphan detector condemning a live conversion (#409)

A 22 MB drawing was told its conversion was dead while it was still running,
and the message it was given asked the user to remove the drawing and upload it
again. Deleting was the one operation blocked at that moment by the
conversion's own row lock, so the advice on screen and the state of the system
were in direct contradiction. The reporter followed it several times and then
rebooted the machine.

The detector now reads the heartbeat the conversion writes rather than how long
the row has sat there. A conversion that is still reporting itself alive is
left alone however long it takes, and one that has stopped reporting for six
intervals is declared orphaned as before. Rows carrying no heartbeat keep the
old elapsed-time rule, which is the only population it was ever right about:
they predate the column, so nothing else can be said about them. A running
conversion cannot fall into that branch, because the first heartbeat is written
in the same commit as the transition to processing.

The beat runs on its own session, opened and committed per beat. Sharing the
conversion's session would put every beat inside whatever transaction the
conversion has open and hold a row lock for the length of the work, which is
the defect this whole area was just fixed for.

Reading a drawing no longer writes to it. The stale verdict used to be
persisted during a GET, which is how an inference the request had made became a
durable fact about the row, and before e65dbf587 that write also queued behind
the conversion it was declaring dead. The verdict and its message are derived
and returned instead, so the record says only what actually happened.

A conversion that finishes after its drawing was deleted now says so. The
version insert carries a NOT NULL foreign key, so a missing parent raised an
integrity error that a detached task logged as a conversion failure, which was
false: the conversion had succeeded and the drawing was gone. It checks first
and reports what occurred.

Tests are in the PostgreSQL lane because that is the only lane that gates
anything. Two of the nine matter most. One sets a drawing an hour past the old
cutoff with a fresh heartbeat and shows it is left alone, and its pair sets the
same row with no heartbeat and shows it is still condemned, so the heartbeat is
demonstrably what changed the verdict. The other shows a read leaves the row
untouched, and is followed by a control that makes the write the old code made
and proves the same check catches it, because a test asserting nothing changed
passes just as happily against a check that cannot see changes.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(dwg-takeoff): pin the null-heartbeat semantics by name

A missing heartbeat means no conversion has run for this row, not that one
died. Every row predating the column reads null, so getting this backwards
declares the whole drawing register orphaned on the first read after an
upgrade.

The existing coverage happened to constrain it, but only as a side effect of
testing something else. This names the rule so the test that goes red points
straight at it. What it guards against is a tidying-up rather than a mistake:
folding the two branches into one line that reads the silence since the
heartbeat and treats a missing one as infinite silence is shorter, looks
neater, and is wrong in the worst possible direction.

The drawing has never been converted at all, which is the case with the most
rows behind it. The assertion is that it is not reported dead rather than
naming the state it is in, because the choice between processing and
needs_conversion turns on whether a converter binary exists on the machine
running the test, and that is not what is being pinned.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(dwg-takeoff): clear the converter spreadsheet the conversion leaves behind

A DWG conversion writes a <name>_dwg.xlsx beside the upload, reads the entities
out of it, and left it there. On every path: the five error branches, the
success path, and drawing deletion. Nothing else ever reads it.

The cost runs the wrong way round. The spreadsheet is larger for a larger
drawing, and a conversion that fails is the one people retry, so the copies
accumulate fastest on the installation that has just failed to convert
something big. The reporter in #409 retried a 22 MB drawing several times.

Cleared in the background task's finally rather than inside the conversion,
because that is the only place every ending meets. _handle_dwg leaves by one of
five returns, a raise, or success, and a removal written at each of those is a
removal that gets missed the next time an ending is added. Deriving the path in
the caller costs nothing, since it is the same input the conversion derived it
from, and the derivation itself now has one definition with three callers so
they cannot drift apart.

Drawing deletion clears it too, as a backstop rather than a duplicate. A
process that dies mid-conversion leaves the spreadsheet with nothing alive that
knows it exists, and deleting the drawing is the last moment anything can
connect the two.

Removal never raises. Cleanup that can fail a conversion is worse than the
litter it removes, and a killed converter on Windows can hold the handle open
a moment longer than the process that held it.

The tests assert the file is present before the act that should remove it, not
only absent afterwards, because the second half passes just as happily against
a test that never created it. The conversion under test fails rather than
succeeds, since cleanup on the happy path is the easy half and the failure
paths are where the file used to survive.

A user reported at 11.2.0 that the control did nothing. The code behind it
had not changed since, so it still applied to 14.x.

Two things kept it quiet. The native side asked the OS to open the URL and
treated the spawn as its answer, so a machine with no usable default browser,

the toast says what actually went wrong instead of a generic warning.

on it, since xdg-open can exec the browser in place and outlive the click.

fixed helper. This reports what the OS reports and no more: Windows start
still exits 0 when it puts up the file association chooser.

chore(costbase): track the cost base pipeline and put it behind a blocking gate

The code that builds the parquet cost base editions people download from us lived
inside WORLD_COST_BASES, a directory .gitignore excludes in full. That rule was
written to keep tens of gigabytes of parquet out of the repository and it swept up
the pipeline source with it, so the thing producing a public artifact was untracked,
unreviewable and covered by no gate. Nothing in git could see it, which is why a
Turkish edition could ship with its content in English and stay that way for weeks.

Code moves to tools/costbase_pipeline and is tracked. Data stays out. The suite runs
in CI (PostgreSQL), the only merge-blocking lane that runs pytest; it needs no
database, and pandas and pyarrow are already base dependencies of the backend
package that lane installs. A dedicated fast lane would be a better home and is left
as a separate decision rather than added as new shared machinery here.

One behaviour change comes with the move and it is the reason the move needed care.
The base directory was Path(__file__).parent.parent, correct only while the code sat
inside the data directory. Relocating it repointed that expression at a directory
holding no parquet, and nothing would have gone red: every test builds its input
with an explicit source_path, so the suite stays green while the production entry
point quietly resolves nothing and reports an empty run. The directory now comes
from --base-dir or OE_COSTBASE_DIR and an unset value is refused rather than
guessed. tests/test_base_dir_resolution.py pins that, including a ban on the exact
expression that broke, and it fails against the code as it was before this change.

The 12 one-off translate_g0* scratch scripts are deliberately left behind.

fix(validation): say when the quality score is capped by blocking errors

The screen showed a quality score of 3 percent labelled "Poor" directly
beside "Rules checked 4975" and "Passed 4721". Read together those two
figures contradict each other, and a user has no way to tell which one to
believe.

Both are right. The score is not a pass rate. It is severity weighted and
then capped: any blocking error limits it to 0.5 / (1 + errors), so a run
carrying about fifteen errors reads near 3 percent no matter how many of
the other checks passed. That is deliberate, since one blocking error
should never read as 99 percent quality, but nothing on the screen said
so, which left the headline number looking broken.

The ring now carries a line naming the cap whenever the run has blocking
errors. The count itself is already in the summary beside it, so the line
stays free of a number and needs no plural handling.

fix(cost-explorer): give the search pool a total order so a rate can be cited twice

The candidate pool was ordered by concept-match count alone. For a one-word
query, which is what an estimator actually types, every row that got past the
WHERE matches exactly one concept, so the sort key was a constant and the LIMIT
cut kept whichever rows the plan happened to produce. Three identical searches
returned three different sets of work items at different rates, all of them
labelled a full match. Nobody could return to a rate they saw a minute ago,
cite it, or hand the search to a colleague and get the same answer.

The order now ends on a unique key so it is total, and the terms ahead of it
mirror what the caller ranks by, so the cut keeps the rows the service is about
to rank highest rather than an arbitrary sample of the match set. The typed word
sorts ahead of a synonym we injected for the user, then the concept count, then
the shorter description. A query that builds no predicates at all had no
ORDER BY whatsoever and is covered by the same terminal key now.

The score itself is untouched. It saturates at 1.0 for any row containing the
typed word, which is why every row reads as a full match, but the low-confidence
threshold reads that same number and changing the formula moves which searches
show the did-you-mean hint. That is a separate change.

Tests assert an explicit expected sequence rather than running the query twice
and comparing, since two runs in one session can agree while the order is still
undefined. All three fail at the previous commit.

fix(build): give both halves of the build a heap limit

The build script never set a heap size, so it ran under Node's default, which is
4288 MB on an ordinary workstation. npm run build started dying with exit 134
and a V8 out of memory trace. This is a provisioning gap rather than a size
problem. The flag was always missing and the threshold was only ever a matter
of time.

Seven workflows had each worked around it by exporting NODE_OPTIONS, which is
why CI stayed green while a fresh clone did not. The bare command is what
CONTRIBUTING.md asks contributors to run, it is what the server prints when it
finds no frontend, and make build-wheel calls it to produce the pip artifact,
so building a wheel yourself failed unless you already knew the trick.

tsc and vite are two separate processes and the flag reaches only the command it
is written on. The first attempt raised tsc alone, on the reasoning that tsc was
where the trace pointed. The build then died in vite at 4055 MB against the
4288 MB default, which is why both halves carry it now. The earlier measurement
could not have told me otherwise: it was taken with NODE_OPTIONS exported into
the shell, so it covered both halves at once and hid which one needed the
headroom. The margin is not narrow either. On the green run vite's working set
reached about 5.9 GB, so the default was never going to be close.

The number is 9216 rather than 8192, and the reason is worth stating because it
is easy to get backwards. An explicit --max-old-space-size on the command line
overrides the value inside NODE_OPTIONS, so whatever the script sets becomes the
effective ceiling for every workflow that used to export its own. 9216 is the
highest value any workflow currently uses. Setting anything lower would have
quietly reduced ci.yml, which is the lane that has been red on tsc running out
of memory, and that number is presumably there for exactly that reason. Taking
it away while fixing a memory bug would have been an odd trade. The green run
was measured at 8192; the shipped value is higher, and since the flag is a
ceiling rather than an allocation, and V8 aborts on reaching it, a build that
completed under 8192 cannot abort under 9216.

Nothing is added to dependencies: node runs each entry point directly, which
behaves the same in cmd.exe and in a POSIX shell.

fix(assemblies): count a recipe's components instead of measuring an empty list

Cards on the Assemblies screen read "0 components" while their own hover panel
listed three. The list query loads assemblies without their components on
purpose, so a page of fifty does not drag every component row across, and the
response builder then took the length of that collection. An unloaded
collection is indistinguishable from an empty one, so the zero was not a count
of anything. The hover panel calls the detail endpoint, which does load them,
which is why the two numbers on one card disagreed.

This is the case the loading policy names: noload does not raise, it returns an
empty collection, so the wrong answer reaches the screen instead of an error.

The number now comes from one grouped COUNT over the page, and the response
builder takes it as a required argument rather than deriving it, so there is
nowhere for a silent zero to come from. The single-object endpoints ask for the
same count, since they fetch through get_by_id and do not load components
either. The template response keeps its len(), because a template's components
are a JSON column and that list is real.

Assemblies with no components stay absent from the count map rather than
carrying a zero; the call sites read it with a default, and the tests pin that
so an empty page cannot turn into an IN () with no values.

currencies, is a schema change and is not in this commit.

newly leaked one; a set of key/locale pairs can.

byte-identical to en.ts outside that declared set, so the same shape of
mistake fails a commit instead of shipping silently. It does not repair
anything and it does not scan for untranslated English generally - a byte
comparison is structurally blind to a wrong-sense translation that isn't
English (mn's field_jurisdiction is one such case, tracked separately,
not in scope here). Wired into repo-hygiene.yml as a fourth guard next to
the existing file, trailer and escape checks, and into .pre-commit-config
so a new leak is caught at commit time too.

Repair of the 7965 known cells is a separate, larger decision on scope and
ordering, tracked in #182.

merged legitimate-identical and leaked-identical into one file. Neither
matches the actual shape of the problem: a full en.ts scan at >=24/28
non-en locales found 127 keys the original 295-key sweep missed entirely,
the largest a whole module (progress, 44 keys) with no .insights. family
to have found it by. A sixth origin commit turned up in the process,
f0226a272 (2026-07-26 16:20), an ordinary feat(progress) commit that
happened to add keys - the mechanism is any commit that adds locale keys
without a 27-locale pass, not a labelled i18n commit or a 53-minute
window. Three of six origin commits say nothing about English or Russian
in their bodies at all, so commit text was never a reliable census.

allowlist keys where every one of 28 non-en locales matches en on
purpose, and 119 keys that don't fit either tell (a handful of locales
translated, most match by coincidence - transliterated proper nouns and
the like) parked in a third, non-gating pending-review list rather than
forced into a list they'd corrupt.

The rebuilt checker scans the whole keyspace every run instead of only
rechecking known debt, and requires every hit to land in exactly one of
the three lists. Two new failure modes: a baseline cell leaving the
leaked set is only accepted as a real repair if the key is still present
in that locale (fallbackLng=en means a deleted key still renders
English), and a within-file loose-quote scan catches entries the strict
double-quote parser can't see, without false-positiving on locales that
legitimately carry more keys than en.ts from richer CLDR plural

fix(demo): replace real vendor names in module seeds and the formwork catalogue

Second pass over the demo data after the pack work in a3c4ea6bb. The
equipment, carbon, service and hse_advanced seeds handed out real
manufacturer names, and the starter formwork catalogue shipped eight rows
named after actual products from four suppliers, which is not something a
demo dataset should carry.

Machinery, fuel, EPD, maintenance and PPE names are now coined roots with a
trade word and a legal form that matches the locale, each one checked
against a plain search and against a search scoped to its own sector before
it went in. The formwork rows went the other way: the name field there was
supplier plus product with nothing left once the supplier came out, so the
eight rows now describe what the system is (steel framed wall panel,
aluminium slab deck panel, self-climbing core system) and the supplier field
is null, which is what the two generic plywood rows already did.

None of this reaches a database that has already been seeded, but the four
seeds and the formwork catalogue get there by different routes. Equipment
short-circuits on the EQ-0001 sentinel, service on any existing contract,
hse_advanced on any populated table of its own, and carbon on a CarbonInventory
row count held by the caller in demo_enrichment, so on an existing install all
four skip wholesale and a re-run inserts nothing at all. Formwork is the one
that keys on the name: seed-defaults counts inserted against skipped per row,
so re-running it there leaves the eight old rows in place and adds the eight
new ones beside them. Renaming those rows on an existing install is safe if we
decide to, since assignments reference the catalogue by id and neither rate
column is touched.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(formwork): carry the catalogue de-branding to installs already seeded

0ff65d60c took the eight trademarked rows out of the starter formwork
catalogue, but seeding compares per row on the name and skips what is already
there, so that fix only ever reaches a fresh install. Every tenant who
installed before today keeps the old rows, which leaves the thing we set out
to stop exactly where it was. This revision renames them in place.

It also closes a second path. Because seed-defaults matches on the name, a
tenant who upgrades and re-runs it today gets the eight new rows inserted
beside the eight old ones, sixteen rows for eight systems. After the rename
there is nothing left for the old names to match and seed-defaults skips all
eight.

The revision keys on the exact old name, so a row the tenant renamed
themselves is left alone, and it only clears the supplier where that field
still holds the original brand, so someone who repointed a row at their own
hire yard keeps that value. It will not rename a row onto a name already
present for the same tenant, which is the state an install lands in if it
already re-ran seed-defaults; those rows are counted and reported rather than
merged, since the old row may carry assignments and choosing between the two
is a judgement about a tenant's own data. No price moves: assignments join the
catalogue by id and neither rate column is touched. The downgrade is a no-op
on purpose, because reversing this would write real company names back into
tenant databases and keep a copy of them in the source tree forever.

The test had to write the pre-rename state itself. create_all builds the table
empty and the catalogue in the tree already carries the new names, so running
the revision against a fresh test database updates nothing and passes without
executing a single branch. Both new tests were confirmed to fail before they
were trusted: dropping the duplicate guard fails the first, and changing the
one non-ASCII literal fails it too. That mutation went green against the
second test, which seeds from the revision's own mapping, so that test now
states a different invariant instead, that the names the revision writes are
names a fresh install would have.

The seed-defaults test that walks the whole catalogue was checking that the
labour rate was above zero and the strip time at least one day, which is true
of any catalogue anyone would write. It now compares against the shipped
figures and asserts no row arrives carrying a supplier, so the de-branding is
held at the API and not only in the file.

feat(resources): let an assignment name the schedule activity it is for

A user asked how to assign a resource to a task and could not find a way. The
reason was not a missing button. An assignment could point at a to-do Task or
at nothing, but never at the schedule activity the Gantt chart draws, so the
object the user was looking at had no place to hold who is working on it.

Adds a nullable activity_id to Assignment, alongside the existing task_id
rather than instead of it, and carries it through the schemas, the repository
filters, the service and the create, propose and patch endpoints. Adds
GET /assignments/by-activity/{activity_id} for the schedule direction of the
link; it takes project_id as a query parameter so the access check has a scope
to verify and an activity id on its own cannot be used to enumerate.

Three validation rules, all warnings and all on demand: an assignment outside
its activity's date window, an assignment naming both an activity and a task,
and an activity_id that resolves to nothing.

The migration declares the column as String(36), not native uuid. GUID renders
as VARCHAR(36) on PostgreSQL too, so the referenced column is text and a uuid
column cannot be constrained against it. The neighbouring revisions get this
wrong and PostgreSQL refuses the constraint outright. A refused DDL also aborts
the enclosing transaction and would take alembic's own version bump down with
it, so the foreign key is created inside a savepoint.

fix(cad): stop reporting a converter Windows refuses to start as healthy

A user opened the BIM page and Windows put a Bad Image box on screen naming
a Qt6 library beside the DGN converter, error 0xC000007B. Behind it our own
status card said nothing was wrong.

Two things were wrong and the quiet one is worse. That exit code was not in
the set the health check recognises, and every unrecognised code falls
through to the branch that calls the install healthy. So the check was
answering a question it had not asked: it saw a number it did not know and
said yes. Added the two loader codes that were missing, invalid image format
and entrypoint not found, alongside the two that were there.

The box itself is drawn by the loader inside a process we start, so nothing
we write reaches the screen until somebody dismisses a dialog the
application does not know exists. A child inherits its parent's error mode,
so the probe now holds SEM_FAILCRITICALERRORS while it spawns and the
failure comes back as an exit code we can explain.

0xC000007B also gets its own wording. It means every file is present and one
of them is built for the other word size, so the advice for the other codes,
re-download the Qt plugins, sends somebody to fetch what they already have.

Worth saying plainly, because the report reads like it: no part of the
application links Qt. The converters are separate console binaries from the
DDC pipeline and they carry their own runtime beside them, which is where
the library in the message lives.

The tests are in the PostgreSQL lane, which is the only lane that blocks a
merge. Six of them go red against the old code set.

fix(demo): spread seeded service tickets across the SLA outcomes

The demo maintenance desk reported a 100 percent SLA breach, which reads as a
broken feature rather than as a contractor under pressure. Two independent
causes, both a deadline compared against a window it was never drawn from.
Open tickets were aged a flat zero to seventy-two hours against a response
window of fifteen to four hundred and eighty minutes, so nearly the whole
queue was already overdue the moment it was written. Closed tickets carried a
flat four hour due date against a resolution drawn from one to twenty-four
hours, so most of the history breached by construction.

Both sites now draw the elapsed time as a fraction of the tier's own target,
weighted 72/18/10 across met, ran close to the wire, and breached. The target
comes from the module's own compute_sla_response_and_resolution rather than a
second reading of severity_levels, so the seeder measures a ticket against the
same deadline the product computes for it, and a bronze contract is no longer
judged by silver's promise. Every timestamp is relative to the moment of
seeding, so the estate cannot drift into the past between releases.

On a seeded estate that lands at two of thirty open tickets overdue and
nineteen of two hundred closed tickets late. The new tests assert those rates
as bands rather than asserting that some ticket somewhere is on time, and each
of the two causes reddens its own test when reverted.

The maintenance customers in the same file now carry an address on their own
Contact record instead of a generated per index mailbox. It is a separate
concern that happens to live in this seeder and could not be split off.

providers fell to a fallback that still handed them the full system prompt,
which names about twenty tools and instructs the model to use them first,
while passing no tools array at all. The models did as they were told in
whatever call syntax their training used, and it arrived in the chat bubble
as literal text. The tool name in the user's screenshot is one of ours, which
is what points at our prompt rather than at provider noise.

Those providers now get a system prompt that says plainly there is no live
data access and not to emit call syntax. The fallback also returned before
the shared tail, so the turn was never persisted, the response carried no
message id, the thumbs feedback POST answered 404, and the token count never
reached the daily budget. It runs through the shared path now.

Not fixed by parsing or stripping the text form. A scrubber has to guess at an
open set of vendor dialects, and a wrong guess eats a real answer, so there is
no detection pattern here for a future report to trip over. Provider name now
reaches the error message on HTTP failures too, which on a branch serving
seventeen providers is the difference between a usable report and none.

fix(users): drop erased accounts from the user management list

Deleting a user anonymises the row in place instead of removing it, because
projects point at it through owner_id and activity rows through actor_id, and
the projects foreign key cascades, so a hard delete would take the user's
projects and their BOQs, costs and documents with it. The row has to survive.

It should not stay on the management page though, and it did. The
administrator kept seeing the account with a blank name and a
deleted+<hash>@deleted.invalid address, which reads as a deletion that failed,
and deleting it a second time answered 404 because the erasure path refuses a
row that is already erased.

The list query now filters on deleted_at. The predicate sits on the base
select, so the total that feeds the pager and the page itself apply the same
condition. Suspended accounts are deliberately untouched: erasure also clears
is_active, so a filter written on that column would have hidden the accounts an
administrator merely suspended and has to find again in order to reactivate
them. The new test in the PostgreSQL lane pins that difference.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(subcontractors): keep the rating provenance record off the wire

A rating stores a basis column recording how each score was reached. Part of
it, under sources, is a per metric pair of the count accumulated from our own
events and a count taken directly from the NCR, safety incident and schedule
tables. That direct count is a raw COUNT(*) filtered only by subcontractor and
month, with no project or tenant predicate, while those same tables are gated
by verify_project_access when read through their own modules. The basis is
returned by the rating endpoints, which ask only for the viewer role, so the
pair handed a viewer an exact tally of another tenant's non conformances and
safety incidents.

The redaction sits on the response schema rather than in a router because
three routes return a rating and a rule written in one of them would leave the
other two open. The column itself is untouched, since the audit trail is why
it is written.

This narrows the exposure and does not close it, and the test says so rather
than implying otherwise. The counters beside sources are max of accumulated
and direct, and the scores are computed from them, so a subcontractor busier
outside the reader's projects than inside them still shows a number the reader
could not otherwise obtain. Closing that means deciding whether a rating is
per project, per tenant or deliberately shared, which changes both what the
query may count and what a stored row means. That is a product decision and it
is recorded rather than guessed at.

fix(tests): read a workflow step's working directory before believing its paths

The lane coverage guard collected every pytest call in every workflow and
matched the path arguments against the backend test trees. It did not read
working-directory, so the cost base pipeline step, which runs pytest tests
inside tools/costbase_pipeline against its own suite and its own conftest, was
counted as a bare run of backend/tests. By prefix that matched every tree, and
the guard reported tests/integration, tests/modules, tests/eval,
tests/benchmarks and tests/perf as fully gated on push by a job that collects

Those five are exactly the trees the file exists to keep honest, so the effect

strongest, which is the failure it was written to catch, happening to itself.

is removed later. The other is its control: excluding by directory must not
exclude the lane itself, since dropping every invocation would leave every
tree unclassified and the recorded map asserting nothing.

hiding it.

fix(costs): give every loadable price base a currency, and repair the rows that lost theirs

A CWICR work item parquet carries no currency column, so the region a base is
loaded under is the only statement of which money its rates are in. The importer
resolves it once per import and stamps every row, which works only if the
currency table covers the regions the importer accepts. It did not. The set of
loadable bases comes from base_registry, the currency table was built from the
v3 snapshot registry plus a hand kept alias list, and twelve of the thirty eight
loadable regions were in the first and missing from the second. An import of one
of those resolved to an empty string and wrote a whole catalogue of prices with
no unit of money on them.

Measured on the running database rather than taken from the earlier survey:
55 718 of 123 485 cost rows carried a blank currency, every one of them source
cwicr and region ZH_SHANGHAI. The other regions in the same table were complete,
so this was one import and not a systemic write. The earlier figure came from a
legacy SQLite file the application can no longer open, and it named the wrong
region as well, so the revision's own note is corrected to what the live
database holds.

The table now comes from the registry the importer itself reads, so a base that
can be loaded can be priced, and the response schemas bind the same object
instead of a second copy of the same construction kept in step by a comment.
PT_SAOPAULO resolves again. It was excluded as a mislabel on the reasoning that
Sao Paulo is Brazil, which is true of the v3 snapshot key and false of the
global family, where it is the region id of a card the loader will happily
import. The cost item service fills a blank currency from the region too; it
used to persist whatever the caller sent unless the item belonged to a catalog.

A region no base declares still resolves to nothing. Stamping a default there
turns "we do not know" into a wrong answer that reads exactly like a right one,
so the backfill leaves those rows blank and reports the count instead. On the
measured database there were none to leave: all 55 718 filled, none left over.
Run twice, the second pass reports zero blank before and zero filled, and a row
already carrying a different currency under the same region comes through
untouched.

The tests read the stored column, never a response schema. Three read paths
already fill a blank currency from the region on the way out, so a test that
creates an item and reads it back through the API layer stays green with every
write path broken.

ci: gate t() keys that no locale file can answer

Both locale guards we already run start from a key that exists. The escape
guard reads locale files, the leak guard compares a locale value against
en.ts, and neither can say anything about a key that is in no locale file at
all, because there is nothing to read and nothing to compare. The call site
still renders, since t(key, {defaultValue}) falls back to its default, so the
string reaches all 29 languages in English while tsc, the build, vitest and
all three hygiene gates report green.

That is how #175 shipped. service.sla_breached and service.sla_late were
converted from English literals into keys, no locale file ever received them,
and the SLA chip read in English in every language through a full release.

The new guard resolves every t() call site carrying a defaultValue against
all 29 bundles and fails on any key fewer than all of them can answer.
Counting CLDR plural forms matters: a counted key is reached through its
category, so meetings.attachment_n need never exist as a bare key, and
ignoring that reports 23 gaps where there are 13. The options object is
brace matched rather than regex matched, because a defaultValue is very
often a template literal and stopping at the first closing brace drops real
call sites and makes the guard quietly narrower than it says it is.

The 13 keys it finds today are recorded in i18n_orphan_baseline.json as an
explicit key to missing-locale set, the same shape the leak baseline uses and
for the same reason: a count cannot tell a repaired locale from a newly
broken one, and a bare key list goes green on the first locale filled in. The
set may only shrink. Fixing them is task #200, and it is not a locale add:
all eight of the wholly missing ones pass a JS template literal as their
default, so the call sites have to hand their values to i18next first.

An empty parse fails rather than passes. Finding nothing and not having
looked must not print the same result.

fix(desktop): bundle PostgreSQL's own loadable modules on Linux and macOS

The desktop app stopped at "Starting the local database" on Ubuntu based
distributions because initdb could not load $libdir/dict_snowball, which it
needs while running snowball_create.sql during bootstrap.

The hook that collects the embedded PostgreSQL tree used PyInstaller's
collect_data_files. That helper is documented to return only files which are
not shared libraries, and it decides that from the suffix alone: it excludes
every entry in importlib.machinery.all_suffixes(). On Linux and macOS that list
contains .so, which is exactly how PostgreSQL names its own loadable modules,
so dict_snowball, plpgsql, pgoutput, the pgvector module and every encoding
converter were dropped from the bundle. On Windows those same modules are
named .dll, which is not a Python extension suffix, so they came through and
the Windows installer worked. The versioned support libraries were never
affected either, because a name ending in .so.5 does not match the .so suffix,
which is why the cluster got far enough to run initdb and fail inside it.

The hook now walks the pginstall tree itself and classifies each file by where
it sits rather than by what it is named, so the layout PostgreSQL needs to

points at the rows. The new PG test compares row ids across the rename, because

feat(contracts): let a tenant author and version its own clause templates

A clause template was a module constant. You could read the eleven standard
forms we ship and you could not create, amend or version one, which makes them
samples rather than a feature, and it is the first thing the community request
named.

Two new tables hold authored templates and their clauses. Versions of one
template share a code and are told apart by a version number, so uniqueness is
on the pair. A template is editable while it is a draft; publishing freezes it,
and the next edit opens version N+1 with the clauses copied by value rather
than mutating a version some contract already names. Archiving retires a
version without deleting it, because a contract drawn from it still has to
resolve.

The built-in catalogue stays where it is, as constants. Seeding it into the
table would reach almost nobody: the deploy path is create_all plus alembic
stamp head and never walks the revision chain, and the module startup hook gets
no session and is not ordered against table creation. The two halves meet in
one repository method instead, and every entry it yields carries source and
editable so a caller never has to infer which half it came from. No database
constraint can stop an authored code shadowing a built-in one, since half the
namespace is not in the database, so that check lives in a single function
every write path calls and the property it exists for is a test.

Contracts gain template_code and template_version, both or neither. A code
without a version would mean the contract was drawn from whatever is current,
so publishing version 3 would quietly restate what an already signed contract
says it came from. The version is resolved when the contract is created and
kept from then on. A built-in stores version 0, which reads as not a versioned
template. A clone carries the source's pair rather than re-resolving, so
cloning a 2024 contract does not silently upgrade it to this year's clauses.

Writing the tests turned up a real fault in the version chain. The guard
against a second open draft was reading the current version, which answers with
the latest published row, so once version 2 was open as a draft the guard never
fired and another call would branch version 3 off version 1. It asks the whole
lineage now.

Sixteen tests in the PostgreSQL lane, which is where they belong: the union of
constants and rows, the unique constraint, and a contract keeping its pinned
version after a later one is published are all things a stub would pass without
telling you anything.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(contracts): author clause templates and put a contract up for signature

Two halves of contract lifecycle management that were missing. Clause templates
now have versions, and a contract can be sent for electronic signature from the
screen that decides whether signing is allowed at all.

Templates get a lineage. A built-in can be forked into an editable copy that
keeps its clause numbers, a published version refuses edits and opens the next
one, and only one draft can be open at a time. The contract records the exact
version it was drawn from, because a version that nothing points at is
decorative. A contract drawn from no template stores neither half rather than
half a pair.

The signing side had a gap that looked like a feature. Contracts carried their
own sign endpoint that only moved a status, and the signing module knew how to
collect signatures from named parties but had no idea contracts existed. The
new bridge builds a document reference and a content hash from the contract and
its party register, so a session is filed under the contract it is about and
the signatories come from the parties rather than being typed again. The hash
covers the commercial terms and the party list and deliberately leaves out
status, signed_at, metadata and the timestamps, since those move because of
signing, and folding them in would make every signature stale the moment the
next one was recorded. Editing anything that matters recomputes the hash and
pushes it onto the open session, which is what lets the screen name the parties
who signed an earlier version and ask them to sign again.

Opening a session runs the same compliance check the gate runs. Finding out
that a contract is blocked after every party has signed is finding out too
late. Only a draft can be put up for signature, one session can be outstanding
at a time, and applying the outcome holds the contract in draft until every
required role has signed rather than activating on the first signature.

The panel lives inside the gate modal for the same reason, below the findings,
and stays disabled until the gate has answered, because an unknown status is
not a draft. On a declined or expired session it does not say anyone is
awaiting a signature, since nobody can act on that.

Contracts does not import signing at module load. If the signing module is not
installed the endpoints answer 503 and the rest of the register carries on.

Eighty locale keys across all 29 languages. Ten of them are the signing
module's own capability and status labels, which its page was already asking
for and no locale file carried, so every language was rendering them in
English.

fix(contracts): stop inventing a signatory, and stop the gate closing itself

by reading it.

A contract with nobody on its party register used to get a signatory made up
for it. The register carries a counterparty type, which is a category, and a
counterparty id that may point into either the contact register or the
subcontractor one, so no name is reachable from the contract row itself. The
gap was filled with the contract's own title, which produced a signature
record attesting that a party named after the document had signed it. On
paper whose only purpose is to record who agreed to what, a placed name is
worse than a refusal, so the session is now refused with a message naming the
fix. The refusal is a stopgap in the wrong place and there is a task open to
turn it into a compliance rule, so the gate disables the button with its own
reason instead of the user learning by pressing it.

Every test in the bridge suite built its contract with parties, which is
exactly how the invented name shipped. Two cases now cover the empty register
and the register that holds only a consultant, who is not a signatory to the
contract.

The compliance gate closed itself on any click inside it. The drawer that
opens it closes on a click reaching its outermost element, and that element is
also the React parent of the modal. A portal moves the DOM node to the end of
the body but React still routes events to the React parent, so pressing
anything in the gate read as a click on the drawer backdrop and tore both
down. Nobody hit it before because the gate's other buttons close it anyway;
it only shows on a control meant to leave the modal open, which is what the
signing panel is. The close handler now sits on the backdrop it belongs to,
and WideModal contains its own clicks so no other caller inherits the same
trap. The test for it fails on the old code.

stays a draft. Every contract shipping as active left the register with
nothing standing between agreeing a deal and billing it: the compliance gate
and the signature only appear on a draft, so the demo could show the whole

being tuned towards each other.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(migrations): shorten a constraint name PostgreSQL cannot accept

Reported from a production upgrade. v3280 named a foreign key at 65
characters, PostgreSQL truncates identifiers at 63, and SQLAlchemy
refuses to emit a name it knows will be cut, so the revision raised
before sending any DDL. PostgreSQL runs DDL inside a transaction, so
that rolled back the entire upgrade and a site coming from 14.0.0
received none of the eighteen pending revisions rather than stopping at
the offending one. The contracts feature could not be installed on
PostgreSQL at all.

The name is now scoped to its own table without repeating the referenced
table, which is how the primary key and the unique constraint either side
of it on the same table were already spelled.

Every test we had passed, because they run on SQLite, where the limit
does not exist, which is how this shipped. So the scan comes with it: it
walks every revision and fails on any identifier over 63 characters, as a
string scan rather than a database round trip so it stays cheap enough to
sit in the blocking lane without a service container. It carries its own
red proof, feeding the detector the exact name that broke the release and
asserting it is flagged, and a second case pins that prose and raw SQL
are not reported, because a guard that cries wolf gets muted. One
offender existed in the whole history and it is this one.

Reported by bvisible.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(dwg-takeoff): give a block its geometry and stop filing it as a sheet

The parser stored a bounding box and the service recomputed one from the
same entities, and the two disagreed about the same drawing because the
parser read a field no writer emits. Nothing compared them, so both were
green for as long as they have both existed. There is one function now
and both callers ask it.

Block definitions were filed as layouts, which is why the sheet picker
offered entries that are not sheets and why auto-selecting the first
layout could land on a door. A definition now carries a block tag and no
layout at all, so the existing sheet filter drops it without an edit, and
the geometry it was already carrying becomes usable instead of dead
weight. Each referenced definition ships once and the client places it
per insert using the scale and rotation that have been on the wire and
unread since before this issue. A server side join would have multiplied
geometry by placement count, so five hundred placements of a forty entity
block would cost twenty thousand records instead of forty.

Definition members carry their own authoring layer, usually zero rather
than the layer of the insert that places them, so the layers filter has
to exempt them or the block arrives empty. Their visibility belongs to
the insert, which is the CAD rule anyway.

Rotation was ezdxf degrees for text and inserts on the DXF path and
radians on the DWG path, and the viewer feeds it straight to a canvas
rotate, which takes radians. A right angle was rendering as ninety
radians. Both writers emit radians now.

chore(release): bring the desktop crate into the version check

The release check read six version literals and the desktop crate was
not among them, so the manifest and its lockfile had drifted eleven
minor releases behind everything else without anything noticing. They
are read now, which makes nine literals across eight files, because the

separately rather than together, since breaking both at once cannot
tell you whether the second one is read at all.

fix(sheets): read a title block field without taking its neighbours

The scale pattern allowed \s inside its character class, and \s matches a
newline, so the capture ran past the end of the label line and the trailing
\S* took the first token of the next one. A title block reading "SCALE: 1:50"
above "REV C" was stored as "1:50\nREV", and the stored value is what the
sheet detail drawer prints.

Bounding the capture to one line is not enough on its own. A title block lays
its fields out in columns and the text extractor joins the cells sharing a
visual row into a single line, so "SCALE: 1:50    DRAWN: AB    DATE: ..."
arrives as one line holding three fields. The value now ends at the first
column gap or at the next field label, whichever comes first, in a helper that
can be tested on its own.

Two more faults in the same pattern, found on the way and covered by nothing.
There was no "=" in the character class, so the imperial form was cut at the
equals and stored as the first half. The pattern that reads that form
correctly sits below the labelled one in the list and therefore never ran on a
page that labels its scale. And the sheet title pattern captured to the end of
the joined row the same way, so a title sharing a row with the drawn-by cell
was stored carrying it. The title keeps the wider bound of the two: it is free
text, and wide letter spacing inside one cell produces the same run of spaces
a column gap does, so only a following label ends it.

Written scales survive unchanged. NTS, N.T.S., VARIES and AS NOTED all read as
written, which the earlier draft of this fix would have lost.

fix(sheets): let a re-uploaded drawing set supersede the previous one

Splitting a PDF wrote every row with is_current true and previous_version_id
null, and nothing else ever wrote those two columns. So uploading a revised
set gave the register two rows per sheet number, both claiming to be the
current revision, distinguishable only by which parent document they came
from. The columns to say otherwise were already on the model and the read path
that follows them was already written; nothing populated them.

It reached further than the register. check_completeness reconciles a project
against a drawing index by number and reads current_only, so it was handed a
doubled ACTUAL set and every re-uploaded sheet looked like a duplicate.

A sheet number already current in the project is now superseded: the new row
points at the one it replaces and that one stops being current. Nothing is
deleted and no column is overwritten. The chain key is the project and the
sheet number, deliberately not the parent document. canonical_name_for
composes the document id into the FileVersion chain key so that two unrelated
PDFs do not merge into one history, which is right for a file index and wrong
here, because a revised set arrives as a new PDF and recognising that its
A-201 supersedes the previous A-201 is the entire point.

Two cases decided explicitly rather than by accident. A page whose title block
cannot be read has no key, so it never chains; otherwise every unreadable page
in a project would collect into one bogus history. A number carried by two
pages of the same upload is a fault in that file: the earlier page takes the
link, the later stays current and unlinked, and it is logged, because
otherwise the duplication reads as ours.

get_version_chain sorted on created_at alone while its own comment claimed
otherwise. Rows from one create_many share a flush, so ties fell to whatever
order the walk appended. Dead decoration until now, load bearing from now, so
it gets a stable tiebreak.

fix(tasks): ask PostgreSQL for containment instead of for a string match

Filtering tasks by a BIM element returned a server error on PostgreSQL, on
every deployment, since the filter was added. That is the call the BIM viewer
makes to show the defects and inspections attached to whatever element you
clicked, and PostgreSQL is the only database we support in production, so
there was no configuration where this worked.

The column is declared as portable JSON so SQLite can carry it too. On that
type SQLAlchemy compiles contains() to a string LIKE rather than to the JSONB
containment operator, and the bound value still arrives typed as JSONB, so the
statement is rejected outright. Compiled both forms against the PostgreSQL
dialect to be sure rather than reasoning about it:

  before  bim_element_ids LIKE '%%' || $1::JSONB || '%%'
  after   CAST(bim_element_ids AS JSONB) @> $1::JSONB

Failing loudly is the lucky half of this. A string LIKE that had happened to
compile would have matched on substrings of ids and returned plausible wrong
rows instead.

The same lookup exists for requirements, and it is correct. Its docstring says
it mirrors this function, so it was written by copying this one, the author hit
this exact problem, fixed it in the copy with a comment explaining why the cast
is required, and never came back. The comment above the original claimed the
containment operator the code did not use, which is why it read as fine.

Verified against real PostgreSQL, not only by compiling: the integration test
that had been failing with invalid input syntax for type json now passes.

fix(core): ask for the permission key that exists, not a bare "admin"

Three routes were gated on the literal "admin": enabling a module, disabling
a module, and fetching the daily ECB reference rates. No module registers a
permission by that name. RequirePermission returns False for a key the
registry has never seen, and an admin caller short-circuits above that check,
so all three behaved as admin-only and nothing could tell the difference. The
fixtures authenticate as an admin, so no test could either.

Nothing was over-granted, but two things were quietly broken. The admin

namespace unclaimed, so the day any module registered a permission spelled
"admin" the access policy of all three would have changed with it.

system.modules.disable, which register_core_permissions has been registering
at admin level all along and which nothing was using. The rate fetch gets the
permissions.py the module never had, plus the on_startup hook that runs it:
the loader auto-imports router, models, hooks, events and validators, but
never permissions.py, so a module without that hook registers nothing.
