feat(einvoice-clearance): record what a tax authority actually answered

The platform could already build an EN 16931 invoice and hand it to a
network. What it could not do is deal with the countries where an invoice
is not valid until a government says so. Those three regimes look alike
from the outside and are not. Under clearance the authority's identifier
is what makes the document legally valid. Under reporting the invoice was
already valid and the filing is either late or not. On a network there is
no authority at all, so a delivered document has been delivered and
nothing more.

That is why there are nine statuses rather than eight. A routed network
document is delivered, never cleared, because calling it cleared would
tell a reader a tax authority answered for it when none exists. The
adapter never picks the status. It reports whether the platform accepted,
and the regime decides what accepting meant.

Submission is gated by the rules run directly rather than through the
validation engine, because the engine's call is guarded so that a broken
rule cannot stop somebody recording state, and a guard that swallows a
failure is the wrong thing to stand between an invoice and a tax
authority.

A document whose adapter died before the platform answered stays
submitted rather than being resent or reverted, and an operator resolves
it from what the portal shows, with a note and, in a clearance country,
the identifier. Resending risks two cleared invoices for one sale and
reverting loses the fact that something was sent.

No government adapter ships. The reference one is offline, deterministic,
and refuses a profile that is not marked sandbox. 75 tests.

feat(tax-withholding): deduct what the statute says, not what one country's rule says

Retention was already handled twice over, once on a progress claim and
once on a subcontract ledger, and both release the money back at
practical completion. Statutory withholding never comes back. It goes to
a tax authority, and whether a payment is subject to it depends on the
payee's verification status on the day rather than on anything in the
contract. So this is a new register rather than another column beside
retention, and nothing here is called withholding_amount, which is a name
retention already owns in two places.

The taxable base is where a plausible shortcut goes wrong. Gross minus
materials minus tax reads like the rule because it is the rule in the
United Kingdom. Under section 48 EStG the deduction is taken from the
Gegenleistung, which includes the tax and carves nothing out for
materials, so a flat rule would under-withhold on every German payment.
Each subtraction is a property of the scheme, and an unqualified record
is judged the strict way rather than the lenient one.

An expired verification moves the payee to the higher band rather than
quietly keeping the reduced one, which is the direction that does not
leave somebody owing a tax authority the difference.

Five schemes and four reverse-charge rules ship as data rather than in
the migration, and none of them installs itself. A fresh deployment has
an empty regime table until somebody chooses the rates, because rates go
stale and a stale rate that arrived on its own is worse than an empty
table somebody has to fill. 67 tests.

feat(payment-clock): treat a payment deadline as the statute treats it

In the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore and
Malaysia the dates around a payment application are fixed by statute, not
agreed between the parties, and missing one has a defined legal
consequence rather than a commercial one. Silence past the payment notice
deadline makes the sum applied for the notified sum, and the payer owes
it. A contract register that stores a due date as a plain field cannot
express that, because the interesting value is not the date, it is what
happens when nobody answers by it.

The module holds the regime, computes the due date, the notice deadlines
and the final date for payment from the reference date, records the
notices that were actually served, and reports the consequence when a
deadline passes unanswered. Eight regimes ship as data rather than in the
migration, so a jurisdiction can be corrected without a schema change.

The clock points at a progress claim or a subcontractor payment
application by plain id and never by foreign key, so neither of those
modules has to be installed for this one to load. Category is regional:
a deployment that never works in a security-of-payment jurisdiction
should be able to switch it off.

The tests are named in the PostgreSQL lane in the same commit. Anything
under tests/unit that is not named there runs in no lane that blocks a
merge, so a guard added without the step would pass review and gate
nothing.

fix(desktop): sign what the sidecar unpacks, not only the wrapper around it

The macOS app reached "Starting the application server" and stopped there,
on a clean machine whose owner had already cleared Gatekeeper by hand:

  code signature in '.../_MEIxxxxxx/Python.framework/Versions/3.12/Python'
  not valid for use in process: mapping process and mapped file
  (non-platform) have different Team IDs

An ad-hoc signature carries no Team ID, so two ad-hoc binaries can never
mismatch. The real Team ID was not on the process, it was on the payload.
The build machine's Python framework is signed by whoever built that
Python, PyInstaller packs it into the archive verbatim, and the onefile
bootloader extracts it to a temporary directory at launch and dlopens it
from there. dyld compares the two signatures and refuses the load, before
a line of Python runs.

So the fix is to make the payload's identity match the process's rather
than to grant the process permission to ignore the mismatch. Setting
codesign_identity in the spec makes PyInstaller ad-hoc sign every Mach-O
it collects, not just the executable wrapped around them. That needs no
entitlement and no hardened runtime, so the ad-hoc rule in
docs/desktop/MACOS_NOTARIZATION.md still holds: sign with "-", no
timestamp. It is macOS only, because naming the option on Windows would
be a lie about what the build does there.

This is also a prerequisite for notarization rather than a stopgap. The
notary service sees a onefile sidecar as one Mach-O and never inspects
the archive appended to it, so a notarized build made without this would
sign the wrapper, pass review, and still fail to start, with the mismatch
now against a real Team ID instead of none.

The second half matters more than the first. Nothing in this workflow ever
executed the sidecar it built. The bundle check reads the archive's table
of contents, which answers whether a file is present and cannot answer
whether the binary starts, and the signature step at the end is explicitly
non-fatal on every branch. A binary that cannot reach its own interpreter
passed both. There is now a step that runs the signed sidecar with the
version subcommand and fails the job on a non-zero exit or a missing
version line. It runs on all three platforms, because "does it start at
all" catches the missing-database-module class of break more directly than
reading the archive does, and it costs seconds. Team ID matching does not
depend on the quarantine flag, so the runner reproduces the user's failure
even though nothing there was downloaded from the web.

Signing moves into the sidecar job, ahead of that run, so the binary being
tested is the binary users get and a signing change has a test loop that
does not involve the release path. The bundling job still verifies the
signature survived the artifact round trip. A manual run now defaults to
sidecar only, because the bundling step names the release after the git
ref and a manual run from a branch would otherwise open a draft release
called "main".

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

ci(desktop): measure the signature inside the archive, not only on its wrapper

The control run built from this workflow with the spec's codesign_identity
reverted started on the macOS runner just as happily as main did. That kills
the meaning the smoke step was carrying: green there does not tell us the
signing fix works, because red never happens there either. Whether dyld
enforces Team ID matching depends on the policy applied to the process, and a
binary built on the machine that runs it, never downloaded and never
quarantined, is judged leniently.

So measure the property instead of the behaviour. The failure the user hit is
about what the onefile archive carries: the bootloader unpacks those members at
launch and dyld maps them into a process that has no Team ID of its own. A
member signed by someone else is the mismatch, and that is a static fact about
the artifact, readable without executing anything and without depending on this
machine choosing to enforce the rule.

The new script opens the built executable as the PyInstaller archive it is,
extracts every Mach-O member and groups them by Team ID. Run on both arms it
answers what the smoke test cannot: whether the spec line changes the payload at
all. It reports and never decides, so it can print evidence on every build.

The comment on the smoke step claimed the runner reproduces the user's failure.
It does not, and leaving that sentence there would hand the next reader a green
gate to trust.

fix(tests): build the pg schema from the same metadata the tests read back

The PostgreSQL lane went red on 0c94892b0 with "relation oe_translation_cache
does not exist". The table is declared on Base.metadata at import time by
app.core.translation.cache, and nothing imports that module until something asks
for a translation. The lane registers models, calls create_all, and only later
runs seeders that pull the translation path in. So the import landed after the
schema was built: the table was in the metadata and not in the database.

That is invisible until a test walks the metadata to decide what to query.
test_no_user_facing_seed_text_says_demo does exactly that, on purpose, so that a
leak in a column nobody thought about still fails. It asked PostgreSQL for every
character column the metadata knows, including one no CREATE TABLE had reached.

Registering the module with the other core imports puts the table in the
metadata before create_all runs, so the schema the lane builds and the metadata
it reads back are the same thing. Nothing changes for the running product, where
the cache creates its table on first use with checkfirst.

fix(desktop): read the artifact instead of reasoning about it

The macOS start failure reported against 14.4.0 was diagnosed from the error
text and from the build machine, never from the file that fails. The file
disagrees. The 14.4.0 sidecar was taken apart member by member, along with two
later builds that differ only in how the packer is told to sign, and all three
are the same artifact in this respect: 402 Mach-O members, every one ad-hoc
with no team identity at all. Nothing inside the archive can disagree with the
process about an identity none of them carries, so whatever supplies one on the
affected machine comes from outside the file, and the signing change written
for this cannot be what makes it start.

The archive reading becomes a gate on that basis rather than a diagnostic,
which is a narrower claim than the one it replaces: it fails the build the day
a dependency or a packer upgrade starts sealing a vendor-signed binary inside
the archive, and it says nothing about the report that prompted it. The
comments that asserted the old explanation are replaced by what was measured.

PyInstaller is pinned rather than taken from a range. It decides how every
collected binary is laid out and re-signed, so when one build behaves
differently from the one before it, the first question is whether the packer
changed, and a range cannot answer that later.

fix(dwg-takeoff): paint one sheet at the size the drawing asks for

Issue 426. A drawing came back from upload looking nothing like the source,
and reloading showed it briefly right before it changed. Two defects, and the
second of them shipped twice.

The scene handed to the fit was the union of every sheet, because the sheet a
reader has not picked yet was resolved by an effect that runs after the first
frame is on screen. Model space and paper space share neither origin nor scale,
so a box around both frames neither: an 18 m building and a 400 mm title block
fitted together collapse the sheet to a speck drawn over the plan. The sheet on
screen is now derived rather than latched, so the first painted frame and the
frame after somebody touches the sheet strip are the same frame. A pick naming
a sheet the current drawing does not have is treated as no pick, which is what
stops a file switch painting an empty canvas. The union survives for a drawing
whose entities carry no sheet at all, where it is the right answer.

Text was clamped to a readable band. The band was removed in f936eace4 and put
back five hours later in 14aef60d5, with a docstring arguing it was intended,
and both commits are contained in v14.4.0, so that release advertised the fix
and shipped without it. Nothing in the suite could tell, because every fixture
in it was small enough that the band never bound. A label now reaches the
screen at its authored height times the zoom, so a heading authored eight times
a room tag arrives eight times its size and the 800:1 range in the fixture
reaches the screen as 800:1 rather than as 9:1. The two defects are one bug
seen from two ends: font size is a function of the viewport, the viewport is a
function of the scene, so the wrong scene made the same 8 mm title block label
occupy 123 mm of the sheet.

Text display is a reader preference now rather than a constant, with the size
multiplier applied to the authored height rather than to a banded result, since
applied to a banded result it can only move every label together and leaves a
flattened sheet flattened at every setting.

Approving a timesheet posts its hours and then writes any daywork lines
through to a daywork sheet. That second half is deliberately best effort, and
the code said so, catching every exception and logging it so an approval is
never held hostage by it. On PostgreSQL that promise was not kept. A failed
statement puts the surrounding transaction into an aborted state, so catching
the exception changes nothing about what comes after it: the status update that
posts the hours fails too, and the approval fails with a rollback error naming
nothing to do with daywork. The write-through now runs inside a savepoint,
which confines the damage to the daywork writes and makes the docstring true on
the database we ship.

Sheet numbers come from the highest number already used rather than from the
row count. A count only produces a free number while the existing numbers run
one to n with no gaps, and they do not have to: a deleted sheet, or a sheet
numbered by anything other than this method, leaves a count pointing at a
number already taken, and the unique constraint then rejects the insert, which
on PostgreSQL takes the caller's whole transaction down with it.

The module also seeds demo data now. It shipped without a seeder, so a demo
project showed the module empty, which reads as a module that does nothing. It
runs after variations so a daywork booking can name an open variation order and
after the equipment seed so plant hours price off a real rental, and it guards
per project on an existing timesheet rather than on a global marker, so
enriching one project again does not depend on what another project holds.

Covered by two tests in the PostgreSQL lane, seven cases: the seed is
idempotent per project and its rows come back through the schema, and an
approval survives a daywork write-through that fails.

ci: let the release signing workflow reach a release again

It has not run since v8.0.0 on 13 June, so every release published after
that one, fourteen minors including 14.5.0, carries no checksum file and no
signature. Nothing reported this, because a workflow that is never
triggered has no red run to notice.

The cause is the trigger. release.yml creates the release with
softprops/action-gh-release authenticated by secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN, and
GitHub deliberately does not start a workflow from an event that a
GITHUB_TOKEN produced, so the release published event this listens for is
never delivered. It listens for the completion of Desktop Release now,
which is the run that finishes last with installers attached and therefore
the first moment there is a full set of assets to check. A Desktop Release
started by hand against a branch is filtered out, since head_branch is a
branch name there and there is no release behind it.

The second half is worse and would have made a manual run useless. The
upload step carried if github.event_name == 'release', which is the one
event that cannot arrive here. Every reachable path therefore downloaded
the assets, produced SHA256SUMS, signed it with cosign, and then skipped
the upload: a green run that published nothing. The filter is gone.

Backfilling signatures for the releases between v8.0.0 and 14.5.0 is not
done here. That is thirty-odd tags and it should be a decision rather than
a side effect of this fix.

ci: publish the licence inventory that stopped shipping at v8.0.0

The SBOM and licence workflow hung off `release: [published]`, the same event
Release Signing hung off, and it died on the same day for the same reason.
v8.0.0 was published by hand, so the event arrived and both workflows ran. Every

None of the three jobs carried a timeout, so each inherited the six hour
default. A hung leg therefore cost six hours of runner time, and the matrix runs
three legs in parallel, so a wedged sidecar build could hold eighteen hours
before anything noticed. Nothing had gone wrong yet; the exposure was simply
open.

The caps come from measurement rather than from a guess, over v14.3.0, v14.4.0,
v14.5.0 and five sidecar-only runs. Sidecar: Linux 14.4 to 15.2 minutes,
Windows 15.6 to 17.8, macOS 25.6 to 34.4, capped at 75. Desktop: Windows 27.8 to
29.6, macOS 26.4 to 36.2, Linux 119.2 to 123.5, capped at 240. Windows signing
runs in well under a minute today because there are no signing secrets and it
downloads nothing, so it is capped at 30 rather than at anything close to its
current cost, since the day the secrets arrive it starts moving two installers
of about 350 MB each and the timeout should not be what discovers that.

Every cap is roughly twice the slowest leg ever observed, so none of them can
fire on a healthy build. The Linux desktop leg is the interesting number: at
about two hours it is four times the other two, it is stable within four minutes
across three releases, and it is the normal cost of building the bundle there
without a Rust cache rather than a symptom. A matrix job takes one timeout for
every OS in it, so that leg sets the value.

distribution and one certainly is not, so each cap sits an order of magnitude

fix(desktop): stop turning on a runtime we have no identity to satisfy

The macOS app stopped at "Starting the application server" with an error
naming a Team ID mismatch on Python.framework, and every census of the
sidecar archive came back clean: 402 Mach-O members inspected, none carrying a
Team ID, so none able to disagree with the process about one. The census was
right and it was measuring the wrong file. It runs on the raw PyInstaller
output, two signing passes before anything reaches a user.

Read from the shipped bundle instead, the sidecar carries
flags=0x10002(adhoc,runtime) with no entitlements. Ad-hoc plus the hardened
runtime means library validation is enforced with nothing able to satisfy it.
Library validation does not ask whether the process and the file it maps agree
on a team, it asks whether the mapped file carries the loader team or a
platform identity, and an ad-hoc file carries neither. So an ad-hoc process
under the hardened runtime is refused its own unpacked payload, and macOS
words that refusal as a Team ID disagreement although no Team ID exists on
either side. That is the one shape a member census structurally cannot see:
every member is clean and the load still fails.

Nothing in this repository asked for the hardened runtime. It is serde
default_true in tauri-utils, and our config set only signingIdentity, which is
why grepping for the flag proved nothing. The config now says so out loud and
points at Entitlements.plist, which has sat in the tree unreferenced by any
build step since it was added. Notarization is what makes the hardened runtime
worth having; until then it costs a launch and buys nothing, so the
notarization guide now flips the line back to true as part of that change
rather than treating it as a fresh addition.

Two measurements are added so this cannot hide again. The round-trip re-sign
now prints the identity it leaves behind, because --verify says a signature is
intact and never says whose it is, and two signing passes sit between the two
censuses. And the census now runs a second time on the sidecar inside the
produced .app, with --require-member so the file named in the failure report
cannot clear a run by never having been opened. It warns rather than fails
while the measurement is new: no healthy baseline exists for it yet, and a red
run here skips the Windows signing job for a reason unrelated to Windows.

The verdict in the census script was one-sided as well. It caught members
carrying a team against a wrapper without one, and reported the reverse as all
clear - which is the shape a real Developer ID would produce, over members
PyInstaller leaves ad-hoc. Both directions now report, and a run that could
not read enough to decide says which items it could not read instead of
printing a count.

Not tested on a Mac from here. The mechanism is measured off the shipped

feat(module-builder): let a module be described as data and rendered from it

Installed modules now live in the instance data directory rather than in the
source tree, so a platform upgrade cannot take a user module with it and an
operator running a packaged build has somewhere to put one. The loader imports
by package path, so the runtime directory is appended to app.modules.__path__
at startup and everything downstream finds it unchanged. Appended and never
prepended: a shipped module always wins a name collision, and the installed
copy that will never be imported is named in the log rather than left to look
like it is running.

On top of that, a module builder whose input is a specification rather than
code. A ModuleSpec says what the record is, which fields it carries and which
rules must hold; the generator renders manifest, models, schemas, repository,
service, router, permissions, validators, locales, tests and a readme from it,
deterministically. An assistant drafting a module writes the spec and never
Python, so the worst a bad draft can do is describe something the spec layer
refuses. Identifiers are checked against the shape of an identifier, the
keyword list and the names the generated row already uses, because a field
called id or metadata parses fine and collides at import time on the user
server.

The generated screen is not a React page. The frontend is a compiled bundle,
so a module installed at runtime cannot add a compiled screen without a
rebuild; each generated module serves its own spec instead and the platform
renders list, detail and form from it.

Tests assert the strong claim rather than the cheap one: a spec that validates
renders a module that compiles, that ruff accepts at the project settings, and
whose own generated tests pass. That caught two real defects in the rendered
code, a method shadowing a builtin and a branch-local datetime import that made
a sibling branch raise UnboundLocalError.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(module-builder): let a generated module create the table it declares

A module installed at runtime lives outside the repository, so it cannot
carry an Alembic revision. A revision file in the instance data directory is
either invisible to upgrade or, once made visible, collides with the
repository head on the next platform upgrade. Until now the generator
rendered a model and nothing created the table, so the first read against a
freshly installed module would have failed on a missing relation.

The module now creates its own table from the same model the code reads,
through Table.create with checkfirst, called from the on_startup hook the
loader already awaits. That hook is also where permissions are registered,
which is where the rest of the platform does it.

Scoping matters more than it looks. MetaData.create_all and drop_all take a
tables argument that filters tables and only tables: standalone sequences on
the shared metadata are visited regardless, so dropping a generated table
that way took a sequence belonging to another module with it. The PostgreSQL
lane caught it on DROP SEQUENCE oe_progress_entry_seq_seq and now asserts the
sequence listing is unchanged on both create and drop.

Two more things the new tests found. The generated model imported GUID from a
module that does not export it, so no generated module could ever have been
imported. And the import block was a fixed list, so a spec without dates, money
or a project scope rendered imports nothing used and ruff refused the module
the builder had just written.

Money now uses the platform MoneyType rather than a bare Numeric. It still
compiles to NUMERIC(18, 2) on PostgreSQL and it returns Decimal on every
backend, where plain Numeric can hand back a float.

Deleting is a manager action now, separate from writing, as elsewhere.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(module-builder): install a described module into the running server

The builder had a renderer and a place to put what it renders. This adds the
half a user meets: a service that drafts a spec through the connected
assistant, refuses one that cannot be built, previews every file before any of
it lands, installs, lists and removes again.

Installing is one step or none. If the files land and the module then fails to
load, the directory goes and the key is free, because a module nobody can see
that still owns its name is worse than a refusal. Removing keeps the table by
default, since regretting a module is not the same as wanting to lose what was
recorded with it, and dropping the data is a separate ask under its own
permission.

Three things had to be fixed under it. A module's own tables and mapped classes
outlive the import, so reinstalling a corrected module raised a duplicate table
error and could only be recovered by restarting. Uninstalling left the module's
permissions registered, still granted to roles with nothing behind them.
And the core-module guard on the persisted state fired in both directions, so
loading a generated module's dependencies failed with a message about disabling
a module nobody had asked to disable.

Where a module is served now comes from one place. The loader mounts on the
hyphenated form of the directory name, so a key with an underscore answers on a
path without one, and the API reports that path rather than leaving the screen
to reassemble it.

fix(module-loader): take a disabled module's routes down again

Disabling a module removed its router by filtering app.routes on the path of
each entry. That worked while including a router copied its routes into the
application's own table. Current FastAPI does not copy: an include appends one
marker object holding the router, and the paths are resolved when a request
arrives. A marker has no path, so the filter matched nothing, removed nothing
and logged that it had removed the routes, while every endpoint of the disabled
module kept answering until the process restarted. The module builder's
uninstall goes through the same call, so a module whose files had been deleted
carried on serving from memory.

Removal now finds the router by identity, which is exact and takes the legacy
underscore mirror with it in the same pass, since both includes carry the same
router object. The prefix sweep stays for the releases that do copy and for
anything mounted under the prefix by other means. Editing app.routes in place is
invisible to the published schema, which is cached against a counter only the
router's own methods bump, so the cache is dropped as well; without that a
document generated before the removal kept describing a module that is gone.

Two readers of the route table are corrected the same way. _has_live_routes
decides whether enabling reloads a module, and answering no about a mounted one
made every enable mount it a second time. The AI security test walks the
application to prove the rate limit is still wired onto the four endpoints that
spend money with a provider; it had gone red on its own and was in no lane, so
nothing said so. Both now read through served_routes, which returns what the
OpenAPI document describes and behaves the same on either FastAPI.

feat(module-builder): build a module from a description and have it answer at once

A control in the top bar collects what a register has to hold over four
steps and installs the result into this instance's runtime module root,
where a platform upgrade cannot reach it. The assistant drafts the
description and never the Python: every file that would be written is on
screen before anything is written, and pressing install is what writes
it. The module is loaded straight after, so there is no restart to plan
and no second switch to find. That is the one place in this codebase
where a confirmed result takes effect immediately, and the confirmation
is the review step rather than a checkbox.

A module installed at runtime cannot ship a compiled screen, so there is
one screen for all of them. It reads the specification the module serves
and builds the form, the table and the account of what the module
refuses out of that. The route carries the module key and the address
comes from the server, because the loader owns the key to URL rule and a
second copy of that rule on this side would be a second place for it to
drift. Resolving it needs only the read permission, which every signed
in user has, while building and removing are administrator work and are
separate permissions from each other.

Money and quantities stay strings the whole way to the wire, so a bill
does not lose its last cent to a double on the way through a form. A
time typed into that form leaves as a zoned instant rather than as a
naive local one, without which the generated validator reads now as the
future for everyone east of UTC and refuses the record. An edit sends
the fields that changed and nothing else, so opening a record and
closing it does not rewrite a decimal nobody touched.

Eighty three strings in all 29 languages, none of them counted, so no
locale needs plural forms it does not have. The three pure TypeScript
test files join the named frontend list in the PostgreSQL lane. The five
component tests are left out on purpose and the reason is written beside
the list, because a silent omission there reads as coverage.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(i18n): compute a new locale key set instead of copying English

Adding a language here is not copy en.ts and translate it. en.ts carries 32,367
keys while every translated locale carries about 35,932, because English is
supplied at the call site as a defaultValue and only reaches en.ts when someone
put it there by hand. A locale built from en.ts silently drops 3,565 strings and
no gate notices, the new language just shows English on those screens forever.

No single locale is a safe template either. Arabic has plural forms a two-form
language never asks for, and Finnish, the obvious sibling for another one/other
language, is itself missing 33 ordinary keys. Grounding a new language in one
sibling inherits that sibling's gaps.

So the target set is computed: the union of every locale on disk minus the plural
categories the new language lacks, with the categories read from the language
through ICU rather than assumed. English source text is harvested from en.ts,
then the call site defaultValue, then the English field beside a Key field in the
playbooks and guides, and plan names the keys it found nothing for, because a key
with no English anywhere is its own bug.

The suffix alone never settles whether a key is a plural form. Of 58 stems ending
in _other, 34 are the dropdown word Other. Of 116 keys ending in a category word,
8 are ordinary sentences carried by all 29 locales, among them "Pick two
different versions" and a division by zero error. Dropping those from a two-form
language deletes real strings and then fails the orphan gate. A category form
counts as a plural only when the stem has a one or other sibling somewhere.

feat(costs): let the base picker say how deep each catalogue goes

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(dwg-takeoff): anchor the hatch to the drawing, and let the readouts move

Two findings from an external tester's report on the viewer, one about overlaps
that go away when you zoom in, one about navigation feeling slow.

The hatch spacing was the literal 8 and the pattern cache keyed on the colour and
that literal, so the pattern never answered the zoom at all. A hatched region
drawn small received the same 8 pixel grid as one drawn large, which filled it in
solid and covered the geometry underneath, and the same region drawn large kept a
grain far finer than the drawing had asked for. That is the whole shape of the
report: the overlap is not near a boundary, it is a hatch painting over its
neighbours, and zooming in does not fix it so much as make the region big enough
that a fixed grid stops swallowing it.

The spacing now moves with the view like everything else on the sheet, rounded to
whole pixels so the tile cache stays bounded against a continuous zoom, and
clamped at both ends. Below the floor the lines would fall closer together than
the screen can resolve, which is exactly the case that produced the solid block,
so the region is filled flat there instead, the way a drawing board stops
hatching a detail it has zoomed away from. The same flat fill covers a region too
small to hold one repeat. The screen extent that decides this comes out of the
vertex walk the path already does, so it costs four comparisons a vertex. The
decision is a pure function with its own tests, and the one that would have
caught the original is that two different zooms must not agree.

The coordinate box and the zoom badge were reading refs inside JSX. A ref does
not re-render, and the frame loop deliberately keeps React out of the drag path,
so through an entire pan or zoom the drawing moved while both numbers held
whatever the last render had captured. The canvas was never the slow part, but an
interface that does not answer the gesture is read as slowness. They are written
from the frame loop now, before the dirty check rather than after it, because a
re-render can put the inline display back while nothing is dirty and a readout
that waits for the next dirty frame is the same defect in a smaller window. Each
write is guarded by a comparison, so a still canvas does no DOM work.

While there: the group holding the zoom badge and the Fit button was gated on the
extents ref, which is filled in an effect. On the render right after a drawing
loads that ref is still null, so the Fit button was absent until some unrelated
re-render came along. It is gated on the entity list now, and the fit handler
already refuses when there are no extents.

Not addressed here, and both said plainly rather than quietly skipped. The block
name labels could also crowd each other when zoomed out, but that only matters if
the drawing has unresolved block references and there is nothing available to
establish that, so it stays a question on the issue. The text height clamp is
version dependent: it exists in v14.4.0 and was removed after it, so whether the
tester is looking at a live defect cannot be answered without the version string.

Reported through issue 58.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

perf(dwg-takeoff): stroke a run of same-styled entities once, not once each

The other half of the tester's report about navigation. The frozen readouts were
why the viewer looked unresponsive; this is what it actually costs to draw.

Every entity opened its own path and stroked it, and set five or six context
properties first. A canvas charges for both. A drawing is thousands of short
segments that mostly agree about their colour, so nearly all of that was spent
telling the canvas the same thing again.

Consecutive entities that would be stroked with the same style now go into one
path and are stroked once. Runs, not groups, and that is the whole design
constraint rather than a shortcut: sorting the list by colour would batch far
harder and would also change which line lands on top of which where two cross.
A viewer is judged on looking like the drawing, so the order stays exactly as it
arrived and only neighbours merge. A file whose colours alternate entity by
entity gains nothing and behaves exactly as before, which is what makes the run
form the safe form as well as the cheap one. On the one real fixture in the tree,
ten strokeable entities collapse to three stroke calls, and that measurement is
in the code rather than a claim about DXF in general.

Mechanically the five stroked types grew a path builder that appends to whatever
path is open, and the exported render functions became wrappers that open and
stroke one of their own, so a caller that wants a single entity drawn keeps
exactly what it had. The arc builders move to their own start point before
curving: inside a shared path, arc() is joined to the previous subpath by a
straight line, and that stray chord across the drawing is the one way this could
have changed a pixel. There is a test for it. Anything that fills or writes text
closes the batch first, so a half-built path is never left open across a fill.

The selected entity is given a style key nothing else can match. It has a wider
stroke and a glow, and it must break the run on both sides rather than lend that
to a neighbour or borrow a neighbour's plain style.

even though they are carried as strings, which is safe here in a way it is not
for arithmetic, because a double is precise enough to say which of two amounts

directions: flipping them to the top would open the column on a screen of
nothing and bury what was asked for.

empty list with what this module checks, which reads as checks that failed to

fix(i18n): stop the playbook English harvester from pairing keys with a neighbor's text

sibling_pairs() matched each <stem>Key field to its English sibling by
searching a 400-char window for the nearest occurrence of the sibling field
name. Two failure modes came out of that: a dense run of same-named sibling
fields (every case-playbook step's own label/title/what/why) made the
nearest-in-window match belong to an adjacent entry rather than the one it
was found for, and a paragraph-length value (longDescDefault and some
what/why text) could run past the window entirely, so the closing quote
never appeared inside it and the key got no source at all.

Replaced the window with exact token-sequence adjacency: tokenize every
`field: "value"` in the file in order, and pair a `<stem>Key` token with
whichever immediate neighbor carries the matching field name. There is no
"nearest" to get wrong, only the one token actually sitting next to this key
in its object literal. Verified against a from-scratch ground truth built by
parsing all 144 case-playbook files directly: 3983 pairs, 0 disagreements,
0 missing.

Also fixed escape() in cmd_assemble, a separate defect a locale session
found while translating: it doubled backslashes before checking for a real
newline, so a translated value that kept extract's own literal `\n` marker
untouched (the common case - most translators only retype the surrounding
words) came out as `\n` in the assembled .ts file instead of `\n`.

held the payment's gross against it without ever asking what currency the payment

feat(i18n): gate the plural form a language needs and English does not have

The orphan guard asks whether a key can be reached at all, and says in its
own comments that it deliberately stops there: a Russian file carrying only
_other counts as reachable, because reachable and complete are different
questions and conflating them would let one gate fail for a reason its
message does not state. This asks the second question.

It matters because i18next does not fall back inside a language. When the
form for a count is missing it walks the fallback chain and prints the
English, so a Turkish file holding _other and no _one shows an English
sentence for every count of one. Nothing else we own can see that. The key
is reachable, the value is not byte-identical to English, no escape was
dropped, and tsc and the build never read locale content at all.

Categories come from the language rather than from English. English has two
and would hold Arabic to two when it has six and Polish to two when it has
four. The table is generated from Intl.PluralRules, which is the same source
i18next consults at runtime, and it is embedded rather than read from node
because the hygiene lane is Python only. Six languages here have a single
category, and an absent _one in those is the right answer, not a gap.

The first draft grouped keys by their suffix and reported 586 findings,
nearly all of them nonsense: err_div_by_zero is division by zero and
pick_one is an instruction to pick one. A suffix is not a plural. It now
takes the counted keys from the call sites, which is exactly the population
where i18next consults CLDR, and reports fifteen. That makes it narrower on
purpose, since a count passed through a spread is invisible to it, and a
gate that misses a case can be repaired while one that cries wolf on five
hundred ordinary keys gets switched off and then catches nothing.

The fifteen are real, two keys translated with English's two forms into
languages that need up to six, and they are baselined so this blocks new
holes instead of demanding unrelated work on the day it lands. The baseline
may only shrink, the same rule the orphan baseline carries.

Checked that it can fail, not only that it passes: removing each of three
plural forms from en.ts produced exit 1 naming the missing form, and every
file was restored byte for byte and the restore verified by reading it back.

fix(i18n): put the English keys inside the object i18next reads

A locale file is one object holding one member, "translation", and i18n.ts hands
i18next that member alone. A key written after "const resource = {" is a sibling
of the dictionary rather than a member of it, so it sits in the file and never
reaches the bundle. English arrives by a second path as well, resources with an
en entry, where a sibling becomes a namespace of its own holding a string, which
is no more reachable than the first way.

On main right now en.ts carries 210 such keys, the entire English source for
tax_withholding, einvoice_clearance and payment_clock, and they arrived in the
previous i18n commit. This puts them where they belong. Every one of the 210
comes back with its value unchanged, nothing already inside was dropped or
reworded, and the dictionary grows by exactly the number moved plus the strings
described below.

Nothing we own caught it. The orphan guard asks whether a key appears, never
where it appears. The value guards ask about the value, and every value was a
correct translation. tsc and the build accept either shape, because the object
literal is valid either way and the trailing "as" assertion is not a check. And
no screen looked broken, because every call site passes the English as a
defaultValue, so a failed lookup renders English rather than a raw key.

check_i18n_key_nesting.py guards the shape from here, in pre-commit and in repo
hygiene, with no baseline, because a key beside the dictionary is never correct
and a baseline would only record how many were wrong the day it was written.
localeKeyResolution.test.ts guards the behaviour, resolving keys through the same
member the app reads. The second one matters more than it looks: every check we
had proved a key was present, and present was the thing that was never in doubt.

The same 30 files also carry this round's translations, because they cannot be
separated from the repair. Those are the three statutory modules in 29 languages,
which had shipped in English only, and the strings for the three screens the next
commit adds.

fix(costs): let a repriced region reach the assemblies built on it

Three code paths write CostItem.rate. Two of them publish costs.item.updated
and the assemblies subscriber pulls the new price through to every component
and parent total. The third, reprice_region, is the one that rewrites a whole
region from the resource price sheet, and it published nothing. So a user
moved the prices for a region, the cost items changed, and every assembly
quoting them kept its own unit_cost snapshot. A budget built from assemblies
never saw the reprice. Reported from a self-hosted install running unit price
analysis, where assemblies are the whole method and the stale copy is the
number that goes into a tender.

reprice_region now publishes costs.region.repriced after the commit, once for
the region rather than once per item, because a single run is capped at 250000
items and a per item fan out would be its own outage. Publishing after the
commit is deliberate: the subscriber opens its own session, and a detached
subscriber that wins the race against an uncommitted write reads the old rate
and writes it straight back.

The assemblies side gets refresh_region, which joins Component to CostItem on
region so the work scales with the number of components rather than with the
size of the catalogue, then re-totals only the assemblies it actually touched.

A rate that cannot be read as a number leaves its row alone and is counted.
The obvious way to write that loop reuses _safe_decimal, which answers 0 for
anything it cannot parse. That is right for a missing factor and catastrophic
for a price: one unreadable rate would zero every component built on it and
collapse the parent to nothing. The test for that case fails against the
_safe_decimal version and passes against the guard, so it covers the guard
rather than restating the happy path.

fix(assemblies): print a currency to the precision it actually has

Reported from a self-hosted install in Chile: a unit price analysis totalled
"82000.00 CLP". The Chilean peso has no minor unit, so those two digits are not
a rounding choice, they are a quantity the currency cannot express, and this is
the figure that goes into a public tender.

Both currency tables already knew it. money.py carries CLP at zero decimals,
currencyMinorUnits.ts lists it under ZERO_DECIMAL, and formatCurrency asks the
CLDR data directly. The assembly screens reached past all three and wrote a
literal 2, so the one number a Chilean estimator actually reads was the single
place where none of it applied.

formatCurrency stays the right answer wherever a caller can hand over the whole
amount. These callers cannot: they right-align a mono column and print the ISO
code in its own element, so switching would render the code twice. What they
were missing is only the digit count, which is now currencyFractionDigits, and
it reads the same CLDR table formatCurrency reads.

The existing preview-totals test caught the change on the currency that proves
it. Its mixed-currency case used XOF, which also has no minor unit, so the
expectation moved from "1000.00 XOF" to "1000 XOF".

The BOQ editor carried a worse version of the same fault. Saving a resource
into the user's own catalogue rebuilt the currency code from the display
symbol, recognised three symbols and answered EUR for everything else, so a
project in CLP, BRL, PLN or INR wrote its catalogue rows in euros. It could
also be confidently wrong rather than merely wrong, because the Chilean peso's
symbol is a dollar sign. The project's own code was already memoised two
thousand lines above and simply was not used.

Where the project never set a currency the field is left out of the payload
rather than sent blank. That distinction matters more than it looks. The create
schema carries a default and the column carries one, but both apply to an
absent value, not to an empty string, and nothing between the router and the
column fills a currency in. A blank string would have validated, stored, and
left a catalogue row naming no currency at all, which is a quieter fault than
the euros it replaces. A unit test now pins the half this relies on, that an
omitted currency comes back as a usable code, since that create path had no
test of any kind before.

Left alone deliberately: quantities, which are not money and keep their own
precision, and price_breakdown/model.py, which quantises stored values rather
than displayed ones and needs its own change.

feat(cad-import): read a DXF without the converter binary it never needed

An upload of .dxf was resolved through a format alias to the DWG converter,
which is a proprietary binary published for x86-64 only. So a self-hosted
install on ARM could not open a DXF at all, even though the platform already
reads DXF in pure Python for the takeoff module. The drawing data never needed
that binary, only the DWG container does.

dxf_native reads the file with ezdxf and writes the same element table a
converter would have written, one row per entity, so parse_cad_excel,
group_cad_elements, the column picker and the AI summary all work unchanged.

The routing decides on the file's own suffix rather than on the extension
argument, because the callers resolve the alias first: takeoff passes
_CONVERTER_FORMAT_ALIASES.get(ext, ext), so a DXF arrives labelled dwg and a
check on the label would never fire. The three preflights that gate an upload
on converter availability now exempt a natively readable format, otherwise they
reject the file one call before the code that reads it.

Lengths come out in metres and areas in square metres, because
group_cad_elements sums those columns into length_m and area_m2 without asking
what unit they arrived in. A drawing whose unit cannot be established leaves
the cells empty rather than passing raw drawing units off as metres.

The alias itself stays. It is still what finds an explicitly installed DWG
converter for a .dxf on the health and capability paths.

fix(price-breakdown): print a unit price at the currency's own precision

A unit price analysis in Chilean pesos read 82000.00 CLP. The peso has no minor

feat(methodology): price a Colombian and a Brazilian tender the way each country reads it

Both countries already had a template, and both reached a total the same way
everything else does: overhead, then profit, then tax on the lot. That road gets
the wrong number in each country, for a different reason.

Colombia quotes markup as AIU. Administracion, imprevistos and utilidad are each
a share of the costo directo, so nothing compounds, and IVA on a construction
contract for immovable property falls on the utilidad alone rather than on the
contract value. On a million pesos of direct cost the difference between those
two IVA bases is 231 800 pesos, which is more than a fifth of the job.

Brazil quotes BDI, and its tax term divides rather than adds, because PIS,
COFINS and ISS are levied on the invoiced amount, the amount that already
contains them. A percentage of the subtotal under-recovers every time. Rather
than bake a pre-grossed-up constant into the template, which becomes a defect
the moment a contractor types the nominal rate, the cascade engine learns a
third step kind: gross_up, base times rate over one hundred minus rate. It
refuses a rate of a hundred or more, since at that point there is no price left
for the tax to be a share of.

The flat templates for both countries stay where they are. An internal budget
priced flat is not wrong and keeps working.

Colombia was also missing from the e-invoicing regimes, alone among the Latin
American countries we carry. It clears through DIAN and the identifier is the
CUFE.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(requirements): let a requirement say why, who, when, how and which work

A requirement stored as an entity-attribute-constraint triplet says what is
required. On its own that is a fact without a life. Nobody can tell who asked
for it, at which point of the job it applies, how anyone would prove it was met,
or why it exists at all, and it could name exactly one priced position.

The five missing answers are now columns. Rationale is why, originator and
originator role are who, phase is when, verification method is how. A
self-reference lets a client demand be decomposed into the constraints that
satisfy it without losing the trail back to the demand. Each of these is stored
as a neutral key rather than a display word, so one row reads as
Ausfuehrungsplanung in Germany and Technical Design in Britain instead of being
readable in one country and untranslatable everywhere else.

Which work a requirement governs moves to its own table. One column could only
ever hold the most recent position, and "every exterior wall is F90" governs
every wall in the bill. Every existing value is copied across and the old column
stays, so callers that genuinely wanted one position keep working and the new
read-through property answers from both. The reverse direction now exists too:
open a bill item and see what it has to satisfy, which used to mean scanning
every requirement in the project.

A requirement set carries the wording its project reads in, ISO 19650 or
neutral. It renames concepts and never changes which ones exist, so it is safe
to flip at any time, and the tests hold both vocabularies to the same set of
terms. The phase spine maps onto HOAI Leistungsphasen, RIBA stages and the ISO
19650 delivery and operational phases, and a system is allowed to have no name
for a phase: RIBA has no separate permit stage and HOAI does not pay for a
strategic one, so forcing an equivalence would state something the standards do
not. The HOAI titles are checked against the ones the DACH pack already ships.

Four defects surfaced on the way and are fixed here.

The label lookup had no regional fallback, so es-CL, es-CO, es-MX and pt-BR
skipped a perfectly good Spanish or Portuguese label and rendered English. The
chain is now exact, then base language, then English.

The priority pattern accepted "may" while the label catalogue knew "could" and
"wont". One value rendered as a raw key in every language and two were
unreachable through the API. All four MoSCoW words are now accepted, "may" is
kept as the legacy spelling of "could" and ranks with it.

The column set was written out by hand in three places, two service
constructors and the response builder, and none of them could notice a field the
others had. A field added to the schema was validated, stored by one caller,
dropped by the other, and returned as a default. All three are now derived from
the schema, and a test fails if a validated field has nowhere to go.

The deliverable due date pointed at a milestone through a bare id with no
foreign key, so a deleted milestone left rows aimed at nothing. The constraint
is in place; values that already named no milestone are cleared and counted
rather than silently dropped.

The reverse lookup is addressed by position rather than by requirement set, so
it had no set to read a project off and shipped without a project gate on the
first attempt. The route census caught it on the commit that added it, which is
what that census is for. It now resolves the project through the bill the
position sits in, and all four new routes are in the register.

No frontend and no new interface strings. The vocabulary is served from
/vocabulary rather than shipped in the bundle, because the phase spine and the
verification methods are domain data that moves with the platform.

fix(requirements): stop the second position link erasing the first

A requirement governs work, plural, and the link table added last commit is
what holds that. Two writers reach it and only one of them knew. attach_position
adds a link row. link_to_position, which predates the table, writes the single
linked_position_id column and nothing else, so linking position A and then
position B left the requirement naming B with nothing at all remembering A. That
was the honest answer while one column was the whole model. It stopped being the
honest answer the moment linked_position_ids started reporting every position a
requirement governs, because then the route quietly dropped data the model
claims to hold.

The old route now writes both representations. The column keeps its meaning,
the most recently linked position, so a caller reading it sees exactly what it
saw before, and the link table accumulates. Relinking the same position is not
an error and does not reach the unique constraint.

Three readers counted coverage from the column alone.

The project dashboard's requirements_coverage and the project intelligence
collector's items_linked_to_boq both asked whether linked_position_id was set. A
requirement attached to ten positions through the newer route answered no. Left
alone, both figures would have fallen as people moved to the attachment that
holds more, which is the opposite of what happened. Both now count a requirement
as linked through either representation.

The third is the BIM element brief. bim_hub defines RequirementBrief as a local
subset of RequirementResponse to avoid importing requirements and creating a
cycle, which is a fair trade, but the only thing holding the two shapes together
was a docstring saying they must stay in sync. Nothing ran. The failure is
quiet in the direction that matters: drop a field upstream and the brief keeps
declaring it, pydantic fills it from a default, and the viewer renders a
plausible wrong value with no stack trace. There is now a test, and it is
one-directional on purpose, because the brief is meant to be smaller.

feat(einvoice): let an invoice carry a different VAT rate on every line

A construction invoice routinely mixes rates. Standard-rated own works sit
beside a subcontract under reverse charge, or beside a reduced-rate supply.
The exporter applied one rate to every line, derived from the header, so any
such invoice went out with a VAT breakdown that misstated what was taxed at
what rate, and the receiver would either reject it or book the wrong tax.

The line now carries its own rate and category, and the breakdown is built as
one group per distinct pair, each group's basis being exactly the lines that
belong to it and its VAT following from that basis and that rate. Where the
lines name rates, the VAT total is derived from them, because a breakdown and
a total that contradict each other is the thing the calculation rules exist to
catch.

has no rate of its own and falls back to the invoice-level rate, so every
invoice already issued renders the figures it rendered before. Inventing a
rate for those rows would assert a tax treatment nobody entered.

Both places that flatten lines for a document renderer now share one mapping,
and so do the two places that persist a line. Written out per caller, a field
added for one document is missing from the other and the export quietly falls
back instead of failing, which is how the single rate survived this long.

Also carries the seller bank account through from the e-invoice settings, so
the payment means only claims a credit transfer once there is an account to
back it.

fix(tooling): stop a shell fragment becoming the commit subject

Twelve commits in this history open with "@" before the sentence their author
actually wrote, and one of them is the commit the v14.6.0 tag points at. A
PowerShell here-string opener written on the same line as git commit -m is
consumed as the start of the message, so git takes it as the subject and the
real subject lands underneath. It reads correctly while you are writing it and
wrong in git log forever, and nothing between the two says so.

The repo already declared a commit-msg hook in .pre-commit-config.yaml, but
pre-commit was never installed in the working checkout, so no message was being
checked at all. That is the reason twelve got through rather than one.

check_commit_subject.py guards the narrow thing: the subject must not be a piece
of the shell that produced it. It deliberately does not ask for a conventional
commit, because several hundred subjects here are not one and that is a separate
decision nobody has taken. The rules that do run are anchored so an ordinary
subject cannot trip them, so bumping @types/node is fine and a subject that ends
in a closing code span is fine, since a continuation backtick is the one that
has nothing opening it.

The twelve are published and one carries a released tag, so they are listed by
SHA as history rather than treated as failures. A test asserts each of those
SHAs still resolves and still carries the defect, because an exemption that no
longer names anything real has stopped being a record and become suppression.

The long-dash rule runs only against a message being written. Style has wanted a
hyphen for a long time, but 2094 existing messages use a long dash, so scanning
history for it would report a decision rather than a defect.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(upgrade): let an upgrade outlive the request that started it

The in-app upgrade reported a failure it had no way to know about. Downloading a
release, resolving its dependencies and installing them takes as long as it
takes, and on a slow link that is minutes, but the work ran inline in the
request. The browser gave up at 45 seconds and told the user the upgrade had
failed while it was still running, and in most cases still going on to succeed.

The wrong message was the smaller half of it. Because the install ran in the
event loop of a single worker process, the server answered nothing at all for
the whole duration, so the one screen that could have told the user what was
happening was also the screen that had stopped responding. There was no way to
tell a stuck upgrade from a slow one.

The request now starts a job and returns its id, the work runs in a thread, and
the client polls the state. One job runs at a time, and asking again while one is
running hands back the job already in flight rather than starting a second pip
against the same site-packages.

The registry lives in this process's memory deliberately. An upgrade ends by
asking the user to restart, and the restart is what discards the record, which is
the right outcome: afterwards the installed version answers the question the job
was tracking, so there is nothing left to remember. An install running more than
one worker cannot share a lock this way and should turn the route off with
ALLOW_RUNTIME_UPGRADE=false, which is what a pipeline-managed deployment wants in
any case.

pip is given ten minutes before the job is failed rather than left hanging, so a
genuinely stuck install still resolves into an answer instead of a spinner.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(field-time): record a day with no signal and send it exactly once

A foreman in a basement or a lift shaft has no data, and the hours still
have to reach the office. The device now keeps the day in a local queue
and replays it when there is a signal. That replay is at-least-once by
construction, since a reconnect can fire twice and a request whose
response was lost on the way back is indistinguishable from one that
never arrived, so the server side is built around the assumption that
every delivery will happen more than once.

Each logical day carries a key minted on the device. The key is recorded
in the shared field sync ledger, so a redelivery returns the timesheet
the first delivery produced instead of writing a second one. An op
carries the entry's whole state rather than a diff, which is what makes
a replayed correction safe without a revision counter: applying the same
content twice leaves the same content. A withdrawal keeps its row in the
ledger, so a create that overtook its own withdrawal cannot resurrect a
day the foreman deleted.

Replay cannot move money. This path only ever produces a draft or a
submitted timesheet, and approval, which posts labour actuals and takes
the worker day claim, stays a desk action. The withdrawal is refused
once a day is past draft for the same reason: the claim is released by
reversing the timesheet and nothing in the database ties the claim to
the row, so deleting an approved timesheet would leave a claim that
nothing could ever release and that day could never be costed again.

Two things the key alone cannot be trusted with are checked before the
entry is touched. The ledger is shared with the field diary and its
uniqueness is on the client op id alone, so a key already spent on a
diary op resolves to a row this module does not own, and following it
would repoint the diary's row and destroy its replay guard. A key also
says nothing about which project it belongs to, so one replayed against
a different project would otherwise reach that project's day. Both are
refused, the second as a 404 so the answer does not confirm that the
entry exists.

Hours are compared on their value rather than their spelling when
deciding whether a delivery is a redelivery or an edit. The column is
Numeric(18, 4), so eight hours reads back as 8.0000 while the device
sends 8, and comparing them as text called every redelivery an edit and
quietly rewrote the day each time.

Two validation rules read the offline block on the timesheet: a device
clock well ahead of the server, and a day that reached the office long
after it was worked. Both are warnings. Nothing orders anything by the
device clock, and hours recorded in a basement and synced a fortnight
later are still true hours, but the approver is the last person who can
notice that a valuation has already closed. Refusing a real shift over a
wrong phone clock would be worse than saying so.

On the device, a second queue database is used rather than a second
store in the existing one, because onupgradeneeded only fires when the
version rises and a browser that already opened the first database at
version 1 would never create a newly added store. Every write would
throw and the adapter would swallow it, so the queue would accept days
and lose all of them.

The queue is drained while the Field Time page is open, and the wording
of the panel says so rather than promising that the day travels on its
own.

empty string everywhere else, so that default is gone too.

fix(jobs): stop eager dispatch borrowing the app's connections into a rival event loop

Every Celery dispatch ran its coroutine on a brand-new thread with its own
fresh event loop, but the coroutine drew its database connections from the
app's one pooled engine. A connection checked out on the main loop and later
reused from a dispatch's new loop made asyncpg refuse it outright with "Task
... got Future ... attached to a different loop". Severity was worse than a
deterministic break because it depended on pool warmth: an empty pool handed
the new loop a fresh connection and the dispatch succeeded, so a cold smoke
test passed while the same dispatch failed once request handling had warmed
the pool. Pre-existing since v10.6.0, byte-identical at the 14.8.0 release
commit.

Every dispatch now builds its own throwaway NullPool engine inside the
dedicated thread's own loop, pointed at the same database the app's pooled
factory resolves to, and disposes of it in a finally block, so no connection
can outlive the loop that opened it. _dispatch_job_sync's signature and
app/database.py's global factory are untouched, and eager mode is not
special cased: _run_async_in_dedicated_thread's docstring is corrected too,
since it claimed production asyncio.run would Just Work, when eager mode is
actually the documented dev and lightweight-deployment default and the
function has always treated both cases the same way.

Verified with a deliberately two-state scratch test: on the old code a warm
pool raised the cross-loop RuntimeError while a cold pool did not, which is
what proves the scenario exercises the bug rather than passing on a lucky
cold pool. On the fixed code neither state raises. tests/integration/core
(4 files) and tests/unit/core (8 files) are gated into ci-postgres.yml in

fix(migrations): let the currency backfill keep what it filled when it is interrupted

The cost item currency backfill issued one UPDATE per region on the migration's
own connection. That reads as batching and is not. Alembic wraps a whole upgrade
in a single transaction, so every superseded row version from every region stayed
on disk until the last one committed, and peak demand was the entire table
rewritten no matter how many regions the loop had. On a 1724 MB table with
553 360 rows to fill and 804 MB free it died extending a relation.

The worse half was that the WHERE predicate makes the work look resumable and
inside one transaction it is not. The abort rolled back the regions that had
already succeeded, so every retry started from zero and needed the same peak.
Freeing a little space and running again could never make progress.

The writes now go through a second connection in autocommit, chunked and
committed as they go, which makes an interrupted run resume from where it
stopped. Committing only makes dead tuples eligible for reclamation rather than
reclaiming them, and autovacuum will not keep pace with chunks issued back to
back, so this vacuums explicitly on a row budget of about 400 MB. Per chunk
would be correct and far slower, since a vacuum scans the whole table however
little it reclaims.

A second connection cannot be assumed. A database older than the costs module
creates the table in a revision inside this same uncommitted transaction, and
querying such a table from another connection blocks on the catalog lock instead
of failing, which would wedge the upgrade with no way to tell what happened.
The probe is to_regclass, which answers from the second connection's own catalog
snapshot and takes no lock, and lock_timeout turns any future revision holding
this table ahead of us into a clean fallback. When the probe says no, the
original in-transaction loop runs, which is right because that case means the
table is new and therefore empty.

Chunking by ctid rather than by the primary key keeps this independent of what
the key is called and how it is typed.

The tests pin durability rather than throughput, because a table small enough to
run in CI completes under either implementation and "the rows came out filled"
cannot tell them apart. The central test rolls the migration's own transaction
back and asserts the fill survived, and a control forces the fallback path and
asserts the same rollback loses everything. The two disagree on identical data.
The peak itself is a property of a 1724 MB table and still needs verifying
against one.

chore(migrations): add a report-only scan for upgrade() rewrites against tables it did not create

#126 was a migration that filled a pre-existing 1724 MB table inside the
single transaction Alembic wraps a whole upgrade() run in, and died with
DiskFull on a real box. Nothing in CI would have caught that class of
migration before it shipped, and nothing catches the next one. This adds a
standalone scan: for every revision in backend/alembic/versions, does its
upgrade() (including helpers it calls, not just its own body) issue an
INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE against a table that revision does not itself create.
Creating a table and filling it in the same revision is not flagged, since
there is no pre-existing data to make a transaction-sized copy of.

Grep cannot do this: every migration here builds its raw SQL as an f-string
over a module-level constant, so a sweep for a literal verb next to a
literal table name returns a confident, wrong zero. ScriptDirectory's own
walk_revisions() cannot either, since importing every migration module to
build the chain drags in a live DATABASE_URL requirement at collection
time. Revisions are read as source text and parsed with ast instead, the
same approach test_migrations_roundtrip.py uses for the same reason, kept
independent here so this script carries no pytest or psycopg2 dependency.

Every table name is resolved with a confidence tier attached (literal,
derived, or unresolved) rather than guessed at silently, and a statement
this script cannot classify at all is listed separately rather than
dropped. Validated against nine files confirmed by hand across the actual
call shapes this codebase uses (direct f-strings, sa.text() wrapped and
bare, Core .insert()/.delete() on a sa.table() object, bulk_insert, a
value threaded through a local variable and an if/elif chain, and SQL
built in a helper function the migration calls rather than inline), plus
five known-clean files (DDL-only). One real false positive turned up
during that validation, in the audit-log migration: two unrelated for
loops both used "table" as their loop variable, and an earlier version of
this script's scope model unioned the two, making the first loop's UPDATE
look like it also touched the second loop's tables. Fixed by switching the
scope model to plain last-write-wins rebinding, matching how Python itself
has no per-loop block scope.

Full run across all 320 revisions: 23 flagged carrying 36 statements (32
resolved directly from a literal, 4 via a loop-derived value), and 6
revisions carry 11 statements this could not classify at all - mostly
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY / ALTER TABLE issued through a helper whose
table-name argument is a function parameter this script does not trace,
which is DDL and would not have been a finding even if resolved, plus one
genuine multi-condition Core read this script does not model as boolean
expressions. A random sample of the flagged list read by hand (fifteen of
the twenty-three files) turned up no false positives.

Report-only. Not wired into any CI workflow. Exit code is always 0 when
the scan itself completes, so it cannot fail a build - the decision on
whether this class of finding should ever block a merge is separate from
building the tool that finds them.

feat(einvoice): refuse a German invoice whose address is only a country

EN 16931 accepts a postal address that names nothing but its country, because
BR-8 with BR-9 and BR-10 with BR-11 are the whole of what it asks for. XRechnung
asks for more, and a document that satisfies the European standard and no more
is rejected by the receiver in Germany rather than accepted with a note. Four
rules now say so before the file is written.

BR-DE-3 seller city (BT-37), BR-DE-4 seller post code (BT-38), BR-DE-8 buyer
city (BT-52), BR-DE-9 buyer post code (BT-53). All four are fatal, which is what
KoSIT flags them, and blank counts as absent because the schematron asserts on a
normalised value. The identifiers and their business terms are read off
itplr-kosit/xrechnung-schematron v2.5.0, the artefact for XRechnung 3.0.2, which
is the version our CustomizationID already claims.

They apply to the xrechnung profile and to nothing else. A receiver in the
Netherlands or on Peppol validates against its own specification and would never
quote a BR-DE identifier, so firing there would hand a user a rule id that means
nothing to the party refusing the document.

The two sides are fixed in different places and the messages say which. Seller
city and post code are columns on the standing settings, so those findings name
the settings screen. The settings row holds no buyer fields at all, so the buyer
findings name the invoice, in the same words the country findings settled on.

Four test fixtures rendered German documents with a country and no city, and now
fail. They were fixed by filling in the addresses, not by softening the rule: a
fixture that could not be sent to a German authority should not have been our
picture of a valid document.

Our own seeded demo invoices do not survive this, and did not survive what came
before it either. All 284 of them, 43 on German projects, carry no e-invoice
metadata at all, so every one already failed BR-6, BR-7, BR-9, BR-11, BR-CO-26
and BR-DE-15 before these four rules existed. The count of invoices that could
be exported as XRechnung yesterday and cannot today is zero, because it was zero
yesterday. Seeding a party is a separate job and this is not it.
