feat(desktop-signing): make an unsigned Windows build say so, and a half-configured one stop

The signing job checked one of the five AZURE_KV_* secrets. With the other
four empty it still installed .NET, still installed AzureSignTool, still
downloaded the installers, and then called azuresigntool with -kvu "" and
-kvt "" to fail several minutes later with a message about the vault rather
than about the secret nobody set.

Three more ways the job could succeed at doing nothing. The download ended in
"|| true", so a download that failed outright left an empty directory, the
signing step said "nothing to sign" and exited zero, and the job went green
having signed nothing. Verification piped signtool into "|| echo", and a
missing signtool exited zero, so the only step able to catch a bad signature
could not stop one. The re-upload had no failure path either, which meant a
release could keep its unsigned installer while the job reported a signed one.

Preflight now reads all five names as a set, before anything is installed, and
splits into three outcomes that are three different colours. None of the five
set is an annotated skip that writes an unsigned notice into the job summary,
because that is every release to date and turning it red is the founder's call.
Some subset set is a hard failure naming the missing ones. All five set means
every later step is allowed to fail the job, and they now do: the download
checks composition rather than count, since two .exe and no .msi would
otherwise ship one signed installer and one unsigned one.

WINDOWS_SIGNING_REQUIRED, a repository variable, closes the remaining hole.
Once signing works, the likeliest future failure is an expired Entra client
secret, and without the variable that would put the pipeline back into the
quiet green skip it is in today.

desktop/README.md said the installers "are signed" with a GlobalSign
certificate in an Azure Key Vault HSM. No such certificate exists and none of
them are signed. docs/desktop/WINDOWS_SIGNING.md is the walkthrough for
creating one, including why a public CA can no longer issue a .pfx file.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(desktop-signing): stop a failed build leg from silencing the signing job

The preflight added in the previous commit can only speak if the job runs.
With a bare `needs: build-tauri`, it does not: a failed dependency skips this
job outright, and a skipped job produces no annotation, no summary block and
no exit code, only a grey tile.

That is reachable. build-tauri is a matrix with fail-fast disabled, so the
legs that succeed still attach their installers to the release while the job
as a whole reports failure. A macOS leg failing after the Windows leg had
already uploaded its .exe and .msi leaves those two files on the release with
nothing having looked at them, and WINDOWS_SIGNING_REQUIRED cannot fire
because nothing ran to read it. The silence removed from inside the job was
still available at its boundary.

The job now runs whenever build-tauri reached a conclusion and stands down
only when it was skipped, which is the sidecar-only dispatch where there is
no release to sign against.

Also checked, since making verification authoritative is only safe if the
check is capable of both answers: signtool verify /pa parses an MSI, walks
the chain and validates the timestamp, exiting 0 on a correctly signed one
and 1 with WinVerifyTrust 0x80096010 on the same file with a byte flipped.
The gate can fail, and it will not false-red the first signed release.

feat(release-signing): answer the four signature questions instead of assuming one

"Is the release signed" has four different answers in this project and they do
not agree. A git tag signature, a Sigstore signature over the published bytes,
a macOS Developer ID plus notarisation, and a Windows Authenticode certificate
are separate mechanisms produced by separate jobs. Reporting them as one number
is how "macOS signing resolved" came to describe a fix to the integrity of an
ad-hoc seal, which is a real fix to a real bug and not that claim.

scripts/release_signature_inventory.py reports all four and labels every answer
with how it was obtained, because they are not obtained the same way. Tag
signatures come from the tag objects in the clone and are invisible to the API,
so a run that only talked to the API would report nothing missing for the
mechanism where everything is missing. Sigstore is read off the published asset
list. The two platform signatures cannot be read from an asset list at all, so
they are argued from whether the pipeline hands the credentials to the tool that
would use them, and that inference is marked as one everywhere it appears.

Three things the script refuses to do, each of which would produce a confident
wrong answer. A short API page is rejected against a dated floor rather than
printed, because a truncated fetch looks exactly like a healthy repository with
fewer releases. A credential counts as wired only when the step that invokes the
signing tool receives it, not when the name appears in the file: the new macOS
status step names all four APPLE_ secrets in order to report their absence, and
matching on names read that as notarisation being configured. And the tool is
matched as an invocation rather than a mention, because a comment explaining
what azuresigntool does with empty secrets otherwise nominates the preflight
step as the signing tool.

The current position, which the script produces on demand and the new document
states as a rule rather than a table: no tag of the 325 is signed, Sigstore runs
from v14.5.0 with a patchy earlier history, no macOS build has ever been
notarised across 113 desktop releases, and no Windows installer has ever been
Authenticode signed. Windows is wired and waiting on a certificate. macOS is not
wired: the build step is handed none of the Apple credentials, so creating them
would change nothing by itself. Those two absences look the same from outside
and have different fixes.

In the workflow, the reason the three preflight outcomes have the shape they do
is now written next to them. The dangerous state is not unsigned, it is believed
signed. An unsigned installer that says so is honest and the reader can decide.
A half configured pipeline that emits something signature shaped without
verifying it is the state where everyone downstream assumes a guarantee that
does not exist. So the skip is a heading in the run summary rather than a line
in a log, and the macOS job now states its own signing status every run, decided
by reading which credentials exist rather than by asserting a fixed answer, so
it starts reporting the other outcome on its own the day someone wires it up.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(fonts): serve our typefaces ourselves, and stop claiming a script we cannot draw

index.html preconnected to two Google origins and pulled Plus Jakarta Sans and
Instrument Serif from them on every app load. Both families now live under
frontend/public/assets/vendor/fonts/, with the same subsets, weights,
unicode-ranges and font-display values the Google stylesheet used, so the
rendered result is unchanged and only the origin moves. Workbox already globs
woff2, so the files are precached and the desktop build renders with no network.

One face is deliberately not mirrored. Google declares a Plus Jakarta Sans face
labelled cyrillic-ext over U+0460-052F, but the file behind it is 1716 bytes and
holds seven codepoints: CR, space, A, nbsp, A-acute, A-breve and the hryvnia
sign. There is not one Cyrillic letter in it, and no other subset carries any
either. The label exists because the hryvnia sign happens to fall inside the
range that names the subset.

A unicode-range is what the browser uses to decide whether to fetch a face, so
that mis-declared range made Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Mongolian strings download a
font that could not draw them; the letters fell through to the system stack
anyway. Measured over the locale files, it covered 51.5% of Kazakh words, 24.3%
of Mongolian and 20.7% of Kyrgyz, against 0.0% of Russian and Bulgarian, which
have no letters in the extended block. The face is kept, because UAH is a
currency we support and the glyph is real, but declared over U+20B4 alone. After
the change no locale in any script selects a face that cannot render it, down
from three.

The CSP came with it. font-src, style-src and connect-src all whitelisted the
Google font hosts, the last because the service worker used to precache the
files with fetch(). Leaving them would keep permitting exactly the third-party
fetch this removes, so the test now asserts their absence instead of their
presence.

scripts/font_coverage_probe.py is the measurement, reporting each locale under
both definitions of coverage: the declared unicode-range, which drives the
download, and the range intersected with the font's real cmap, which drives what
is painted. The gap between those two columns is where this defect lived.

kept its address as a single free text line, so BR-7 and BR-11 had no input

name; the invoice list resolves that label for every row, so one such record

feat(release-signing): settle the signing history against the bytes, not the current config

The inventory said no macOS build was ever signed and no Windows installer was
ever Authenticode signed. Both were universal claims about the past resting on
evidence that is entirely about the present: the workflow as it stands now, and
the secret list as it stands now. A secret that existed a month ago and was
deleted since leaves no trace in either.

For macOS the history settles it. No file under .github/ has ever contained an
APPLE_ credential reference in any commit on any branch, so no build ever
received one and none could have been signed, whatever secrets existed.

For Windows it did not settle it. The Azure step has been wired since 2026-06-09
and could in principle have signed anything published after that. So the script
now reads the artifacts. --check-artifacts fetches the first 8 KB of every

feat(release-signing): let a backfill sign old bytes without minting a new component list

Signing a release published weeks ago is not the same run as signing one
published minutes ago, and the difference is the SBOM. It gets generated at run
time from whatever the dependency ranges resolve to today, so attaching it to an
old release would put a component list on that page describing software the
release never contained, and the manifest would then cover that list and sign
it. A missing component list is a gap. A signed and wrong one is worse than the
gap, because it is the kind of wrong that nobody rechecks.

So workflow_dispatch takes a backfill flag, and the SBOM job is skipped when it
is set. Skipped rather than left to fail: both leave the release without an
SBOM, but only one of them says that was the intention. The sign job already
tolerated a missing SBOM through !cancelled(), so nothing else changes.

The run states which of the two it was, and a backfill run says why there is no
SBOM beside the signature. Without that the result looks like a broken run, and
the obvious repair is to generate the SBOM that the skip exists to prevent.

Scope this is built for is v14.0.0 through v14.4.0, the seven releases on the
current major that carry no signature. Nothing is dispatched here.

fix(release-signing): read the signature back off the release, do not infer it

The signing job depends on the SBOM job, and a backfill skips the SBOM job. A
job whose dependency is skipped is itself skipped unless its own condition is a
status expression, which this one is, so signing should still run. That is the
documented behaviour and I believe it is right, but the workflow was relying on
it without ever checking, and if it is wrong the result is the worst shape
available: resolve succeeds, sbom skips, sign skips, every job reports green and
nothing is signed. That is the same failure this workflow already had once,
where the upload step was gated on an event that could not reach it and every
run produced a signature and threw it away.

So the run now ends by asking the release what it holds. If SHA256SUMS, its
signature and its certificate are not all on the release page, the run goes red
and says which are missing and what the signing job reported, because a skipped
signing job points at the graph rather than at cosign. A release that cannot be
read is reported as not measured rather than as unsigned; those are different
and only one of them is a claim about the artefact.

This checks the release, not the run, which is the point. It says nothing about
a release nobody dispatched a run for, and the docs say so rather than letting a
green run be read as a guarantee it does not carry.

feat(scripts): gate the tree against proprietary classification content

The check has two heads, because the two leaks look nothing alike. The first catches a
division code sitting next to the official title that belongs to it, which is the shape
a reproduced table takes. That needs two discriminators rather than one, since half
those titles are ordinary trade words: the number has to be the official number for
that exact title, and a file has to carry enough distinct divisions to be the
compilation, so that a crosswalk repeating four terms across fifty line items is not
mistaken for a copied table. The second head catches the standard's name where a user
reads it as a description of our own content, while leaving the all lowercase form
alone, because that one is the technical key we exchange over the API. Places that
legitimately name a standard, such as a picker, a preset or a validation rule, are
allowed by location rather than globally, so the exemption cannot spread.

The denylist is kept as hashes, so the script does not itself become the copy it exists
to prevent, and a finding reports the division number and the location without echoing
what it matched. The sweep also refuses to call an empty run clean, which is how it
caught itself listing the tree relative to the caller's directory instead of the
repository root and reporting success over zero files.

The security advisory RUSTSEC-2026-0097 lands on rand 0.7.3, which nothing of
ours asked for. It arrived through tauri-utils 2.9.1, which pulled kuchikiki,
which pulled selectors 0.24 and phf 0.8, which pulled rand 0.7. Pinning rand

already sits at its newest compatible release.

Moving the tauri crates to the current 2.11.5 line resolves it properly. That
version no longer reaches for kuchikiki, so the dead html stack behind it goes
too, 36 crates in all including the whole phf 0.8 and rand 0.7 family. The only
rand left in the tree is 0.8.6, the patched release. The manifest already
allowed all of this, so the change is the lockfile alone.

Verified with cargo check on the same command before and after the update, both
green, and the version sync gate still reads 14.8.1 from the crate entry.

The other open advisory, RUSTSEC-2024-0429 against glib 0.18.5, has no fix
available yet. It wants glib 0.20, but glib reaches us only through the GTK3
bindings that tauri uses on Linux, and that binding line ended at gtk 0.18.2 and
requires glib 0.18. There is nothing to bump until upstream moves off GTK3.

shrinks by a metre, the door count goes to eleven, the slab and the relocated
wall keep their quantities, and taking the old wall down arrives as new scope.
The German register's chain is that same pair, so its archived and its current
issue are different drawings.

Seed idempotency moved from the project to the document and is keyed on a seed
key rather than a file name: a re-run stays a no-op, an install that predates
index B receives it, and the sheet it already holds is renamed and re-served
from the current fixture instead of gaining a twin. A project holding a
document this seeder did not write is still left to its owner.

feat(einvoice-clearance): seed the German registration and the document behind it

The module shipped complete and unseeded, so the clearance screen was empty on
every install. A visitor could read the explainer about what a tax authority
answers and then look at a screen where nothing had ever been answered.

The seed now files a German registration and puts the showcase invoice through
it, ending as a delivered document with the transmission id the platform
returned and the whole trail behind it. Nothing is written as rows: the
document is prepared, checked and submitted through the module's own service,
the same three calls the router makes, so the statuses, their order and the
identifier come from the state machine rather than from a second description of
it that could drift. The payload is the real XRechnung the export route
renders, hashed from the exact bytes that were sent.

The invoice is resolved by the number the demo pack declares, on the project
that pack installed, and never by position. The installer picks its invoice
list with a lookup that falls back to the generated one, so a list added for
this pack later would change which invoices exist and in what order, and a
seeder taking the first receivable would quietly file against the wrong
document. A project that cannot answer gets a log line and nothing is written,
because a clearance document pointing at no invoice is a fiscal record of
nothing.

The registration is a sandbox one and the submission acknowledges the warning
that says so, which is what the module is: the offline reference adapter
refuses a live registration outright, so the alternative is not a more
realistic demo but a rejected document. Demo estate only, and idempotent per
invoice, so one sale never ends up with two submissions.

fix(takeoff): keep the seed from adopting a document it did not write

Adoption re-copies the fixture over the file path of the row it takes over, so the seeded-row test now also requires an empty source_document_id. A takeoff document opened from Project Files builds its metadata from scratch today and cannot carry the seed marker, but the guard belongs on the side that overwrites bytes rather than on the side that happens not to set the key.

fix(einvoice): every compliance finding speaks the reader's language

Thirteen rules had no entry in the translated catalogue, among them the ones a hand-made invoice trips first: the missing unit of measure, the VAT that does not match its group, the unknown category code. The screen fell back to the engine's English sentence, silently, in the frame the whole e-invoice case is built around.

Findings now carry the values their sentence interpolates, so a translation can name the same line and quote the same amount instead of being reworded into something weaker. A new gate reads the rule ids straight out of the engine and fails when one of them has no sentence, and a second one fails when a translation drops a value the English entry names.

fix(i18n): name the clearance screen and the project switcher correctly in German

The clearance page carried its English route title into the header while the sidebar beside it said E-Rechnungs-Clearance, because the title map had no entry for that route and fell back to the literal. The project switcher borrowed its empty-state label from the schedule module, so on any screen without a project open it invited the reader to go and manage a construction programme. Four clearance toasts had no key in any locale, English included, which is why no locale gate ever reported them. The finance intro now says Obligo where it used to use a participle as a noun.

fix(finance): an invoice status the lifecycle knows can now be read on screen

Demo invoices were seeded as submitted, which the finance state machine has never had, so those invoices sat in a state no user action could leave. The field carries no pattern, so nothing refused the value on the way in, and the wide seed vocabulary scan reads vocabularies out of Pydantic patterns and could not see it either.

The opposite gap was sent, a real state the screen had never learned: no label, so the badge printed the database word; no colour, so an invoice the client is holding looked like an unsent draft; and no entry in the filter, so it could only be found by clearing the filter. Same for credit_note_issued. A new gate reads the lifecycle out of the state machine and fails when the seed speaks a word outside it or the screen cannot say one inside it. The German and English labels landed with the previous commit.

fix(finance): keep the e-invoice dialog and the invoice table in one language

The profile picker printed the registry label unchanged, so a German heading sat above Netherlands, Norway, Singapore and international. The display name now comes from the catalogue per profile, which keeps the standard's own name intact while the country beside it can be translated, and a gate fails when a profile ships without one.

The e-invoice action is now offered on receivable invoices only. On a supplier's invoice it opened a compliance report about our own missing seller details on a document we are not issuing, and there were more of those on the German demo project than of the one it was meant for. Invoice and payment dates in the dense list rows render numerically, which is the form the regional settings ask for. The dry-run response field the dialog never rendered is no longer declared.

fix(i18n): backfill invoice status, project selector and e-invoice profile keys across 38 locales

finance.status_sent, finance.status_credit_note_issued and projects.select_active
existed only in en/de and tripped the orphan-key guard. Also carries the
e-invoice clearance error toasts, the seller/buyer party labels and the
ten profile picker entries (EN 16931, UBL, Peppol, ZUGFeRD, Factur-X,
XRechnung, NLCIUS, EHF, Peppol A-NZ, Peppol SG) that were English-only
outside en/de. Standard names stay verbatim per format spec; only the
parenthesised country name is localized.

test(finance): guard the e-invoice action at both call sites

The predicate was covered but the call sites were not, and the defect was a call site: the action was offered on payable invoices, where the dialog reports our own missing seller details on a document the supplier wrote. The scan reads the page source, since both sites are inline in a long page with no component to mount alone, and the regression to catch is a third site shipping unguarded. A planted sample proves the scan comes back dirty when it should.

Also records why sent and approved share one badge colour: five variants cover seven states, and those two read the same to an eye scanning the column, in flight and not yet money.
feat(cases): the PDF takeoff case now ends by issuing the bill as GAEB
fix(cases): stretch the case hero photo to the header row height

fix(progress): number a healed seq column the way the migration does

The boot-time schema heal adds oe_progress_entry.seq with ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT nextval(...), and PostgreSQL evaluates that default while rewriting the table, so every row that predates the column is numbered in the order it happens to lie on disk. The Alembic migration numbers the same rows by recorded_at, created_at, id. Every latest-wins query in the progress module leads with seq, so three readings lying physically 90/10/50 with their timestamps running 10-50-90 reported 50 as the current reading on a boot-healed database and 90 on an Alembic one. Same product, same rows, different answer depending on which path built the schema.

A fixup owned by the progress module now runs immediately after the heal, at both places that call it, and puts those rows back into observation order. It heals itself on the next boot and asks nothing of the operator.

Detection is one index-ordered scan that counts strict descents, so a database that never diverged pays a single pass and stops. Rows written inside one transaction tie on both timestamps and are not a descent, which keeps the repair away from a bulk write whose only real ordering is the one seq already holds. When it does fire, the renumber writes above the current maximum, because the column is unique and a permutation of its own values cannot be applied in place, and it then parks the sequence above the result so the next reading recorded still outranks the history it tops.

feat(deps): ship the vector store clients in the standard builds

The unified image installed ./backend[server] and the desktop lock was compiled
with no extras, so qdrant-client and lancedb reached neither. Every stock deploy
then ran the CWICR matching path against a client that was not there: _get_client
raised ImportError, the ranker fell through to its metadata-only branch with no
store to read, and /match-elements answered an empty 200 rather than failing
loudly. The same builds already set VECTOR_BACKEND=lancedb while lancedb was
equally absent. Railway, Render and the terraform droplet all deploy this image,
so one install line covers all five targets.

Both clients now sit in a new semantic-clients extra that carries no embedding
model. The image installs it and the desktop lock is compiled with it, which is
why the regeneration command in the lock header changed. The encoders stay
optional in [semantic]: FlagEmbedding and sentence-transformers pull torch, which
the PyInstaller spec excludes outright. polars stays there too, because the rate
parquet it reads is an operator-supplied file that nothing ships or downloads.

The lock alone would not have reached the desktop channel. Both clients are
imported inside function bodies, so PyInstaller never sees them in the static
graph and would have dropped the wheels again; the spec now collects both
packages by submodule. Verified on Windows by freezing a probe that opens an
embedded Qdrant store and a LanceDB connection. The guard test now checks both
directions, that the clients are present and that no torch stack resolved.

refactor(cases): retire the PDF pricing case in favour of the German takeoff route

The old card walked a flat PDF to a priced bill in five steps, and the German
takeoff case opens on the same ground, so the hub was offering one route under
two names. The case file goes with its line-art scene, its bespoke photo
mapping and the 37 content keys it carried in 38 locale files. Takeoff
from DWG and quantities from BIM stay where they are, they start from other
data.

The cases tests now anchor on the surviving case, and they assert the retired
slug resolves to nothing, so restoring the data file by accident cannot put the
card back on the hub without a test saying so.

chore(brand): let a UI string name the CAD tool, with its mark on it

The authoring tool our converter reads from stays named in the interface,
because naming it is what tells a user which files actually go in, and the
first mention in each string now carries the registered sign. The marketing
site has read that way since July, so the app matches it rather than
inventing a second house style.

The gate's own header claimed the opposite, that no vendor product name may
appear anywhere, while practice had already made this exception. It now
documents what we enforce, and a second check holds the line: the name is
allowed, an unmarked first mention is a finding. That check stores the word
rather than a hash, because here the word is permitted and a report that
names it is more useful than one that masks it.

Two shapes it must not get wrong, both covered by tests. A later mention
inside the same string stays bare, so correct wording is never rejected. A
following hyphen is not an exemption, which is what German, Dutch and the
Nordic locales need, since there the name compounds into the next word. Only
the converter's own repository slug is exempt, so that URL stays byte-exact.

chore(i18n): carry the registered sign on the CAD tool name in every locale

Nine keys name the authoring tool on purpose, and each now carries the sign
on its first mention across all forty locale files. A later mention in the
same string keeps its plain spelling, which is how the name is meant to be
written, and the German and Nordic compounds take the sign on the name
itself rather than at the end of the compound.

The converter's repository slug is left exactly as it was. It is part of a
URL, so a sign inside it would be a broken link rather than an attribution.

Japanese had also put the product name into five strings where English
deliberately says RVT, or names no tool at all and calls the layout a model
browser. Those follow the English source again, which is a translation fix
that happened to surface while marking the rest.

refactor(packs): rename the US pack away from a vendor brand

The pack was named after a commercial cost database that it does not ship and
could not ship. It is now us-costdata, and the neutral name reaches the
directory, the python package, the manifest slug, the onboarding field keys
and the city index rule pack. The pack finally has a README, and it says
plainly what the situation is: no cost data of that class is bundled, the
licence of any such database forbids bundling it, and what the pack gives you
is the structure to import the rates you are licensed to use.

The same brand also sat in places that had nothing to do with the pack. The
cost item source vocabulary listed it as a provenance value, the plugin
manager used it in a usage example, a migration docstring borrowed it as an
adjective, and the US methodology doc built a whole mapping example around it.
Those now say what they mean, a commercial unit cost database import. A stale
module inventory snapshot is brought back in line with the manifest it was
generated from. Shipped release notes keep the old name, they record what was
released and are not rewritten.

fix(deps): keep lancedb out of the standard builds

The semantic-clients extra shipped two clients. Measurement says only one of
them earns its place. qdrant-client and its gRPC stack are 22 MB in the image
and 33 MB of site-packages on Windows, and they are what makes /match-elements
work on a stock install. lancedb is 157 MB on Linux and 196 MB on Windows,
almost all of it a single unstripped Rust extension, which would have taken the
desktop installer from 191 MB to roughly 320 MB.

It would not have bought the feature it looks like it buys. core/vector.py's
get_embedder() only tries sentence-transformers, and nothing in the tree imports
fastembed, so the generic semantic store has no encoder in a stock install
whether or not the client is present. Paying 157 MB for a path that stays dead
is the opposite of what this project optimises for, so lancedb goes back to
[vector] and the extra now carries the client that fixes something.

The deploy targets still set VECTOR_BACKEND=lancedb against a backend the image
does not carry. That mismatch predates this work and is left alone on purpose:
it is a question about whether the generic store should exist without an
encoder, not something to settle by shipping the wheel.

The lock removal is exactly the lancedb family and nothing else, and the guard
test simply stops requiring lancedb rather than forbidding it, since it is a
client and not an embedder.

test(modules): merge the module bundles the way the running app does

The registry card test built its German store by loading the locale first and
merging the module bundles over it. The app does the opposite: the module
bundles go in while app/i18n.ts evaluates, and the locale arrives later on its
lazy chunk. Both merges overwrite, so a key that a manifest and a locale file
both define is won by the locale file, not by the manifest.

Nothing changes today, because no manifest ships a German string that differs
from the locale file for a shared key. The moment one does, the old order would
have had this test assert a word the reader never sees.

fix(costs): point the client-missing hints at the extra that fixes them

Three messages told a user with a missing qdrant-client to install [semantic],
which pulls torch and a multi-gigabyte encoder to solve a 22 MB problem. They
now name [semantic-clients], the client-only extra.

Only the messages that are actually about the client changed. The embedder
status card, the /qdrant-search 503 and the reindex script's "no embedding
model" branch still say [semantic], because those paths genuinely need the
encoder and pointing them at the client extra would promise something it does
not install. The reindex script's LanceDB branch was wrong in the other
direction, telling users to install [semantic] for a package that has only ever
lived in [vector]; it now names [vector].

The supervisor hint also carried a claim that went stale: it told users that
packaged builds cannot install the client and to switch to a source or
container install. The container image and the desktop build both ship it now.

fix(progress): lead the latest-entry readers with seq

Three readers picked the current reading by recorded_at alone and never
went through _latest_first, so they answered a different question from
the rest of the module. A correction appended after the reading it
corrects lost to that reading whenever it carried an earlier timestamp,
which is what a back-dated fix looks like.

That row is not cosmetic. The contracts progress claim bills the percent
it reads from get_latest_for_position, and the client progress report
takes its headline figure from get_latest_project_entry and its window
figure from element 0 of get_entries_for_period.

recorded_at cannot decide this on its own. It defaults to the database
now(), which in PostgreSQL is the transaction timestamp and is therefore
identical for every row one transaction writes, and it is back-datable
by the caller. seq is the append counter and settles both cases.

The new test pins the discriminator as well as the outcome: it asserts
that ordering by recorded_at alone still returns the superseded row, so
the scenario cannot stop telling the two orderings apart and leave the
assertions passing for the wrong reason.

feat(documents): retire the drawing pair the German revision chain replaces

An install seeded before the chain existed kept the English general arrangement pair, whose archived and current issues serve one file, so the register showed a revision that changed nothing right next to the chain written to fix exactly that. The top-up now removes it, and only it: rows this seeder wrote, matched on its own marker and on the sheet number, on the German showcase projects, and only once both issues of the chain are really on the project. A row some takeoff document was opened from is left alone, because takeoff keeps its source as a plain id column with no foreign key and deleting underneath it would strand the measurements filed against it. The files stay on disk, since each project is seeded inside a savepoint that can still roll back and a surviving row whose bytes were deleted is worse than an orphaned demo PDF.

ci(full-suite): spread the database-heavy tests across enough shards to finish

The nightly has never produced a complete result. With no stored durations
pytest-split partitions by test count, and this tree is not uniform in cost:
on the 2026-08-14 run shard 3 finished 3288 unit tests in 143 seconds while
shards 1 and 2, which held tests/integration and tests/modules, were still
going when the 120 minute ceiling cancelled them. A cancelled shard reports
no test result at all, so two eighths of the tree had never been measured.
Shard 1 also ran the service container out of its 100 connections.

Going from 8 shards to 32 spreads those 5875 database-backed tests over about
seven shards instead of two. The split stays count-based and pathless so the
union of the shards is still exactly the collected tree.

Both jobs now run unbuffered and verbose. The two cancelled shards logged not
a single test name in two hours because pytest block-buffers stdout when it is
not a terminal and the buffer died with the process, which left the PostgreSQL
container log as the only evidence of where they had got to.

fix(documents): retire the old pair on a project whose chain landed earlier

The retire only ran beside the pass that files the German chain, so an install reseeded between the chain landing and the retire landing kept both. That install never takes the top-up path again, because the sheet is already filed, and the early return it does take now runs the retire as well. The condition is unchanged: the chain has to be on the project, whether this pass wrote it or an earlier one did.

fix(brand): gate the English that ships inside components, not only locales

The trademark check read locale files and nothing else, and locale files are
not the whole UI. An i18n default written into a component renders whenever its
key is missing, and guide.eac.selectors.body has no entry in any of the forty
locales at all, so its default is the only English that string will ever show.
It named the CAD tool with no sign on it and every gate reported green.

The check now also reads default-shaped lines anywhere under frontend/src. What
selects a line is its shape rather than the file it sits in, because a check
that shouted at an identifier, or at a comment explaining the converter, would
be switched off within a week. Those two shapes are tested next to the findings
for that reason, along with the link that carries the repository slug and a
marked default on one line.

Two defaults in the requirements import had also drifted from their own English
source. The locale there says RVT shared-parameter on purpose, and the defaults
still carried an older wording that named the product. They follow the locale
again rather than gaining a sign, because the locale is what a reader sees.

The script is rewrapped to the width ruff format applies under scripts, which
the previous change had exceeded.

fix(dwg-takeoff): let the export's own block table say what is a sheet

Block geometry has been arriving and being placed since the viewer learned
to expand references, but the sheet picker was still offering block
definitions as if they were sheets. A real 17 MB export produced 456 of
them against a single drawing, and a 36 MB one produced 1108. The strip is
hidden only for a drawing with one layout, so instead of a clean viewer the
reader got a wall of thumbnails, none of which is a sheet.

The classifier could only recognise a definition by finding a reference
that places it. That misses two whole families. A dimension owns its
anonymous record implicitly rather than placing it through a block
reference, which accounted for 1018 of those 1108, and a definition that
the drawing never places is referenced by nothing at all.

The export answers this itself and was not being asked. Its block table
rows carry a layout flag that is true for exactly the records a sheet was
built around: 809 records came through with the flag true for two of them,
model space and paper space, and false for the other 807. Reading it takes
the same drawing to two sheets and no false ones. The name based tests stay
as a fallback for a build that ships no block table, and a table that flags
nothing as a layout is dropped rather than believed, because reading that
one literally would classify every owner as a block and leave the drawing
with no sheet at all.

The join this rests on was unverified when the block work started. It holds:
on a real export the block id column carries record names, and 577 of the
579 names some reference places appear there as owners.
