chore(brand): mark the CAD tool where the label is written straight into the page

Six display strings never went through i18n at all, so neither the locale sweep
nor the check on i18n defaults could see them. A radio label built from a
ternary, the accepted-formats line on quick estimate, a block description in the
palette, two release summaries and the message shown when a mesh arrives with no
stable reference. All of them name the tool to a reader, so all of them take the
sign on the first mention.

The rule-pack names and their descriptions are still left alone. They read like
display text, but the same wording is the pack identity in data/bim_rules, and
moving one side without the other would leave the two disagreeing about what a
pack is called.

chore(brand): leave the shipped release notes as they were written

The previous change marked the tool name inside two release summaries, for
6.7.0 and 3.4.1. Those entries describe what those versions did on the day they
shipped, and editing them turns a record into something maintained, which is
not what the ruling asked for. The rule covers how the product names things
now, and the live labels it names are already marked.

fix(ci): stop the zero-width guard from failing on how Persian is spelled

The guard scanned U+200C to U+200F, which are not stray invisibles but the
way several of our languages are written. fa.ts carries 34602 ZWNJ because
Persian needs one wherever a prefix must not fuse into the next word, bn.ts
uses ZWJ for Bengali conjuncts, and he.ts and ar.ts use LRM so a Latin file
extension renders the right way round inside a right-to-left sentence. That
is 34698 characters the job called defects, and it failed on every run.

The earlier answer was to except ar.ts from the scan entirely, which hid six
real zero-width spaces sitting in three of its strings. Kazakh had a seventh,
in the middle of a word. Those seven are gone and the file exception with
them, so the guard now covers every locale with nothing waved through.

What is still scanned is what actually broke React reconciliation in task
135: the zero-width space, the word joiner and invisible operators, the bidi
isolates and the byte order mark. The scan finds none of them anywhere in
frontend/src, across 2718 files.
fix(cases): keep the takeoff photograph with the case that inherited the route

fix(ci): make the tenant isolation job select the tests its name promises

The job claimed its four keywords picked exactly the security suite. They did
not, because -k only ever sees the node id. It cannot see a fixture called
two_tenants, a docstring that says IDOR or an assertion that says LEAK. Of the
5875 tests in the integration and module trees the old chain took 515 and left
behind about 87 real cross-tenant tests, including the one that checks a grant
on one project does not leak another and the one that checks a credential
cannot be planted on a foreign project. Those were gating merges only through
the nightly, which is the hole this job was added to close.

The chain now selects 658, measured with pytest rather than estimated. Every
word was checked for what it drags in before being kept: security was rejected
at plus 353 because it matches whole files by name and brings in decimal
arithmetic and magic byte gates, scope at plus 138 for validators and currency
conversion, forbidden at plus 11 for a submittal state machine. cross_tenant
and outsider are not in the list because they add nothing, already covered by
tenant and isolation.

At the measured 3.9 seconds per test that projects to about 43 minutes, which
fits the old 45 minute cap with 5 percent to spare. That is not headroom, so
the cap goes to 60.

A keyword chain leaks by construction and the next oddly named test will slip
through it again. The durable fix is a tenant_isolation marker selected with
-m, and this is the interim.

chore(deps): take the patched nanoid in the frontend lock

GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8 covers nanoid below 3.3.18, where a custom generator can
loop forever on a zero size. The alert never appeared in the open list because
Dependabot auto dismissed it as a development scope finding, so the count of
open alerts said nothing about it. The version is still one we resolve and run
in the build toolchain, so the lock should carry the patched release.

postcss is the only thing in the tree that asks for nanoid, and it asks for
^3.3.16, so 3.3.18 was already inside the range it declares. No manifest edit
was needed and none was made. The change is the lockfile alone, three lines on
the single nanoid entry, with its development scope unchanged.

fix(packs): stop a pack renaming a unit it cannot convert

The US pack's en-US locale remapped modules.boq.unit.m3 to "cu yd", kg to "lb",
m2 to "sq ft", m to "lin ft", l to "gal" and t to "ton". Nothing converts the
number beside the label, so a cubic metre read as a cubic yard is wrong by
1.308 and a kilogram read as a pound by 2.205. The six remaps are gone. The
pack keeps its honest imperial labels on the imperial keys, and imperial output
stays a real feature that needs a real conversion rather than a rename. A new
test walks every pack locale and fails when the measurement system of a key
differs from the system of its label, passing translations and composite trade
units through untouched.

The Canadian pack no longer presents a commercial vendor's database as its data
source, in either its README or its distribution description. It now says what
the US pack says: no commercial cost database is bundled and none can be, the
pack is the structure and the import path for rates you are licensed to use.

The classification gate now reads .md and .toml. It scanned neither, which is
how the Canadian claim survived every green run. One limit remains worth
knowing: the gate matches a field assignment, so it reads the TOML description
but not the same claim written as markdown prose.

Five packs declared a readme they did not ship, so their source distributions
could not be built at all: bimhessen-de, brazil-sinapi, modular-prefab,
renewables-epc and uk-jct. Each has a real README now, written from its own
manifest rather than its marketing description, and a test asserts that every
declared readme path exists. All seven pack sdists build.

ci(e2e): give the macOS runners a cap the tests can finish inside

The 45 minute ceiling, not the test result, was deciding this lane. On the
nightlies that passed, macos/webkit took 39m28s, 41m01s and 43m31s, so
2026-08-13 cleared the cap with 89 seconds in hand. On the nights it did not
clear, the job was killed at 45m49s, and on 2026-08-12 all three macOS engines
went together at 45m25s, 45m32s and 45m36s.

A timeout is reported as cancelled, which is an absent result rather than a pass
or a fail. On those nights the lane said nothing at all about whether the product
runs on macOS, which is the failure mode worth removing: a check that comes back
blank for a reason unrelated to the code under test stops being read.

Linux and Windows are nowhere near the ceiling, 22m36s for ubuntu/chromium and
34m23s for windows/firefox on 2026-08-14. The cap only decides when a hung job is
killed and reserves no capacity, so a generous one costs a nightly lane nothing.

fix(brand): mark the rule pack descriptions and gate the literals nobody translated

A rule pack description reaches a user from two directions, the copy seeded by
the frontend and the YAML the loader reads into the pack it serves, so the sign
goes on both of them and on the copy the seed file embeds. The pack name stays
bare on purpose: the same string is the pack's identity in data/bim_rules, and a
sign on one side would rename it there and nowhere else.

The form check now reads the third place English ships, a quoted literal that
never went through i18n and that no translator ever sees. Template literals stay
out of it, because the first mention inside an embedded YAML document falls in
that document's own comment, and so do test fixtures and the shipped release
notes. The test-file filter also covers the sibling naming convention, which the
earlier one missed.

fix(boq): read a typed ton as the short ton, not the metric tonne

The unit normaliser folded "ton" and "tons" into "t", so an estimator who
entered a weight in short tons had it stored as 1000 kg tonnes and every
such quantity came out 10.2 percent heavy. The catalogue also carried no
imperial mass unit at all, so the pound that the US pack declares as its
weight default never resolved and formed its own bucket beside the
canonical units.

There are now two imperial mass canonicals, lb and ton_us, and a typed
"ton" resolves to ton_us. That is the reading the rest of the platform
already uses: the conversion tables on both sides, the BOQ unit system
rules and the IFC unit parser all treat a bare ton as 907.18474 kg.
Anyone who means the tonne still has t, tonne, tonnes and mt, none of
which is ambiguous in any market.

Units are normalised on write and never on read, so rows already stored
with the literal string "ton" keep the meaning they were entered with.
The demo catalogue and cost model seeds hold such rows, priced per metric
tonne, and they are deliberately left alone.

The new canonicals are also taught to the places that would otherwise not
recognise them and would quietly go blind: the imperial and dimension
sets in the validation rules, the mass dimension table that takeoff and
printed reports convert through, the GAEB export map, and the UN/ECE
codes on e-invoice lines. GAEB has no short ton code, so ton_us is
forwarded verbatim rather than mapped onto a token that would read back
as the tonne.

Tests pin the factor and not just the token, and a new gate walks every
regional pack and asserts its declared quantity defaults resolve to a
canonical, with the superscript and Cyrillic spellings named explicitly
rather than skipped.

fix(us-pack): state the true division count and drop the form designations

The US pack told the onboarding reader that MasterFormat carries 50
divisions. Our own division list in the us_pack module carries 35, so the
number was wrong in the step body, in the radio default and in both of its
options. The rule pack repeated it in its name and in covers_divisions,
where the range string additionally implied divisions 24 and 47 that we do
not carry at all. Both now read as the runs we actually cover, and the
methodology doc no longer claims fifty either.

Payment application form designations are trademarks and have no place in
pack data, so the two onboarding fields are named and labelled by what they
do rather than by the form number. The rule pack description follows. The
three rule ids that carry the same token are left alone on purpose: they
are resolved against the live registry by the pack coverage resolver, so
renaming them there would change what that resolver reports.

The cost item source comment gives up a vendor name for the function it
stood for. The token was never written as a value of that column.

feat(ui): give the sent invoice status its own badge colour

Seven invoice states shared five badge variants, so approved and sent came out the same blue. They sit one row apart in the same status column, and an invoice that has gone to the client is not one that has only been approved internally. Adds a purple variant and gives it to sent, leaving approved on the blue it has always had.

Purple rather than the semantic info cyan, which is close enough to brand blue that the split would not survive a glance. Tokens are defined for both themes and measured: 8.13:1 on the light pill, 7.58:1 on the worst dark surface, against the 4.5:1 the badge text needs. Hue is a weak channel on its own, so the label stays the thing that carries the meaning.

fix(packs): restore the Canadian pack's supplier attribution

The supplier this pack names as its cost-data source is a real partner, so
the mention is legitimate and rewriting it was wrong. Both files go back to
exactly what they said before, in the French summary line and in the
distribution description.

The signal was already in the tree and was missed: the pack's README says
the name is used under partnership agreement, and its manifest carries a
powered_by_text naming the partner. Two packs beyond this one say the same
thing, so a supplier named inside a partner pack is not evidence of a
borrowed brand.

The classification gate carries an explicit allowlist entry for the pack now,
so a later sweep cannot reopen this as a finding. That entry was measured
rather than assumed: with it the two files yield no findings, without it the
distribution description is flagged, so it is the entry doing the work. The
README mention is prose and was never reachable by the gate either way.

feat(registers): correspondence and inspections report how much of the log you see

Both list endpoints returned a bare array capped at the server default, so a
project past the cap showed its first page and nothing said so. They now
return the {items, total, offset, limit} envelope that schedule and finance
already use, with total as the count the filter matched rather than the length
of the page, and both registers carry the truncation notice under the list.

The inspections Total tile counted loaded rows, so it read 50 for a project
with 500 inspections. It now reads the register count. The dashboard quality
card turns one page into a pass rate, which is a sample and not a project
figure, so it carries the notice too.

Correspondence built its URL through a ternary whose empty branch was
unreachable, the limit above it being unconditional. Written as one literal it
is also a URL the envelope gate can read end to end, which is what lets the
gate bind the endpoint to its callers instead of reporting zero call sites it
never inspected.

feat(punchlist): report how many snags exist, and count the KPIs over all of them

The punch list router asked the repository for a page and its total, then
returned only the rows. So the register showed the newest fifty items and
nothing on screen said there were more, and the search box, which filters in
the browser, answered no matching items for a snag sitting on page two.

The KPI strip was worse than silent. Three of its six tiles - urgent open,
closed this week, average open age - were counted in the browser by walking
that same page of rows, under a comment calling the list project-wide. On a
project with five hundred snags the strip reported the urgency of the newest
fifty, and drifted further from the truth the more work the project carried.
Those three are server aggregates now, counted over the whole project, and
urgent open uses the same two statuses the open tile sums so the two cannot
contradict each other.

The list route returns items, total, offset and limit. The register shows a
truncation notice, the pin board keeps its own row query under its own key
with its own notice, and the issue hub asks for a hundred instead of taking
the default fifty. The gate entry for the endpoint went in with d71d2278e,
which picked it up from the working tree; this is the code it describes.

feat(daily-diary): the diary says how much of itself it is showing

The diary list, the day's photo grid and a diary's entries all returned bare
arrays, so a project past the server default showed its first page and nothing
said so. All three now return the {items, total, offset, limit} envelope, and
the archive, the photo grid and the entries timeline carry the truncation
notice. The project widget deliberately asks for one diary and shows one, so
it unwraps the envelope without a notice.

The entries route took no offset or limit at all and returned however many
entries the diary held. It now pages, bounded like the photos route in this
module, and reports the count it matched. That is a new bound rather than a
preserved one: a day's diary is small, but the bulk-create route beside it can
write a month into one, and a response whose size is set only by the data has
no ceiling.

The paged read is a separate repository method rather than a limit added to
the existing one. The five callers of the existing one are the day's PDF, the
completeness check and the workforce rollup, and each of those is wrong rather
than merely short when handed a page: a diary export that quietly drops its
last deliveries is worse than one that takes a moment longer. The paged read
also orders by id after entry_time, because a bulk import writes a whole day
on one timestamp and ties let a row repeat on two pages while another is never
returned at all.

feat(auth): honour the permission list an API key declares

An API key has always carried a permissions column. It was written at
creation, echoed back when the key was listed, and read by nothing that
made an authorization decision, so a key could never reach less than its
owner did. The column read as enforcement while enforcing nothing, which
is the worst state for anyone about to build a headless integration on
top of it.

The key's list is now the narrowing half of the decision. Authority is
the intersection of what the owner's live role grants and what the key
declares, so a key can be held below its owner but never raised above
them. An empty or missing list declares no narrowing, which is the shape
every key issued so far has, so existing keys behave exactly as before.
The narrowing runs ahead of the admin bypass on purpose, because holding
an admin's key below its owner is the case the column exists for and a
check placed after the bypass would never run.

The ICS calendar feed is stricter. Its credential rides in the
subscription URL, where a third party stores it and intermediaries log
it, so it is the most exposed thing we hand out and it now demands the
narrowest key we can express. A key must name integrations.calendar_feed
outright; the empty list stops being a pass there. That is the one
deliberate behaviour change here, and it is safe to make now because no
screen issues keys yet, so nobody has one in a calendar client. The feed
also checks that the account behind the key is still active, which it
never did.

Project reach stays the owner's. There is no project column on a key and
adding one half formed would be worse than not adding it, since no
endpoint can revise a key after creation.

fix(gaeb): the export summary stops claiming prices a bill does not have

The Prices tile answered Yes for any bill carrying at least one rate, so
an LV with one priced line out of four hundred announced itself as a
priced bid to the bidder about to receive the file. It now reads the
whole bill: Yes only when every line item has a rate, Partial with the
count of lines still missing one, No when none of them do. X81 keeps
saying No, since that phase drops prices by definition.

The Pos. column also holds the width its longest Ordnungszahl needs. The
fitted width was only a starting width and sizeColumnsToFit handed it
straight back to a hardcoded 70px floor, which ellipsised an ordinal
like 09.01.0030 again as soon as the viewport got tight. An ordinal is
an addressable identifier that gets typed back into an inquiry, so the
floor now tracks the data instead.

docs(punchlist): say what the truncation notice really does over an empty search

The comment above the register's notice claimed the empty state was left
exactly as it was. That is not true and was never meant to be: the notice is
gated on the server page having rows, not on the filtered rows, so a
client-side search that matches nothing still shows it above "no matching
items". That is on purpose and it is what the finance register already does,
because a search that finds nothing is exactly when the reader has to be told
only part of the register was searched.

A project with no items at all is unaffected either way, since then the total
is zero and the notice renders nothing. Loading, error and no-project stay
gated out. Comment only, no behaviour change.

fix(dwg-seed): the demo plan states its own count and is labelled in German

The seeded drawing carried an element count that was never about it. Both
seeders read the count off the demo spec entry for a converted CAD file of the
same format and handed it to the DXF the seeder authors at seed time, so a plan
holding eight entities advertised the 5480 of a different drawing. The count
now comes from the parse of the file it describes, and the parameter that
carried the other number is gone rather than left there to be filled in again.
A reference row seeded without ezdxf states no count at all, because nothing on
that path has read a drawing.

The room labels read LIVING 6.0 x 4.0 and BED 2.4 x 4.0 on a plan presented as
a German Grundriss. They now read Wohnen 3,60/4,00 and Schlafen 2,40/4,00,
which is the wording and the notation a German plan uses, a decimal comma and
width over depth. The living room label also repeated the 6.00 m of the outer
wall while sitting in the 3.60 m room the partition leaves, so each label now
states the room it labels and the two labelled widths add up to the envelope.

Both are pinned against a real database. The count is compared with a walk of
the DXF on disk rather than with the number the seeder wrote, which is the only
comparison that is not two copies of one value, and the labels are read back
through the same entity reader the viewer uses.

test(dwg-seed): compare the labelled room widths at the tolerance the file uses

The two new label assertions were written at a relative tolerance of 1e-9,
which the current two room plan meets exactly but which is tighter than the
addition of parsed decimals guarantees in general. Every other geometric
comparison in this file compares at 1e-6, and a test whose point is surviving
the plan gaining a room should not fail on the third summand.

fix(i18n-gate): the e-invoice profile names are standards, not translation debt

The leak gate has been red since yesterday evening over six values in the
einvoice.profile family: EN 16931 in both syntaxes, Factur-X, Peppol BIS
Billing, XRechnung and ZUGFeRD. All six are identical in all 39 locales, and
the four siblings in the same block that carry a country in brackets are
translated in ru and zh, which shows translators worked this block and left
the bare standard names alone on purpose. That is the allowlist, with
reason_category standard_code.

The other new cluster is da, de and fr sharing International, Navigation and
National (1) with English. Their neighbours in those same files are real
translations, ru translates all three, and Spanish is not in the set because
it says Internacional, Navegacion and Nacional. Three Latin cognates spelled
the same way in three languages is not a leak, so the locale set is recorded
as an accepted cluster rather than declared as debt.

fix(case-routes): a module screen is a declared route too

The case-route guard read only App.tsx, but modules mount their own routes
into the same Routes block through useModuleRouteElements. The first two cases
to link the GAEB Exchange screen turned the lane red for a route that works:
the module declares /gaeb-exchange in its own manifest and ships enabled.

The guard now reads every manifest under frontend/src/modules as well, which
is what cases.test.ts already did. Modules that ship disabled stay out,
because their routes really are unreachable until the reader turns the module
on, and regional-exchange is exactly that case with its twenty country
screens. An empty module read is a failure of its own now, so a scan that
stops finding manifests cannot pass by measuring nothing. Both manifest
extensions are read, since regional-exchange keeps its own in a tsx.

i18n: three waves left their new strings in English, so translate them

Three groups of keys, all of them added over the last day and none of them
reaching a reader outside en and de.

The e-invoice rule messages are the largest: thirteen BR rules, already
written in en and de, now carried into the other thirty-seven locales. mn is
deliberately not among them, it is out of the supported list.

gaeb.prices_missing turned the orphan-key gate red. It is a counted key, so
every locale gets exactly the CLDR categories its own language resolves to
rather than a copy of the English pair: six forms in ar, four in cs, pl and
ru, three in the Romance locales and in he and hr, one in id, ja, ko, th, vi
and zh. The wording follows the position noun each file already uses for
gaeb.import_btn, so the warning reads like the button above it.

settings.date_format_auto and the two federated file-picker strings belong to
the date-format and takeoff-files work. They land here first, before the code
that calls them, so no push in between can show an English string to a reader
who did not ask for one.

feat(modules): the registry page reads in every language, not just English

A module manifest declares the name and description the registry page prints.
Most of them shipped an English literal or a key only English and German
answered, so a French or Japanese reader saw either the English string or the
raw key, and nothing failed because the type is string either way.

Every first-party manifest now carries its name and description in the
locales the app ships, and two tests hold the line. manifestI18n.test.ts is
the statement about the data: every name and description is a key, English
and German answer it, and no locale a manifest carries repeats the English
string back. ModuleTogglesSection.i18n.test.tsx is the statement about the
screen, rendering the cards through the real i18next wiring with the English
fallback switched off, in German and in French, because a fallback makes an
untranslated card look finished.

Three strings only reached the page as raw keys and are translated here:
converter.ifc.name and converter.rvt.name, which the sweep had added a
description for but not a name, and modules.regional_exchange.description,
whose manifest is the one .tsx in the directory and was skipped by a scan
looking for .ts. The Filipino name of the takeoff viewer was the English
string again and now follows the word its own description already uses.

feat(settings): the date format you pick is the date format you get

The regional setting stored a date format and offered three of them, but no
rendering surface read it back, so picking one changed nothing on any screen.

Dates now go through formatDateWithPreference, which reorders the day, month
and year to the chosen pattern and leaves everything else to the language:
the calendar, the numbering system, the time zone and the time fields are
untouched, so an Arabic reader who asks for MM/DD/YYYY keeps Arabic-Indic
digits and only gets the fields in a different order.

The default is the new value auto, which means follow the interface language
and runs the original code path unchanged. That matters because there was no
unset state before: both the account column and the store defaulted to the
concrete DD.MM.YYYY, so wiring the preference up without auto would have
silently changed what every existing account sees. The server default stays
DD.MM.YYYY for rows already written; only the Python-side default moves, so
no migration is needed for a value that renders identically either way.

Two test files carry the guarantee: one proves auto is byte for byte what the
old expression produced across locales, the other renders the three surfaces
a reader recognises and drives the preference through all of them, including
the case where the setting changes while the page is open.

feat(files): the project files dialog shows the takeoff plans too

The takeoff module keeps its documents in its own table, and the dialog
called "open from project files" listed only the documents area. A plan that
was open in the takeoff viewer could not be found by name in a dialog whose
title said it held the project's files, which is not a gap in a list, it is
the list saying something untrue.

The listing endpoint now takes a set of kinds rather than one category, so a
caller that needs two sources asks once and gets a single project-scoped,
permission-checked, paged answer instead of merging two listings on the
client and paging neither. An unknown kind is a 400 rather than a quietly
empty page: a typo there returns rows the caller did not ask for and nothing
on screen would say so. The kind set is derived from the Literal that already
typed it, so a new kind cannot be accepted by the type checker and rejected
by the endpoint.

The picker groups by kind, marks what the calling module already holds so the
same plan cannot be added twice, and says which sources it is showing. The
database properties behind this are cross-table and project-scoped, so they
are tested against a real cluster rather than a mock.

test(auth): a permission refusal is not a UUID oracle, so stop banning 403

The IDOR shape test banned status_code=403 anywhere in the integrations
router. That was the right rule while every 403 would have been a verdict
about a row: "this exists but is not yours" is distinguishable from "this
does not exist", and the difference is what leaks a UUID.

The calendar feed now refuses a key whose permission list does not include
integrations.calendar_feed, and it refuses before it looks at the project at
all. That answer is identical for a real project id and a made-up one, so it
tells an attacker nothing. The rule is therefore not "no 403" but "every 403
here refuses the caller by permission", which its own message has to say, and
a resource verdict never does.

The scope test proves the ordering rather than asserting the status alone: it
records whether the project guard was consulted and fails if the refusal read
the row first.

fix(page-gate): an invalidation must not borrow the next query's fetcher

The shared-key scan counted a call site as a read when a queryFn turned up
within six hundred characters after the key. invalidateQueries names a key
without consuming the value, and the scan knew that, but the window is wide
enough to reach the next useQuery in the file and pick up its queryFn.

ProcurementPage is where it showed: the file invalidates ['finance-invoices']
inside a mutation, the next query up the file reads a different endpoint, and
the gate judged the invalidation against that neighbour's type argument and
called the file unmigrated. No edit to the file could have cleared it, which
is the failure mode the URL scan in the same script already guards against by
binding to the nearest preceding call.

The window now stops at the next queryKey, because a second key starts a
second call object and a queryFn past it belongs to that one.

feat(pagination): eighteen more lists say how much of themselves they show

These endpoints already returned the envelope with a total in it; the screens
reading them threw the total away and rendered the first page as if it were
the whole set. A contact search that silently stops at fifty is worse than
one that says so, because the reader concludes the record does not exist.

Migrated here: quick estimate, contacts and the shared contact search box,
contracts, CRM, CVR, the dashboard rollups, the ERP chat history and its
panels, the FX panel, procurement and the delivery modal. Each reads items
and total from the envelope and shows the truncation notice when the page is
not the whole list.

The progress register gets a database fix rather than a UI one. It paged with
OFFSET and LIMIT ordered by recorded_at alone, which is not a total order:
recorded_at defaults to the transaction timestamp, so every entry a bulk
import appends carries the same value, and the database is free to arrange
the tied rows differently for each offset it serves. A walk through the pages
could hand back one entry twice and never return another, with every page
looking correct on its own. Ordering also by seq makes the order total. The
test walks the pages against a real cluster and asserts the multiset of ids,
because a partial order is invisible to any single-page assertion.

fix(progress-test): identify the ordering key by name, not by object identity

The PG lane failed on the one assertion in that file that never touches the
database. ProgressEntry.seq.asc() coerces the mapped attribute through
__clause_element__, so the expression's .element is the annotated Column, and
that is not the InstrumentedAttribute the model exposes, nor the plain entry
in __table__.c. An identity comparison against any of the three fails on a
correct ORDER BY, and the failure message said as much: it reported that the
order must end on seq rather than on oe_progress_entry.seq.

The key is now identified by table and column name, and the two assertions
below it still check what seq is actually relied on for, which is that the
final key is unique and NOT NULL.

fix(updates): stop asking GitHub again every time it says no

The release check calls api.github.com anonymously, where the rate limit is
per IP address. An office behind one address burns it and gets 403 for the
rest of the hour, and the widget is mounted in the sidebar, so it is on every
page.

Only a successful answer was cached. A refusal was not recorded at all, so
every mount in every tab asked again and the browser logged another failed
request each time. The failure is now cached like an answer, on the same TTL,
which is what a negative cache is for.

The second hole was the cache guard in useUpdateCheck. It returned early only
when the cached release was newer than the running version, so the ordinary
case, an install already up to date, fell straight through to the network on
every mount and the cache guarded nothing. A fresh entry now ends the
question either way, which is what the sidebar widget already did.

VITE_DISABLE_UPDATE_CHECK turns the check off for an install that has no
outbound internet to begin with: on-premise behind a proxy, an isolated site,
a machine being recorded. There is no answer we could show it, and without
the flag it asks once an hour forever.

fix(i18n): two menu entries that share a label lead nowhere in particular

Variations and change orders are separate screens, and so are the daily diary
and field reports, but eleven locales printed one label for the first pair and
German printed one label for the second. A sidebar with the same word twice is
not a gap the reader can work around: there is no way to tell which entry
leads where, and both look like the same page listed by mistake.

In most locales it is the variations key that carries the change-order
wording, so that key gets the term its own screen is about. Where the legacy
nav.changeorders spelling already carried a distinct change-order label, that
wording moves onto nav.change_orders instead and the variations key keeps the
domain term it already had, which is how French and Portuguese resolve.

German follows the ruling of 12.08 that never reached the file: Nachträge
stays with variations, change orders become Änderungsaufträge, and field
reports become Baustellenberichte so the diary keeps Bautagebuch to itself.

fix(variations): offer back the contract standard the German seed writes

The German demo seed puts VOB_B on its variation rows, and the registry of
supported standards never carried it. Nothing failed loudly: the rows saved
and the clause reference rendered, but opening a seeded row for editing
offered a list that did not contain the contract that row is under, so a
save moved it to a different standard without saying so.

VOB_B now resolves to § 2 Abs. 5 VOB/B, the price consequence of a change
the client orders under § 1 Abs. 3. Work never agreed at all falls under
§ 2 Abs. 6 and states its own clause on the row.

The test reads the standards straight out of the seed source rather than
repeating them, because a list written twice is the shape of the bug.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(daily-diary): write a German site register the showcase projects can be filmed with

The four German demo projects carried ten diaries each with English notes, no
entries, no photos, a "closed" badge over a null closer and five of the ten
dates falling on a Sunday or a public holiday. The rich seeder that would have
filled them never ran, because its guard asks whether the project has any
diary at all and the project installer had already written the thin headers
itself.

Rather than unblock the generic seeder onto these projects, which would have
kept the English wording and added a unique key collision on
(project_id, diary_date), there is now a dedicated seeder for them. It writes
thirty consecutive German working days ending today, skipping weekends,
federal holidays, the Land holidays of Hesse and Baden-Wuerttemberg and the
two December days a German site is shut anyway. Each day carries four entries,
three weather readings and up to two photos taken from the project's own
committed site photography, referenced by the URL the documents module already
serves rather than by copying bytes.

The status ladder runs through the service, so a closed day names who closed
it and an archived day carries the signature and content hash production code
computes. Both timestamps are moved back to the evening of the day in question
afterwards, which is safe because neither field feeds the content hash, and
the test recomputes the seal from the stored rows rather than trusting it.

The list of showcase demo ids now lives in one place, app/core/demo_showcase.py,
because three writers have to agree on it: the generic diary seeder and the
project installer both filter it out before their own guards run, and the
variations seeder was already carrying a private copy.

fix(field-time): offer the project's own crews in the timesheet picker

The resource picker on the day recorder and the timesheet editor listed every
resource in the tenant, so a foreman booking hours on one site scrolled past
the crews of every other one. The repository has scoped listing already, home
project or unhomed company pool, but the argument stopped at the service: the
router never accepted a project and the service never passed one on.

The endpoint now takes an optional project_id and both field time screens send
the project they are already showing, keyed so switching projects refetches
rather than reusing the previous roster. Calls without the parameter keep the
tenant wide list they had, which is what the resources register itself wants.

fix(routing): show the project the address bar names, not the one the switcher remembers

Eighteen screens mounted under /projects/:projectId read the global project
switcher directly and ignored the route. Opening a shared link to another
project's variations, contracts, diary or takt schedule silently rendered
whichever project the recipient had last selected, with the correct id sitting
in the address bar the whole time.

useActiveProjectId already encodes the rule the rest of the app follows, route
first and switcher second, so these screens now call it. Flat routes such as
the resources register keep reading the switcher, which is correct there
because no project is named in the address.

Five further screens reachable at /projects/:projectId, equipment, service,
subcontractors, portal and the BI dashboards, resolve no project at all and
list the whole company on both their flat and their nested route. That is a
different defect, scoping their queries rather than choosing between two
sources, and it is left alone here.

fix(i18n): the page heading and the browser tab follow the language the rest of the screen speaks

The heading over a page and the title of the browser tab both come from the
English literal a route hands to its page wrapper, translated through a map in
the header. The map had grown to cover about half the routes, and the half it
missed included the opening screen of most modules, so a German session read
"Field Time" and "Payment Clock" over a page whose every other word was German,
and the tab said the same.

Every title added here already has its words translated somewhere in the
bundle, usually under the very key the sidebar uses to name the same
destination, so this is mapping work and not new strings. Where the sidebar
words the destination a little differently the sidebar wins, because the point
of the map is that the menu entry, the heading and the tab can never disagree.

Two entries had been pointing at keys that exist in no locale at all. They
looked correct and behaved exactly like a missing entry, because the same
fallback that prints the English literal also catches a key nobody answers.
Both now point at the assemblies module's own names.

The test reads the routes straight out of the router, so a route mounted
without a mapping fails rather than quietly shipping an English heading, and it
checks every key against both English and German rather than English alone, a
key present in one and missing in the other renders English anyway. Eleven
titles stay English on purpose, all of them developer or admin surfaces, and
the list has to stay honest in both directions: a title that gets translated
later has to leave it, and a title whose route is gone has to leave it too.

fix(i18n): a module page is headed with the word the reader's own language uses

An installed module renders under a route that heads every one of them with the
literal "Module". Nothing replaces it later, the page never touches its own
title, so the heading and the browser tab said "Module" in all forty languages.

The word itself was translated everywhere already, but as a filter label inside
the quantities module. A page heading has no business reading its name out of
another module's namespace, since whoever renames that filter would silently
rename this heading, so the modules namespace now carries the word too and the
values come across unchanged from the ones already in the bundle.

That leaves ten route titles English on purpose, all of them developer and
admin surfaces, and the list that records them stays a gate rather than a note.

feat(demo): seed the cost-value register and the earned-value baseline

Two modules of the cost control walkthrough opened on an empty screen because
the demo registry never called them. Both seed now, and they read the same
commercial profile out of app/core/demo_commercial, so the reconciliation's
cost to date and the baseline's actual cost are one number rather than two
estimates of it. A viewer walks from one screen to the other, and the two have
to be the same job.

The profile carries the eighteen month spend curve, six cost heads with their
own margin and their own overrun, and the window each head is open in. A head
that opens late and closes early is what makes the margin move from month to
month; a fixed multiple of overall progress keeps every head's share of the
total constant forever and reports the same margin at every date.

The earned value figures come from the module's own compute_metrics rather than
being written out here, so the demo cannot show a CPI that does not follow from
its own EV and AC. Observations are rounded to the cent before they go in,
because the engine derives the variances from the raw inputs and would
otherwise store a schedule variance that misses EV minus PV by a fraction of a
cent, which is a register that visibly does not add up.

Baseline validation is left pending with no findings and no score. Stamping an
approval without running the rule set would be inventing one.

Fifteen tests on the PostgreSQL lane cover the periods and their German titles,
the falling margin, the cashflow that starts out of pocket and closes on the
bill, the identity between the two modules' view of actual cost, a second run
that changes nothing, and a project outside the demo estate that stays empty.

feat(i18n): name the payment clock states and the resource types in every locale

Eighteen keys existed in no locale at all. Every call site passes a
defaultValue, so the screen printed the raw server enum, the English word
travelled onto a German page, and no gate could see it: a key absent from en.ts
and from de.ts alike leaves no gap for a gap check to find.

Both vocabularies are closed and come from code, not from user data, so the key
set is enumerable. The four application states, the five breach events and the
three notice types are the tuples in payment_clock/models.py; the six resource
types are the build-up rows in the bill of quantities grid. The German wording
follows the trade rather than the dictionary, so the rate build-up reads Lohn,
Material, Gerät, Gerätebediener, Nachunternehmer and Sonstiges.

The regional Spanish and Brazilian files repeat their parent wording. These are
statutory and estimating terms with no regional split, and inventing one is how
a locale drifts away from its own family.

One entry lands in the leak allowlist with its evidence. Material is the same
Latin loanword in nine of the locales, which the leak detector reads as a
cluster of files copied from English; French, Polish and Russian all differ,
which is what makes it nine languages agreeing rather than nine copies.

fix(demo): the diary guard now asks who wrote the row it is looking at

The demo installer lays down a handful of empty diary headers before the
module seeder runs, and the guard asked whether the project holds a diary at
all. Every project answered yes, so the ninety day register with entries,
weather, photos and signatures was written, tested and never once inserted on
any install. Nothing looked broken from the outside because the screen was not
empty, it showed the installer's headers.

The guard now asks who wrote the row. This seeder and its German sibling mark
their own work, the installer marks its placeholders with the demo id, and a
row carrying neither is somebody's actual diary and still stops the project
cold, which is the reason to have a guard in the first place.

The placeholders are removed on the projects that go on to be filled, because
project and date are unique together and a header standing inside the ninety
day window would collide with the day being written. A project the seeder
skips keeps everything it had, so nothing comes out emptier than it went in.

Five tests on the PostgreSQL lane, one per case the guard has to tell apart.

fix(demo): write the demo domains the way a German firm registers them

Twenty addresses across the three retail packs and the project installer put
an umlaut in the domain: vergabe@sommerfeld-kaeltetechnik.de was written with
the umlaut in it, and so were the cooling, groundworks and landscaping firms
around it. A domain label cannot carry one on the wire. It has to be punycode,
and punycode on screen reads as line noise, so what a German firm actually
registers is the folded spelling. On camera the old form read as a typo.

The name is not the address. Sommerfeld Kaeltetechnik GmbH keeps its umlauts
in the company name and always should; only the part after the at sign is
constrained. Website hosts were folded alongside the addresses so a firm whose
mail now resolves is not left with a site that does not.

A test reads the two spans separately and fails on either half getting it
wrong, which is the distinction nothing in the tree was making. It runs in the
PostgreSQL lane with the other demo seed checks, because a test that blocks no
merge is the same as a test that does not exist.

fix(routing): stop three company registers pretending to be project scoped

Equipment, subcontractors and the partner portal were each mounted twice, flat
and under /projects/:projectId/. The second mount promised a filter the data
cannot express: only a hire carries a project, not the machine; only an
agreement carries one, not the firm; portal users, access rules and sessions
carry none at all. Both mounts therefore rendered the whole company register,
and the one with the project in its address was the more misleading of the
two, because it said the list had been narrowed when it had not.

The project-scoped addresses now redirect to the flat ones rather than being
deleted, so a link somebody saved still lands somewhere true. Nothing in the
navigation pointed at them, so no menu entry changes.

Service and BI dashboards keep both mounts. Their records do carry a project,
so there the route is a promise the data can keep and the work is to honour it
on the page, which is a different change.

feat(i18n): head the diary calendar in the site's own language

The seven column headings above the diary month were printed through a
defaultValue fallback and the keys existed in no locale, so a German site
diary was headed Mon Tue Wed. It is the most looked at row on the page and the
one the seeded Bautagebuch sits under.

Seven keys, a closed set, in every locale. The abbreviations are the ones each
language actually uses rather than the English three letters transliterated,
so Estonian gets single letters and Chinese gets the numbered days. Hebrew
names its days by their ordinal from Sunday, which puts the second day against
Monday and the first against Sunday.

fix(frontend): drop the two imports the project-context change left behind

93ea75f4a moved both pages from the context store to useActiveProjectId but
kept the old import standing. The tree has noUnusedLocals on, so tsc -b
failed with TS6133 on ContractsPage and ConstructionControlPage, which means
the frontend build has been red on main since that commit. Nothing but the
import lines is touched, and tsc -b is clean afterwards.

feat(service): scope the register to the project the route names

The module is mounted twice, flat at /service for the tenant-wide dispatcher
view and under /projects/:projectId/service. The second mount was a lie: the
page loaded the same tenant-wide lists and printed them under one project's
name. Contracts, tickets and recurring schedules could already be filtered
server-side, so the page now asks for the route project and keys its queries
by it, and a contract or schedule created from inside a project is struck
against that project instead of vanishing from the list it was created in.

Work orders needed the filter built. They carry no project of their own, the
project sits two joins away through the ticket and the contract, so the
listing gets a by-project branch rather than a narrowing in the browser. The
difference is not cosmetic: the listing is paginated, so filtering after the
page would take the newest hundred work orders across the whole tenant and
then drop the foreign ones, and a quiet project would show an empty tab while
its own work orders sat just past the boundary. tests/pg pins that case.

The ticket listing accepted status and priority and silently dropped both
whenever the caller scoped by project. Fixed the same way, with its own test.

Equipment, portal and subcontractors were the other three project-scoped
mounts and they stay redirects: those registers carry no project dimension at
all, so there is nothing there to filter by.

fix(service): derive the selected contract so a pick cannot outlive its scope

Moving between /service and /projects/:projectId/service re-renders the page
without remounting it, so the contract chosen on one route survived onto the
other while the list it came from was replaced. The Assets tab reads that id,
which means a contract from outside the project could put its assets under
the project's name, which is the defect the scoping had just closed.

Derived from the loaded contracts rather than reset in an effect, so there is
no render in which the picker and the assets query disagree.

feat(demo): give the seeded bids the lines the price comparison compares

The leveling matrix and the budget comparison are both built by indexing a
bid's line_items on position_id. The demo installer wrote line_items=[], so
both screens rendered a full grid of empty cells however many bidders had
submitted, and the page whose entire purpose is per-line spread had no
per-line data in it at all.

Each bidder now prices the package scope line by line. The submitted total
stays an input rather than becoming an output: several packs state their bid
figures in the package description and derive the bid factor from them, so
the lines are the documented total spread across the scope, not a new number
replacing it. Within that the rates move deterministically around the
reference rate, so there is real spread to colour and a reseed produces the
same comparison, and a later bidder leaves a few lines out entirely so the
imputation path has something to impute. Short packages keep every line,
where dropping one would remove a visible share rather than a detail.

Line totals are the exact product of rate and quantity, because the matrix
reads any disagreement between the two as a scaled bid line and badges it. A
column lands within a few cents of the submitted total and no closer; closing
the last cents would need exactly that disagreement.

Multi-package tenders now split the priced lines into one contiguous scope
per package instead of every package pointing at the whole bill.

Separately, the tendering module's own demo seeder wrote line rows keyed
unit_price / total_price / code. Nothing in the tree reads those names: the
API returned the rows, the page typed them as LineItem, and the columns
rendered blank. They now use the vocabulary BidLineItem declares. Those
packages still carry no reference BOQ, so there is nothing to level against
there, which is a separate gap.

fix(tendering): compare a package against the lines it was raised over

Both comparison screens load the package's BOQ, and a package covering part
of a bill still points at the whole thing. So the lines nobody was asked to
price landed on the reference side, where every bidder read as having omitted
them: each out-of-scope line was imputed at the bidder's own mean rate, and a
lot worth a quarter of a bill levelled its bids to roughly four times what
they quoted, then measured them against a budget four times their own. The
summary counted three imputed lines for every matched one.

A package can now say which lines it covers, and the leveling matrix and the
budget comparison both read it. Two writers already knew the answer and said
it differently, so either form is accepted: create_from_boq freezes the lines
it chose into line_item_template, which until now nothing read, and the demo
installer records a plain list of position ids. A package that declares
nothing covers its whole BOQ, which is what every package written before this
carries, and a scope that matches no line in the BOQ is stale metadata rather
than an empty package, so it widens back out instead of emptying the screen.

The installer's split of a bill into one scope per package now cuts on the
running total rather than on line count. Every package's bids are the same
share of the grand total and the comparison measures a bid against its own
lines, so a scope worth half of what its bidders quote would put all of them
100% over budget for a reason nobody can read off the screen. BOQ lines differ
by two orders of magnitude in value, so equal counts are not equal money. A
bill of fewer lines than packages still gives one line to each rather than
crowding them into the first, and an unpriced bill has nothing to balance and
falls back to counting.

The integration is what the tests pin. The pure filter has its own unit tests,
but the failure lived in the join between a stored package's metadata and a
stored BOQ's positions, which is how it shipped past a suite that covered the
arithmetic. The PG tests level real bids against a real bill, once with the
scope declared and once without, and the second one states the shape that was
wrong so it cannot come back quietly.

i18n(clash): name the four severities in every language

The clash page builds the key from the value it is naming, t(`clash.severity.
${s}`), and no locale had a key for any of the four. A missing key falls back
to the defaultValue, which here is the raw server value, so the severity
column, the filter chips, the facet list, the bulk menu and the engine's
suggestion all read critical, high, medium and low in English on a screen that
was otherwise fully translated. The status half of the same vocabulary has had
its keys all along, which is what made the gap invisible: the two columns sit
side by side and only one of them was ever in the reader's language.

The words are not new. High, medium and low are the ones the dashboard already
uses for this exact scale, and critical comes from each locale's own severity
vocabulary, so the page now says what the rest of the product says. Where the
language inflects, the form is the one that agrees with the other three: the
Russian statuses on this page are feminine, so the severities are too, and
Czech, Croatian and Bulgarian take the masculine to match theirs.

Both vocabularies are closed and both are decided by the server, so the test
asserts the whole set rather than a sample: every locale names every severity
and every status, and German is resolved through a real bundle to show the
line is reachable and not merely present. Checked against a value the server
does not send, the same assertion fails in 41 of 42 cases, so it is measuring
the locales rather than agreeing with them.

fix(schedule): the resource histogram picks from this project's roster

The picker on a schedule's resource tab listed the tenant, then defaulted to
whatever came back first and drew its histogram from it. Across a tenant with
more than one project that first row belongs to whichever roster sorts first,
so the tab opened on a demand curve for someone who has never worked on this
schedule, and the dropdown offered every other project's crews as the way to
correct it.

It now asks for the project the schedule belongs to. The server already knows
what that means for a shared pool: the crews homed on the project plus the
unhomed company pool, which is the same narrowing the site surfaces use. The
histogram endpoint takes a resource id and is unaffected.

The name lookup on the activity grid stays tenant-wide on purpose. It resolves
ids that assignments already carry rather than offering a choice, and an
assignment can point at a resource homed on another project, so narrowing it
would print raw ids in place of names.

i18n(payment-clock): say the sum's reason in the reader's language

The sentence under the sum payable is the answer the module exists to give,
and it arrived as finished English prose. The server has to assemble it - the
four possible answers are not the same statement and each names dates, a
statute and a figure - but it can only assemble it in one language, so a
German screen carried an English sentence under a translated heading.

The server now names which sentence it is and the values that go in it, and
the page says it. The prose stays: it is the API's answer, it is what a
reading stored before the codes existed carries, and it is the page's
fallback. source could not serve as the code, because three different answers
share undetermined and they are different statements. The window-still-open
case is two codes rather than one with an optional tail, since a language that
puts the date first cannot reorder a clause glued on after the fact.

Seven sentences in forty languages, and the four tolerance presets on the
clash page in the same pass, which had no key at all and read Coarse, Fine and
Precise everywhere. The completeness gate that already covered clash severity
and status now covers both families: every locale names every value its
screens build a key from.

feat(cases): wear the specialist as a honeycomb over the case, not beside it

A case card banded the two: the person on one side, the diagram of the work on
the other, meeting through a soft mask. The person arrived first, which was the
point, but it cost the diagram nearly forty percent of its width and the
diagram is what says what the case does. On the dashboard tiles, a sixth of a
row wide, a band would have left the drawing unreadable, so they carried no
person at all.

Both now keep the whole diagram and cut the portrait to the honeycomb cell the
marketing site uses on the cards these cases came from, sitting over one
corner. The dashboard deals its faces from the same helper as the hub, so a
case wears the same person in both places rather than two different ones. The
photographs stay decorative: the role is named in the card text, so nothing is
said only in a picture.

The no-project panel every gated module falls back to now points at the thing
it is talking about. It said to pick a project from the header and left the
reader to find the header; the arrow leans up and towards the start edge, where
the switcher is, and mirrors under rtl by rotation so it keeps pointing at the
control rather than away from it. Same words, same action, on a panel that
reads as a card rather than a blank page.

fix(finance): show the overdue money the dashboard already had

The finance dashboard endpoint returns total_receivable, total_overdue and
overdue_count, and the page declared all three and read only the first. So the
screen a finance lead opens to see what is late showed what is owed and never
what is past due, while the reporting page drew the same field from the same
endpoint as a money tile.

The tile now sits beside Receivable, red while anything is overdue and green
when nothing is, and it borrows the reporting page's label so one number is not
called two things on two screens.

perf(punchlist): fetch the pin board only when the pin board is shown

The register loaded a hundred rows for the pin board on every visit, including
the visits that never show it. Everything that query feeds - the board and its
truncation notice - renders inside the pins branch, so on the list view the
rows arrived and were dropped.

It is now gated on the view, the same way the drawings query beside it already
was. The KPI band had already stopped reading the list in favour of the server
summary, so with this the screen makes one request for items instead of two.

fix(cost-model): the number on the budget badge agrees with its arrow

The three KPI badges say "vs budget" and printed the headroom left instead of
the deviation from it, so a project 11.1 million under budget read "+11.1M vs.
Budget" in green with a downward arrow. Arrow and colour were right and the
number said the opposite, which is the half a reader looks at.

All three now come off one quantity: over budget is a plus, under budget is a
minus, and the arrow and the colour keep meaning what they meant.

fix(demo): a progress period carries the year it happened in

The S-curve on a seeded project fell 36.7 points in a single month and
finished the year below its own July. The readings were fine, one cumulative
percentage per month and climbing. The label was not: it kept the project
start year and wrapped the month with a modulo, so a programme starting in
April 2026 named its thirteenth month 2026-04, exactly like its first.

Everything downstream is keyed by that string. The cumulative endpoint keeps
the latest entry per period, sorts the periods as text and subtracts
neighbours, so a month holding three readings kept whichever one the dedupe
picked and the ladder came back shuffled. Of the 34 seeded templates 33 drew
a falling curve and 30 named at least one month twice.

The label now carries the month into the year. The test pins the property
rather than the expression: one label means one month, and reading the
percentages in label order climbs, on every template.

Installed demo data keeps the old labels until the project is reseeded.

fix(cost-model): one page, one reading of each index

The 5D page carried two SPI/CPI pairs and two numbers called EAC. The
Performance card read the latest stored EVM snapshot while the Earned Value
panel a screen above it recomputed live, so a German reader saw SPI 0.90 and
CPI 0.96 beside SPI 0.75 and CPI 0.19, one saying the job is close to plan
and the other that it pays five euro for one euro of work. The card now reads
the live computation and keeps the snapshot only as the fallback for a
project whose EVM cannot be recomputed.

The two forecasts are genuinely two methods and both belong on the page: the
tile sums the forecast each budget line carries, the panel divides BAC by
CPI. Only one of them may be called EAC. The tile now says which forecast it
is, in every locale, built from the words each locale already uses for
Forecast and for budget lines.

Four German strings on the same page were machine translated and read as it:
a noun that was an adjective, two words run together into one that means
nothing, a lower-case noun, and the wrong gender on Endergebnis.

fix(ui): compact money is written in the reader's language

A German cost report printed "203.1M EUR". Both halves are wrong for the
person reading it: a point is a thousands separator in German, so that reads
as two hundred and three thousand, and M is not a magnitude letter that
language uses. On one screen there were twenty of them.

No locale check could see it. The string was assembled in code, and four
screens had each grown their own private version of the same six lines, every
one of them with a toFixed and an English suffix. They now share one helper
that asks the engine, which knows both halves per locale and has since the
locale data was written: 203,1 Mio. € in German, EUR203.1M in English,
203,1 млн € in Russian.

The card on the project list gains a second thing from this. Its formatter
was built once at import from whatever language the app started in, so it
could not follow a language switch; the shared one reads the locale per call.

fix(ui): a percentage is written the way the reader writes one

The other half of the same screens. A German cost report printed 68.3% and
-36.7%, where that reader writes 68,3 % and reads a point as a thousands
separator, and a Turkish reader gets the sign after the digits when their
language puts it in front. The shape that produced all of them is a template
literal with toFixed and a per cent sign glued on, so no locale check can see
it: there is no key to be missing.

fmtPercent asks the engine instead, and the two screens the audit measured
now go through it - the earned value figures and the variance on the 5D page,
and both percentage helpers on the progress page. The rest of the tree still
has the old shape in about a hundred places; they are the same one-line
change and follow separately.

fix(demo): a project reports the progress it has, not the progress it will have

The same building answered three different questions with three different
numbers on two screens: the progress page said 85 per cent complete, the
earned value panel derived 11 from the 4D schedule, and the schedule itself
was right. A demo installs into a story that starts in April 2026 and runs
for two years, and the progress seeder wrote a reading for nearly every month
of the programme, so a job in its fifth month filed itself as almost finished
with readings dated into 2028.

Actuals now stop at the month the reader is in, which is the clock the
schedule already reads when it works out how far each phase has run. The
planned S-curve still covers the whole programme, because that is the shape
the chart is drawn from: a planned line to the end and an actual line that
stops where the site is. A twenty-two month job now reports 17.7 per cent in
its fifth month instead of 88.

Installed demo data keeps the old readings until the project is reseeded.

fix(ai): a self-hosted endpoint belongs to the user who saved it

Reported as GHSA-wfpw-cv5v-64j5. Saving an Ollama or vLLM base URL wrote it
into a module-global provider table, so the endpoint belonged to the worker
process rather than to the person who saved it. Anyone whose next AI call
routed to a self-hosted runtime sent their prompt, and the project text in it,
to the host named by whoever last touched their own settings. Only these two
providers are tunable, which is the whole reachable surface, and the
dispatch-time URL guard is no help against it: that guard blocks link-local
and cloud-metadata addresses, and an ordinary public host is what it lets
through by design.

The endpoint is now bound when the settings of the user making the call are
resolved, and read back at the single dispatch point. The binding is a context
variable, so it reaches the dispatch without every signature in between having
to carry a URL, and it reaches nothing else - a task inherits a copy of the
context, so one request can neither see nor overwrite another's. It is bound
on every resolution, including the ones that find no endpoint, so a batch that
walks several users in one task cannot carry the first user's host into the
rest. An explicit argument still wins, which is what the connection test
sends before anything is saved.

Saving no longer touches shared state at all, and the function that did is
gone rather than left unused, because a single new caller would be enough to
bring it back. Operators who want one endpoint for the whole instance still
set OE_OLLAMA_URL or OE_VLLM_URL, which is the mechanism that was always meant
to be the global one and which a user could previously overwrite at runtime.

ci(ai): the endpoint isolation test runs beside the other AI security tests

It was added as a step of its own a commit ago. The lane already has a step
for exactly this subject, and two steps that mean the same thing drift.

fix(ui): the top bar calls a screen what the menu calls it The page title came from a literal English string written at the route, `

`, so a German cost-control session read Progress, Earned Value and Cost-Value Reconciliation over three pages that were otherwise entirely German, while the fourth was in German because that page happens to set its own. Nothing could report it. There is no key to be missing, so no locale check has anything to look at, and 256 routes carry the same shape. Every one of those screens already has a translated name on its own sidebar row, so the title asks the catalogue for it and keeps the written English only where no screen claims the path. Matching mirrors the icon lookup deliberately - longest prefix, nested project routes on their trailing segment - so the name and the glyph in the same chip always come off the same entry. A row that points at a tab of a screen resolves to the screen, because a screen has one name.

fix(ui): the rest of the tree writes percentages the way the reader does

The sweep the previous commit left open. 104 places across 61 files printed a
percentage by gluing a per cent sign onto toFixed, which is English and only
English: a German reader gets a point where they write a comma, and a Turkish
reader gets the sign after the digits when their language puts it in front.
None of it was reportable, because a string assembled in code has no key for a
locale check to miss.

They all go through fmtPercent now. What was deliberately left alone is the
three files that assemble a document rather than a screen - the HTML report
export, the Excel sheet and the PDF - where the label beside the number is
English prose anyway and localising half a line reads worse than not
localising it. That choice belongs with the export formats.

Mechanical, one shape, and the build is the check that every rewritten
expression still is one.

Revert "fix(ui): the top bar calls a screen what the menu calls it"

This reverts commit 00a78672d.

The defect it fixed had already been fixed. The top bar translates the
English literal through TITLE_I18N_MAP in Header.tsx, with a test that every
route has an entry and every entry resolves, and Progress, Earned Value and
Cost-Value Reconciliation have all been in that map since 14 August. I read
an audit written before that landed and did not re-measure it.

What the revert restores is one mechanism instead of two. Deriving the title
from the screen catalogue is arguably the better of the two, because there is
no map to keep complete, but that is a replacement to argue for on its own
merits rather than a second path bolted beside a working one - and with both
in place the module routes that pass an i18n key as their title would stop
reaching the branch that handles them.

The gate the commit added for navCatalog.test.ts is kept: that file was
running in no lane at all.

test(dashboard): the snapshot shows the honeycomb the card now draws

The case tiles on the dashboard gained a hex portrait of the specialist the
playbook came from, and the visual-regression snapshot still described the
card without one. The suite runs in no lane, so nothing said so at the time;
it turned up on a full local run.

fix(punchlist): the assignee column says who, not which id

assigned_to and verified_by are free text, and three things legitimately
land in them: a name somebody typed, a contact id, and a user id. The
seeder and the field integrations write a contact id, the assignment
control on the screen writes a user id, and the register printed whichever
it got. So a punch list read "Assigned to 3f2b8c1e-9a44-..." on every row
of the table, on every kanban card, in the detail drawer, along the axis of
the insights chart and in the issues hub, with an avatar lettered from a
hex digit.

The API resolves the ids now and sends assigned_to_name and
verified_by_name beside the raw values. It is two queries for a whole page,
one per register, rather than one per row: this screen is already the
slowest in the module and a lookup from the page would have added a request
per row on top. Free text is never sent to the database, because a name
somebody typed is already the answer.

An id that resolves to nothing does not come back as unassigned. The snag
has an owner, we just cannot name them, and telling a site manager it is
unassigned invites a second assignment. Both lookups are fail-soft and run
in their own savepoint, so an instance without the contacts module, or a
contact that was deleted, costs a name and not a punch list.

fix(punchlist): the exported list names the same party the screen names

Resolving the assignee stopped at the screens. The PDF, the spreadsheet and
the CSV fallback still printed the column as stored, so a Mangelliste handed
to a subcontractor read "3f2b8c1e-9a44-..." under Assignee while the page it
was exported from said Bauunternehmung Keller. One concept, two renderers,
disagreeing, which is the shape the resolution existed to remove. Measured
on a real workbook: the name is in the file and the id is not.

An id that resolves to nothing still prints as the id rather than as a blank
cell. Whoever receives the sheet can at least look it up.

Also stops the lookup depending on what shape the driver hands back. Ids
arrive as text from a free-text column and as whatever the type decorator
returns from a row, which is a UUID today and the raw string for any value
it cannot parse. Comparing one shape against the other resolves nothing and
raises nothing, so the screen would read "Unknown" for every owner and no
test would say why. Both sides go through one normalisation now, and the
stub hands back a string row to prove it.

fix(i18n): five number formatters kept the language the page opened in

The language switcher does not reload the app, on purpose, so every string
flips with no English flash. An Intl.NumberFormat built at module scope does
not flip with them: it reads the language once, when its lazy chunk first
loads, and formats that way for the rest of the session. Five of them sat at
module scope, on the BOQ register, the templates page, the projects register
and the dashboard project card.

What it looked like: a German reader who arrived in English saw 12,550,880

Leistungsverzeichnis, LV for short, and that is what a tender, a GAEB exchange and a Vergabe

saying LV against 339 still saying BOQ, so the same object was named two ways on neighbouring
screens.

The loan word also arrived without a settled gender. Some strings borrowed it as feminine and
others as neuter, which is how the file came to carry both Bepreiste BOQ and Bepreistes BOQ for
the one thing. LV is neuter after Leistungsverzeichnis, so the sweep moves the article and the
adjective with the noun rather than only swapping the letters, and thirteen strings that already
said LV behind a feminine article are corrected too. An adjective keeps its weak ending after a
definite article, so das bepreiste LV stays as it is.

that really is called a BOQ in those markets, and one takeoff string glosses the German term
