fix(costs): a search that never ran is not a search that found nothing

Semantic search caught the missing optional stack and answered 200 with an empty list. The cost
grid draws that exactly the way it draws a query that matched nothing, so on a deployment without
an embedding model the reader was told their search had no results when the search had never
started. Every neighbouring endpoint in the same router already answers 503 for this condition,
and the orchestrator above them documents 503 as the graceful degradation signal, so the one that
stayed silent was the odd one out rather than the careful one.

It now answers 503 with the same sentence its neighbours use, and carries the reason in a header
so an operator can tell a missing library from a model that failed to load from one nothing has
asked for yet. Those three states have three different remedies. A probe reports them without
triggering a load, so a status page cannot pay the multi-second download cascade.

The cost page still falls back to the text search, which is the right behaviour and was already
there, but it now says that is what it did. A fallback the reader is not told about is a
different answer wearing the same clothes.

feat(tendering): say which part of the bill a package was raised over

Creating a package from a bill has always recorded the chosen sections in the package metadata,
and nothing has ever read them back. The comparison and levelling screens narrow their arithmetic
to that scope, so the number a bidder is measured against already depends on it, but on screen a
package covering one trade looked exactly like a package covering the whole bill. The reader was
being shown a comparison whose boundary they could not see.

The package detail now names the sections and how many of the bill's positions they hold, and it
only says anything when the package is partial, because telling someone a whole-bill package
covers the whole bill is noise.

Two writers declare a scope and they say it differently. Creation names the sections; the demo
installer records a flat list of lines. When only the flat list is there the sections are derived
by walking each line up to its top-level ancestor, which gives the same answer whenever the scope
was built from whole sections and an honest approximation when it was not, and the screen says
which of the two it is. Section ids that name nothing in the bill are treated as a bill that was
replaced, so they fall back to the derivation rather than printing empty rows.

The derivation is a plain function over positions, tested the way the scope filter beside it is,
without a database.

perf(http): send the bundle compressed, since the browser was already asking

Two screens were reported as slow, the snag register at 4.3 s and the bill editor at 4.1 s, and
the audit guessed they shared a root without saying what it was. Measured against the local stand,
three runs each: every endpoint those screens call answers in under a tenth of a second. The punch
list is 89 ms, its summary 95 ms, the bill 103 ms, the project list 62 ms. The API was never the
problem.

What both screens do pay for is the shell. The application bundle is 2,496,962 bytes and the
English locale chunk 2,267,263 bytes, and both came back at exactly those sizes when the request
carried Accept-Encoding gzip, deflate, br. Nothing on the server ever compressed anything. That is
4.8 MB of text before either page draws, against page chunks of 65 KB and 59 KB, which is why the
two timings sit so close together: the difference between them is their own code and the rest is
the part they share.

Text responses whose length is known are now gzipped. Starlette ships a middleware that would do
most of this, but it decides by length alone, so it also spends CPU on PDF exports and photo bytes
that are already compressed and come out slightly larger, and it buffers streaming responses to do
it. On a 2 GB box that is the wrong trade, so this one asks what the body is first and passes
everything else through untouched. A response that already carries Content-Encoding is left alone,
and Vary names Accept-Encoding so a cache cannot hand a compressed body to a client that did not
ask for one.

The guard covers the asset mount as well as ordinary routes, because the mount is what serves the
4.8 MB and it is a different path through Starlette.

ci(migrations): fail the build when the revision graph forks

Three revisions were written in parallel today and two of them chained off the same parent. Each
author ran alembic heads inside their own piece of work, each saw a single head, and each was
telling the truth: they ran before the other files existed. The fork was visible only to someone
looking at all three at once, which is a job for a gate rather than for a person.

It matters because alembic upgrade head refuses to run against an ambiguous head. A fork that
ships is found by whoever upgrades first, and on a release that is the user.

The check reads the revision files rather than asking Alembic. ScriptDirectory would answer the
same question more authoritatively and would also import the whole SQLAlchemy stack, which on at
least one machine here wedges for minutes on an unrelated Windows management call. A gate that
hangs is a gate people turn off, so this one needs no database, no driver and no config.

The price of reading text is that the parser has to be right, and the first draft was not. It read
down_revision with a single line regex, so every merge revision whose parents are a tuple across
several lines lost them and was counted as a base. It reported 43 heads over a tree that has one.
The heads number looked alarming but plausible; the bases number, 18, is what gave it away,
because an Alembic graph has exactly one base. So the summary line prints edges and bases and not
only the answer it was asked for, and there is a floor under the revision count, because a scan
over an empty directory reports a single head for the same reason a test suite with no tests
reports success.

It also fails on two files claiming one revision id, which Alembic resolves by loading whichever
it walked last and dropping the other without saying so.

and es-CO resolve through es, pt-BR through pt, and en-US through en. That is what lets an
American English file hold 1499 keys instead of a 2.4 MB copy of the 33771 English ones.

and counted a variant that leaves a word alone as a locale that cannot answer it, so the day
en-US.ts appeared the guard printed 25280 errors. Every one of them was wrong, and the cheapest

only because their gaps had been written into the debt baseline one key at a time, which does not
scale to a locale that overrides four percent of the keyspace on purpose.

A variant is now missing a key only when its base is missing it too. Falling back into the base
language is the designed behaviour and the reader gets their own words; falling past the base into
English is the silent defect this guard was written for, and that still fails. English answering a
key covers nobody but the English readers, or the guard would have nothing left to catch.

mirrored table would be a second copy of a decision, and the copy is the one that goes stale, as
this guard just demonstrated. The run now prints which variants it resolved through which base, so
a derivation that stops working is visible instead of quietly demanding a full keyspace of
everyone.

proven against the author's idea of the repository. The docstring also stops saying 29 languages.

test(i18n): a stray brace in any locale value is a 500, and nothing looked for one

The braces in a locale value are code rather than text. t() runs str.format over whatever the
file holds, so the placeholder is the one part of a translated string that a translator must
carry across untouched, and it is also the part a translation tool is most likely to eat.

What t() catches decides how bad each mistake is. It catches KeyError and ValueError, so a
renamed field degrades quietly to the uninterpolated string, which is wrong output but a live
page. It does not catch IndexError, so a positional field, a bare pair of braces or a {0} left
behind by a tool raises out of the call and takes the whole route with it. Verified against the
running module rather than read off the except clause: t() on a value holding {0} raises
IndexError, and on a value holding an unknown named field returns the string untouched.

Both are now asserted per locale against the fields en.json declares for the same key, so a
value may not lose a placeholder, gain one, or rename one. Doubled braces are left alone on
purpose. All nineteen boq.mvp values carry {{count}}, which passes through format as literal
text and is resolved on the client, so treating it as a backend field would fail every locale
that is correct.

Seven English keys carry a single brace field today and every one of the twenty seven locales
already agrees with them, so this goes in green and blocks no work in flight. It is going in
now because the locales are being filled at the moment, and the cheapest time to catch a
swallowed placeholder is the commit that writes it.

fix(i18n): losing the locales directory quietly restored a catalogue missing most of its strings

load_translations checked whether locales/ existed and, if it did not, created it and filled it
from a copy of the catalogue embedded in the module. That recovery path is deleted here, about
three thousand lines of it, and the missing directory is now a FileNotFoundError naming the
directory and how to restore it.

The reason for removing rather than updating the copy is that its failure is invisible. It knew

the platform came up serving a catalogue missing most of its strings. Nothing downstream can see
that state: every file is present, every file parses, the files agree with each other, and the
catalogue guard compares locales against en.json, which would have been restored just as small.
The English fallback in t() then does its job and the whole platform quietly speaks English. A
recovery path that recovers the wrong data is worse than no recovery path, because the wrong
data looks like success.

It also could not be kept correct. The copy drifted the moment anyone edited a JSON file, and it
had drifted by more than four thousand keys, so keeping it would have meant maintaining a second
catalogue by hand forever to serve a case that cannot legitimately arise.

The case cannot arise on a real install. The locale files are tracked, so a source tree restores
them with git checkout, and pyproject force-includes the whole directory into the wheel, so a
pip install carries them. Reaching the old path meant deleting a directory git will hand straight
back. The comment on that force-include said the recovery would rescue a wheel built without it,
which was never true in the way it read, and it now says the wheel fails at startup instead.

that could load what it fetched, so start_background_download asked

beside qdrant-client, because every import of it sits inside a function body

is a separate asset no desktop install downloads, so they would be weight with no
reachable code path. Recompiling the lock in place kept every existing pin except

the lock against the spec's excludes. A name in both files means the build
downloads a dependency and then freezes a sidecar without it, which is what

feat(packs): give Texas and California the state rules a bid actually turns on

The US pack has always been national, so a Texas bid and a Californian one
came out of it looking the same. They are not the same, and the differences
are the kind that move money rather than wording. Texas splits the sales tax
on materials by the form of the contract, and then reverses the whole rule for
nonresidential repair work by taxing the labour too. California makes the same
contractor the consumer of what it installs as material and the retailer of
what it installs as a fixture, which is two treatments inside one invoice.
Texas publishes no state wage schedule at all and leaves the rate to whichever
body awards the contract, while California runs its own regime that a federal
determination does not satisfy. The retainage caps differ and the Texas one
turns on a contract value threshold. And since the start of this year
California caps retention on private work as well, which is new enough that a
pack written from memory would have missed it.

So this adds two backend modules carrying that as data, two activatable packs
around them, and four payment regimes so the clock computes real dates instead
of describing them. Every rule names the statute it came from, and every one
carries an effective date field even when the answer is that the commencement
was not established, because a reader has to be able to tell that from an
oversight. The test suite fails a rule with no citation, which is the point:
an estimator who sees no retainage rule goes and looks the cap up, while an
estimator who sees a wrong one bids it.

Nothing here restates what the national pack already owns. The classification
structures, the contract families, the payment application and the units stay
where they are, and both configs decline to redeclare VAT for the same reason
the US pack does.

test(i18n): gate the numbers a reader sees against the language they picked

Scans every source file under frontend/src for a number written without the
reader's language and fails with the file, the line and the source of anything
it finds. It covers two shapes that are one defect by different routes: a call
that takes a locale and was not given one, and a fixed-decimal call that takes
no locale at all, so no argument fixes it and the site has to move onto a
formatter instead.

Nine rules carry the categories that repeat and say in a sentence why each is
locale-independent by requirement: a rounding round-trip whose string never
reaches a screen, a row of a CSV, a formatter fallback inside the catch that
formatting threw from, CSS geometry and colour, coordinates, React keys, request
bodies, string surgery on the result. Sites that fit no rule are argued one at a
time in an allowlist keyed on the snippet, so an exemption covers only the line
it was written for, and a snippet that no longer appears in its file fails
rather than decaying into a blank exemption over everything else in that file.

Export is deliberately two categories. A CSV is parsed by whoever opens it, so
its separators cannot follow the reader. A PDF or an HTML report is read, and a
German estimator wants those figures written the German way. Both come out of a
function called handleExportSomething, so the rule matches the sink rather than
trusting the scope alone.

The gate searches for the shape it wants removed, which means it cannot see a
site converted in error. That limit is written into the file so the next person
does not mistake a green run for proof that every conversion was right.

The gate reads each locale for its own term and for the rival phrasings that

perf(desktop): take the CPU build of torch, not the CUDA one

Shipping the encoder cost Linux about 2.7 GB against about 190 MB on Windows,
and the whole difference was CUDA. torch's Linux wheels on PyPI declare the
nvidia stack as hard dependencies, so the lock pulled cuBLAS, cuDNN, cuFFT,
NCCL, cuSOLVER, Triton and nine more onto a headless HTTP server that has no
GPU to address and no code that would look for one. Recompiling with
--torch-backend=cpu drops eighteen packages and takes the Linux install to
about 259 MB, measured as 182.9 MB for the manylinux CPU wheel plus the 76 MB
the rest of the closure weighs there. Windows and macOS are unchanged, because
their PyPI wheels were already CPU-only, which is why only Linux was ever the
problem.

The CPU wheels are not on PyPI, so pip needs the index named on the install
line. It is deliberately not written into the lock. That index publishes its
own copies of ordinary packages and some are years stale, so offering it to the
resolver as a general source is not free: it serves urllib3 1.26.13 against
qdrant-client's floor of 1.26.14, and compiling the lock with the index in
scope fails outright on that conflict. On the install line every version is
already decided, so pip only has to find the pinned files rather than choose
between them, and that was confirmed by running the step as the workflow runs
it. The torch wheel came from the pytorch index, everything else from PyPI, and
every package landed on the version the lock names.

A new guard fails if a future recompile forgets the flag. It checks both the
symptom and the cause, because they are separable: no distribution may start
with nvidia, cuda or triton, and the non-macOS torch pins must carry the +cpu
local version. macOS is exempt by necessity, since there is no CUDA build for
it and therefore no +cpu variant to ask for.

documents hub. That is convenience work, the model is already saved by the time
it runs, and the comment above it said failures were swallowed for exactly that
reason. The swallow did not deliver what it promised.

carrying on therefore does not rescue the request, it only moves the funeral:
every statement after this point raises about a transaction that can no longer
continue, and the upload fails several frames away describing something other
than what went wrong. We have paid for this before, when deadline notifications

caught exception could not revive.

except to SQLAlchemyError, because a NameError or a TypeError in that block is a

feat(semantic): fetch the encoder in the background and report which of five states it is in

The encoder the semantic search path needs was never downloaded anywhere. The
download now runs in the background on a deployment that wants it, never blocks
startup and never fails the boot. An install that cannot or will not fetch it
keeps working: lexical search still answers and the surface says plainly that
the semantic half is unavailable.

Five states rather than a boolean, because the reader's next move differs in
each one. library_missing needs the extra installed, downloading needs
patience, failed needs a retry or the error text, ready needs nothing, and
not_requested needs a tick. One "is it ready" flag collapses four different
remedies into a shrug.

The transfer resumes rather than restarting. Files land under a .part suffix
and are renamed only once complete, and the marker that declares an install
finished is written last, so an interrupted download can never be mistaken for
a finished one. A single lock keeps a second request from starting a second
transfer.

reset_embedder() clears the failure latch when weights arrive. get_embedder()
latches its failure for the life of the process on purpose, and without this a
first boot with no weights would set that latch and never look again at a model
that landed a minute later, which would make the download decorative. It leaves
a working embedder alone deliberately: evicting one puts a cold model load
inside a request thread, which is exactly the blocking this feature promises
never to do, and the prize would only be a better model than the one already
answering.

fix(vector): a reindex that wrote nothing is not a success

The reindex button reported "Reindex complete" over any 200, including the one
that indexed nothing at all. index_many() catches a failure to encode a batch,
logs it at debug and moves on, and reindex_collection() then returns
skipped = len(rows) - indexed. So an absent or unreachable encoder produces a
perfectly healthy response in which every record was skipped, and the card told
the operator the collection was searchable at the exact moment it was not.

Three outcomes now instead of one. Nothing indexed with records skipped is a
warning that says the collection is not searchable and names the likely cause.
Nothing indexed with nothing skipped is an empty collection, which is not a
failure and should not send anyone hunting for a broken encoder. A reindex that
wrote something stays a success.

Partial skipping stays a success deliberately. Rows with no indexable text skip
on every healthy run, so warning on those would fire constantly and the warning
would stop being read, which would cost more than it saved.

feat(certified-payroll): the weekly certified payroll for public works

Public works require a payroll every week naming each worker, the trade they
worked as, the hours they worked each day, the rate they were paid and how much
of it was fringe, with a signed statement that the rate met the wage
determination covering the job.

The module records the determination as a document with an authority, an
identifier and a date, and holds every craft under it with the basic hourly wage
and the fringe rate in separate columns. No rates ship with it. Determinations
are issued per craft, per county and per awarding body, so what the product
keeps is which one was used and what it said, never a copy of somebody else's

one. Where both cover the work the higher total package governs, and the week
records the determination it used together with the arithmetic that chose it.

A draft week owns no rows. It derives them from the payroll hours already
recorded, so nothing is typed twice, and certifying freezes them with the words
spelled out, so renaming a craft next month cannot rewrite a statement somebody
signed. Seven validation rules run before a week can be certified and each one
names the mistake rather than reporting that something is invalid. Serialises to
form WH-347 and to CSV.

fix(doctor): prove the native extras import instead of locating them

The vector and encoder checks asked find_spec whether the module was on disk.
That is the wrong question for the two optional extras that are mostly compiled
code. lancedb is almost entirely one Rust library and sentence-transformers
imports torch, a pile of native shared objects, so either can resolve perfectly
and still fail to load. Reporting that as "installed" leaves the operator with
no way to tell a working install from a broken one, which is the failure this
command exists to prevent.

It is not hypothetical. A frozen desktop build was measured answering
"sentence-transformers installed" while carrying no torch at all, and lancedb
enters the desktop sidecar for the first time in this release.

The file had already learned this once. _import_error, twenty lines above the
checks that needed it, imports in a child process precisely because a native
extension that will not load resolves fine and because one that segfaults would
otherwise take the diagnostic down with it, and it falls back to an in-process
import on frozen builds where sys.executable is the app binary rather than an
interpreter. It was wired to the PDF readers alone. The two checks with the most
native code under them were the two still only looking.

The report now has three states rather than two, because absent and broken are
different problems with different fixes. Absent stays a warning and keeps its
install hint, since a stock server is meant not to carry these. Present but
unimportable is an error, carries the actual failure line, and its hint is a
reinstall rather than an install, because telling someone to install what they
already have is not a fix. The cheap lookup still runs first and short-circuits,
so an install that simply lacks the extra pays exactly what it paid before and
doctor does not start importing torch on every run.

The tests were run against the unmodified file as a control. Five of the seven
fail there, including all three that assert a broken extra is an error and the
one that proves the import probe runs at all, so the absence assertions are not
vacuous.

sees an import written inside a function body. The paragraph above it, about
the vector-store client, said the same thing in the same words and was left
alone, and it has since been quoted back as grounds for a different decision.

docs(boq): say which of the two markup engines a bill's total comes from

The platform has two markup engines and neither one said what it was for.
The bill's stack is BOQMarkup rows resolved by _calculate_markup_amounts, and
the estimating methodology is compute_cascade in the methodology module. They
have different jobs, but a reader who found the second one first had nothing
in the file to tell them so, and the question of which owns a bill's total had
to be asked out loud rather than read. Both now carry the answer, and both say
the bridge runs one way: a methodology may seed a bill's markup lines, and
nothing computes a bill's total from a cascade.

The same paragraph records the rounding difference at both definitions. The
cascade quantizes every step immediately and feeds the rounded amount forward;
the bill's stack keeps full precision and quantizes once at the rollup. On the
same numbers they disagree by cents. That is deliberate and it is not being
reconciled here, because moving either one changes the total of every estimate
already stored, which is its own decision with its own migration rather than a
side effect of a passing edit.

Recording why a third markup surface is the wrong answer, so the next person to
propose one meets the argument before the code. A separate module composing
over the bill's stack cannot work: the cascade is a private function over ORM
rows, so the new module either reimplements the compounding order, and then two
implementations of the same money drift apart the first time one is fixed, or
it reaches into another module's internals, which is the coupling the module
system exists to prevent. Anything that reads a bill's markup lines belongs in
the module that owns them, and the four gaps in that stack land on BOQMarkup
additively for the same reason.

feat(i18n): label the computed t() families from their producer

A key assembled at runtime, risk.status_ with the status token appended,
never reaches the orphan scan and never reaches a translator, so 97 families
had no members in any locale at all. What every reader saw instead was the defaultValue, and the
defaultValue was usually the token with its underscores swapped for spaces.
The screen said "on hold" where the product means "On hold", and it said it
in English to everyone, in all 29 languages.

The wording here comes from each vocabulary's producer, the enum or check
constraint or seeded list that decides what the token can be, and not from
the call site that renders it. That distinction did real work: several of
these vocabularies are produced in the frontend, by an as-const array inside
the same .map() that builds the call site, or by an exported constant in a
sibling feature. Searching the backend for those returns a clean and entirely
misleading zero.

372 keys land in en.ts only. The other 28 locales are a translation job and
they follow separately. Landing English into them would hide the gaps from
the very scan that has to find them.

review_authority.move_to_* is the one family that does not land. Nine keys
with a status name welded into each key name would freeze "Move to X" as an
assembled sentence in all 29 locales at once, and a language that inflects
the status after that preposition cannot reach it once the sentence arrives
built. It is one key now with the status interpolated, and the status word
itself goes through the cycle_status_ keys that the badge beside it already
uses, so the button and the badge cannot drift apart.

The gate is three paths and they only work together.
check_i18n_computed_keys.py finds every computed key and asks whether its
family exists in en.ts. i18n_computed_key_baseline.json records the 118
families with no English landed yet, and against each one the reason. The
reasons are not all the same kind: most are families whose producer is
unbounded, but two are families whose producer exists and contradicts itself,
which is a different job for whoever picks them up. The
repo-hygiene job runs it. Split them and the result is either a job that
fails on the day it lands or a script that nothing runs. The baseline is a
dict rather than a list of prefixes because the reason a family is on it is
the only thing that lets a later reader judge whether it can come off. It
also prints, without failing, when a baselined family has been answered or
has lost its last call site, because a baseline nobody prunes is a baseline
that rots into permission.

Two notes for whoever takes the next wave. romEstimate.reconcile.desc_* is
four sentences that share a member set with four badges, which is exactly the
shape that gets truncated by someone assuming the two sets carry the same
length of text. They do not. And property_dev declares doc_type three times
over: _VALID_DOC_TYPES as a frozenset of 6 in service.py,
_VALID_DOC_TYPES_HTTP as a set of 12 in router.py, and _DOC_TYPE_PRESETS as
18 whose own comment says it is not a constraint at all. Nothing here depends
on resolving that and nothing here changes it, but the family that reads
doc_type cannot be closed until it is.

fix(i18n-tools): assemble refuses to publish a corpus that still reads as English

The extract guard stops the batches being wiped. It does not stop the wiped
batches being published, and assemble is the step that does the damage: it
overwrites the shipped locale file from whatever the batches hold, and after
that write there is nothing left to resync the real translation out of.

The check had to be a proportion rather than a match. Every locale keeps some
values identical to English, so refusing on any of them would refuse every real
assemble. Measured across the 41 shipped locales, the English-identical share
runs from 0.7 percent in fa to 4.8 percent in nl. Uzbek, about half translated
at the time, sat at 59.2 percent, and a corpus extract has just rewritten is at
100. A quarter separates those cleanly, five times the worst finished locale and
far below anything unfinished.

So assemble now counts the values that still equal their English source and
refuses over a quarter, naming the file it would have overwritten. It is a
tripwire for batches nobody filled in, not a quality bar, and --force is still

feat(boq): let a section carry its own markup rate

A markup set could say what a company charges and nothing else. There was no
way to write down a standard with an exception, so an estimator who wanted 4
percent overhead on fit-out and 10 everywhere else had to change the number for
the whole bill and remember what it used to be. Two nullable columns on the
markup row fix that. A line can name the position it is confined to, and it can
name the bill-wide line it stands in for inside that subtree. Both null, which
is every row that exists today, still means what it meant: the company
standard, applied to the whole direct cost.

The arithmetic composes over the cascade rather than restating it. The direct
cost is partitioned into buckets of leaves that see the same set of overrides,
the existing cascade runs once per bucket, and each line's amount is what it
earned across the buckets it applied in. A bill-wide line overridden in one
section still reports the money it made everywhere else.

Two decisions worth knowing about. An override keeps the place of the line it
replaces in the compounding order, not its own, because the order is the
standard's decision and an exception is about the rate; letting it move would
change what every later line compounds on without anyone editing them.
Overrides nest, with the nearest scope winning per line, so a trade exception
inside a phase exception behaves the way it reads.

Nothing moves on a bill that has no scoped line. That is asserted rather than
assumed: all fourteen shipped regional templates are priced through both paths
and the amounts have to be identical, not close. The buckets are also made to
sum to whatever direct cost the caller reported, so a rollup that converts
currency and one that does not each partition the figure they actually
published. Duplicating a bill remaps both references onto the copy, since
carrying the source ids over would leave the new bill inheriting where the old
one made an exception.

Recording why a third markup surface is the wrong answer, so the next person to
propose one meets the argument before the code. A separate module composing
over the bill's stack cannot work: the cascade is a private function over ORM
rows, so the new module either reimplements the compounding order, and then two
implementations of the same money drift apart the first time one is fixed, or
it reaches into another module's internals, which is the coupling the module
system exists to prevent. That is why this landed on BOQMarkup additively.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(boq): check the markup stack and tell the estimator, never refuse them

Nothing checked the markup stack. An estimator could put contingency on top of
profit, leave two lines fighting over the same place in the order, or type 300
into a percentage box, and the bill priced all of it and exported it to a
client without a word. Four rules now say so, on the validation report, in the
language the reader has selected.

Every one of them is a warning and none of them rejects anything. A rule that
rejects is a rule people route around, and the routes around a markup check are
worse than the check: a percentage typed into the wrong box, a line switched
off to get past a gate and never switched back on. There is a test that pins
this rather than a comment, because the temptation to tighten the schema to
match a rule is exactly how the property gets lost: the create schema still
accepts the percentage the band rule flags.

The rules are contingency not charged a profit margin, every line declaring its
own place in the order, a percentage inside a plausible band for its category,
and a cumulative line having something in front of it to compound onto. They
are named, not numbered, because a finding has to say what it is about to a
person reading a report.

The last one deserves a note. The brief asked for a rule that a cumulative
entry must not reference a later entry, and in this model that rule cannot
fail: cumulative means every line before me in the order and names nothing, so
there is no reference to point the wrong way. The engine that does have
referenced steps already refuses forward references outright. What is checkable
here is the neighbouring mistake, a line labelled as compounding on preceding
markups while nothing precedes it, so it quietly computes on the direct cost
and changes base the next time someone reorders the stack.

The templates the platform ships are held to the rules it ships. Every regional
default is priced through all four and has to come out clean, except the UK
set, which places risk after main contractor overheads and profit deliberately
under NRM1 and is expected to raise the contingency flag. That expectation is
written down in the test, so if either the rule or the template moves, the
report says which one.

feat(boq): price a bond off its rate card and an escalation off the index

Two shapes the markup stack could not hold. A surety quotes a rate card, not a
rate: the first tranche of the contract sum at one percentage, the next at a
lower one, the rest lower still. Charging the whole sum at any single band
over-prices or under-prices every job that is not sitting exactly on a band
edge, and until now a bond line could only be a single percentage. And a bill
priced in one month and built in another was escalated by whatever number an
estimator typed, with nothing connecting it to the cost index the platform
already stores.

Both arrive as markup types rather than as new ways of saying what the base is.
That is the part worth reading. apply_to says one thing, which lines a markup
is computed on, and it stays saying only that. Making it also carry "index this
from March to June" would have turned a one-word statement about a base into a
small language, and a second cascade language inside the module that exists to
not have two cascades is the thing that was worth avoiding. A type says what
kind of number the line is; a base says what it is a share of. They compose,
and an escalation line can still be cumulative like anything else.

The date-to-date arithmetic is called, not copied. The factor comes from
price_index.resolve_factor over the stored series, so a bill and a rate library
escalated across the same two months can never disagree about the ratio. The
BOQ module reads the series through the price-index module's own accessor
rather than its table. There is a test that computes the expected amount from
resolve_factor rather than from a hand-typed constant, so a reimplementation
that rounded differently would fail rather than pass.

Three decisions worth knowing about. A falling index reduces the price instead
of being clamped at zero, which makes this the one place a markup line can be
negative; clamping would report a bid at a price the index does not support.
An escalation whose series or period cannot be resolved contributes zero and
logs, because a list endpoint pricing many bills at once must not fail all of
them for one bad reference. And a banded or escalation line is refused at
create and update time when its configuration is missing, since a line that
prices at zero for want of a rate card looks exactly like a line somebody meant
to be zero.

The set of types the schema accepts and the set the engine computes are now
asserted to be one set, read out of the engine's own source. That is how
per_unit used to fail: accepted, stored, and silently worth nothing.

fix(pagination): the guard can see a read that goes through a wrapper

check_page_envelope_consumers.py binds a URL literal to the call standing
next to it, and the only call it recognised was apiGet. Project overview does
not call apiGet. It calls useGracefulQuery, a local wrapper that swallows an
ApiError and answers null so a widget for a module nobody installed renders
empty rather than red, and seven reads of already migrated routes went
through it. Those seven were not judged, and they were not counted either, so
they were absent from the report rather than green in it and the per endpoint
totals understated what had been inspected.

One of the seven was wrong. The variations counter asked for
VariationRequest[] from a route enveloped in wave 6, and the widget iterates
that value, so on the path where it runs it throws rather than counting
nothing. It runs only when the widget is mounted without the rollup provider,
which is why nobody had met it. It reads the page and takes items now, the
way the other six already did.

The wrapper is named in a list rather than written into the expression, and
the bar for that list is written beside it: the URL literal and the type
argument must both appear at the call site. That is what makes a wrapper
bindable at all. A helper taking a path does not qualify however convenient
it looks, because it holds the type argument in another function, so naming
it would count callers while inspecting none of them. The contracts wave met
that shape and it was fixed at the caller instead. The two are opposite
directions and worth telling apart, so the reasoning sits in the file rather
than only here.

Writing the fixture produced two narrowings. The bare array hint is built
from the same list as the binder, or a wrapper call gets counted and then
acquitted on an items that belongs to the line unwrapping it rather than to
the type argument, which is exactly how the variations counter looked. And
the window after the URL now stops at the next call, the way the window
before it already stopped at this one. Only the earlier half had ever been
narrowed, and the later half can go wrong in both directions: it convicts a
migrated call of the bare array belonging to the call underneath it, and it
acquits an untyped apiGet on the next call's unwrapping.

Reads the guard binds and judges go from 76 to 83 of the 121 URL literals
that resolve to a migrated route. The 38 left are 31 writers, skipped by
design because a POST or a DELETE returns no page, six test mocks and one
literal with no call within reach. The guard is green on the tree and red on
the widget as it stood before this commit.

feat(i18n): tell a mid-translation locale from a genuine gap

The orphan and computed-key guards could not tell a locale that is missing
a key from a locale nobody has finished translating yet, and both read the
same to either guard: a hard error. That made SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES the only
place strictness could live, and it does not answer the question by itself,
because a file can sit on disk mid-batch or sit there abandoned and look
identical from a bare key count.

Both guards now read frontend/src/app/i18n.ts for SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES first.
A locale on that list is offered to a real user today, so every gap in it
stays a hard error, no exception, regardless of anything else. A locale off
that list gets classified by how much of its file still matches English word
for word: a locale still mostly English reads as mid-translation and its
gaps downgrade to a loud, counted line instead of an error; a locale that
reads as finished but was never added to the list is its own anomaly and
gets enforced the same as before, just named for what it is rather than
passed as an ordinary miss.

The threshold was measured against the committed tree rather than guessed.
Every finished locale sits under 5% identical to English, from ordinary
overlap like numbers, unit codes and acronyms such as BOQ or MEP, with the
highest at 4.83%. The one locale actually mid-translation at the time sat at
40%. Ten percent sits in the gap between those two groups with margin on
both sides.

An earlier version of this would have read a directory the translation-batch
tool writes under .i18n-work/ to tell the two states apart. That directory is
gitignored and nothing in CI ever populates it, so the signal would have been
invisible on the one machine that runs these guards for real. Deriving the
same fact from the committed locale files instead means the classification is
visible wherever the guard runs, self-corrects as a locale is translated with
nothing to remember to unset, and never depends on a flag anyone could set
once and leave stale.

Neither guard's enforcement changes for anything in the tree right now: uz is
still on SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES, so its gaps are still hard errors regardless of
how translated the file is, and mn, the one locale currently off the list,
reads as finished rather than in-progress and stays enforced under the new
anomaly wording. This is a mechanism for whichever way SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES
reads, not a relaxation of what it enforces today.

Proven with a synthetic three-locale fixture exercising all three branches
directly against both scripts' real functions: a listed locale's gap stays
enforced regardless of translation quality, an unlisted mid-translation
locale's gap is excluded and reported only in the downgrade line, and an
unlisted finished-looking locale's gap stays enforced under the anomaly
wording. All three assertions hold on both guards.

test(i18n): the number census says what it could not judge, and both ways round

Two gaps in the same file, and they turn out to be one gap.

The first is that the rule read a receiver and had almost no way to recognise
one. It knew `rows.length` and it knew `row.updated_at`, and everything else
went past unjudged and uncounted, so an empty offender list meant either that
every number was in the right place or that nothing had been recognised as a
number, and nothing on the run told the two apart. The file said so about
itself in a comment: six of the thirty six figures in the held documents were
dates and "the other thirty are numbers", which was subtraction rather than a
reading, because the walk could recognise the six and could not look at the
rest.

So the reading is wider now and it is one reading rather than two. Four
questions in `verdictAt`, in order of how little each assumes: the receiver
where it settles the matter, then the options argument, which names one
formatter or the other outright and cannot be argued with, then the single
declaration of a bare receiver name in the same file, then its single
annotation. Both directions call it, so the rule about numbers and the rule
about dates cannot drift apart into two lists maintained separately, which is
what happens when the same question is asked twice.

Measured on the branch before any of it was written, because a widening that
turns a gate red is a defect report and a widening that does not is a change
of coverage, and which one this was is a fact rather than a hope. Screens on
the interface language: 37 seen, 0 numbers, 35 dates, 2 unjudged. Everywhere
on the number preference: 269 seen, 83 numbers, 0 dates, 186 unjudged.
Documents held back: 36 seen, 27 numbers, 6 dates, 3 unjudged. Every one of
the sixteen newly resolved sites on the screens is a date, which is why this
lands green, and the twenty seven in the documents are the figures a recipient
rule will have to move when there is one.

Each run prints its census. The unjudged count is the honest half of it: the
backward direction judges 83 of 269 and says so rather than being tuned until
the number looked better. Refusal is deliberate everywhere it happens. A
receiver bound twice in a file stays unjudged instead of the gate picking one,
and a dotted receiver is never resolved against a same-named local, since
`a.value` ends in `value` too and that is how a census turns into a wrong red.

The census goes to stdout rather than through console.log, which is the
obvious way to write it and does not work. Vitest intercepts console and
gives it to the reporter, and on a green run the default reporter prints
none of it, so the first version of this was invisible in exactly the case
it exists for. It came back only under --disableConsoleIntercept, which
nobody passes. Caught by looking for the line in the run output instead of
assuming it was there.

The counts are floors on the two rules that walk the whole tree, because those
counts describe the branch while the walk reads the working tree, and an exact
number there goes red on a half converted copy with no way to tell that from a
regression. In the held documents they are exact, which is safe only because
the per-file totals are already pinned and fail first, with the message that
tells the reader not to edit the number.

The second gap is the contract nobody wrote down. Every other assertion here
checks that a number follows the reader, and that has two clauses: with no
preference the number moves with the language, and with a preference it stops
moving with the language. Only the first was asserted. The test that proved a
chosen format wins rendered in exactly one language, which a build that
ignored the preference entirely would also have satisfied whenever the
fallback happened to agree. Reading one amount in four languages tells "the
preference won" apart from "the preference agreed", and the negative control
beside it keeps that from passing on a surface that renders one frozen string
for everybody. A quantity is asserted as well as an amount, because it reaches
the locale through a different component.

The tree walks carry explicit timeouts now. They were running close to the
default fifteen seconds on a loaded machine and doing more work per file after
this, and a walk that fails on the clock reads exactly like a walk that failed
on the rule.

fix(demo-seed): every demo project prices its work in its own currency

The assembly recipes, the plant rates and the resource pool are written once
and reused by all thirty-one packs, and their numbers were euro figures
written out verbatim whatever the template said. A square metre of plaster
and paint came to 42.30 in Berlin, in Sao Paulo, in Delhi and in Dubai, with
only the currency code changing, so the catalogue quietly claimed that a
euro, a real and a rupee buy the same amount of building. Nothing caught it
because every figure was well formed and carried the right code beside it.

There is a cost level per currency now, with material and labour kept apart.
The two columns are the whole point rather than a refinement: the Gulf
imports its cement at world prices and hires its crews well below German
wages, so a single blended factor would be wrong in both directions at the
same time. Equipment follows the material column, because a plant rate
tracks the capital cost of an imported machine and not the wage of whoever
drives it, and a whole of works figure such as a subcontract sum takes the
mean of the two. Thirteen currencies are covered, which is every currency
any pack declares.

This is not an exchange rate, and the code says so in the place a reader
would have to be told. It is a demo data device, a single number carrying
both the conversion and the local price level, picked so that somebody in
that market recognises the figure instead of having to convert it. Real
money still comes from the bill, which every template hand authors in its
own currency, and the euro projects are unchanged by construction.

The gate runs the real generator on the Berlin template with only the
currency replaced, so anything that differs between two runs came from the
levelling. It holds four separate things: that no currency still prints the
euro figure, that material and labour move apart rather than together, that
the euro literals survive untouched, and that every currency found by
reading the pack files on disk has a row. That last one counts from the
packs rather than from a list kept beside them, because a census that reads
its own list is blind to exactly the currency a new pack brings, and it
fails loudly when it has read no files at all. Every assertion was
falsified: nineteen deliberate breakages, nineteen reds.

per megabyte and stays linear, so 100 MB of real rows parses in roughly three

at 1 MB and 1.72 at 8 MB, climbing, and parses to no rows at all. That is how a
26 MB upload spent 61 seconds in this handler. The cost follows the shape of a
file rather than its size, so a byte cap cannot bound it at any value, and the
guard for it belongs in the parser. That work is tracked separately.

The integration test keeps a probe from the other side: an ordinary upload is
not turned away on size, which is what makes the refusal above it meaningful.
Nothing sends a body over the cap, because moving 100 MB through the client to
watch one comparison buys less than stating the number does.

ci(desktop): take the rpm off the critical path of a release

v15.0.0 shipped without a single Linux installer, without SHA256SUMS and
without a cosign signature, and none of that has anything to do with Linux
installers. The ubuntu job hit its 240 minute cap and was cancelled, which took
the run to cancelled, and the signing workflow gates on the run concluding
success.

What ate the four hours is measurable and it is one step. On v14.8.1, with a
369 MB sidecar, Rust finished in 5m29s, the deb was written in 13 seconds, the
rpm took 1h48m43s and the AppImage 1m53s after it. On v15.0.0, with a 732 MB
sidecar, the deb took 25 seconds and the rpm was still running 3h33m later when
the cap fired. That is the same throughput both times, about 56 KB of payload a
second, so it tracks whatever the sidecar weighs and the next thing added to it
moves the cap again. The deb packs the identical payload to the identical size
four hundred times faster, so this is not compression and no setting we own
changes it.

The rpm is the most downloaded Linux package we publish, 15 against 9 for the
deb and 4 for the AppImage on v14.8.1, so it is not something to drop. It is
something to keep out of the way. It gets a job of its own that needs only the
sidecar, so it starts alongside the others, and continue-on-error, so running
out of clock now costs the rpm and nothing else. The run still waits for it
before completing, which puts the signature a couple of hours later than it
used to arrive; that is unattended, and it is the trade that stops a slow
bundler taking a whole release with it.

Two more things came out of the same reading. The comment on the old cap
explained the Linux two hours as the cost of building the Tauri bundle with no
Rust cache, and the Rust build was five and a half minutes, so that is
corrected in place rather than left to mislead the next person who reads it.
And a tag push takes its workflow file from the tag's own commit, which means a
pipeline fix landed afterwards can never reach that run, and is why none of the
above could have repaired v15.0.0 by itself. There is a tag input now: the
source is checked out at the tag, the pipeline comes from the branch it is
dispatched from, and every job that touches the release reads the tag from one
place instead of from whichever ref it happens to be running on.

fix(desktop): ship the locale catalogue the sidecar reads while starting

Two users on Windows 11 upgraded to 15.0.0 and got an app that never opened,
reported as issue #434 and by mail with a full launcher log. The sidecar exits
during startup with FileNotFoundError on a locales directory inside the
temporary folder it unpacks itself into, and the desktop build had in fact
never contained one.

The catalogue resolves as a directory sitting next to the app package rather
than inside it, so the line that ships backend/app does not carry it and it
lands at the bundle root, where nothing put it. The wheel has force-included
the same folder at the same path for exactly this reason and says so in a
comment; the spec was simply never told. Adding it is one line, and the line is
unconditional on purpose, so a build assembled without the catalogue stops at
PyInstaller instead of producing another installer that cannot start.

What made a packaging gap this old invisible is worth stating, because it is
the part that will repeat otherwise. Until this release a missing catalogue was
a warning, and the loader refilled the directory from an embedded copy carrying
20 of the languages and a much smaller key set. The desktop channel had
therefore been serving a partial catalogue for its whole life while looking
healthy: every file present, parsing, and agreeing with every other file, which
is a state no check we have can see. Replacing that recovery with a hard error
was right, and it converted a silent degradation into a dead app on the same
day. The error message went with it, since it asserted the catalogue is
force-included in the wheel and so can never be absent, which is true of a
wheel and false of a frozen bundle, and then advised a git checkout or a
reinstall to a user for whom neither can work.

Three guards, because the fix alone only closes today's instance.

A unit test compares the wheel's force-include map against the spec's data
list. Force-include exists precisely for files the package walk cannot see,
which makes it the register of what a frozen build is most likely to miss. It
executes the spec with the PyInstaller API stubbed rather than reading it,
because a text search passes on a spec that computes a path and never appends
it, which is this bug exactly. Its denominator is the wheel map, so a directory
missing from both files has no anchor and stays invisible; that limit is
written into the test rather than left to be rediscovered, and alembic.ini is
named there as the case that sits in it deliberately.

The preflight report gained the line its twin already had. Both force-included
paths needed one, the frontend bundle had it and the catalogue did not, and the
new check asks the loader instead of testing the directory, for the reason the
frontend check spells out at length: a check that reimplements the lookup it is
checking is right only by coincidence.

The release workflow now runs that report against the frozen artefact. It
already ran the sidecar, but under a name wider than its measurement: the step
called "check the sidecar starts" runs the version subcommand, which proves the
bootloader unpacks and the app package imports and never touches the server
startup path where the catalogue is read. A dead sidecar passed it on all three
platforms. The step keeps its narrow job under an honest name, and a second one
beside it exercises the startup path and fails on the build rather than on a
user's machine.

Two smaller things fall out of the same log. The launcher knew the real cause
and threw it away: the termination handler names the exception the moment the
sidecar dies, then the startup timeout fired nine minutes later and replaced it
with a sentence saying only that the backend had not started in time. It
guarded on the readiness flag, which is set when the backend goes healthy and
therefore never when it dies, so the guard was true in exactly the case it was
meant to exclude. The two reports show both halves of it, one user quoting the
real exception and the other quoting the timeout, for one identical failure.
Readiness and "the user has already been told why" are now separate flags,
which is what the guard needed to ask about all along.

Fixes #434

fix(desktop): start the sidecar somewhere it is allowed to write

Ten registers ship an attach button that cannot work on a per-machine Windows
install. Eighteen upload roots across those ten modules are declared as
working-directory-relative literals and create themselves with mkdir on first
use, going around the data-dir plumbing the rest of the platform answers to.
Nothing set the sidecar's working directory, so it inherited the launcher's,
and the Start Menu shortcut of a per-machine install starts the app in the
install folder under Program Files. Creating a directory there is denied to an
unelevated user, so attaching a file to a request for information, a submittal,
an inspection, a punch item, a letter, a diary entry, a lien waiver, a closeout
item or a compliance document answered with a bare 500. In one of them the
mkdir sits outside the try that wraps the write, so not even the module's own
error handling saw it.

Measured against a real install rather than reasoned about: the shortcut's
working directory reads as the install folder, and the same mkdir the routers
perform fails there with an access denial for a user who is not an
administrator, leaving nothing behind.

The existing note beside the spawn is correct and was not enough. It says that
leaving --data-dir unset keeps the data directory writable under Program Files,
which is true, and says nothing about the working directory, which is a second
path the same process resolves against. That is also why this survived: both
development and CI run with the repository root as the working directory, which
is writable, so all eighteen look healthy everywhere anyone has ever watched
them.

This is a floor rather than the repair. It moves them somewhere writable
without editing the eighteen declarations, and they still want fixing so they
answer to OE_CLI_DATA_DIR like everything else; until they do, a relative path
written by a new module lands in the right place by accident rather than by
design. Falling through silently when the home directory cannot be read is
deliberate, because an inherited working directory is exactly what shipped, so
that machine is left no worse off than it is today.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(desktop): stop believing a pidfile whose number now belongs to something else

The launcher told a user the local database was ready and the application
server was not, in the same breath. Both statements came from the same
leftover file. A force-killed postmaster leaves postmaster.pid behind, the
check that clears it asked only whether the recorded number is alive, and
operating systems reuse process numbers. Windows reuses them quickly.

Measured on a real machine rather than reasoned about. The file was written
on 31 July and named process 5336. That process is alive and it is a
licensing service with no relation to this cluster. The check saw a live
process, kept the file, the wrapper attached to the port the file records,
and reported the cluster ready. Nothing was listening on that port, so the
backend then failed with a connection refusal and the user was left with a
diagnostics screen that says the database is fine and the server is not.

This is the ordinary aftermath of upgrading rather than a rare accident.
The installer hooks force-kill the sidecar and its children on every install
and every uninstall, by design and for a good reason, which is the file lock
that would otherwise block the write. So the product creates the condition
itself, on the happy path, and then needs only the operating system to hand
that number to someone else.

The pidfile carries the postmaster's own start time on its third line, and
that is what tells the process that wrote the file apart from whatever holds
the number now. A creation time that does not match means the number was
recycled and the file is stale. Where there is no time to compare against, a
process name we can read that is not a postmaster says the same thing.

Only positive evidence of recycling counts. The opposite mistake is far
worse, because deleting the pidfile of a live postmaster invites a second one
onto the same data directory, so anything unreadable or uncertain answers no
and the file is kept. That is why the recorded time decides on its own when
it is present, instead of being overruled by a name.

The test was watched failing against the previous behaviour before it was
kept, and its failure text names what the user sees rather than what the
function returns.

fix(desktop): announce the local database only once something answers it

The stage that reports the embedded database ready fired on the strength of
the attach returning a handle. Attaching reads the cluster's own files, so a
data directory left describing a postmaster that no longer exists hands back
a perfectly well formed object pointing at a port where nothing is listening.
The launcher then tells the user the local database is ready and the
application server is not, in the same breath, which is the least useful pair
of statements the product could make about one cause.

The probe that would have caught it was already written and already correct.
It was wired only to the branch where the attach had raised, so it guarded a
cluster that was visibly recovering and left the path where everything looked
fine unguarded. That is why two fixes landed next to this line without
touching it: both were reading the failing branch, where the check was.

Readiness is now a connection rather than a return value, on both paths. On a
healthy boot the first connect succeeds and the cost is not measurable, which
is asserted rather than assumed. When it does not answer, the cluster is not
there whatever its files say, and saying so lets the existing bounded retry
clear the leftovers and start one, instead of handing a stale port to the
first asyncpg connection and surfacing it as a network error a stage later.

This is the second of the two holes behind the same screen. The first was the
pidfile check asking whether the recorded number is alive rather than whether
it is still the same process. Either one alone reproduces the failure, and
closing only one would have left the report true but the screen unchanged
whenever the other fired.

fix(desktop): ask the cluster on the family it actually listens on

The probe that now proves the local database is ready before announcing it
asked 127.0.0.1. That is the only address a Windows cluster has, and on Linux
and macOS it is an address the cluster does not have at all: the postmaster
pixeltable-pgserver starts there listens on a unix socket and opens no TCP
listener, which its own log states in as many words. So the probe reported a
cluster that was up, healthy and serving as dead, and the bounded retry then
tore it down and rebuilt it twice more before giving up. The PostgreSQL lane
went red on the commit that introduced it and green on the one before.

The knowledge was already in this file, thirty lines above the probe, where a
comment explains that get_uri() hands back TCP loopback on Windows and a unix
socket elsewhere and that the loopback guard below it is skipped on the unix
path. The probe was written next to that paragraph without reading it.

Readiness now asks whichever family the cluster offers, and the pidfile says
which. Line 5 is the unix socket directory, empty on Windows, and the socket
inside it is named after the port on line 4, so one number serves both. Line 6
is the first listen address, empty when there is none. The socket is tried
first where there is one, and that order is not a preference: a system
PostgreSQL on 5432 would accept a TCP connect and satisfy a probe asking about
a cluster in a temporary directory it has never heard of, while the socket path
comes out of this cluster's own pidfile and belongs to it alone. A pidfile too
short to answer is read as allowing TCP, because a probe that rules out a
family on missing information is the failure this helper exists to prevent.

The recovery probe shared the same assumption and now shares the same helper.
It survived only because it was wired to the branch where something had already
gone wrong, which is the same reason the assumption went unnoticed in the first
place.

Four cases cover it, and the one that matters asserts that no TCP connection is
attempted rather than that a socket answers, so it holds on a machine with no
unix sockets. The behaviour it pins was measured on the previous commit rather
than argued: the old probe dials 127.0.0.1:5432 and returns false in fifty
milliseconds.

fix(desktop): refuse a data directory PostgreSQL cannot open, and say how to keep the data

The embedded cluster was started against whatever pgdata the machine already
had. When the bundled PostgreSQL major moves, that directory is unreadable to
the new binaries, and the failure arrived three retries deep as a connection
error with nothing in it about versions. Reinstalling does not help, which is
what makes it the worst kind of wall: the obvious remedy is the one that
cannot work.

boot() now compares the major recorded in PG_VERSION against the major the
bundle carries, before anything touches the cluster, and refuses there. The
9.x case keeps both components, because before PostgreSQL 10 the second one
was part of the major. Everything about the check fails open: no PG_VERSION,
an unreadable bundled version, a pg_config that will not run, and the boot
proceeds as before.

The message names the major found, the major expected and the path. It offers
DATABASE_URL and pg_dump first, because they keep the data, and says that an
explicitly truthy OE_USE_EMBEDDED_PG overrides DATABASE_URL, which is what
--embedded-pg sets and would otherwise send the reader straight back into the
same directory. Only then does it name --reset, in a sentence carrying its own
warning that every project, price, document and user in the cluster is gone
permanently.

The launcher checklist line names both versions too. That line is the only
surface a desktop user stuck on a window that will not open ever reads; the
full paragraph goes to a log file they are not looking at.

nothing, which is why Android and iOS are matched ahead of the desktop

feat(procurement): an order raised against a bill position commits against its cost line

Committed against remaining has read zero on every project since the report
was written. The read side was complete: po_committed_by_cost_line joins the
order lines to their orders, converts by the order currency and groups by cost
line, filtering the rows where cost_line_id is set. Nothing ever set it. The
column, the report and the dashboard all existed, and only the writer was
missing, so the number stayed honest and useless.

A purchase order line now carries the link from the moment it is written. The
buyer picks a bill position, because that is the language of the job, and the
resolver follows the position to the cost line it rolls up into. Nobody raising
an order is asked what a cost line is.

The resolution happens on write and not on read. An order is a commitment made
on a given day against the scope as it was understood on that day, so
repointing that position next month must not rewrite what last month's order
committed against. A test asserts exactly that by repointing the position after
the order is issued and reading the committed total again.

There is a distinction under this that the schema alone does not tell, so it is
written out in the module docstring of procurement/cost_spine.py. The estimate
reaches the rest of the platform along two links that are not interchangeable.
Quantity modules carry boq_position_id, because a delivery note or an installed
quantity is a fact about a measured item of work. Money modules carry
cost_line_id, because estimate, budget, committed, actual and claimed have to
meet on one row before any of them can be compared. So POItemCreate accepts
boq_position_id as an input field while the table stores only the cost line: a
schema field and a column are allowed to differ, and here they must, or the
next person adds the wrong column to the wrong table.

The resolver refuses another project's position and another project's cost
line, both with a 404 raised before the order row exists, so a refusal cannot
burn a number from the project sequence. A position whose project has no cost
spine yet resolves to nothing, which is a valid order that simply commits
against nothing so far. Minting a cost line from here was considered and
rejected: the generator derives a control account from the position
classification and skips section headers, and a line minted outside it would be
absent from the account rollups that give a cost line its purpose.

The tests carry the negative cases first. An order line naming no position must
leave the column empty and must keep the committed aggregate empty with it,
because a writer that does nothing passes a positive only test, and that is the
family of bug this change repairs.

Material requisition lines resolve the same way. That path takes its items as
dicts because the module exposes no requisition endpoint and so has no create
schema to carry a field, and it is wired now so the link is right on the day
that endpoint lands.

fix(procurement): correcting a quantity no longer strips the order off the cost spine

them, so the rows are built from scratch every time. The rebuild did not
resolve the cost line, which means the first correction to a quantity would
have unlinked the whole order and dropped it out of the committed report for

tell the two apart. It creates a linked order, issues it, corrects the quantity

feat(costmodel): read back what the site did, one row per bill position

The Cost Spine rollup already answers what a scope item cost, per cost line and
in money alone. That is the right shape for a cost report and the wrong shape
for the person who wrote the estimate, who works in bill positions and wants
one row per item of work with a quantity and a rate on it.

So GET /projects/{project_id}/spine/position-actuals/ turns the rollup around.
It is keyed by bill position, carries the position ordinal, description and
unit, and puts two physical facts next to the money that the cost line does not
hold: how much of the item the crew reports installed, and how much material
the store has issued against it and what that material cost. One row can now
say the thing that was not visible anywhere: you billed 120 m3 at 180, you have
committed 1800 of it, the crew reports 40 percent installed, and 55 m3 worth
9900 has been consumed.

Uncommitted is reported signed rather than floored at zero. Ordering more than
was estimated for an item is a finding, and clamping it would draw the one row
a cost manager needs to see exactly like a row that is merely fully committed.

Assembling this crosses the two links the platform keeps apart, which is why it
lives in a file of its own rather than being read ad hoc wherever it is wanted.
Money is keyed by cost line, progress and inventory by bill position, and the
position carries the cost line it rolls up into, which is the only bridge
between them. Nothing here writes either link.

A position with no cost line still gets a row, with its estimate and its
progress and zeros for money. The crew's work is real whether or not the
project ever generated a spine, and a row that vanished for want of a link
would read as no work done. The response counts those rows separately so a page
of zeros can say which of its two causes it has.

Waste is excluded from consumed quantity on purpose. It is material that left
the store without becoming part of the works, and counting it would report an
item as further advanced than it is. Site inventory reports waste on its own.

Six queries whatever the size of the bill, and boq_id or position_id narrows
the selection before the aggregates run, so a drawer opened on one position
does not pay for the whole project. No user interface in this change.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(costmodel): let a picker search the whole bill instead of a page of it

The cost line list served two hundred rows and took no search parameter, so
anything offering the spine as a choice had to page the whole project into the
browser and filter what it had loaded. A filter that can only see what was
loaded denies the existence of rows the register holds, and a buyer who types
the code in front of them and gets nothing concludes their position is not on
the spine. That is a worse answer than an error.

So the narrowing moves to the query. `search` matches code or description as a
case insensitive substring, with the wildcards escaped, because a bill is full
of codes carrying an underscore and an unescaped one silently matches any
character in its place. `linked_to_position` selects the lines that answer to a
bill position, so the rows returned and the count returned describe the same
set rather than the caller dropping rows afterwards and reporting a total that
covers rows it never showed. `boq_position_id` resolves one known position,
which is how a control opened on an existing order can still name the line it
was attributed to when that line sorts past the page.

Every test seeds more than one page, and that is the point rather than an
incidental detail. A search test over five rows passes whether the search
reaches the database or not, since five rows all fit on the first page and any
filter in the browser would find them too. The only assertion that separates a
working search from a broken one is that a line the unfiltered first page does
not contain comes back when searched for, so each test states the control
first: not on page one, found by search.

The picker follows. Whether it renders at all is decided by the unsearched
list and never by the current results, so a search matching nothing leaves the
control in place to be corrected rather than making it vanish mid keystroke.
The unsearched list is still one page and can still be partial, so it now says
so instead of presenting itself as the whole register. The selection is fetched
by its own id when the page does not hold it, because a control that cannot
find its own value renders as unselected and the next save writes that back,
which is the quiet way an attribution made months ago disappears.

The search parameter is only sent when something was typed. It is declared with
a minimum length, so posting an empty string for a cleared box would answer 422
and turn "show me everything again" into an error the buyer cannot get out of.

fix(procurement): an awarded tender commits against the spine like any order

Wiring the money link into the order form covered what a buyer types. It did
not cover the largest single commitment the system makes. Awarding a tender
turns a whole package into a purchase order inside an event handler that builds
its own line items, and that handler wrote the bid line's position id into
wbs_id as text while leaving the money link null. So the package landed on the
project total and nowhere in the breakdown, which is the same defect the order
form had, on a much larger number.

The position was already in hand, which is what makes this worth fixing rather
than scheduling: the bid line names it, and the same resolver the order form
uses turns it into the cost line the day the award is recorded.

Resolution is best effort here and deliberately so. It raises when a position
has moved out of the project, and refusing to record an award because one line
points at stale scope would lose the commitment itself. A missing attribution
is a reporting gap somebody can close later. A missing purchase order is money
nobody knows was spent until it has been.

The position id keeps going into wbs_id as well. It has been landing there
since the handler was written and the coding check counts it, so taking it away
while adding the cost line would trade one gap for another on every project
whose spine has not been generated.

The tests drive the coroutine rather than the subscriber that wraps it. The
subscriber launches the work as a detached task and returns at once, so an
await on it proves nothing, and sharing one connection with the test session it
runs the two concurrently until the driver refuses. They also read the
committed aggregate rather than the column, because a resolver that runs and
returns nothing leaves the column exactly as a resolver that never ran.

The sibling handler, the one that builds an order from a priced bid submission,
is left alone. Its lines resolve through the bid package line, which carries a
code and no position, so there is nothing there to resolve and the fix would
have to start with the schema.

Every test for the coded check hands it a dict written by hand in the test
file. The dict the rule actually reads is built by the service from an explicit
field list, and no test in that file could see the list. So the assertion that

a permanent one, on orders that are correctly linked, and a warning nobody can

just the symptom.

fails alone, the control keeps passing, and so does the hand written positive
test one class above, which is the whole reason this one had to exist.

No database and no session. The builder only reads attributes off the
instances, and a repository constructor only stores what it is handed.
