feat(procurement): an order line reads back the position it was ordered against

A buyer picks a bill position, the order resolves it to a cost line and stores
only that, because a money row carries no position column and should not grow
one. The storage decision is right and it left a hole on the read side: the
response returned the cost line and nothing else, so a form reopening the order
could not put the buyer's own choice back into the picker. The control renders
empty, empty reads as never coded, and the next save writes it back over a real
attribution. Accepting a field on write that you cannot return on read is how
an edit form forgets what somebody chose.

IF YOU ARE WIRING THE FORM, READ THIS PARAGRAPH. What comes back is the
position the cost line names today. CostLine carries boq_position_id and an
update can re-point it, so this is a derivation and not a record of what was
typed. Echoing it back for a line the user never touched could therefore
relink the order, and nothing would look wrong at the time. The clean round
trip is to send back the cost_line_id you were given for untouched lines, and
boq_position_id only for lines the user actually changed. resolve_cost_line_ids
gives an explicit cost line priority precisely so that works.

The resolver sits beside the write-side one, in cost_spine.py, keyed by cost
line as text like every other map in this layer, batched so a page of orders
costs one query rather than one per row.

Five of the six endpoints returning a single order spelled out the same pair of
lookups, so they collapse into one _po_response helper and each site is now a
line. Brevity is not the reason. A seventh endpoint that copied only the vendor
lookup would answer null for every position, and null there reads as a line
nobody ever coded rather than as a lookup somebody forgot. A wrong answer
wearing the costume of a legitimate one is the thing worth designing out.

Nine tests, five on the query and four on the stamping, and the map key was
mutated to check they discriminate: pointing it at the item id instead of the
cost line fails exactly the two that assert a real position comes back, while
both negative controls and all five query tests keep passing. A control that
cannot fail is decoration.

The negative cases are deliberate. A line with no cost link and a cost line
generated from no position both have to come back bare rather than carrying a
neighbour's position, because the map is keyed by cost line and a wrong key
reads exactly like a missing one.

fix(audit): a dropped audit row stops taking the caller's write with it

log_activity has always promised that a failed audit write leaves the caller's
transaction intact so the business write continues. Catching the exception was
not enough to keep that promise. A failed flush puts the session into a
rolled-back state where every later statement raises PendingRollbackError, so
the caller was handed a broken session and a swallowed error, and the audit row
took the business write down with it.

This was seen on a first run of the shipped 15.2.0 desktop build. A long
blocking model download starved the connection pool for about ninety seconds,
the audit flush timed out, and the timeline bridge then failed its commit on a
session this function had already poisoned. An audit row and a timeline event
were both lost where only the audit row was ever meant to be at risk.

The fix is a savepoint around the add and the flush, the same idiom already
used elsewhere in core for exactly this purpose. The savepoint rolls back on
its own and the caller's transaction survives, which is what the comment above
the block already claimed happened. One function changes and all 103 call sites
across 40 files inherit it.

The failure log line now says the audit row was dropped and the caller's
transaction is still usable. The old wording said only that a flush had failed,
which left a reader unable to tell whether their own data had landed, and that
is the one thing they most need to know.

The test drives a real database error rather than a patched one. entity_type is
a 64 character column and PostgreSQL rejects a longer value at flush time. That
distinction carries the test: a mocked flush that merely raises does not put the
session into the rolled-back state the test is about, so it would pass with or
without the savepoint and prove nothing. Checked in both directions, and on the
previous code it fails with the same PendingRollbackError seen in the field.

fix(desktop): a listening socket stops counting as a running database

The readiness probe opened a TCP socket and called whatever answered a
database. A postmaster keeps its listen socket for as long as the process
lives, including after it can no longer serve a session, so the probe
measured the one thing still working and reported the cluster ready. The
launcher then announced the local database and failed every connection it
made in the next breath.

That state is reached by an ordinary sequence rather than a rare one. A run
that dies after bringing the cluster up leaves the postmaster alive. Its
pidfile keeps naming a live process, so the stale pidfile sweep correctly
refuses to touch it, pixeltable attaches to it instantly, and every retry
attaches to the same unusable server. Nothing in the module could clear it,
so the machine stayed broken across relaunches and across upgrades, and
reinstalling did not help because nothing about the installation was wrong.

Reported from a real launcher log. Two runs of one release crashed on a
packaging fault after the cluster had started, and the release that fixed
that fault could not start either, because it kept attaching to the
postmaster the earlier crash had orphaned. The ready stage and the failure
share a timestamp in that log, which is the shape of the whole defect.

Readiness is now decided by sending a StartupMessage and reading the reply.
Any reply counts, including a refusal: "the database system is starting up"
and "sorry, too many clients already" both prove a server is there to say
so. Only silence, EOF or a reset mean nothing can serve, and that is the one
state the recovery acts on.

Detecting it is only half. A cluster that accepts and stays silent is now
stopped so a working one can take its place, which is what turns a clearer
error into a machine that starts. The guards around that are deliberately
strict, because being wrong there does not mean a failed boot, it means
ending a process that belongs to somebody else: the pid must still be the
one that wrote the pidfile, and it must hold the port the pidfile names.
The port check reads the system wide socket table on purpose. The per
process view returns an empty list on Windows for a process whose handle we
do not hold, without raising, which reads as "owns nothing" and would have
handed the decision to a guess about the process name.

A cluster replaying WAL is untouched by all of this. It has not opened its
listen socket yet, so it reads as closed and is waited out exactly as
before, and the three states stay distinct for that reason.

Verified against a real cluster rather than only against the fake used in
the unit tests, since a malformed startup packet would have made a healthy
server look mute and got it stopped, which is worse than the original bug. A
fresh cluster answers in 15ms and the recovery refuses to touch it. A
postmaster held in the stuck state is reported mute, is reported healthy by
the old probe, and a following boot clears it and comes up, after which a
client query succeeds. That last run takes about ninety seconds because
stopping a postmaster means the next start replays WAL.

One existing case asserted that an open socket is an answer, which was the
rule that shipped. It is inverted rather than deleted: the question was the
right one to ask and only the expected answer was wrong. Three more cases
used a bare listener as a stand-in for a healthy cluster and now use one
that speaks, including the unix socket case, which would otherwise have
taken the PostgreSQL lane red on Linux while skipping on Windows.

fix(project-route): an upgraded database keeps the naive timestamp the model no longer declares

classified_at was the one naive DateTime column among 197 aware ones, and the
service has always stamped it with an aware datetime, which asyncpg refuses to
put into a naive timestamp. Declaring the column with timezone=True fixes a
fresh installation, because create_all builds it correctly from the start, and
does nothing at all for an existing one. Module tables here are not in Alembic,
356 of 602 have no migration, and the auto-migrator that stands in for one only
ever adds columns and never retypes them.

So the widening runs at boot and at init-db, next to the sequence repair that
lives there for the same reason. It reads the current type by reflection rather
than assuming which version the database is coming from, and it converts with
an explicit AT TIME ZONE 'UTC'. Without that clause PostgreSQL reads the stored
values in the session time zone and shifts every historical classification
instead of relabelling it, which a test proves by widening under a session
deliberately set to another zone.

The rest of the test drives the upgrade itself: it puts the column back the way
an older database has it, widens it, checks the reflected type changed, and
checks that the boot after that one does nothing at all.

question is about the built-in pack. Modules register into that same set name as

named rather than created, because boot already builds the whole chain with
parents of its own. That is the same shape the cross platform end to end
workflow uses, and its windows jobs have been green throughout. Set
OE_TEST_PG_ROOT to override on a machine that has the same trouble with its own
temp dir.

The reaper reads the same resolved root. One looking in the system temp dir
while the session writes somewhere else would quietly stop collecting anything,
and a reaper that collects nothing reports the same silence as one with nothing
to collect.

fix(embedded-pg): the cluster directory is left for initdb to create

Bringing the local database up on Windows could fail before it started, with
initdb reporting that it could not change the permissions of the very directory
it had just been pointed at. The directory was ours: it was created ahead of
initdb, and initdb then took its path for an existing directory, which begins by
fixing the permissions on it.

That chmod is the one it cannot do. initdb re-executes itself under a restricted
token, dropping the Administrators group so that a cluster is never owned by an
administrator, and the child it becomes cannot always write a directory the
elevated parent made. Handed a path that is not there yet it creates the
directory itself, owns what it created, and never touches anything of ours.

So only the directory that holds the cluster is created now, and the cluster
directory inside it is left to initdb. Nothing downstream needed changing,
because all of it already had to work on a machine where none of this exists
yet. An installation that already has a cluster is unaffected, since that
directory is present either way.

Every Windows shard of the backend matrix died on this, three of three, and it
is the same code path a desktop installation takes on first start.

listening sockets needs root on macOS, so the call raised AccessDenied before

started ourselves, which macOS does allow. That keeps the test doing its work
on the platform rather than turning it off there. The walk covers the child and
its descendants because a virtualenv launcher re-executes, so the listener can
be a grandchild, and the point of the test is that a pidfile names whoever
actually holds the socket.

machine-wide call forced to raise the way macOS raises it, the walk returns the

test(embedded-pg): the stand-in socket is bound somewhere its address fits

directory, so the code under test is asked exactly the question it was asked

and nothing else.

fix(health): the memory figure stops being a number that can only climb

On Linux and macOS the health endpoint filled memory_mb from getrusage, which
returns ru_maxrss, the peak resident set since the process started. That number
never falls again. A demo seed drives it into the gigabytes and it stays there
for the rest of the process life, so anyone watching the endpoint sees a gauge
that only ever climbs and never recovers. Windows took a different branch and
reported current RSS through psutil, so the same field meant two different
things depending on where it ran, and comparing one deployment against another
compared a high water mark against a live reading.

This was not theoretical. A packaging check this week read 1805 and 2509 MB off
two Linux runs and those figures were about to be quoted as what the application
uses, when both were high water marks left over from seeding thirteen demo
projects. At rest the same build sits near a tenth of that.

Current RSS is what the field is named after, so it is now preferred wherever the
platform will produce it: /proc/self/statm on Linux, psutil elsewhere if it
happens to be installed. The peak is still reported, under memory_peak_mb, so
nothing is lost and the two are told apart. Where neither path can produce a
current figure the field falls back to the peak rather than disappearing.

psutil stays best-effort on purpose. It is not a declared dependency and the
Linux path deliberately needs nothing beyond the standard library.

Measured on both platforms by allocating and releasing 200 MB. Linux now reports
memory_mb 9.9 then 210.1 then 10.1 while memory_peak_mb holds at 210.1. Windows
reports 18.3 then 218.3 then 18.3.

fix(desktop): the startup window outlasts the database it waits on

The launcher allowed 600 seconds for the whole of startup. The backend allows
600 seconds for bringing embedded PostgreSQL up on its own, which is what
OE_PG_BOOT_TIMEOUT defaults to. The two were the same number, so a database that
spent its budget recovering left the launcher with nothing at all for everything
that comes after it: the migrations, the module load, creating the tables and
preparing first-run data.

That ordering is not a remote possibility, it is what an upgrade does. The
installer stops a running copy by ending its process tree, which crash-stops the
embedded database, so the first start after every upgrade is exactly the log
replay that the 600 second budget exists to cover. A user in that position had a
healthy backend that was still working, was told it had not started in time, and
got the same result on every retry because nothing had actually gone wrong for
retrying to clear.

The comment above this line already said the window should sit comfortably above
the backend's own budget. It named the previous 240 seconds and was never
revisited when the inner budget grew, so the intent was right and the number had
stopped matching it.

Doubling it to 1200 restores the margin. It costs nothing when a start has
genuinely failed, because that is reported the moment the sidecar dies rather
than when this window closes, which is why a backend that cannot find its locale
catalogue still reports itself within the first minute or two.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix: the clean database stop can now happen on a machine that has run us before

The headline of this release could not fire for anyone upgrading. The database
library records one process identifier per process that opens the cluster and
stops the server on the way out only when the list it reads back names the
exiting process alone. It appends on the way in, edits on the way out, and
never removes a process that was killed rather than allowed to exit. Ending
the process tree, which is how every version until this one stopped on Windows,
is exactly that kind of killing, so every existing install already carries a
list naming processes that no longer exist. Measured on a machine that has run
the product for a while: nine recorded holders, eight of them gone.

That made the clean stop a one time event. It could fire on a data directory
nobody had ever force killed, which is what a fresh test machine is, and was
skipped everywhere else. It was skipped silently too, because a skipped stop
and a completed one are indistinguishable from outside, and the launcher log
said the backend closed cleanly either way since both things it checks were
true. So the live test that passed was not wrong, it was run on the one kind of
machine where the fault does not exist.

Recorded holders whose process is gone are now dropped, on the way in as well
as on the way out, since a machine whose graceful stop keeps failing falls back
to ending the process tree and never reaches the shutdown path at all. Only a
process that is demonstrably gone is dropped, and never this one: removing a
holder that is alive would stop the database underneath something still using
it, which is much worse than not stopping it at all. Removal goes through the
library's own list object, so the two cannot disagree about the format. When
the stop is skipped because someone else really is holding the cluster, that
now appears in the log rather than looking like a stop that happened.

Deciding whether a process still exists no longer depends on a package we do
not require. psutil is not a declared dependency, nothing in the runtime
requirement set pulls it in, and the old check answered "may still be alive"
whenever it could not be imported, which would have kept every recorded holder
and skipped every stop on an install without it. Both platforms can answer the
question from the standard library, so they are asked first and psutil is a
refinement rather than the answer. On Windows an exit code also tells a running
process apart from one that has ended and is still held open by its parent,
which a check by name gets wrong.

The category name for enterprise modules is translated in the thirteen
languages that have a word for it and stays as it is in the six where it is the
word those languages use.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix: the data directory override is honoured by the command line too

Everything in the platform that resolves a data directory reads the same three
variables in the same order: OE_DATA_DIR, then DATA_DIR, then OE_CLI_DATA_DIR.
The uploads root does it, the signing secret does it, the demo seed does it,
the partner pack state does it. The command line did not. It took the home
directory and nothing else, and then exported that as the active data directory
for the rest of the process.

So an operator who pointed OE_DATA_DIR at a mounted volume got a split. Uploads
and the signing secret went to the volume, because those resolve it themselves.
The database, the embedded cluster and the config file stayed in the home
directory, which on a container is the layer that disappears on redeploy. A
documented override that is honoured by some of the writers and not the others
is worse than one that is ignored outright, because nothing reports the half
that was dropped. An explicit --data-dir still wins; this only supplies the
default.

While comparing the two, one smaller disagreement turned up. The storage
resolver took an override that was only whitespace at face value and resolved
the data root to a directory named a space, where the other two treated blank
as unset. A compose file spells "not set" as an empty value, so blank now means
unset in all three, and a padded value is trimmed in all three.

The version command was pointing people at the wrong directory. It printed a
line labelled site-packages against the interpreter's own folder, which is
Scripts on Windows and bin elsewhere, so anyone who followed it went looking
for the package where the package is not. It now names where it is installed,
which interpreter is running it, and which data directory is in effect, since
that line is what someone pastes when an install is misbehaving and the data
directory is how an operator confirms their override was taken.

The tests put the two resolvers side by side under the same environment and
fail if they ever part company again. The one case where they are allowed to
differ, a source checkout with nothing set, is pinned with its reason so it is
not mistaken for the same fault.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix: the release cannot ship a wheel with no user interface in it

The publish workflow has a step called "Sanity check wheel" whose job is to
refuse a wheel that does not carry the built frontend. It asked whether any
file in the archive had the string "_frontend_dist" somewhere in its name. That
question cannot be answered no. The build hook creates frontend/dist/.placeholder
whenever that directory is missing, on purpose, so that the force-include map
always resolves on a cold clone, which means every wheel we will ever build has
at least one file under that path. A wheel whose entire user interface was a
123-byte placeholder satisfied the check and printed "wheel OK". The substring
also matched _frontend_dist_prev, so a wheel that carried nothing but a stale
bundle from a previous build passed as well.

It now asks for the thing the step exists to prove. The page the server serves
has to be in the archive, and every script and stylesheet that page asks for
has to be in the archive with it. On the wheel PyPI is serving today that is
index.html plus fourteen assets, all fourteen resolved. On a wheel built with a
broken frontend it fails on the first line, and on a wheel carrying only the
previous bundle it fails there too. Both were checked against the published
artifact rather than against a description of it, by rebuilding that artifact
with each of the two faults injected and nothing else changed.

Two more payloads that a pip install cannot work without had no check at all,
so they got one. The migration tree and alembic.ini only started shipping in
15.4.0, and without them alembic cannot run after an install and the version
table is never stamped. The locales sit outside the app package and are reached
by force-include alone, so a wheel that misses them starts and then serves a
catalogue with most of its strings gone. Neither absence would have shown up
in the job, which is the whole problem with a gate that reports on a substring.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(upgrade): an upgrade cannot replace the binaries it is running from

pip does not know that some of the files it is about to overwrite are being
executed. The embedded PostgreSQL binaries ship inside site-packages under
pixeltable-pgserver, and on an install where the local cluster is up, the
postmaster serving the request is running out of that directory. On Windows the
running image is locked, so pip fails partway and leaves an install that is
neither the old version nor the new one. Everywhere else it succeeds and the
process quietly becomes a mixture of the two, because this codebase imports
inside functions in many places and every later import reads the new file.

The command line upgrade now asks whether a cluster is live before it starts and
stops with one line naming the process and the data directory when one is.
Asking the machine is not the same question as asking this process, which is the
one is_running answers, so it reads the pidfile and then asks the operating
system whether that pid is still there. A pidfile left behind by an unclean stop
is exactly the leftover that would otherwise refuse an upgrade for no reason, so
a recorded pid whose process is gone reads as no cluster, and any failure to
answer reads as no reason to refuse.

The same hazard reaches the HTTP upgrade endpoint through force-reinstall, which
does not stop at our own package but reinstalls the whole dependency set. That
path now refuses with a conflict while the embedded server is up and says what to
run instead. The plain upgrade beside it is left alone, since it only moves what
changed and the ordinary case moves pure Python.

Carried in the same commit and unrelated to the above, the health endpoint was
rebuilding the alembic script directory on every call, which opens and compiles
all three hundred and some revision files. Health is polled on a timer by the
desktop shell, by container healthchecks and by whatever watches a deployment, so
that ran in a loop rather than on a rare diagnostic path. The head the installed
tree declares is now parsed once per process and keyed by the ini path, so a test
pointed at a different tree is never answered from the previous one. The database
revision it gets compared against is deliberately not cached, because that one
does change while the process runs, and caching it would turn "has the schema
fallen behind" into "was it behind when this process started". That part has no
test of its own.

feat(einvoice-clearance): the module has a way in, and it speaks every language

The first step had no control anywhere. The page explained that a registration
has to exist before anything else can happen, the list below it said there were
none, and nothing on the screen would make one, so every step downstream was
unreachable on a new installation. That is what a reader means when they say they
cannot tell what to do here.

There is now a registration form and a document form. Both are built from the
module's own meta endpoint rather than from a list in the frontend, so a country
asks for the fields it actually registers with: Mexico for a certificate
reference, Germany for a network participant id, and neither is shown the other
one's box. A country added to the backend registry appears with the right fields
and no frontend change. What the country platform does with a sent document is
said before anything is typed rather than discovered at submission time, since
the three regimes mean three different things by acceptance and the reader
should not have to know which one they are in.

Fifty one strings were new and they are in all forty two locales: seven for the
plan room flow, nine document statuses, three regimes, and the thirty two
national field names the country registry declares. The cancellation window is
passed as count and under no other name, because count is the only one i18next
resolves plural forms from, and completeness was checked against each language's
own CLDR categories rather than against English.

One near duplicate was avoided. The branch for a platform that cannot cancel
wanted a string that already existed, already translated everywhere, already
saying exactly that. It interpolates the platform name as well as the correction
mechanism, so both are passed. Reusing the key with half its variables would
have printed the word undefined into forty one languages with every gate green.

The write body for the country fields was typed as unknown and is now a string
map, which is what the server declares. A looser type there only moved the
failure from the compiler to a request an operator had already filled in.

fix(desktop): the installer stops the database it could not see

The hook that stops our processes before an install or an uninstall filters by
the install directory, and the one process that matters is never in it. The
embedded PostgreSQL postmaster runs out of the temporary directory the onefile
backend unpacks itself into, so its path is under the user's temp folder and
the filter matched it zero times. The cost of that is the whole complaint:
after the application was gone the postmaster was still running, still holding
its data directory and still holding the port, so the next install came up
against a cluster it did not own, and an uninstall left a process behind with
nothing on disk to explain it.

Looking for an image called postgres.exe would have been the same mistake one
layer down. A developer machine or a server may well be running an unrelated
PostgreSQL, and stopping someone else's database because it shares an image
name is what the blunt taskkill did before, only closer to the data.

So the postmaster is now identified the way PostgreSQL identifies it, through
the pid file it writes into its own data directory. That file names exactly one
process and by construction it names ours. Two guards sit on top of it, because
a pid file outlives the process that wrote it and Windows reuses pids: the
process found under that pid must still be called postgres, and its start time
must still be the one the file recorded. A recycled pid fails the second check
even when it passes the first.

The data directory is resolved through the same three environment variables, in
the same order, that the backend itself uses, and the test asserts that order
against the backend's own source rather than against a constant copied into the
test. If the backend ever gains a fourth override, the installer fails here
instead of quietly looking in a directory nobody uses.

The stop runs after the window has been asked to close, not instead of it, so
in the ordinary case the launcher has already shut the cluster down cleanly and
there is nothing left to act on.

The tests execute the PowerShell that ships rather than a retyped copy of it,
and on Windows they run it in all three directions that matter: it stops a
postmaster its own pid file names, it leaves a process that is not a postmaster
alone, and it leaves a recycled pid alone. A guard that refuses everything
passes a one-sided test, which is why the positive control is there. The static
checks also bound each generated command against the NSIS string limit, since a
command past that limit is truncated rather than rejected and still looks like a
working script.

fix(cli): the data directory is declared once and resolved once

Commands that take a data directory each declared the flag themselves and each
resolved it themselves, so the two could drift and did. Both are now single
points: one declaration helper serving six commands, one resolver. A command
added later either uses them or has no data directory at all, which is the
only arrangement that stays true without anyone remembering it.

Three real consequences fall out of that, and they are the reason this was
worth doing rather than a tidy-up.

The doctor's provider-key check read the default directory and took no data
directory at all, so `doctor --data-dir X` reported on one install while the
data-directory check in the same run reported on another. It now reads the
directory it was given.

The upgrade command guards against upgrading while a cluster is live, and it
looked for that cluster in the default directory with no way to say otherwise.
An operator whose data lives elsewhere was told nothing was running while it
was. Every writer of the cluster directory already resolved the path; only
this reader did not, so it was the odd one out rather than the new case.

An empty `--data-dir ""` resolved to the working directory, which under a
per-machine install is wherever the shortcut happened to point. A blank now
falls back to the default, the same way the environment resolver already
treated whitespace as unset.

The count in the report that prompted this does not survive measurement, and
the measurement is the useful part. Three independent instruments were run
over the file: an AST pass classified by expression root, a line pass, and a
third pass that dedups nested joins and follows one assignment hop. They
disagreed with each other, and each of them saw something the others missed,
which is exactly why a repaired count reported from any single one of them
would have read as complete. What survives is the denominator: of the path
expressions in this file, ten still hold a variable rather than a literal in
the path slot, and no literal-anchored instrument can audit those. Eight are
benign or deliberate and are named in the tests. The other two are the real
version of the defect and are not in this file at all: module installation
writes into site-packages, which is what actually fails under Program Files.
That is left for its own change rather than smuggled in here.

The sweep test asserts its own denominator and carries a negative control,
and both polarities were checked out of band: healthy, six examined and none
flagged; with the default forced relative, six examined and six flagged. A
sweep that can only pass is not a sweep.

fix(costs): six money surfaces stop overruling the currency

Six places built their own formatter with the digit count written in by hand,
two minimum and two maximum, against a currency that arrives as a variable.
That is a claim that every currency reaching those screens has two minor
units, and it printed a forint with fillér that the currency does not have.

The load-bearing fact is that the product had already answered this. The
shared money component renders a forint with no decimals and did so before
this change. These six surfaces were the only ones disagreeing with it, so
what is removed here is six overrides of an answer that already existed, not
a new answer. The digit count for any currency is still decided in one place,
the locale data the resolver reads, and it is still the only place. Nothing
here settles which currencies get how many digits; it makes those six screens
follow whatever that place says instead of ignoring it.

One consequence is worth naming rather than leaving to be discovered. For a
fractional amount in a zero-decimal currency the display now rounds: half a
forint disappears from the screen rather than being shown as a fraction of a
unit that does not exist. No stored value, no arithmetic and no rounding rule
was touched, and the shared component already behaved this way.

The item that prompted this named five sites. There were six. The extra one
is the mass-pricing preview, which keeps four maximum digits on purpose: a
derived unit rate is a working figure and a posted amount is not, and that
asymmetry is deliberate rather than an oversight.

The ratchet that was supposed to hold this line is emptied in the same change,
because it had become the more dangerous half. It budgeted five sites across
four files, which was honest while those five existed. With the sites gone the
census reads zero, the assertion compares a count against a ceiling, and a
ceiling of five over a real count of zero passes while five regressions walk
back in unremarked. The gate was green and toothless at once. With no entries
every file has a ceiling of zero, so the first site to reappear fails wherever
it lands.

Emptying a budget creates the opposite risk, which is that a probe which
quietly stopped recognising the shape also reports zero and also passes. So
the probe is now handed the exact thing it exists to catch and required to
catch it, and handed a literal currency code and required not to. The file
already asserts its own denominator to guard the walker; this guards the
matcher.

fix(desktop): the build stops inventing module names it cannot import

The sidecar spec declared six layers for every one of 191 module packages
whether the file existed or not, so 1337 names went into the analysis and 167
of them named nothing on disk. Every desktop build therefore printed 167
hidden import errors, and a genuinely missing dependency would have arrived as
one more line in that list. The discovery loop now asks the disk before it
declares a layer, which takes that channel from 173 lines to 6. The six that
remain are upstream: psycopg2 probing optional backends it does not need,
cffi's generated parser tables, and one lazily imported scipy module.

Excludes were the obvious tool and the wrong one. That list carries a stated
meaning, which is that nothing in the sidecar imports the name, and another
test reads it under exactly that contract. Adding 167 module names there would
have made the list say something false and would have needed editing every
time a module gained a file. Generating the layers from disk means the name is
never emitted in the first place.

The guard is a unit test that executes the spec with the packaging symbols
stubbed and reads the hidden imports that actually reach the analysis, rather
than a local variable that may or may not be the same list. It stats every
module name and asserts a floor as well as the failure, because a check that
counts can pass by going blind, and it prints the offending names rather than
a number. Both controls are exercised: a fabricated missing dependency in a
copy of the spec fails the gate, and the pre-fix cross product replayed
through the same checker flags 167, matched by an independent census.

It runs in the PostgreSQL lane immediately after dependencies and ahead of
every database step, because a failing step skips what follows it, so a guard
placed at the end only runs on the days nothing else is broken.

chore: the runtime upload directory stops being published

Eighteen files written by test runs sit in `backend/uploads/`, which is the
directory the application writes user uploads into at runtime. The path has
been ignored for a long time, but an ignore rule does not untrack what was
already committed, so those files went out with every release and are readable
in the public repository.

None of them is referenced by anything. The templates are artifacts of the
custom-template tests, including two written to prove that a path traversal
and a tenant boundary are refused, and the four under the buyer portal are
placeholders whose entire contents are the words "real pdf" and "hi". They are
harmless in themselves, which is precisely why they were never noticed: what
they demonstrate is that anything a test uploads lands in a tracked directory
and is then published, and the next such file may not be a stub. Names like
`passport-<id>.pdf` under a folder called kyc also read to anyone browsing the
repository as exactly the thing we would never store there.

Only the index entries are removed. The files stay on disk, the directory
keeps working the way it always has, and nothing in the application or the
tests reads them by path.

fix(health): the signal the launcher acts on stops answering what it does not know

The desktop shell refuses to attach to a backend it judges unhealthy and starts
its own instead, which means a wrong verdict does not merely mislead a reader:
it puts a second server on the same data directory, the accident the attach
check was written to prevent. Two of the fields that verdict rests on could not
tell "no" apart from "I never found out".

The migration head is the first. A desktop bundle carries no migration tree at
all, and a package built before the tree shipped carried none either, so the
comparison had nothing to compare and answered false, which reads as "this
backend is behind". A database created before the stamp existed reports the same
way while physically carrying the columns of the newest revision, so an entirely
correct installation reported degraded forever. An undeterminable head now reads
as unknown and only a determinable mismatch degrades. The two launcher functions
that judged the same question and disagreed, one treating stale migrations as
acceptable and the other not, now delegate to a single judgement, and the tests
drive the real probe over a real loopback socket and assert both polarities as
well as the version mismatch they are meant to disagree about.

The schema heal is the second, and it had the same shape one field along. It
reported failure or success, and a deployment where the heal never ran reported
success, because the whole block sits behind a PostgreSQL check. It now has the
three states it always needed, and the verdict lives on the application it
describes rather than in a module global that a second application in the same
process would inherit from the first.

The public payload also stopped carrying the reason. That endpoint takes no
authentication, and a database error stringifies with the statement and often
the parameters attached, so anyone who could reach the probe could read the
schema and the failing SQL off it. The boolean already told the operator what
they need, the cause is kept where it always was, in the log and on the
application object, and the docstring now says plainly that if it is ever wanted
over HTTP it belongs behind the same role check as the upgrade endpoints.

Below that, a leftover pid file can no longer free a cluster that is alive. The
recorded start time is compared against the process actually holding the pid, so
a recycled number is recognised as a different process, and every uncertain
answer still counts as alive, since freeing a live cluster is the failure that
costs a user their data and refusing to free a dead one costs a restart.

One comment was wrong and is corrected rather than left to justify a future
decision: psutil does reach an installation, transitively, because the embedded
server package requires it outright. The guard around it stays conservative for
the reason that is actually true, which is that no requirement of ours names it,
so it lasts exactly as long as an upstream requirement we do not control.

test(desktop): the line that carries the module tree is load-bearing for imports

The module loader imports four layers of every module by name, under a
suppressed import error, so a layer that fails to resolve fails in complete
silence: no error, no log line, and a module whose event subscribers simply
never register. None of those four layers is named in the packaging spec's
hidden imports, which raised the question of whether they resolve inside the
frozen application at all.

They do, and the answer was measured against the published installer rather
than a fresh build. Ninety-eight such files exist on disk, and every one of
them reaches the bundle: seventy-one are frozen because something imports them
statically, and the remaining twenty-seven arrive only as source, inside the
module tree the spec ships as data. That route works because a frozen package
whose submodule is absent from the archive falls back to an ordinary file
finder on the extracted directory, which is precisely where that tree lands. A
minimal executable built in the same shape confirms it in both directions: with
the tree present a data-only layer imports, and with the tree removed it does
not resolve and says nothing about it.

So the entry that ships the module tree is load-bearing for imports, while its
own comment describes it as carrying translation files and validation rules.
Narrowing it to the file types it claims to carry would look like housekeeping,
would slim a bundle that ships two thousand source files beside as many frozen
modules, and would silence twenty-seven modules with every gate still green.

This adds the guard that stops that. It reads the layer names out of the loader
rather than listing them, so a layer the loader learns tomorrow widens the check
instead of falling outside it, and it asserts each file reaches the sidecar by
one of the two routes that genuinely suffice rather than insisting on the
stricter one. Narrowing the data entry in a copy of the spec fails it with the
ninety-eight names printed.

fix(validation): a project's measurement system comes from the pack that claims its country

Two mechanisms were facing each other, both switched on, neither reaching the
other. A validation rule asked the engine for the project's measurement system
and nothing in the application had ever written that key, so on every real run
it read nothing and returned nothing: registered, enabled and unreachable. On
the other side every regional pack declares the system it works in, and no
consumer read that either. The pack now answers the question the rule was
asking, and both come alive at once.

The resolution is deliberately conservative. A project's country is matched
against the packs' own country and region fields rather than a hand-written
table, so adding a pack extends the mapping without editing anything else. A
country claimed by more than one pack resolves only when those packs agree, and
a country claimed by none resolves to nothing at all rather than to a default,
because guessing imperial or metric is worse than declining to judge. Both
entry points into bill validation call the same resolver, so they cannot drift.

What proves the wiring rather than merely exercising it is the opposite case:
the same imperial bill that validates cleanly under a project in the United
States is flagged under a German one, and the finding carries the system it
expected. Presence of a pack cannot produce that difference; only its declared
value can. A project in a country no pack claims stays silent, which is the
control that asserts nothing rather than duplicating the positive case.

Turning the rule on exposed the second half. Every pack declares default units,
and six of them were not in the vocabulary the rule judges by: the United States
pack's own square and cubic feet, and all four of the Russian pack's units,
which are written in Cyrillic and are preserved verbatim by the unit normaliser
rather than folded to Latin. The rule ignores an unrecognised unit rather than
flagging it, so a position written in square metres inside an imperial bill was
invisible to the very check that exists to catch it. The vocabulary now includes
them, and the guard is written as a property rather than as six more literals:
every unit any pack declares must be recognised by the system that pack claims,
and must not be recognised by the other. A future pack is covered without
anyone remembering, and a pack that omits its measurement system fails rather
than dropping quietly out of the parametrisation.

Two documents were saying things that are not true and are corrected here. The
tax module's docstring described itself as aggregating rates from the regional
packs; it does not, it carries a hand-transcribed table and imports nothing but
decimal. It now says so, and says plainly that the two can drift apart with
nothing to catch it, because a file that names a guard which does not guard is
worse than one that admits the gap. And a test that had been red asserted a
project-level unit system field that has never existed, then validated a
hand-built payload that ignored the project, bill and position it had just
created, so even past the impossible assertion it could only ever have proved
the rule is callable. It now drives the shipped endpoint and asserts the value
the client never sent. Its docstring records that resolving from the pack is a
statement of what ships today rather than a decision against a per-project
override, and that this file is where such an override's precedence would go.

fix(boq): a second bill on a project is a question, not a coin toss

Three places decided by themselves which bill of quantities to write into.
Each read the project's bills, ordered them by creation time and took the
first, which on a project with one bill is correct and invisible, and on a
project with two is a silent choice between them. None of the three logged
the choice. Two of them had no way for a caller to say which bill was meant,
so the guess was not even a fallback, it was the whole mechanism.

What they write is not cosmetic. The quantity map creates priced positions
from model rules. The project intelligence actions write unit rates onto a
bill's positions, attribute a validation report to a bill, and derive a
schedule from one. The element matcher appends confirmed groups as positions.
On a project holding an approved estimate beside a working one, the oldest is
usually the approved one, so the guess preferred exactly the bill a user would
never have picked, and the lock that exists to prevent edits was not consulted
at all.

They are three defects rather than one repeated, and the fix says so. The
ambiguity rule is universal and now lives in one place: more than one
candidate is a refusal that names the candidates, none is a refusal that says
so, one is an answer. What counts as a candidate belongs to the caller, and
that distinction is the reason this is not a single blanket predicate.
Restricting every site to unlocked bills would have broken validation and
schedule generation on every project whose only bill is approved, which is the
normal end state of a project, so the read-only callers count every bill and
the writing ones count unlocked bills. The refusal carries the same reason
codes the change order module already returns, so a client that learned them
there reads these the same way.

Ambiguity is refused where the refusal can still reach the caller. In the
quantity map that is the run, not the per-rule step, because each rule runs in
its own savepoint under a blanket handler that would have turned the refusal
back into the silence being removed. A dry run reports the ambiguity as a flag
instead of raising, since it writes nothing and its job is to tell the user
what would happen. Each refusal was checked at the boundary rather than in the
service alone, because a detail that is stripped by a response model is a
refusal the user never sees.

A fourth guess of the same family was found next to the first and is fixed
with it: the branch that locates a target position by ordinal matched across
the whole project with no bill filter and no ordering, so with two bills it
returned an arbitrary row. It now orders deterministically and declines, with
a log line, when the two candidates come from different bills.

The tests assert both polarities at every site, and the positive side asserts
that the write actually landed, so a resolver that answered nothing at all
could not pass them. The locked case is covered in both directions, which is
where the regression this change could plausibly have introduced would show:
a project whose single bill is approved still validates and still generates a
schedule.

test: the platform smoke run stops pretending to be a test suite

A sixteen hundred line file sat in the integration test tree behind a
module-level skip. It is not a suite. Its functions are sequential steps that
take a live API client and a result collector and hand their ids to the next
step, so pytest could only ever report them as fixture errors, and for several
releases thirty-five collected errors read at a glance like thirty-five healthy
tests.

The skip was the honest part. What it hid is that nothing in the file was ever
executed by anything, so removing it costs no coverage, and that was measured
rather than assumed before the move: zero assertions on either side, the same
thirty-five functions on either side, and all but a handful of the sixteen
hundred lines byte for byte identical, the difference being line endings.

So it moves to where a script belongs and says in its own docstring what it is,
what it needs and how to run it. It wants a server already listening and the
demo account seeded, it walks the API across five languages, six regions and
three cost standards, it prints a summary, and it exits non-zero when anything
failed, which is what makes it usable as a smoke gate after a deployment. That
is a thing we did not have. A suite that cannot run is not one.

ci: a lane that puts the current code in front of a database another release built

Eighteen workflow files and not one of them had ever done that. Every lane that
touches a database creates an empty one, and an empty database is the case the
product handles best: the migration environment recognises a blank database,
short circuits to create_all and stamps the newest revision, so a run against
one executes no revision at all and proves nothing about upgrading. The only
appearance of an alembic upgrade anywhere in the workflows is inside a comment
explaining why a forked head matters, in a job that reads revision files as text
and never opens a database.

That gap has a shape, and the shape is what this lane is built around. The boot
sequence heals a schema by adding what is missing, and a column the model marks
NOT NULL with no server default is added nullable rather than refused. Nothing
raises. The column name appears, so every presence check we own reports the
upgrade complete while the constraint the model promises is simply absent. A
check that asks whether a column exists cannot see that, and until now that was
the only kind of check we had.

The database is aged by installing the previous release from the index into its
own interpreter and booting it once the way a real install of it boots, because
wheels before 15.4.0 ship no revision tree at all and there is no migration
entry point in that interpreter to call instead. Rows are seeded and they are
load bearing rather than decoration: PostgreSQL accepts a NOT NULL column with
no default on an empty table and refuses it only once rows exist, so an unseeded
database would let the exact break this lane exists to catch sail through. The
aging script also refuses to run if the package it imports resolves inside the
working tree, since a mis-wired path would build the current schema and then
every check downstream would pass against it.

The verification refuses to be vacuous before it begins. If the set of things
the current code declares and the aged database lacks is empty, the lane fails
rather than going green, because that means the pin was moved onto a release
with no schema change and the run would otherwise report success for having
tested nothing. After that it asserts the schema moved, that every column
declared NOT NULL is NOT NULL in the database, that every mapped column of every
table that was behind can actually be selected, and that the account the
previous release created can still log in and read the row it wrote. The
register is read with a token on purpose, because an anonymous call answers 401
and a 401 satisfies any assertion written as "not a server error".

What makes the lane worth its runtime is the negative run. Breaking it with a
NOT NULL column on a table that has rows turns exactly one check red. The schema
moved: fine. The health endpoint: two hundred, the heal reports no failure, the
migration head reports a match. Login: fine. The register: fine. Every signal
the product owns about its own health reports a clean upgrade on a database
where the constraint does not exist, and only the nullability comparison
disagrees.

The limits are written into the job and into the script rather than left for
someone to discover. The comparison covers presence and nullability and nothing
else, so a widened or narrowed type reads as unchanged, a rename reads as an
addition while the old column keeps the data, and a revision whose work is a
data rewrite produces no schema signal at all. Also recorded at the pin: the
head check passes today only because a pre-15.4.0 wheel records no revision, so
the stamp lands at head. Pinned at a later release the database arrives already
stamped at an older revision and that check reads false, which would be a true
statement about the product rather than a fault in the lane.

One result falls out of the passing run and is worth stating: the upgrade from
15.3.1 to today adds nullable columns only. This particular upgrade is safe, and
that is a measurement rather than an absence of one.

fix(converters): the installer stops fetching executables from wherever a branch points today

The application downloads converter executables from a repository directory and
runs them on the user's machine, and it asked for them by branch name. A branch
name is not a version, it is a pointer to whatever was pushed last, so two users
installing the same release of this product an hour apart could receive
different binaries, and nothing in the download path compares a hash or a
signature against anything. The desktop release workflow baked the same moving
reference into the installer it publishes.

Both now name one commit. The environment override survives, and a second, newer
variable is read first so a deliberate move stays possible; the older variable
still works for anyone who set it. An empty value counts as unset, because a
runner exporting an undefined variable would otherwise ask for an empty
reference and fail every listing call with a not-found.

A commit rather than a tag, and that is a measurement rather than a preference:
upstream publishes no tags and no releases at all, so a commit is the only
pinnable reference that exists there. The pinned tree was compared against the
branch tip it replaces, entry by entry, and they are the same tree, so the pin
changes what we promise without changing what anyone receives today.

The guard asserts that the two sides are equal rather than merely well formed.
Two independent shape checks would let the application and the workflow drift to
two different commits and stay green, which would put two builds of the same
native libraries on one machine, and that is a worse failure than either side
being wrong alone. It rejects the shapes that would quietly reintroduce a moving
target, a branch name among them, and it fails rather than skips when an input
is missing, since a skipped guard reads as a passing one.

What this closes is drift and substitution by force push, because a
commit-addressed path cannot be rewritten under us. What it does not close is
that nobody checks the bytes. A signature verifier for exactly this purpose
already exists in the tree, and it has no call site on the path an install
actually takes.

fix(i18n): Persian gets its letters back, and the rule that took them exists once

A cleanup rule deleted thirty five thousand two hundred and eleven characters
from the Persian locale, and they were not formatting. The zero width non
joiner is a letter level character in Persian orthography: without it the word
for backup is not spelled differently, it is spelled wrong, and so are the words
for setup, import, and the auxiliary that turns a verb into can. Bengali lost
fifty four of the joiner that renders its ra phala, and Hebrew lost twenty five
of the mark that keeps a file extension the right way round inside a right to
left sentence. The product has shipped that way since the seventeenth of August,
which includes a release.

The reason it happened is the part worth fixing. The rule lives in two places, a
continuous integration job and an npm script, and only one of them was narrowed
when this exact danger was noticed three days earlier. The other kept the old
character class, kept failing on correct Persian, and kept printing an
instruction to run a script that still deleted those characters. Someone
followed the instruction, which is what an instruction is for.

The restore is mechanical and its rule is stated so it can be checked rather
than trusted: a key is restored only where the current value equals the old
value with the zero width characters removed. Fourteen thousand seven hundred
and seventy five Persian keys, fifty two Bengali, twenty Hebrew. The key sets
are identical before and after, every line number is unchanged, and the set of
keys whose value moved is exactly the set the rule selects. Twelve Persian keys
were retranslated after the loss and no longer match their own stripped form, so
the rule leaves them alone; they are still misspelled and they need someone who
reads the language, which is a smaller and more honest remainder than a
mechanical guess would have produced.

The script that did the deleting can no longer do it. It counts those four
characters and reports them as letters and marks rather than stray formatting,
and it says in its own opening lines which language needs which one and what the
run in August cost. It still removes a stray zero width space, which was always
the real target. The file specific exception it used to carry is gone, because a
tool that cannot delete a letter does not need a list of the files where letters
live.

The rule itself now exists once, in one module, with its reasoning beside it,
and all three consumers delegate to it rather than restating it. A self check
runs on every invocation and refuses when a caller drifts, proven by making them
differ five different ways and watching it refuse each time. One of those ways
needed a different mechanism worth recording: a restatement inside Python cannot
be found by looking for escapes, because Python spells the character as a
function call with no backslash in it, and comparing values at runtime compares
a module against a second copy of itself. So that caller is checked structurally
instead, and may not assign those names at all, which forbids even a copy that
is byte for byte correct today.

A census of every locale file the damaging commit touched confirms the loss is
bounded to these three and is now entirely repaired. It also turned up something
that looks identical and is not: two other languages hold none of these
characters either, and the earlier commit that removed them from one of them was
correct. Its counts give it away, four languages that use neither joiner each
lost the same one hundred and thirty one of each alongside the same number of
genuinely stray characters, because what it removed were machine inserted
triplets appended to English strings. That was the bug it existed to fix. So
there is one data loss here, not two, and what remains in the other language is
a question for a translator rather than a repair.

fix(changeorders): an approval that cannot place its scope refuses instead of losing it

Approving a change order moves the budget and writes the approved scope into a
bill of quantities. When the project held more than one unlocked bill the
service declined to choose between them, which was right, but the approval
carried on regardless: the caller received a success, the order became approved,
the budget moved, and the scope was written into no bill at all. Nothing in the
response said so.

That is worse than the guess it replaced, and the reason is the shape of the
approval rather than the size of the mistake. Approving is idempotent by early
return, and the write has exactly one call site inside it, so once an approval
lands there is no request left that could place the scope afterwards. A user who
noticed the missing lines would have had no way to act on what they noticed.

So the refusal now happens before anything is written. It sits ahead of the
status write and ahead of the event publication, because an event is published
detached and a refusal raised after it would leave the notification sent while
the rows rolled back. The whole approval rolls back, the caller is told which
bills it could have meant, and it retries the moment it names one. The same
check guards the final step of a multi-step approval chain, before the update
that stamps it, since that path reaches the same write.

Not everything unwritten is refused, and the distinction is deliberate. A
project with no unlocked bill at all still approves: the caller has no answer to
give, and plenty of projects run change control without ever opening a bill.
What is refused is exactly the set the caller can do something about.

The preview was making the same promise. One sentence claimed a number of
positions would be created, in every case, including the two cases where nothing
would be. It now has four branches and the two that write nothing say so as a
warning rather than a promise. The screen that asks the question also gained the
control to answer it, listing unlocked bills only, since the approval refuses to
write into a locked one and offering it would be offering a refusal.

Two things found on the way in are fixed with it. The item count returned zero
on any failure, and the new check used zero to mean "no line items, nothing to
place", so an unreadable count would have skipped the question entirely and
rebuilt the exact silence being removed; it now reports that it could not tell,
and an unknown count asks anyway. The picker was gated on being an administrator
or a manager, while the chain approval endpoint has no such requirement, so an
editor named as an approver in a chain got the decision buttons, no picker, and
a refusal with nothing to answer it in.

The refusal is proven at the boundary rather than in the service alone, over
real HTTP through the assembled application: an ambiguous approval answers with
a conflict that names both candidate bills, both bills keep their position
counts, the order stays submitted, and the budget does not move. The positive
control runs on the same transport, because a server that refused everything
would otherwise pass.

fix(money): a total is written the way its own currency is written

Several tables built their own number formatter with the digit count spelled out
as a literal, so a column of money printed a fixed number of decimals whatever
currency it was in. A currency with no minor unit gained two digits it does not
have, and a summary pinned to none dropped the minor unit from a currency that
uses it. Each of these sat in a footer or a comparison row, which is where a
reader looks for the figure they are going to act on.

The repair is delegation rather than a better literal: these surfaces now ask
the shared resolver what the currency wants, and the two shapes of that question
are used deliberately rather than interchangeably. A site that prints the symbol
itself asks for a formatted amount; a site that lays out its own number and
prints the code beside it asks only for the digit count, because handing it the
symbol-printing helper would have produced the symbol and the code together.

One of them needed splitting rather than delegating. A single formatter served
four money cells and one quantity cell, so pointing it at a currency would have
changed a count of items as well. Quantities keep their own formatter and their
plain two-decimal convention, which is a convention about numbers rather than a
claim about money, and the money cells get one that reads the currency. That
currency has to arrive from the project rather than from the rows, and the
reason is in the backend: subtotals are converted into the project's base
currency before aggregation while each row keeps the currency it was priced in,
so reading the digit count off a row would ask about one currency and answer
about another.

What stops this returning is a gate that asks a property of a surface rather
than keeping a list of known offenders: does this footer build its own
formatting engine with a literal digit count. It judges helpers by their body
rather than their name, so a helper called money is caught and one that merely
forwards is spared, and passing a digit count to the shared resolver is
deliberately spared because that is a display decision somebody made and can be
reviewed. Every assertion prints the whole census by name, because a bare number
cannot be acted on.

The gate had to be shown failing twice before it could be trusted, and both
times it was passing while blind. Its reader first stopped at a function's
parameter list, so every body came back empty and nothing could be convicted at
all. Then, one defect further out, it stopped at a memo that delegated to the
real engine one hop away and cleared a formatter that had been re-pinned on
purpose to watch it fail. Both were found by breaking the tree deliberately and
watching, which is the only method that says anything about a matcher: one that
has never been shown to fail proves nothing when it passes. The file records
both, and the reader now follows a helper into the helpers it calls.

Where the matcher cannot read a footer as money, the answer is a written verdict
from a person rather than silence, and a test refuses to let a new formatting
footer arrive in that group without one. That is a human gate and it is left
labelled as one, because the group is clean today and still shaped to hide the
same defect tomorrow.

Two things are recorded and not closed. A pinned digit count inside an imported
shared helper is invisible to a per-file matcher by construction, and one table
reads back as clean for exactly that reason. And a census of the whole tree found
the shared helper the private copies appear to have been copied from, along with
every other surface of the family, sorted by hand into the amounts a reader
compares against an invoice and the headline figures where dropping the minor
unit is a legitimate choice. That list is a decision, not a defect, and it is
waiting for one.

feat(bim): the screen that asks which bill to write into can now answer

Refusing to guess between two bills of quantities left the quantity map with a
question and no way to answer it. The apply button raised the ambiguity, and the
only place a bill could have been named was a per-rule field, which would have
meant leaving the screen, editing every rule that creates positions, and coming
back. So the answer now lives on the request, where the question is asked.

The picker appears only when the project holds two or more unlocked bills, since
with one there is nothing to choose and the behaviour is unchanged, and it lists
unlocked bills only, because the apply refuses to write into a locked one and
offering it would be offering a refusal. Choosing nothing means letting the
project decide, which is exactly the old single-bill path. The chosen bill is
held in the screen's own state and is dropped if it stops belonging to the
active project, so switching projects cannot redirect a write.

Two tests cover the path the picker created rather than the path that already
worked: a dry run with a bill named reports an answer instead of a flag and
writes nothing to either bill, since resolving a target is not writing through
it, and a bill belonging to another project is refused for that reason rather
than accepted for being a valid bill somewhere.

No new translated text was needed. The two labels this control wants already
exist in all forty three locale files, which was confirmed by counting them
rather than by trusting a search that reported them missing.

fix(ci): a required lane stopped existing instead of going red

A job-level environment block named the runner context. That context is not
available where a job-level value is evaluated, because the value is resolved
before a runner is assigned, so the whole file was rejected. The consequence is
not a failing job. It is a run named after the file path, carrying no jobs at
all, with a required lane simply absent for two commits.

Absence is the dangerous half. A red lane is a thing someone looks at. A lane
that produces a run with nothing in it reads as not finished yet, and the
merge-blocking check that is supposed to speak up says nothing, because there is
nothing left to say it.

Both instruments that were supposed to cover this passed while blind, and they
passed for the same reason: neither was measuring what decides whether the file
runs. A YAML parse succeeded and reported four jobs, because the file is
perfectly good YAML. A lane-coverage test read the file as text and found the
job it was looking for, because the job is there. What is wrong is where a name
stands, not whether it parses or exists.

So the guard checks placement. For every job-level key that is evaluated before
a runner exists, it refuses any context that is not available at that moment,
and it says in the failure what the consequence is rather than only what the
rule is. It is narrow on purpose and does not pretend to validate a workflow,
because a partial validator believed to be a whole one is worse than none at
all.

It is proven against the file that caused this rather than only against an
invented one, and in both directions: the published broken version is convicted
by name, the repair is cleared, and a step that names the runner is left alone,
since a step runs on the runner and may say so. A check that forbade the context
everywhere would be enforced by deleting it.

fix(costs): building a vector index is given the time it takes, and HEAD imports itself again

Indexing a cost database is minutes of work behind a request whose client budget
was forty five seconds. The request was cancelled from the browser while the
server carried on and finished, so the screen reported a failure over an index
that had been built, and pressing the button again started the same work a
second time. Two of those calls were raw fetches with no client budget at all
and read an error field the backend does not send, so a genuine failure arrived
as an empty message.

Every call that starts or continues indexing now takes the long budget instead
of the default one, and when the client still gives up first it asks the server
what actually landed rather than guessing. A status poll that finds a finished
index reports the success, and the threshold it accepts is the same count the
page already uses to decide an index is ready, so a first committed batch cannot
read as a finished one. Four English sentences that had been written into the
toast calls became translated keys, which the locale files were already carrying.

The transport change is one optional field and one condition. A caller may ask
for its own timeout not to raise the shared toast, which matters because that
toast is throttled: suppressing it inside the window would have stamped the
throttle and silenced twelve seconds of real warnings belonging to every other
request on the screen, so the flag is read before the window rather than inside
it. No existing caller passes it, and the branch it sits in is only reached when
our own controller fired, so a response of any status never enters it.

What forced this to land as one commit is that part of it was already committed
without the rest. The bill editor was pushed importing a module that was never
added and setting a field the shared transport did not have, so a clean checkout
of the previous tip had an unresolved import. Nothing said so, because the
frontend gate builds the working tree, where the file exists. A build that is
green on a tree nobody ships is not a gate on what was pushed, and this is the
second time that particular blindness has cost us a broken tip.

feat(procurement): a purchase order line can say which bill position it buys

A purchase order was written beside the bill of quantities rather than against
it. The line carried a description typed by hand, so nothing connected what was
ordered to the position that priced it, and committed cost could not be read
back against the estimate without somebody matching text by eye.

Each line item now carries the position it belongs to, chosen from a picker
under the description rather than typed, and the field is optional because
plenty of orders buy things no position describes. The backend already accepted
and stored it, so this is the half that was missing rather than a new contract.

One defect went with it. The row key was built from the first twenty characters
of the description, so every keystroke produced a different key, the row was
remounted, and the input lost focus after each character. Anyone typing a
description longer than a word had been retyping it in fragments.

fix(variations): a linked change order opens the change order, not the register

The pill that shows a variation has been promoted into a change order carried
the id it needed to decide whether to draw itself, and then navigated to the
bare register, throwing that id away. On a project with a few hundred orders the
reader arrived at a list and had to find the one they had just clicked.

It now passes the id the way the register already reads it, which was confirmed
by reading the consumer rather than by trusting the intent: the change orders
page picks the parameter up and highlights the row. The contract pill is
deliberately left pointing at its plain register, because the contracts page
accepts no such parameter, and a test pins that difference so the two are not
quietly made uniform by someone assuming they should match.

test(teams): four stranded-team tests look at the tab their subject lives on

The teams page gained a tab bar and now opens on people. Four tests written
before that still queried the team cards directly, so they were asserting
against a tab that was not showing. They now open the teams tab first, which
restores what they were written to check rather than changing it.

test(i18n): the Uzbek script check stops convicting the English it was given

The gate refused any Cyrillic inside a translated Uzbek value, which is right in
general and wrong for one key. That key's English source lists sample
spreadsheet headers in several languages, Russian among them, as data to be
recognised rather than as prose to be translated, and the Uzbek translation
correctly keeps them verbatim.

The check now allows a Cyrillic run that also appears in the English source, and
refuses every other one. Measured over the real pair of files that is one
offender before and none after, and the single spared key is that header sample.
A self-test proves the relaxed form still catches an ordinary Uzbek word written
in Cyrillic, so the exemption is the shape of the evidence rather than a hole.

fix(money): four more surfaces ask the currency how many decimals it has

Four screens formatted money with the decimal ceiling written out as a literal
and no floor. Under a currency style the engine supplies the floor itself, so
this was invisible on a currency with two minor units and wrong on the ones
either side of it. A currency with no minor unit printed a tenth of a unit it
has no coin for, and a currency with three lost its third digit. On an older
engine, which the desktop build still reaches, a default floor of three under a
ceiling of two raises out of the render and costs the page rather than the cell.
The regional settings preview was worse than any of them: it never asked the
resolver at all, so the sample it shows to explain the setting could disagree
with every screen the setting governs.

All four now delegate to the shared formatter, which means the digit count for a
currency is decided in one place and these follow whatever is decided there. No
digit count is written down here, and every fixture uses a currency that the
standard and the locale data agree on, so none of this touches the currencies
whose decimal count is still an open question.

Two consequences worth knowing. Fixing a helper fixes every call site in its
file, which is twenty two of them across the three pages, all carrying the same
defect. And a blank currency now renders a plain grouped number instead of a
fabricated euro or dollar sign, which is what the shared formatter does and what
the surrounding code already expected.

The proof is a controlled revert rather than an assurance: the pre-fix files
were restored from the commit, the new tests were run against them and six
failed by name, and the restored files were checked byte for byte before the
suite was run again and passed. Each test mounts the real component and asserts
agreement with the shared formatter rather than a literal string, and asserts
that the old formatter and the new one disagree on the same input, so a fixture
that could not tell them apart would fail rather than pass quietly.

fix(validation): the imported rule check tests the namespace it exists to protect

An integration test asserted that imported requirement rules keep the plain
identifiers they arrive with. Rules have been namespaced to their project since
June, so the assertion had been impossible to satisfy for two months, and it had
never gone red because no lane runs the file it lives in. The one job that
touches the integration tree selects by keyword and deselects this file
entirely, while reporting success, which reads from the outside like a whole
tree passing.

The line was worse than stale. It accepted an identifier with the project prefix
stripped off, which is exactly the leak the prefix exists to prevent, while
