rejecting what the endpoint really produces. It could neither pass nor catch.

It now checks both halves through one helper, that the identifier is namespaced
and namespaced to this project, and that what remains is recognisably an
imported rule. A control drives the helper through a dropped namespace, another
project's namespace, and a correctly namespaced rule that is not an imported
one, so the checker is shown refusing each before it is trusted to accept.

The fixtures no longer point at a schema we cannot redistribute. The licence
forbids sharing a modified copy and ours was modified, so the file is gone and
the ten fixtures name the published schema by its own address instead. That
address was verified by reading the bytes it returns rather than the status line
it returns them with, since the host answers a challenge page with a success
status to anything that does not look like a browser, and all ten fixtures were
validated against the genuine schema before the hint was repointed, so this
cannot have traded a missing schema for a failing one.

fix(interface-management): the demo register always has something on the overdue tile

Every status in a seeded interface register was drawn at random, so whether the
register held anything overdue was a lottery. It lost about once in every
eighty seven projects, and when it lost, the dashboard tile that exists to show
overdue interfaces photographed as a zero and the screen looked broken to
someone seeing the product for the first time. The rate is not a guess: at the
register size the demo uses only five positions could carry an overdue row, each
lost independently with probability nine in twenty two, and the fifth power of
that is one and a fifteen hundredths of a percent, which is what twenty thousand
draws of the old seeder produced.

The first four positions are now reserved rather than drawn, and one of them is
reserved specifically for an unsettled status dated into the past, so the tile
and the status breakdown both have something behind them on every draw. The
reserved pool is filtered through the register's own predicate rather than
against a copy of the exempt list, because a paused interface handed a past date
is never counted overdue and a seeder that restated the rule would drift out of
step with it the first time the rule changed. That predicate is now named and
exported for exactly this caller, which has to choose a status before it holds a
row to ask about.

Twenty thousand draws through the fixed seeder produced no losing register at
all, and the same harness reproduced two hundred and twenty nine losses over the
same ids through the old one. Zero across a whole population is normally the
most suspicious result a census can return, so it is stated here with its
structural reason rather than as a measurement: the reserved position exists in
every register size the demo uses and always carries a status the report counts.
The property test drives four hundred draws across five ordinals and two party
pool sizes, and asserts not only that something is overdue but that the reserved
row is the one carrying it, since without that second half it would go on
passing by luck once the guarantee broke. Pointed at the old seeder it fails on
the first draw.

The lane assertion that went red over this used to say only that the tile
photographed as a zero. It now prints the status census beside the census of
rows already past their date and names which of those the register exempts,
asking the predicate rather than restating it, so the next person to see it red
is told why rather than only that.

fix(formwork): a database that predates the debrand stops carrying the names

Eight formwork catalogue rows were seeded under manufacturer product names. The
seeder stopped writing them, and a migration was written to rename the rows that
already existed, but a database brought up through the ordinary boot path never
runs that migration: the boot creates tables and stamps the current head without
executing a single revision, so an installation carrying all eight trademarked
rows reports itself as fully migrated. Nothing about that database looks unwell.

The rename now also runs from the module's own startup hook, which fires after
the tables exist, so an installation repairs itself the first time it is
started. It is one call site rather than three on purpose: the only rows this
can help are rows that predate the install, so any database built by the
initialiser is repaired by the first ordinary start.

It declines where the migration declines, using the same condition rather than a
new one: a tenant that already holds a row under the replacement name keeps both
and nothing is renamed. There is one divergence in the other direction, and it
is written down in the code rather than left to be discovered, because it is
narrower than the migration rather than wider: where one tenant holds two rows
under the same old name, the loop renames the first and the second then reads as
a clash, while the migration's single statement renames both. That half is read
off the SQL and has not been run, and the comment says so.

Proven on a real cluster in both directions. The eight rows were planted as the
old seeder wrote them, the ordinary boot sequence was run, and all eight were
still there with the version table reporting head. After the repair the query
returns nothing and all eight replacements are present. A table seeded from
today's defaults is snapshotted whole before and after and compared row by row,
so an untouched database is shown untouched rather than merely shown not to
raise. Running it twice changes nothing.

Two teeth checks, because a test that has never failed says nothing when it
passes. Removing the commit leaves all eight names in the database and the test
goes red, which matters because most of the suite runs inside a savepoint that
is rolled back and would have passed whether or not a commit ever landed.
Removing the call from the startup hook fails a test that never names the repair
function, so the wiring is what is being checked rather than the code behind it.

The eight old names live in one file in shipped code, with the reason they are
there written above them, since the next brand sweep will ask.

fix(documents): a failed write inside an upload stops taking the upload with it

Three writes on the upload path had no savepoint around them: the registration
of a file into its version chain, the pair that adds a new version and retires
the previous one, and the fan-out to whatever else had subscribed to the upload.
A failed flush in any of them poisons the session, so the upload did not fail
where it went wrong. It carried on and died at its own commit, reporting a
transaction problem rather than the thing that actually happened, which is the
least useful moment and the least useful wording available.

Each of the three is now wrapped, so a failure is contained where it occurs and
the surrounding work either continues or reports what failed. The version pair
is one savepoint on purpose rather than two, and that is a change to what the
database holds rather than only to what is reported: previously a retirement
that failed left the new row written with the old row still marked current, so
the chain had two current versions and no error anywhere. Now both roll back
together.

The tests are shown failing against the previous code rather than merely passing
against the new. Four of nine fail there, each with a session already poisoned by
an earlier statement, which is the shape the fix is for.

One thing worth stating because the wrapper is inside a handler that only logs:
the savepoint resolves on whatever session object it is handed, so a caller
passing something that does not implement one would lose the write silently
rather than loudly. Every caller was checked and none does. The suite for the
whole radius of those helpers was run, forty six tests, and the single failure in
it fails identically against the previous code and is about something else.

test(bim-hub): the drawing upload proves the savepoint it depends on is there

The router already contained the savepoint and the narrow exception around the
cross-link write. Nothing checked that it stayed, and this write is the one that
connects an uploaded drawing to the record it belongs to, so losing it means an
upload that succeeds and a link that quietly does not exist.

The tests reach the real router and fail if the savepoint is removed. That the
injection actually arrives is proved by two of them rather than assumed: one
asserts the failure is logged and one asserts a wrongly typed failure still
raises, so the savepoint test cannot be passing because nothing reached it.

fix(property-dev): completing a handover stops returning a server error to everybody

Completing a plot handover failed with an internal error for every caller. The
service updated the handover and then read a field off it, but the update expires
the row it has just written, so the read went back to the database to refresh a
value it no longer held, from a place where a synchronous query cannot run. The
plot never moved to handed over and the buyer never advanced, so the last step of
a sale did not complete and nothing downstream of it could start.

Every field is now read before the row that holds it is written, on both the
handover and the buyer.

A test that covered this was skipped, and the reason attached to the skip blamed
the test transport and the shape of the subscriber graph. That was wrong. It was
production code failing, and the skip had been hiding a live server error rather
than a test infrastructure problem. It is unskipped because it passes, which was
established by running it, not by deciding the reason no longer applied.

fix(desktop): a database that will not start says what to do about it

When the embedded database library cannot be imported at all, the log said so
and nothing else. On a frozen desktop build that is the one case where the
person reading has no way to act on it, because the import failing there means
the bundle is missing a piece rather than that something is misconfigured, and
the two need different responses.

The message now carries the repair, and only on a build where that repair is the
right one. Everything else is unchanged: the whole edit lives inside the handler
for that import failing, so on any installation where the import succeeds, which
is every healthy start and every upgrade, none of it runs, and the function
still reports failure the same way.

The care here is about what the handler is allowed to touch. A lazy import
inside an error handler that itself raises would turn a reported failure into an
unhandled one, in exactly the damaged case the branch exists for. The module it
reaches for imports only the standard library, has no path back to this one,
starts nothing at import time, and is already loaded by the time this can run,
because the entry point imports it eagerly, which also means the packager
includes it.

docs(boq): the comments name the setting that actually exists

The converter reference was renamed from a branch to a reference some time ago
and the code was updated everywhere it runs. The comments in one file were not,
so anyone reading them was told to set an environment variable that has no
effect. Every changed line here is a comment and nothing executable moved.

test(desktop): the wheel comparison records an omission instead of failing at it

A test asserting that the desktop bundle ships everything the wheel force
includes has been failing, because the wheel includes the migration tool and its
configuration and the bundle does not. Failing was the honest first answer, but
it is not a useful standing state: a permanently red test is read as noise and
then ignored, which costs the coverage of everything else it checks.

The omission is now recorded as deliberate with the reason attached, so the file
says why rather than only that. It comes with a second test that expires the
exemption: if the wheel ever stops force including those files, the record of
the omission becomes wrong and goes red, so the exemption cannot outlive the
condition that justified it.

test(changeorders): the stub session answers the query the service now makes

Two of the change order tests fail because the service learned to look for every
open bill on a project and the stub session in the test was never taught to
answer that shape of query. The stub returns the same object either way, so the
test failed on a missing attribute rather than on anything about change orders.

test(tendering): the addendum and levelling tests stop claiming the feature is absent

The whole file was skipped with a note saying the feature does not exist yet. It
does. Addenda can be created, published and acknowledged, and the levelling
matrix is built and returned, all of it shipped and reachable. The skip had
outlived its reason by long enough that the file was no coverage at all while
looking like it was.

The tests are rewritten against the signatures that actually ship and they pass.

fix(contracts): one commercial change stops being added to the contract twice

A variation promoted into a change order creates a mirrored order in the change
register, and two independent subscribers add money to the contract total. Each
deduplicates against its own record of what it has already posted, and neither
knows the other exists, so where both can see the same contract the same change
is counted twice. Measured on a contract of a hundred thousand carrying one
change of twenty five thousand, the total came to a hundred and fifty thousand
instead of a hundred and twenty five.

The plain promotion is safe, and that is worth stating because it narrows the
exposure rather than widening it: the mirror is created without a contract link,
so the change order subscriber returns before it opens a session and the money
moves exactly once. What opens the hole is one ordinary edit. The mirror arrives
in the register as a draft asking to be filled in, and saying that it amends the
contract its own variation order already names is the natural thing to do. That
edit merges rather than replaces, so the variation link survives and the contract
link is added, and now both subscribers are pointed at the same contract.

The refusal is keyed on the mirror relationship rather than on the contract,
which matters because keying on the contract would decline legitimate second
postings. The change order already carries the variation order it mirrors, so
approval now puts that on the event, and the contract subscriber declines when
that variation order has already been counted. The decline is recorded under its
own name rather than dropped, and deliberately not added to the list of posted
change orders, because the dashboard counts that list and a skipped posting there
would raise the count with no money behind it.

The negative controls are the point here, since a guard that declines everything
would pass the positive one. A change order raised directly against the same
contract with no variation link still posts and the total genuinely moves, and a
mirror whose variation order names no contract still posts, because there the
mirror is the only route the money has.

One case is left open and it is left open on purpose. Approving the linked mirror
before the variation order completes posts twice again, because this guard keys
on money already applied and at that moment none has been. Closing it needs one
side to suppress on the prediction that the other will post later, and when that
prediction is wrong the money never lands and nothing retries. A contract quietly
too low is a worse failure than one visibly too high, so which record is
authoritative for a mirrored pair is a decision rather than a patch.

fix(catalog): the formatter and the type that declares it agree again

The price formatter here learned to take a currency, its call sites were updated
to pass one, and the type declaring it as a property of the panel that receives
it was left describing the old one argument shape. That combination compiles at
the point of handing the function over, because a function taking an optional
second argument satisfies a type that promises only the first, and fails at the
three places inside the panel that pass a currency. So the frontend did not
build, and had not since the change landed.

The reason nobody saw it is worth writing down rather than only fixing. A
signature and the type that declares it are one edit, not two, and the tooling
that would have said so is a production build, which was not run between that
commit and this one. Every check that did run passed, because none of them
compiles the tree. This is the second broken tip in a week from the same shape,
the first being an import of a file that was never added, and both were invisible
for the same reason.

fix(supplier-catalogs): the commodity codes mean what their names say

Forty two of the sixty two rows in the shipped classification seed carried a
code that means something other than what the row describes. The defect is in
the number rather than the text: in most of them the name and the description
agree with each other and disagree with the code, which is the signature of
someone writing a sensible taxonomy from knowledge of the trade and attaching
plausible numbers to it. Four of the codes are not positions in the standard at
all. They continue a real run past the point where it stops, which is what
happens when a number is produced by incrementing digits rather than looked up.

Twenty seven codes and eighteen names are corrected to the published values, and
the level and parent columns follow, since both are arithmetic on the digits
rather than opinions about them. The file ships in the wheel, so this has been on
disk at every installation, although nothing transmits it: there is no exporter,
no screen, and the table fills only on an explicit request.

Two corrections are deliberately not applied. Each of them wants a code that
another row is currently sitting on, and both of those rows are ones with no
correct code anywhere in the standard, so they are decisions rather than repairs.
That collision is not bad luck. The author inserted a discipline the standard has
no class for, everything after it slid by one seat, and undoing the slide
telescopes back onto the inserted slot. The consequence of applying them anyway
would have been silent, because the loader upserts per row and the later line
simply wins, so one of the two rows would have vanished with nothing raised, and
which one depends on the order they happen to appear in.

Three claims in the model documentation were false and all three are corrected
rather than the one that was reported. The field said to reference this table
holds free text and is checked against nothing, the foreign key it names does not
exist anywhere in the codebase, and the analytics it claims to feed do not exist
either. An example naming a code for a particular cement named a code for
something else entirely.

The gate is a property of the file rather than a list of the rows that were
wrong: a declared level has to agree with the shape of its own code, and a
declared parent has to be the nearest ancestor the file actually contains. Run
against the file before the repair it fails on thirty five rows and four parents,
which is what makes it worth having; run after, it is clean. Both counts were
measured a second time with a differently written rule, because a matcher that
agrees with the thing that produced it is not a second opinion.

The check digit the other scheme drops is deliberately still dropped. Adding it
would be a silent break in customer data rather than in ours, since the field on
a catalogue item is free text with no key behind it, so every value already
written through the interface would stop resolving the moment the lookup changed
shape.

fix(file-trash): restoring from the recycle bin stops failing on six kinds out of eight

Pressing Restore returned a server error for photos, sheets, models, takeoffs,
reports and markups. The item stayed in the bin, the row never came back, and
what the user saw was an internal error with nothing to act on. Documents and
drawings worked, which is why this survived: the two kinds most people try first
are the two that were fine.

The restore decided which stored values to convert back out of storage by the
name of the field rather than by the type of the column it was going into.
Anything whose name ended in a way that looks like an identifier became one, and
anything that looks like a timestamp became a date. A name is not a type. Ten
columns across six kinds are ordinary text columns that happen to carry such a
name, one of them holding a timestamp the reporting service writes as text on
purpose, so the restore handed a text column an object it cannot store and the
database refused the insert.

The conversion now asks the column what it is. Every column on all eight kinds
was classified rather than the two that happened to fail: nineteen genuinely need
the date conversion, twenty three are identifier columns where it makes no
difference because the layer beneath already accepts text, and ten were being
converted wrongly. The identifier branch is kept even though it changes nothing,
because it states what the code means to do.

What was missing was an instrument. Everything that existed drove the delete and
the restore separately from values written by hand, so nothing ever went round
the loop, and a hand-written value is by definition one that fits. There is now a
test that deletes and restores a real row of every kind through the endpoint, in
the shape the screen actually sends, and asserts the values come back unchanged
rather than that a row reappeared. It carries its own guard: if a new text column
arrives with a name the old rule would have converted and nothing fills it in the
test, the test fails, because a round trip that leaves those columns empty passes
straight over the defect. The first draft of the test did exactly that and caught
two kinds instead of six.

Two things checked and deliberately left alone. Deleting a report was never broken
for a user: the screen sends no snapshot and the service then reads the row
itself, so the missing fields the failing test complained about could only ever
be missing in a hand-written payload, and that test's payload was simply stale.
And the required-field check is stricter than the database it is protecting, since
it runs again on the way back in against data the database has already accepted.
Every text column it could refuse was traced to its writer and none of them can
produce an empty value, so that one is latent rather than live and loosening it on
speculation would be trading a real check for an imagined case.

fix(validation): every surface asks the same question about a project, and an empty bill stops passing

Seven places built the payload the validation engine reads, and each assembled
it by hand. Six of them left out the project's measurement system, so the same
bill validated from two different screens could reach two different verdicts,
and nothing anywhere reported the disagreement. The rule that reads that value
does not fail when its input is missing, it returns nothing at all, which is
why this was invisible: a surface that never supplied the value looked exactly
like a project no regional pack claims.

There is now one function that builds that half of the payload, and it always
writes the key, nulls included. That is the change that makes the rest
checkable. Absent now means nobody built the payload; null means the question
was asked and no pack answered. Before, the two were the same thing.

It takes the caller's session rather than opening its own, because validation
frequently runs inside a transaction that has not been committed, and a second
session would see nothing and report that as no pack answering.

Four of the seven were known. Three were not, and one of those was found by the
gate on its first run rather than by anyone reading, which is the argument for
the gate in a sentence. The gate asserts a property rather than keeping a list:
anywhere a payload carrying bill positions reaches the engine, it came through
the builder. A second check asserts the builder is the only thing that writes
those keys, so calling it and then overwriting what it returned does not count.
Three offending shapes are convicted by name and four legitimate ones are
spared, including one a naive check would have wrongly caught. Both directions
run in the lane that blocks a merge.

Two limits are written into the gate rather than left to be discovered. It reads
source, so a payload assembled inside a helper the call site merely invokes is
invisible to it, and that blind spot was audited rather than declared: seven
payloads are built inside helpers today and none of them is a bill. And it knows
the builder by name.

The rule now says when its input is missing instead of going quiet. It reports
that as an engine problem naming the key and the function to use, kept separate
from the findings so an otherwise clean bill still reads clean while the gap has
a name.

Writing that complaint exposed a second defect that nobody was looking for. The
same rule returned a passing result for a bill with no lines at all, which gives
an empty bill a compliance signal and makes it read as fully passed at a perfect
score. That contradicts a documented platform rule that an empty bill is skipped
rather than passed, and that rule has its own test which has been passing for a
different reason. This was live, and it was measured rather than argued: the
previous version of the rule was loaded from the commit and run against an empty
bill with the measurement system present, and it returned a passing result and a
report scoring one. It survived because almost nothing populated the key, and
unifying the seven surfaces would have widened it to all of them.

Two expectations asserting that passing result are replaced. They are not
expectations bent to fit new code: they contradicted a written contract that has
its own test, and the measurement above is about the released version rather
than about this change.

What this could disturb elsewhere was measured rather than estimated. Two test
files hand the engine a payload for this rule set. One is the empty bill case
above. The other asserts there are no engine problems, and rather than weakening
that assertion its payload now goes through the builder, which is what the
product does, so it goes back to measuring the thing it was written for.

fix(reference-data): the Romanian rate is current, and the sample files stop teaching the wrong codes

Romania raised its standard rate of value added tax over a year ago and our
table still carried the old one with no end date, so anyone in that jurisdiction
who let the product supply the default was quoting and invoicing a percentage
point too low. The row is split rather than overwritten, so the old rate keeps
the period it was correct for: a document re-rendered against a table that had
forgotten the previous rate would silently change what it said about the past.

The two periods meet exactly and neither overlaps, which is checked on the two
boundary dates rather than on today, since a test that only asks about today
passes against a table with no history at all. Six dates spanning nine years each
resolve to exactly one row, and before the split all six resolved to the old one.

Whether this could even be seeded had to be established before it could be
trusted, because both rows share their country and their code, and a uniqueness
constraint would have made a fresh install raise on the only path this reaches.
There is none. The obvious cheap precedent proved nothing, since no other country
ships two rows under one code, so the model and its migration are what settle it.

This corrects what a new installation is given. An existing database keeps what
it has, because the seeder does nothing once the table has rows. Healing those is
a data migration and writing into customer tables on upgrade is a decision rather
than a fix.

The sample import files carried seven rows whose code means something other than
what the row describes: brickwork filed under stairs and ramps, a vinyl floor
under wall finishes, soil and waste under water installations, a boiler under
sanitary fittings, reinforcement under cast concrete, concrete blocks under clay
brick, and a rooftop unit under self-contained units. These are the files a
person downloads to learn our import format before building their own, so a
wrong code here is not a wrong row, it is a wrong code copied into somebody's
catalogue. Two of the corrections swap position, because the file is strictly
ascending everywhere else and fixing the numbers without reordering would have
broken an invariant it was holding.

There were two tracked copies of every sample and the first sweep found one of
them. The second copy was missed because the search was looking for build output
and this one is a source, which is the same mistake as fixing a symptom in the
place it was noticed. Both are corrected by the same anchored edits rather than
by copying one over the other, since they differ in ways that predate this.

Two things are recorded rather than acted on. The check we already ship for these
codes would not have caught a single one of the seven, in either of the two ways
it could be read: every wrong code is well formed, at the right depth, and inside
the right division. A check that the code agrees with the description would need
the standard's own tables, which we are not licensed to bundle, so this class is
caught by a person who knows the standard or by a customer's own licensed tables,
and saying so is better than shipping something that makes it look covered. And
the drift that let the rate go stale is now visible in the data: not one row in
the whole table had ever closed a period, so every past rate change was an
overwrite and the table had no way to record that anything had changed. That
census cannot be run twice, and a standing check for it would have to know a rate
changed, which is the thing the table cannot tell you.

fix(dashboard): the value tile stops inventing a tenth of a yen

The per-currency chips on the Total Value tile pinned a ceiling of two decimal
places with no floor under it. That reads like "two decimals" and is not: with
no minimum stated the engine takes the floor from the currency itself, so the
ceiling only ever bit the currencies whose own count is not two. A yen amount
below the compact threshold printed a tenth of a yen, a unit the yen does not
have, and a dinar lost its third digit, a unit the dinar does. Euro and dollar
render identically either way, which is why it read as correct for as long as
it did.

The ceiling now belongs to the compact branch, where one decimal is the whole
point of compacting, and the full-length figure says nothing and leaves the
count to the currency. Nothing changes for any two decimal currency and the
compact tiles are untouched.

The guard that comes with it is a property rather than a file list: a currency
styled formatter, a currency arriving as a variable, a maximum naming two or
more, and no minimum at any value. A ternary names two numbers and the largest
wins, which is what catches this spelling. Every file starts at a ceiling of
zero, so a legitimate whole unit tile needs no permission from the gate, and
the five deliberate sites are outside the rule by what they say rather than by
where they live. The census prints in every run, passing or failing, including
the count of ceilings the rule cannot read, which is asserted at zero rather
than merely reported.

fix(demo): the waste report always has waste to report

The site inventory demo booked each material's waste on a coin toss, so on the
smallest register a project could come up with no waste movement at all and the
waste report, whose entire purpose is to state a waste ratio, stated zero. It
happened on about one project in two hundred and thirty, measured at 88 of
20000 draws against an analytic 0.3737 percent, with the whole distribution
matching term by term rather than only the tail. Nothing would have caught it,
because a demo that is right ninety nine times out of a hundred passes every
test that runs once.

The first metered material that consumed anything now books its waste whatever
the draw says, and every material after it is drawn exactly as before. The draw
is still made for the reserved material so the generator advances identically
and nothing downstream of it moves.

The wider sweep behind this is worth recording, because the answer to it is a
structural reason rather than a count. Only thirteen seeders draw from a
generator seeded by the project id, which is what makes a fresh lottery on
every install rather than the same demo every time; the rest seed a constant
and are out of the class entirely. Of those thirteen, most already derive their
register size and their reserved content from the project's ordinal, which is
the idea this fix applies. That is why one instance was left rather than many.

Three registers that were already built correctly gained the check that was
missing, which is the one on the precondition rather than on the outcome: that
the reserved position is inside the shortest register the seeder can produce,
and that the value sitting there is one the report will count. The strongest of
them closes the last real draw in the temporary works path, where which item
lands on a position is drawn and the resolved status may rewrite a planned one
to suit the item, so the test walks the whole catalogue and asserts that no
item can rewrite either reserved status. Without it the guarantee would have
been a lottery over which item was drawn onto the reserved position, which is
the same defect one level down.

The negative control does not wait for a rare draw in either direction. Both
seeders run with the draw turned off, the saved pre-fix copy and the fixed one,
and the pre-fix seeder books nothing on every ordinal while the fixed one books
exactly one, on the first metered material, every time. The plan test is
controlled by mutating the real constants: eight mutations, eight convictions,
and every assertion clear again once they are undone.

Two deterministic absences found on the way are recorded here rather than
fixed, because nothing displays either today. A construction control outcome
sits at an index two of the four register sizes can never reach, and the value
module gates every credited row on a set filtered at import, so a rename there
would silently empty it for every project at once.

feat(costs): the install sentence tells the reader which case it is in

The embedder status endpoint returned English prose telling the reader how to
install the optional semantic extra, and that prose was the one untranslated
thing on an otherwise fully translated panel. It could not be otherwise: prose
cannot be translated by the client, and recovering the case by parsing the
sentence would break the first time anybody reworded it.

So the payload now names the case alongside the sentence, either a pip install
with a command to run or a frozen bundle that ships a fixed set of packages and
has no pip to add to them. Those are the two branches the endpoint was already
choosing between, so this states a decision it was already making rather than
introducing one.

The three fields come off a single call, which is what makes the combination
that would render an empty copy box impossible: a code saying pip cannot arrive
beside an empty command, because one branch decides all three. The obvious
later edit is to compute the code from the desktop mode setting or from an
environment variable instead, and either would answer a different question than
the command answers, so the agreement is pinned by a test rather than left to a
comment.

The prose keeps being sent. It is what a frontend older than this change reads,
and it is the fallback rung for a newer one on any code it does not recognise,
so the field cannot become optional now that the code exists. The code is an
open set for the same reason, and the test says out loud that adding a value to
it without a translation behind it downgrades every language back to English,
which is the exact thing this was added to remove.

The last test is the control the other three need. Each of them holds inside a
single install, so all three would still pass if the branch stopped branching
and returned one constant answer, which is precisely what a broken frozen check
would produce. Two answers that come back equal are the finding rather than a
coincidence, so the difference between the two installs is asserted. Both
polarities are driven by setting the interpreter flag the real check reads
rather than by replacing that check, since a test that stubs the branch it is
checking proves only that the stub works.

fix(i18n-foundation): Canada gets its provinces and Nova Scotia gets its cut

The shipped tax table carried three Canadian rows where the country has ten
live rates, and one of the three was the same defect the Romanian entry had:
Nova Scotia at fifteen percent with no end date, wrong since April 2025. That
row is now split, fifteen up to the thirty first of March 2025 and fourteen
from the first of April, so a document dated before the cut still prices at the
rate that applied to it.

Seven provinces were simply absent. New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador
and Prince Edward Island run the harmonised tax; Quebec, British Columbia,
Saskatchewan and Manitoba run their own alongside the federal one. The table
was already keyed on the tax code rather than one row per country, since two
harmonised provinces were sitting in it that way, so this follows the
convention the file already had rather than inventing a second one.

The tax type is used to say something rather than to decorate. Quebec is
recorded as a value added tax because it is one, with input credits, while
British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are retail sales taxes with no
credit at all. That is the difference between an invoice in one province and an
invoice in another, and it now lives in the data instead of in somebody's head.
One consequence to know about: a filter on value added taxes now returns a sub
national row beside the country level ones, which nothing reads today.

China was checked and deliberately left alone. Thirteen percent standard and
nine for construction, both correct and unchanged since April 2019. The value
added tax law that took effect this year re-based the statute without moving
any rate, so adding a row for it would have recorded a change that did not
happen.

Two things this does not do, said here rather than left to be found. The
Canadian history is closed where a defect was found and not swept: several
provinces and the federal rate itself had earlier rates that are still absent.
And a row says what it charges without saying how it combines, which matters
more than any number in it: the harmonised provinces replace the federal rate
while the others stack on top of it, and nothing in the row distinguishes those
two. Adding the rates without that field makes the gap reachable rather than
creating it, and it is the next thing to settle.

Existing installations keep the old rows either way. The seeder skips the table
entirely once it holds anything, so this reaches new installations only.

fix(tests): the decimals census refuses to read half a match

The reader behind the minor-units census took the capture group off a matched
pattern without checking it was there. Under this tree's strict index checking
that is a type error, so it was also the thing keeping the build red, but the
type error is the smaller half of it.

The larger half is what the code would have done had it compiled. A pattern
that matches while its group comes back empty is not a formatter without a
ceiling, and reading it as one files the call under "leaves the count to the
currency", which empties the convicted list, which leaves a gate that is green
and blind. That is the exact failure this file exists to catch in other
people's code, so it does not get a pass in the file's own reader: it throws,
and it names the site it was reading when it broke, which is why the two
readers now take the label the census loop already knows.

The same habit had a second instance and it was in the self-test, where a
subscript on a list that came back empty and an optional chain on a reading
that came back null both compile and both turn a reader that has stopped
reading into an assertion that still passes. The fixture helper now proves the
fixture holds exactly one call and that the reader agreed to read it, throwing
with the fixture text on either miss. After both, the only non-null assertion
left in the file is inside a comment quoting the shape being warned about.

The two-direction proof was re-run on the edited reader rather than inherited
from before it. One run breaks a file the rule had spared and adds a
whole-unit formatter to a file that had none, and the census shows the first
leaving the spared list for the convicted one while the second joins the
spared list and the total seen rises, so both sites were read rather than one
being skipped. Both files were restored and the restore verified by checksum
rather than by intent.

fix(contracts): a promoted variation is counted once whichever half is approved first

Two independent paths add money to a contract total, one following the
variation and one following the change order it was promoted into, and the
release before this one taught them to recognise each other. It only worked in
one direction. The check asked whether the money had already been added, so
approving the mirrored order before the variation completed found nothing on
the contract and posted, and the variation then posted the same amount again. A
contract of a hundred thousand carrying one change of twenty five thousand read
a hundred and fifty thousand.

A key on whether money has arrived is order dependent by construction, so it is
replaced rather than repaired. Both halves now compute the same string naming
the commercial change itself, and a contract records which sources it has
already posted for. That is the shape the cost spine and the purchase order
markers on the same field already use, and it does not depend on who goes
first. Either ordering now lands the amount once and records which half was
skipped.

Recording is not paying, and the fix nearly lost that distinction. A variation
raised in a currency the contract does not use is appended to the contract's
list of variations before the currency check refuses it, so that list says the
variation was seen, not that it was paid. Deriving the posted sources from it
would have let a foreign currency variation block the one half still able to
post, and the money would have arrived by neither route. Anything sitting in
the currency mismatch record is subtracted, and a test raises the variation in
one currency, corrects the mirror to another, and asserts the amount lands
exactly once.

fix(docs): the formwork design document stops naming the products it compares against

The module design document listed eight suppliers by name in its opening
section, named products in its category tables, put product names in the
wireframe cells and built the whole of its differentiation section around named
vendor tooling. The brand gate convicted ten tokens in it. Ten was the
misleading number: the two most common names in the document are not on the
denylist at all, so a repair scoped to what the gate could see would have left
the document full of brands with the gate green over all of it, which is the
same instrument shaped failure that let eight formwork rows survive the first

So the closure was cleared rather than the convictions, and the gate was used
as a floor rather than as the specification. The check is a word boundary sweep
over twenty eight tokens, and because a zero over a whole population is the
result least worth trusting, the same sweep was run against a file known to
contain those names and found them.

Nothing was sanded flat to achieve it. The differentiation section was
rewritten by category of tool rather than deleted, since none of its claims
were ever about the names, and it now says something stronger than it did: a
contractor renting from any of the large suppliers can run this on top of the
rental contracts they already have. The wireframes are character exact, because
each replacement was fitted to the fixed width column it sits in.

One entry in the documentation site's regional pack table named a national
standards body rather than a competitor, in a column that also carries FIDIC
and JCT, which are standards and stay. It is removed rather than renamed
because there is no pack behind that row, so an allowlist entry would have read

Brazil's reference and covers the rest under local norms, which is what the
India and Middle East rows already do.

against each other rather than assumed to differ. One pins the entries nothing
else was watching, since a token that has a replacement is already held by the
pairing check, and one floors the total. Removing a pinned entry while adding a
decoy leaves the size unchanged and only the first guard fires; truncating the
list while sparing every pinned entry only trips the second.

feat(i18n-foundation): a tax rate records how it combines with the one above it

The table carried rates and left it to the reader to work out how two rates in
one country relate. In Canada that is not a detail. A harmonised provincial
rate replaces the federal one, so Ontario is thirteen and not five plus
thirteen, while a separate provincial rate adds to it, so British Columbia is
five plus seven. Both kinds sat in the table looking alike, carrying the same
type, distinguishable only by a naming convention nothing enforced.

That left three readings available and no way to choose between them from the
data. Adding every active row gives a hundred and seven percent, which is
absurd enough to be caught. The dangerous one is the obvious implementation,
federal plus my province, because it is right in British Columbia and wrong in
Ontario, so whichever province you happened to test in decided whether you
believed it.

The field is four values rather than a flag, because a flag can only answer a
question with two answers and this one has more: the federal rate itself, a
rate that replaces it, a rate that stacks on it, and a rate in a country with
no federal layer at all. It is a real column and not a key in the existing
metadata blob, since a blob cannot carry "present on every row" as a property
anything can enforce, and being silently omissible is the defect rather than
an inconvenience.

All seventy nine shipped rows carry an explicit value: sixty six national, two
federal, six replacing and five stacking. The United States turned out to be
the third structural case and was not expected. It carries a row stating that
the federal sales tax is zero, which is exactly the layer a state rate adds
to, so California falls out of the same arithmetic as British Columbia rather
than out of a rule of its own. Brazil and India are recorded as national and
flagged, because their sub-national structure exists in the world and not in
this table, and encoding a structure we do not carry would be worse than
naming the gap.

The tests compute the combined rate for eleven jurisdictions from the shipped
data alone, and the function they call branches on this field and on nothing
else. It does not know that a harmonised rate is harmonised. Two controls run
in opposite directions: marking Ontario as stacking produces exactly eighteen,
asserted as that number rather than as merely different, and removing the
federal row leaves Ontario at thirteen while taking British Columbia to seven.

The migration adds the column nullable, backfills it, and only then makes it
NOT NULL. The one step form is what has silently landed as nullable here
before, and every health signal called that a clean upgrade. It was proved on
a database aged to the previous revision and upgraded, rather than on a blank
one, because a blank database here never walks the chain at all.

One case is deliberately left open and is worth knowing about. The column and
the create schema both default to national, so a provincial row created
through the interface without the field inherits it, and a harmonised rate
recorded as country-wide drops out of the arithmetic and computes as the
federal rate alone. That is a quieter wrong answer than the eighteen. The
default stays, because a single tier country genuinely is national and making
the field required would break every existing caller of an endpoint that has
never carried it. What is closed is the path where it would become permanent:
the shipped file cannot hold a Canadian or American row that names a
subdivision while claiming to be country-wide, and the seeder reads the field
without a fallback, so a row missing it fails loudly rather than defaulting.

Alongside it, a gate over the three hand-maintained rate tables that had no
way to disagree out loud. They do not disagree today, on any of the forty five
comparable pairs, and nothing would have said so when they started. Absence
never convicts, only keys carried by two or more tables are compared, the
compared population is printed rather than counted, and every tax code must be
either classified or excluded with a stated reason so a new code cannot
silently shrink what is checked.

test(ci): the tenant isolation lane selects a property instead of a spelling

The lane that gates cross tenant and IDOR tests chose them with a twenty six
word keyword chain. Because that kind of selector matches the whole node
identifier, the module filename included, a hundred and fifty of the six
hundred and seventy eight tests it selected were pulled in by the name of the
file they sit in rather than by anything they assert, and several of its words
were quietly collecting their homonyms. One took foreign currency and foreign
keys, one took a provider secret never shown to its own owner, one took indexed
columns and reporting periods, one took a soft deleted row, and one took a
lease agreement written for a renter.

It missed more than it over took. Ten files were invisible to it in full,
fifty eight tests, among them the dedicated security suites for reports,
permissions registration and daily diary. Worse, it opened other files and took
a fraction of them: one of seventeen from the finance security suite, two of
fifteen from procurement, one of seven from payroll. Which tests survived was
decided by whether an author happened to write foreign rather than other.

Every test now carries a marker, and the marker is registered together with the
definition it is applied by, in a comment block above it, so the rule is
readable at the place it is enforced. A test earns it when identity is the
variable under test: the test establishes who is asking and asserts what that
identity may or may not reach. Both polarities belong, because a lane holding
only denials is satisfied by a gate that denies everyone, exactly as a lane
holding only grants is satisfied by a gate that grants everyone.

The swap is not a widening. It selects seven hundred and seventy four, adds a
hundred and fifty two and drops fifty six, and only the two sets show that. The
net of plus ninety six reads as pure gain and is not.

The dropped fifty six matter more than the arithmetic suggests, because the
sharded backend job runs the unit tree alone. These two trees are gated on push
and pull request by this one lane and by nothing else, so a test this lane
stops selecting stops gating a merge entirely. They are none of them tenant
isolation tests and they were gated by accident, and gated by accident is still
gated. A second run in the same step takes exactly the set the chain used to
select and the marker does not, proved to be a strict superset of the fifty six
by node identifier, and it passes. It is a ratchet to be drained rather than a
lane to be maintained: each member should eventually earn a marker of its own
or move into the unit shards, and the chain frozen beside it is a record of
what used to be gated rather than a rule anyone should extend.

Two things the guard on this workflow caught before it went green, both worth
knowing because both produced a confident wrong answer. Splitting a command
across continuation lines left a line based reader seeing both trees and no
selector, so the lane recorded as running everything. And a comment sentence
containing the words of a bare invocation was read as one, which recorded full
coverage for every tree in the repository. A comment could fabricate coverage,
which is precisely the false green that guard exists to prevent, so it now
skips comment lines.

test(money): a decimal ceiling is a claim about a currency, and it is checked

The seventeen file sweep that stopped screens overruling the currency they
print left nothing to stop the next one. This adds the check, and one of the
sites it would have convicted is deleted rather than repaired: a preferences
store carried its own currency formatter with two decimals written into it,
duplicating the shared resolver, and nothing in the tree called it.

The rule ignores the floor and only reads the ceiling, which took three
attempts to get right. A ceiling of two or more is a statement about how many
minor digits a currency has, and only the currency knows that, so writing one
next to a currency the code does not name is asserting a fact about an unknown.
A ceiling of zero or one is a statement about the tile rather than about the
currency and is true of all of them, which is why two is the boundary. An
earlier wording said the floor and the ceiling must not straddle the currency's
own count; it was measured against the tree before being written and would have
convicted five correct whole-unit summaries, because a written ceiling of zero
makes the engine default the floor to two and then clamp it down.

The second rule is about the shape that hides the first. A one sided override
is not wrong in itself, but the ones here exist because the surrounding call
can fail, so each must sit where a failure reaches a fallback. Writing that
check honestly cost two false convictions, both recorded because they are the
reason to trust the third version. Asking merely whether a catch returns
convicted two sites whose fallback sits on the enclosing function's last line,
which is the better idiom rather than the worse one. And measuring the span by
counting braces went wrong on a regular expression written between the try and
the call, which balances by luck, so the reader now blanks strings, templates,
comments and regular expression bodies to spaces before it counts, with its own
fixtures for the two cases that decide whether a slash opens a pattern or
closes a tag.

Both rules were proved in one run, each against a file it spares, and the
spared file was restored and the restore verified by checksum rather than by a
command that takes its meaning from a ref.

Three defects were found in the reader itself during a type audit and all three
had the same shape, which is the shape this file exists to prevent. A match
that found nothing defaulted to an empty string, which read as a function body,
which narrowed the span the containment rule searches, which convicts correct
code. A slice taken from an unmatched position handed the keyword test the tail
of the file instead of nothing. And a verdict rested on whether a match array's
first element is always present, which is a question about the compiler rather
than about the code being read. A reader that has quietly stopped reading still
prints a plausible census, so the census now carries a floor on its own
population and asserts at zero the number of ceilings it cannot read, and says
in the file what its first legitimate occupant will be and that the answer then
is to teach the reader rather than to relax the assertion.

fix(bim-hub): a Chinese bill row measured in pieces keeps its piece count

The guard that stops model geometry overwriting a hand entered count knew the
count units of two languages and not of the third. A row measured in one of the
eleven Chinese count words, linked to a model element, had its count replaced
by a volume. The two shipped Chinese demo packs carry sixty four such rows.

The eleven join the set that already carries the German abbreviations, and not
either measurement system set, which is a distinction worth stating because
nothing had stated it. Those two sets are only ever read as the wrong one: a
metric project is judged against the imperial set and an imperial project
against the metric one. A count of discrete items has no dimension, so it
cannot be the wrong measurement system, and putting a Chinese piece word into
the metric set would flag every such row on an imperial project as a mismatch.
The English count words follow the same pattern and always have, without anyone
writing down why.

The metric vocabulary gains the Chinese spellings alongside the Cyrillic ones
that were added for the same reason, along with the full width Latin forms a
Chinese input method produces when left in full width mode, since nothing on
the write path normalises them and lowercasing folds a full width capital to a
full width lowercase rather than to an ASCII one.

Two compatibility glyphs that appear in ordinary Chinese cost documents are
deliberately absent. They cannot be stored at all: the unit shape check
requires a letter, a digit or a percent sign first, and those glyphs are
symbols, so an imported row measured in one is rejected before it reaches any
vocabulary. Adding them would have been decoration that a later reader would
trust. A test asserts the rejection instead, so the day the write path learns
to normalise them the test fails and says to extend the vocabulary.

That half of the vocabulary is staged rather than live, and the commit says so
rather than implying otherwise. The unit system rule reads a value resolved
from whichever regional pack claims the project's country, and no pack claims
China, so the rule returns nothing for a Chinese project before it looks at a
single unit. Adding a Chinese pack to the Asia Pacific one would have made the
rule run and handed every Chinese project an Australian currency and locale,
which is worse than silence. What is needed is a China pack of its own, which
is a routing decision rather than a vocabulary one.

Both Chinese demo packs cited GB/T 50500-2013, which is wrong twice over: the
2013 edition was GB, a mandatory code, and it was superseded on the first of
September 2025. Both now cite the current edition in both languages, with the
supersession recorded. The item codes are NOT renumbered and are recorded as
unverified, because the current measurement standard's text could not be
obtained and a confidently renumbered code is worse than an old one, which is
at least traceable.

One row is removed from each pack rather than recoded. A geotechnical
investigation report was priced as a measured item under the code for site
clearance. It is not a measured item under any edition; it is an owner cost
outside the bill. Stripping the wrong code would have left an uncoded row in a
measured section, which a live rule correctly fails.

The Shanghai pack's description claimed a total of about one point eight
billion over a bill summing to six point nine hundred million, which needs a
hundred and sixty one percent on top for measures, other items and tax and is
not a defensible build up. It now names the measured works figure and says
explicitly what it excludes. Shenzhen's headline is left alone: it claims a
figure its own bill supports once tax is added, so it was already true, and
making the two symmetrical would have meant changing a correct number to match
a corrected one.

fix(subcontractors): an award gate that could not read a date now reads one

Expired insurance was recorded, displayed on the vendor page and did not stop
an award. The gate read an administrative blocked flag and a prequalification
status, and neither of those is a date, so the one fact that lapses on its own
was the one fact the gate could not see. The register was right, the screen was
right, and the decision was taken without either.

The gate now reads three axes and reports all of them together. The certificate
set is a required argument rather than a defaulted one, because a default would
let any caller keep the old blind behaviour by not passing it, which is the
defect itself wearing a keyword. The date is a required argument too, so the
gate never reads a clock: a decision taken today passes today and a replay of a
historical decision passes the historical date, and the payment path now hands
the same day to both gates so the two cannot disagree about which day it is.

The boundary is inclusive. Expiring on the thirtieth means valid on the
thirtieth and refused from the first. That is what every other reader of the
column already does, and two gates disagreeing about the same day on the same
column would be worse than either choice on its own. Every comparison is a date
column against a date, with no timestamp anywhere in the path, so no offset can
move the boundary by a day. A caller holding a timestamp reduces it itself and
thereby chooses whose midnight applies, which is now written down rather than
being true by accident.

Missing and expired are different findings and get different answers, which is
a deliberate departure from the instruction to report both alike. Both are
reported, and only expired and revoked refuse. A prequalification marked pending
is explicitly awardable today, so a gate that also refused on a missing document
would stop every new supplier on its first day and be switched off within a
week, which is the more expensive failure. The payment gate keeps the stricter
line and still refuses on missing, so the two together read as work may be
awarded before the certificate arrives and may not be paid.

Only the types that block payment can block an award. An expired quality
certificate or bond does not refuse, and that is asserted rather than assumed.

One defect was introduced here and caught on review, and it is worth recording
because of why the tests missed it. The insurance backstop originally fired
whenever no live certificate existed, so a lapsed policy could produce both a
missing finding and an expired one for the same document, carrying two
different dates for one lapse. That is precisely the unreadable refusal that
gets overridden at the counter. The register is now authoritative whenever it
holds any row at all, live or lapsed or revoked, and the denormalised date on
the vendor row speaks only where the register is silent, replacing the missing
finding rather than joining it. One document, one verdict. The tests did not
catch it because they asserted a set of states and a dictionary keyed by
document type, and both of those collapse duplicates silently. A cross product
of four register states against three vendor row states now asserts that no
document type appears twice.

The legacy payment gate delegates the same arithmetic and rebuilds its old
reason codes byte for byte, so no existing reader changes and the invariant
that blocked equals a non empty reason list still holds.

Two things are known and open rather than fixed. A missing document currently
lands on a structured field that the award banner does not read, because the
banner only walks the reasons when the award is refused, so it renders green.
That is a frontend line and it is the same shape as the defect one level down.
And the survey of how else an award can be reached found five paths. One of
them resolves a contact identifier the gate can already use and simply does not
call it, which is the cheapest real gap left. Two others cannot be gated as they
stand, because they identify a supplier by free text with no key to anything.
A second procurement stack turned out to carry its own vendor table, its own
purchase order writers, a status field of the same shape as the flag replaced
here, and a fourth expiry register that is the only one keyed to a counterparty
by a real foreign key and whose scheduled expiry marking no writer consults.
The defect has an exact twin one stack over, sitting on the better shaped data.

Two of the four expiry registers in the platform cannot be read by a gate like
this at all. One identifies its holder by a free text name and the other carries
no counterparty column whatsoever, so joining either would be a gate that fails
open on a typo, which is worse than no gate. That narrows this work rather than
widening it and is the reason only two sources are read.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

i18n: the strings for the demo refusal and the encoder sentence, in every language

Fourteen keys into forty two locale files, carrying the text for two changes
that land immediately after this one. Thirteen belong to the read only demo and
one to the sentence the element matcher shows when its encoder is not present.

They land before the code rather than with it, deliberately. A key that exists
before anything reads it is inert. Code that ships before its key is a raw
dotted identifier printed on screen in forty one languages, which is the defect
this repository has shipped more than once, so the ordering is the safer of the
two and not an accident of who finished first. The two string sets share these
files and cannot be separated by path, so they share a commit; that is stated
here rather than left for a reader to work out from the diff.

The demo strings say what the public demonstration is and why it will not save
anything. That the projects on it are examples, put there so a visitor can see
the product working on real material. That everyone looking at the page sees the
same ones, which is the actual reason nothing can be written. That the product
itself runs on the visitor's own machine, that installing it takes a few
minutes, and that their projects, their prices and their drawings stay where
they put them. Then the six ways in: an installer for Windows that brings
everything it needs, a disk image for Apple silicon, a Debian package and an RPM
and an AppImage for Linux, a container image from the public registry, the
Python package, and the source with one command. A refusal that only says no
teaches the reader nothing; this one is the moment the product explains itself,
so it carries the whole answer rather than an apology.

Both failure modes were measured rather than assumed, because they are invisible
to different instruments. A missing key shows nothing at all on screen and no
gate reports it. An English string sitting in a non English file renders
perfectly and is the leak itself. So both were counted: no key is absent from
any of the forty two files, and across the forty one non English files not one
of the fourteen values is byte identical to its English counterpart. Zero and
zero, from a census over the whole population rather than a sample.

The forty third file on disk is deliberately untouched. It is a partial delta
that carries none of the sibling keys and inherits them, so adding these to it
would make it something it is not.

fix(migrations): the tax combination backfill declares what it rewrites

The revision that adds the combination column backfills every existing row and
did not carry the acknowledgement the hygiene gate requires, so the gate has
been red on every push since it landed. The gate was right and the migration
was the thing that was wrong.

The table is a shipped catalogue of tax rates, seventy nine rows, one per
jurisdiction we carry. It grows when someone adds a jurisdiction and not when
someone uses the product, so it is bounded rather than tracking tenure, and the
distinction matters because the two classes carry different risk on a large
install. A rewrite of every row in a catalogue is a different object from a
rewrite of every row in a ledger.

The acknowledgement says what it is acknowledging rather than only naming the
table. Every row is rewritten, and that is the point rather than a cost: the
column is being introduced in this same revision, so there is no row that
already holds a correct value for the rewrite to destroy. It also records the
ordering, which is the part a later reader would otherwise have to reconstruct.
The two statements run narrowest first, the explicit sub-national cases and then
a single sweep of whatever is still null to the default, so a row matched by the
first is never reconsidered by the second.

Nothing about the migration's behaviour changes. This is the file stating a
property it already had.

fix(requirements): a row is checked against the project of whoever asked

Three routes in the requirements module reached a row by identifier and acted
on it without asking whose it was. Linking a bill position to a requirement
took any position identifier and stored it, so a requirement in one project
could point at another project's priced item, and the traceability matrix then
printed that item's description, unit and quantity to a reader with no access
to the bill it came from. The additive route that names the position in the
request body rather than in the path had the identical defect, and both are
fixed in one change, because a rule installed at one of two call sites is a
rule tested at the call site that was already right.

The position check lives in the service rather than in the router, which is
the opposite of what the rest of the module does. A router level project check
answers whether the caller may reach the position's project, and that is a
different question from whether the position belongs in this requirement set.
Someone who legitimately holds both projects passes the first and must still
fail the second, and the helper that answers it returns early for any caller
whose stored role is administrator, so a check built on it can read as working
while asserting nothing about containment. The service compares the position's
bill to the requirement set's project, which is the containment rule itself
rather than an access rule standing in for it. A position that does not exist
and one belonging to somebody else return the same status and the same wording,
because a distinct message for the second confirms the identifier is real and
turns the endpoint into an existence oracle for other tenants' bills.

The third route is the text import, the only set scoped endpoint in the module
with no project check of any kind while twenty nine of its neighbours carried
one. Its own docstring said a new set was created, which would have made the
absence harmless. The service resolves the set named in the path and appends
to it, so the call wrote rows into another tenant's set and returned that
set's name, project and contents in the response body. The docstring is
corrected along with the route, since the wrong description is part of why the
gap survived. This one takes the module's ordinary router level check, because
the set named in the path is the object whose ownership is in question, so
whether the caller reaches its project is exactly the right question.

Each guard is proved by disabling it and confirming that exactly its own test
reddens, and each disabled file is restored from a copy and checked by hash
rather than by a command that takes its meaning from a ref. With the import
guard removed the refused call returns a 201 carrying the foreign set's
contents, so the before state is recorded rather than described. Every
boundary test asserts the status and the body separately, since a 404 that
echoes the identifier it refused has already confirmed that identifier is
valid, and each carries its positive half, because a lane holding only denials
is satisfied by a gate that denies everyone.

Eight tests in the second link suite paired two randomly generated project
identifiers and asserted a 404 from that. They were passing on the absence of
both rows rather than on the containment rule, so they now build real projects
and real bills, and they fail without the fix. They carry no marker, which is
right because identity is not the variable under test in them, and it also
means neither the lane that gates this class of change nor the chain frozen
beside it selects them. Measured rather than assumed: both selections collect
nothing from that file. They are the regression tests for what the rule means
and they run on push nowhere.

The test application builder threads permissions instead of hardcoding an
empty list and defaulting every caller to administrator, so the boundary cases
run as an editor holding exactly the one permission each route requires.

One further finding is recorded and not fixed. The requirement to model
validation route gates on the set's project and then takes a model identifier
from the request body which is never compared to it, so a caller can validate
their own requirements against another tenant's model and read element counts
and property values back in the report. The model does carry a project, so the
comparison is available, but the rule for who owns a model belongs to the
module that defines it and not to this change. Every other route that reaches
a row by identifier was read and is contained by an argument it already
carries: the bulk delete scopes each row to the set, the deliverable routes
scope each row to the requirement, and the detach is keyed on both sides.

feat(cases): the country a case belongs to is something you can see and pick

The case library knew which market each case came from and showed it as an
eighteen pixel flag on a pill, in the smallest type on the page. A reader
looking for the German cases had to know they were there. There is now a shelf
across the top of the library, one card per market, each carrying the flag at
forty four pixels, the country's name at the size of ordinary text, and how many
cases it holds.

Picking a market does not merely filter, it changes the shape of the page. The
grid drops from eight columns to five and each case card goes from roughly a
hundred and fifty pixels square to two hundred and fifty by two hundred and ten,
which is one and two thirds the width and a little over twice the area. A
market with one case in it gets a page that looks deliberate rather than a page
with one small tile stranded at the top left. The unfiltered view is untouched,
so the library a reader lands on is the same library it was.

Those numbers are measured off the rendered page rather than read off the
stylesheet, at a fixed viewport, through the development server so that nothing
was built and no bundle was written. That distinction has cost this project
real time before: a card that is larger in the stylesheet and unchanged on
screen is the failure mode here, not a hypothetical one.

Four defects in the surrounding filter went with it, each confirmed by driving
the page and reading the document afterwards rather than by reading the markup.
The active filter list did not name the market or the stage, so a reader could
see that something was filtered and not what. Neither could be removed from the
list. The clear control appeared only when certain other filters were set, so
picking a market and nothing else left no way back except reloading. And the
choice of market was held in a component, so it did not survive a reload, which
on a page reached from a link is the common case rather than the rare one. It
now lives with the rest of the library's state and is validated by shape on the
way in, so a stored value from an older version cannot break the page.

Two strings are added and both are new, so nothing is retranslated. Every one of
the forty two locale files that carries the sibling keys carries these, and the
forty third is the partial delta that inherits them. The two failure modes were
counted rather than assumed, because they are invisible to different
instruments: no key is absent anywhere, and across the forty one non English
files not one value is byte identical to its English counterpart.

Three cases gain the market they always belonged to, one of them the United
Kingdom, which needs no name of its own because the country name comes from the
reader's own locale rather than from a table we maintain. Every market on the
shelf resolves to a flag, checked rather than assumed, because the flag
component returns nothing at all for a code it cannot place and would have left
a country name floating beside empty space with no gate to catch it.

One thing is deliberately left alone. The summary line above the cases counts in
a key that has no plural forms, so a market holding exactly one case reads one
cases. That was already true and was hard to reach before, and this change makes

rather than buried under a diff this size.

fix(demo-packs): section titles stop borrowing a classification we do not license

The gate that stops a proprietary classification's division titles entering the
tree read fifteen strings in two files. A whole tree census over eight thousand
files found forty nine matches in seven, and a second extractor of a different
shape found an eighth. The disagreement between the two is reported rather than
resolved in favour of the larger number, because the first matcher undercounted
in exactly the way the shipping gate did, and a census that agrees with itself
has only been run once.

Three of the eight repaired files were never convicted by the widened gate
either. Their titles are single words and sit below the eight division
threshold that keeps the gate from firing on coincidence. They were repaired
because the rule applies to them, which is the difference between fixing a
gate's output and fixing the defect it exists to describe.

Two title positions that the hash table does match are deliberately left alone
and recorded as such. A Mexican pack numbers its sections as partidas, and nine
of its ten numbers contradict the standard's divisions while one coincides;
the same pack carries a hundred and two explicit mappings in a separate key, so
it already distinguishes the two namespaces itself. A trade table carries
Japanese codes fifteen and sixteen, and in the same file the Italian, Korean
and Polish fifteen is electrical, so the numbering is national and the

printed one file scanned and exited zero: the directory failed a file test and
was dropped silently, and the guard for a sweep that reached nothing fired only
when there were no arguments at all, so an explicit selection resolving to
nothing passed. Directories now expand, a path matching no scannable file is an
error that names the argument, and a selection that scans nothing fails. The
packs directory goes from one file to thirty one.

The census also convicted a comment inside the gate, where an official title
had been written out as an illustration. It now carries a placeholder.

The leak has been shipping since the end of May. Every revision of each
repaired file was read out of git and put through the widened matcher, with the
term carried as a hash so that no title is written into this repository to test
for it. One file was cleaned once already, in early August, and one line
survived that pass.
