fix(cases): the count of cases picked for you reads correctly when there is one

The persona shelf prints how many guided cases match the reader, and the string
was written once with a plural noun in every language. A reader matched by a
single case was told so in the plural. On the case page that is not a rare

fix(certified-payroll): every route in the module answered with a server error

All nineteen access checks in the module passed their arguments in an order the
function does not have. The check takes a project, a user and a session, in that
order, and each call handed it a session first. Nothing about that is caught
before the request runs, so every endpoint in the module raised on its first
statement and returned a server error. Wage determinations, classifications and
the payroll reports themselves were all unreachable, which is the whole module.

The failure is uniform, which is why it survived. A module where one route in
twenty is broken gets reported by whoever needed that route. A module where
every route is broken looks from the outside like a module that is not wired up
yet, and the report that reaches us is that the feature is missing rather than
that it is failing.

The order is confirmed against the single definition rather than against the
neighbouring modules, because the neighbours do not settle it. Several carry a
private helper of almost the same name, distinguished only by a leading
underscore, and that one genuinely does take the session first. Reading the
tree for calls that look wrong finds forty one of them and every one is a
correct call to the other function. A check written to look for the wrong order
has to name the function precisely enough to exclude its near namesake, or it
convicts correct code in bulk.

value rather than on either spelling, and the test exercises both, because a

was an honest record of a live defect rather than a stale excuse, and it is

and the static check both go red, and only those two.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(demo): a public demo can refuse every write and say why

A deployment that strangers can reach has one job that a self-hosted install
does not: what the last visitor typed must not be what the next visitor sees.
Until now the only way to get that was to reseed on a timer, which means a
visitor can still spend ten minutes on a screen somebody else has already
edited, and can still delete the project they were about to be shown.

Turning this on refuses every request that would change persistent state, and
answers with a refusal that names itself rather than a bare status code, so the
interface can explain what happened instead of reporting a failure. Reads are
untouched and signing in still works, because a demo where you cannot sign in
is not a demo of anything.

It is off by default and it is an operator decision. A self-hosted install
behaves exactly as it did before, byte for byte, and nothing about this reaches
it. It is also deliberately separate from the switch that governs analytics and
redaction on the same box, which is a different question with a different
answer, and the hosted demo sets both.

There are two independent layers and the second is the reason the first is
allowed to be imperfect. The first refuses at the endpoint, chosen by the
endpoint's identity rather than by its URL, because the module loader mounts
every module twice under two spellings of its name and a rule keyed on the path
would cover one spelling and miss the other. The second sits at the database
cursor and refuses a write that the first let through. That layer is not
route-dependent, so a route the first layer has not been taught about still
cannot write. What an incomplete first layer costs is the shape of the error a
visitor sees, not the integrity of the data behind it, and a test drives
exactly that case with the first layer bypassed on purpose.

The write scope is set inside the guard, after it has already decided to refuse,
so the path that permits a write cannot be reached by a request the guard turned
away. A curated list of the writes that must still succeed is exercised with the
flag off, and an edit that only updates is refused with the row afterwards
verified byte for byte unchanged, because a refusal that still writes is worse
than no refusal at all.

WHAT IS NOT PROVEN, stated here rather than left for someone to discover. The
first layer has not been swept across every mounted endpoint. The mechanism that
enumerates them changed behaviour in the web framework, returning a handful of
entries where it must return thousands, so the property and the instrument built
to check it were broken by the same change. What the tests establish is that
both layers fire independently and that the refusal contract is exact. That is
evidence the mechanism is correctly built and not evidence it reaches every
route, and those are different claims.

This commit also carries two lines that belong to other work, because they live
in a file this change cannot be separated from. One is an install hint reworded
so it reads correctly on a desktop bundle, and the other adds a traceback to two
skips that were swallowing one. Splitting them would have meant leaving this
module uncommitted while a file that imports it went in without it, which is a
tree that cannot import itself.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(requirements): adding a requirement no longer answers with a server error

Adding a requirement through the interface returned a server error, and so did
adding several at once. That is the module's main way of getting anything into
it, so for anyone using the interface rather than a file import, the module
could not be filled in at all.

A row that has just been inserted has never been queried, and the strategy that
loads its related rows runs on a query. Inserting and writing the row out does
not count, so the new row comes back with its related collections not loaded,
and with any column the insert did not name not loaded either. Writing the
response then reads one of those collections, which asks the database for rows
from a place that is not allowed to wait for an answer, and the request fails.
The handler caught the failure and reported that the requirement could not be
added, which was true and told nobody anything.

The repository now puts a freshly inserted row into the state a query would have
left it in, without asking the database anything. A collection that is empty
because the row was created a moment ago is recorded as empty, and a column the
insert did not supply and the database does not fill in is recorded as absent.
Both creation paths go through it, and so does the third caller that builds its
rows by hand, which a fix placed on the shared factory would have missed.

Two things are deliberately left alone and the code says why. Relationships that
are declared to refuse a silent query stay unloaded, because recording one as
absent would answer that a requirement belongs to no set when it belongs to one.
A column whose value the database chooses is left unloaded rather than guessed,
because a wrong value that reads as real is worse than a loud failure.

Nothing caught this because the tests build their rows through helpers that
refresh them afterwards, and a refresh is a query. Every requirement any test
had ever looked at was therefore in the loaded state, and only a row created the
way the service creates one was not. A green suite over the whole module said
nothing about it. The one path with no tests at all was the bulk one, so the new
tests exercise both, and the hand-built path as well.

A comment on the model claimed the loading strategy guaranteed the collection
was present. That sentence is the reason the defect was written, so it is
corrected here rather than separately: the guarantee holds for a row that was
queried, and only for one.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(desktop): an install hint words itself for the build it is read on

A diagnostic that told the operator to run a package install was written for a
server install and read the same way everywhere. The desktop bundle carries no
pip, so on that build the advice sent the reader after a thing that is not
there, and for packages the bundle does ship it hid the fact that reinstalling
the app is the actual repair.

Every hint that names a package now routes through one function, which chooses
its wording from whether the process is a frozen build. Where the package is in
the desktop lock the frozen reader is told the bundle is damaged and to
reinstall from the installer, which leaves projects and settings alone. Where it
is not in the lock, and three of them are not, the reader is told the build
ships a fixed set of packages and needs either a build that carries it or the
server install. The embedder card goes further and sends an empty install
command, so a copy box that could only hand over something unrunnable disappears
rather than sitting there looking usable.

Two remedies a desktop reader can actually follow were sitting inside the routed
argument and so reached only the reader who has pip. The offer of online
analysis when the drawing reader will not load, and the reassurance that
everything else keeps working without the vector client, now sit outside the
call and survive on both builds. Four sentences joined their routed tail with a
semicolon, which read correctly while that tail was a clause and read as a
capital letter after a semicolon once it became a whole sentence, so they join
with a full stop now.

A test walks every install instruction under the application and fails on any
that is not routed, naming the file and the line. It also drives four of the
sites on both builds and asserts the wording each one must not produce, because
a check that only looks for the absence of the word pip is satisfied by either
frozen sentence and so cannot tell a correct choice from a confidently wrong
one.

test(interface-management): the seeder and the register agree on what can be late

The register refuses to count three statuses as overdue, and the demo seeder
chooses a status before it decides what dates a row carries. The two rules
therefore have to agree, and nothing made them. They disagreed once already:
the seeder reused its own settled pair, handed a paused row a date in the past,

meets it, rare enough that nobody reproduces it, and silent when it happens,

The property is asserted across five hundred draws, because the failure is a

proves nothing about the run that will not. It needs no database, since this is
a fact about two rules rather than about anything written down.

fix(demo): the service register belongs to the projects it covers

Every service contract was written with no project on it. The module's own
screen passes no project filter and so looked correct, while the tab a
visitor actually reaches it from, inside a project, filtered by project and
came back empty on all thirteen. Tickets, work orders and assets carry no

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(requirements): a set cannot be validated against a foreign model

Validating a requirement set against a BIM model checked the caller against
the set and checked nothing about the model. The set was resolved honestly and
the access check on it was correct, so the route looked right from the outside.
But the model identifier arrived in the path and was read straight from the
database, which meant a caller entitled to their own set could name any model
in the installation and have every element of it read, measured against their
requirements and written into a report filed under their own project. The data
left through the report rather than through the response, which is part of why
it was easy to miss.

The model is now resolved inside the set's own project. A new method on the BIM
model repository returns a model only when it belongs to the project asked for,
and returns nothing otherwise, so the not found error the validator already
raised now covers a foreign model in exactly the same words as a model that was
never there. That sameness is deliberate. A refusal that reads differently for
"not yours" than for "no such thing" confirms that a row exists somewhere the
caller cannot see, and a private model list can be enumerated one identifier at
a time through a pair of them.

The rule is containment rather than a second permission check, and it is written
to be independent of who is asking. An administrator is entitled to be told yes
in both projects, and neither yes makes it correct to measure one project's
requirements against another project's model, because the report is stored
against the first while everything in it was derived from the second. That is a
wrong record rather than a permission somebody lacked, so it has to hold even
for callers a permission check waves through.

The unscoped lookup stays and is not deprecated, because the other caller in the
tree is asking a different question. Validation holds no project and needs to
find out which one a model belongs to before it can check access at all. This
module already holds the project and needs to know whether the model is inside
it. Both methods now say which case they are for, so the next reader picks one
rather than assuming the newer retired the older.

Two neighbouring routes were checked and left alone. Linking a requirement to
BIM elements stores caller supplied identifiers without resolving them, so
nothing foreign is read and a nonexistent identifier is accepted exactly like a
real one, which is a data quality question rather than this one. Listing
requirements by element verifies the caller against the project first and then
searches inside it, so a foreign element simply returns nothing.

The tests prove the refusal rather than the status code. Before the foreign
request is made, the owning tenant validates its own model successfully and the
other tenant validates its own model successfully, so the route is known to work
and the caller is known to be sufficient. Only then is the foreign model asked
for, and the test also asserts that no report was written, because the read is
the damage and a status code would not have seen it. A second test asks for a
foreign model and for an identifier that never existed, substitutes out the
values the caller supplied, and asserts the two refusals are then identical.

fix(tests): an export name is not a value a user reads

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(change-intelligence): a notice period can say whether its days are working days

Every notice period in the contractual time bar was a bare integer, and the
engine counted it with its own date arithmetic that knew nothing about
weekends. That has been right by coincidence rather than by design, because
every standard configured so far counts in calendar days. The first standard
that counts in working days would have been entered as a plain number and come
out roughly four days early, silently, showing a plausible date with nothing on
screen to contradict it. A deadline that is wrong in the direction of less time
than you have, on a notice whose failure can invalidate a claim, is the worst
shape this kind of error takes.

A period now carries its own basis, resolved from the same row as the count.
The basis tables are built from the period tables rather than written beside
them, so a period cannot exist without one, and there is a check that names any
that lacks it. The lookup resolves in the same order as the count does, the
standard's own table and then the neutral fallback, so a number and the rule
for counting it can never come from different rows.

There were two implementations of this arithmetic, not one. The payment clock
had a correct one and the notice engine had its own. The correct one has moved
into a shared module that depends on nothing but the standard library, and both
callers now use the same objects rather than the same behaviour. The reason it
moved rather than being imported across is that the payment clock is a regional
module a deployment is meant to be able to switch off, while the notice engine
is always on, and an always-on module must not break when a switchable one is
disabled.

Holidays are unchanged and deliberately not improved on. The shared module
ships no lists and defaults to none, callers supply their own, because a wrong
holiday list is worse than an honest count of weekends that a user can
reproduce. A test asserts both halves of that: a supplied holiday moves the
answer, and none is supplied by default.

No standard was added. Only the ability to express one.

Proving that nothing moved needed more than a passing suite, and this is worth
recording because the passing suite is weak evidence here. Every configured
standard is calendar-day, so the existing tests return the same answer whether
the basis is honoured or ignored entirely. They are a regression check and not
a verification. The wiring was therefore checked by mutation: removing the
basis from the call sites, and separately mispairing one so a clock reads
another row's rule. Both were caught, and the mispairing is the case nothing
else could see, because every basis holds the same value today. The test that
catches it declares exactly one notice type in working days and asserts the
other four did not move.

One period was left alone with its reasoning written down rather than decided
quietly. One standard excludes public holidays from a reckoned period, which is
calendar minus holidays and neither of the two bases. Its rows are reminder
windows rather than a statutory bar, so they stay calendar until somebody who
knows that contract decides otherwise.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(variations): a standard's timer stops reading like a template to copy

The function that derives quotation and assessment deadlines for one contract
family counts in weeks, which is calendar arithmetic and is correct for that
family. The problem was never that it was wrong, it was that it is the obvious
thing to copy when the next standard needs timers, and a standard counting in
working days copied from it inherits calendar arithmetic with no field anywhere
to be wrong about. That is why such a copy would be silent.

It now goes through the shared day arithmetic the rest of this area uses, and
deliberately takes no basis parameter, because no caller can make this family
count any other way and a setting nobody can name a caller for is an invitation
to set it wrong. What it gained instead is a paragraph naming the trap and
pointing at the notice period table, which is where a working-day standard
actually belongs. The chaining is preserved with the reason written beside it:
the second window is measured from the first deadline rather than from the
notification, and a rewrite that based both on the notification would not have
been caught by anything.

Nothing moved, proved twice. The existing tests pin literal dates and still
pass untouched, and a sweep of two thousand combinations against the previous
arithmetic returned identical answers.

Three tables hold contract standards and they are not being merged. They look
like duplicates and they are three different things sharing a vocabulary, which
the granularities show: the document catalogue has a row per standard form and
option, so two options of one family are two rows with one identical set of
notice periods; the clause reference has a row per edition, because a clause
number is edition specific; the notice periods have a row per family, because
the windows are stable across editions and options. A single table would have
to reintroduce per-field granularity immediately, which is what three tables
already are, and these strings are persisted in columns, so a common vocabulary
would be a data migration rather than a refactor.

What they need is not merging but a guard on the bridge between them, and that
is what this adds. Every catalogue entry and every clause entry must reach a
family that has notice periods, and every family with notice periods must have
a clause reference, unless the code is on a deliberately absent list. The lists
hold the consequence of each absence rather than the bare code, and a test
enforces that, so a list cannot decay into names nobody can act on. The gate is
proved non-vacuous rather than assumed to work. And one test checks that a
catalogue entry's declared family agrees with what the bridge resolves it to,
because the bridge matches on a substring and a code that had drifted would be
timed as one family while being reported as another.

Two absences are recorded rather than filled. Two families reach the neutral
fallback for their notice periods even though they are named on the record, and
the fallback's own documentation says a named standard takes precedence. The
number it returns happens to equal one real standard's, so what a reader sees
is a plausible date beside a different standard's clause label. Supplying the
real periods means asserting domain facts, so they are listed with that
consequence spelled out instead.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(demo): the same file is stored once rather than once per project

Every demo project is handed the same native CAD sources, and the seeder wrote
them into a folder per project. A seeded install therefore carried ten
byte-identical copies of one eighteen megabyte model and ten of the same IFC,
and most of what the uploads folder weighed was repetition rather than content.
The bytes now go to a content-addressed store that the whole install shares.

The measurement depends on which box you take it on, so both are worth stating.
Where the optional CAD samples folder is present, which is a developer machine
or a deployment that sets OE_DEMO_CAD_SAMPLES, uploads falls from 214.5 to 26.8
megabytes. On a package install, where the multi megabyte native sources are
simply absent and only the committed IFC materializes, it falls from 30.6 to
8.4. The count of distinct files is seventy two either way, before and after, so
nothing was lost but the repetition.

The store is deliberately dull. A blob is an ordinary file whose name is the
digest of its own contents, with no symlinks, no hard links and no index, so a
demo install stays a directory anybody can copy and the whole store can be
checked with a hash function rather than with our code. A blob is written under
a temporary name and renamed into place, and because the final name is the
digest, there is no state in which a half written file passes for a finished
one. The row is added only after the rename, so an install that dies partway can
leave a file nothing points at, which is recoverable, and never a row pointing
at a file that is not there, which is not.

Idempotency is now checked against the disk as well as against the database. The
old code saw a Document row, called that entry done and moved on, so a row whose
bytes had gone stayed broken through every later run, and an install that
already exists would have reclaimed nothing at all. A row whose file is missing
is repaired, and a row whose file is fine but still sits in a per-project folder
is moved into the store and the old copy removed once nothing else names it.
Without that second part the saving would only ever have arrived on a data
directory that starts empty, which is not the situation any running deployment
is in.

Sharing a file between rows changes what deleting one of them means. Deletion
unlinked the blob unconditionally, which after this change would have taken one
project's model away from every other project and left rows that look healthy in
every listing and answer 404 on download. A file another document still points
at is now kept, the last reference removes it, and a failure to answer the
question counts as keeping it, which is the trade the rest of that path already
makes. The cost is one count per deletion against a column with no index, which
is nothing at the scale a delete happens.

The tests live in the PostgreSQL lane because both properties are properties of
rows in a database. They assert both directions rather than one, since a seeder
that rewrote every blob on every run would pass a test that only counted files,
and a delete guard is worth nothing if the suite also passes without it.

fix(documents): a document stops claiming to be in a language it is not

A generated document is served with a header naming its language, and that
header was written by middleware from whatever the reader asked for, while the
document itself was rendered by a resolver that knows two languages. So a
reader who asked for French received an English contract labelled French, with
a two hundred response and nothing anywhere to contradict it. This was not a
silent gap, it was an affirmative statement of something untrue, made on every
request in every language we do not render.

The middleware now only supplies that header when nothing else has, so a route
that knows what it actually rendered outranks it, and three document routes now
say what they really produced. What this changes is not how many languages we
print. It is that failing to have a language stops looking like having it, so a
client, a test or a monitor can now see the degradation instead of being told
everything is fine.

The document is still served rather than refused. Refusing would break every
current caller asking for any of the forty languages we do not render, all at
once, and that is a decision to stage rather than to make as a side effect of
correcting a header. Whether some jurisdictions should be able to demand a
refusal instead, where a document in the wrong language is worse than no
document, is left open on purpose.

Two identical copies of the resolver and its formatting helpers had grown in
two modules, byte for byte apart from their docstrings. They are one shared
module now, which is a deleted copy rather than a refactor.

The tests are the reason this was hard to see, and they have been corrected
along with the code. The unsupported case was written as French. That is a real
language which we will one day render, so the assertion read as a decision that
English was right for a French reader, and anyone proposing to fix it would
have found a test apparently defending the behaviour. There were ten such
assertions rather than the two about the fallback, the rest being other
mechanisms that had merely borrowed French as a convenient stand-in. All of
them now use a permanently unassigned tag, which cannot become valid and so
cannot turn into a defence of a defect later.

What remains is recorded rather than implied. Twenty-one places build a
document and four of them consult a resolver at all. One route serves a stored
file whose language nobody knows, and it cannot be corrected by this mechanism
because a route can currently outrank the middleware but cannot ask it to stay
silent.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(boq): the Chinese fee stack is filed the way Chinese practice files it

The bundled Chinese markup template listed five charges as siblings, and two of
them do not belong at that level. Under the bill of quantities pricing method
the management fee and the profit form part of the composition of a unit rate,
not separate heads standing beside the measure item head. Because one of those
heads was categorised as overhead, the price analysis reported sixteen percent
of overhead on a bill whose management fee is eight, which is a wrong number on
a screen a Chinese estimator reads first.

Nothing is repriced. Every base is unchanged, so a newly seeded bill totals
exactly what it did before, and the template is read only at seeding time so
existing rows are untouched.

Two limits are stated rather than glossed. The two rate composition charges are
still bill level rows, because there is currently no way to declare a
percentage that informs a unit rate without also applying it to the bill, so
ordering them first and categorising them as the rate's composition is as close
as the model reaches. And the question of what those percentages should be
taken on was deliberately left alone. Chinese practice appears to take some of
them on the measure item total rather than on bare direct cost, but that is an
inference from practice rather than something read in the standard, and acting
on it would have repriced every new Chinese bill as a side effect of a
categorisation fix. It is a decision to take on evidence, separately.

The larger finding is that the same stack was stated in four places and they
disagreed about one charge three different ways, so two demo packs were putting
a statutory charge inside the rate composition and reporting ten percent of
overhead on rates whose management fee is under five. One name now resolves to
one category across every source that states one, and a check holds them
together.

Alongside this, two smaller things. A column that would record how a change was
valued had been declared on the model and was reachable from nothing, so it now
carries a closed set of three values taken from practice rather than from any
one edition's wording, which means a later change of vocabulary moves the
labels and leaves the stored codes alone. And the font layer can now render
Chinese at all: the only bundled face has no CJK coverage, so every generated
document printed Chinese as empty boxes. The renderer ships a suitable face
already and simply had to be asked for it, with no new dependency and nothing
added to the bundle. Two things about that are deliberate and pinned by tests.
The face is referenced rather than embedded, so identical rendering everywhere
would still need an embedded font, and the choice is made per document rather
than once per process, because the face names are module level and a per
document choice written into them would have re-faced every German and Russian
document produced afterwards in the same worker.

The font is available and no generator asks for it yet, so documents still
print boxes until one does. That is recorded rather than implied.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(demo): a public demo can forget the files strangers upload to it

A demo deployment kept every file every visitor ever uploaded, forever, with no
retention of any kind. On the deployment we run that is the largest thing we
own that grows, about thirty megabytes a day against a disk that had reached
ninety-eight percent, and a full disk stops a database writing rather than
merely filling up.

A sweep now removes visitor uploads past a window, defaulting to fourteen days
and configurable. Fourteen is chosen rather than rounded to: it is longer than
any demo session and longer than a weekend, so somebody who comes back to show
a colleague still finds their file, and it turns unbounded growth into a fixed
few hundred megabytes.

It cannot run anywhere it is not wanted. Arming needs both the read-only demo
flag and a positive window, so an ordinary install where real project files
live is unaffected by construction rather than by nobody mistyping a setting,
and the registration returns before creating anything at all when either is
absent.

Seeded content survives structurally. Whether a row is seeded is read off the
row's own metadata, which every seeder already stamps, rather than guessed from
a filename, a directory or a project, so a visitor uploading into a demo
project is still a visitor and a seeded file somebody renamed is still seeded.
A row that cannot answer the question is kept, never removed.

The order is the row, then the commit, then the file, one candidate at a time,
and the two possible residues after a sudden death are deliberately not
symmetric. Stopping after the row leaves a file nothing points at, which is
invisible, costs only disk, and the platform already ships a repair for it.
Stopping after the file would leave a row pointing at bytes that are gone, and
nothing can put those back. Committing per candidate rather than per batch
bounds the residue to a single file whenever the process dies.

Three hazards found in the data rather than assumed, each pinned by a test.
Files are shared between tables, so opening a document in another module reads
the same bytes rather than a copy. The recycle bin keeps a file alive after its
own row is gone, with the path recorded in the bin's payload. And two doomed
rows can name one file. A single rule covers all three: remove the bytes only
when no live row in any registered table and no bin entry names that exact
path.

Every run reports, including a dry run and a run that removed nothing, because
the failure this is modelled on is a nightly job that failed safe into a log
nobody read. Three states are distinguished rather than blurred into one: not
armed, which is the healthy answer on an ordinary install, failed, which needs
a person, and stopped at a cap with work still behind it, so a large number
removed is not mistaken for a finished sweep. A stale timestamp in that report
is itself the signal that the job has stopped running.

Two sources are deliberately not swept because their rows carry no metadata,
which means an unseeded row cannot be told apart from a seeded one, and the
exclusions are recorded with that reason next to them rather than as bare
names. A check fails if a source is added whose rows cannot answer.

The Toronto condo pack shipped three bidders, so the tendering and leveling

Three bids compare. They do not level, because leveling is the work of

the real-firm gate, which reads the pool the installer actually consumes rather

rather than clustering, so the high bid has something to be high against.

declared list, so the length was never load bearing and this is data rather
than behaviour.

The wider observation is recorded rather than acted on. Twenty-nine packs
declare a bidder pool, twenty-two of them declare exactly three, and five packs
already declare five, so five is a precedent in the shipped data and not an
invention for one country. Whether the other twenty-two should follow is a

one of them.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(pdf): the generators now ask for the face that can draw Chinese

The font layer learned to render Chinese and no generator asked it to, which
was recorded at the time and is the whole of what was wrong. Every document
the product produced still printed Chinese as empty boxes, and it did so
while returning two hundred and a valid PDF, so nothing downstream noticed.
Seven generators now ask: the bill of quantities, the tender award and
rejection letters and the award record, both meeting minutes renderers, the
punch list, the report exporter and the site diary.

The choice is made per string, not per document and not per process. Neither
face covers both scripts. The bundled DejaVu has no Han glyph at all, and the
Adobe Simplified Chinese face has no Latin-1 accented forms, so a bill written
in German for a Chinese subcontractor renders correctly only if each string is
drawn with the face that can draw it. A document-level switch would have had
to sacrifice one side or the other, and a process-level one would have refaced
every German and Russian document produced afterwards in the same worker.

Most generators already funnel their user-controlled text through one escaping
helper, so the face is chosen there, once, and the whole generator is wired.
Where a table holds bare strings rather than paragraphs the face comes from a
list of FONTNAME commands appended after the table's own style, because a
paragraph-level choice cannot reach a cell whose font the TableStyle decides.
That is where a half-wired generator keeps printing boxes while every other
assertion passes, so the punch list assignee, the meeting location and the
action owner are asserted by name.

The proof is the produced bytes rather than a passing call. With the CID face
the Chinese codepoints survive into the content stream under the standard
Adobe-GB1 CMap and a reader recovers the characters. Without it reportlab
embeds a DejaVu subset that has no Han glyph and writes every Chinese
character as glyph zero, which extracts as a run of NUL bytes and is
unrecoverable. Each generator is checked in both directions: the same document
built with the switch forced off comes back boxed, so the tests measure the
wiring rather than the PDF library. A German document built after a Chinese
one in the same process is asserted unchanged, which is the regression a test
that builds one document cannot see.

Two things are deliberately not done. The face is still referenced rather than
embedded, so a document that must render identically everywhere still needs an
embedded font and a reader without an Adobe Simplified Chinese face still
shows nothing; that is a decision with a size cost attached and it was not
taken here. And the detector was left as it is. It was measured against our
own Chinese data and covers all of it, but the squared unit forms a Chinese
bill writes are outside it, and widening the range would send a Latin document
containing one of them to a face with no umlauts. That trade wants evidence,
not a side effect.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(demo): the websocket half of the read-only claim is actually driven

The test that was meant to cover websockets on the read-only demo shipped red
and nothing noticed, because the tree it lives in is reached by a single
filtered step in a workflow that is red often enough that a failure there stops
nobody. What it was red for had nothing to do with the guard. The file carries
a future import, so the probe endpoint's annotation was the string WebSocket,
FastAPI resolves string annotations against the endpoint's own globals, the
import sat inside the test function body, and the parameter was therefore
treated as a required query parameter and the handshake closed with 1008. The
trap is worth naming because any socket endpoint written with a function local
import gets a query parameter instead of a socket and a close code instead of
an error.

The synthetic probe is gone rather than repaired. It built its own application
and proved only that the guard does not break a throwaway socket, which is not
the claim anyone cares about, and it was where the bug was. The test now drives
the real notification socket on the real application by speaking ASGI on the
suite's own event loop, so there is no second thread fighting a loop bound
connection pool and no new dependency.

Connecting is not the claim either, so the test goes further than the old one
did. It mounts a socket that deliberately tries to write, asserts that socket
inherited the same dependencies the real ones carry, and drives both
polarities. With the flag on the write scope inside the handler is none and the
statement is refused. With the flag off the identical statement on the
identical socket succeeds. The second half is the load bearing one: an earlier
version of that control used a statement that failed on a not null column in
both polarities, which reads exactly like a working guard and is a pass that
means nothing.

The self check that refused to let the test prove nothing is kept and widened.
Both sockets are named, so losing one to a rename fails instead of quietly
shrinking the coverage, and the driver catches nothing, so an exception from
the application is a failure rather than a printed dictionary.

One asymmetry is recorded in the docstring rather than left for someone to
find. Everywhere else this guarantee is two independent layers, so a mistake in
an allowlist is cheap. On a socket it is one, deliberately, because the request
guard only refuses http scopes and an http exception is not something a
handshake can carry. A socket is therefore held by the database tripwire alone,
and that tripwire has one known blind spot in a helper that writes through a
raw cursor. Neither socket goes near it, which is why the claim is true today.
A socket that later reached that helper would break it silently, and the person
adding that socket should read this before they do.

fix(demo): the Toronto structural tender actually has five bidders

Two firms were added to the Toronto pack so its structural tender would show
five bids rather than three, and they landed in a field this pack does not
build its bids from. A pack that declares tender packages overrides the pack
level company list, so the five names fed the derived firm data and the bid
loop never saw them. The structural package still built three bids.

The two firms now sit in the package that carries the tender, beside the three
they were chosen to sit with. The pack level list is deliberately left in
place rather than removed, because it is still read for the firms that appear

was working correctly and still said nothing useful. It reads the field the

all. A green result with real denominators is evidence about exactly what it

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(property-dev): the twelve property documents can draw a Chinese name

The reservation receipt, the sale-purchase agreement, the handover and
warranty certificates and the other eight documents in this module printed
every Chinese character as an empty box. The module offers Chinese in its
locale picker, but the wiring is not really about the picker: a buyer, a
developer or a plot can be named in Chinese in a contract whose template
locale is English or German, and that is the common case rather than the
exotic one. Every paragraph in the module now goes through one helper that
picks the face the string itself needs, and the header, the watermark, the
footer and the page number do the same on the canvas.

The choice stays per string, matching the seven generators wired before this
one. Two alternatives were tried and rejected against the code rather than in
principle. Keying the face on the document locale is wrong twice over: it
misses the Chinese buyer in an English contract, and because this module ships
no Chinese translation and falls back to English text, it would also drag an
otherwise English document onto a face chosen for text that is not there.
Re-facing the paragraphs at the single build seam does not work at all,
because reportlab resolves the face when the paragraph is constructed, so
assigning a new style afterwards is silently ignored and the document still
comes out boxed.

The tables needed nothing. Every cell in this module is already a paragraph
rather than a bare string, so the cells inherit the choice from the helper and
the table styles were left alone.

Proved on the produced bytes. A Chinese receipt names the CID face, carries no
notdef run and gives back the development name, the buyer and the plot code. A
German receipt built immediately afterwards in the same process does not name
the CID face at all and gives back its umlauts and its sharp s, which is the
regression a suite that builds one document cannot see. The style factory is
asserted separately to still hand out Latin faces after a Chinese render. The
same document with the switch forced off comes back boxed, so the tests
measure the wiring and not the PDF library.

Not done here: the face is still referenced rather than embedded, so this
changes what a reader with the Adobe Simplified Chinese face shows and not
what a reader without it shows.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(realtime): a binary frame no longer drops a live socket

Both realtime channels read their keep-alive loop with receive_text(), which
raises KeyError on a frame carrying bytes rather than text. The exception
unwound into the handler's catch-all, logged that the websocket crashed and
dropped a working connection. On presence that took the caller out of the
editing roster and out of every peer's view of them, and on notifications it
stopped that user's pushes until something reconnected. Any client can send a
binary frame in one line and several browser keep-alive helpers do, and this
is present whatever the read-only demo flag is set to, so it reaches every
deployment.

The loop now reads the raw message and ignores anything that is not the one
text frame it understands. Closing on an unexpected frame was the alternative
and it is the wrong trade. Both channels already ignore unrecognised text, so
ignoring an unrecognised binary frame is the symmetric choice rather than a
new policy, and losing a presence roster to a stray frame costs the user more
than silence does. The channels are server-push only, so client input is a
keep-alive nicety and there is nothing to be gained by refusing it loudly.

Both channels get a regression test that sends a binary frame and then a ping,
where the answered ping is the assertion. The notifications socket had no test
of its own, so it also gains a handshake policy check and a greet-and-ping
case. Worth knowing for whoever sees one of these go red: against the unfixed
handler these tests do not fail fast, they stall, because the handler returns
without closing and no close frame ever reaches the client. It is the per-test
timeout that turns that into a red test, so a hang in either of them is this
defect coming back rather than a flake.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(demo): the demo fills the projects it is curated around, not the first three

Five seeders filled a prefix of the project list rather than a set anybody
chose. Each took the first three ids it was handed, and the list arrives in
creation order with the flagship moved to the front, so on a clean thirteen
project install the deep cost model, accommodation, markups, change control and
the Last Planner schedule landed on the flagship, residential Berlin and the
Dubai warehouse and nowhere else. Frankfurt, the Paris school and the US
medical project opened those five modules empty. Nothing chose that; it fell out
of which project happened to install first.

The projects are now named where the seeders are called rather than counted
inside each one, because a rule written once per caller is a rule the next
caller forgets and there were five callers of this one. The seeders take the
whole list they are given. Measured on a fresh install the five modules now
land on the flagship plus all five curated projects and stay off the other
seven, which is the shape the demo is meant to have.

Widening the Last Planner seeder exposed a second fault in it. Four of its
counts were fixed totals shared out across whatever rows sat above them, so how
deep one project's board went depended on how many other projects the estate
had. Doubling the projects halved them: Berlin fell from four weekly plans to
two, and one of those two is the week still in progress and carries no PPC,
which leaves a single closed week and no trend to read. They are rates now,
four weeks per master schedule, thirteen constraints per look-ahead, sixteen
commitments per weekly plan and ten deltas per baseline, so a project looks the
same whether the estate holds three of them or thirteen.

The root cause register was the same fault in a different shape. It capped at
fifty reasons for the whole estate, and it drew them from a query that read
every missed commitment in the table rather than the ones the run had just
written. At three projects the cap sat above the number of misses, so in
practice every miss carried its reason and the cap looked harmless right up
until the estate grew. Every miss carries its reason again, and the rows come
off the objects the loop created, so the seeder can no longer reach a
commitment it did not write.

The fallback is deliberately the old behaviour rather than a wider one. Where
none of the curated ids resolve, which is a partner pack workspace or a customer
install with no demo projects in it, these seeders keep touching exactly the
three projects they touched before instead of suddenly reaching further into
somebody's own work. Four of them also moved off the every project list onto the
demo set, so what they can write to only ever narrowed.

Tendering was left alone on purpose. It has the same cap, but every project
already carries tender packages written by its own bundle, in its own language,
and this seeder adds three generically named ones. Widening it would put English
placeholders next to Außenanlagen and the Shanghai superstructure package rather
than fill a gap, so it is a candidate for removal rather than for widening and
that is a separate decision.

The flagship ids the seeders held are gone with the slices that needed them.
They existed only to put the flagship back after a prefix dropped it, and with
no prefix there is nothing to put back, so keeping them would describe a special
case the code no longer makes.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(service): the recurring schedules tab opens on a register instead of nothing

The service module materialises tickets from RRULE-driven schedules, the tab is
built and the endpoints work, and every project opened it on an empty table. A
screen with nothing in it reads as an unbuilt feature, and this one is the
register a maintenance planner actually works from: the jobs that come round
again rather than the ones somebody raised this morning.

Each project now carries three rules bound to its own service contract, drawn
from a list of five so two projects opened side by side do not read as copies.
The wordings are the job as a planner would write it, a fire alarm and emergency
lighting test on the first of the month, a quarterly filter change and coil
clean, a weekly generator run-up. Statutory examinations are named generically
rather than after one country's regulation, because the estate spans five. One
rule per project is paused so the register shows both sides of the enable
toggle rather than a column that reads the same all the way down.

The next run is computed from the rule rather than typed, so a seeded row
carries the same date the materialiser would work out for it. A rule the
library cannot read leaves the field empty, which the worker treats as not due
rather than as due now.

It is a separate seeder rather than a section of the existing one, and that is
the point rather than a detail. The service seeder returns as soon as any
contract exists, which on an install that has been seeded once is always, so a
register wired into it would only ever appear on a database that started empty.
This one asks the question per project, which is safe because it is handed the
projects the caller has already proved are demo projects. A project that has a
schedule already is left alone, including one somebody wrote themselves, and a
project that is still empty is filled on the same run.

A project with no service contract is skipped rather than filled. Every
occurrence stamps its ticket against a contract, so rules seeded without one
would populate the tab with rows that fail the moment the worker reaches them,
which is worse than the empty tab they replace.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(calendar): Canada gets Canadian holidays instead of American ones

The shared calendar served Canada the United States federal holiday list, under
a comment saying it was simplified and close enough. It is not close enough. It
gave Canada the fourth of July and Memorial Day, and it withheld Canada Day,
Victoria Day, Boxing Day and the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. The
overlap is what kept it alive: five dates coincide, so any spot check picked one
of those and came back clean.

Canada now has its own function, computed by rule from the standard library so
it holds for any year rather than for one that somebody typed out. Ten federal
statutory days, the scope a function named for the country can actually keep.
Family Day and the August civic holiday are provincial, fall on different days
in different provinces, and are left out with the reason written down, because
an accurate national list with a stated limit is worth more than a fuller list
that is wrong in seven provinces.

Weekend substitution moves forward, which is where Canada differs from the
American rule this used to borrow. The American rule observes a Saturday
holiday on the Friday before it; Canada moves to the following working day in
both directions, so Canada Day on a Saturday is observed on the Monday. The
first of July 2028 is the case that separates them, and taking the American
direction would put a Canadian date three days early. Early is the dangerous
direction here, because these dates are what deadlines and notice periods are
counted from, and a date that arrives early looks confident while costing
somebody their remaining time.

Christmas and Boxing Day sit next to each other, so a substitution can land the
second one on the day the first already holds. Held in a set, the duplicate is
absorbed without a word, the year quietly loses a holiday and the working day
count goes up. The later day now moves on to the next free weekday instead, and
2026 is a year where that happens.

The tests discriminate rather than merely pass. Canada Day against Independence
Day is asserted in 2025, not 2026, because in 2026 the fourth of July falls on a
Saturday and the weekend would mask the difference well enough for the old
behaviour to pass. Victoria Day is asserted the same way and is the cleaner
signal, having no American counterpart at all. Remembrance Day is deliberately
not used, since it shares a date with Veterans Day and would prove nothing.
Every one of the eleven goes red against the old alias.

The computed set for 2026 is also checked against the Canadian row already
shipped in the seeded work calendars, and they agree on all ten dates including
the Boxing Day substitution. A rule derived from first principles and a table
somebody typed by hand agreeing date for date is better evidence than either on
its own, so that agreement is asserted rather than noted.

Nothing else in the file moves. Austria still borrows the German list, the Swiss
list is still three dates, and the four Gulf countries still share one function.
Those are the same class of problem and they are a separate change.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(i18n): Saudi Arabia stops shipping a four day working week

The seeded work calendar gave Saudi Arabia work_days of 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4. The
consumer matches those against isoweekday, which returns 1 through 7 and never
returns 0, and nothing anywhere normalises a zero. The row was written in a zero
based convention where Sunday is 0, so it meant Sunday through Thursday, and
what it produced was Monday through Thursday. Every Saudi working day count came
back a fifth short, and every date derived from one landed early. It never
raised, never logged and returned a number that looked reasonable, which is why
it survived: 29 of the 30 seeded rows are Monday to Friday and give the same
answer whether the code is right or wrong, so the one row that differs is the
only one that could have shown it and nobody read it.

Sunday to Thursday is what the row meant, corroborated three ways inside the
repository rather than chosen. It is the only row of the thirty that departs
from Monday to Friday, so a different week was deliberate. The shared calendar
lists Saudi Arabia under a Sunday to Thursday week. The Middle East pack spells
the same week out by day name, which carries no convention at all. Seven, one,
two, three, four is that week written the way the consumer reads.

A test had already found this trap and written it down. It names the zero based
convention as the cause, calls it a live input validation gap rather than
intended behaviour, and asserts the broken arithmetic on the same literal. It
used Germany as a stand in, so searching for the country finds nothing, and it
guarded the write schema while the bad data came in somewhere else entirely: the
seeder builds the row straight on the model and never passes through a schema.
The guard was real and the data walked around it. Its name also promises a
louder failure than it found, a week where no day is a working day, while the
assertion is a fifth short, and a reader skimming the name waits for a crash
that never comes.

So the write path now refuses a weekday outside one to seven, and a separate
check reads the shipped file itself and fails on any value the consumer cannot
match. That second one is the check that would have caught this, because it
inspects the data where the data is actually written rather than where the
schema sits. It carries two floors, a minimum row count and a minimum number of
weekday values, so a file that had been emptied could not pass by having nothing
left to object to. Read responses stay unconstrained on purpose, with a test
saying why: a row written before the guard still has to be readable, and
refusing to serialise it would hide the very calendar an operator needs to see
in order to repair it.

Installations that already seeded the bad row are repaired by a data migration,
and it repairs exactly one shape, Saudi Arabia holding that precise set. Anything
else out of range is printed with its country and value and left alone, because
two zero based conventions are in reach of whoever wrote a row and the same five
numbers mean Sunday to Thursday under one and Monday to Friday under the other.
Guessing would trade one silently wrong week for another. Rows already inside the
valid range are never touched. It is idempotent on the data rather than on a
marker, so a partly migrated database is safe, and the downgrade is a documented
no operation because reverting would mean writing the defect back.

The characterisation test keeps every assertion and its literal, since the value
still reaches the column two ways the schema cannot see. Only its docstring
changes, to say where the guard now stands and which check would have caught the
shipped row.

The same authoring mistake was swept for one level wider. Thirty eight other
occurrences of that literal sequence across ten files are all legitimate code in
the other calendar system, which counts Monday as zero, and no other file feeding
this path mentions work days at all. The two calendar systems disagreeing is a
known and separate problem, and the reverse of this defect has already been seen
once in the other direction.

fix(calendar): the United Arab Emirates works Monday to Friday

The shared calendar gave the UAE a Sunday to Thursday week, grouped with the
other Gulf states under one comment. The UAE moved to Monday to Friday in 2022
and is the only state in the region to have done so, so it no longer belongs in
that group and now carries its own entry with the reason next to it.

Nothing in the running product reads this yet. The working week has one reader,
and that reader has a single application caller which passes Germany. So this is
a loaded gun rather than a fired one, and the value of fixing it now is that the
first caller to ask about the UAE gets the right answer instead of a plausible
one. The sweep for other readers turned up mostly false friends worth recording,
since AE is also the reverse charge tax category in EN 16931, and the rest of the
hits are IBAN lengths, currency, phone and address validation, tax rates and
carbon factors. None of them consults a calendar.

The change quietly disarmed a test, and that is the part worth reading. A test
asserted that 16 May 2027 is not a working day in the UAE, anchored on Eid
al-Adha. That date is a Sunday. Under the old week Sunday was a working day, so
the assertion could only pass because the holiday lookup found the Eid, which
made it a real check that the Islamic date conversion reached the public
interface. Under the new week Sunday is a weekend, the function answers at the
weekday test and never consults the holidays at all. The assertion still passes
and now proves nothing. The whole suite stayed green while it happened.

That was demonstrated rather than argued: with the entire UAE holiday set emptied
the old anchor still passed, and the new one correctly failed. The test is
re-anchored to the Monday of the same Eid in the same year, which is a working
day under both weeks, so it isolates the holiday instead of the weekend.

The general form is worth stating because it will happen again. Widening a
weekend silently removes the discriminating power of any test anchored on a date
that has just become a weekend, and it does so without a single failure to point
at. A test that never discriminated is a known problem; a test that discriminated
until an unrelated change took the ability away is a harder one, because the
change that broke it is not the change anyone would look at.

Two documentation claims that stated the old week are corrected with it. The
public example asserted a January Friday was a weekend, which is now false, and
the shared holiday function opened by declaring a Sunday to Thursday week for
countries that no longer agree on one. That docstring now points at the working
week table rather than restating it, since restating it is what let the two drift
apart.

One known limitation is now written down where the next reader will meet it
rather than left to be rediscovered. The Middle East holidays are a single set
shared by four countries, so it returns UAE National Day for Saudi Arabia, Qatar
and Kuwait as well, and the Saudi national days are missing entirely. Separating
them means splitting the function per country, which is a wider change than a
working week and is deliberately not attempted here. Bahrain and Oman have a
working week and no holiday function at all.

Nothing else in the file moves. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman
keep their weeks, and no line naming any of them is added or removed.

test(documents): the Chinese render tests exercise the shapes production sends

Two of the stand-in values these tests hand to the document builders did not
match what the product actually passes, so two of the assertions were being made
about a document the product never produces.

The report builder takes a generated-at value that is a string column, and the
service passes the stored value straight through. The test was handing it a
datetime, which the builder stringifies on its way into the header, so the test
rendered a space and six digits of microseconds where the product renders the
stored ISO text. The assertion still passed, on different characters than ship.

The punch list builder resolves a party name through a lookup map before falling
back to the raw column, because the assignment control writes an identifier
there while the seeder writes a different kind of identifier. The test passed an
empty map, so every case took the fallback and the resolved route, which is the
common one in production, was never exercised at all. The Chinese case now puts
an identifier in the column and the name in the map, and the German case keeps
the stored-name route, so both real shapes are covered rather than one.

A third mismatch was left alone deliberately, with a comment recording why. The
punch list identifier is annotated as a parsed value and receives text, but both
uses in the builder are plain interpolation with nothing type-specific, and the
text passed is character for character what stringifying the parsed value gives.
Changing it would satisfy a type checker and alter nothing that is drawn.

Scope of what these tests can be read as proving, since the difference matters.
They start at the builder boundary. They establish that a builder selects its
face from the text it is given and that the produced bytes carry the codepoints
rather than a missing-glyph marker, with the control run in both directions so
the wiring is measured rather than the library's own behaviour. They say nothing
about the route and service layers above the builder. Two of the wired renderers
have no glyph coverage here at all: one is covered only by an older test that
asserts nothing about glyphs, and the other is written inline in a request
handler and cannot be reached without a database.

fix(pdf): the face is chosen by asking the font, not by guessing from the codepoint

Face selection asked whether text was Chinese. The question a renderer actually
needs answered is whether the face it is about to draw with can draw the
characters it has been given. Those two coincide for Chinese and come apart
everywhere else, and the gap between them was producing wrong output in both
directions.

Selection now asks the font. A TrueType face is asked for the glyph; a built-in
Type 1 face is asked through its encoding vector and codec. Text walks a ladder,
starting from whichever face the generator already uses, then the bundled
Unicode face, then the Chinese pack, and takes the lowest rung that can draw
every character it holds. Answers are cached per face and codepoint, except a
face the library cannot resolve at all, which is deliberately not cached: that
usually means registration has not run yet, and remembering the miss would make
it permanent for the life of the process.

Three defects surfaced the moment the question became per character, and none of
them would have shown up in a passing suite.

The squared metre sign fell off the ladder and came back as the Latin face,
which cannot draw it, so a bill written in Chinese units rendered its unit column
as boxes while the surrounding text was fine. It is not in any Chinese codepoint
range, which is precisely why a range-based test never caught it.

Where nothing on the ladder covered the whole string, the previous code returned
the first rung rather than the best one. That pinned Korean and Thai to a face
with no glyphs for either, and worse, pinned any Latin text sharing the string
with them. It now returns the widest available face, which was checked rather
than assumed: across all two hundred and eighteen printable Windows Latin
codepoints the Unicode face draws everything the built-in draws, the only
exception being a control character no document contains.

The Chinese pack is the one face the library cannot be asked directly, because it
carries neither a character map nor widths and leaves the mapping to the reader.
Its repertoire is now taken from the encoding table already shipped with the
standard library, unioned with Windows Latin so that a mixed string does not have
to give up its ideographs in order to keep its ASCII. That is still a declaration
rather than a measurement and the docstring says so, but it is a published table
instead of a hand-typed one, and it puts Korean, Thai, Arabic, Hebrew and
Devanagari correctly outside the pack.

Two claims made in an earlier commit are corrected here. That the Chinese pack
has no Latin-1 accented forms is not supported by measurement and should not have
been written. That it has no kana is simply wrong; the repertoire has carried
them since the 1980 national standard, and they now resolve correctly. Neither
affects the design, which rests on the half that is proven: the Latin face has no
glyphs for Han, and boxes are unrecoverable.

The older script-range helper is left exactly as it was, with its tests. It has no
caller outside its own module and tests, nothing on the selection path consults
it, and redefining what a shipped name answers is worse than leaving it beside a
better one. It is now documented as a question about scripts rather than about
whether anything can be drawn.

The negative control changed to match. It used to replace the predicate, which
tested the test; it now disables the Chinese rung, which is the switch the
product itself would throw, and it still fires.

fix(einvoice): the invoice can draw the names it is issued to

The hybrid invoice builder set a Latin built-in face at all ten of its drawing
sites and registered nothing else, while drawing the seller name, the buyer name
and every line description. Any character outside Latin-1 came out as a box, so
this was never only a Chinese problem: Cyrillic, Greek, Hebrew and Arabic names
all failed the same way, on a document that is issued as a legal record and on a
product that ships forty-two languages. The module is also one of the few that
already consults a language resolver, so it knew what it was drawing and drew it
wrong anyway.

The face is now chosen from the text at each drawing site, not for the document
and not for the process. A single invoice can carry a buyer in one script and a
seller in another, and each string is drawn with a face that can draw it.

Existing invoices are unchanged, byte for byte, and that is tested rather than
argued. The test recovers the previous builder from the last commit, runs it, and
compares its whole output against the new one for a German and an English
invoice. Nothing is excluded from the comparison: the library's deterministic
mode pins the creation date and document identifier, which are the only bytes
that vary for reasons unrelated to fonts, and with those pinned the files are
equal. The test carries its own control, since a Chinese invoice through the same
builder must not produce those bytes, so it cannot pass by comparing something
against itself.

That identity depends on setting the face only when it changes. The library
writes a font operator on every call without checking whether the font is
different, so selecting per string unconditionally would have moved the bytes of
every invoice ever issued even where the answer was the same Latin face each
time. The helper draws directly when the base face can already draw the string,
and only selects, draws and restores when it cannot.

The document stays a hybrid and stays unembedded. There is no font program of any
kind in the output, the Chinese face is referenced through the standard character
map and left to the reader, and the embedded structured invoice, its metadata and
the relationship that binds it to the document all survive, each held by a test.

Two width problems were measured while doing this and neither is fixed here,
because fixing them moves Latin bytes and that belongs in its own change. The
seller name clears its column comfortably, at 82.5mm against 90mm available for a
long Chinese company name. The buyer name has only 80mm and the same name
overruns it slightly. The line description is far worse: it is truncated at sixty
characters and drawn into 95mm, and sixty Chinese characters measure 169.3mm,
which runs straight across the quantity, unit and price columns. The cap is a
width budget written as a character count, and it is already close to the edge
for Latin at roughly 90mm of the 95 available, so this is a pre-existing
weakness that non-Latin text merely makes visible.

A claim repeated in a test docstring is corrected in place rather than only in a
commit message, since a false statement left in the tree outlives any message
about it. The Chinese pack does carry a good part of the accented Latin range,
including the u-umlaut, contrary to what was written; it stops short of the
o-umlaut, the sharp s and the euro sign, all three of which appear on an ordinary
German invoice. The conclusion the docstring drew still holds, now for a reason
that is true.

fix(calendar): each Gulf country gets its own holidays instead of a shared set

One holiday function served four Gulf countries, and two more had a working week
with no holidays at all. It is now six functions, one per country.

The defect that mattered was not a missing date but a borrowed one. The shared
set returned the National Day of the United Arab Emirates, on the second and
third of December, for Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Kuwait as well. A missing holiday
reads as absent data and somebody eventually notices. A borrowed one returns a
confident wrong answer, and a deadline in Riyadh moved for a day that country
does not observe. That is now asserted directly: no Gulf country returns another
country's national day.

Read the removal first, because it is the only one. Five countries gain dates and
Saudi Arabia loses exactly one, the Gregorian New Year, which the shared set gave
it and which Saudi Arabia does not observe. Being the only date taken away it is
the only change that could regress without announcing itself, so it has a test of
its own, and that test carries a control asserting the UAE and Kuwait still keep
the first of January. Without the control it could not tell a corrected Saudi
calendar from a New Year line deleted for everybody, and both mutations were run
to confirm it distinguishes them.

Bahrain and Oman were not a split, they were absent. Both had a working week and
no entry in the holiday table, so the lookup fell through to an empty set and
every day that was not a weekend counted as a working day. No Eid was ever
reachable for either country. That class now has one member left: China still has
a working week and no holiday function, and Chinese New Year is lunisolar and
needs a curated table rather than a rule.

Each country carries its own fixed days, sourced rather than borrowed. Two sets
are deliberately partial and say so in their own docstrings, along with the
consequence, which is that a short holiday list overcounts working days and
therefore pulls derived deadlines earlier. Naming the direction matters more than
naming the gap, because early is the direction that quietly costs somebody time
they were entitled to.

One seam is left open and named rather than papered over. The Eid conversion is
correctly shared, since the first of Shawwal and the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah fall
on the same Gregorian day everywhere and there is nothing national about the
arithmetic. The number of days each Eid runs is policy, announced annually by each
government, and it remains one placeholder applied to six countries, closest to
right for the country it was originally written for and too short for Saudi
Arabia. Rather than invent six numbers, the docstring and the Eid test both state
that the test covers the conversion and not the observance.

A test written two commits ago broke here and deserved to. It used the first of
December 2026 as its example of an ordinary working day in the UAE, and the first
of December is Commemoration Day. The old shared set had never heard of that day,
so nothing could contradict the choice at the time. It is the same shape as a
test whose anchor stops discriminating, arriving from the other direction: the
assertion was sound until the data underneath it got better.

The same trap was avoided while writing the new anchors. Every national day was
checked to fall on a working weekday in its own country before being used, which
is how Qatar National Day on the eighteenth of December 2026 turned out to be a
Friday, and therefore a Qatari weekend. Routed through the public working-day
call it would have passed with no holiday data at all, so it is asserted by set
membership instead, where no weekend rule can short-circuit it.

The audit for such tests was itself the most useful finding, and it is worth
recording because the instrument was wrong before the answer was. A search over
the test source for calls naming a country found twelve calls and flagged one.
Replacing it with a wrapper around the function itself, installed before
collection, found twenty-eight calls and flagged four. The three it had missed
all passed the country through a loop variable rather than a literal, which the
search could not see. The coverage of the audit was being decided by the shape of
the call when the question was about coverage at all. Where the question is every
call to something, wrap the something; a search over source is bounded by syntax.
All four flags are correct by intent and none is changed: they sit in the two
working-week tests where the weekend rule is the mechanism under test.

Nothing in the running product reads any of this yet. The public working-day call
has a single application caller and it passes Germany.
