feat(calendar): China gets a holiday table, and it checks its own arithmetic

China had a working week and no holidays, so every day that was not a weekend
counted as a working day. It was the last country in that state; every country
with a working week now has a holiday function behind it.

Four of the festivals are lunisolar and none of them can be computed from
anything this module depends on, so they come from a curated table covering 2024
to 2030, following the pattern already used for the other calendar that needs
one. New Year's Eve is derived as the day before Spring Festival rather than
stored beside it, so the two cannot drift apart in a later edit.

The 2025 reform is a real threshold rather than a rounding of history. Before it
the statutory count is eleven days a year, after it thirteen, because that reform
added New Year's Eve to the Spring Festival block and a second day to Labour Day.
One year in the window returns twelve rather than thirteen, because Mid-Autumn
lands on the third day of the National Day block, and the test states that in its
own parameter so the number is not filed as a bug by whoever meets it next.

Running out of the window is loud. A year past the table warns rather than
logging quietly, and returns only the six fixed Gregorian days. A test pins that
exact set, asserts the warning fires, and carries a control asserting that a
covered year does not warn. Silence at the edge of a curated table is how a table
becomes wrong without anyone finding out.

The table guards its own arithmetic, which matters because the real risk to a
hand-curated table is a future editor adding a row by guessing. Lunar festivals
sit a bounded distance from the same year's own lunar new year, so every row is
checked: Dragon Boat between 120 and 124 days after that row's Spring Festival,
Mid-Autumn in one of two bands depending on whether that year carries a leap
month. One year in the window has its leap month falling between the two
festivals, so the pair have to disagree with each other in a particular way
rather than moving together, which is what gives the check teeth rather than
merely a shape. What it cannot catch is a table shifted uniformly, since every
offset is relative, and the docstring says so. Qingming is a solar term and sits
outside the scheme entirely, so it gets only a narrow calendar bound that limits
the damage rather than proving the date.

That guard was proved against a real defect rather than a synthetic one. The
seeded work calendar for China carries two 2025 festival dates inside a row
labelled 2026; dropping those into this table turns the offset check red.

The direction of error is stated honestly and it is not the reassuring answer.
China reassigns working days each year, moving particular weekends to bridge
holidays, and that arrangement is announced annually and is not derivable, so it
is not modelled. It is a swap rather than a grant, so the two unmodelled halves
pull opposite ways: unmodelled days off count real holidays as working and pull a
deadline earlier, unmodelled working weekends push it later, and because the
arrangement borrows about what it spends they roughly cancel across a year. What
is wrong is less the annual total than which days carry it, and the sign of the
error on any given span depends on where that span begins and ends relative to a
festival. So China has no guaranteed safe direction, and the docstring says that
explicitly and says how it differs from the two partial sets nearby, which can
only ever be conservative because they are merely short.

Two of the new anchors could not be asserted through the public working day call,
for the same reason found earlier in the Gulf: one festival falls on a Sunday and
one of the Labour Day pair on a Saturday, so a weekend rule would answer before
any holiday was consulted. Both are asserted by set membership instead. The
control day was chosen the same way and one candidate was rejected during
writing, a Monday inside the National Day block, which is a genuine day off in
China while this function calls it working. Asserting it would have written the
known limitation into a passing test.

fix(i18n): the Chinese work calendar stops holding last year's festivals

The seeded Chinese row is labelled 2026 and carried two 2025 dates. Dragon Boat
sat on the thirty-first of May and Mid-Autumn on the sixth of October, which are
the correct dates for 2025 with only the year advanced. The day and month were
left alone, which is what makes it a copy-forward rather than a typo.

The arithmetic identifies it without needing any external source. A lunisolar
festival sits a bounded distance from the same year's own lunar new year, so
Dragon Boat belongs 120 to 124 days after it and Mid-Autumn 219 to 222, or
249 to 252 in a year carrying a leap month. Measured against Spring Festival
2026 the seeded values came to 103 and 231, both outside. Measured against
Spring Festival 2025 the same day and month come to 122 and 250, both inside.
The corrected dates come to 122 and 220.

New Year's Eve was missing and is added. It is a statutory day since the 2025
reform and it falls the day before Spring Festival, so its absence removed a
real closure from the middle of the block.

This one is reachable, which is what separates it from the calendar corrections
around it. The working-days calculation is exposed as a public endpoint and
subtracts exactly these rows, so the count moves: 2026 goes from 251 working
days to 249, and holidays landing on a working day from ten to twelve. The
thirty-first of May was a Sunday and cost nothing; the two corrected dates are
both Fridays, so both bite. Before this, every Chinese deadline derived through
that endpoint arrived two days early, and early is the direction that quietly
takes time away from whoever is relying on it.

The row survived because it was half right. Spring Festival and Qingming are
correct for 2026, so anything that checked a date rather than the whole row came
back clean.

The rest of the seeded data was swept for the same authoring mistake rather than
assumed clean. Of 367 exception entries across thirty rows, 44 are lunar or
lunisolar and can be phase-checked; 40 are correct. Every Islamic date across
four countries lands within a day of its anchor, and the uniformity of that
offset is itself evidence the check is calibrated rather than lenient. So this is
two bad rows, not a systematic vintage problem.

Two findings from that sweep are deliberately not in this commit. Korea carries
the same defect on the same festival, three adjacent days shifted together, and
is a separate country on the same endpoint. India has a spring festival sitting
on a new moon when it is a full moon observance, which is a different mechanism
and whose correct replacement is a convention choice rather than a computation,
so it is left for someone who can settle the convention.

test(i18n): the seeded lunisolar festivals check their own spacing

The Chinese row shipped two festival dates carried forward from the previous
year, and nothing in the tree could have noticed. This adds the arithmetic that
would have.

A lunisolar festival sits a bounded distance from the same year's own lunar new
year, so a row can be checked against itself with no external source at all,
which is what makes it worth having on data that is curated by hand. Dragon Boat
falls 120 to 124 days after that row's lunar new year; Mid-Autumn and Chuseok
219 to 222, or 249 to 252 where a leap month intervenes.

It reads the shipped file rather than the schema, for the same reason the
weekday guard does: the seeder builds rows straight onto the model, so no write
schema ever sees this data. Guarding the door does not help when the data came
through the wall.

The anchor is the row's own named lunar new year, matched exactly so that an eve
or a second day cannot answer in its place. That choice is deliberate and its
alternative is pinned by a test rather than left to a comment, because anchoring
on the first date of the block instead would not fail today: an eve is one day
earlier, which spends a day of the tolerance and still lands inside the band. It
would only surface years later on a row sitting at the edge, long after anyone
remembered the anchor was chosen carelessly.

Two floors, so the check cannot pass by having nothing left to inspect, and the
vacuity case is demonstrated rather than argued: renaming every festival so
nothing is measurable leaves the comparison green and turns the floor red.

Three limits are recorded next to the guard rather than discovered later. It
cannot catch a table shifted uniformly, since every offset is relative to
another date in the same row. It does not prove Qingming, which is a solar term
and gets only a narrow calendar bound, kept in its own test named as the weaker
check so a clean run is not read as verification. And it is blind to a festival
that is simply absent, which is precisely the half of the original defect that
was found by reading rather than by arithmetic.

One row is exempt with its reason attached, because Korea carries the same
defect on the same festival and has not been repaired yet. The exemption is a
ratchet rather than an amnesty: a further test fails as soon as an exempt row
stops violating, so a repaired row cannot leave a stale exemption behind to
quietly cover the next defect.

fix(schedule): the Monday-zero calendar refuses an ISO weekday

The seeded calendar was taught to refuse a zero, which cannot be an ISO weekday.
This is the mirror: the other calendar system counts Monday as zero and Sunday as
six, and it accepted a seven, which cannot be one of those either. The engine's
own docstring already recorded a seven arriving as a known mistake, so this is a
gate on something that has happened rather than something imagined.

Tracing what actually reaches the engine found a second entrance nobody had
named. Beyond the calendar schemas, a schedule carries a free-form metadata
dictionary that is persisted verbatim, and the calendar resolver reads a working
week straight out of it into the engine without any schema in between. Gating
only the named schemas would have left the mirror half open, so both refuse now.

The bound and the check live beside the engine because both schema modules
already depend on it, which avoids a cross-module import the codebase elsewhere
goes out of its way to defer. The literal range inside the parser is replaced by
the same constants, so the range is stated once rather than in three places.

The engine itself is unchanged and still tolerates what it always did. This gates
the writers, not the consumer, and the existing test that requires the engine to
swallow an out-of-range value still passes. The two calendar systems remain
separate; nothing here reconciles one convention with the other.

No migration, and that is a decision rather than an omission: no shipped value in
this system is out of range, so there is nothing to repair.

The instrument had a defect of its own, found after it looked finished. Its
failure message sorted the offending values directly, which raises on a list
mixing text and numbers, and that line sits in the branch that only runs once
there is something to report. It would have crashed exactly when it finally had
something to say, and no test covered it because every real week in the tree is
whole numbers. The first repair was also wrong: splitting the values by
membership silently loses a boolean, since a boolean compares equal to a number.
Both are fixed and pinned.

Recorded without being acted on: a third table states a different Gulf working
week again, and every value in it is in range, so no gate here will ever flag it.
A fourth representation stores day names instead of numbers. Anyone assuming
there are two opinions about the working week should know there are four.

fix(packs): the China pack stops naming standards it does not enforce

The pack declared eight validation rule packs and one of them exists. The other
seven name real Chinese standards, the quantity calculation code, four structural
codes, the fire code and the green building assessment standard, and behind each
of those names there is nothing: no rules in the core engine and no reference
pack files in the pack itself. They are now removed from the declaration and kept
as a comment naming each one as planned rather than built, so nobody re-adds a
slug believing it once worked.

The measurement is worth stating because the first one was wrong. Resolving the
slugs against the engine returned nothing at all, including for the one that is
real, and the reason was the reader rather than the pack: the rule registry is
empty until the built-in registration runs, and a bare import never runs it. With
the registration performed first, the surviving slug resolves to exactly two
rules, both over the bill of quantities item code, one requiring it to be present
and one requiring a 9-digit or 12-digit national code. A zero from a reader that
has a default is a fact about the reader.

Nothing shipped was silently broken by the seven, and the pack's own apply path
is why. It sorts declared rule packs into those the engine knows and those it
does not, and reports the remainder as documentation-only in a warning. So an
operator applying this pack has always been told, in a sentence at the bottom of
a dialog, that seven of its eight promises are documentation. The defect was that
the manifest, the package description and the docstring all said otherwise, and
those are what a buyer reads.

The edition label is corrected in the same pass and in the same spirit. The pack
said GB/T 50500-2024. The shipped 9-digit item codes were authored against the
2013 text, that is the only edition whose text is in hand, and the 2024 edition
along with the GB/T 50854-2024 measurement family could not be obtained, so
conformance to them is not claimed. The prefix carries the distinction and is the
reason the label cannot simply be dated: the 2013 edition is GB, a mandatory
code, and the 2024 edition is GB/T, a recommended standard. The classification id
keeps its original spelling because it names the pack directory and the key the
item codes are filed under, not an edition, and a comment above it says so
because it is exactly the kind of thing a later reader would correct back.

The description now lists what the pack actually does: Simplified Chinese and

string cell came out as empty boxes even after the document had registered

attendee and action tables, the BI dashboard report table and the property

were left alone, they pick their own face and were never affected.

control run in both directions: with the pack registered the glyphs resolve,

fix(einvoice): a wide name is clipped at its column, not across the page

Making the wide scripts legible did not create the column overflow, it widened
one that was already there. Sixty Han characters in the line description drew
128.9mm of Helvetica boxes against a 95mm column before the face wiring, and
169.3mm of real glyphs after it, so the page went from an unreadable overrun to
a readable one. Measured rather than assumed, because the two answers meant
different things and only one of them was ordinary work.

The clip is a monotone tightening. It takes the narrower of the character cap
that was already there and the width measured in the face that will actually
draw the string, so it can only ever shorten what the page drew and never
lengthen it. A Latin description inside both limits is returned untouched,
which is why the byte-identity test still passes without being relaxed. A Latin
description that already overran is now cut at the column edge, and that is the
only case where Latin output moves at all.

Measuring in the face that draws matters more than it looks. Helvetica and the
CID pack do not share a width table and a Han character is close to a full em
where a Latin one is about half, so measuring a Chinese name in the base face
under-counts it by nearly half and clips it in the wrong place. There is a
control asserting the two measurements really do disagree, since a clip that
measured in the wrong face would still pass a naive test.

No ellipsis is appended, and that is a decision against the instruction this
change was written to. The instruction was to watch the marker's own width so
it sits inside the budget, which assumed a marker. Adding one at all would move
the bytes of any Latin invoice whose description is cut at the character cap
but still fits its column, and those invoices are precisely what the identity
guarantee protects. A silent cut is worse to read than a marked one, so this is
a real cost, but it is the smaller one: the guarantee is worth more than the
marker, and a marker can be added later on its own terms once someone decides
which existing invoices may move.

Four strings a party controls are clipped, each at the offset that follows it
rather than at one shared number: the seller name at 90mm where the bill-to
column starts, the buyer name at 80mm because its block starts 90mm in and ends

One instrument correction that came with it. The first version of the width
test looked for the longest leading run of a name in the whole extracted page

fix(property_dev): a name reaches the document as text, not as markup

Seven strings we ship carry a bare ampersand and are drawn through a corrupting
path today. They are clause headings in the jurisdiction packs, "Governing Law
& Jurisdiction" and "Completion & Possession" among them, and they go into
generated sales contracts. This is not a fault waiting for an unusual customer
name, it is product data going through the parser on every contract that uses
those packs.

A reportlab Paragraph takes a small HTML-like markup, so every value these
generators interpolated into one was parsed rather than printed. Nothing
raises. The file opens, looks plausible and goes to a regulator.

Measured against the unfixed renderer, the parser does four different things.
A left angle bracket starts a tag, so "Baufeld <Nord>" draws as "Baufeld" and
the rest of the name is gone. An ampersand followed by a letter reads as an
unterminated entity and a semicolon is injected after the next word, so "R&D
Tower" draws as "R&D; Tower" and "AT&T Plaza" draws as "AT&T; Plaza". A name
stored with a literal "&" decodes to a bare ampersand. And an ampersand
followed by a space is left alone.

That fourth behaviour is why nobody has ever seen this. Every one of the seven
shipped headings uses ampersand-space, so all seven render correctly and always
have. It is also why the first version of the test could not have caught the
bug: it used "Meyer & Sohn", which passes against the broken renderer, not
because the path is safe but because the input dodges the parser. The cases
that carry the finding are the ones where an ordinary name is corrupted, so the
test now separates the inputs the parser mangles from the ones it happens to
tolerate and asserts both directions.

The fix goes in the funnel. Two hundred and forty of the two hundred and fifty
three paragraph sites in the module go through the _p helper, so _p now escapes
by default and takes an explicit markup flag for the eleven sites that write
reportlab markup on purpose. Opting out is not a way to skip the work, it only
moves the escaping inside the markup, so all eleven escape whatever they
interpolate. The list of new owners escapes each name before joining them
rather than joining first. The thirteen direct Paragraph calls bypass the
funnel and escape at the value, in the regulator disclosure in service.py and
in the regulatory report renderer. The one interpolation deliberately left raw
is the font face name inside a font tag attribute, which is our own output and
would break the tag if escaped.

A correction about how completeness was checked. The first version of the gate
reported the fix complete, and it was wrong in a way worth recording: it
carried an exemption clause, written into it by hand, that skipped any site
mentioning the translation helper. It therefore could not tell a site that
escapes its translated label from one that merely names the helper. With the
exemption removed the gate flagged eight real misses, all of them signature
lines interpolating a translated label unescaped. Those labels come from a
locale loader that accepts a user-written override, which makes them
user-authored in a deployment rather than translator-authored, so they belong
in the same class as a party name. They are escaped now and the gate runs with
no exemptions at all.

The escaping idiom follows the rest of the codebase, which already solved this
in boq, closeout, contracts and daily_diary with a module-local helper and a
bare html.escape. No new dependency, html is stdlib.

Proved on the produced bytes with the control in both directions: the same
seven strings through the fixed funnel come back unchanged, and through a raw
Paragraph five are still corrupted and the two ampersand-space cases are still
untouched. A separate assertion holds the other edge, that the summary values
are bare table cells rather than markup and must not be escaped, or the
entities would print literally.

Deliberately not done. The duplicate renderers in this module are left as they
are and not merged. This lands with six module-local escape helpers across the
codebase, which is one rule in six places and is not a finished decision; a
follow-up consolidates them onto one helper and does nothing else, so that this
correctness fix does not wait behind a refactor of six modules.

test(demo): the route sweep stops seeing five routes out of three thousand

The demo read-only guard proves its guarantee by sweeping every mutating route
and checking each one is covered. On the FastAPI version CI resolves, that sweep
was seeing five routes. The application mounts 3225.

From 0.141 an included router is stored as an opaque wrapper rather than being
flattened into the application's route list, and the wrapper carries neither the
methods nor the path the old loop filtered on. So every router-mounted route fell
out of the census silently, and websocket routes were not visible at the top level
at all. What survived the filter was the handful of routes declared directly on
the application. The test went green over a sweep of five, which is the worst
shape a guard can take: it did not fail, it stopped looking.

The fix walks the structure recursively, following each wrapper to the router it
wraps and accumulating the prefix from the include context, falling back to the
route's own path where neither is present. Measured against the same nested and
mirrored application on both versions it returns identical results, prefixes
included. On the real product it finds 3225 mutating routes on the pinned desktop
version and 3225 on the version CI resolves.

FastAPI's own flattening helper was tried first and rejected on measurement. It
resolves HTTP paths correctly and yields an empty path for every websocket route
on 0.141, so it cannot enumerate the sockets this guard exists to check. The
walker is used for both, and the generated schema is kept as a second opinion for
HTTP only, which is what the assertions say.

The census now asserts its own denominator, because that is the part that would
have caught this. A floor of one thousand mutating routes fails loudly if the
traversal collapses again, and the failure message names the routes it did find
and points at the walker, so the next reader does not have to re-derive any of
it. Restoring the old traversal produces exactly that failure, listing the same
five routes another census had independently arrived at. The cross-check against
the schema asserts the walker is at least the schema count rather than equal to
it: the loader mirrors each underscore-named module at a legacy prefix with the
schema flag off, so 3225 against 2248 is the mirror, not an error, and both
numbers are floored independently.

A second version-dependent defect turned up while proving the first, and it was
in the test rather than the product. On 0.141 the dependency list on a
router-mounted socket route is empty: application-level and include-level
dependencies are no longer copied onto each route when it is included, they are
applied from the router chain when the request arrives. The assertion read that
empty list and reported that a live socket carried no guard, which would have gone
red in CI and read as a security failure while nothing was wrong. Driving a real
handshake in both directions shows the guard runs and refuses exactly as it does
on the pinned version. The check tested where a dependency is stored, which has
now changed once, instead of whether it applies. It now unions the route's own
dependencies with those inherited from the router chain and the application.

That union is known to be narrower than the merge the older version performs: a
dependency passed to the include call itself is reconstructed by neither of the
two lists this reads, and it passes today only because nothing in the product
passes dependencies that way for these sockets. That is luck rather than
correctness and it is being fixed on top of this, separately, by the reader who
found it. It is recorded here rather than left for someone to discover, because a
guard that is right by accident is the same class of thing as the sweep this
commit repairs.

The suite runs in no blocking lane today, which is why none of this was caught,
so it is added to the access-control job. It runs on its own deliberately: a
background sweeper moves data underneath it when it shares a lane. Both versions
pass the whole file, 21 tests each.

docs(pdf): state what we do to Arabic and Hebrew, and pin it

Right-to-left names escalate to the bundled Unicode face like any other script
the base face cannot draw, so the glyphs exist and the correct codepoints reach
the content stream. What does not happen is layout. No bidirectional reordering
and no contextual shaping run, so Arabic is drawn in isolated forms rather than
joined, and both scripts go down in logical order and read backwards on the
page.

That is a deliberate trade and it was worth writing down rather than leaving
for the next reader to discover. Boxes replace the codepoint with glyph zero
and nothing downstream can recover it; escalating gets the presentation wrong
but keeps the data right, which is the better failure on a document whose text
has to be checkable against the structured data beside it. It is still wrong.

So the limitation is now in the module docstring in plain words, where someone
opening the file meets it, and two tests pin the current behaviour. The first
asserts the half that is right: the name escalates rather than boxing, and
every codepoint survives. The second asserts the half that is wrong, that the
text comes back exactly reversed. It asserts the exact reversal rather than
just inequality, so that a partial implementation reordering some runs and not
others fails too.

The second test is meant to fail the day bidirectional layout is implemented.
Its message says so and says to replace it with a real layout assertion, which
is the difference between a documented limitation and an undiscovered one.

Deliberately not done. Bidirectional reordering and shaping are not implemented
here. That is a substantial piece of work with its own decisions and it does
not belong in a font-selection change.

fix(demo): the demo seeders stop writing into projects nobody asked about

Several demo seeders were pointed at every project in the database. On a
developer machine that is only noisy. On an installation where somebody has
created real projects, it means invented tender packages, change orders and
accommodation bookings appearing inside their work, authored by nothing they did.

The worst of it was a fallback that guessed. When the curated set of demo
projects could not be resolved, the code took the first three projects it found
and treated them as the demo set. There is no ordering that makes those three the
right three, and on a populated installation they are simply three customer
projects. The fallback is gone. The focus set is now the flagship plus the
curated demo ids and nothing else, and when none of those are installed it is
empty, which is correct rather than a failure: with no demo projects present
there is nothing for a demo seeder to fill.

The tendering seeder is removed outright rather than repointed, and this is the
one deletion here so it deserves its reason. It was invoked across every project,
and the demo packs already build their own tender packages and bids as part of
the project they describe. So it was a second source of the same kind of row,
writing to projects that had not asked for one, competing with data that is
authored to match its project. Nothing imports it, in the tree or at the previous
commit beyond the two lines removed here, and no test names it.

The schedule seeder had the opposite defect and it is worth stating because it
reads as the same word. It was gated on a table-wide marker, so the moment any
one project had a board, the seeder concluded its work was done and returned. A
project joining the curated set afterwards was never filled, and nothing reported
it, because a skip on a marker looks identical to a skip on completion. It guards
per project now, which is what the marker was always meant to express. The other
seeders in this change carry the same per-project guard for the same reason.

There is no test here and that is a gap rather than an oversight I am hiding.
These paths run at startup against a live database and the existing demo tests
assert the flagship project's contents rather than which projects were touched.
The assertion worth having is the negative one, that a project outside the
curated set gains no rows, and it needs a fixture with a project that is not a
demo project at all. That is the shape to build next.

docs(calendar): two rows carry the leap band, not one

The offset guard's docstring said the 2028 row is the one that proves the test
has teeth, because its leap month falls between Dragon Boat and Mid-Autumn so the
two offsets have to disagree with each other rather than move together. That is
true of 2028 and it is equally true of 2025, which carries a leap sixth month
where 2028 carries a leap fifth. Their Mid-Autumn offsets are 250 and 251, both
inside the wider band.

Only the prose undercounted; the guard already handles both and no assertion
changes here. It matters because it is prose an editor adding a row would trust,
and reading it would leave them expecting exactly one row in the leap band. A
second one is then a defect rather than the arithmetic working, which is the
wrong way round. The docstring now says two rows land there and that this is
expected.

The dates behind the guard were verified against sources rather than recalled,
which is the half no internal consistency check can supply. A row measured
against its own anchor cannot detect a table shifted uniformly, and only an
outside source closes that. All 28 lunisolar dates across the seven-year window
are correct. The lunisolar and solar-term dates come from the Hong Kong
Observatory Gregorian-Lunar conversion tables, which compute on the 120 degree
east meridian on the same astronomical basis as the mainland calendar under
GB/T 33661-2017, parsed independently in the two formats they publish and
cross-checked against each other. The statutory holiday counts come from State
Council Order 795, and the arrangement for two separate years was checked against
the annual State Council notices, including the 2025 leap-month year, which is
the one most likely to expose a divergence between the two sources. It does not.

fix(closeout): the cover page draws the names it is built from

The closeout cover escaped its text and then drew it on a style that names a
fixed face, so it was safe from markup and still boxed every non-Latin
character in the document. A Chinese project name, package title, slot title or
evidence reference came out as empty boxes, and a box is unrecoverable: the
codepoint is replaced by glyph zero and nothing downstream can undo it.

Escaping and facing are two different questions about the same string, and a
module can pass one while failing the other. This one did.

Every paragraph in this document already went through one helper, and every
table cell in it is one of those paragraphs rather than a bare string, so the
fix is the helper asking for a face that can draw the text it was handed. That
is the same shape the bill of quantities and the daily diary already use. The
choice stays per string, so text the base face can draw comes back on the style
it came in on and the existing Latin output does not move.

Proved on the produced bytes in both directions. With the Chinese rung
available the four fields come back as characters and no glyph zero appears;
with the rung removed the same document boxes, which is the switch the product
would really have thrown. A third test builds a German cover after a Chinese
one to catch a per-process switch leaking between documents, and a fourth holds
the escaping that was already there, so that adding the face selection did not
cost it.

fix(i18n): 288 Chinese strings stop reading as English with Chinese words in it

The Chinese locale carried a class of string that is not a clumsy translation but
a word-by-word substitution, and the tell is that English function words survive
as standalone Chinese characters doing a job Chinese does not give them. "No rooms
to schedule yet" had become four characters meaning roughly not, room, to, schedule
followed by a dangling not-yet. "No matching this filter" was three fragments with
no verb. A reader of Chinese does not find these hard to read, they find them
unparseable, and there is nothing in the string to signal that it was ever meant
to say something.

288 strings are corrected. 178 of them are in the bill of quantities, which is
where a Chinese estimator spends the day, and the rest are spread across property
development, projects, costs, element matching, accommodation and admin.

The shapes, since they are not all one thing. 253 change a term or a particle,
which is where the mistranslations live: one of them used the word for a job
vacancy to mean a line item in a bill, so an estimator was being told that adding
a vacancy had failed. 25 keep exactly the same characters and only reorder them,
which is the pure calque: a phrase built in English order out of Chinese words,
correct in every part and wrong as a sentence. 10 are rewritten because there was
nothing recoverable.

The check that matters for a locale edit is not the wording, which cannot be
verified mechanically, but that the edit changed only what it claimed to. The key
set is identical before and after, 38175 keys in the same order, so nothing was
added, dropped or moved. Every changed line is a value line. Every replacement
carries Chinese characters, so no English leaked in behind a translation, and
every replaced line already carried Chinese, so this is a repair of Chinese rather
than the filling of a gap. Interpolation placeholders were compared against the
English source key by key across all 288: none regressed, and none was introduced
that the English does not have. That last one is the check worth keeping, because
a placeholder that does not exist in the source renders to the user as literal
braces and no reviewer reading for fluency would catch it.

Verified through a build rather than a type-check, since a locale file is a
TypeScript module the bundler has to be able to read. Full build clean, the
Chinese chunk emitted at 2.7 MB carrying the new wording, and the built page
resolves every asset it references.

One instrument note, because it nearly produced a false alarm of the worst kind.
Reading this change by pairing adjacent removed and added lines in the diff makes
it look like catastrophic corruption: values appear to land on unrelated keys, a
button labelled add-failed appearing to become add-a-custom-column. That is an
artefact of the diff format. With no context lines, a hunk removes several lines
before adding several, so pairing them positionally aligns each key with a
different key's value. Compared key by key instead, every one of the 288 is a
faithful edit of its own string. A locale diff has to be read as a mapping, never
as two adjacent columns.

feat(boq): bill column presets for China and Canada

Two presets, so an estimator in either country starts from the columns their own
bill actually has rather than building them by hand.

The Chinese one follows the comprehensive unit rate. Item code and feature
description as text, then labour, material and machinery as sums over the
resources carrying those roles, then management fee, profit and risk as free
input percentages. The last of those three is beyond a strict reading of the
composition and it is there deliberately: a comprehensive unit rate is the three
cost elements plus management fee, profit and risk, and leaving risk out gives a
Chinese estimator a composition that is one head short.

The feature description stays free text rather than becoming structured fields,
and that was a real decision rather than the easy path. Its content is prescribed
per item code across the whole of the measurement standard, so no fixed column
list can express it, and a preset that pretended otherwise would be wrong for
most item codes.

The three fee columns take free input instead of the derived percentage hint. The
hint renders read only and no resource role denotes a management fee, so it would
print either a resource share or a flat hundred and then refuse the correcting
edit. A test pins that they stay free input, because the hint looks like the
obvious thing to reach for.

The Canadian one is a rate composition rather than a second classification. The
existing North American preset covers classification and productivity and carries
no derived columns and no tax treatment, so this is a gap rather than symmetry.
Labour, material, equipment and subcontract as resource sums, overhead and profit
as free input, and a tax regime as a selector naming the regimes rather than
carrying rates, because provincial rates move and a stale rate in a preset is
worse than no rate. Its id names no standard, matching a decision already recorded
in the tree that the country has no single national one.

The Chinese preset is labelled GB 50500-2013. The label was written against the
2024 edition first and corrected against the tree: the shipped item codes were
authored to the 2013 text, that is the only edition whose text is in hand, and the
prefix carries the distinction, since the 2013 edition is a mandatory code and the
2024 edition is a recommended standard. The preset id keeps its original spelling
because it identifies the pack and the classification the codes are filed under
rather than an edition, and a comment says so, because that is exactly the thing a
later reader corrects back.

No new locale keys, because the dialog renders a preset name verbatim and every
existing preset uses a literal. The Chinese characters here are display names and
nothing else: eight lines carry them and all eight are a display_name.

Verified by a full build rather than a narrowed type check, since a narrowed
program is a fact about the program you selected. The whole-application type check
runs out of heap on this machine, exit 134 with no type errors reported, which is
a fact about memory rather than about this code. Twenty-four tests pass.

fix(finance): the Brazilian invoice draws the client it is addressed to

The invoice escaped its input carefully and then drew it on a style naming a
fixed face, so a client name or a service description outside the Latin range
came out as empty boxes on a document that was otherwise correct. Measured
before it was fixed: a Chinese client name produced glyph-zero runs on the
rendered page, which is unrecoverable, since the codepoint is gone rather than
merely mis-drawn.

Escaping and facing are two different questions about the same string.
Escaping decides whether the value is read as markup; facing decides whether
there is a glyph for it at all. This module answered the first one carefully,
and the care is why the second went unnoticed: a reader looking for injection
finds the escaping and stops.

Every cell of all four tables here is a paragraph built by the module's own
helper rather than a bare string, and nothing bypasses that helper, so facing
the helper faces the whole document. This is the same body the bill of
quantities and the daily diary already use. The choice stays per string, so
Portuguese text comes back on the style it came in on and the ordinary invoice
does not move.

Four tests, both directions. The Chinese invoice renders its client name and
service description; the control removes the Chinese rung and asserts the same
invoice boxes; a Portuguese invoice built after a Chinese one catches a
per-process switch leaking between documents; and the fourth holds the
escaping that was already here. That last one is not decoration. The helper
exists to stop a hidden-text attack arriving through the metadata block, so
losing the escaping while adding the facing would have been a security
regression, and the test asserts the attack string is still printed rather than
parsed.

The header above WORK_CALENDARS said the table defines hours_per_day,
working_days and typical holidays. Only the first of those is true. The second
is misnamed, the key is work_days, so anyone who grepped the name the comment
handed them found nothing. The third has never existed. And label, which every
entry carries, went unmentioned.

ref, in both quotings, returns nothing at all: the comment arrived together with
the table in 9e266fced and the capability it named has not existed for a single

against names catches the first kind and is structurally blind to the second.

fix(demo): a seeded resource buildup adds up to the rate it sits beside

The BOQ grid derives its resource columns by summing quantity times unit_rate
over a position's leaves, so the labour, material and plant columns are only
right if the leaves add up to the position rate. Across the seeded demo data
they did not. Of 4174 priced positions, 274 added up on the reading the grid
uses, 640 were off by more than five percent, and the worst was short by a
third of its own rate.

The cause is not the shares the branches declare, it is what happens to an
hourly leaf on a cheap position. The quantity of a labour or plant leaf is its
money divided by the crew rate, and it was stored to two decimal places. The
thirty percent labour share of a 0.42 rebar spacer is 0.13, and against a 50 an
hour crew that is 0.0026 hours, which rounds to 0.00 and prices the leaf out of
existence. Twenty-one leaves across the demo data carried no money at all, and
the rows they sit on read as pure material with no crew time on them, which for
a rebar spacer is a wrong answer rather than a rounding artefact. Four decimal
places is the coarsest precision at which nothing rounds away, and it leaves a
sub-cent residue behind.

That residue lands on the material leaf, and which leaf absorbs is forced
rather than convenient. An hourly leaf holds a quantized quantity against a
fixed crew rate, so the money it can express is a multiple of that rate and it
cannot land on an arbitrary remainder without distorting the rate itself. The
material leaf holds quantity 1.0 and carries its money in unit_rate, so it can
express any value exactly. Every one of the 4174 positions carries exactly one
such leaf and it is first in all of them, measured off the built objects rather
than read off the source. No position drives that leaf to zero or below, which
is the failure this arrangement could have introduced and did not.

Fixing the sum without fixing the precision would have been worse than leaving
it alone. The absorbing leaf would have swallowed the money the annihilated
leaves lost, so all 4174 positions would add up while the rebar spacer read as
a hundred percent material against a declared sixty-five, thirty and five. That
is a correct total over a buildup that no longer describes the work.

Two branches declared a composition summing to 0.95, the concrete branch and
the generic fallback, covering 1235 positions between them. They are corrected
to 1.00 by raising the material share, not because the arithmetic needs it, the
absorbing leaf would have covered the difference either way, but because the
source should not declare one composition while the code produces another. The
material share is the one raised because the missing five points belong there.
Raising plant instead would have put concrete pumps at twenty percent of a
concrete rate, closing the sum and degrading the buildup in the same motion.

Both consumers now read the same number rather than two nearly equal ones. Each
leaf's total is the money that leaf actually carries, so the grid, which
computes from quantity times unit_rate and never looks at total, and the
breakdown rollup, which prefers total, agree by construction. All 4174
positions are now exact on both readings, and the largest gap between the
composition the source declares and the one the code produces is 1.67 points,
on a position priced at 0.42.

The test asserts the identity over every position of every registered demo
template rather than a sample, which is the whole point: this was a
per-position rounding effect that only bit on cheap rows, and a sample would
have walked past it. It also pins the structural reason the identity is
reachable at all, so a branch added later with only hourly leaves fails by name
instead of drifting, and it pins the declared shares at the source so a short
composition cannot hide behind the absorbing leaf again. The three assertions
that carry the fix were each checked against the previous behaviour restored at
runtime, and each goes red on it.

Scope. This covers _make_resources, the buildup every demo template goes
through. The separate _resources_for_position helper has its own remainder
logic and a single call site and is untouched.

fix(finance): seven invoice cells stop printing their own bold tags

The Brazilian invoice asked for bold by writing inline markup into text it then
handed to the helper whose whole job is to escape what it is given. The escaping
worked, which is the problem: the page drew the tag characters. Every column
heading of the line item table and the net payable line printed the opening and

cell interpolates a formatted amount rather than carrying a literal, so an opt-out

the document that states what is owed, exactly the hole the escaping exists to
close. Weight through the style cannot go wrong that way, because it leaves no
route by which text reaches the parser unescaped.

says the tags are gone from the page text. The second says the six headings and
the net figure draw in a bold face, read off the font of each drawn run rather
than off the source. Deleting the markup and drawing plain text passes the first

assertions fail.

Without one the two are the same number, the figure appears twice on the page,
and a search for it cannot tell the bold row from the plain one. The first
version of that test had no retention and passed by reading the wrong run.

commit asserts that ordinary Latin output does not move, and fixing the tags

test(demo): the socket half of the census asserts wiring instead of a state nothing can reach

The websocket test in this file drove a probe socket that deliberately wrote,
to show the database tripwire refusing it. That was the right test while a
handshake was never refused, because the tripwire was the only thing holding a
socket. It is about to stop being the only thing, and once a handshake can be
refused the probe asserts a state the application cannot enter: a socket that
reaches the write is by definition one the allowlist named, and an allowlisted
socket is not what that assertion was about.

A test for an unreachable state is worse than no test. It passes, and it reads
as coverage, so the thing it used to prove quietly stops being proven while the
suite stays green. So the half that can no longer mean anything is removed
rather than adjusted, and what it used to cover moves to
test_demo_read_only_sockets.py, which asserts it against real and allowlisted
sockets in both polarities. The rewritten test names that file and the three
cases that went there, so the coverage can be followed rather than assumed.

What is left here is the half that belongs beside the HTTP census, and sockets
are the sharper case for it. A socket carries no method, so the mutating-route
sweep skips it by construction, and it is absent from the OpenAPI schema, so
the cross-check cannot see it either. Whatever is asserted about the wiring of
sockets is asserted here or nowhere.

It asserts the set rather than a floor, and that is the lesson of the census
one level up. "Every socket I found carries the guard" is a claim about the
sweep as much as about the guard, and it passes just as well on a sweep that
found two of three as on one that found all of them. Comparing against the
declared set makes a shrinking census a failure instead of a quieter pass, and
the message reports both directions separately because they mean opposite
things: a socket missing from the sweep is a census defect, one that appeared
is a socket nobody has decided about yet. Three entries for two declarations,
because the loader mirrors an underscore-named module at a legacy prefix.

Adding a socket is meant to fail here. That is not a side effect of using an
exact set, it is the reason for using one: a new socket should cost a line in
this file and a moment's thought about whether it belongs in the demo
allowlist.

Verified with the file it hands its cases to, in one process on the FastAPI
version the lane installs, 25 passed.

feat(demo): a read-only demo refuses a websocket it never allowlisted

Every HTTP route on the public demo is default-deny: the guard reads the method,
refuses anything unsafe, and an allowlist names the handful that stay live. A
websocket was exempt, and the comment said why, that an HTTPException is not
something a handshake can carry and neither of the two sockets we ship writes
anything. Both halves are true and the conclusion was still wrong. A socket
carries no method, so there is nothing to key a safe-versus-unsafe decision on,
and the only honest reading of no method is not known to be safe.

What the exemption cost is depth rather than a hole today. Everywhere else the
guarantee is two independent layers, so an allowlist mistake is cheap because
the other layer catches it. An exempt socket rested on the database tripwire
alone, and that tripwire has one documented blind spot, the raw-cursor bulk
insert in the costs router, which for an HTTP route layer 1 is exactly what
covers. Neither socket goes near it, which is why the claim held; a socket
added later that did would have broken it silently, and nothing would have
said so.

So sockets are default-deny too. Two endpoints are allowlisted by function
identity rather than by path, which covers every spelling in one entry: the
loader mirrors an underscore-named module at a legacy prefix, so presence is
mounted at two URLs that resolve to the same endpoint. A refused handshake
closes with 1008, which is policy violation and is what this is, and is already
the code both sockets use for their own auth refusals, so a client needs no new
case. The reason carries the machine-readable key and nothing else, because a
close reason is capped at 123 bytes and would not fit the message the 403
carries.

The comment on the allowlist is written for the person adding the third socket,
and the thing it tells them is that the cost of forgetting is silence. Measured
on the two clients we ship, neither of which reconnects: the notifications hook
has no close handler at all and degrades quietly to polling, and the presence
hook renders an empty roster, which a visitor cannot tell apart from nobody
else being here. A socket left out of the list does not fail loudly anywhere a
user or an operator is looking. It stops working on the demo and stays green
everywhere else.

The tests drive both polarities on one application, because either half alone
proves nothing. An allowlisted socket must still open with the flag on, or the
guard has simply broken the demo's realtime features rather than protected
them, and a stranger must be refused with the flag on and open with it off, or
the refusal is not the guard doing it. The stranger is mounted through an
include with a prefix rather than declared on the application, because that is
the only shape the product uses and the two are not equivalent. Its handler is
defined at module level, which is load-bearing: this file uses postponed
annotations and FastAPI resolves an endpoint's types out of its globals, so a
handler defined inside a test body has no resolvable annotation and the
handshake dies for a reason that looks exactly like the one under test.

Verified with the census file in one process on the FastAPI version the lane
installs, 25 passed together, and the pair now runs in that lane.

ci: the socket guard runs beside the census, and the step says what it really requires

The demo read-only step ran one file and said it ran alone on purpose. The
reason was real: the census counts every table, so a neighbour in the same
process that leaves a collaboration lock behind turns it red when the sweeper
reaps it, which is a true observation about a background worker and a very
confusing way to learn it.

Run alone was always a proxy for that, and the socket file is the case that
shows the difference. It was measured against the actual requirement rather
than the proxy: the presence socket reads the current lock rather than
acquiring one, and the file takes none, so it can share the process. Adding it
under a sentence that says the step runs alone would have left a false comment
guarding a real hazard, which is worse than no comment because the next person
trusts it. So the sentence is replaced by the requirement itself, that nothing
sharing the process may leave a collaboration lock behind, followed by what was
measured and the instruction to check anything added later the same way. The
protection survives; it no longer rests on a property the step has stopped
having.

The two files are complements and neither covers the other. The census proves
the guard is attached to every mutating HTTP route. The socket file proves a
handshake the allowlist does not name is refused, which the census cannot see
at all: a socket carries no method, so no count of mutating routes includes it,
and the database tripwire only speaks once a query is already on its way, by
which point the connection is established. Naming them in the same step means
neither can be dropped while the other keeps reporting green.

Cost, measured rather than guessed: 25 tests, 0 failed, 248 seconds on the
FastAPI version this lane installs, on a contended local box, and the same pair
came back 25 passed in 210 seconds on a second run. Nearly all of it is one
application build plus the cluster boot this job already pays for, which is why

fix(i18n): the working week outlives the year the seed file covers

The seeded work calendars cover exactly one year. All thirty rows are labelled
2026 and all 367 exception dates fall inside it, so any range ending after the
thirty-first of December leaves the data behind. That is not a January problem,
it is any forward-looking schedule longer than about four months.

For a range with no calendar in its own years, the last rung of the fallback
used a hardcoded Monday to Friday. It was written as though a country without a
calendar in the requested year had no calendar at all, when in this file it
always has one. Thirty rows, thirty countries, and exactly one of them is not
Monday to Friday. Saudi Arabia is seeded Sunday to Thursday, and past 2026 it
came back exactly inverted: Friday counted as a working day and Sunday as
weekend, the calendar upside down for a date range anyone can request today.
Our own 2026 row says Sunday is a working day there and our own 2027 answer said
it is not, so nothing external was needed to call it wrong.

The diagnosis is an asymmetry inside a single function. The working week already
had a fallback carrying the neighbouring year forward, described in the
docstring, covered by a named test, and sitting under a comment that explains
the Gulf move from Sunday-Thursday to Monday-Friday as the reason it exists. The
holidays beside it got none of that and are still confined to the years in
range. Same function, same data, one rung apart: one axis got a documented
fallback, a named test and an explanation, the other got silence. A working week
is a rule and can be carried forward, a holiday is a date and cannot, which is
why this change covers only the week. The holiday gap stays open and is now
stated in the docstring instead of left to be discovered.

Everything is asserted per day and never per year, and that is precisely why
this survived. Sunday to Thursday and Monday to Friday are both five days, so an
annual total comes out the same under either. Before this fix Saudi Arabia and a
country code we have never heard of both returned 261 working days for 2027. A
test asserting a yearly total here would be worse than no test because it would
pass, so the new suite pins the blind spot rather than stepping around it: one
case asserts the two totals are equal across 2029, a year beginning on a Monday
where the two weeks tie exactly, then shows the disagreement one day at a time.
Under a mutation disabling the new lookup that case fails on its per-day
assertion after its total assertion has already passed, which demonstrates the
blind spot instead of arguing it. The Monday to Friday control passes under the
same mutation, so a fallback that merely stopped resolving cannot hide there.

One more thing worth a sentence, because it is the third instance of it today.
Every existing test in this package builds its calendars with make_calendar,
including both cross-year tests, so the mechanism is proven green and is
structurally incapable of noticing that the shipped file holds a single year. A
fixture certifies the code and says nothing about the data, while reading in
review as coverage. The tests added here load the real seed through the real
seeder, and fail loudly if the row they depend on ever changes shape rather than
passing on an assumption that has quietly expired.

feat(i18n): the working-days answer says which years it was informed about

The seeded work calendars cover a single year, so a range ending after the
thirty-first of December is answered from a fallback rather than from data.
Refusing such a range was the alternative and it is the wrong one. A schedule
running past December is ordinary use, and turning a quiet wrong answer into a

fix(collab-locks): the presence frame stops calling an unread lock free

The first frame a presence socket sends carries the current lock holder. When
that read failed the handler set the lock to null and sent the frame anyway,
and null already means nobody holds it. So a lock the server could not read
arrived as a lock nobody holds, asserted with exactly the confidence of the
truth, and nothing was logged either way.

The frame now carries lock_state, which is held, free or unknown, because the
lock field on its own has no way to say unknown. The failed read is logged too,
but the log is not the fix. A log tells the operator which of the three
happened and leaves the client holding the same false statement.

This cannot be made visible to a user today, only correct, and a reader going
looking for the user-facing symptom should stop here rather than conclude the
commit overstated itself. Nothing renders the field. PresenceIndicator is the
only component that reads it and nothing imports PresenceIndicator; the one
live consumer of the presence socket reads the roster and never touches the
lock; and no write path anywhere consults a lock, so the editing conflict a
stale reading might have caused is prevented by the compare-and-swap in the
acquire path instead.

The reason to fix it now is that the trap is already written. PresenceIndicator
derives its holder from a falsy test on the lock field, so a failed read and a
genuinely free lock produce the identical "nobody is editing" badge. It is
coded and merely unmounted, and the first person to put that badge on the grid
inherits the lie without touching either file.

Three tests rather than one. A test that only expects unknown passes just as
well against a handler that answers unknown every time, which would be the same
defect with the polarity reversed, so free and held are asserted beside it.

The entity resolver in the same file moves from debug to exception. Failing
closed is right and being quiet about it is not: a database or import error and
a genuinely unreachable entity produce the same refusal, and at debug level
production had no way to tell them apart.

fix(pdf): a line break stops sending plain Latin to the Chinese face

The face ladder asks each rung whether it can draw every character of the string
and settles for its widest face when none of them can. That fall-off is right for
a script nothing carries, which is what it was written for: Hangul and Thai render
as much as any face manages instead of being swapped for a different box. A line
break is not a script. No face reports a glyph for one, so every rung failed and
any string carrying a newline, a carriage return or a tab landed on the widest
face, which is the Chinese pack. A bare newline on its own did too.

Those three characters now leave the question before it is asked. They are listed
one at a time with the reason beside them rather than taken as a category, because
a category wide enough to hold them also holds the zero-width marks, and those are
real characters that a face either has or has not got.

What it would have cost, since this is latent rather than live. The AIA payment
application writes its table headings with embedded newlines. Wiring that module's
paragraph helper, which is the next commit, made ten of its thirteen faced calls
escalate on whitespace alone, so an English-only payment application drew its
column headings in a Chinese CID face and grew by 1114 bytes. Nothing already
shipped is affected: wrapping the ladder and running the document suites gives
zero escalations that survive removing the never-drawn characters, across 117
tests and about 2700 ladder decisions. It goes live the moment the AIA module is
wired, which is why this lands first and on its own.

It was found by going to prove a byte-neutrality claim rather than by making it.
The first render after the facing change came back 1114 bytes larger, which was
not believable, so the instrument was checked before the result: two runs with no
change at all hash identically under reportlab's invariant mode, so the difference
was real rather than an artefact of the creation date.

Twelve cases in six tests. Each of the three characters gets a case inside Latin
text and a case on its own, and a ratchet asserts the excluded set is exactly
those three, so widening it later cannot skip its evidence. The controls are the
load-bearing half. Hangul and Thai still escalate off the base face, and the
discriminating pair is the one worth reading: a heading and a Hangul name differ
only in whether a character no face can draw is present, both carry the same
newline, and the first keeps its base face while the second does not. Without
those the change reads as the ladder escalating less, which is something a later
reader could widen until the feature stops working. With the fix reverted the six
whitespace cases fail and every fall-off control still passes, which is the shape
a boundary should have.

Deliberately not done. font_can_draw_all is untouched and goes on meaning
literally what its name says; the knowledge that a line break is layout rather
than a glyph sits at the call that makes a layout decision. No generator changed
and no document moved. The zero-width marks stay in the coverage question on
purpose.

fix(ws): a socket that cannot judge a token stops saying the token was bad

Both WebSocket handlers answered every authentication problem with a 1008
policy close and the reason "unauthenticated". Measured against the real
handlers rather than read off them, every failure those clauses were written
for already arrives as an HTTPException and is answered on the narrow path
above: a malformed, expired or wrong-type token, a subject that is not a UUID,
a user who does not exist or is inactive. So the entire live population of the
broad clauses was things that are not authentication failures, the database
being unreachable and configuration or programming errors, and each of them
was reported to the caller as rejected credentials. That is not a vaguer
answer than the truth, it is a lie about whose fault it is.

The broad clauses stay broad, which is right for a socket handler. They raise
instead of returning None, and the caller closes 1011 for a fault while
keeping 1008 for a genuine refusal. This is not an invention: the presence
handler already draws exactly this line twenty lines further down, closing
1008 when authorization refuses and 1011 when it fails unexpectedly. The
authentication step was collapsing a distinction its own caller took care to
preserve.

What makes it worth a close code rather than a better log line is that neither
frontend client reconnects. A socket that closes stays closed here, so a
momentary database fault did not degrade presence and notifications, it ended
them, and nothing came back when the database came back. The user saw an empty
roster and no notifications and nothing on screen suggesting anything had gone
wrong.

The tests assert both directions on both sockets, and that is not symmetry for
its own sake. A test that only checks 1011 on an outage passes just as happily
against a handler broken into answering 1011 for a genuinely rejected user,
which is the same defect with the polarity reversed and a worse one to meet: it
tells someone with a stale token that the server is broken. Proved by mutation
rather than by argument. Reverting the close code produced "assert 1008 ==
1011" with "notifications WS user re-hydration failed" in the log, so the test
discriminates on the mechanism and not on the constant.

One correction from the measurement is worth recording, because believing it
would have produced a confident wrong answer. The first probe reported that an
unknown user fell through to the broad clause, which would have been a real
defect. It was the probe: it ran outside the application lifespan, so the
schema did not exist and what actually escaped was a missing table wearing an
authentication failure's clothes. Re-run inside the lifespan, the unknown-user
path raises HTTPException and the narrow clause catches it correctly. A probe
that manufactures the exact confusion it was built to detect is worth saying
out loud.

Two of the nine broad clauses in these files are deliberately unchanged. The
keep-alive catch-alls log with exception, so they conceal neither existence nor
severity, and their job is to guarantee the cleanup in the finally block runs.
Narrowing them would trade a real guarantee for tidiness on a list.

fix(demo): the form of contract a pack declares now reaches the notice engine

Every demo pack states its head contract form in project metadata as
general_contractor_form, and nothing read it. The notice engine resolves a
project's standard from Contract.terms, the seeded head contract carried no
terms at all, and so every demo project in the product fell through to
standard-neutral periods. Abu Dhabi is the case that makes it visible: the pack
names FIDIC, the engine has known FIDIC all along, and the tower still computed
generic clocks. A project that names a supported standard and gets the fallback
anyway is not a missing feature, it is a wire nobody connected. The key had no
consumer and the engine had no input, and those turned out to be one finding
rather than two.

The head contract now carries the declared form in its terms, where the resolver
already looks. The value is stored in the pack's own words rather than
normalised on the way in, and that is deliberate. normalize_standard already
maps a free-text hint onto a canonical token, and it belongs to the change
intelligence module. Writing its output into the seed would put a second copy of
another module's decision into the demo data, and the copy would go stale the
first time that mapping changed, silently, because nothing compares them. The
seed records what the pack said. Deciding what that means stays with the module
that owns the meaning.

Where the engine does not know the declared standard the answer is still
standard-neutral, and that is the intended outcome rather than a gap left
behind. Naming a standard and resolving to UNKNOWN is honest. Coercing it onto
some standard the engine does happen to know would make the screen look
finished while putting a fabricated deadline in front of somebody under a
standard's name, and a fabricated deadline is worse than no deadline, because a
wrong date gets acted on and a missing one gets asked about.

The tests are driven from the shipped pack templates rather than from a
hand-built contract, since a hand-built fixture is exactly what let this sit.
One of them asserts that the packs still contain both a standard the engine
knows and one it does not, so the rest cannot go green over a population that
quietly lost its interesting members.

Four variants were run against the suite to establish that it discriminates.
The tree as it stood before this change fails three tests, the ones that sit on
the seam between the seed and the resolver, and that is the proof the suite
would have caught the defect. Writing the terms under a key the resolver does
not read fails the same three, identically. The identical failure is the correct
result rather than a weakness: the defect's shape was that the resolver had
nothing to read, both variants reproduce exactly that, and a suite that told
them apart would be asserting something about the cause that it has no way to
know. The fourth variant, an unknown standard forced onto a known one, passes
all three and fails one test alone, the one whose reason is written above. That
test is the spine of this change. If someone later makes an unknown standard
green by mapping it onto a neighbour, exactly one thing goes red and it says
why.

A second test file pins a hazard with no victim yet. The standard matcher works
by substring, so a contract whose text merely contains the letters of a standard
family name matches it. Connecticut contains nec, and a document described as
Connecticut general conditions resolves to NEC today. No pack triggers this and
nothing is being changed about the matcher here, because narrowing it is a
change to another module's behaviour and wants its own reasoning. The test
records the shape of the trap and names the four other families that share it,
so that whoever narrows the match has the case in front of them.

Only the head contract is touched. Subcontracts are left as they were, since the
form a general contractor works under is a property of the head agreement and
inventing one for every subcontract would put words in the seed that no pack
said.

feat(core): one question that every country-shaped registry can be asked

The product varies by country in several places and each of them was invented
where it was needed, so each has its own shape: a tuple of dicts carrying a
country_code field, a dict keyed by region with a DEFAULT entry, a dict of
functions keyed by ISO code, two seeded JSON files. Nothing could answer "is
this country covered", and the honest answer for Canada turned out to be that it
has three working calendars and no payment regime, which nobody had noticed
because there was nowhere to look.

This centralises the question and not the data. Every registry stays in its own
module and keeps its own shape, and a probe here knows how to ask it. Adding a
country is still an edit in the module that owns the table. The plugin principle
is the reason the manifest is a list of probes rather than a table of countries,
and it is not traded here.

The vocabulary is six verdicts, because the useful distinctions are between the
shades of no. COVERED is a row of the country's own. FALLBACK is something that
resolves by default or alias rather than on the country's terms, where the
caller sees an answer and cannot tell it was not written for them. MISSING is a
registry that is country-keyed, is populated, and does not have this country.
NOT_KEYED is a registry with no country axis at all, where a per-country answer
means changing its shape rather than adding a row. ABSENT is no such registry
anywhere. UNRESOLVED is the probe failing to answer.

Keeping MISSING and NOT_KEYED apart is the distinction that pays for itself
immediately: four of the eleven dimensions come back NOT_KEYED for every country
in the world, being contract standard families, the credential vocabulary, the
estimate class ladder and labour rates. Reported as gaps they would look like
forty-four missing rows across eleven countries. They are four shape decisions,
and no amount of data fixes them.

UNRESOLVED is counted apart from all five answered verdicts, everywhere, and
that separation is the point of the file rather than a detail of it. An
instrument that reports what it could not measure as an absence converts "I do
not know" into "there is nothing there", and the second reads as a finished
question. The first run proved this was not theoretical: three probes could not
import their modules, and the ordinary except-return-missing would have reported
Germany and the United States as missing a working calendar. Both plainly have
one. An empty population is treated the same way, because a probe that resolves
its symbol and then finds nothing has more likely lost the shape than discovered
an empty world.

Calendars are probed as four registries rather than one. They were written
independently, they are read by different callers, and they disagree, so a
single collapsed row would hide the one thing worth seeing. Canada is the
present example and it was found this way rather than looked for.

Where a registry has a resolver, the probe calls the resolver and the table is
not accepted as a substitute. This was measured rather than assumed. The work
calendar table is keyed by a mixed vocabulary of ISO codes, one non-ISO
abbreviation, regional blocs and English country names, and its resolver puts
two further aliasing layers in front of it, so reading the table for membership
calls nine countries uncovered that in fact resolve. That probe now reports
UNRESOLVED when its resolver cannot be imported, rather than fall back to a
proxy it has measured to be wrong. Elsewhere, a source parse without executing
the module is allowed and is labelled as such in the report, because it answers
structural questions about what is written, which is a different kind of claim
from what the running product does.

The command line takes country codes and its exit code reports the health of the
instrument rather than of the product. A country with real gaps still exits 0,
because that is a finding and the tool found it. A probe that could not resolve
its registry exits 1, because then the zeroes must not be read as coverage.

The tests are about the instrument and not the coverage. A country lacking a
payment regime is a finding for the register and not a failure there. Each of
the five answered verdicts is asserted to occur somewhere in a twelve-country
sweep, since a vocabulary nothing ever returns describes an imaginary product,
and the sweep asserts its own size first so the floor cannot pass over a
collapsed population. One test exists only to prove the calendar resolver is
importable under the harness, without which its FALLBACK branch would report
unresolved in every environment and the suite would go green over a verdict it
had never once produced.

Four mutations were run in memory to establish that the suite discriminates.
Making the probe wrapper return missing on failure is caught, both directly and
through the public entry point. Treating an empty population as missing is
caught, with the populated case held alongside as a control so the catch is
specific rather than a blanket break. Collapsing the four calendar sources onto
one is caught. Every baseline holds and every restoration holds.

fix(finance): a Brazilian invoice stops being labelled German

The RPS renderer has no locale input of any kind. Its labels are Portuguese
literals, its money formatter is an unconditional pt-BR separator swap, and
the string "locale" does not appear in the file. That is correct and it should
stay that way, because an RPS is a Brazilian fiscal document and there is no
reader preference that could ever make it something else. What was wrong is
that the route serving it declared nothing, so the Accept-Language middleware
supplied the reader's requested language instead, and Portuguese bytes went out
to a German reader carrying a header that named the document German.

This is worse than the surrounding cases rather than another instance of them.
Sixteen other document builders hardcode English and are equally undeclared,
but none of them ever made a language decision, so their header is merely
uninformed. This one made a decision, made it correctly, and the header
contradicted it in a field receivers act on.

The fix is a literal because there is nothing to resolve. A resolver here would
be machinery standing in front of a constant, and worse, it would invite a
later change to wire a reader preference into a document that has exactly one
language. The value carries a region subtag deliberately: the product already
ships pt and pt-BR as separate locales, so pt-BR is the tag the product itself
uses for Brazilian Portuguese. The shared document resolver truncates to
primary subtags and could not produce this value at all, which is not an
argument against the value but an argument for where it lives. A document with
one fixed language is precisely the place a region tag can be stated, because
no resolution step exists to flatten it.

Two tests, and the second is not a restatement of the first. One pins the
value. The other pins that the route is the author of the header, read off the
response the handler returns before any middleware has seen it, which is the
property that actually regressed. A test that only asserted the header was
present on a served response would pass just as happily against a route that
declares nothing while the middleware happens to supply the same string, and
that is the defect wearing the fix's clothes.

Proved by mutation rather than by argument. Removing the header line produces
two failures and sixteen passes in that file. The first version of the second
test failed on a KeyError rather than on the comparison it announced, so it was
gating the right thing while reading as though it gated something else; it now
uses a lookup that returns rather than raises, and the control was re-run to
confirm it fails on the assertion at the line the test names.
