fix(price-breakdown): a per-unit norm stays per-unit however large the position is

The price analysis divided every resource amount by the position quantity, on
the belief that a second convention existed in which resource amounts were
whole-position figures. No writer in the tree produces those. The division left
the sheet correct only for positions of quantity 1 and understated every other
one by a factor of its own quantity, and because the sheet reconciles only
against itself, nothing anywhere disagreed with it.

The belief was reasonable when it was written, which is the part worth
recording. A resource row does carry a total, and a total is the sort of field
that usually means the whole of something. Read that way the numbers on a large
position come out looking like a unit rate, and a mason booked at half an hour
per square metre reads as ten hours once the quantity is folded in, which is a
figure a planner would recognise. The reading is coherent. It is just not the
one the platform stores.

The platform invariant is that every resource quantity is a per-unit norm, the
amount one unit of the position consumes, so unit_rate equals the sum of
quantity times unit_rate over the resources, and whole-position demand is that
product times the position quantity. The invariant is stated in
resource_summary.aggregate and implemented by both writers that produce a split:
the resource-driven rate derivation in boq.service, which sums the per-unit
subtotals with no division by quantity, and the assembly apply path, which keeps
the per-unit norm as the raw component quantity and says so in its own comment.
The stored total is written as quantity times unit_rate and is per-unit for the
same reason.

The basis parameter is deleted rather than defaulted. A switch between two
readings of the same stored number is a switch between correct and wrong, and
offering it makes every reader responsible for a decision the data already
settled. Flipping the default and leaving the parameter would have left the next
person believing two populations exist and reaching for the lever. from_position
has one production caller, the position price-analysis endpoint, and no call
site anywhere passes basis, so removing it is a safe change rather than a
hopeful one.

What it looked like. A 250 cubic metre concrete position at 100.00 per cubic
metre, built from two hours of mason at 20.00 and one cubic metre of concrete at
60.00, printed 0.008 hours of mason, 0.004 cubic metres of concrete, a direct
cost of 0.40 and a unit rate of 0.40, with a position total of 100.00 instead of
25000.00. It now prints 2, 1, 100.00, 100.00 and 25000.00. Eight thousandths of
an hour of mason per cubic metre of concrete is not a buildable norm and any
estimator would have said so, but nobody was shown it on a page that argues with
anything else. This is the German EFB 221 sheet with a markdown download, so
those figures went to public authorities.

A test in the suite already vouched for the wrong convention, and it is worth
looking at rather than only counting. Its fixture carried the comment "Resource
totals are for the whole position (quantity 20)" and booked a mason at ten hours
per square metre of blockwork. Ten hours per square metre is absurd. Ten hours
across a twenty square metre wall is half an hour per square metre and perfectly
ordinary, so to anyone who had accepted the convention the number read as sane,
and the test then stood behind the convention that had produced it. The fixture
is rewritten as a position that adds up: 1.05 square metres of blocks and half an
hour of mason per square metre, with the rate carrying overhead and profit on
top. It still asserts a direct unit cost of 52.50, so the expected figure has not
moved, but it is now reached by reading the stored norms rather than by dividing
a larger number down to them. Under the old code the same fixture yields 2.625
and fails, which is what separates a rewrite from a moved goalpost.

The 250 cubic metre case is pinned as a test in its own right, with every
assertion written twice, once for the honest figure and once against the one the
division produced, so a reinstated divisor fails rather than passing quietly.
The zero-quantity test keeps its behaviour but loses the comment that vouched for
the divisor, since nothing divides by the quantity any more and a zero quantity
is no longer a special case in this module at all.

One judgement call left in place. The mapper still prefers a stored total over
recomputing quantity times unit_rate, and that preference is kept rather than
tidied away. Every writer sets the total to exactly that product so the two agree
in practice, and changing which one wins would be a second behaviour change on
top of the divisor. The recompute is not dead code: the flagship seeder writes
resource leaves with no total field at all, so that branch carries every position
in the flagship demo data.

a DNS label are ASCII by convention, so vergabe@kurpfalz-kaelte.de is the
correct address and the accented form would be a broken one, while the company
that answers it is called Kurpfalz Kaeltetechnik GmbH with the umlaut. Twenty of
the twenty-nine lines carry both forms side by side, which is what says the
authors applied the rule deliberately rather than getting tired halfway through
a file.

That made this worse than a false positive. The gate prints an instruction, to
write the accented form, and following it on any of the twenty-nine breaks the
address. The gate then goes green, because the stripped spelling it objected to
is gone. A gate that only passes once the data is wrong is worse than no gate,
and this one was one careful reader away from taking twenty-nine working
addresses with it.

The exemption is per occurrence rather than per literal, because a single line
carries both the display name and the address for the same firm, and one exempt
hit must not excuse a real one beside it. That is the most likely way to get
this wrong and it is the one case the tests pin on its own.

Scoped to email addresses and nothing wider. A bare hostname or a URL carrying a
stripped spelling would need the same treatment, and none appears in the
denylisted files today, so the pattern says where to add it rather than covering
it now on speculation. An email-only rule was measured to cover all twenty-nine
before it was written, which is why it is the rule.

Seventeen tests, and the controls are the point of them. A test asserting only
that an address is ignored would pass just as well against a gate that had been
switched off, so the file also asserts that a stripped spelling in a display
string is still reported, that things which merely resemble addresses are not
exempt, and that the shipped packs now pass with a nonzero count of files
actually scanned. Both mutations were run. Removing the exemption fails seven of
the seventeen. Making it per literal instead of per occurrence fails exactly one,
the control written for that case.

The gate had no test file before this. It is on the pre-commit hook and in no
merge-blocking lane, which is how it stayed red long enough to be noticed by
being run on purpose rather than by stopping anything.

test(finance): the Brazilian invoice is safe by content, not by construction

A font census of the Brazilian invoice shows Helvetica among the document's
resources, which is exactly the shape a half wired document has: bare string
cells drawn under a table that names no FONTNAME, falling back to Helvetica and
boxing everything outside Latin-1. That reading is wrong here, and it cost a
detour to establish, so it belongs in the record rather than in someone's head.
Helvetica is reportlab's default canvas font. It is selected 184 times around
empty cells and page setup and it draws no glyphs at all: filtering the
extracted runs down to those actually carrying text leaves Helvetica with none.

The module was measured before anything was written. It builds five tables
holding 68 cells, every one of them a Paragraph, and pdf_table_font_commands
returns an empty list for all five. Every cell already takes its face from its
own style, which the paragraph facing sets, so there is no cell left for a
FONTNAME command to help. The wiring the other generators needed would have
been four lines here that changed no byte of any document.

What is worth pinning is the reason it is safe. The file names no FONTNAME
command anywhere, so nothing stands between a bare string cell and Helvetica.
Today no such cell exists, but that is a property of what the cells currently
are rather than of anything in the code, and a property that holds by content
and not by construction is what a test is for. The test builds the invoice with
a Chinese client and description, captures every table through the module's own
Table name, and fails naming the table, the row, the column and the value if
any cell is not a flowable.

The instrument guards itself in the other direction too. If the module ever
stops building its tables through that name the spy stops firing, and a test
that captures nothing would otherwise pass for free, which is the same failure
as having no test but much harder to notice. So the number of captured tables
and cells is asserted before the cells are examined. Both directions were run:
making one header cell a bare string fails with that cell named, and building
the tables through a module level alias fails on the capture count rather than
passing.

commands were added to a document that has no cell needing one, and the

fix(boq): a labour share is measured against the rate, not against the buildup

percentage_of_unit_rate divided one resource sum by the total of all of them.
The name said unit rate, four of the five pieces of prose around it said unit
rate, and the arithmetic said something else. A column built that way cannot be
wrong on its face, because the roles it can name always add up to its own
divisor, and that is the same thing as saying it can never report the one
disagreement it is positioned to see. It was a share of the buildup wearing the
label of a share of the rate. It now divides by the position's stored
unit_rate.

Where a buildup obeys the platform invariant the two divisors are the same
number and nothing on screen moves, so every consistent position keeps the
figure it had. They differ only where the buildup and the rate disagree, which
is exactly where a reader needs to be told.

The old divisor was not biased in one direction, and that is what made it hard
to read past. Across the 18 priced items in starter_seed_data.json the buildup
falls short of the rate on 61 percent of rows and exceeds it on 39, with the
ratio running from 0.65 to 1.60. Across the 10 priced rows of cwicr_items.json
it is 40 short and 60 over, out to 3.84. The median sits near parity, so the
aggregate labour share barely moves and nothing looks wrong in summary, while
single rows moved by 20.9 points up and 33.4 points down. A uniform bias a
reader can correct for. This one they cannot, and it is the shares that an
escalation clause multiplies.

One function computes the share, and it is called from the value getter and
from cellClass rather than each of them working it out. That is not a tidiness
preference. The rendered value goes through fmtFixed, which writes the reader's
separators, so a German user's cell reads 137,40 and parses back as 137. A
second implementation that formatted first and compared afterwards would not be
a duplicate of the first, it would be a different answer, and a cell that prints
one number while the styling that judges it is decided by another is worse than
either mistake alone. Three call sites now, which is why it is a function.

A share above 100 prints the real figure and marks the cell rather than being
clamped. The reasoning is the one from the head contract change: a wrong number
that is shown gets asked about, and a plausible one gets acted on. 137.4 in red
tells an estimator that two numbers stored on this position contradict each
other, and a tidy 100.00 tells them nothing while looking finished. The tooltip
on a marked cell says which resources are worth more than the whole rate, since
a mark with no reason is half a signal. A missing, non-numeric or zero rate
renders empty, because a share needs something to be a share of, and printing
one against nothing is the same failure in a quieter voice.

Both branches move, and the resource sub-row was the trap. A resource row
carries a unit_rate of its own, the price of that one resource, so a divisor
read off the row would have divided every resource by its own price and printed
its quantity as a percentage. The parent has to be resolved through
_parentPositionId, and that has a test to itself.

All five pieces of prose move with the arithmetic: the type doc comment, the
cell tooltip, the API doc comment, the ÖNORM preset comment, and the comment in
the preset index that described the old divisor accurately and would otherwise
have been the only false voice left in the tree. A commit that fixes arithmetic
and leaves a comment vouching for the old arithmetic has not finished.

Every case where the two divisors differ is asserted twice, once for the value
it must produce and once for the value it must not. not.toBe("50.00") is the
old answer for a short buildup and not.toBe("100.00") is the old answer for an
over-full one, so a future simplification back to the resource sum fails rather
than passing quietly, and the control sits in the assertions instead of in a
comment that a rewrite can delete.

The gate for this is a build, not a type check, and it had one. tsc over the
whole project runs out of memory on this tree and is not what says a frontend
change is finished. The five files were built together with the tree settled
beforehand, exit 0, and dist/index.html present with all 11 asset references
resolving, which is the pair of facts that answers the question rather than the
exit code alone.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(core): an answer can say how it was arrived at, one axis at a time

Wave one of the jurisdiction work. The product resolves a great deal from a
country: working weeks, payment clocks, notice periods, tax rates, phone and
address rules. Until now the resolved value travelled alone, so a caller handed
a number could not tell a row written for its own country from a default that
happens to be shaped like one. Several surfaces went further and stamped the
requested country onto an answer the generic rules produced, which is not a
missing feature but a false statement.

This adds the vocabulary for saying it, and nothing else. No resolver is changed
here. Four modules are about to adopt this at once, and four hand-rolled
versions of the same idea would be four vocabularies that drift, so the shape
lands first and the adoptions follow.

It is a field beside the value rather than a wrapper around it, and that is the
one design decision worth arguing. Provenance is per axis. A wrapper keyed on
jurisdiction paints an answer green while a second axis is silently wrong, and
the tax engine is the worked example: it raises on an unknown jurisdiction,
which is honest, and returns the same bytes for a zero-rated supply and for a
date it holds no rate for, which is not. One envelope would have called that
engine covered. So a function with two axes returns two provenances and asks
weakest() which one governs.

The pattern is not invented here. carbon.resolve_grid_factor has shipped it for
some time, returning the country requested, the country used and an explicit
fallback flag, and its docstring already states the thesis better than the plan
does: a reviewer is never handed a country-specific-looking number that is
really a world average. This is that pattern given a name.

The constructor refuses combinations that contradict themselves, which is the
reason it is a type rather than a convention. Declared with the requested and
used values differing is precisely the shipped defect where a config endpoint
says these are one country's rules about the generic ones. Fallback with the two
equal is the same lie told backwards. Both raise. A caller can still record
something false about the world; it can no longer record something the fields
themselves disagree about.

Unavailable is kept apart from fallback for a reason with a body behind it. A
fallback is an answer and may well be the right one. An unavailable is the
absence of an answer, and the two must never share a code path, because the
failure that motivated the distinction is a holiday calculation raising, being
swallowed into an empty set, and every day of the year silently becoming a
working day. No holidays and I could not work out the holidays are different
things, and only one of them is safe to compute dates from.

The axis is free text rather than an enum. Modules own their dimensions and the
core holds only the question, so a closed set here would mean editing core to
add a dimension, which is the coupling that would end modules being plugins.

Twenty-four tests, and the ones that assert a successful construction carry no
weight on their own since they would pass against a dataclass with no validation
at all. The load-bearing ones assert a raise, and each is written from a defect
that shipped. The parametrised table over the five sources exists for its middle
row, where answered is false and usable is true, because that is the amber state
the plan depends on and a test of only the two ends would pass against an
implementation where those two properties are the same function. weakest is run
with its arguments both ways round, since an implementation returning the first
or the last would pass either call alone. The source strength order is pinned as
pairs rather than as the whole member list, so that adding a sixth source at its
true strength does not turn a correct change into a red test and teach the next
reader to edit tests rather than read them.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(core): a fallback must name what answered in its place

The provenance type refused a fallback claiming it used the very thing it was
asked for, and accepted one that named nothing at all. So a record could say a
default stood in, decline to say which default, and still report itself usable.
A caller reading that is told it may compute with a value whose origin the
record does not carry, which is the condition this module exists to make
unspellable. It was refusing the loud contradiction and admitting the quiet one.

The hole was found by a module adopting the type rather than by the type's own
tests, and the shape it takes is the reason it matters. Nobody sits down to
write a nameless fallback. They write fell_back(axis, code, table.get(code, ""))
because that reads as reasonable, and an absent key hands the constructor an
empty string. Four modules took this vocabulary up on the same day, so the
choice was to close it once here or to meet it four times over the next week
with four different workarounds.

Only the fallback is tightened, and the asymmetry is deliberate rather than an
oversight. A declared answer with no used value is under-informative and not
untrue, because a source that answered on its own terms has already named what
answered: it is the thing that was requested. A fallback is the only source
whose stand-in cannot be derived from any other field, which is exactly why it
has to be written down. Unavailable keeps its empty used and now serves as the
escape route the refusal points at, so an adopter told a nameless fallback is
illegal has somewhere honest to put the case where genuinely nothing answered.

The token requirement is light on purpose. A stand-in does not have to be a
country or a year; INTERNATIONAL and GREGORIAN_ONLY are what the adopting
modules already pass, and naming one is a sentence of thought rather than a
lookup. That is the whole cost, and it buys a record where every fallback can
be read back to the thing that produced it.

Three tests, and only the first carries weight on its own. It asserts the raise,
in the exact shape the adopting module hit. The second is its control: the
honest fallback with a named token must still construct, because without that
the constraint could be satisfied by a type that refuses every fallback and the
first test would pass against something nobody can use. The third pins the
escape route, since a refusal that points at an alternative is only honest if
the alternative exists.

Verified by mutation rather than by argument. With the new guard removed and
nothing else changed, the refused construction succeeds and reports used as the
empty string with usable true, which is the defect as reported. With the guard
present it raises. The named-token control constructs under both, so the guard
discriminates rather than blanket-refusing, and the source file was sha256
identical before and after. The two modules that already call fell_back pass
unchanged, sixty five tests between them, so nothing in the tree was relying on
the hole.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(validation): the phone and address rules say whose rules they are

The phone validator emitted numbers that cannot exist and reported them valid.
Asked to normalise 301234567 for France, which has no rules here, it returned
+301234567, which is well formed and belongs to Greece. Given the same number
with a trunk zero it returned +0301234567, which is not a possible E.164 number
under any numbering plan. Both came back with passed True and country_code FR,
so the one field that could have warned the caller was instead confirming the
mistake.

That field was an echo throughout. get_phone_rules returned the generic
patterns stamped with the country that was asked about, so a config endpoint
could tell a UI these were France's phone rules when France has none here.
validate_phone stamped the same code onto every result, and so did
validate_address. The address getters made the opposite mistake and said
nothing at all: get_address_rules and get_address_field_order returned the
generic table unlabelled, so two uncovered countries came back byte identical
with no way to tell either was a stand-in.

Both now carry a Provenance from app/core/provenance.py beside the value: what
was asked for, what answered, and whether that was a fallback. country_code
keeps meaning what it always meant, the code that was asked about, because
DEFAULT is not a country code and putting it in that field would replace an
echo with something worse. What answered is jurisdiction.used.

The E.164 hole needed more than a field. No number of provenance fields
rescues a fabricated value: a label saying these are the generic rules, sitting
beside a string no telephone network can route, is still a labelled lie, and a
caller that trusts the label still holds +0301234567. A national number can
only be turned into an E.164 by a dial code and only a real country row carries
one, so where there is none e164 is now None. passed still reports what the
syntax check found, because a fallback is an answer and the generic pattern may
well be right about the digits. Success therefore no longer implies an E.164
form and the docstrings say so in both places that used to promise it.

Error messages moved with it, because a message saying a number does not match
the national format for country FR is itself a claim that France's rules judged
it. They now name whichever rules did. On the address side only the required
field message could ever have been wrong that way: the generic rules carry no
postcode pattern and require no state, so those two checks are unreachable
unless a real row answered, and a comment says so where they still name the
country.

How much this repairs. Nothing in this repository calls any of these five
functions. There is no import of app.core.validation.phone or .address
anywhere, the package __init__ is two lines of copyright so nothing is
re-exported, and there is no router, no test and no frontend reference. Both
files carry four commits, three of them repo wide sweeps and the fourth the
bulk commit that created them, whose siblings in the same commit got tests and
callers while these got neither. So this is speculative code that never had a
caller rather than a regression that lost one, and what the fix buys is that
the first consumer is not misled rather than that live output is repaired. The
claim stops at the repository edge on purpose, since packs resolve through
importlib.resources and an external one is out of reach of a grep.

Which is also the argument for fixing rather than deleting. The field diary
module needed to validate a phone number and wrote its own regex against a
local pattern instead of importing the validator that exists to do it. That is
demand routing around the capability rather than an absence of demand, and the
answer to something people needed and did not use is to make it correct, not to
remove it and guarantee the next module writes a third regex.

One axis each, and that is measured rather than assumed. The dial code was the
candidate second axis for phone and it is perfectly correlated with coverage,
since all fourteen entries carry one and the generic rules carry none, so a
second provenance would have repeated the first in every case rather than
distinguishing anything. Address resolves postcode pattern, required fields,
field order and the state flag from a single row.

Forty tests, and the controls are the point of them. A covered country is
asserted to be declared rather than merely not a fallback, and an uncovered one
to be a fallback rather than merely not declared, so an implementation
answering one fixed verdict fails in both directions. Each pair is also
asserted to disagree with the other, since two separate constants would satisfy
everything else. The E.164 tests name the two strings the old code produced
rather than checking only for None, so neither can return and still pass.

The test that carries the most is the inversion, because it is a relation
between two calls rather than an expected value and cannot be satisfied by
accident: Canada, which has rules, rejects the nine digits that France, which
does not, accepts. The generic pattern takes six to fifteen digits and is
looser than every national rule in the table, so coverage was turning a
rejection into an acceptance. Coverage asymmetry is pinned for the same reason,
since Canada has phone rules and no address rules and neither surface's answer
can be assumed from the other's.

Three mutations, run rather than reasoned about. Restoring the echo so the
requested country is stamped as declared fails twelve of the forty and leaves
every covered case passing. Writing that echo down literally, declared with
used set to the generic table, fails thirteen, one more, because the
constructor refuses it outright. Restoring the fabricated E.164 fails five, and
only the tests written for it. The covered and uncovered cases fail differently
under each, which is what says the tests measure the distinction rather than
the shape.

One defect is recorded rather than repaired, and pinned by two tests so it
cannot be rediscovered by a crash. The address rule dicts are not of uniform
shape: postcode_optional is carried by the generic rules and by none of the
thirteen country rows, and postcode_note by GB and UK alone. A consumer
branching on either key gets a usable value for every country we do not support
and a KeyError for every country we do, which is the wrong way round twice over
from one cause. Filling it in means deciding what postcode optional means for
eleven countries whose authors never said, which is a question about the data
rather than about provenance, so the tests assert the shape as it stands and
will fail the moment somebody answers it.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(i18n-foundation): the working-days answer says whether it knew the country

WorkingDaysResponse carried country_code, and it was the query parameter coming
back. For a country with a calendar that reads as a fact about the calendar. For
a country without one it reads the same way and means nothing of the kind: the
week used there is a hardcoded Monday to Friday belonging to no country at all,
and the field naming that country was the only thing on the response that
looked like a verdict.

The response now carries a Provenance from app/core/provenance.py saying which
it was. country_code keeps meaning what it always meant, the code that was asked
about, and jurisdiction.used says what answered.

This one was closer to right than it looked, which is worth saying because the
rest of the file is the reason. The per-year disclosure was already honest and
already tested: work_week_source is three valued, declared or carried or
default, work_week_from_year names the year a week was carried from, and
holidays_applied is a separate flag because a week is a rule that carries across
years and a holiday is a date that does not. That is per-axis provenance done
properly, and done before we had a name for it.

What was missing is that all three of those axes are about time. Whether the
country was known at all is a fourth, and it was derivable rather than stated:
every entry in years reads default exactly when no calendar exists. Derivable is
not stated. A caller should not have to reconstruct a fact about a country by
scanning a list about years, and a single year range gives it nothing to compare
against.

The case that proves the axes are separate is a range past the seeded year. The
country is known, the year is not, so the jurisdiction reports declared while
the year reports its week as carried. One flag across both would have to pick a
side and would be wrong about the other.

Second thing in the same function, and the same family of failure. The
out-of-range lookup built a mapping of year to working week and then asked only
whether the mapping was non-empty. A calendar row declaring no working days put
a key in the mapping and nothing in the week, so the year reported its week as
carried from a real calendar, which was true, and then counted no working days
in any range, for ever, with a 200 and no failure anywhere. Not an error, a
plausible number. Such a row is now ignored in both places it can enter, with a
warning naming the calendar, and its holidays are ignored with it so that
holidays_applied cannot disagree with the row it describes. A country whose only
calendar is one of these reports a jurisdiction fallback, because nothing in
that row contributed and the week used belongs to nobody.

No shipped calendar has an empty week. All thirty seeded rows declare five days,
and exactly one of the thirty declares something other than Monday to Friday,
Saudi Arabia at Sunday to Thursday. So the five tests written for the empty week
are the only thing that will ever reach it, which is the reason to write them
rather than a reason not to.

Eleven tests. The controls are the point of them, so a seeded country is
asserted to be declared rather than merely not a fallback and an unseeded one to
be a fallback rather than merely not declared, and the two are asserted to
disagree with each other, which two separate constants could not satisfy. The
country used for the unseeded case is asserted to be absent from the seed rather
than assumed to be, since a test that quietly stopped describing an uncovered
country would still pass. The carrying control uses Saudi Arabia's Sunday to
Thursday week deliberately: both weeks are five days, so the totals match and
only the individual days differ, which is why a count could never have caught
this. It asserts a Friday and a Sunday rather than a fortnight.

Both guards were disabled in turn and the tests run against them. Disabling the
in-range guard fails two of the five; disabling the out-of-range guard fails
three. They are not independent, and the extra one is the interesting part: with
the in-range guard active an empty row is kept out of the declared mapping,
which sends the request into the widened lookup, so the second guard is what
catches an in-range row as well. Both negative controls hold under each, which
is what says the guards are not simply switching carrying off.

The route test that asserts the whole response body failed on the way, as its
own comment says it exists to do, and was updated rather than loosened.

One mapping does not fit, and I would rather name it than bend either side.
work_week_source has three states and only two land cleanly on Source: declared
is DECLARED and default is FALLBACK, while carried is neither. The reason is
that the field is not one axis. Declared and carried differ over which year
answered; default differs over whether the country answered at all. Now that
jurisdiction is its own field the second question is asked there, and what is
left of work_week_source is a year axis on which carried is simply a fallback
with the year it came from beside it, exactly as the carbon resolver reports a
nearest year. I have not changed the field. Renaming its states would touch the

fix(calendar): a failed holiday computation stops reading as a year with none

_get_holidays collapsed four situations into one frozenset of dates. A country
we cover completely, a country whose year falls outside a curated lunisolar
table, a country nothing covers, and a computation that raised all arrived at
the caller as a set, and a bare except Exception turned the last of them into an
empty one. Since is_working_day reduces that set to a bool, a broken holiday
computation did not fail. It produced a year in which every weekday was a
working day, and the only trace was a log line, which is not something a caller
can branch on.

resolve_holidays now returns the dates beside two Provenance fields from
app.core.provenance, one for the country and one for the year. Two rather than
one because the axes fail independently: a country we cover completely can still
be asked for a year its curated table does not reach, and a single flag keyed on
the country would have called exactly that case covered. A caller wanting one
verdict passes both to weakest, and holiday_provenance does that for it.

Three empty sets, three meanings, and they are now different. A country with
genuinely no public holidays is DECLARED with no dates, which is an answer. A
country nothing covers is a FALLBACK to a working week with no public holidays,
which is a weaker answer and still one you can schedule against. A computation
that failed is neither, and it raises. That third case is the whole reason
UNAVAILABLE is kept apart from FALLBACK, and the type refuses to record it as
anything else: a provenance saying nothing answered while naming what answered
does not construct.

The failure is deliberately not cached. Caching it would have been the more
natural fix and the worse one: the first call would raise and every call after
it would read a plausible empty set back out of the cache, so the original
defect would survive wearing a raise. The tests assert the failure twice, at the
resolver and again through is_working_day, because a single call cannot tell
those two apart. HolidayCalculationError carries the UNAVAILABLE provenance so
that catching it does not mean rebuilding one by hand and getting the source
wrong.

Sharing a holiday function is now read two different ways, because it means two
different things and the table already said which is which. GB and UK are two
spellings of one state, so neither falls back to the other. AT is served by
Germany's function under a comment saying Austrian holidays closely mirror
Germany's, and a close mirror is an approximation, so Austria reports a fallback
naming DE. Getting this wrong in either direction is a defect: calling Austria
declared hides a borrowed answer, and calling Britain a fallback raises an alarm
that is false, and a provenance field that cries wolf stops being read. Both
polarities are mutation tested.

Partiality is decided from the curated tables themselves rather than from their
first and last year. Membership is tested directly, so an interior gap cannot
read as complete, and the bounds are not copied into a second place that would
have to be kept in step. The detail string names the holidays that were dropped
instead of quoting a window, for the same reason. _holidays_cn already knew
exactly which festivals it was dropping and said so in its warning, so the
information existed and only the channel was missing. The warning stays.

The set of curated tables was checked rather than assumed, and a test now holds
it to that: it counts the year-keyed tables the module actually defines and
fails if one is not registered. Today there are two, the Chinese festivals and
the Hindu holidays, and both are listed. The Gulf holidays are not a third
table, they are an arithmetic conversion from the Islamic calendar with no
window at all, so they are complete on the year axis.

_get_holidays keeps returning a frozenset and became a thin accessor. Returning
the mapping from it would have been tidier and would have silently broken a live
assertion: test_calendar.py proves Bahrain and Oman have holidays at all by
asserting the return is truthy, and a non-empty mapping is truthy however empty
its dates are. The neighbouring assertions on length and equality would have
failed loudly. That one would have gone quiet.

Mutation matrix, measured against the new file, with the source restored to a
byte-identical sha256 after each. Baseline thirty nine passed, and one hundred
and two with test_calendar.py alongside it. Restoring the swallow fails four.
Raising but still caching an empty answer fails two. Treating a curated-window
miss as complete fails four. Calling every shared table a synonym fails one, and
forgetting the synonym table fails one the other way. Calling an uncovered
country declared fails three. Dropping one Gulf country from the span registry
fails three. Restored, one hundred and two passed.

Coverage answers whether rows are present, and it does not absorb accuracy. The
six Gulf countries have their rows, so both axes stay declared and that is a
true sentence. What is not true is that their Eid lengths were computed:
_gcc_eids applies one span of three and four days to all six, because the length
is announced annually by each government. So there is a sibling field beside
omitted. omitted names what exists in the world and is missing from our data.
placeholder_spans names what is in our data with an extent nobody worked out.
Folding the second into partial was the tempting move and the wrong one: partial
is derived from curated-window membership, and one slot answering two questions
resolved two different ways is the wrapper mistake in miniature, which is the
thing this whole change exists to stop.

The name is load-bearing rather than cosmetic, and this is the paragraph worth
reading before tidying it. The obvious objection to flagging the Gulf at all is
that flagging one case makes its own absence speak for every other: nobody has
verified the German table either, and a marker on the one place we happen to
know about would quietly claim the rest were checked. What defeats that is
naming the field for the mechanism instead of for the quality. Absence of a
placeholder means no placeholder we know of, which is modest and true anywhere.
A field called approximate, or unverified, would have an absence meaning
verified, and that is a claim this tree cannot support for a single table in it.
Rename this field to describe how good the answer is and it starts lying about
every country it does not mention.

For the same reason it records the mechanism and not the grading. The docstring
on _gcc_eids says the span is closest to correct for the UAE and too short for
Saudi Arabia. That grading is deliberately ignored: all six are registered
identically, because closest to correct is still not computed, and how far off
each one runs is policy rather than something to derive. The registry is checked
against the source rather than trusted, by a test that finds every holiday
function calling _gcc_eids and fails if one of them is unregistered.

There is a live consequence, which is why this was worth settling before the
commit rather than after. A case cannot publish as jurisdiction-specific if a
dimension it uses falls back, and that rule reads coverage. Saudi Arabia answers
complete on a span the module's own source says runs short, so a consumer
applying that rule has to read placeholder_spans as well as the two provenances,
and the field has to exist for it to read. Switzerland is a different mechanism
and is deliberately not marked here: its lambda carries three dates under the
comment simplified, which is a short roster rather than an uncomputed span, and
stretching this field to cover it would blur the one distinction that makes its
absence safe.

Two more seen and left alone. The coverage probe in country_coverage.py still
reads _HOLIDAY_FUNCS as a set of keys, which remains accurate for the question
it asks. next_working_day still returns the cap boundary after sixty iterations
under a comment calling it unreachable, which is the same silent wrong answer

fix(property-dev): a date with no rate is refused, not quoted at zero

compute_vat returned Decimal("0.00") when the contract date fell before a
rate's effective_from, and twelve lines further down the genuine zero-rate
branch returned the same thing. The two were identical down to as_tuple, so
nothing downstream could separate a tax-free supply from one the engine had no
rate for. net_from_gross had the same shape, returning the gross unchanged,
which asserts that no VAT was baked into an inclusive price rather than
admitting it does not know.

What that priced. A GB contract for 100000 signed 2010-12-31 came back with
grand_total 100000.00 and a breakdown of exactly ['Net price']. One line, no
VAT row at all, on a date when UK VAT was 17.5 per cent and the real figure was
17500. The same contract dated inside the band returns 120000.00 with a VAT
row, so the whole difference between a correct quote and a silently wrong one
was the line that went missing, and the wrong one is the one that looks tidy.
The trigger is stored data rather than a request field: the service derives
effective_on from the contract's own signing_date, so any contract signed
before 2011-01-04 for GB, or 2007-01-01 for DE, was quoted this way.

The two zeros looked identical and were not. A zero-rated line carries 0.00 and
that zero is a fact about the supply, expressible in the contract and correct.
The zero for a date with no rate was an invention. Same digit, opposite
epistemic status, and the defect is precisely that nothing on the wire could
tell them apart.

Why refusing is the only honest answer, rather than reaching further back for
an older rate. The table holds one band per rate class, and that is a property
of its shape rather than of its contents: there is no room for a second band,
so it cannot express a rate change at all. The docstring promising that an
earlier contract uses the rate in force on its signing date was not describing
an unimplemented feature, it was describing a structure the file does not have.
There are two effective_from keys in the whole table and no prior-rate entry
anywhere, so there is nothing to fall back to and any number produced for an
earlier date would be invented rather than approximate. That is also why this is not the
shape carbon uses for grid factors: a year catalogue can legitimately answer
with a neighbouring year and flag the substitution, because it has other years.

Stated in the vocabulary that landed in app/core/provenance.py, because this
fork will be met again. That module keeps UNAVAILABLE apart from FALLBACK on
purpose: a fallback is an answer and may well be right, an unavailable is the
absence of one, and the two must never share a code path. The plan rule that
amber is a working state governs fallbacks. It does not govern this. There is
no international VAT rate to fall back to, so refusing is not an exception to
that rule, it is its other branch.

The engine's own module docstring is the evidence that this was believed rather
than overlooked. It promised that a contract signed pre-band-change "uses the
rate that was in force on its signing date", which is precisely what it did not
do, and four lines above that it stated the principle it was breaking on every
axis but one: "Unknown jurisdiction to explicit error - never falls back to a
silent default that would generate billing-incorrect invoices". A wrong comment
is merely stale. A docstring stating the principle four lines from the code
breaking it is a belief that was written down and never implemented. The same
rule is settled elsewhere in the product too, in boq/markup_templates: "0" is a
real rate and does override, because a zero-rated jurisdiction is a statement,
not a missing value.

compute_vat and net_from_gross now raise RateNotInForceError, carrying the
jurisdiction, the rate class, the date asked about and the effective_from that
governs. The router maps it to a 422 with those four fields in the detail dict,
which is the pattern the three clauses above it already use. A raise alone
would have thrown away the jurisdiction axis that resolved honestly on the way;
the mapped response keeps it. A caller told that no rate was in force on
2010-12-31 and that the earliest one begins 2011-01-04 can correct the signing
date or add the historical band to the YAML. A caller handed 0.00 could do
neither, and had nothing to indicate there was a question.

Nothing between the raise and that clause catches it, traced frame by frame
rather than by confirming that something somewhere catches something.
compute_vat has two callers, both in this file. gross_from_net calls it
unguarded and has no production caller at all, so that path is dead rather than
dangerous. compute_total_taxes_for_contract calls it inside a try that catches
UnknownRateClassError alone, to let VAT-less jurisdictions through quietly, so
the new exception passes straight by the one construct that would look like
coverage to a reader skimming for a try. Its net_from_gross call is inside no
try at all. From there it is a bare return in the service and then the endpoint,
so the router clause is the only thing that handles it and the only thing that
needs to.

The three ways this endpoint can refuse stay three. An unknown jurisdiction, an
unknown rate class and a date outside the band each keep their own error token
and their own fields, because collapsing them into one 422 shape would rebuild
the original defect in the error path, and the error path is where nobody
looks.

The dates go into that dict as isoformat strings, not date objects. FastAPI's
default handler renders the detail through json.dumps, which has no encoder for
date, so the refusal would have come back as a 500 and been a worse outcome
than the zero it replaces. Checked in both directions on a throwaway app rather
than assumed: raw date gives 500, isoformat gives the intended 422 with the
date on the wire.

test_vat_effective_from_before_band_change_returns_zero asserted the defect and
its comment rationalised it, "A contract signed before that date should return
0 (no band yet in force)", which is the strongest evidence available that this
was believed rather than overlooked. The case it covers is right and is kept
verbatim; only the expectation is inverted, and the test now also asserts the
four fields a caller needs to act.

Two controls guard the fix from passing for the wrong reason. A genuinely
zero-rated supply must still return zero without raising, so the change cannot
be satisfied by refusing every zero, and an endpoint test pins that a contract
signed inside the band still quotes, so GB cannot go offline behind a green
suite. The main invariant is asserted on the pair rather than on a number: a
test that pins a particular value is blind to this defect, because the wrong
answer was an ordinary zero. Both directions were run by reverting the fix and
by making every zero raise, and each broke the case it was supposed to break
and left the other passing.

Deliberately not done here. The zero-rated supply still prints no breakdown
line, because the summariser only appends a row when the amount exceeds zero,
and fixing that changes the shape of a live payload rather than a wrong number,
so it lands separately. The swallowed UnknownRateClassError in the summariser
is a different axis and lands separately too. Neither the response schema nor
the frontend panel is touched, and the two rate tables in the product stay two.

docs(pdf): the line-break comment names the route the code actually takes

The comment above _NEVER_DRAWN reached the right conclusion by the wrong
mechanism, and it was mine. It said that no face reports a glyph for a line
break, so every rung of the ladder fails and the string lands on the widest
face, which is the Chinese pack. Two of those three claims are false.

Latin string carrying a newline, Helvetica reports no glyph and the bundled
Unicode face reports no glyph, but the CID pack reports one, because it answers
coverage from a codepage that encodes a line break. So it satisfies the loop
and is returned on its own merits, and the settle-for branch is never reached.
The widest face is also not the Chinese pack: it is the bundled Unicode one,
and it exists for scripts nothing on the ladder covers, Hangul and Thai among
them.

The conclusion survives untouched. Such a string is drawn in the Chinese pack,
which is the byte-moving accident _NEVER_DRAWN prevents, so no behaviour and no
test changes here and none should. But the whole job of that comment is to
explain why the constant exists, and a reader working out the fallback path
from it would build the wrong model of the ladder and then act on it. A comment
that is merely stale is a nuisance; one that describes a mechanism the code
does not have is worse than none, because it is confident.

Found while reading the ladder to answer a question about the hand-rolled PDF

being checked against what the functions return.

fix(boq): a total says how much of it was never converted

A BOQ resource priced in a foreign currency is converted to the project base
before it joins the rollup. When the project holds no usable rate for that
currency the amount is summed in its own units anyway. That is deliberate and
it is the right call: a row is never zeroed and the rollup stays deterministic.
The cost of it is that the grand total can be a blend of currencies, and until
now nothing on the resource-summary response said so.

A user hit this and it is the only defect in the current sweep with a witness
rather than a reasoned argument behind it. They changed a resource's currency
from one code to another and watched the total not move. The reason was that
the first currency had a rate in their project and the second did not, so the
conversion was skipped rather than applied. The pair is what made it
diagnosable. One unchanged total reads like a screen that failed to refresh,
whereas two currencies behaving differently under the same action on the same
screen is a diagnosis.

The response now carries the unconverted money per currency, quantised with the
same quantum and rounding mode as the total it qualifies so the two subtract
cleanly. No published figure moves. What changes is that a reader can see that
fifty thousand dollars are sitting inside a euro total, instead of being left
to assume that none are.

The existing missing-rate warning was not enough for two separate reasons, and
both are worth naming. It reaches the grid per position and never reaches the
summary at all, so the surface that does the blending was the one surface with
no signal on it. And it carries the currency code without the amount. A warning
that names a problem without sizing it invites the reader to assume it is
small, and assuming it is small is the failure mode.

The conversion policy also stops being written out by hand. It existed in four
places, three helpers in the service and a fourth copy inline in the router,
and an inline re-implementation of a shared rule is the kind of thing that
drifts on its own because there is no shared name to grep for. It is now one
function, returning a factor rather than a converted amount so that a Decimal
caller and a float caller can share the decision without either changing its
arithmetic. It returns None when a conversion is needed and cannot be done,
which is the distinction the whole change rests on: None and 1.0 produce an
identical total and mean opposite things, and collapsing them is precisely how
an unconvertible amount joins a base-currency total unnoticed.

The router copy carried an extra guard that skipped the branch entirely when a
project had no FX table at all, which is the case where the most value goes
unconverted and so the worst one to stay silent about. Conversion behaviour is
unchanged, since no rate is no rate either way, but that case is now reported.

This is half of the work. Whether an unconvertible amount belongs in a grand
total at all is a product judgement about what a grand total means, it moves
numbers customers have already signed off, and it is not being decided here.
The channel is the shared prefix of both answers: nothing can be excluded from
a total until it can be reported separately, so this code is required either
way and is thrown away under neither.

Five places in the tree answer "money in more than one currency" and they give
five different answers, which is why this lands as a survey rather than a fix.
Variations converts what it can and returns the rest separately, never folding
it into the total. The CRM analytics types never blend, and carry per-currency
arrays as the truth. Property development's profit and loss excludes foreign
rows from every accumulator and sets a flag, so it understates and says that it
is understating, which is a working state. The sales kanban blends every
currency in a column into one total with no flag anywhere, which is not a
figure at all. And the BOQ, here, converts what it can and blends the rest.

Two of those five are already correct, and they are left exactly as they are.
They are the reference.

One thing found while measuring that is worth recording beyond this change. The
BOQ helper and the variations helper read as though they agree, because their
comments use the same vocabulary about determinism and never zeroing a row,
while their behaviour is opposite on the only question that matters. Two
functions that appear to agree are more dangerous than two that obviously
disagree, because nobody re-reads the one they believe they already understand.
The two docstrings only gave it away side by side.

fix(property-dev): a quote stops depending on which price field it carries

The same contract, the same jurisdiction, the same missing rate class, and two
different answers from the API depending on which price field the contract
happens to hold. compute_total_taxes_for_contract wrapped its compute_vat call
in `except UnknownRateClassError` and left its net_from_gross call twelve lines
above it bare, so a contract carrying `net` returned 200 with vat 0.00 and no
VAT line, while the identical contract carrying `total_value` raised and became
a 422. Measured across every case rather than argued, with region_subcode
supplied so that stamp duty could not refuse first on an unrelated axis:

  US standard  no VAT block in the table   net: 200 vat=0.00   total_value: 422
  BR standard  no VAT block in the table   net: 200 vat=0.00   total_value: 422
  RU reduced   has a block, lacks a class  net: 200 vat=0.00   total_value: 422
  GB standard  control, ordinary case      net: 200 vat=20000  total_value: 200

Nobody would write that down as a rule. The honesty of the answer was not a
property of the question asked; it was a property of which of two equivalent
fields the caller filled in.

Who that exposes is worth stating rather than leaving to assumption. The
service builds its contract input with a net key and never a total_value one,
so our own screens take the first column every time and the second is
unreachable from them. This is shipped surface on an open API rather than a
path our UI walks, which means the fix protects integrators rather than us.
That is a reason to fix it rather than to defer it, since an integrator on the
second column has no way to discover that the first exists and answers
differently.

Underneath it, UnknownRateClassError was two errors sharing one name. US and BR
have no vat or gst block at all. RU has a block holding exempt and standard and
the caller asked for reduced. Those are not the same event: one is a fact about
what the table holds, the other is a caller naming something that does not
exist. Neither the type nor the message text separated them, and the summariser
flattened both onto the same zero that the previous commit had just finished
separating from the zero-rated one. One slot carrying two questions resolved
two different ways is the same mistake as folding accuracy into a coverage
verdict, with different nouns.

So the event is split. A jurisdiction whose table holds no VAT or GST block
raises NoVatBlockError, which the summariser handles at both call sites and
turns into a real zero, because a quote for a country with no modelled VAT
should still be a quote. A rate class that does not exist in a jurisdiction
that does have a block keeps UnknownRateClassError, and it now propagates from
both call sites to the 422 clause that was already there, which is what removes
the asymmetry. NoVatBlockError is deliberately not a subclass of the error it
was split out of: making it one would leave every existing except on the parent
swallowing the child, and the split would be a rename.

The new error is named for the table, not for the world. It says the rate table
holds no VAT or GST block, which is checkable by reading the YAML. It
deliberately does not say the jurisdiction has no VAT system, because that is
true of the United States, which has no federal VAT, and false of Brazil, which
levies ICMS, ISS, PIS and COFINS on property transactions and is simply not
modelled here. A message asserting the second thing would be a regression
dressed as a fix: today Brazil quotes a silently wrong zero, and under that
wording it would quote a confidently labelled wrong zero, and a label is what
stops the next reader looking. The wording is a placeholder for a marker the
table does not yet have, distinguishing no-VAT-by-law from not-modelled-yet.
Once that exists this message should be sharpened to say which of the two
applies. That marker is scheduled; this is what is honest until it lands.

On the control that produced the table above, because the first version of it
was wrong in a way worth recording. It used US without a region_subcode, and
both arms raised: the net arm on MissingRegionSubcodeError from stamp duty, an
entirely different axis, several steps before execution reached the line under
test. The two arms did differ, which was the shape being looked for, so it read
as a clean discriminating pair. What exposed it was a disagreement between two
instruments rather than a re-measurement: the hypothesis predicted that arm
would return a swallowed zero, and it raised instead, and a prediction of a
return does not get to count a raise as support for itself. The second tell was
the exception identity, since MissingRegionSubcodeError had no business
appearing at all if the account of the mechanism was right. A control that
reaches the wrong raise first measures the wrong thing and looks conclusive
doing it, so every unrelated input a call path needs must be supplied before a
refusal means anything.

That is also why the new test asserts the expected kind of each row and not
only that the two columns agree. Agreement alone is satisfied by refusing
everything and by quoting everything, and each of those breaks one row while
leaving the other three. Both were run: guarding one call site again fails
exactly the two no-block rows and leaves the control rows green, and making the
new error a subclass fails exactly the test that says the split is real.

Deliberately not done here. The zero this leaves behind carries no provenance
yet, so a caller still cannot tell it from a zero-rated one; that is the next
commit, because it adds a response field and is purely additive where this
changes what existing requests return. The rate table is untouched, so Brazil
still quotes zero and is merely honest about why.

fix(validation): the phone and address rules say whose rules they are

The phone validator emitted numbers that cannot exist and reported them valid.
Asked to normalise 301234567 for France, which has no rules here, it returned
+301234567, which is well formed and belongs to Greece. Given the same number
with a trunk zero it returned +0301234567, which is not a possible E.164 number
under any numbering plan. Both came back with passed True and country_code FR,
so the one field that could have warned the caller was instead confirming the
mistake.

That field was an echo throughout. get_phone_rules returned the generic
patterns stamped with the country that was asked about, so a config endpoint
could tell a UI these were France's phone rules when France has none here.
validate_phone stamped the same code onto every result, and so did
validate_address. The address getters made the opposite mistake and said
nothing at all: get_address_rules and get_address_field_order returned the
generic table unlabelled, so two uncovered countries came back byte identical
with no way to tell either was a stand-in.

Both now carry a Provenance from app/core/provenance.py beside the value: what
was asked for, what answered, and whether that was a fallback. country_code
keeps meaning what it always meant, the code that was asked about, because the
thing that answers a missing row is not a country and putting it in that field
would replace an echo with something worse. What answered is jurisdiction.used.

The stand-in is named for what it is rather than for the slot it fills.
DIGIT_COUNT_ONLY for phone, because what judges an uncovered country is a count
of digits and nothing else, with no dial code and no numbering plan behind it.
PRESENCE_ONLY for address, because what stands in there checks that street,
city and country are non-empty and examines the shape of nothing. A reader who
has never opened either file learns the shape of the risk from the token, which
is the whole job of the field: DEFAULT would have told them only that the
non-default did not answer, and answered already says that. Neither is called
INTERNATIONAL, which would assert a standard behind a regex whose purpose is to
accept anything.

The token is descriptive and never a discriminant. Anything deciding whether it
holds a country-specific answer reads source, or answered for the boolean, both
of which are defined once in core and cannot drift. Comparing the token against
a literal is the wrong idiom and would miss every fallback whose stand-in is
named something else.

The E.164 hole needed more than a field. No number of provenance fields
rescues a fabricated value: a label saying these are the generic rules, sitting
beside a string no telephone network can route, is still a labelled lie, and a
caller that trusts the label still holds +0301234567. A national number can
only be turned into an E.164 by a dial code and only a real country row carries
one, so where there is none e164 is now None. passed still reports what the
syntax check found, because a fallback is an answer and the generic pattern may
well be right about the digits. Success therefore no longer implies an E.164
form and the docstrings say so in both places that used to promise it.

Error messages moved with it, because a message saying a number does not match
the national format for country FR is itself a claim that France's rules judged
it. They now name whichever rules did. On the address side only the required
field message could ever have been wrong that way: the generic rules carry no
postcode pattern and require no state, so those two checks are unreachable
unless a real row answered, and a comment says so where they still name the
country.

How much this repairs. Nothing in this repository calls any of these five
functions. There is no import of app.core.validation.phone or .address
anywhere, the package __init__ is two lines of copyright so nothing is
re-exported, and there is no router, no test and no frontend reference. Both
files carry four commits, three of them repo wide sweeps and the fourth the
bulk commit that created them, whose siblings in the same commit got tests and
callers while these got neither. So this is speculative code that never had a
caller rather than a regression that lost one, and what the fix buys is that
the first consumer is not misled rather than that live output is repaired. The
claim stops at the repository edge on purpose, since packs resolve through
importlib.resources and an external one is out of reach of a grep.

Which is also the argument for fixing rather than deleting. The field diary
module needed to validate a phone number and wrote its own regex against a
local pattern instead of importing the validator that exists to do it. That is
demand routing around the capability rather than an absence of demand, and the
answer to something people needed and did not use is to make it correct, not to
remove it and guarantee the next module writes a third regex.

One axis each, and that is measured rather than assumed. The dial code was the
candidate second axis for phone and it is perfectly correlated with coverage,
since all fourteen entries carry one and the generic rules carry none, so a
second provenance would have repeated the first in every case rather than
distinguishing anything. Address resolves postcode pattern, required fields,
field order and the state flag from a single row.

Forty tests, and the controls are the point of them. A covered country is
asserted to be declared rather than merely not a fallback, and an uncovered one
to be a fallback rather than merely not declared, so an implementation
answering one fixed verdict fails in both directions. Each pair is also
asserted to disagree with the other, since two separate constants would satisfy
everything else. The E.164 tests name the two strings the old code produced
rather than checking only for None, so neither can return and still pass.

The test that carries the most is the inversion, because it is a relation
between two calls rather than an expected value and cannot be satisfied by
accident: Canada, which has rules, rejects the nine digits that France, which
does not, accepts. The generic pattern takes six to fifteen digits and is
looser than every national rule in the table, so coverage was turning a
rejection into an acceptance. Coverage asymmetry is pinned for the same reason,
since Canada has phone rules and no address rules and neither surface's answer
can be assumed from the other's.

Three mutations, run rather than reasoned about. Restoring the echo so the
requested country is stamped as declared fails twelve of the forty and leaves
every covered case passing. Writing that echo down literally, declared with
used set to the generic table, fails thirteen, one more, because the
constructor refuses it outright. Restoring the fabricated E.164 fails five, and
only the tests written for it. The covered and uncovered cases fail differently
under each, which is what says the tests measure the distinction rather than
the shape.

One defect is recorded rather than repaired, and pinned by two tests so it
cannot be rediscovered by a crash. The address rule dicts are not of uniform
shape: postcode_optional is carried by the generic rules and by none of the
thirteen country rows, and postcode_note by GB and UK alone. A consumer
branching on either key gets a usable value for every country we do not support
and a KeyError for every country we do, which is the wrong way round twice over
from one cause. Filling it in means deciding what postcode optional means for
eleven countries whose authors never said, which is a question about the data
rather than about provenance, so the tests assert the shape as it stands and
will fail the moment somebody answers it.

feat(property-dev): a regulator report carries the language it was drafted in

The quarterly regulator report is generated for four regulators and three of
them are drafted in English. The fourth, the 214-FZ filing, is drafted in
Russian, because Russian is the language the filing is made in. The route
served all four without saying anything about language, so the Accept-Language
middleware labelled every one of them with whatever the reader had asked for.
A German reader downloading the Dubai disclosure received a document declared
German, and a Russian reader downloading the Russian filing received the one
document on the route that really was in their language, also mislabelled.

The language is a property of the regulator here rather than of the reader, and
that is the whole reason a literal at the route would not do. A Russian filing
does not become English because a London office opened it, and it does not
become German because the browser asked for German. So RegulatorReport now
carries a language field beside the bytes, each generator states what it wrote,
and the route reads it off the report. The field is deliberately required rather
than defaulted, so adding a fifth regulator forces the question to be answered
instead of quietly inheriting English.

Writing the four values down turned up the argument for recording rather than
inferring. The module header describes the CMA disclosure as bilingual, Arabic
and English. There is no Arabic prose anywhere in the file, so the rendered page
is English throughout and the field says English. A route clever enough to work
out its own language from the surrounding declarations would have believed that
header and declared Arabic on a document with no Arabic in it. The field records
what the generator wrote; the header records what somebody once intended. Those
two diverged and stayed diverged, which is why the generator is asked and not
the module.

The payload branch is untouched and still carries the request-derived header.
Whether a machine submission declares a language is a separate decision from
this one, and the same call was made for the e-invoice XML in 5dc0f8115.

The warranty claim sheet in the same router declares English on both of its
branches, the PDF and the text fallback. A fallback that dropped the header
would have made the language of that document depend on whether reportlab
happened to be importable.

One limit on the evidence, stated because it is not visible from the diff, and
one thing found while establishing it. The JSON envelope branch of the
compliance route is executed by no test. Searched three ways: the path fragment,
the response model name, and the bare route name in case a test assembled the
URL. Both tests that reach the endpoint take the 422 path and the as=pdf path
and return before the envelope is built, and the response model is named nowhere
under tests at all. So the new required field is checked by the accompanying
declaration test, which reads the route's syntax, and not by any request.

That branch is not dead code, which is the part worth acting on. The web client
calls it with no as parameter, in fetchRegulatorReport, so the envelope is the
shape a user of the compliance page actually receives while the two shapes the
tests cover are the two nobody's browser asks for. The gap predates this change
and is not closed by it; it is written down here because the field being added
travels on that untested branch.

feat(documents): twelve exports stop letting the middleware name their language

Twelve routes rendered a document and said nothing about what language it was
in. Saying nothing is not neutral here. AcceptLanguageMiddleware sets
Content-Language on every response with setdefault, so a silent route does not
ship an undeclared document, it ships one labelled with whatever the reader
asked for. A German reader downloading the tender package received English
bytes that claimed to be German, and neither the browser, the archive nor the
next person to open the file had any way to know a fallback had happened.

Each of these is a literal rather than a resolver, and for the same reason the
RPS was in 5dc0f8115: nothing in these builders takes a locale from anywhere.
Their labels are English literals, so English is what the page is. The
declaration is not a promise to keep them English, it is an accurate statement
about what is being served today, and it turns every silent fallback on these
routes into a visible one at no cost.

The routes are the four tendering exports, both meetings exports, the AIA
payment application, the methodology export, the punch list, the field report
and the form submission record. The reporting download declares for every
format it serves rather than only the PDF, because all of them are built from
the same English literals.

A thirteenth belongs with these and is not in this commit. The BOQ estimate
export got the same declaration for the same reason, and it landed inside
be4de421c because that file was carrying an unrelated currency change at the
same time and a pathspec cannot take half a file. It is named here so the
header on that route can be traced to this argument rather than to the commit
message it arrived under.

Two of these documents are worth a note beyond the header. The tender package
export and the form submission record are not rendered with reportlab at all:
each writes a single Courier text stream through latin-1 with errors="replace",
so any character outside Latin-1 in a bidder's name or an inspector's answer is
replaced with a question mark before it reaches the page. Declaring English is
accurate about the labels and is not a claim that the data survived. That is
the script axis and it is tracked separately.

Gated by tests/unit/test_document_language_declarations.py, which is two tests
because they fail for opposite reasons. One names every rendering route and
fails when a declaration is removed. The other searches for PDF-serving routes
and fails when one appears that is in neither the rendering list nor the
serves-stored list, which is the case a list alone can never catch. Both were
run against a deliberately broken tree first: removing one header, unclassifying
one route and relabelling the Russian filing each turn the expected test red,
and every file was restored byte-exact afterwards.

fix(calendar): a span nobody computed stops reading as a computed one

Two changes in one pass, both on the same file, because visiting it twice costs
more than the changes do.

The stand-in token for an uncovered country is renamed. It was INTERNATIONAL,
which names a category rather than a thing: it would have been equally true of
every international default in the tree, and that is the disqualifier the
provenance module states outright. Worse, it claimed a standard. There is no
international convention under which nobody has public holidays, and what
actually answers for an uncovered country is precisely that, an absence.
NO_PUBLIC_HOLIDAYS says what the caller is holding and asserts nothing behind
it. GREGORIAN_ONLY already passed the same test and is untouched. The constant
is private to the module and the tests assert against the constant rather than
the literal, so nothing outside moves.

The larger half is a third axis. Six Gulf countries and Switzerland hold
holidays whose dates are computed and whose extent is not. _gcc_eids applies one
span of three and four days to all six, because the real length is announced
annually by each government, and the Swiss function is a hardcoded three-date
roster under a comment reading simplified. Both are answers a caller can compute
dates with, and neither was worked out.

So holiday_extent is a FALLBACK and not a kind of coverage. Coverage answers
whether rows are present; all seven have their rows and both of the other axes
stay declared, which is a true sentence. What the third axis says is that
something stood in for the extent, and it names what stood in, as a fallback now
must. Switzerland sits beside the Gulf deliberately: a hardcoded roster is as
uncomputed as a hardcoded span, and marking one while leaving the other would
make the absence of the mark mean less than it should.

The naming is load-bearing and this is the paragraph to read before tidying any
of it. The obvious objection to marking these seven at all is that marking the
cases we happen to know about makes the silence everywhere else say something
false, and nobody has verified the German roster either. What defeats that is
naming the axis and its tokens for the mechanism rather than for the quality.
An absent stand-in means no stand-in we know of, which is modest and true
anywhere. An axis called approximate, or unverified, would have an absence
meaning verified, and this module cannot support that claim for a single table
in it. Rename any of this to describe how good the answer is and it starts lying
about every country it does not mention.

For the same reason it records the mechanism and not the grading. The docstring
on _gcc_eids calls the span closest to correct for the UAE and too short for
Saudi Arabia. That grading is deliberately ignored and all six are registered
identically, because closest to correct is still not computed, and how far off
each one runs is a judgement rather than something to derive.

There is a live consequence and it is the reason this is worth a commit rather
than a comment. Nothing publishes as jurisdiction specific while a dimension it
uses falls back, and that rule reads the verdict. Before this change Saudi
Arabia answered fully covered on a span its own source says runs short, so the
rule read the answer and never saw the caveat. holiday_provenance now weighs
three axes instead of two, so the verdict goes amber on its own rather than
depending on a consumer remembering to read a second field. There is a test
asserting exactly that, at the level a consumer would hit it.

placeholder_spans keeps its meaning and becomes the data beside the new
provenance, the way omitted sits beside effective_year. A test holds the two
registries together, because a country carrying the names of holidays nobody
computed while reporting the axis clean is the worse half of that pair to lose.

Mutation matrix, measured, with the source restored to a byte-identical sha256
after each. Baseline fifty five passed, one hundred and eighteen with
test_calendar.py alongside. Restoring the swallow fails four. Raising but still
caching an empty answer fails two. Treating a curated-window miss as complete
fails four. Calling every shared table a synonym fails one, and forgetting the
synonym table fails one the other way. Calling an uncovered country declared
fails three. Dropping one Gulf country from the span registry fails three.
Calling every uncomputed extent a computed one fails eight. Restored, one
hundred and eighteen passed. With the Nigeria and Bulgaria file alongside, one
hundred and thirty.

Nigeria and Bulgaria need nothing here and get nothing. Neither has a curated
year window nor a stand-in extent, so both register as nothing on the second and
third axes and read as fully declared, which is what the tables say about them.
