docs(tests): the money serializer guard names the practice it codifies

The test that keeps an or-zero fallback unreachable now says, in its own
docstring, that property_dev/schemas.py already splits its money serializers on
exactly this distinction. The required serializer ends in a zero fallback, the
optional one carries none and returns a nullable string so an absent value
serializes as null, and computed_price sits correctly on the optional one.

That sentence is worth seven lines because of what it does to a reader meeting
the test for the first time. A guard that introduces a rule invites an argument
about whether the rule is right. A guard that names an existing convention and
says where it is already practised is answerable by reading one file. The
convention was there before the test and was written down nowhere, which is the
condition under which a convention quietly stops being one.

Placed directly after the paragraph explaining why the fallback is a landmine
rather than dead code, so the reader meets the convention before the failure
instructions rather than after them.

fix(i18n-foundation): the stand-in week is named for the week it is

The working-days answer already says whether it knew the country. When it did
not, the provenance named what stood in as DEFAULT, which is the one thing a
reader did not need to be told: that the non-default did not answer is what

defined once in core where they cannot drift. Nothing in the shipped tests

fix(boq): the estimate class rung is named in the reader's language

The classification panel printed the class label straight from the API, so the
rung name read in English in every language the product ships. The fifteen keys
around it were fully translated, which made the result worse than an untranslated
panel: the words Accuracy, Methodology and Definition Level arrived in the
reader's language and the thing they labelled did not.

It now resolves through estimateBasis.class.label, and no parallel key set was
minted. That namespace already existed and the estimate basis surface already
used it for the same five rungs, so this panel joins an arrangement rather than
starting one. The reuse is safe rather than lucky, and the evidence is that the
five English values in en.ts are identical to the five labels in the class table
the API serves them from, so pointing the panel at the keys cannot change a word
of what an English reader sees. One ladder, one key namespace, and a translator
who improves a rung name now improves it on both surfaces at once.

absence had any effect, because the regional variants resolve through their base
language before English, so a key missing from es-MX is answered by es and a key

and a key that was never looked up render identical English.

render and does not match the new one. Proving it that way rather than by

obvious way to show a test has teeth is to break the file other people are
working in. The assertion is made against the source of the call site rather
than a rendered component for a plainer reason: the property is about one line,

feat(payment-clock): Bulgaria and Nigeria get their own payment clocks

Two of the seven cohort countries missing from payment.prompt_payment_regime
now have rows: bg_commercial_act_303a and ng_ppa_2007. Five remain (Canada,
Russia, China, India, Brazil).

Nigeria's clock is Public Procurement Act 2007 section 37, not section 35.
A secondary source cited 35 with a confident paragraph attached, and it was
wrong about the citation while roughly right about the substance, which is
the worse combination: a reader who checks the substance and finds it
plausible has no reason left to check the number. The Act's own section
order settles it, 35 is mobilization fees, 36 is the performance guarantee,
37 is interest on delayed payments. Section 37(2) deems a payment delayed
past sixty days from invoice or valuation certificate submission; 37(3) sets
no statutory rate at all, it points at the contract, and 37(4) obliges every
contract to carry one, so the row's interest basis is "contract" by express
statutory command rather than by the Act's silence. The Act reaches public
procuring entities only. No private-sector Nigerian statute was found, so
the row ships alone rather than paired with an invented private one, and the
absence is stated in its own notes rather than left for a reader to assume.

Bulgaria's Commercial Act Article 303a turned out to be a real national fact
rather than a re-statement of the EU Late Payment Directive's floor: fourteen
days absent agreement against the Directive's thirty, and ten percentage
points over the BNB base rate against the Directive's eight over the ECB
rate. Bulgaria's transposition is stricter than the minimum on both counts,
which is what makes bg_commercial_act_303a a row of its own rather than a
case the existing eu_late_payment regime already answers. The figures come
from two independent legal-practice guides rather than the Commercial Act's
own text, and the row's notes say so, along with the one thing that was not
checked, whether Bulgarian public procurement carries this same period or a
separate one the way the Directive's own Article 4 treats public authorities
differently from transactions between undertakings.

Registry shape was checked before either row was written. The public against
private split and a two-stage certify-then-pay clock both already have room,
proved by the shipped US and Australian multi-regime entries and the four
independently nullable dates every regime is built from; neither country
needed it widened. One real gap surfaced during that check and is not fixed
here: PaymentRegime carries no effective-date range, so a statute that was
superseded, Brazil's procurement law and Russia's 44-FZ both qualify, has
nowhere to record the window it was in force. Bulgaria and Nigeria do not

fix(calendar): two stated limits that nothing enforced now reach the caller

Both of these are the same defect as the swallowed holiday computation, on the
same axis, which is why they travel together. A limit the code knows about and
the caller cannot see is not a limit, it is a wrong answer with a comment.

THE HIJRI WINDOW

_hijri_dates_in_gregorian_year caught the converter's range error and returned
an empty list, and its own Returns section documented that as a feature: empty
if the year is outside the converter's supported range or no match exists. One
value standing for a defect and an answer at the same time, written down as
intended behaviour, and there was a test asserting it. So this was a decision
rather than an oversight, which is worth saying plainly because reversing a
decision deserves more than reversing an accident.

What it did. The converter reaches 1924-08-01 to 2077-11-16. Past that, every
Islamic holiday vanished and the year reported itself fully covered on every
axis, so is_working_day counted Eid al-Fitr as a working day. Measured, the UAE
holds thirteen holidays a year and returned four from 2078 onward, Saudi Arabia
nine and returned two, Nigeria eleven and returned eight.

Nigeria is in that list because it converts Hijri dates directly, not through
the Gulf helper. It joined the affected set the day it was added, and anybody
writing the list from memory as "the Gulf countries" would have missed it. That
is why _HIJRI_DEPENDENT is held to the source by a test that finds every holiday
function reaching the converter, and why the test asserts equality rather than
containment.

A year past the window now raises, which surfaces as UNAVAILABLE, and
is_working_day refuses rather than returning a confident wrong answer. The year
that straddles the end of the window, 2077, is a fallback on the year axis
naming HIJRI_WINDOW_EDGE, because the reachable part of it did answer.

2077 is the interesting one. The window ends in mid-November, so that year
converts in January and fails in December, and the UAE reported twelve holidays
for it against a healthy thirteen. Twelve sits inside the band that ordinary
lunar drift produces, so the year that was already wrong is the one that looked
healthy, and no threshold anybody would have set could have found it. The flat
four from 2078 was merely the part that was obvious.

ON THE EMPTY LIST, WHICH IS THE PART I GOT WRONG FIRST

The argument for raising was originally that an empty result is sometimes a
legitimate answer, since the docstring says a fixed Hijri date can fall in a
Gregorian year zero, one or two times. The zero is false. Measured over the
converter's entire window, 1925 to 2076, all four Hijri dates this module uses
land once or twice in every single year and never zero, and it is arithmetic
rather than luck: consecutive occurrences are about 354 days apart and a
Gregorian year is 365, so two of them cannot straddle one.

So the ambiguity the docstring advertised never existed in the data. Every empty
list this function ever returned was the defect and none of them were answers,
which makes raising simply correct rather than a judgement call. The docstring
is corrected in place, with the reason, because it is what made an empty return
look like it might mean something.

THE JAPANESE FORMULA WINDOW

_equinox_day states "accurate for the years 1980-2099" and enforced nothing.
Japan at 2100 and at 2500 returned sixteen holidays and declared on every axis.
The boundary is earned rather than copied from somewhere: the formula corrects
leap years with offset // 4, which treats 2100 as a leap year where Gregorian
does not, so it goes one day out at 2100 and never recovers. It yields March 19
for 2100 against March 20 for 2099 and 2101.

Outside the window the year axis is now a fallback naming EXTRAPOLATED_EQUINOX.
That takes the other edge with it: 1979 returns nineteen holidays against
sixteen for 2000, because the modern roster is applied to a year before the law
that created it, which is the same lie at the opposite end.

WHY THESE TWO FIXES QUOTE A BOUND AND THE CURATED TABLES DO NOT

Deliberate, and it will look like an inconsistency to anyone tidying. A curated
table names particular years and can be missing one in the middle, so
_CURATED_TABLES is tested for membership and never for bounds, or an interior
gap would read as a covered year. A formula's validity and a library's window
are continuous and cannot have interior gaps, so there the bound is the fact
rather than a second copy of one. Do not unify them on the grounds that they
look alike.

TWO TESTS BELONGING TO OTHER PEOPLE CHANGED, AND BOTH WERE ASSERTING SOMETHING
THAT IS NOT TRUE ANY MORE

test_hijri_out_of_range_year_does_not_raise asserted the old behaviour and its
docstring called it degrading gracefully. It is rewritten to the new contract,
keeping the observation that the behaviour was deliberate. Silence a caller
cannot detect is not graceful.

test_neither_country_has_a_curated_year_window probed 2099 on the reasoning that
a year far in the future is as good a check as one nearby. That holds for
Bulgaria, which is Easter arithmetic with no horizon, and not for Nigeria, which
inherits the converter's. The probe year moved and the half the assumption was
hiding is now its own test: Bulgaria answers for any year, Nigeria stops at the
converter.

Mutation matrix, eleven mutations across the three calendar test files, source
restored to a byte-identical sha256 after each. Baseline one hundred and fifty
two passed. Restoring the holiday swallow fails nine, raising but still caching
five, a curated-window miss as complete four, every shared table a synonym one
and forgetting the synonym table one the other way, an uncovered country
declared four, dropping a Gulf country from the span registry three, every
uncomputed extent computed eight, restoring the hijri swallow five, no longer
enforcing the Japanese window three, and dropping Nigeria from the
hijri-dependent set two. Restored, one hundred and fifty two passed.

Left alone on purpose. next_working_day still returns its cap boundary after
sixty iterations under a comment calling it unreachable. It is unreachable with
shipped data, because no working week in the table is empty, and it becomes
reachable the day one lands that is. That is a latent hole rather than a
demonstrated defect, and bundling it here would make this commit argue for three
things at three different strengths.

fix(calendar): the rulings land where the next reader will actually look

Four things, three of them decisions that were made about 0f08854d0 after it
landed and had nowhere durable to live, and one defect in that commit.

THE CLAIM THAT COMMIT DISPROVED SURVIVED IN FOUR PLACES

0f08854d0 measured that a fixed Hijri date never lands zero times in a
Gregorian year, corrected the docstring that said otherwise, and left three
more copies of the claim in the same file plus one in its own test. The module
argued both ways depending on which docstring a reader opened.

The loudest survivor was HijriRangeError, the class written for the correction.
It said an empty list is the honest answer for a year in which an Islamic date
genuinely does not fall, and offered the shorter lunar year as the reason that
happens legitimately. That fact proves the opposite: consecutive occurrences
are about 354 days apart against a Gregorian 365, which is exactly why none is
impossible. Anyone reading only that class would have concluded the raise was a
judgement call between two readings.

The other three were the HIJRI_COVERED token comment, the _gcc_eids docstring
repeating the zero, one or two wording, and the test asserting the new
behaviour justifying it with the claim its sibling test disproves.

Worth naming why they survived, because the search was the failure and not the
care. The copies were hunted where the old code had been. Three of the four
were in prose written as part of the correction itself, which is where nobody
looks, because that is the part you are sure you got right.

TWO DEFECTS SHARING A TOKEN NOW STAY TWO CLAUSES

EXTRAPOLATED_EQUINOX covers a formula run outside the range it was fitted to
and a modern holiday roster applied to a year that predates it. Separate
faults, one axis, and the detail string ran them together as one sentence with
a long explanation, so a reader could not tell which one their year had.

They are not symmetric, which the blended sentence also hid. The extrapolation
applies at both ends of the window. The roster is only wrong below it. Carrying
the roster clause on a year above the window is a true sentence about the wrong
year, which is the quiet way a detail string stops being evidence.

Two clauses now, and the second is emitted only when it is true of the year
asked. There is a test rather than a comment on it, because the failure mode is
somebody tidying two clauses into one and prose does not survive that. Both
mutations kill it: blending the clauses fails one test, carrying the roster
clause above the window fails one test, 153 passing either side.

WHY THE GULF HORIZON IS UNAVAILABLE, AND WHAT WOULD REVERSE IT

This was ruled on rather than assumed and the record only held the ruling, not
the argument, which is the shape that gets re-derived from nothing in a year.

The obvious argument is wrong. A shipped test used to assert graceful
degradation, so somebody noticed the limit and chose to degrade past it, which
is the same shape as China's declared curated horizon. What decides it the
other way is that is_working_day is the only production consumer in the
backend and it returns a bare bool. A FALLBACK here would be a correct label on
an answer nothing in production reads, attached to a Gulf year missing every
Eid. Degrading gracefully requires somebody downstream capable of noticing.

So the reversing condition is written down next to the ruling: if
is_working_day ever grows a way to surface a degraded answer to its caller,
FALLBACK becomes the honest choice and this should be reopened deliberately.

THE EDGE IS THE FINDING, NOT THE CLIFF

On HIJRI_EDGE, because the token is where somebody meets this. A year fully
past the converter's window lost every Islamic holiday and was obvious: the UAE
returned four against a healthy thirteen. A straddling year returned twelve,
inside the ten to seventeen band ordinary lunar drift produces. The year that
was already wrong is the one that looked healthy.

The cliff was findable by counting and the edge never was, because the edge is
where the defect and the healthy signal overlap, and any instrument tuned to
catch the obvious part of a defect reports that overlap as fine.

Two of these four were asked for in a commit message. A commit message is not
where the next person looks, so they are in the source as well, and this note
says so rather than quietly substituting one for the other.

feat(property-dev): the table says whether a missing VAT block is the law or us

Two jurisdictions in the rate table carry no VAT or GST block, and until now
the table could not say why. The US levies no federal VAT, so zero is the
right VAT figure for a US quote. Brazil levies ICMS, ISS, PIS and COFINS, and
this table carries none of them on the VAT path, so a Brazilian quote has no
VAT figure at all and a zero understates it. Read from the table the two rows
were indistinguishable, and any single answer about them is wrong for one.

This is a field because the answer cannot be derived, and not a labelling
improvement. A two row yaml edit reads as cosmetic, so to be plain about it:
the next commit has to put a provenance source on the quote, and there is no
expression over this table that returns the right source for both rows. The
engine already knows the block is missing and raises NoVatBlockError for it,
but nothing in the table says whether the absence belongs to the law or to us.
Twelve jurisdictions are here and exactly two are blockless, so the population
splits one and one with no majority to round toward, and any single answer
covering both is wrong for half of what it covers. The alternative was
shipping that wrong source onto live quotes and adding the field afterwards.

The key is vat_absence, its two values are by_law and not_modelled, and it
sits at jurisdiction top level rather than inside a vat block. That placement
is deliberate: _has_vat_block reads vat and gst only, so a sibling key leaves
it returning False for both rows exactly as before and no existing path
changes behaviour. No computed amount moves in this commit.

The load-time validation is the part that carries weight, more than the two
YAML lines. A blockless jurisdiction that declares nothing is refused, a
declared value outside the pair is refused, and a jurisdiction that has a
block and declares the key anyway is refused, which is the same shape of
contradiction the provenance type rejects, told about a table instead of an
answer. The check runs before the cache is assigned rather than after, so a
refused table is not left behind for the next caller to read as though it had
passed, and there is a test holding that rather than a comment vouching for
it. Refusing rather than defaulting is the whole point. A default is how
the next jurisdiction would acquire an answer nobody chose, resolving to
whatever the accessor happened to return with nothing to notice. It costs
nothing today because both blockless rows are marked, so the refusal cannot
fire on the shipped table. It exists for the row somebody adds next year.

Two values and not three. The pair names where the gap lives, which is a
question with two answers and no middle. A third value such as partial would
answer a different question, how completely something is modelled, and no
caller can derive anything from a degree. A comment saying so would not stop
anyone, so the loader raises instead.

The tests assert the property rather than the pair that satisfies it today.
Every blockless jurisdiction declares a marker and every declared marker is
one of the two, which survives a third row being added; asserting that the
set is US and BR would go red on that day and teach whoever added the row to
edit the test rather than read it. The refusals go through the loader rather
than calling the validator directly, because a validator nothing calls would
satisfy every one of them while the shipped table went unchecked, and a
well formed synthetic table is loaded as the control, since without it a
loader that rejected everything would pass all four refusal tests.

Verified by mutation rather than by argument. With only the call to the
validator removed and the validator itself left in place, the eight refusal
cases fail and the two property cases still pass, which is the split that
distinguishes a guard that discriminates from one that is merely wired. The
file was sha256 identical before and after. Seventy five tests in the engine
suite, a hundred and thirty two across everything that reads the table
including the drift gate, and eleven on the quote endpoint. The full unit
suite was not run; it does not finish inside ten minutes on this machine.

Deliberately not done here. No provenance is emitted yet; the accessor exists
so the next commit can derive a source instead of inventing one, and putting
both in one change is what would make this file hard to review. The docstrings
name app.core.provenance in prose but nothing imports it. And
pis_cofins_residential on the Brazil row is left exactly as it was: it is read
by nothing in the backend, which is worth someone's attention, but wiring a
rate changes what Brazilian contracts are charged and that is not a decision
to smuggle into a commit about a marker.

fix(supplier-catalogs): the three-way match refuses what it cannot compare

SupplierCatalogsPage.tsx:873 already settled this for the cheaper decision. A
raw Number(unit_price) comparison across vendor rows would crown 100 JPY cheaper
than 5 EUR, so a single cheapest may only be picked when every compared row
shares one currency. That ruling was made in this module, for choosing which
vendor looks good. It applies with more force to approving an invoice for
payment, and match_invoice was not honouring it.

VendorInvoice.currency and SupplierPurchaseOrder.currency are independent
columns, each defaulting to EUR, and neither was read. The header subtraction
and the per line subtraction ran regardless, so an invoice in one currency
matched against an order in another produced a variance that is not a number of
anything. When the nominal figures happen to sit close, the variance lands
inside the tolerance band and the invoice is auto approved for payment.

The route that makes this urgent is not the button. It is the Peppol ingest,
where auto_match defaults to True and the match runs on receipt, with no person
in the loop to notice that the two documents are priced in different money.

Not converting is the point. Reaching for an FX table here would trade a loud
wrong answer for a quiet one, and this module references the fx module zero
times, so there is no rate available that anyone has agreed to. Instead the
match declines to run, which is the same shape as the tax engine refusing a date
it has no rate for and formwork blanking a label it cannot name honestly.

Refusing needs somewhere to put the refusal, and that is the substance of the
change. Today "no variance" and "I cannot compute the variance" are the same
value, because MatchResult.price_variance is a required Decimal and every
refusal path has to invent one. The only values available are lies, and zero is
the worst of them, since zero variance is the exact figure that means nothing is
wrong. So the variances become optional and None means the comparison was not
performed. rfq_bidding/comparison.py:439 already does this with
normalised_amount, so this is existing practice in the tree rather than a new
idea. The no PO branch is folded in for the same reason: it was returning
Decimal("0") for a comparison it had not performed either, and leaving it would
have put two refusals side by side in one function with opposite doctrine.

three_way_match_status takes a new value, not_comparable, distinct from
exception. An exception means the match ran and the figures disagreed. This
means the match could not run, so the invoice may be perfectly correct. The
column is String(32) with no CHECK and no enum, so a fourth value costs one
literal and no migration. invoice.status deliberately does not move: refusing to
compute and then declining to write a verdict are the same decision, and writing
any status would be a smaller version of writing a zero.

The event is new rather than reused, and the subscriber is why that matters.
INVOICE_EXCEPTION has exactly one subscriber, in notifications, and it acts on a
person rather than on data. It writes a persisted warning to whoever ran the
match, with the reason truncated to 200 characters, and nothing automated reads
it. So the entire consequence of this defect is delivered to a human being in
their own language, as a sentence we compose, and until now that sentence stated
a price variance that does not exist. Reusing the exception body key would have
sent an operator hunting a pricing dispute rather than a data problem.

Two type unions in the frontend are corrected in the same commit, because they
are in the blast radius either way and both were wrong before this change.
MatchStatus declared auto_matched, a value that column has never held.
InvoiceStatus omitted disputed, which its column does hold, while declaring
matched, which the backend writes only to the other field. Both are inert and
each is referenced once, at the field it annotates, with nothing branching on
either. Two declarations were wrong for their entire lives without anyone
noticing, which is a fair measure of what a union costs when nothing consumes
it.

Covered by a test that builds an order in one currency and an invoice in
another for the identical amount, and asserts the refusal, both variances None,
both codes named in the reason, the invoice status unchanged, the new event
published, neither the matched nor the exception event carrying the invoice, and
no ThreeWayMatchRecord row written. That last one is deliberate: the record's
price_variance column is NOT NULL defaulting to zero, so the only row it could
store here is the lie this commit removes.

The notification carries two new English strings and no others. Every other
locale falls back to English until they are translated, which is a visible gap
rather than a silent one, and the remaining forty one files follow separately
so this fix is not held behind a translation pass.

refactor(core): one Content-Disposition helper instead of three

Three places built the RFC 6266 download header. app/core/content_disposition.py
exported attachment_disposition, app/core/http_headers.py exported
content_disposition_attachment, and bim_hub built the header inline in its model
geometry route. All three emitted the same pair of parameters and all three
carried their own comment explaining the same HTTP 500.

They did not arrive by degradation. The inline copy in bim_hub came first, the
http_headers helper came months later out of a stability sweep, and
content_disposition.py is the newest and the best of the three: it folds an
umlaut down to its base letter rather than to a question mark, and it replaces
the characters that are illegal in a Windows filename so the browser does not
have to. Each author solved the problem better than the last and nobody removed
the previous answer.

The older helper survived for a reason, and this change had to deal with it
rather than around it. content_disposition_attachment accepted inline=True and
attachment_disposition did not, so the two were being used as attachment versus
inline rather than as duplicates. record_publishing/router.py imported both on
adjacent lines and called one for each. The capability moves into the better
helper as a keyword argument, and only then does the other one go.

No download changes how it behaves. Nothing that used to save to disk now opens
in a tab and nothing that used to open now saves. The three routes that send an
inline disposition, a captured invoice document, a published record and the BIM
model geometry, send exactly the same disposition type as before; the keyword
exists so they can keep doing that through the better helper. Counted rather
than assumed: three inline call sites before this change and three after, one
for one.

What a user can see is the legacy filename= parameter, which is what a browser
falls back to when it ignores filename*, and every one of these headers sends
both. A German document name that used to be offered as B?rogeb?ude
Frankfurt.pdf is now offered as Burogebaude Frankfurt.pdf. A Cyrillic or Chinese
name gets underscores where it used to get question marks, which matters because
a question mark is not a legal filename character on Windows and the browser was
mangling the name a second time on the way to disk. An ASCII name is
byte-identical. The filename* parameter, which is the one every current browser
reads, is unchanged in every case, verified against the previous implementation
rather than against a description of it.

The test that should have prevented this asserted that each converted file calls
attachment_disposition or content_disposition_attachment. A guard written to
accept either helper cannot report that there are two, and it stayed green
through every commit that added a caller to the worse one. It now names a single
function.

What was run, and what it covers. The RFC 6266 filename suites, 81 tests, which
are the direct subject. Then every suite that asserts a Content-Disposition or
exercises a converted route, found by grepping the test tree for the header
rather than by picking files: record publishing, daily diary and its PDF locale,
the Brazil invoice PDF, cost catalogs, the design options comparison and the
export download filenames integration test, 197 tests, exit code 0. Then an
import check over all thirteen changed modules, because an import rename can
fail in a way a filename assertion cannot see; twelve import standalone and the
finance pair imports in the package order its own comment prescribes, which is a
pre-existing cycle in a file this change does not touch. ruff format and ruff
check are clean on all thirteen.

That is the coverage. The module suites for bim_hub, closeout, forms, schedule
and tendering were not run in full, so those five files rest on the import check
and on ruff rather than on their own tests.

feat(payment-clock): Ontario and India join the cohort

ca_on_construction_act and in_msmed_2006. Two more of the cohort's seven
missing countries. Canada is Ontario specifically, the province whose
prompt payment provisions commenced 2019-10-01; the federal Prompt Payment
for Construction Work Act is a second Canadian row for later, not retrieved

Ontario's dates were retrieved directly rather than taken at second hand:
the Ontario Association of Architects' Construction Act practice tip, which
cites the Act's own sections throughout, confirms 28 days to pay a proper
invoice, 14 days to serve a notice of non-payment, both counted in calendar
days stated explicitly rather than assumed, and a 7 day subcontractor
pass-through this regime does not compute. Missing the 14 day window means

Section 6.9's interest mechanism does not fit any of the four interest
bases: the contract rate governs whenever the contract specifies one, and
the Courts of Justice Act prejudgment rate is the default the section
supplies only when the contract is silent, a fallback rather than a floor

statutory default sitting behind it.

India's MSMED Act 2006 section 15 caps the payment period at 45 days from
acceptance or deemed acceptance; section 16 sets compound interest, with
monthly rests, not simple interest, at three times the Reserve Bank of
India's notified bank rate. Neither the multiplier nor the monthly
compounding has a field of its own: interest_basis, interest_margin_percent
and interest_fixed_percent were built for an additive margin, a single
prescribed source, or a flat rate. Written into interest_reference_rate as
text instead, and the notes say this costs nothing today because nothing in
the module computes a currency amount from these fields, only a
description, and would cost real accuracy the day something does. The Act
is buyer-size-scoped, reaching a buyer purchasing from a micro or small
enterprise, not construction-scoped, the same shape as Nigeria's
procurement-scope row; whether a shorter default period applies when no
date was agreed at all was not confirmed and is not encoded.

feat(property-dev): a tax quote says how it arrived at its VAT figure

Three quotes put the same bytes in the vat field and mean three different
things. A zero-rated first sale in the UAE has a rate, and the rate is zero.
The United States levies no VAT, so zero is the whole truth. Brazil levies
ICMS, ISS, PIS and COFINS, and this table carries none of them on the VAT
path, so its zero is a placeholder and a total that adds it understates
itself. Read from the amount the three were indistinguishable, and the two
that are safe to add to a total could not be told from the one that is not.

The quote now carries a vat_provenance beside the vat, on the vocabulary in
app.core.provenance rather than a private flag. A rate found for the
jurisdiction is declared. No VAT in law is a fallback, because a fallback is
an answer, the generic rule applied and the answer it produced is correct.
Nothing modelled is unavailable, which is the absence of an answer, and the
two must not share a code path. That is the module's own distinction and this
is the case it was written for.

The stand-in token is NO_VAT_IN_LAW. The test a token has to pass is whether
it would be equally true of the other blockless row, and this one is not:
Brazilian VAT is missing from our table while being present in Brazilian law,
so nothing about Brazil is described by saying the law levies none. The
summariser used to say the table models no VAT here, which was written when
the two rows were indistinguishable and would have covered both. Brazil
carries no token at all, and the type is what enforces that rather than a
convention: an unavailable that names something raises. The question is
written next to the token rather than only here, because it is a check a
reader can run on the next token on any axis, while naming the thing that
answered is a description a reader has to interpret.

The provenance is set in step 2 of the summariser and nowhere else, which is a
correctness point rather than tidiness. On a contract carrying total_value
rather than net, the step 1 handler fires as well, so setting the field in
both places would be two chances to disagree about one contract. The step 2
call is unconditional, so one place covers every path. Checked before relying
on it: NoVatBlockError has a single raise site, guarded by not
_has_vat_block, which is also what makes calling vat_absence inside that
handler safe, since it raises for a jurisdiction that has a block.

The resolver refuses a marker it has no rule for instead of letting one fall
through to unavailable. That branch cannot be reached through the loader,
which rejects a third value at load time, but the alternative is a future
third marker silently acquiring a provenance nobody chose, and the cost of
that is a wrong answer on a real quote rather than an error. This function and
VAT_ABSENCE_VALUES have to move together, and raising is what makes forgetting
audible.

On the wire the field is the dataclass itself, following
i18n_foundation.WorkingDaysResponse, which already ships a bare Provenance on
a response model. So there is no mirror type to drift. The answered and usable
properties do not cross the wire, and a test pins that: they are derivable from
source, and shipping both would invite clients to branch on the copy that
cannot be extended. The router needed no change, since it builds the response
with model_validate over the engine's dict.

The discriminating test asserts both halves, that the three amounts are equal
and that the three sources are pairwise different. The equal-amounts half is
the reason the field exists at all, and checking each source against its own
expected value would stay green if two later collapsed onto one. The existing
price-field invariant now carries the source too, so the new field sits inside
the invariant its own docstring calls load-bearing rather than beside it. The
wire test measures all three zero amounts rather than only the one it builds,
since the claim on the schema is about three cases and pinning one of three is
how a sentence like that quietly stops being true.

Verified by mutation rather than by argument, and in both directions, because
one direction is not evidence about the other. Collapsing the two markers onto
fallback is the old defect back, a Brazilian placeholder reading as an answer,
and all five discrimination tests fail. Collapsing them onto unavailable is
the opposite defect, a correct US zero reading as missing, and there three of
the five fail while two stay green. Those two are right to stay green: they
only ever look at Brazil, which that mutation leaves correct. The declared
control passes under both, so neither mutation is merely breaking the
function. The file was sha256 identical before and after each round. Eighty
one tests in the engine suite, and a hundred and sixty one across that suite
plus country coverage, carbon, the tax table drift guard, the or-zero fallback
guard, the quote endpoint and the property development IDOR suite. The full
unit suite was not run; it does not finish inside ten minutes on this machine.

Deliberately not done here. grand_total still adds a vat the provenance has
just called unusable, so a Brazilian total still has a placeholder in it.
Marking an axis unusable labels the answer and does not stop arithmetic, and
moving an amount because a label makes it look wrong would be choosing a
behaviour for its consequence. That was equally true before this field
existed; the field is what makes it visible, and a test pins it so that
changing it later is a decision rather than a drift. What a quote for an
unmodelled jurisdiction should actually say is a breakdown question and
belongs with the zero-rated line work. pis_cofins_residential on the Brazil
row is still read by nothing and is still untouched.

fix(bid-management): parity analytics stop blending currencies

A bid priced in another currency was compared against the rest as though the
numbers were the same money. Three bidders at 100 EUR, 110 EUR and 1000 USD
came back stamped EUR with a mean of 403.33 and a max of 1000.00, both of
which are USD, and the docstring one line above the call said money is never
blended across currencies.

The costly part is not the average. The USD bidder was flagged an outlier and
given a review verdict, and the line was marked high dispersion at a cv of
104.61. The defect does not merely mislead, it accuses. A named bidder is
marked for review on the strength of an unconverted currency, on a tender
leveling surface, which is the number that gets somebody set aside.

Off-currency bids are now held out of the maths and counted into a new
excluded_off_currency field on the response, beside a mixed_currency flag.
Nothing is converted. A rate table we cannot promise is complete would trade a
visibly wrong answer for an invisible one, and the module already takes the
hold-out approach in compute_price_spread and compute_bid_summary.

Two things had to come with it, or the fix would have been worse than the bug
on the very input that motivated it. The currency vote now runs over the valid
submissions the matrix is actually built from, because a rejected foreign bid
could otherwise set the label stamped on the domestic bids that remained, and
under the new filter it would have excluded every one of those and emptied the
analytics. That case needs a milder trigger than the blend does: one foreign
bidder who submitted and was ruled invalid is enough to relabel the entire
domestic field. And an unlabelled bid neither votes nor is excluded, because
the currency column defaults to an empty string, so blank means unknown rather
than foreign, and letting blanks vote throws out the one bidder who did record
a currency.

The filter names the bidders positively identified as carrying another code
rather than keeping the ones the vote could place. A bid the vote cannot see,
such as one whose header total is stale while its lines are priced, is in
neither the kept rows nor the excluded count, so keeping the placed ones would
have deleted it from the comparison. It stays, which makes the change
non-narrowing rather than only intended to be, and that is asserted.

The two response fields are not decoration. The endpoint validates the result
through a response model, and unknown keys are dropped there, so a count the
service computed and the schema did not declare would have been thrown away
one line before the reader, which is this defect's own failure mode reproduced
inside its fix.

Verified against three packages that fail today, each measured before the
change and again after, with the expected numbers written down in advance:
the blended median, the manufactured outlier verdict, and a package whose
label read USD while every number in it was EUR. Twelve tests added, 84 pass
in the two bid_management unit files.

i18n: the currency mismatch notification speaks every language

The three-way match learned to refuse an invoice it cannot compare against
its purchase order, and the refusal is delivered to a person rather than to
a machine. It reaches them as a persisted notification in their own language,
which meant two new English strings and forty one files still falling back to
English. This closes that.

The register is the part that needed care rather than the words. This is not
a rejection and not an accusation. A supplier sent an invoice denominated in
one currency against an order denominated in another, and the platform
declines to subtract one from the other because the difference between them
is not a number of anything. The invoice may be entirely correct. So each
translation says the match could not be performed, not that the invoice
failed or was refused, using whatever vocabulary that language already
established for invoices, orders and the match itself in the neighbouring
keys rather than a fresh coinage.

The three interpolation variables survive verbatim in every file, checked
programmatically rather than read. Word order around them moved wherever the
language wants it moved, which is the reason they are variables.

Two files are out of scope for reasons that belong on the record. en-US.ts is
an overlay by its own design and carries only keys where American usage
differs; neither of these strings has a US spelling or term to override, and
a key copied across unchanged would have to be kept in step with en.ts
forever for nothing. mn.ts and uz.ts are in, although the registry has them
disabled while they are brought up to standard, because both are live source
that resumes rather than dead weight, and leaving two more English strings in
a file that is catching up is the wrong gap to reopen.

Every locale in one commit. A key that lands in thirty files and not the rest
is harder to detect than a key that landed nowhere, and it is how a locale
quietly falls behind.

feat(ci): a gate against a shared test clock the suite does not have

The backend suite holds 99 fixed date constants across 77 files naming 40
distinct instants. NOW is five different days, TODAY is six, AS_OF is
2025-01-01 in one file and 2026-07-16 in another. None of that is a bug
today, because every one of them is file-local and nothing lets two of them
meet inside a single run.

It stops being harmless the moment a date lands in a conftest or in a helper
that two test modules import. Then a test pinning one instant locally and a
helper reading the shared one disagree about what day it is inside a single
run, and the failure surfaces a long way from either date.

Rewriting 99 correct constants to defend against a fixture nobody has
proposed is churn whose cost is certain and whose benefit is hypothetical.
Forbidding the fixture is one check, so this is that check. It keys on the
binding rather than on the identifier, so a name nobody has thought of yet
is caught as well. Exactly one shared anchor is permitted, at one declared
location under one declared name, and taking that slot means changing this
script in the same commit.

A parameter default is not an anchor, and neither is a document that merely
contains a date, so the row factories and the exchange-rate fixture pass.

Twelve controls, in both polarities. Two of them were added after the rest
were green and are the ones worth naming: the declared slot is exercised and
proven to be accepted, and a different name in that same file is still
caught. The other ten only ever proved the gate can say no, and the slot is
the one route the failure message actually tells people to take. The scan
prints its denominator, so a run that stops seeing the test tree cannot
report clean the way a passing suite with zero tests does.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

ci: Repo hygiene stops asking for nineteen runner slots to do two minutes of work

Repo hygiene has not returned a verdict on anything since 10:02 this morning.
Every run created after 10:04 is still queued, the oldest at over two hours,
and the queue depth grew across seven consecutive pushes without once
shrinking. Eight commits landed with no verdict at all. Nothing is broken and
no runner label is wrong. It is starvation, and our only blocking gate has
been silent through it.

The cause was the shape of the file rather than the scripts. Nineteen jobs,
eighteen of them running exactly one step, each doing its own checkout of an
8764-file tree and its own Python install in order to run a script that
finishes in seconds. Measured end to end, all twenty-one scripts take about
131 seconds of actual work, and they were asking for nineteen runner slots to
do it while competing with CI (PostgreSQL) for the same pool. The gate was
never slow. It was wide.

So the single-step jobs are grouped by what they read: the tree (structural,
ten scripts), the locale files and the key space (i18n, ten scripts), and git
history (commit-history, one script). Twenty jobs become three. Every script
that ran before runs now, on the same trigger, with its step name and the
comment explaining why it exists carried over intact. The script set was
diffed against a measured baseline rather than against the old file's
intentions, and it comes back equal at twenty-one both sides.

The property that made this worth doing carefully: nineteen independent jobs
meant one run told you every check that failed. A job stops at its first
failing step, which would have turned one red run into a queue of pushes each
revealing the next failure, and discovering failures one push at a time in a
queue two hours deep is worse than the queue. So every check step carries
`if: !cancelled()` and runs whatever failed before it, while a failed step
still fails its job, so the verdict depends on the whole set. Nothing uses
continue-on-error, which is the thing that would have quietly broken that.
`!cancelled()` rather than `always()` for one reason worth stating: cancelling
a run should genuinely release the slot, and slots are the resource this
layout exists to conserve.

The trailer guard stays alone and has to. It is the only guard that reads git
history instead of the working tree, so it is the only one needing
fetch-depth 0. Folding it into either group would hand it the default shallow
checkout, where it would scan the one commit it can see, find nothing, and
pass. A green tick for a guard that had stopped running is worse than no
guard, so the reason it sits alone is written next to it.

This also lands the shared-test-clock check as a step rather than a twentieth
job.

absent VAT block. VAT absence is a claim about a rate, and a rate is a
percentage regardless of which country charges it, so tax_engine's
NOT_MODELLED is closable by writing a row with no change to the table's
shape. A prompt payment regime is a claim about the shape of a law.
NO_STATUTE and NOT_MODELLED carry the same two ideas across, no such law or
a law not yet reduced to a row, both closable the same way once the
research is done. DIFFERENT_SHAPE is not closable that way: Brazil's Lei
14.133/2021 art. 141 obliges the public buyer to pay invoices in the order
they were registered, an ordering rule rather than a deadline measured in
days from an event. No amount of research turns "pay in registration
order" into a days-to-pay figure, because elapsed time since an event is
not the thing the statute regulates. Two of the three values are gaps this
registry can close by adding a row, one names a country whose statute the
row shape cannot express at all, and collapsing the three into the tax
engine's two would erase that distinction.

_validate_no_regime_reasons() runs at import time, in data.py, not deferred
into seed_payment_regimes the way tax_engine defers to _load_table.
tax_engine's deferral is about a YAML file an operator can edit on disk
without running anything, so deferring means a bad file fails the first
caller loudly instead of breaking import for everyone who depends on the
module. Neither half applies here: NO_REGIME_REASONS is a Python dict
literal that cannot reach a deployment without passing ruff and pytest
first, and country_coverage.py's probe reads it directly, never through
the seeder, so a validator placed at the seeder's call site would leave
that read path unvalidated. A guard placed where the data is written
protects nothing when the data has a reader that does not go through the
writer.

The validator checks (set(NO_REGIME_REASONS) | NO_REGIME_HELD) &
_COUNTRIES_WITH_A_REGIME as one set operation, rather than only walking
NO_REGIME_REASONS, so a country added to NO_REGIME_HELD that also picks up
a real row is caught too. Iterating NO_REGIME_REASONS alone would have had
a blind spot: HELD is never iterated by that narrower check, so a held
country that later gains a row would pass silently and the probe would
report it as held forever.

Nothing anywhere compares against NO_REGIME_HELD as a whole, asserts its
size, or asserts its exact membership. Every use is either "country in
NO_REGIME_HELD", one jurisdiction at a time, or an emptiness check on an
intersection, both of which hold at any cardinality. A held jurisdiction is
a per-jurisdiction fact and the code says so about one at a time; adding or
removing a held country later is a one-line data change, not a code change.

What this vocabulary keeps apart, stated directly: a country with a
confirmed reason in NO_REGIME_REASONS is one we looked at and can say
something about, in one of the three ways above. A country in
NO_REGIME_HELD is one we are actively looking at and cannot yet. Every
other country not in PAYMENT_REGIMES is the third and largest state,
silent by default, and the vocabulary does not touch it: no entry, no
flag, no signal that anyone has looked. A missing row alone cannot tell
these apart, and collapsing NO_STATUTE (the law itself has nothing) into
the same bucket as unresearched silence would say a country has been
checked when it has not, which is the wrong direction to be wrong in for
something a quantity surveyor may bill against. The probe test below
checks this directly: BR, CN and an untouched country produce three
different sentences, not the same missing-row sentence three times.

CN and RU are the two entries in NO_REGIME_HELD, and neither gets a
NO_REGIME_* value. The Brazil measurement's search method does not transfer
to them: a wrong-instrument result is evidence about the instrument used,
not about the jurisdiction it was pointed at, so carrying a category over
from a different country's search would have recorded a conclusion nobody
reached. "Held" says that plainly rather than reading as unstated backlog.

country_coverage.py's _payment_regimes probe rewrites detail text only when
the verdict is already MISSING, via dataclasses.replace, and never changes
the verdict itself. MISSING is defined in this file as country-keyed,
populated, and this country not in it, which is exactly Brazil's and
China's situation; FALLBACK means something resolves by default or alias,
which is not true here, nothing resolves for Brazil at all. So the shared
six-verdict vocabulary every other probe also depends on is untouched. A
held jurisdiction and a missing one are not reported by the same words: a
reader querying Brazil gets MISSING naming NO_REGIME_DIFFERENT_SHAPE and
pointing at NO_REGIME_REASONS; China gets MISSING saying held and why,
pointing at NO_REGIME_HELD; a country nobody has looked at gets the bare
generic MISSING sentence _keyed already produces. Three distinguishable
answers to the same question, at the same verdict, drawn from the same
detail field the rest of the file already uses to carry this kind of
nuance.

The probe calls no_regime_reason(country) rather than reading
NO_REGIME_REASONS.get(country) directly, so the accessor has a caller
instead of shipping in __all__ with nobody using it. The call sits inside
the report.verdict != MISSING early return, so the accessor's own raise,
reserved for a country that has a row of its own, can never fire from this
call site; said so in a comment at the call.

tests/unit/test_payment_clock_module.py: TestNoRegimeReasons, nine tests.

second of which is the exact bug a narrower validator would have had, a
held country that gains a row; one is the closed-set refusal; one checks

tests/unit/test_country_coverage.py: one new test asserting BR, CN and an

deleted and the probe fell back to the same generic sentence for all three.

fix(supplier-catalogs): stock cost stops averaging two currencies into one number

A goods receipt rolls the accepted price into the balance's running average.
That average carried no currency, so receiving the same item under a EUR order
and then a USD one stored the mean of the two prices, which is money in
neither. Every reservation, issue and stocktake then copies the balance's
average onto its own movement row, so a single blend spread from one balance
into the whole audit trail behind it, and none of the copies could be told
apart from a correct one.

The average now belongs to one ISO currency or it is not stated. StockBalance
gains a currency and a cost_state of single, mixed or unknown, and unit_cost_avg
becomes nullable so that "there is no single-currency average here" stops being
spelled as the price zero. StockMovement gains the same currency alongside its
own unit_cost, which is also now nullable: an issue out of a balance whose cost
is not knowable has no unit cost to record, and a zero there would read as
stock that went out for nothing.

Mixed and unknown are kept apart on purpose. They need different things said to
the operator - one means we know exactly what happened and cannot express it as
a single price, the other means we cannot see what happened - and collapsing
them into one null would throw that difference away.

Two behaviours are worth stating because they are decisions rather than
consequences. A balance issued down to zero and then restocked becomes single
again, since none of the blended stock is left to be wrong about, which makes
this self-repairing for anyone who cycles their inventory. And an unlabelled
receipt makes a balance unknown rather than agreeing with the next unlabelled
one: a blank code is not a currency two rows can share.

The migration classifies rather than recomputes, and that distinction is what
makes it safe. Each balance is judged on the set of purchase-order currencies
behind its inbound movements: every receipt movement names its goods receipt,
every goods receipt names an order, and every order has a currency. One
currency means the stored average was correct all along and it is kept, now
labelled. Two or more means it is a blend, and it is withdrawn. Untraceable, or
no receipts at all, and it is withdrawn as unknown.

No replay is involved and none would work. The stored average is not a function
of the receipts alone: issue and stocktake rewrite quantity_on_hand, which is
the weight the next receipt blends against, so replaying inbound movements
would not reproduce what is stored. Classification does not care, because a set
has no order and no weights, and neither outcome recalculates anything. A mixed
balance is deliberately not repaired at historical FX either: that is a
decision about how this product values inventory, and a schema migration does
not get to make it on anyone's behalf. What this can do, which was impossible
before, is say which balances are affected.

The outbound history of a single-currency balance is labelled too. An issue, a
reservation and a stocktake adjustment never priced themselves; each copied the
balance's average at the moment it ran. If every receipt into a balance is one
currency then every prefix of them is, so the average at any past moment was a
blend of that currency and the figure copied from it carries it. That is a
derivation and not an estimate - no ordering, no rate, no replay. Without it the
day of the upgrade would split every history in two, everything before it
unlabelled and everything after it labelled, in a warehouse where nothing about
the money ever changed.

One case is excluded because the derivation's premise fails there rather than
because it is awkward. It assumes the balance had already received something,
and a stocktake can write an adjustment against a balance with no receipts at
all, copying the creation default, which is denominated in nothing. That row is
identifiable without an order over the movements because the value it copied is
exactly zero, so outbound rows with a zero unit cost are left unlabelled and
counted. A zero there is either that default or a genuine zero-priced copy, and
performed_at cannot arbitrate: it is a nullable String(40) with no sequence
behind it.

Historical movements keep their unit_cost even when their balance comes out
mixed or unknown. Withdrawing the number on the balance is right, because a
balance is a current valuation and a blend is not a price. A movement records
what the system did at the time and may already have been posted onward into
project cost, so nulling it would be destroying an audit row to make a
classification tidy, which is not a schema migration's call.

Both tables are acknowledged growth=tenure for the data-rewrite gate. The
movement table appends a row per receipt, issue, reservation and adjustment and
never deletes one, so it tracks operating history exactly as the table in #126
did. The balance table would be more comfortable to call bounded and that is
not the true answer: a batch-tracked item adds a row per lot received and lots
are never merged away, so the count follows receipts rather than the catalogue.

Nothing is written until every decision is made, and then it is one statement
per distinct written value rather than one per row. The rule that makes the
grouping safe is that every grouped statement's WHERE clause must key on
something that uniquely determines every value it writes, which is why the
single-currency balances group by currency and not by cost_state - grouping by
the state would collapse rows that differ in the value being written. The two costs a
tenure-growth table creates are addressed separately and it is worth not
conflating them. Peak disk is the acknowledgement's job: Postgres keeps every
superseded row version until commit however the writes are grouped, so nothing
here reduces it, and the ack exists so somebody asks the size question before
this ships. Round trips are the batching's job: one statement per row on a
table with years of movements behind it is that many round trips inside one
transaction, holding its locks throughout. Grouping makes the statement count a
function of how many currencies a deployment trades in rather than of how long
it has been trading, and a test pins that: same data, twenty times the rows, same number of
statements. Every other test here would pass just as happily against a per-row
loop.

The counts are printed, including how many balances matched an inbound movement
at all and whether each labelled movement took its currency from a purchase
order or from the balance it was drawn against, and the unresolvable ones are
split into two stories: a movement that
never carried a reference, and one whose goods receipt has since been deleted.
po_id is ON DELETE CASCADE while reference_id has no foreign key, so removing a
purchase order takes its receipts and orphans those rows silently.

The join is guarded rather than trusted. Balances store "" for no batch and
movements store NULL, and a join that stops matching does not raise - it
returns nothing, classifies every balance unresolvable, withdraws every average
in the database and reports success. If any inbound movements exist and not one
balance matched one, the revision now aborts inside its own transaction and
changes nothing.

The warehouse balances table was rendering every unit cost under whatever
currency the operator had picked in settings. That defect needed no blend to be
wrong - a warehouse that had only ever received in EUR was mislabelled too, in
every deployment, on correct data. It could not be fixed before now because
there was no currency on the balance to render, and the comment above it said
as much: it chose the settings currency so the column would show a unit instead
of an em-dash. Cosmetics were traded against correctness knowingly and the
trade was written down. That was the only reader of the preference in the file,
so the whole read is gone with it.

Also corrects a docstring that described this weighted average as FIFO.

Verified against an aged database rather than a blank one, which matters here:
env.py short-circuits an empty database to create_all plus a stamp, so "empty
database, upgrade head" runs no revision at all and still reports success. The
new PG test builds the four tables in their pre-migration shape, seeds one
balance of each outcome, runs the real upgrade() over them, and separately
provokes the broken join to prove the guard fires.

i18n: the warehouse cost column says what it cannot say, in every language

Stock cost learned to refuse an average it cannot denominate, and the refusal
is a cell in a table rather than an error. Two English strings went in with
that change and forty one files were still falling back to English. This
closes them in one commit.

Neither string is a failure and the register was the part that needed care.
Mixed currencies means the platform knows exactly what happened and declines
to express it as one number: this warehouse received the same item under
purchase orders in two currencies, so an average across them would be money
in neither. Not available means it cannot trace where the stock came from and
will not print a figure it cannot vouch for. Both belong in a narrow column
next to a quantity, so short wins over literal wherever the language allows.

Two vocabularies were already settled in these files and both were reused
rather than reinvented. The empty-cell phrase comes from each file's own
schedule.evm.not_available, exact string, because a data table that says
nothing to show in two different ways in two places is a table that looks
translated by two people. The currency noun comes from the adjacent
supplier_catalogs.mixed_currencies, which is two lines away in en.ts and means
almost the same thing.

That neighbour phrases it as different currencies while the new key says mixed,
and a short column header reads better as one adjective and one noun than as a
clause. So where the language has a natural compact form it is used, and where
mixed would read stiffer than different the neighbour's own wording is kept
instead. Same meaning either way; this is a two-word label, not a translation
of a sentence.

Three files needed a judgement rather than a lookup. fil.ts uses pera for money
in this neighbourhood rather than a currency loanword, unlike its own invoice
keys, and the closer neighbour won. bn.ts and ur.ts already code-switch the
English currency word into their own script in that same key, so the new labels
do too rather than reaching for a purer form the file does not otherwise use.
uz.ts had no local noun to borrow because its own neighbour is still an English
placeholder, so both strings were translated fresh, using the same word chosen
for that file in the previous batch so the two do not disagree.

Placement is anchored on supplier_catalogs.unit_cost_avg, the column these two
stand in for, rather than on alphabetical position. These files are not mirrors
of en.ts: the supplier_catalogs block is contiguous everywhere, but partway
through it several of them switch from insertion order to alphabetical, and
alphabetically avg_cost_ would sit between address and batch, nowhere near the
column it describes. Anchoring on the sibling keeps the three keys together in
every file without touching the sort order of anything around them.

en-US.ts is out of scope by its own design. It is an overlay carrying only keys
where American usage differs, neither string has a US spelling or term to
override, and a key copied across unchanged would have to be kept in step with
en.ts forever for nothing. mn.ts and uz.ts are in, although the registry has
them disabled while they are brought up to standard, because both are live
source that resumes and leaving two more English strings in a file that is
catching up is the wrong gap to reopen.

No interpolation variables in either key, so there is nothing to preserve
across word order. Every file is exactly two added lines and nothing else,
checked programmatically rather than read: both keys present exactly once in
all forty one, no duplicates, no other line touched.

fix(ci): the byte identity tests get the history they have never had

Three tests named for byte identity were failing without ever comparing a
byte. They rebuild the pre-wiring PDF builder out of git and compare its
output to today's, which is the only way the claim that Latin documents did
not move can be checked against the real previous implementation rather than
against a copy of itself. Finding that previous implementation means walking
the file's history. The checkout was shallow, fetch-depth 1, so the walk had
one commit to search, found nothing that predates the wiring, and stopped at
its precondition. The assertion that fired reads as a statement about the
history, and it was one, but it looked like a statement about the documents.

This read for a while as a macOS and Windows split, and it never was. The
reason ubuntu looked clean is that every ubuntu shard was failing ruff before
it reached the file. Once that was fixed in 03412806d the shard that owns this
file reached it and failed the same way, which is the confirmation the
diagnosis wanted: depth 1 applies to every runner on every platform. Measured
on 31be1dcfa, ubuntu shard 4 of 6 reports three failed and three thousand
eight hundred and fifty five passed, the three being these tests and nothing
else in that shard. The same run has four failing jobs in total, that shard,
the two cross platform shards, and the rollup derived from them. All four are
these three tests, so this is not three tests unblocked, it is the lane.

The two jobs that run tests/unit now check out with fetch-depth 0 and filter
blob:none. Full history without blobs costs 11 MB and three seconds, against
221 MB and nineteen seconds for the shallow clone it replaces, because a
depth 1 clone still pulls every blob of the tip tree and a blobless one pulls
none. Plain fetch-depth 0 was measured too and rejected: 933 MB and around
eighty five seconds per job at the throughput the runners actually show,
twelve jobs a push, which would have slowed a blocking gate to buy a property
on tests that were not running at all. The other five checkouts are untouched
because they do not run tests/unit.

Blobs now arrive on demand, so a git show in these tests may fetch from the
origin. That is stated in each docstring, and the walk keeps check=True with
no except around it, so a fetch that cannot happen fails the test rather than
skipping it. A skip that CI does not count is a pass wearing a different word,
and this file exists because of defects that hide behind things that look like
they worked.

The lookup also follows renames now, in a second pass rather than the first.
A rename of the builder would otherwise lose the pre-wiring commit and the
test would fail with the identical wording for an unrelated reason, which is
the worst kind of latent breakage because a diagnosis already on file would
point at the fetch depth. The reason it is a second pass is cost: follow
detects renames by diffing blobs, so against a blobless clone it fetches every
blob it compares, measured at 188 MB and fifteen seconds against 11 MB and two
seconds for the plain walk. Only a rename needs it, so only a rename pays for
it. Checked rather than assumed: with the real marker one pass runs and finds
the version, and with a marker present in every revision both passes run and
the follow form executes cleanly.

What these tests will report in CI is genuinely unknown. The first green after
this is the first time they will ever have executed their comparison there.
This does not restore a working state, because there was no working state to
restore, and if they come back red on some platform that is new information
rather than a regression.

Deliberately not done. The precondition assertion is untouched. It is the
guard that stops the test passing by comparing a copy of itself, and relaxing
the guard against a quiet failure would be the defect this file is about,
told as a joke. The three lookups remain three near-identical copies, now
carrying the same two-pass walk in each, which is real duplication and a
sensible thing to factor into one helper. That is a merge of one decision
living in three places and it is not being done unasked.

fix(property-dev): overdue is claimed on money that was never demandable

issue_instalment_demand() attempted `pending -> overdue` whenever an
instalment's due_date had passed, but `_INSTALMENT_TRANSITIONS["pending"]`
never allowed "overdue" - only "due" does. Both were written in the same
original commit, 0f40f5377, and never touched since (checked with
git log -L). The guard admitted a source state the table never granted,
so any pending instalment past its forecast date 409'd instead of letting
a demand letter go out.

The fix is not to widen the table. "pending" means the construction
milestone that creates the obligation has not fired yet (see
_fire_milestone()'s docstring - it is the thing that moves an instalment
"pending" -> "due"), so the due_date on a pending row is a forecast
derived from the signing date, not an operative one. The buyer does not
owe this yet, and "overdue" is a statement with real consequences -
interest, penalties, in some contracts grounds for rescission. Recording
it here would be recording that a buyer failed to pay money that was
never demandable. The guard is narrowed to `ins.status == "due"` only,
so the transition-to-overdue attempt is never made for a pending row
regardless of its forecast date.

Not raised here, and worth saying plainly rather than leaving it looking
lost: a pending instalment sitting past its forecast date is still a
real signal, it says the project is behind schedule, which is a schedule
surface rather than a payment one.

Also worth one sentence and not a blocker: the two sanctioned writers of
pending -> due, _mark_first_pending_due() and _fire_milestone(), both
call update_fields() directly without going through _ensure_transition()
- they bypass the same guard this function is being made to respect. A
separate consistency question.

Second defect in the same branch, reachable once the guard above is
correct: update_fields(ins_id, status="overdue") expires the row, and
the five fields written into the event payload right after were being
read off that now-stale ``ins`` object - MissingGreenlet under
aiosqlite/asyncpg, same idiom already fixed next door in
waive_instalment() (d780b1b01). Snapshotted schedule_id, amount,
amount_paid, due_date and milestone_label right after the initial fetch,
before either code path can expire the row, and used the snapshots in
the event payload on both paths.

Neither half of this branch had ever run: the one test covering this
method relied on its SPA's default signing_date staying in the future,
which aged into the past and made the method 409 instead of testing
"not overdue". Split it into two tests that no longer depend on wall
clock. One pins a signing_date far in the future and asserts the
instalment stays "pending" and the event still publishes. The other
walks a fresh plot through the full FSM to countersigned with a
signing_date in the past, so _fire_milestone() has genuinely moved the
instalment "pending" -> "due" before due_date is checked, and asserts
issue-demand marks it "overdue" - nothing exercised that path before.
