fix(licences): bundled fonts are attributed by the pipeline, not by hand

Ten font files under three licences ship inside the wheel and the desktop
installer, and none of them appeared in any generated inventory. That was
structural rather than an oversight. pip-licenses and license-checker both
enumerate installed packages, and a font committed into our own tree is not
a package, so no scanner could ever have listed them however long they
shipped.

Worth being precise about what was and was not wrong, because the two get
merged easily. The licence obligations were being met the whole time.
Bitstream Vera requires its copyright and trademark notices and its
permission notice in all copies of the font software, OFL clause 2 requires
the copyright notice and the licence and explicitly allows a stand-alone
text file, and in both cases the text travels in the artefact beside the
fonts it governs. That was verified inside the installed package for both
channels rather than reasoned from packaging defaults, and the desktop spec
ships the directories whole. What was wrong is that NOTICE and
THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md each present themselves as a complete inventory and
neither mentioned a font.

The fix is one script in two modes. check_bundled_font_licences.py walks the
declared asset roots, resolves the licence governing each font, and either
gates the tree or emits the THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md section. Sharing the
walk is the point. A separate generator would be a second source of truth,
and the published inventory could then drift from the guard without either
looking wrong.

It checks the packaged result rather than the tree. "A licence file sits
next to the font" is the weak version, and here it would reintroduce the
failure it exists to prevent, because backend/pyproject.toml excludes
**/_*.txt and LICENSE_DEJAVU survives the wheel walk only by having no
extension. A future _LICENSE.txt beside a new face would sit right next to
its font, pass a presence check, and be dropped from the wheel. The exclude
patterns are read out of pyproject.toml at run time so this follows any edit
to them, and matching is case-sensitive in both places so the gate cannot
answer one way on Windows and another in CI.

LICENSE_DEJAVU is three statements rather than one licence, and the NOTICE
entry keeps them apart. The DejaVu changes are public domain, the outlines
are Bitstream Vera under Bitstream, Inc., and imported glyphs are Arev under
Tavmjong Bah with its own separately binding notice clause. A row reading
"DejaVu, Bitstream Vera Fonts License" loses two of the three.

Building it caught one bug worth recording. Resolving a licence by taking
the first match in a directory filed all four Plus Jakarta Sans faces under
the Instrument Serif licence, because both OFL texts sit in one licenses
directory beside eight fonts. It credited the wrong authors in a legal
document and no count in the output looked wrong. Resolution is now by
longest shared filename prefix, and several candidates sharing nothing with
the font name is reported as ambiguity rather than guessed at.

NOTICE needed one hand edit because nothing generates it. The guard asserts
that every licence governing a shipped font is named there, which makes that
a one time cost rather than a recurring one.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(schema): the heal keeps the NOT NULL it has a default to backfill with

The upgrade lane went red on one column. oe_supplier_catalogs_stock_balance
.cost_state is declared NOT NULL by the model and accepted NULL in the database
after boot. Nothing else noticed, and that is the part worth writing down: the
column existed, it selected, every table and column the code declares was
present, schema_heal_failed read False and alembic_head_matches read True. Six
signals agreed it was a clean upgrade. The seventh was the only one asking
whether the column had kept its constraint.

What boots is not the migration chain. app/main.py never calls alembic upgrade;
it runs postgres_auto_migrate and then create_all, which is why the heal exists
at all. The heal would only write NOT NULL when it could also write a DEFAULT to
fill the rows already in the table with, which is correct, because ADD COLUMN
NOT NULL with nothing to backfill fails outright on a populated table. It looked
for that default in server_default alone. cost_state declares its default in
Python, so the heal saw none, added the column nullable and moved on. The
alembic revision for the same column does declare a server default and is
correct, so a database that ran the chain was always right and only the healed
one was wrong. That is why two lanes disagreed and why the upgrade lane was the
one telling the truth.

So the heal now reads a scalar model-side default too. Callables are excluded
deliberately: uuid4 and utcnow have to run per row, and one frozen value would
be wrong for every row after the first. So are containers, because a JSON
default is a Python object rather than SQL text and rendering one would be
guessing at the dialect. Booleans are tested before integers because bool is a
subclass of int and DEFAULT 1 on a boolean column is a type error.

The radius is not small and is better stated than discovered later. 1176 NOT
NULL columns across 621 tables will now arrive with a default and their
constraint rather than nullable, when they arrive by heal. On a fresh install
nothing changes, because create_all already builds those columns correctly. So
this only ever touches the upgrade path, which is exactly the path that was
wrong.

Because of that radius there is a fallback. If the database refuses the
constrained form the plain ADD COLUMN is re-issued and logged, so a default this
code renders badly costs a constraint rather than the column, and an ORM read
that used to work cannot start returning 500 because of a change meant to make
the schema stricter.

The test is in tests/pg, which is a lane that blocks, and it strips the column
from a populated table before healing rather than from an empty one. It asserts
both halves: that the column comes back NOT NULL, and that the row which
predates it reads the default. The second is not redundant. A NOT NULL column
that arrived without backfilling could not have been added at all, so the
nullability check alone cannot tell a filled row from a table that was empty.

Verified with the fix disabled from a plugin outside the tree rather than by
editing anything: the new case fails with the wording CI printed, and the
existing case in the same file still passes. tests/pg entire, 742 passed.

fix(finance): a budget line reads back the same whichever way you ask

Creating a budget and then reading the same row gave two different numbers
for the same money. The POST response carried "500000" and every later read
of that row carried "500000.00", because MoneyType is NUMERIC(18, 2) on
PostgreSQL and create returned the object it had just built in memory
instead of the row the database had stored. A flush does not expire
attributes, so the instance still held the caller's own string.

The part worth knowing is why the update path did not have the same
problem, because it is not by design. update_budget opens with a call to
get_budget whose only stated purpose is to raise a 404, and it is that
load, not the re-read at the end, that puts the row in the session at the
column's scale. The response format of a PATCH currently depends on a
existence check kept for an unrelated reason. Delete it as redundant one day and
the response silently changes shape, with nothing failing to say so. That
is the actual defect here; create and update disagreeing is how it showed
up.

create_budget now refreshes the row before returning it. refresh rather
than expire on purpose: expiring defers the load to attribute access during
serialisation, and a lazy load at that point is where MissingGreenlet comes
from under async SQLAlchemy, so the I/O is done explicitly under await
instead.

Verified by running it rather than by reasoning about the ORM, which is
what a first pass at this would have got wrong: session.get on an instance
that is already in the identity map and has not expired returns the same
object and issues no SQL, so the obvious one line fix would have been a no
op that looked like a change and passed review.

Two assertions in the critical-flows suite moved to the stored form. That
direction was not a guess. Across the whole backend suite there are 115
assertions comparing one of the 62 MoneyType column names to a numeric
string literal, and 86 of them already expect decimals; those 86 sit on
read paths and would be red today if they did not. The create response was
the outlier, not the standard.

The stub session in the finance unit tests grew a refresh. It had no such
method, so the service calling one raised an AttributeError from inside the
code under test, which reads as a defect in the service rather than a gap in
the stub. It is a no-op, and says so: there is no database behind it, and
the stored form is a property of the column type and the database, so it can
only be asserted where both are real. It is, in the integration suite above.

One more assertion in that file moved, and it is a different defect that the
population sweep turned up rather than a consequence of this change.
test_create_evm_snapshot posted spi "0.95" and asserted the response said
"0.95". The service derives every index itself, EV over PV here, and stores
it quantised to four places, so the answer is "0.9500" and always has been.
The test was asserting that the server echoed the client, which is the one
thing this endpoint is documented not to do, and it fails identically at
HEAD, in isolation, and on both database backends, so it is neither new nor
caused by the refresh above.

It had been failing unseen because no lane that blocks a merge runs
tests/integration. CI (PostgreSQL) runs tests/pg and a named list from
tests/unit; the only job that reaches this file is CI, which is red for
unrelated reasons and is not a gate. A red test in a suite nothing gates on
is indistinguishable from a green one.

Five sibling create methods in the finance repository have the same shape
and are deliberately left alone here.

Population derived from the two column names this touches rather than chosen:
twelve files in the backend suite mention original_budget or revised_budget,
all twelve run, 185 passed. Two of them were red before this and are the two
described above.

fix(crm): forecast and dashboard publish the currencies they compute

GET /pipeline/metrics is the control. It has published by_currency and
mixed_currency correctly since the day they were added, its response schema
declares exactly the forgiving defaults that broke the other two endpoints, an
empty list and False, and it has still never once been wrong. The route
computes the metrics and builds the response in one breath with every field
passed explicitly, so not one of those defaults is ever reached.

Two endpoints in the same module reach them on every call, and they get there
by different routes.

The forecast loses the fields at the storage boundary. compute_forecast returns
four money scalars and the two currency fields, compute_and_store_forecast
copied the scalars onto the Forecast row, and ForecastResponse.model_validate
read that row back. The two currency fields had no column to land in, so they
fell through to the schema defaults. GET /forecasts/{period} and
POST /forecasts/compute answered mixed_currency false with an empty breakdown
for every period, whatever the deals said, and raised nothing on the way. A
forecast blending EUR, USD and GBP reported itself as single currency
microseconds after computing that it was not, and the one field built to warn
about a blend was the field asserting there was nothing to warn about.

That was not an oversight, which is the part worth keeping. The comment above
those two fields said the defaults were there to keep model_validate working
over a row that "has no per-currency column yet". The gap was known and written
down. What was never written down is what the accommodation cost, that every
answer the endpoint gave was the reassuring one.

The dashboard loses them to a plain omission. crm_dashboard calls the same
compute_pipeline_metrics the control does, then passes seven of the ten fields
into CrmDashboardResponse. The other three came from the defaults. This one is
rendered: the Insights tab reads by_currency and falls back to the blended
scalar "only when absent", which meant it took the fallback every time it has
ever run, on every account.

So neither the computation nor the schema is what separates these three
endpoints, and there is no single boundary to blame either. The mitigation was
written once and holds wherever the computed values are handed straight to the
response. It fails wherever something sits in between, whether that is a row
with no column for them or three arguments nobody typed.

For the forecast the fix is two nullable columns on oe_crm_forecast and the
carry-through into them. Nullable rather than defaulted, and that is the point
rather than a convenience: a row written before this change was never checked,
and NULL is the only value that says so. False on a field named mixed_currency
is not an absence, it is an assurance. For the dashboard it is the three
arguments, and nothing in the frontend needed changing because the fallback it
already carries is correct once the truth arrives.

There is no backfill. The figures could be recomputed, compute_forecast is pure
and still there, but running it today over today's opportunities and writing
the result into a row dated April would stand this month's currencies beside
April's scalars with nothing to say the two halves describe different days. Old
rows stay NULL and fill on the next explicit recompute. A read deliberately
does not recompute, so GET /forecasts/{period} keeps answering null for an
untouched period, which is the honest answer rather than the tidy one.

Two drop sites on the forecast path rather than one. ForecastRepository.upsert
copies fields onto the row already stored for a period and that copy is a hand
written list, so a column added to the model and to the create path would still
have gone missing on every recompute, leaving the previous run's breakdown next
to this run's totals. The stub repository in the crm unit tests is a hand copy
of the same list and had inherited the same omission, which means it would have
certified the gap rather than caught it. Both are level with the model now.

fix(changeorders): publishing a scenario stores one

The button in the change order impact screen has never worked. Publishing a
scenario writes the projection into a JSONB column, the projection carries
order_id as a uuid.UUID, and the default serializer cannot encode one, so the
flush raised and the endpoint answered 500 to every caller. The audit trail this
endpoint exists to write had not received a single row.

It is production behaviour rather than a harness artifact: neither the
application engine nor the test engine configures a json_serializer, so both
reach the same encoder and both refuse.

The projection is now rendered through the response model before it is stored,
which fixes it at the write rather than at the engine. Three reasons for that
placement. It keeps the stored record identical in shape to what the reviewer
actually saw, so an audit row and the screen it came from cannot describe the
same scenario differently. It refuses a payload that is not a projection at the
moment of writing, instead of accepting anything and finding out on read. And
it leaves every other JSONB column in the product alone, which a serializer
swap at engine level would not.

The reason it survived is the more useful half. Nothing had ever called
publish_scenario. The single test that named it reads a list of route names to
confirm the route is guarded, which is a test about the guard and not about the
function, so the name appeared in a passing suite while the function had no
coverage at all. A route census that counts names would have called this route
tested.

Three tests now call it. One publishes and reads the stored snapshot back. One
serialises that snapshot, because the failure was at flush and not at read: a
test that only checked a field was present would pass on a dict still holding a
UUID, and the round trip is the same trip the database makes. One fills the
documented ten scenario cap, which was written and never exercised, since no
scenario had ever been stored for an eleventh to push out.

The integration test proves it over HTTP as well, which is where the trailing
slash in this router turns out to matter: the read is declared "/{order_id}" and
the publish "/{order_id}/publish-scenario/", so a client that guesses the wrong
one is answered with a bare 404 rather than a redirect. Noted where it bit,
not changed here, because changing it changes the public surface.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

refactor(tests): one walk through git history instead of three copies

Three tests rebuild a PDF builder as it stood before the face wiring and
compare its output to today's, and each of them carried its own copy of the
walk that finds that earlier version: the same repo root, the same subprocess
helper, the same loop, differing only in which file to read and which token
marks the wiring. The copies were tolerable while they were four lines. The
commit before this one made each of them a two-pass walk with five lines of
comment explaining what the second pass costs, so the same decision now lived
in three places at fifteen lines each, and the next person to learn something
about it would have to find all three.

They now call one instrument, source_before_the_wiring, which takes the path
and the marker and returns the newest version whose source lacks it. The
explanation of why the walk exists, why it does not read HEAD, why a failed
fetch must not become a skip, and why the rename-following pass is second
rather than first, is written once on that function rather than three times
above its callers.

The assertion stays at each call site rather than moving into the helper. The
helper returns an empty string when nothing is reachable, and the caller turns
that into a failure that names the builder it was looking for. A single raise
from inside would say the same sentence for all three and identify none of
them, which is the thing that made the original diagnosis slow: the message
described the history and read as though it described the documents.

No behaviour change is intended and none is observed. The seventy four tests
in the file pass, including the three that use this, and they pass by finding
the same earlier versions as before, which is what they compare against.

Deliberately not done. The helper stays in this file rather than moving to a
shared test utility. Every call to it is here, all twelve references to git in
the suite were these three copies, and promoting something to shared on the
strength of one file having three users is how a utility module starts.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

brand check: the tokeniser reads accents and other scripts

The check cut a run at every character outside a to z and 0 to 9. That ended a
run at every separator, so a denied name written with a hyphen or a space walked
straight through, and it ended a run at every non-ASCII letter too, which turned
out to be the expensive half.

Three things followed from that second half. Accented words were cut into
fragments, so ordinary Croatian and Spanish prose collided with four-letter
product names in this field, and two names could not be listed at all because of
it. A name written with its own umlaut was unreachable, which is why one entry
in the list had been recorded as the fragment left over after the mark was
dropped, and why another was recorded whole and could therefore never match
anything. And every non-Latin script reduced to nothing at all, so a line of Han
characters produced no run to compare and the check returned clean because it
could not read the line, which is the one result a check must never give.

A run is now any sequence of letters or digits in any script, with the
underscore excluded so that a snake_case identifier still separates into its
parts, and each run is folded to its base letters before it is compared. Marks
are stripped before the run is cut as well as after, because text that arrives
decomposed carries them as separate characters that would end a run exactly as
before, and some tracked files are stored that way. Compatibility forms fold
too, which closes the trick of writing a name in full-width Latin.

Both sides of the replacement pairing move together. The rule that spares a file
which states what it renames a name to compares two reductions of the same text,
so reducing only the scanning side would have broken the exemption the moment
either a name or a descriptor carried an accent. The three files that carry the
old catalogue names deliberately still scan clean.

The entry that existed only in its broken form is re-derived here rather than
afterwards. Folding the input would otherwise have disarmed it while every
signal stayed green, and that is the failure this change was most at risk of
causing, so it is the one the census is built to catch.

Verified by running the previous version and this one over every tracked text
file and comparing what each detects, rather than by checking that the check
still passes. Detections are 38 across 13 distinct tokens before and 38 across
13 after. Exactly one token moves, from six occurrences of the fragment to six
of the whole word, which is the re-derived entry and nothing else. Reported hits
are 5 across 3 files in both, unchanged. A name the previous version missed when
written with its accent is now caught, the same name without the accent behaves
as it did, and a line carrying no denied name stays clean.

That census is enforced from here rather than performed once. The three subject
files are pinned to the number of distinct entries they reach, so a change that
disarms an entry drops the count and goes red, and the tokeniser properties the
list depends on are tested directly: one accented word is one run in both the
composed and the decomposed spelling, a full-width spelling is caught, an
ordinary accented word is not convicted by the fragment it used to produce, and
an identifier still comes apart at the underscore. Each was run against the
tokeniser it exists to refuse, and each goes red there.

It is not slower. Both versions were run alternately in one process to keep the
file cache out of it, and the full pass came out at 114s against 123s, because
the unit here is a line and nearly every line still takes the ASCII path, which
now matches runs directly instead of through match objects.

The allowlist had already recorded this defect once. One of its entries carries
the note that the context it was pinned to stopped matching the moment the demo
packs were given their accents, and that the check went red on a line nobody had
touched. That entry is left exactly as it is.

Separators are still open. A denied name written with a hyphen or a space
remains invisible, because catching it needs a rule over adjacent runs rather
than a better run, and that lands on its own. So does the substring rule for
scripts that do not put spaces between words.

test(interface-management): walk the overdue guarantee end to end

Every seeded interface register reserves a prefix of four statuses so the
register cannot be drawn with an empty overdue tile. The test for that
guarantee asserted its first link only: that the reserved position holds a
status the register is willing to call overdue. Everything after that link was
assumed. The seeder still has to date that row into the past, and the
register's own predicate still has to agree that a row so dated is overdue, and
neither was being checked.

That is the shape where a guarantee quietly stops holding. Change how the
seeder picks dates and the status is still an overdue-capable one, so the test
stays green while the tile it exists to fill goes empty.

The chain is now walked to the end for every seed: the status is one the
register can call overdue, the seeder dates it before today, and is_overdue
says so on the row that would be displayed. The sample is four times larger,
because the property is over every register the seeder can produce rather than
over the ones a smaller sweep happened to reach.

Test only. Nothing in the seeder or the register changed, and the guarantee
held at every one of the seeds checked.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(supplier-catalogs): the absolute price tolerance names its currency

A tolerance profile carries two price bands and the wider one wins: a
percentage of the order total, and an absolute floor. The percentage is safe
anywhere, because a percentage of the order is already denominated in the
order's own currency. The floor was a bare number. A profile is selected by
name and applied to purchase orders in every currency the tenant trades in, so
one number was being compared against amounts it had no defined relationship
to, and the column comment above it read "absolute (currency)" while no such
column existed.

The direction of the error is what makes it worth fixing rather than noting.
A floor that is too small relative to the order's currency never wins the max
and changes nothing at all. A floor that is too large widens the band, and the
invoice is auto-matched, approved for payment, and written to the match record
with no exception raised and nothing for anyone to read. The failure that
costs money is the one that produces no output.

This is latent rather than live, and the distinction is real. Nothing ships a
nonzero floor. No migration inserts a profile row, and
ensure_default_tolerance_profile is called by no application code, its floor
being zero in any case. max(percentage, 0) is the percentage, so every
installation running today is
unaffected. It becomes reachable the moment a tenant posts a profile to
/tolerance-profiles with an absolute floor, which is a supported thing to do
and the only reason the field exists.

It is also not the currency guard that is already there. match_invoice
refuses when the invoice and the order disagree, and that guard compares two
documents to each other. An order and its invoice can agree perfectly and
still be measured against a floor written in a third currency, which that
comparison never looks at.

The profile gains a nullable currency and the floor is dropped at match time
unless it can be shown to be the order's. Dropping rather than refusing the
whole match is the point: the percentage band is still perfectly well defined
without the floor, so there is a correct answer available and declining to
give one would be worse. What it must not do is drop the floor quietly, so
MatchResult now carries the floor that actually applied and a state saying
what became of it, and the three ways it can fail to apply are kept apart
because each has a different remedy. Label the profile, label the order, or
nothing at all, since a floor in another currency is the design working. The
band also narrows rather than widens when the floor goes, which turns a silent
approval into an exception a human reviews. That is the safe direction to be
wrong in.

The floor is read twice per match, once against a percentage of the order
total and once per line against a percentage of a unit price. Both readers
had the same defect, both now take the resolved value, and the line-level one
had no test at all before this: invoices built through the API carry no lines,
so line_results is empty unless an e-invoice was ingested, and the comparison
was never reached. That the two bands are computed on different magnitudes,
so a floor sized for an order total is large next to a unit price, is older
than this change and deliberately left alone. It is a question about how the
floor should be scaled rather than about what currency it is written in, and
answering it would move bands that are correct today for anyone whose floor
is labelled.

Two things were reporting the wrong band and both are corrected here.
tolerance_used_pct is the profile's percentage and was published even on the
matches the floor decided, so the field could not explain why an invoice
passed. And the exception message printed the band and annotated it with the
percentage unconditionally, so on the one occasion the number came from the
floor instead, the text credited it to a percentage it had nothing to do with.
The message now names whichever band set it.

There is no backfill and there cannot be one. A profile is global and has no
order to inherit a currency from, so nothing in the database says what an
existing floor was written in. But the ambiguous case is the only one that
needs an answer, and a floor of zero is the same amount of money everywhere,
so NULL loses nothing there. The upgrade counts the rows it cannot classify
and logs the number rather than assuming it is zero, and the test that checks
the count deliberately supplies a row that makes it nonzero, since a count
only ever run against data that makes it zero is not a count.

The migration speaks about rows that already exist, which leaves the ones made
next. Both write paths are now guarded and both go through the same function,
because they ask the same question. Create refuses a nonzero floor with no
currency outright. Update cannot be expressed the same way, since a partial
update has to be judged on the row it produces rather than the fields it
carries: raising the floor on a profile that already names a currency is fine,
sending the same floor to a profile whose currency is null is not, and neither
is clearing the currency out from under a floor that is already there. That
check needs both halves and so lives in the service.

Two docstrings were describing behaviour that does not exist and are corrected
alongside, since both were load-bearing for the reasoning above. The model
said the default profile ships seeded with every installation, and nothing
seeds it. ensure_default_tolerance_profile said it was called on boot, and its
only callers are tests.

Not included, and worth doing separately: ThreeWayMatchRecord stores
tolerance_used_pct and has no column for the floor, so the persisted audit
trail still cannot show which band let an invoice through. On shipped data
there is nothing for such a column to say yet, which is why it is not folded
in here.

chore(release): 15.6.0

Ten version literals across nine files, and the changelog entry the release
workflow reads its notes from.

What this release is mostly about, for anyone reading the tag rather than the
notes. Every document this product generates chose its typeface by guessing
from the characters in the string, and the guess was wrong in the one case
that mattered: a table cell that named no face fell back to one with no
Chinese glyphs at all, so a name written in Chinese came out as empty boxes or
did not come out. The face is now chosen by asking the font whether it can
draw the text. Alongside it, names reach a document as text rather than as
markup, so an ampersand in a company name no longer prints as an escape or
takes the rest of the cell with it, and a document says which language it was
written in instead of the language of whoever downloaded it.

Working calendars are the calendars of the countries they name. Canada was
using American public holidays, Saudi Arabia was shipping a four day working
week, the Gulf states shared one holiday set, and the Chinese calendar held
the lunisolar festivals of the previous year. A holiday computation that fails
now says it failed rather than reading as a year with no holidays, which is
the difference between an error and a year in which every day is a working
day.

Money that was a blend of two currencies is now either labelled or withheld. A
stock balance that received the same item against a euro order and then a
dollar order averaged the two into a number that is money in neither, and it
spread from there onto every issue and stocktake behind it. The three way
match refuses an invoice it cannot compare against its order instead of
subtracting one currency from another, and the absolute price floor it
compares against either names its currency or is dropped, which narrows the
band rather than widening it.

And an upgraded database keeps the constraints the model declares. What runs
at startup is not the migration chain, it is a repair pass that compares the
live schema against the model, and it would only mark a column required when
it could also supply a value for the rows already in the table. It looked for
that value in one of the two places a model can declare one, so a column
declaring its default in the other place arrived optional on every upgraded
database while every health signal reported the upgrade clean. Eleven hundred
and seventy six columns across six hundred and twenty one tables are affected,
on the upgrade path only. A fresh install was never wrong.

fix(packaging): the demo ships the photographs its captions describe

The wheel carried captions.json for twelve site photographs and none of the
twelve pictures. A first run seeded the captions, logged sixty missing asset
lines and left every demo gallery empty.

.gitignore globs *.jpg for dev screenshots and negates it for exactly this
directory, with a comment saying these are real shipped seed assets. Git
honours the negation, so all twelve are tracked and a checkout has them.
Hatchling reads the same file and does not honour negation, so its package
walk dropped the photographs while captions.json survived by not matching the
glob. Deterministic, so CI built the same wheel.

Fixed with the artifacts key, which is hatchling's mechanism for files the VCS
ignores that the build must ship anyway. Not force-include: that bypasses the
walker, so force-including the directory would add captions.json a second time
on top of the copy the walker already collects, and a duplicate zip entry is
rejected at upload with a 400.

Measured rather than assumed. The wheel goes from 4334 members to 4346, the
twelve added files are byte identical to the tracked ones, nothing is removed
and there are no duplicate entries. The publish job now asserts every file
captions.json names is in the archive, which fails on the old wheel with all
twelve missing and passes on the new one, so the next packaging change that
loses them stops at the gate rather than at somebody's first run.

fix(bid-management): an award names the submission it was made against

A bidder can hold more than one submission in a package, and the two
subscribers of bid_management.package.awarded each decided for themselves
which one an award referred to. The contract subscriber read an unbounded
query with scalar_one_or_none, which raises as soon as there are two rows,
and the handler wraps its whole body in except Exception reporting at debug
level. So the award succeeded, the purchase order was created, and the
contract silently did not exist. One debug line was the entire trace.

Measured through the service rather than read off the source. Two
invitations to the same company in one package, both submissions accepted
by record_submission, and the award then produces no contract at all. The
shape is reachable through the ordinary API: BidSubmission constrains
invitation_id to be unique but not bidder_id, BidInvitation has no
uniqueness on package and invitee, create_invitation has no duplicate
check, and record_submission verifies only that the bidder and the
invitation agree about the package. A re-invitation for a revised round
gets there.

Which row an award refers to is now a decision rather than an accident of
query order. select_awarded_submission states the precedence in one place,
most significant first: validity, then recency, then id so that the order
is total. The last term is not meaningful in itself, but two rows written
in one transaction can share a created_at and without it the winner would
depend on whatever order the database happened to return.

The rule is the one the purchase-order subscriber already applied, newest
valid falling back to newest, so the contract subscriber moves and
procurement does not. What is_valid means for existing rows is deliberately
unchanged: the fix is about which submission gets read, not about which
submissions count as valid, and a test asserts that a later invalid row
still does not displace an earlier valid one.

The selector is scoped by bidder alone. Bidder.package_id is NOT NULL, so
the bidder already carries the package scope, and joining the invitation to
filter on the package as well would be narrower rather than equivalent. It
would drop any row whose invitation and bidder disagree about the package,
which record_submission refuses to create but which may predate that guard,
and silently changing which submission an existing award resolves to is not
this function's decision to make.

The tests live in tests/pg because they cannot be written anywhere else.
The fake session in tests/unit/test_procurement_events.py models neither
order_by nor limit, and its scalar_one_or_none returns the first row where
SQLAlchemy raises, so under that double both the defect and the fix are
invisible. That divergence is now written down in the double's docstring,
and the double gains the first method the selector needs. The regression
test is parametrised over one and two submissions: one submission passed
before this change, so a test seeding a single submission would have gone
green over the defect, and keeping that case is what shows the two-row case
is not passing because the assertion is weak. Reverting the fix fails the
two-row cases and leaves the one-row case green.

Two things found alongside this and deliberately not fixed here. The
handler-wide except Exception that swallowed the failure is still in place,
so a contract subscriber that loses a contract is still quieter than one
that mislabels a currency. And an award whose package carries no currency
can still be described three ways by the records that follow it, which is
the separate currency defect this selector is a prerequisite for rather
than a fix for.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(notifications): a subscriber has to reach somebody from the payload it is sent

A handler that reads a key its publisher never emits resolves no recipient
and sends nothing. Nothing raises, nothing is logged, and the feature is
just absent. Reading the handler does not find it, because the handler is
correct on its own; the fault only exists in the pairing. Thirteen
handlers are in that state today and none of them was noticed by a test.

The rule is one property of one handler, checked by running it twice: once
against a payload holding every key it reads, and once against a payload
restricted to the keys its publisher actually emits. It is starved when
the first produces a notification and the second does not. The first run
is the control, and it is what makes this evidence rather than a lint,
because without it a handler that notifies nobody under any payload looks
identical to one starved by its publisher. That distinction is not
hypothetical: the first version of this instrument reported every handler
broken, and the tell was that one of them creates a contract and correctly
notifies no one.

Because the rule is a property of each handler alone rather than an
assertion about a fixed set, a handler added next month is covered without
anyone editing a list. The thirteen are recorded with the key each one
waits for, and that list may only shrink: a handler on it that starts
resolving a recipient fails the test until it is removed, and so does an
entry that no longer matches any handler.

A cheaper rule was tried and rejected on measurement rather than taste.
Relaxing the second payload to "keys that any publisher anywhere emits"
would need no per-event parsing, but it disagrees with the real rule on 8
of 26 handlers and every disagreement calls a starved handler healthy.
There are about 590 distinct published key names, so common ones like
created_by and actor_id are always emitted by something.

What the test cannot see is written inside it rather than left for the
next reader to discover. Publisher discovery is static and misses an event
name passed as a constant, and a payload built in a variable instead of
written literally at the call site. It also used to miss any publish
reached through a wrapper, which is why the wrappers are now found by
checking that they forward their own event-name parameter to a bus
primitive. Twenty-four handlers have a publisher this cannot read. They
are not exempted and not called defects, because the instrument has no
verdict about them either way; they are counted, and the number of
handlers the test can decide is itself ratcheted, so extracting an event
name to a constant fails the test instead of quietly making it greener.

Two exclusions are decided from the code rather than by hand. A handler
whose body calls no notification function at all is silent by
construction, not starved. A handler that opens a session and loads the
row the event points at takes its recipients from the database, so a
synthetic payload finds nothing and the control cannot fire; those eight
are named with the row each one loads, and their equivalent test has to
seed a database and live in tests/pg. Both lists are checked for staleness
the same way the starved list is.

Discovery is the live bus rather than a scan. The registrars are called
and the handler objects are read back off the registry, which resolves
them whatever shape the subscription tables take. Calling both a master
registrar and the sub-registrars it groups registers each handler several
times, so they are deduplicated by event and qualified name; that is a
property of calling them this way and not of application startup, which
goes through one entry point.

One assertion is about the bus rather than any handler. publish hands
every subscriber the same Event, with no per-handler copy, so a handler
that wrote into event.data would change what the handlers after it
receive. Nothing does today. It is pinned because if it ever starts, every
verdict above becomes wrong quietly.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(release-signing): two runs on one release stop clobbering each other

Every release starts this workflow twice on purpose. Desktop Release dispatches
one as soon as the installers exist so the signature does not wait on the rpm
bundler, which can run for hours, and the workflow_run trigger starts another
when Desktop Release completes. Nothing kept the two apart.

Both runs write the same three files to the same release with gh release upload
--clobber, and --clobber deletes the existing asset before uploading a new one,
so the asset id changes underneath anyone who listed the release a moment
earlier. On v15.6.0 the two runs arrived twenty three seconds apart, the
workflow_run run replaced the licence inventory while the dispatched run was
downloading, and the dispatched run died on HTTP 404 for an id that had been
valid seconds before.

That outcome was the harmless one. Reverse the winner and the release keeps the
dispatched run's manifest as its signature, and the dispatched run is the one
that does not wait for build-linux-rpm, so the release would carry a signed
SHA256SUMS with no line for an installer it ships. Every refusal already in this
workflow exists to stop precisely that, because a manifest over part of a
release verifies cleanly and therefore reads as a complete one.

Serialising on the tag settles it. The runs queue rather than collide, and the
order comes out right on its own: the dispatched run goes first because it is
dispatched first, and the workflow_run run, which has seen the whole release
including the rpm, is the one that writes last. cancel-in-progress stays false
deliberately, since cancelling the run in flight is how you get the half written
release the group exists to prevent.

v15.6.0 itself is correctly signed. Its manifest covers all nine non signature
assets, the checksums match the bytes GitHub serves for every one of them, and
the signature verifies under a certificate whose subject names this workflow on
main and whose OIDC claims name the run that succeeded.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(bid-management): an award tells the people it can name

Awarding a package notified nobody. The subscriber resolves who to tell by
reading winner_user_id, buyer_user_id and actor_id off the event, and the
publisher emitted none of the three, so the handler found no recipient and
returned. Nothing raised, nothing was logged, and no test noticed, because the
handler is correct read on its own and the publisher is correct read on its
own. The fault existed only in the pairing between them.

The payload now carries the two recipients that exist. actor_id is the user who
made the award, which the router already passes down, and buyer_user_id is the
package owner recorded at creation, the same value the contract bridge already
uses. Both are additive: no key is renamed and none is removed.

winner_user_id is deliberately still absent, and that is a different defect
rather than an oversight in this one. A Bidder row is a snapshot of an external
company, holding a company name and a contact email, and carries no user id
anywhere in the schema. There is no value the publisher could put under that
key. The winning company therefore still is not told it won, and cannot be
until somebody decides how an external bidder receives a notification at all,
which means deciding whether a portal identity and a platform user are the same
kind of thing. The key stays in the handler with a note saying so, because it
names a recipient the feature is meant to reach and deleting it would erase the
requirement along with the gap.

Two body values were empty for the same reason and are fixed alongside, since
an award notice that reaches somebody and says nothing is only half delivered.
The amount read award_amount while the payload has only ever published
awarded_amount, so every award notification rendered a blank where the money
should be; the reader moves to the published name rather than the payload
moving, because other subscribers already read the published one. The package
name had no key at all and is now published.

The proof is that the payload contract gate's starved list is one shorter. That
list may only shrink, so a handler on it that starts resolving a recipient
fails the suite until it is removed, which is what makes the removal evidence
instead of a claim. Reverting either half of this reds it: without the
recipients the gate names the handler as starved, and without the amount fix
the pairing test names the key.

One caveat is worth stating rather than leaving for the next reader, and it is
now in the gate's docstring too. The gate asserts that a handler reaches at
least one recipient, which is the right rule for a payload that starves its
subscriber and is exactly why a green from it must never be read as proof that
a feature works. This handler was written to tell three people, now tells two,
and passes. The gate is also structurally blind to the body values above, since
it only follows recipients, which is why those get their own test.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(cli): the version fallback names a version instead of a sentinel

Where the package metadata cannot be read, both version lookups fell back to
Settings.model_fields["app_version"].default. That field is declared with
default_factory, so pydantic keeps the PydanticUndefined sentinel in default and
there is nothing there to read. The sentinel has a __str__, which is why this
survived: nothing raised, the except below it never ran, the value never became
"unknown", and the line printed to the user was

    OpenConstructionERP vPydanticUndefined

on the one path that exists for someone already trying to work out what they
have installed. The frozen desktop build and a source checkout that was never
pip installed are the two ways to reach it.

The fallback now asks the field which kind of default it holds and reads that
one. Both branches are kept because either declaration is legitimate and this
should not break again the next time somebody changes which is used.

cmd_version carried its own copy of the whole lookup while _resolve_version sat
below it describing itself as shared by the version and welcome commands. It was
not shared, it was pasted, so the docstring was already wrong and either copy
could have been repaired while the other went on printing the sentinel. The copy
is gone and the sentence is true now.

Four tests. The one that matters drives the fallback by making the metadata
lookup raise and asserts the answer names a version, which is a stricter claim
than being non-empty, since PydanticUndefined is a perfectly good non-empty
string and a test written the loose way would have passed against the defect. A
control checks the primary path still wins when metadata is readable, so a
repaired fallback cannot be confused with a fallback that has quietly become the
only path. Another asserts on the printed line rather than on the source, which
is what keeps the duplicate from coming back without pinning how the sharing is
written. Verified by reverting the fix: two of the four go red and the captured
output reads vPydanticUndefined.

What the tests cannot do is stated in the file. They stand in for the real cause
rather than reproducing it, so they do not prove the frozen build takes this
branch.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(bid-management): an award settles what money it is, once

An award made on a package with no currency stored the empty string and
published it. Three records then described that one award and disagreed:
the purchase order read EUR, the contract read nothing, the award row
itself read nothing.

Each subscriber of bid_management.package.awarded ran a fallback chain of
its own, and only procurement's consulted the winning submission. The
difference is invisible whenever the package declares a currency, because
the first term wins everywhere, and every existing test passes an explicit
currency in the payload and never reaches the rest of any chain.

The blank package is not a contrived state. BidPackage.currency defaults to
the empty string, and the validation at open_bids that looks like it would
object needs both operands truthy before it will call a currency a
mismatch, so an unlabelled package plus a EUR submission is not flagged,
stays valid and is awardable through the ordinary API.

award_package now resolves the currency once, against the same submission
select_awarded_submission gives both subscribers, and stores it on the
award row and in the payload. The package declares the tender's currency
and still wins whenever it has one, so no labelled award changes; the
submission is consulted only where the answer used to be the empty string.
The subscribers are left alone. With a resolved value in the payload they
take its first term and never reach their own fallbacks, which is why the
fix belongs at the publisher rather than in three places that would then
have to be kept identical.

The control drives award_package and reads the payload it actually
publishes, captured by standing in for publish_after_commit, so what is
asserted is the shipping path. Run against the unfixed tree it fails with
the four labels printed. Removing only the new fallback term reproduces the
failure, and service.py hashes the same before and after the restoration.

An earlier draft of that control fed a hand-written empty currency straight
to the two subscribers, bypassing award_package. It measured a payload the
publisher can no longer emit and would have made the case for changing the
subscribers instead. It was rewritten before the fix was written, not after
it failed to pass.

The fake session in test_bid_management.py answers every query empty, so
select_awarded_submission returns nothing there whatever the repo stubs
hold, and the award's currency always stops at the package. That is now
written into the double, next to the .first() it grew, pointing at the
PostgreSQL test where the fallback is actually exercised.

The empty fallback at the end is not dead code, though it reads like it.
The check above guarantees the winner has a valid submission, but it counts
through submissions_for_package, which joins BidInvitation.package_id,
while select_awarded_submission filters on bidder_id alone. Those are
different sets, deliberately so, for the reason set out in that function's
docstring, and a row the one counts and the other does not is exactly what
the empty string is there for.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(static): a missing asset says so instead of answering with the page

The SPA fallback answered every unmatched path with index.html, which is right
for a client-side route and wrong for a file. A request for a bundle that is not
on disk came back 200 with text/html under a .js URL.

The way this reaches a user is a browser holding a stale index.html after a
redeploy. It asks for a hashed bundle that no longer exists, gets the page back
instead, and fails inside the module loader, so what the operator sees is a
syntax error in a script rather than a missing file. That is several steps away
from the cause and it is where the debugging starts. The 200 also invites the
browser and any proxy in between to keep the answer, so the wrong response
outlives the deploy that caused it.

This is the same failure the /health and /openapi.json aliases in this file
already exist to prevent. The note there says a probe is told a sick service is
healthy. The reasoning was never carried across to assets, and it is the same
reasoning: a caller asking a yes or no question must not be handed something
that parses as yes.

The discriminator is what the request asks for rather than what it resembles. A
file request is one whose suffix is a type this server serves, or anything under
the /assets mount, where the bundler puts nothing else. Client-side routes are
untouched because they carry no suffix, and a route whose last segment happens
to contain a dot keeps its index.html unless that suffix is one we would have
served. The obvious version of this check is "does the path contain a dot", and
that would turn a legitimate route like /projects/tower.a1 into a 404, so there
is a test pinning exactly that case.

Fourteen tests, and the shape matters more than the count. Six assert the new
404 across several types rather than one, because the defect was a property of
the fallback and not of any extension. The rest are controls in the other
direction: a bundle that exists is still served with its own content type, a
root file that exists is still served, four client-side routes still get the
page, and an API path still gets its JSON 404. Without those a blanket 404 would
have passed every positive assertion.

Verified by removing the branch again: six red, eight green, and the six are
exactly the missing-asset cases while every control stays green.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(notifications): a failing wave-5 subscriber no longer disappears

Ten handlers in the cross-module subscriber file wrapped their whole body in a
bare except that logged at debug level and then returned as though nothing had
happened. The bus was told the handler had succeeded, so a broken subscriber
looked exactly like a working one and nothing upstream could count the failure.

Those clauses are gone and the exception now reaches the bus. The narrow except
clauses that catch a specific error and mean it are untouched, twelve before and
twelve after. Most of the diff is the dedent that follows removing the try
blocks, not a rewrite of the handlers.

The new test drives a subscriber that raises and asserts the failure is
reported. Before this change it came back with an empty error list and a result
of None, which is what made the swallow invisible in the first place.

fix(supplier-catalogs): a stock movement with no unit cost stops returning 500

StockMovement.unit_cost is nullable on purpose. A movement out of a balance
whose average is not knowable has no unit cost to record, and writing zero there
would read as issued for nothing. The response schema declared the field
required, so serialising such a movement raised a validation error and the route
answered 500. The database write had already committed by then, which is the
unpleasant part: the operator saw a failure over a movement that was recorded.

Three routes return that schema, reserve, issue and stocktake, and the first
stocktake of an item that has never been received reaches it on an ordinary
fresh install.

The same change also adds currency, which the model has carried all along and
the service writes on every path that creates a movement. Without it the amount
reached the caller with nothing saying what it was denominated in.

This is one half of a widening that was applied to the balance and missed on the
movement, so the new test compares the two shapes rather than only asserting the
new behaviour. That comparison is what would have caught it at the time.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(upgrade): a populated database that names no revision is left unstamped

Releases before 15.4.0 shipped no alembic.ini, so their databases record no
migration revision at all. On boot create_all creates whatever tables are wholly
absent and cannot alter the ones already there, so such a database is left part
migrated, and the boot stamp then wrote head over the top. That claimed a schema
state nothing had verified, and the missing revision was the only durable record
that the database was not at head. Once head is written the evidence is gone for
good, every later upgrade skips the same revisions with no signal at all, and
nothing left in the database can say which version wrote it.

Refusing to stamp is reversible, since the database can always be stamped later
once the repair for this cohort is settled. Stamping is not reversible. While
that decision is open the reversible branch is the one to take, so the stamp is
now declined and the database stays visibly not at head.

The question can only be asked before create_all runs, because afterwards every
database has our tables. So boot captures the answer first and carries it down
to the stamp, and the parameter defaults to off, which leaves every caller that
does not pass it behaving exactly as before.

One false positive is known and accepted. A fresh install that crashes between
create_all and the stamp comes back looking like this cohort and will stay
unstamped until someone stamps it by hand. That is loud, logged with what to do,
and recoverable. The behaviour it replaces was silent and was not.

The test carries the control that has to come out the other way: the same
database through the same call with the guard off, showing head being written.
Without it a guard that returns nothing is indistinguishable from no guard.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(upgrade-lane): the schema check compares nullability in both directions

The lane compared one direction only, the model promising NOT NULL against a
database that accepts NULL. The reverse, a column the database insists on and
the model declares nullable, was invisible, and that is precisely what a
revision which widens a column leaves behind when it never runs. The boot heal
adds columns and indexes and has no DROP NOT NULL, so the old constraint
survives, code assigning None into it raises a not-null violation on an ordinary
write, and the lane called the schema healed.

The two directions are different defects with different repairs, so they are
returned and reported as two lists rather than one count. A reader can now tell
which of the two they are looking at without opening the schema.

Widening the check also widens what counts as evidence that the database under
test is genuinely old. The first check exists so the lane cannot pass vacuously
on a database that was never aged, and on a database whose only remaining
divergence is an over-tight column that check would previously have found
nothing and failed for the wrong reason.

The test loads the gate by path and drives it against a database wrong in both
directions at once, asserting the two lists come back different rather than
merely non-empty. Two lists that came back equal would mean the second direction
is not being computed. Verified red against the previous version, which returns
three lists and does not name the widened column anywhere.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(upgrade): the boot heal can widen a column, not only add one

What runs on upgrade for most installs is the startup schema heal, not the
migration chain. Until now that heal only ever added things: tables, columns,
indexes, constraints. So a revision whose whole content was to relax a column
had no effect on any of those installs. The old NOT NULL survived, the models
went on declaring the value optional, and the first ordinary write that left it
empty failed with a not-null violation from inside a request that had already
written its row.

That is not hypothetical, it shipped. Two cost columns in the warehouse stock
tables were made optional and are still NOT NULL on every upgraded database, so
reserving stock and receiving goods both answer with a server error there. The
release before this one fixed the half of that defect which lives in the
response model, which is what a fresh install hits. This is the other half.

Dropping a NOT NULL is the one alteration of an existing column that cannot be
refused by data already in the table. It only widens what the column accepts, so
no existing row can contradict it, which is why it belongs in a heal that runs
unattended on someone else's database while adding a NOT NULL or changing a type
do not. Primary keys are skipped on both definitions, the models' and the live
one, because the database rejects the statement there and an aged schema can
disagree with the models about which columns those are.

Measured rather than assumed: against the current models on a healthy database
the pass emits nothing at all, and the tests drive it on a table built for the
purpose so both sides of the comparison are exact. With the pass disabled they
go red, which is the only thing that makes them evidence.

The upgrade lane also stops asking a question one cohort can never answer. It
required the migration head to match, and a database from before 15.4.0 records
no revision at all, so that used to pass only because such a database was being
silently stamped at a position nothing had verified. Now that the boot refuses
that stamp, the lane asks each cohort for its own honest answer: a database that
arrived carrying a revision must be at head, and one that arrived with none must
still have none.

chore: release 15.6.1

Eleven fixes and no new capability, so this is a patch inside 15.6.

The one worth reading first is warehouse stock. A stocktake, a reservation and a
goods receipt all answered with a server error, and the defect had two halves
that hit different installs. On a fresh install the response model declared the

has no cost to record. On an upgraded database the column itself was still
mandatory, because the repair pass that runs at startup could add a column but
never relax one, so the change that made it optional had no effect there. Both

Also here: an upgraded database that records no revision is left saying so
rather than being stamped at a position nothing verified, the upgrade lane asks

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(payment-clock): Russia and China get the payment clock they were owed

Two countries were carrying a recorded "still looking" rather than an answer. The
table that holds statutory payment periods named both in a set whose whole purpose
is to say that a search had been run with the wrong instrument, so the absence was
not evidence, and that neither had earned a value yet. This is that search finishing.

Russia gets one row, for public procurement, where the customer has seven working
days from the day it signs the acceptance document. Working days rather than
calendar ones, so the Russian holiday calendar has to be supplied to reproduce the
statutory date, and the year is moved about by decree, which a fixed weekday rule
will not follow on its own. Two cases lengthen the period and the row does not
compute them, so it says which they are and tells the reader to state the date on
the application instead. Nothing is shipped for private Russian construction,
because the Civil Code makes payment fall due on acceptance and leaves the period
to the parties, so there is no number to encode. That is the same stance the
Nigerian row already takes.

China gets two rows rather than one, because the regulation sets two different
periods for two different payers: thirty days for a government or public
institution buyer, sixty for a large enterprise, in both cases owed to a small or
medium supplier. This table's rule is one clock per regime, which is why the two
German entries and the two American ones are also split. Construction works are
named in the operative text, so this is not an analogy borrowed from a goods
statute, and the paragraph a progress claim actually turns on is the one that runs
the period from the day both parties confirmed the settlement amount.

Brazil deliberately gets nothing and stays as it was. The search there did not fail
to find a number, it found that the 2021 procurement law stopped fixing a single cap
for the public administration and put the period in the tender instrument instead.
The figure this registry wants does not exist in the statute to be copied. Giving
Brazil a clock would need a registry that can express an ordering rule rather than
an elapsed time, which is a change of shape and not a row.

Where a source was thin it is left out rather than rounded up. The exact
commencement of the Russian amendment that cut fifteen working days to seven is
disputed between two dates, so the row says so rather than picking one, and a
twenty working day exception that appeared in a single weak source is not written
down at all. Every new row records the limit of its own sourcing in its notes, the
way the Bulgarian row already does.

The interest under the Russian article is a daily fraction of a floating central
bank rate, which is none of the four shapes the numeric interest fields were built
for, so it is written as text and the numbers are left empty. That costs nothing
while nothing computes an interest amount from those fields and it would cost real
accuracy the day something does.

The test that proves this fails on the tree before the change and passes after it.
The one alongside it, which checks that a country still being researched says so
rather than reading as a plain gap, used to name China as its example and would have
quietly stopped exercising that branch the moment China got a row. It now stages a
country into that state itself, so the branch stays covered whoever happens to be
held.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(i18n): a search that finds nothing says so in ten more languages

The empty state of the pipeline step palette, the line a user sees when they have
typed a search term and nothing matched it, was still sitting in English in Arabic,
Bulgarian, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Korean, Mongolian, Thai, Turkish and
Vietnamese.

It survived because the tooling that exists to catch exactly this could not see it.
The English value is written in single quotes, since the sentence itself contains
double quotes around the search term, and both coverage scanners assume every value
opens with a double quote. They skipped the pair, lost their place, and swallowed
the next twenty five keys along with it. So the string was untranslated in ten
languages and no report ever mentioned it. The scanners are being repaired
separately; this is the strings.

Each translation follows the quotation convention its own file already uses rather
than a single house style imposed across scripts, so Bulgarian takes the low and
high marks it uses elsewhere, Korean takes its corner brackets, Finnish takes the
right double mark on both sides, and the rest take guillemets. Thai takes no full
stop, because it does not use one. The placeholder that carries the user's search
term is unchanged in all ten and is checked rather than eyeballed.

fix(i18n): the coverage scanner reads the whole English file

The two scripts that report locale coverage share a parser for the flat
translation block of a locale file, and it was reading en.ts as pure data when
en.ts is not pure data. Two things in that block broke it. There are 130 comment
lines grouping the keys by feature, nine of which carry a quote character in
ordinary prose, and a parser that does not know about comments reads one of those
quotes as the start of a string, loses its place, and drops every pair until it
happens to resynchronise. Separately, two values are written in single quotes
because the text itself contains a double quote, and only the double quote opened
a string here, so those fell into the skip-this-pair branch.

Between them they hid 27 keys of en.ts from every coverage report either script
has ever printed, one whole feature group among them. A missing key cannot be
reported by a tool that cannot see it in the reference file, so those keys were
absent from every locale and from every gap list at the same time.

The English-equal check was wrong in the same place for the same reason. It
compared raw source, and en.ts spells one string in single quotes to avoid
escaping the double quotes inside it while every other locale writes that same
text double quoted with the escapes. Compared as source those two differ, so a
string that was in fact untranslated was being reported as translated. The
comparison is now on decoded text, which is what makes the check mean what its
name says.

The percentage these scripts print is coverage of the English keyspace and not of
the target file, because every locale also carries keys en.ts does not: the
English for the case playbooks and the module guides lives inline in source as a
defaultValue rather than in a locale file. The summary now names that second
count separately, so a number is never printed without saying what it counts.

Greek and Ukrainian are added to the test-only fallback aggregator. Both were in
SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES and shipping, and neither was listed there, so every test
that iterates all locales was quietly skipping them while passing. That is how
Kyrgyz went unchecked before them. The file now also records which locales are
deliberately absent and why, so the next reader can tell an omission from a
decision.

fix(schedule): a country code stops selecting another country's working week

The table that picks a working calendar held two vocabularies in one dictionary
and could not tell them apart. Most of its keys are ISO country codes, which is
what the shipped cost catalogue uses for its region ids today. A few were the
language prefixes of a naming that catalogue has since left behind, and every
calendar in the file still carries a comment naming the id it was built for:
AR_DUBAI, PT_SAOPAULO, ENG_TORONTO, HI_MUMBAI. None of those ids exists any
more. The catalogue renamed them to AE_DUBAI, BR_SAOPAULO, CA_TORONTO and
IN_MUMBAI, and this table did not follow.

So AR went on meaning Arabic while the data started meaning Argentina, and PT
went on meaning Portuguese while the data started meaning Portugal. A project in
Buenos Aires was given the Gulf week of six ten-hour days and one in Lisbon the
Brazilian week of six. Both are Monday to Friday countries. Three of the
overlapping heads agree by luck, DE and FR and RU reading the same either way,
which is why the two that do not went unnoticed. AR_BUENOSAIRES and PT_LISBON
are shipped rows, so these answers were reachable from data this product ships.

Canada was the opposite failure. A Canadian calendar has been in the table all
along and no key reached it, so CA fell to the default and the API reported a
Canadian project's calendar as Standard. Two shipped demo packs carry that
region.

A sweep of all 249 officially assigned alpha-2 codes through the real resolver
found three wrong answers there and two more among the region labels, where a
bare entry for the word United caught every label beginning with it, so the
United Arab Emirates were given the American calendar rather than the Gulf one.
Five wrong answers and one calendar nothing could reach. Two of those were
visible by eye and the other three came out of the sweep, which is the argument
for sweeping rather than sampling.

The one dictionary is now three: country codes on their own, the superseded
heads on their own, and full labels matched in full rather than by prefix.
Nothing may sit in both of the first two, and nothing in the legacy table may be
a two-letter code, so the order they are consulted in cannot decide any answer.
That property is asserted rather than described. Argentina and Portugal are
simply absent from the country table, because no calendar ships for either and
the default really is both countries' week.

The test sweeps all 249 codes, the shipped catalogue ids and the labels, and it
fails on the tree before this change and passes after. Three of its cases exist
to stop the wrong repair: one stages a country into the offending state and
requires the sweep to report it, so a sweep that has quietly stopped looking
cannot pass; one pins the six-day countries, so flattening every week to Monday
through Friday cannot be mistaken for a fix; and one pins the field names the
arithmetic actually reads, because this product carries four structures that all
look like a work calendar and only one of them is consulted here.

Two things this deliberately leaves alone. The core calendar module disagrees
with this table about six countries' working weeks, Sunday to Thursday against
Monday to Saturday in two of them, which is a real disagreement and not a
rounding difference; it is a separate change and settling it will require
changing the assertions added here. And two catalogue ids, SV_STOCKHOLM and
VI_HANOI, begin with codes that belong to other countries; both answer the
default before and after, so they want a data rename rather than a resolver fix.
