fix(contracts): a region name stops picking another country's rules, and a Canadian contract stops being given a deadline nobody wrote

Two defects in the same area, both shipped, and the second is the one to read first.

A change on a Canadian contract was being given a countdown to a legal deadline that no
contract text supports. The registry of notice periods did not recognise the CCDC family,
and an unrecognised form fell through to a generic period rather than declining to answer.
Measured on the tree before this change, a Toronto variation with an event on the first of
August was told the period was twenty eight days, that the deadline was the twenty ninth,
that the status was due soon, and that the basis was calendar days. Every one of those
numbers was manufactured by a fallback. The generic period is a reasonable thing to offer
where nothing better is known and the reader can tell that is what they are looking at; it
is not reasonable when it is presented as this contract's own clock.

That form is now recognised and held rather than answered. It goes into a set of standards
the product knows it cannot yet state a period for, following the convention the payment
clock registry already uses for a country still being researched, rather than inventing a
second way of saying the same thing. The clock is still built and still returned, with no
period, no deadline and a status of unknown, so the refusal reaches the screen instead of
the row quietly disappearing. It also still reports the entitlement as at risk when no
notice is on file, because declining to state the window is not the same as saying there is
no window. A genuinely unrecognised form keeps the generic fallback it always had, which is
pinned by a test so this narrows nothing except the one family it names.

No period was written down for it. The contract documents are copyrighted and are not in
this repository, and a legal deadline recalled rather than read is exactly the kind of
number that should not ship.

The second defect is how a project finds its rules at all. The resolver matched its hint
tokens as unanchored substrings of a free text region name, first match winning, and two of
those tokens are two letters long. So the German pack was reached by the two letters in the
middle of a word. Ciudad de Mexico got the German rules from the Spanish preposition, and
Ile-de-France from the French one. Russia, Belarus, Cyprus and Australia all got the
American rules from the letters in their own names. Denver and Delaware, both American,
got the German ones. The right answers were reached the same way, which is what let this
sit: Houston resolved correctly by containing two of the letters in the American token, and
Baden-Wuerttemberg resolved correctly by containing two of the letters in the German one,
so a test written from the countries the list was built for would have gone green over all
of it.

Resolution now starts from the ISO country code the project already carries in its own
column, and the free text name is a fallback rather than the primary. Three lookups that
cannot overlap replace the one that could: country codes matched exactly, a short list of
superseded codes that are not and cannot be ISO codes, and full labels matched as whole
words. Every key in the label table is longer than two characters, and that is asserted
rather than assumed. Because the tables cannot overlap, the order they are consulted in
cannot decide any answer. This is the same shape the work calendar resolver was given for
the same class of defect, so the product now solves this problem once rather than twice.

One honest regression comes with it. German sub-region labels are no longer matched by
their spelling, so a project whose region reads Baden-Wuerttemberg and whose country column
is empty now gets the default instead of the German pack. It was getting the right answer
by accident and the accident is gone; the country column is where that belongs.

Two things this deliberately does not do. Canada and China still have no rules of their
own, so a correctly resolved project in either lands on the universal pack. That is the
honest answer and it is not coverage, and it is now written down as a test naming both, so
the absence has to be dealt with rather than rediscovered. And the country column remains
ambiguous in a way this change cannot fix: it is mandatory with a German default, so a
project created through the API without a country is indistinguishable from one whose owner
chose Germany, while a project created through the demo path holds an empty string because
an empty string does not trigger a default. The empty string is read as unknown here and
Germany is taken at face value, because demoting Germany would break every project that
really is German in order to protect the ones that never chose. Separating those two needs
a column that can hold nothing, which is a migration and not a resolver change. The
ambiguity is now written above the table where the next reader meets it.

fix(schedule): the Gulf weekend falls on the days the Gulf actually rests

Saudi Arabia and Qatar were being planned on a week that rests Sunday and works
Friday. Their week is the other way round, Sunday through Thursday, so the two
days a project there does not work were both marked as working and the one day
it does work was marked as rest. That is three days out of seven wrong, and
wrong in the way that matters most, because a date pushed off a weekend lands on
the wrong side of it and every date after it inherits the error.

Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman were worse off than wrong, they were absent. A country
with no entry falls through to the default calendar, which is Monday to Friday,
and a country that is missing looks exactly like a country with no special
calendar. There was nothing to tell the two apart, which is why this sat: the
absence produced a plausible answer rather than an error.

The Emirates moved to a Monday to Friday week in 2022 and now has a calendar of
its own rather than sharing one named after the region. Sharing was the original
mistake: a calendar named for a region invites countries to be filed under it by
geography, and the Gulf does not have one working week.

Why nothing caught this before. The API reports the working week as a count of
days, and the days themselves reach a client only as prose inside the calendar's
label. A count of five is correct for a country resting Friday and Saturday and
equally correct for one resting Saturday and Sunday, so every consumer of that
number agreed with the calendar while the calendar disagreed with the country.
A number that is right while the days behind it are wrong is not a small error,
it is an error with no symptom.

So the check added here compares the two tables the product already holds, the
statutory working week in the core calendar and the planning week the scheduler
resolves, and it asserts they never conflict rather than asserting they are
equal. They are deliberately not equal: Brazil, China and India are planned on a
six day construction week while their statutory week is five days, and flattening
one onto the other to make a test pass would be a real regression dressed as a
fix. What is not allowed is a day the country works being a day the planner
rests. It also runs the other way, so a calendar that no country week is ever
compared against cannot hide, since that is precisely how the Gulf calendar
stayed wrong while every test around it passed.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(contracts): the missing rule packs are a checklist rather than a silent gap

The test that names the countries with no compliance pack of their own now says
what has to be true before a name is struck off it, and says that going red is
its purpose rather than an obstacle.

The finding behind it is worth stating plainly. Twenty eight rule set standards
are registered and six are reachable through a pack. The other twenty two, which
include the Chinese and Spanish sets, are not unreachable everywhere: a project
can select them through its own rule sets and they run. What no jurisdiction
reaches is the contract signature gate, because that gate is fed by packs alone.
So the gap is narrower than the raw count suggests and it is real.

The temptation this guards against is closing that gap by wiring the remaining
standards up. Three things now have to hold before a country is added. The
rule sets a pack names have to be sets the engine actually registers, since an
unregistered set does not run and must never read as having run and passed. The
rules have to test something the jurisdiction is about rather than only that a
classification code is present and correctly shaped. And the country has to be
one whose projects should genuinely be blocked at signature by those rules, not
merely one the product supports.

The reason for the bar is the asymmetry between the two kinds of nothing. An
absent pack reads to a user as absent. An empty one reads as coverage, and tells
them they have been checked when they have not. Leaving the gap open and named
is the safer of the two while the rules behind those standards have not been
read.

fix(tests): a timer armed in one test file stops firing after that file is gone

The frontend suite could exit 1 while reporting that every test passed. Six
hundred and thirty four files, seven thousand two hundred and seventy one
passed, none failed, red exit code. That shape is not a flaky test, it is a
failure raised outside any test, where there is no test for the runner to
attribute it to and nothing in the summary to hold it.

The cause is a timer that outlives the environment that armed it. When a test
file finishes, the jsdom globals are deleted, but a timer armed during that file
is an ordinary Node timer and is not deleted with them, so it fires afterwards
into a world where window no longer exists. The grid arms exactly such a timer:
the routine that fits columns to the available width retries on a nought, one
hundred and five hundred millisecond chain for as long as it measures zero
pixels. The last link in that chain lands after teardown, reaches the part of
React that asks the window for the current event priority, and the run dies
there.

Two obvious repairs do not reach it, which is worth writing down so nobody
spends the afternoon on them again. Stubbing the element's width does not settle
the retry, because the retry lands after the test body has detached the element
and a stubbed getter on a detached node no longer describes an attached box.
Unmounting does not help either, measured directly on the grid: the retry
survives cleanup untouched, since the grid armed it and nothing in the React
tree owns it.

Whether the crash becomes visible at all is a race between the timer and the
worker exiting, which the worker usually wins. That is why this reddened one
operating system and not the other two, why it arrived and left without anyone
changing the test, and why it landed on commits whose diff touched no frontend
file at all.

So the setup file now tracks what each file arms and cancels whatever is still
pending once that file's last test has run, which is the only boundary this
needs to beat. Inside a file nothing changes. Timers behave exactly as before,
including the eighteen files that drive them deliberately through the fake timer
clock, which install over this wrapper and hand it back when they uninstall.
Only the timers that would have crossed the teardown boundary are dropped, and a
timer that fires or is cleared normally stops being tracked at that moment
rather than being held to the end.

This deliberately does not silence anything. A timer cancelled here has already
outlived every test that could have asserted on it, so no assertion changes and
no failing test is turned green. What changes is that a component leaking a
timer can no longer take the whole run down with it after the fact.

feat(cases): the case library learns four more markets

The catalogue goes from 164 cases to 202. Canada and China had none at all, Spain
and Britain had one each, and each of the four now has ten.

Canada and China were not researched here. Both had a full set of case
specifications written months ago, sourced and argued, and neither ever reached
the product. Germany and the United States had the same treatment and theirs did
arrive, which is the whole difference between thirteen German cases on the hub
and nothing at all for a Canadian reader. This is those two sets finally being
built. Spain and Britain had no such groundwork and were written from the trade
practice up.

The interesting content is what each case does not claim. Every one was checked
against what the product actually does before a step promised it, and the places
where the product does part of the job are written into the case in plain words
rather than glossed over. So the Spanish certification case names the European
late payment regime and says which Spanish law implements it, because there is no
Spanish row in the statutory payment register and pretending otherwise would send
a reader looking for a date nothing computes. The Spanish exchange-format case
says out loud that the import does not rebuild the decomposition, does not keep
auxiliary prices and captures a coefficient it does not apply, and hands the
reader to the next case to build it themselves. The British measurement case was
written claiming NRM 2 work sections and was corrected before it shipped, because
the classification picker offers the NRM 1 elemental structure and nothing in it
is a work section, so the step would have walked a reader into a screen that
cannot do what the words said. The Canadian prompt payment case names the
provinces as law rather than as something the product selects, since only one
Canadian regime is registered and it is Ontario's.

One of those narrowings found a defect in the shipped product rather than in the
case. The Canadian change case deliberately states no day count and tells the
reader to count the period their contract allows in working days against their
own site calendar. The product was meanwhile showing that same reader a twenty
eight day calendar countdown, manufactured by a generic fallback, for a contract
family it did not recognise. The case and the application would have contradicted
each other on adjacent screens, and the case was the one that was right. That is
fixed separately.

The chips a step carries were copied rather than invented. A module label and the
key beside it decide what different readers see, and a pair that disagrees is
invisible to every gate because nothing is untranslated. Every triple in these
thirty eight files was taken verbatim from one already in use, so no route grows a
second spelling and no baseline needed touching.

The prose is English throughout, including the Chinese set, with standards, forms
and documents named as themselves. That follows what the shipped cases already do:
across all 202 files there is not one accented character in case copy, and the
German cases write Maengel and Verjaehrung rather than carrying umlauts. A market
case names its own vocabulary; it does not switch language to do it.

One snapshot moves with them, and it is worth saying why it is in this commit
rather than looking like noise. A dashboard tile prints the size of the case
library, so thirty eight new files change a number rendered two directories away
from where any of them live. Every gate run while these were being written was
scoped to the cases feature, and a file that is never looked at cannot report
itself, so this would have gone red in continuous integration rather than here.
The update was read rather than accepted: four lines changed, all of them the
count. The snapshot holds no case card, which is what makes this a content
change and not a presentation one.

None of these cases routes a reader to a compliance pack. There is no Canadian,
Chinese or Spanish pack to route to, so rather than gesture at one the cases work
with what the product has. That absence is real and is recorded as its own
finding.

feat(cases): a case says who it is written for and what it walks through

A case has always known which kinds of company it serves and which modules its
steps visit. The catalogue used the first only to filter and showed neither, so a
reader scanning the grid could see how long a case takes and how many steps it
has, but not whether it was meant for them or where it would take them. The
public case pages have shown both for a long time, which made the product the
quieter of the two about its own content.

The card now carries both. Company types and module names sit in the reveal panel
where the fuller story already lives, rather than on the resting card, which is
deliberately dense and stays that way. Both runs are clipped to what fits with a
count for the remainder, and the whole list is available to a screen reader rather
than only the visible part, so nothing is hidden from a reader who cannot see the
overflow.

The case page shows every company type a case names, not a clipped run. Someone
who has opened a case is asking whether it is theirs, and that is the moment to
answer it completely. There those company types are controls rather than labels:
pressing one filters the catalogue to that kind of firm and goes there, because
the reader asking whether a case is theirs is the same reader who wants the rest
of the cases written for them, and the chip is already the thing under their eye.
It replaces any company filter already set rather than adding to it, so the chip
means show me these rather than narrow what I had. Each is a real button carrying
the action as its accessible name and its tooltip, with the company name as its
visible text, so what a screen reader announces is what the control does rather
than the noun it is named after.

On the card the same company types stay plain text, and that asymmetry is the
point rather than an oversight. The card is a single click target, and a nested
control inside it would steal the click the whole card exists to catch. That is
pinned by a test and noted where the card renders them, so the next reader does
not helpfully make the two surfaces consistent and break the card doing it.

The case page chips are drawn without a tint on purpose: the discipline chip
beside them is the one carrying colour, and a second coloured family on the same
row would leave the colour meaning nothing.

Module names are resolved the way the module honeycomb already resolves them,
through the key rather than through the label written beside it. That distinction
is not cosmetic. A chip carries both, only the key is translated, and where the
key exists in English the key wins for every reader including the English one. A
surface that read the label directly would agree with the honeycomb in English and
disagree with it in the other languages, and no locale check could see it because
nothing would be untranslated.

Three strings are new, and every locale that answers for a language of its own has
them in this commit rather than carrying English with a promise to translate
later. That is forty two files, English included. An English string sitting in a
non-English locale is not a placeholder for a translation, it is the leak itself,
and it passes every check that looks for missing keys. Each was written from the
vocabulary its own file already uses for the same ideas rather than translated
fresh, and each file keeps its own separator convention, which is not a colon and
a space everywhere. In the languages that inflect nouns the two card labels are
headings rather than governing constructions, because what fills the slot is a
fixed list of names that cannot agree with a case the label would demand. The
third string is an action label on a control rather than a caption, so it takes
whatever form each language uses for a button, which is an imperative in some, an
infinitive in others and a noun phrase in the rest. The American English file is
deliberately untouched: it holds overrides only, and none of these three has an
American spelling to override.

fix(i18n): the Uzbek string added yesterday uses the letter Uzbek writes with

One string shipped with a plain typewriter apostrophe where Uzbek Latin uses a
modifier letter. The o and g of that alphabet carry a mark that is part of the
letter rather than punctuation, and substituting the ASCII apostrophe for it is
the same class of error as writing a Turkish dotless i as a normal i. This file
already writes it correctly twenty three thousand four hundred and twenty five
times; the string added yesterday was the single exception.

It reached the tree because the check that ran before the commit asked the two
questions that catch most locale faults, whether the placeholder survived and
whether the value was left in English, and neither of those is about the script
the language is written in. The repository does hold a check that would have
caught it, and it was not run against the change.

That check is worth describing, because it is more careful than it first looks.
It ignores any value identical to the English one, which sounds like a hole and
is the opposite: an untranslated value is a different defect with its own report,
and flagging it here would bury the real finding under strings that were never
Uzbek to begin with. Thirty one values in that file are in exactly that state
today. They are a genuine gap and they are not this one.

The mark used here was taken from the file rather than chosen: the correct
codepoint was counted from the twenty three thousand existing uses rather than
picked from memory, because two different marks are in circulation for this
alphabet and a file that is internally consistent should stay that way.

all forty three locale files, and they land in the same commit as the code that
calls them rather than after it. That is not tidiness. A key with a default

So the wiring and the translations are one change or the leak is real.

The set of files was taken from the gate rather than from a directory listing,
and that mattered more than it sounds. en-US is not a full locale, it is an
overlay of American spellings that inherits everything else, so it needs
nothing. And a locale the gate reads as mid-translation is excluded from its
requirements, which is exactly the file a second translator was rewriting at
the time: a sweep over every file on disk would have destroyed that work.

The plural forms were counted per language rather than mirrored from a
neighbour, using the category table the plural gate itself reads and checking
each against the count that is actually reachable today. Three languages carry
a singular that English-shaped intuition says they do not need, and without it
i18next walks its fallback chain and prints English rather than falling back to
that language's own plural. Filipino ends up with two identical forms, which
looks like a copy-paste slip and is correct: the noun does not mark plural when
a numeral is present.

Uzbek, separately. That file was fifty times behind every other language, with
sixteen hundred and fifty four sentence-length values still byte-identical to
English against a median of twenty across the other forty. One thousand and
ninety eight of them are now translated. The remaining five hundred and fifty
six are mostly the case-study walkthroughs, which are the slowest content in the
file and the worst place to trade quality for speed, so they are left for a
pass of their own rather than rushed into this one.

Two defects were caught inside that work and are worth recording because they
are the same shape as the one that shipped yesterday. A possessive suffix had
been attached to a placeholder as though it were a separate word, which is
correct for the filler the author had in mind and wrong for every other one.
And two module names had been drafted in title case, which the file does not
use; that was settled by reading ninety already-translated siblings rather than
by picking a convention.

feat(cases): the catalogue leads with the market the reader's language speaks for

A German estimator opening the case library met the same first screen as
everyone else, with the thirteen cases written for German practice somewhere
below the fold. The catalogue now moves the cases for the market their language
speaks for to the front.

It orders and it does not filter, and that distinction is the whole design
rather than a limitation admitted at the end. Every case stays on the page: a
German reader sees thirteen German cases first and the other hundred and eighty
nine right behind them, Chinese included, with no language change and no
control to find. Defaulting the market selector to the language would have been
the shorter change and it would have hidden the hundred and forty cases that
belong to no single market from exactly the readers whose language names one,
and those cases are the product rather than a backlog. A test asserts every
case in the catalogue is present on the page while the front of it is German,
because an ordering check that only reads the front would pass a filter too.

A language becomes a market through the country each language already declares
for its flag, which is the product's one existing statement of which country a
language belongs to, so there is no second table to drift. A language reaches a
market only if the catalogue actually has cases for that country, and the set of
markets is read from the cases themselves, so a market gaining its first case
starts being answered with no edit.

Five of the forty two languages reach a market. The other thirty seven change
nothing at all, and that branch is a no-op by construction rather than a
feature. What those readers get is the catalogue's own order, which lives in a
number inside each case's own file where a human can find it and move it. No
popularity signal was invented: the product measures nothing that would honestly
back one, and a hand-written ranking buried in a sort function is worse than an
honest default.

The Latin American Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese variants are deliberately
not given the Spanish and Portuguese cases. All ten Spanish cases name a Spanish
instrument or a Spanish law, the exchange format, the procurement act, the
monthly certification regime, the reverse charge. Leading a Mexican reader with
one of those does not merely fail to help, it names a law that does not apply
where they work.

Two limits are stated in the source rather than discovered later. English maps
to Britain and English is the final fallback for every unshipped browser
locale, so most readers worldwide meet the British cases first, which is
defensible from the registry and is still a product decision. And the browser
locale has its region stripped before the app sees it, so an Austrian arrives
as plain German and gets the German cases first; that is survivable only
because this orders instead of narrowing.

A case also now says which kinds of firm it was written for, as a comb of
hexagons beside the modules it walks through, and each one takes the reader to
every case written for that kind of firm. The caption counts against the closed
list of company types rather than a literal, so it cannot start lying when a
ninth type ships. The count key binds the total rather than the subset, because
in "three of eight company types" the noun is governed by the eight: bound to
the subset every inflecting language would agree with the wrong number while
the English output went on looking correct.

feat(dashboard): a first workspace is told where to start, and the case block is readable

Two changes that share one screen and one recorded rendering of it, so
they share a commit: the snapshot of the dashboard holds both, and
separating them would leave whichever landed first describing a page that
no longer looked like that.

Someone who has just installed the product opens the cost database screen and
finds nothing, with no statement of what a cost database is, where one comes
from, or that they are expected to obtain one. The screen was correct and it
was useless: it reported an absence to a person who did not yet know the thing
was supposed to be there.

It now opens on an invitation with two named ways in. Load a regional database
of tens of thousands of priced items for materials, labour and equipment, or
build a price list of your own from scratch, one rate at a time. Each says what
happens afterwards, so the choice is made with its consequence visible rather
than discovered later, and it says plainly that both are available and that
more can be added at any time. Nothing here is phrased as an error, because
nothing is wrong.

The same invitation appears on the dashboard while no database is loaded, in a
one-line density rather than the full panel, and it leaves on its own the moment
one is. It costs no request: the dashboard already loads the figures that tell
it whether a database exists, for the onboarding steps it has always drawn, so
this reads state that was on the page rather than asking again. An invitation
that outstays the question it answers is an advertisement, and this one cannot,
because the condition that draws it is the condition it exists to remove.

The strings were already in the locale files. They were written by an earlier
pass for a screen that had not been built, so they sat with no call site until
today. Two new ones were needed and are translated into every language with
this change rather than after it.

The case block on the dashboard drew ten cases at up to eleven columns, which
made every one of them a thumbnail whose title could not be read. It now draws
twenty three at six, each a portrait beside a title in ordinary type.

The count is not a constant. It follows the width of the block rather than the
width of the screen, because the breakpoints available to a card are the
viewport's, and a card sitting in a third of the dashboard asking for six
columns would draw six unreadable tiles on a wide monitor. So the block asks
its own span how many it can show: six columns at full width, four at three
quarters, three at half.

Three controls in its header shrink it, grow it and hide it. None of them is a
new mechanism. The block is already a registry widget, so the dashboard already
owns both preferences and already surfaces them under Customize, and these
controls write exactly what that panel writes. Shrink and grow appear only when
there is a step to go to, so the block is never offered a width the grid cannot
draw. The hide control names Customize dashboard in its tooltip before it is
pressed, since once the block is gone there is nothing left on screen to offer
the way back, and the tooltip uses that panel's own translated title rather
than a fresh translation of the phrase, so it names the control the reader will
actually see.

One asymmetry is deliberate and worth stating. Hiding is synchronised to the
account and width is not. Width is a property of the screen someone is sitting
at; hiding is a property of what they want to see. Pushing a phone-sized width
onto a desktop would be the wrong kind of consistency.

A defect fixed on the way, and it is the sort that only shows up when two
surfaces are compared. Cases wear a portrait chosen by where they sit among all
cases, which is why the helper that assigns them documents that it has to see

selected, so the same case wore one face on the dashboard and another on the
hub as soon as a role filter reordered the ranking, while a comment above the
call claimed it was doing the right thing. The test that pins the fix sets a
role filter first, because in catalogue order the bug and the fix agree and an
unfiltered test would assert nothing.

The recorded rendering of this block moves with it. That file lives outside the
feature directory, so every gate scoped to the feature was green while it still
described the old block, which is the second time in a day that a snapshot
somewhere else has held the previous version of something. Its diff was read
rather than accepted: the removals are ten copies of the old tile markup and
the old call to action, and nothing else in the file moved.

fix(desktop): an upgrade cannot wait forever on a step that usually does nothing

A user upgrading on Windows reported the installer stopping on "Closing
OpenConstructionERP..." and never moving again, with the task manager the only
way out. Uninstalling by hand first and then installing worked.

nsExec waits for its child indefinitely unless it is given a timeout, and it
was given none. The uninstaller waits for nsExec, and on an upgrade the
installer waits for the uninstaller, so a PowerShell that never returns stops
the whole upgrade on that line. All four calls are bounded now: sixty seconds
for the window close, which already waits fifteen inside PowerShell, thirty for
the database stop, which waits for nothing, and ninety for each by-name
fallback, which was measured at fifty five. On expiry nsExec pushes the string
"timeout" rather than an exit code, and the caller already reads anything that
is not zero as a reason to try the fallback, so a wedged PowerShell now
degrades into the slower path instead of into a hang.

Two things this does not do, and both are worth stating because the second one
is a property of the installer rather than of this change.

It does not identify what wedged. That would need the machine it happened on.
What it does is make the class of failure impossible: no step in an upgrade can
now outlast a bounded wait, whatever the cause.

And it cannot help the upgrade that carries it. On an upgrade the new installer
runs the previously installed uninstaller, from the reinstall page, which
happens before any of the four hook macros the bundler defines. So the hook
that decides whether an upgrade hangs is always the one already on disk, never
the one being installed. Every version we have shipped carries an unbounded
call, which is why this reproduces from any of them, and the fix reaches users
on the upgrade after next rather than the next one.

The guard is worth more than the fix here. Adding a flag between the call and
its argument broke the pattern two existing checks used to find these commands,
and one of them had no count assertion, so it turned into a loop over an empty
list and kept passing. That was caught only because its neighbour did assert a
count and went red. Both patterns are widened, both now assert how many calls
they found, and the new check refuses any call without a bound. It was run
against a hook with one bound removed to confirm it convicts, because a guard
that has never been seen to fail is not a guard.

fix(i18n): a translation cannot ask for a variable nobody passes

The text inside a pair of double braces is not words, it is code. i18next
substitutes by name, so a value that says one name while the call site passes
another renders the braces to the reader and keeps doing it forever. Nothing we
own could see that. The key is present, so the orphan guard passes. Both plural
forms are present, so the plural guard passes. The value is not byte-identical
to English, so the leak baseline passes. No escape is doubled. The build never
reads locale content, and a string literal cannot fail to compile.

Three of these were live at once.

A tooltip in the bid schedule shipped the characters ${variantCount} to the
reader in forty-one languages. The call site writes its defaultValue as a
JavaScript template literal, which is correct where it stands because JavaScript
evaluates it, and whoever filled the locale files copied that source text rather
than the string it evaluates to. The one translator who noticed replaced it with
i18next syntax but guessed the variable name, so the language that spotted the
bug was broken too. It is fixed in all forty-two, and it now reads count, which
is what AutocompleteTooltip passes.

A spelling pass had normalised labor to labour and catalog to catalogue inside
the braces as well as around them. Forty-two translations and en.ts agreed on
labour, so en-US.ts looked like the outlier when it was the only file left
holding a name anything passed. FormworkPage passes labour, so en-US was the
broken one. Its visible words stay American; only the variable moved.

A glossary pass in a French wave had turned count into the French word for
country across thirty-seven strings, plural forms among them, which leaves a
counted key with no number to switch on. That was caught in the working tree
before it landed and is not part of this commit.

The guard blocks one direction only, and that asymmetry is the whole of its
accuracy. A name the source does not have is unresolvable and always wrong. A
name the locale omits still renders, and is often the better translation: in a
language whose one-form means exactly one, writing the word beats printing the
digit. Measured on this tree there are forty-one omissions and forty of them are
right, thirty-five being Arabic and Hebrew one-forms and five being languages
that correctly dropped an English plural suffix. A guard that failed on those
would be wrong forty times out of forty-one, and a guard that is usually wrong
gets switched off.

It compares against en.ts rather than en-US.ts. i18n.ts registers en as the
resource bundle and the fallback, so en is what the call sites are written
against; en-US is an override carrying about 1580 American spellings out of
35255. The first version of this guard pointed at en-US, compared 65212 values
and reported a clean run over everything, when it had seen four percent. Its
negative control is what caught that, so the control now covers all three
failure shapes plus the omission that must stay green.

than a universal one. Chinese and Japanese use their own ideographic comma,
Arabic uses its own, and several languages put a word before the last item. A
reader in those languages saw punctuation from someone else's alphabet sitting
in the middle of their own sentence.

and resolves the reader's language the same way they do, so nothing new was
written and no fresh language lookup was added anywhere. Forty two call sites
move onto it here, across thirty one files.

What decides whether a site moves is who reads the string, not what it looks
like. A list a person reads changes; a list something parses does not. The
sharpest case is in correspondence, where the same field is joined three times:
twice into a form whose save path splits it back on a comma and posts it to the
API, and once into a tooltip. Only the tooltip moved. A sweep that took all
three would have broken recipient parsing for exactly the languages it was meant
to help, and silently, since the failure only appears once someone saves.

The type check earned its place twice, both times by contradicting the name. Two
fields called blocking gate numbers are declared as strings and needed nothing,
so trusting the name would have added a pointless conversion. And one site joins

call site is a different type of the same name holding plain strings. Only the
call site's own binding decides which applies, so searching for the field name
gives a confident wrong answer.

English and Russian output is byte-identical to what it was, because the narrow
conjunction style in those languages is a comma and a space. Nothing moved for
most readers; everything moved for the ones it was wrong for.

feat(ops): a backup that did not happen can now be told from one that did

Production went nine days without a database dump and nothing said so. Every
instrument that could have noticed was reading something other than a backup.

So this reads the artefact and nothing else. It stats candidate dumps and takes
three facts from each, the name, the size and the modification time. It does not
read a schedule, a unit file, a policy document, a log or the application. It
never asks whether a backup was meant to happen, only what got written. That is
the whole design, and it is why no file is a verdict rather than missing input:
a check built on configuration would have read a perfectly valid schedule
throughout all nine of those days and reported healthy.

Size is checked alongside age rather than after it. A dump killed part way
through carries a current timestamp, so age alone waves it past and the truth
surfaces at restore, months later, with nothing to restore from. The floor
defaults to one byte so an empty file is always a complaint whatever else is
configured, and the help text tells the operator to raise it to a real fraction
of a true dump.

Cannot tell is its own exit code, distinct from bad, so a monitor can separate a
broken backup from a broken check. There is no input for which this prints a
reassuring answer it did not earn.

Two things were repaired on the way and the second is the more interesting one.
Listing the directory originally went through a glob whose selector can swallow
a permission error and return nothing. That would not have gone green, an empty
listing is already a complaint, but it would have told the operator there is
definitely nothing there when the truth was I was not allowed to look, which
sends somebody to rebuild a backup regime that may be running perfectly. It now
raises and reports cannot tell. And the test covering an unreadable directory
was skipped on Windows, so on the machine where it runs it had never once
executed while reading as covered. It is driven differently now and runs
everywhere.

The guard was watched failing before it was believed, against seven deliberately
broken worlds: fresh, the nine day outage, a zero byte file, a file that died
after a few kilobytes, an empty directory, a directory that is not there, and a
path that is not a directory at all. One green, six red, each for its own
reason, and the guard's hash is identical before and after that run so nothing
was adjusted to make it agree. Then four deliberate mutations of the guard
itself, removing the size floor, making an empty directory read as healthy,
making the age threshold never trip, and making cannot tell report success. Each
was caught, none survived.

The location is an argument, not a constant, so no real path lives in the script
or the tests.

Worth writing down what this cannot do. Run on the machine that writes the
dumps, it dies with the host it was meant to report on, and a host that is gone
does not report badly, it reports nothing at all. It is fully load-bearing only
once there is somewhere off the box for it to run from.

This finishes the sweep and repairs the commit that started it.

That commit does not compile. Fifteen files in it call the list formatter without
importing the name, so the build fails them for an unknown identifier, and the
tree has been in that state since. The cause is worth more than the fix. The
converter asked whether a file already imported anything from the formatters
module and skipped adding an import when the answer was yes, which is true of
every file that already pulls in a currency or number helper and says nothing
about whether this particular name is bound. The verification then counted the
module specifier and found one, which was also true and also measured the wrong
thing, because the count was already one before the file was touched. A check
that cannot tell an edit landing from an edit not landing is not a check. What
actually caught it was the sibling test run, sixty four unknown-identifier
errors across five suites, which is the first time in this task that a real
consumer looked at the work.

The remaining conversions land with it. A hundred and nine call sites across
eighty three files, which reconciles against the hundred and twenty in the tree
once the eleven that predate the sweep are added.

Three latent type defects came out of it, none of them regressions. Two mapped
arrays whose elements were declared nullable or optional, where a filter in
front of one of them looks like it narrows the element type and does not, and
one array of numbers. The old join accepted all three because it coerces
anything, so they compiled and produced output nobody had reason to distrust.
The stricter signature is what made them visible.

One site is a cast rather than a declaration, and it needed care for a reason
that generalises. The replacement is stricter than the thing it replaces: join
runs every element through a string conversion and never throws, while the
formatter calls a method on the element to trim it. Where an author has asserted
an element type rather than declared one, the compiler accepts the assertion by
definition and no gate here can tell a true cast from a false one, so a numeric
value would reach a user as a crash on a path no test covers. That site converts
its elements explicitly instead.

What decides whether a site moves is who reads the string, and the sweep leaves
thirty seven joins in product code deliberately. Values a browser parses as CSS,
address lines where list formatting is the wrong tool and would write a
conjunction into a postal address, header address lists where the standard
requires a comma, prompts assembled for a model, a mathematical set, a document
that is English by construction, and the round trip cases where a joined field
is split again on save. The sharpest of those is a correspondence field that
goes two places from the same data: into a form value that the save path splits
and posts, which stays a plain comma, and into a tooltip that nothing parses,
which moves. One exclusion carries the word revisit in its own reason, a format
list whose docstring calls itself human readable and which is pinned in place by
three assertions, because a test pinning a defect is a weak reason to keep it.

The test that covers this earns its name now. It drives two real call sites in
four languages with every assertion written to fail against the punctuation it
replaced, and it adds a census of the whole product that pins those thirty seven
as a shrinking list: a converted file goes red because its count moved, a file
at zero has to leave the list rather than sit there dead, and a new join
anywhere goes red asking the author to use the helper or record why the string
is machine facing. The census guards itself first, refusing to pass if the walk
sees implausibly few files, because a scan that resolved the wrong directory
reports a clean product. It was watched failing before it was believed.

English and Russian output is unchanged, because the narrow style in those
languages is a comma and a space. That is also why none of this could have gone

notices a standard added to one table and not the other asked whether the
resolver answered, and used that as a proxy for registered. With a held standard
the proxy is wrong in the dangerous direction: add a clause row for CCDC and the
check would call it registered while the notice engine still cannot time it,
which is exactly the defect the check exists to catch. It had gone blind to its
own class of bug. It now asks the question directly, whether the standard it
reaches has a row in the period table, which is what the sibling check in the
same file already did.

line up inside it, and comparing against unrecognised was only how the file
could say no collision back when CCDC was unrecognised. It now measures the
collision itself: of the six standard tokens exactly one occurs anywhere in the
hint, that one is CCDC, and it stands alone rather than sitting inside a longer
word. A hint dragged into another family by its descriptive tail still fails,
which is the property that was being protected all along.

The matcher is generous on purpose and this file now says so out loud. It
resolves a phrase mentioning Connecticut to NEC, because those three letters sit
inside that word, and that is pinned as a characterisation rather than endorsed,
so anyone tightening the matcher to word boundaries gets a failure to read and a
decision to make instead of a silent change to what every free-text hint

like NEC4 and AIA A201-2017 are recognised by designation and not by accident,
so the generosity is load bearing and cannot be removed as dead weight. And the
sweep over shipped forms now refuses to pass on an empty sweep, because a guard
that swept nothing reports the same green as a guard that swept everything.

Three tests are renamed because their names asserted the old two-state world,
and their bodies now assert the property the file actually needs: that the packs
populate both branches, and that a standard the engine holds no periods for gets
no deadline at all rather than a borrowed generic one. Nothing was deleted and
no assertion was loosened. One test is added, requiring every token in the
mirror table to round-trip through the normaliser, so a mistyped literal cannot

i18n: the pending-review list becomes a shrink list instead of a third state

This list held keys that are neither a declared leak nor an accepted match, and
for its first three weeks it had no cap, no reason on any entry and no record of
who added one. It grew across eight commits, a hundred and nineteen keys to a
hundred and eighty four, and never once shrank. A list like that reads as
neither a solved problem nor an open one, and it made the two lists either side
of it look more decided than they were simply by sitting between them.

Three changes, and the ratchet is the one that matters. The size is now capped
by a constant, and the guard fails when the list is above the cap or below it.
Failing on shrink looks wrong at first and is the whole point: lowering the
constant has to happen in the same diff as the removal, so the cap can never
accumulate slack that a later addition hides behind. Adding an entry means
raising the constant where a reviewer sees it and can ask why.

Every entry now carries a reason and the commit that introduced it, and the
guard fails on an empty one. All hundred and eighty four were mapped to their
real introducing commit from history with none left unresolved. The commit
reference is used rather than a name because every commit in this repository
carries one shared identity, so the hash is the honest verifiable answer to who
put it there.

The reasons are where this got interesting, and the record should show the
corrected version rather than the first one. The first pass wrote a narrative
per commit explaining why each batch was added. Checked against the entries' own
data before being accepted, most of those narratives were wrong: of the thirty
keys added while a locale was being registered, not one names that locale in its
own differs_in set, and six keys said to have been caught by a threshold scan
have counts below the threshold, which makes that claim simply false. Every
reason was rewritten to state only what was actually checked, and where an
entry's own data does not corroborate its commit's framing, the reason says so
instead of repeating the commit message as though it were a fact about the key.
None of the hundred and eighty four has had per-key content triage; a note in
each entry says that, so the next reader inherits the state rather than the
impression.

The docstring had the same shape of problem as the count it used to hardcode. It
described this list as almost-universal matches where a few locales differ, and
the data holds the opposite shape too: keys matching in one locale while
twenty-eight differ, which is closer to an allowlist candidate than to a leak.
It now names both shapes and points at the per-entry fields for what is actually
known.

One limitation, stated rather than papered over. The cap catches count drift, not
a same-commit swap: remove one entry and add another in the same diff and the
count is unchanged, so it is the reason and the introducing commit that force the
new entry to justify itself, not the cap. Catching a swap by the cap alone would
need this guard to read git history, which it does nowhere else.

Separately, the checker used to verify a set of repaired keys was reading its own
key list out of the file it had just emptied, so it passed on zero input. It now
carries those keys as data and refuses to exit clean having checked nothing.

Verified: the guard exits zero on the tree, all hundred and eighty four entries
carry both fields, and the file gained exactly two lines per entry with no
reindentation. Lint findings on the script are the same five it already had.

fix(migrations): three revisions can run against the schema the product installs

The default runtime does not migrate its way to the current schema. env.py sees
a blank database, builds the tables from the models with create_all and stamps
the head afterwards, so a fresh install executes no revision at all. The next
release then leaves that install holding the current columns behind an old
stamp, health calls it degraded, and the obvious repair is to run the upgrade.

On such a database the upgrade died. v3304, v3305 and v3306 add a currency
column each and none of them looked first, so v3304 raised a duplicate column
error, its transaction rolled back, and the two revisions behind it never ran.
Twenty four of the twenty seven revisions between v3273 and the head already
guard their DDL on an inspector and skip what is present. These three now do
the same, in the same shape as their neighbours.

The split inside v3304 is deliberate and worth naming. Its DDL is guarded and
its classification pass is not. An existing column says nothing about whether
the classification ever ran, because create_all makes a column and does not
fill it, so an install that arrived that way has three empty columns and needs
that pass more than a fresh one does. Skipping work because a column exists is
how a repair goes missing.

Found on a real installation rather than reasoned about. The database behind a
local instance was stamped twenty seven revisions back, reported degraded for
it, failed the upgrade exactly here, and after these guards went in reached the
head and reported healthy because it is genuinely there, not because anything
was stamped to say so.

The test builds each of the four tables in both shapes, before and after, and
runs the revision's own upgrade over each. Both directions are asserted: a
guard that returned early every time would pass the re-run test and do nothing,
so the control on the other side is what makes the first one mean something.
Neither shape is reachable from the two checks that already exist, because a
fresh install runs no revision and a chain check only reads how revisions are
linked to each other.

fix(ai-estimator): a booked position keeps the norm the catalogue gave it

The estimator translates a catalogue row into its own resource shape at one
boundary, and there it read the per-unit norm from a key the costs module never
writes. Every component therefore fell through to a default of one, and applying
a position stored, for every resource, a quantity equal to the position's own
quantity.

The catalogue writes that norm as quantity. This is arithmetic rather than a
guess about the field name: resource pricing values a work item as the sum over
its components of quantity times unit price and stores that sum as the item's
unit rate, so quantity is per one unit of the item and never a total.

Nothing showed on review. The unit rate is written separately from the chosen
candidate at apply time, so the money looked right, and the loss surfaced only
when an estimator edited the position and the rate was re-derived from the
buildup. By then the figure could be out by two orders of magnitude. Procurement
demand aggregation squared the quantity and schedule duration derivation
inflated by the same factor.

A component that declares no usable norm still falls back to one, but is now
marked so a reviewer can see which lines are assumed rather than grounded. A
plausible default that changes no visible result is exactly how this stayed
hidden, so the fallback has to announce itself.

The regression test asserts a relationship rather than an expected figure: a
stored resource quantity must differ from the position quantity whenever the
norm is not one. Under the old code the two were always equal for every parent
quantity, so the invariant fails on every case the test covers. Groups persisted
under the older spelling keep their meaning, because a stored group must not
change value when the code that reads it is upgraded.

fix(einvoice): the forint and the rupiah are decided, and decided as zero

Both codes carried an undecided marker on the reading that ISO 4217 gives them
two decimals, CLDR gives them zero, and EN 16931 breaks no tie. The value does
not move. What moves is that it is now a decision with a reason beside it
rather than a pin holding today's behaviour still.

What settles it is not a third standard but the subunit. The fillér left
circulation in 1999 and the sen is likewise gone, so neither amount can be
settled in the unit ISO still lists. A count of two would not be a more precise
forint, it would be two digits no payment can carry.

The reading that made the question look open was that our resolvers disagreed
about it. They do not, and that is worth recording because it was the reason
nobody closed this. The core money registry holds zero for both, the screen
resolver takes CLDR's zero from the running engine, and the document table
holds zero. Four readers, one answer, with only ISO's own list on the other
side. Marking a unanimous position as disputed made every reader of it hesitate
over a question the code had already answered.

The coverage test gains the direction it was missing. It asserted that every
decided code appears in the document table, which caught a code that was ruled
on but never added. It could not assert the reverse while the table was allowed
to hold a code behind an undecided marker. With the marker gone that state does
not exist, so the two sets are now asserted equal, and a code added to the
document table without a decision recorded beside it fails rather than shipping
with whatever count its author happened to type.

fix(i18n): two locales labelled the hour with something that is not an hour

units.h is the canonical hour and it is the only time-valued key in the
backend catalogue, which makes it the only one where a wrong label names a
different quantity rather than reading clumsily. Japanese said 人工 and
Korean said 인. Both now say what this product's own frontend catalogue has
always said in those languages, 時間 and 시간.

These were not two instances of one fault and the difference decides what a
later pass may do. 人工 is the worker-day of Japanese estimating practice, so
it named a longer period than the value carries and a conversion factor at
least exists for it. 인 is 人, a person. It named a headcount beside a rate,
and no multiplier of any working day makes that true, so anything that sweeps
these together and multiplies by a working day would make Korean worse rather
than better. Worth knowing too: units.h being the only time key means 인 was
occupying the sole time slot, so Korean shipped with no word for an hour
anywhere in the file. A missing unit is a different and worse thing than a
mistranslated one.

A worker-day is a unit in its own right, not a translation of the hour. The
BOQ picker already offers day, shift and mh as canonical tokens and the
locale-native 人日 and 인일 beside 時間 and 시간, so an estimator who prices in
worker-days picks that unit today.

The new test is the gate. A units.h label has to be either the ISO 80000-3
symbol h, which is valid unchanged in any language, or an abbreviation of the
name this product gives the hour in that language. Abbreviation is a
subsequence rather than a prefix because German Std comes from Stunde and
Turkish sa from Saat. Run against the committed locale files it rejects
exactly the labels that were wrong and accepts the other 25, and it names its
own blind spot: the two catalogues are its two witnesses, so a label wrong in
both the same way would pass.

Two designs were tried first and rejected against the data. Asserting that a
label is not a string the same locale offers as a different unit reds on
correct Danish and Norwegian, where units.t and units.h are both t, tonne and
time. A list of the known-bad strings is the right answer by a mechanism that
can never produce a new one.

The workflow step is there because a test no blocking lane names cannot fail
anything. It follows the pattern of the steps around it, including the guard
that turns a skip into an error.

fix(storage): five declarations stop resolving against the working directory

The data directory is declared once and resolved once. These are five path
declarations that repair did not reach: each one built a filesystem path on
os.getcwd(), so the same command read and wrote a different tree depending on
where the operator happened to stand.

Two of them are the catalog export in app/scripts, which anchored both its
input parquet and its output directory that way. Run from backend it works.
Run from the repository root it dies loudly on the missing input, which is the
good case. Run from a checkout two levels below the same parent directory it
still finds the toolkit, silently creates a directory inside somebody else's
repository and writes the catalog there. The silent third case is the one
worth fixing, and the path is not theoretical: running the export once to see
where it landed rewrote a version-controlled file,
data/catalog/ENG_TORONTO_Full_Resource_Catalog.xlsx, which was restored from
HEAD with git cat-file. A path nobody could reach by argument turned out to be
live enough to overwrite tracked data on the first run.

Output now goes through resolve_data_dir, which is the repository data
directory for a checkout, so the export lands exactly where it always landed
and lands there from anywhere, including a data directory an operator moved
with OE_DATA_DIR. The input is anchored on __file__ with a CWICR_TOOLKIT_ROOT
override, deliberately not CWICR_PARQUET_ROOT, because that name already
belongs to the costs module for a different layout and reusing it would point
one of them at the other's tree.

The other three declarations are the DWG upload root in the projects module.
dwg_takeoff resolved this correctly some time ago and its own docstring
records why: the body it replaced defaulted to a working-directory root, was
never a member of safe_data_roots, and was what broke drawings marked ready on
standalone, Docker and macOS deployments. Two sites in bundle_import and one
in file_manager_service still carried that same body, so the repair stopped
one module short. A bundle import put the drawing somewhere the module that
serves it does not look, wrote that location into the database where it
outlived the process that produced it, and then the file manager confirmed the
wrong location to the user asking where the files were. Measured from two
foreign working directories, the replaced expression gives two different
answers and fails the safe-root check; the resolver gives one answer and
passes it. A fix that lands in the module that noticed the problem and not in
its neighbours is a class worth naming, not a one-off.

Both new tests run from a working directory that is not the repository root,
and the load-bearing assertions run from two different ones, because a single
foreign directory cannot tell an anchored path from a differently broken one.
They assert on the resolvers rather than through main, because a test that
runs the export needs a private parquet that does not exist on CI and
overwrites tracked files every time. The export test also scans its own module
for both spellings of the working directory, with a negative control that
plants the defect in the same multi-line shape the real one had, so a scanner
that quietly stopped walking cannot pass on an empty result.

Two notes on how these were found, because neither turns up by grepping a call
form. A line-oriented search misses the export input entirely, since the
working-directory call sat four lines above the segment that made it a path;
what finds these is scanning for how a value is born rather than for the
shapes a path can be spelled in. And a content search over the tree returned
one of the two occurrences in bundle_import while reporting no truncation, so
half a fix would have looked complete. The population was measured again with
an AST walk over 2713 files and a plain recursive grep, and accepted only
where the two converged. Two instruments agreeing is evidence only when they
do not share a source.

feat(i18n): the module chip on a case step is guarded in every language

Every step of a case playbook names the module it runs in, and the name is
written twice, as moduleLabel for English and moduleLabelKey for everyone
else. All four renderers resolve it the same way, t(m.labelKey, {defaultValue:
m.label}), so i18next reaches the English label only when the key resolves
nowhere. A key no locale can answer therefore prints English into that
language with nothing on screen to say so. Three of them do that today.
nav.payment_clock, nav.tax_withholding and nav.einvoice_clearance are absent
from 31 of the 43 locale files, held only by bn, de, el, en, fa, fil, he, kk,
uk, ur and uz, which is the same set for all three and so one unfinished pass
rather than three separate gaps. That is 21 chips across 12 cases. The Russian
page for the payment clock case reads its hive as Контракты, Payment Clock,
Финансы, Документы, and the German one reads Verträge, Zahlungsuhr, Finanzen,
Dokumente, because German happens to hold the key.

No gate saw this and one of them should have. check_i18n_computed_keys.py owns
exactly this shape and its docstring names it, but it resolves a key against
its English by anchoring on a field named default-something, and a playbook
names its English moduleLabel, which is a seventh name. No pair forms, all 842
chips fall out of the scan, and the guard reports 259 clean pairs and exits 0
while the defect ships. Its own comment predicted this: a guard keyed to one
name calls the class clean while its siblings go unread.

Widening that anchor is not the repair. The same widening pulls in the 6277
cases.<slug>.* content keys, and those keep their English in the playbook on
purpose and are absent from en.ts by design, so the en.ts question that guard
asks is the wrong question about them and would produce thousands of false
findings. Two populations under one syntactic shape need two scripts, so the
computed guard now counts and names the 3099 sibling-shaped key fields it
cannot resolve instead of leaving them out of its report, and points at the
new script for the chips among them. That change is additive and its exit code
is unchanged.

The new guard checks whether a key can be answered, never whether the rendered
text differs from English. Sameness is not decidable here: nav.bim is BIM in
all 41 non-English locales and nav.crm is CRM in 31 of them, both correct, and
any instrument comparing rendered text against English reports those forever.
An earlier count of ten affected pages was that artefact wearing a number. A
regional variant is covered when its base language answers the key, which is
the rule the orphan guard already applies, so es-MX, pt-BR and the en-US
overlay need nothing of their own.

There is no baseline, because 134 of the 137 chip keys are clean and a
baseline written today would record the three that are not, which is the
defect rather than debt to inherit. For the same reason the step is
deliberately not wired into repo-hygiene.yml yet. That lane blocks every
commit in the repository, and a gate that stops work it was not written to
stop gets switched off by whoever it inconveniences, which guards nothing for
real instead of nothing on paper. Land the three translations, then add the
step, and it starts green and every later failure means a chip really did
regress.

fix(packs): seven packs declared rule sets in a field nothing reads

Seven packs named a standard the engine implements and the rules never ran.
The reported cause was spelling, din_276 against the registry's din276, and
that part is true. It was not the cause. validation_rule_packs has no runtime
consumer anywhere in the tree: nothing reads it to enable a rule set, so a
correctly spelled entry activated exactly as much as a misspelled one, which
is nothing. Correcting the fifteen strings in place would have changed nothing
measurable, and three earlier pieces of work were each correct and each aimed
at a field nothing reads. The path that makes rules run is the project's own
validation_rule_sets column, read by _build_rule_sets in the BOQ router and by
_rule_sets_for in the validation seeder, and no pack ever reached it.

So the field is now two fields. validation_rule_packs keeps its documents and
is documented as running nothing, with every entry required to match a
rule_packs JSON file the pack ships, in both directions. validation_rule_sets
carries engine identifiers, and a project created while a pack is active
inherits them. Inheritance is additive: boq_quality is seeded first, so
inheriting NRM cannot cost a project its universal bill hygiene. That was a
real bug in the first draft and its own test caught it.

An identifier the registry does not know is refused when the pack is applied,
with a message naming the spelling that works, and the route answers 409
rather than 404, because the pack is installed and readable and it is its
contents that are wrong. The check cannot live on the manifest, which is a
module level constant built before any rule is registered, where the registry
reads empty and would either refuse every pack or wave every name through. The
manifest checks the shape of the string and says so, and a well formed name
the engine does not register passes there on purpose.

Nine manifests, not the seven reported. Two more packs had genuine engine
identifiers, gbt50500 and mexico, sitting in the document list where they were
equally inert. The two keyspaces are disjoint now: no document id collides
with a registered set name, and all fifteen near miss ids are covered by a
rule set in the same pack. The severity mix was reported as four warning sets
and five error sets. The fifteen ids collapse to eight distinct sets, of which
six carry error rules and two are warning only.

The blast radius, stated plainly because somebody will hit it and search for
it. Each pack's own demo project is unchanged, newly failing none, because a
demo is built by install_demo_project straight from its template and never
passes through project creation, so it does not inherit. The population that
does inherit is a project made while a pack is active whose positions carry no
classification, which is what a spreadsheet imported without a classification
column produces: the importer reads an absent column as an empty string and
the inference returns an empty dict. Measured on twenty such rows, six of the
seven packs take the bill from passed to errors, one error per line on every
line, and the quality score from 1.000 to 0.024. doker-formwork is the
exception, because its formwork rules are scope gated and say nothing about a
bill of quantities. No rule was weakened to soften that number. The rules fire
correctly on data that genuinely lacks the classification the standard
requires, and the apply preview now says so before the operator commits to it,
naming the sets and counting the error severity rules among them.

The gate added for this recently did not catch any of the fifteen, and the
reason is worth naming because it is a class. It asserted that the set of
defects it found equalled a constant listing exactly those fifteen. An allow
list built from what you found enshrines what you found: it could only ever
catch a sixteenth, and it made the defect permanent by recording it. That
constant is deleted along with the test built on it, and the requirement is
inverted, so a document id naming a standard the engine implements has to be
accompanied by the engine identifier rather than merely noted.

The second hole is the same class wearing different clothes. The registry is
not a constant, since a module registers its sets when its validators module
is imported, so the probes read it in a subprocess. That subprocess swallows
failed imports, and with no database URL ten module validators fail and
formwork, cost_match and saved_views leave the registry. The near miss scan
then finds nothing and passes while measuring nothing. Both test files now
assert that the registry they measured is larger than the core only registry
and contains formwork, which is the same shape as asserting that an
enumeration found anything at all.

Twenty seven tests, written first. Every one that matters carries a negative
control that was executed and reverted: removing a pack's declaration, typing
it one character wrong, neutering the shape validator, and hiding a shipped
JSON file each turn the relevant tests red and name what broke. The formwork
scope test carries a positive control asserting that the formwork rules do
fail a formwork payload, so a clean bill of quantities result cannot quietly
mean the rules were never registered.

Three shipped demos already fail error rules under the sets they declare
themselves, identically before and after this change, which is how we know
this change is not the cause. Nineteen error severity rules iterate every row
rather than the leaf rows and so convict section headers, which carry no rate
and no leaf classification by construction. That is the next commit, not this
one.

fix(i18n-scripts): the locale scripts stop damaging the text they carry

Three separate defects, found while checking how the locale tooling behaves
around invisible characters, and one of them is much larger than the way it
was found.

i18n_extract.py decoded every value with encode().decode("unicode_escape").
That codec takes a string's UTF-8 bytes and reads them back as latin-1, so it
destroys every code point above U+007F: every Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic, Greek and
accented Latin value in the file came back as mojibake. Zero-width characters
were how the defect surfaced, not what it is. The file is already decoded text
by the time the parser sees it, so nothing above U+007F needed decoding at all,
and the codec is replaced by an unescaper that handles the escapes a JS string
literal can actually carry and leaves every literal character alone. Its
surrogate-pair branch comes first so an astral character written as two \u
escapes is rebuilt as one code point rather than two lone surrogates that
cannot be encoded back to UTF-8.

translate_mn_pass2.py and translate_mn_pass6_more_long.py failed a fourth way,
one the usual three-way split does not have a word for. They did not delete
anything, did not corrupt anything and did not crash. They ran green, printed
a count and matched nothing. Their translation tables are keyed by English
source strings, a mechanical pass over the tree had stamped invisible
characters onto some of those keys, and en.ts carries no such stamp, so those
entries were simply unreachable. Seventeen of 452 in pass2 and two of 51 in
pass6 had been dead for as long as the stamp had been there, and every signal
the scripts produce said they were working. That shape is the quietest of the
four, because its report is indistinguishable from a clean run with genuinely
nothing to do, and the fix therefore includes an assertion that the match set
is not empty rather than only a corrected lookup.

Both sides of those lookups now go through a small visible() helper, and there
is one thing about it that must not be missed. Never apply it to locale text
in general. U+200C is required Persian orthography, U+200D forms Bengali
conjuncts, and U+200E and U+200F place Latin tokens inside right-to-left
lines. All four are category Cf, so a Cf-stripper that looks correct here will
silently misspell five shipping languages somewhere else. That warning lives
in the docstring as well, for the reader who finds a working stripper and
reaches for it.

The third defect is line endings. Every mn pass and i18n_apply.py read with
Path.read_text and wrote with Path.write_text, both of which translate line
endings, so a run that replaced nothing still rewrote the whole file, to CRLF
on Windows and to LF everywhere else. Measured on the real locale, a pass2 run
with zero replacements turned 4568560 bytes into 4606848 and introduced 38288
CRLFs. On a host with core.autocrlf=true git normalises that straight back to
LF in the index, so the damage is invisible to git status while being entirely
real on disk, and a developer with autocrlf=false sees every line of the file
change. Both ends now use open(..., newline="") and carry each line's own
ending through, which is the idiom i18n_new_locale.py already documents. The
same change to i18n_apply.py fixes a regex that ended in ,?\s*$: greedy and
matching before any newline, it swallowed the entry's own ending and any blank
line after it, and the replacement then wrote back an ending of its own
choosing.

The nine scripts are deliberately left unformatted. They were already
unformatted before this change, reformatting them would bury a 194-line fix
under a whole-file diff, and ruff reports exactly the same eleven findings
before and after, same rules on the same files, only line numbers moved.

Covered by backend/tests/unit/test_locale_scripts_carry_invisible_characters.py,
which compares code points and bytes rather than rendered strings, because a
rendered comparison is what let all three defects through. Its round-trip
fixture uses deliberately mixed line endings: an all-LF fixture passes on Linux
with the defect still in place and an all-CRLF one passes on Windows, so only a
mixture fails on both. Against the previous revision of these nine scripts the
new tests fail fifteen of sixteen, the one that passes being the control that
checks the unescaper still decodes the escapes it is supposed to.
