fix(zero-width-guard): git decides what the scan is responsible for

Run with no arguments, which is the form .github/workflows/ci.yml uses, the
guard did not terminate on a machine that had marketing-site checked out. It
was killed at ten minutes. marketing-site is 770 MB of generated pages, ignored
in its entirety, and walking it is most of the work the scan was doing. CI never
noticed because a fresh clone has no marketing-site at all, so the gate worked
everywhere except where a person would actually run it, which is the worst way
for one to be broken: the only reader who could have seen it was the reader
whose run never came back.

Scope now comes from git. `ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard` is
everything the repository tracks plus everything a commit could still pick up,
and nothing .gitignore has already excluded, so a file written a minute ago and
not yet added is still scanned while generated output no commit can reach is
not. The character class, the extension list and the two lists of what is stray
and what is spelling are all untouched: the rule did not move, only the set of
files it is asked about.

The set is the same set. Over frontend/src the old walk and the new git scope
enumerate 2905 files each, and comparing them as sets rather than as totals they
are equal, nothing added and nothing dropped. marketing-site goes from a walk
that did not finish to zero files in under half a second, because git answers
from the index instead of from the disk. The whole no-argument run now takes
seven seconds and still exits 0.

Where git cannot answer, in a wheel or a copied directory, the walk is still
there but it has a ceiling and refuses with exit 2 rather than hanging. A gate
that hangs cannot be told apart from a gate that is thinking. Exit 2 already
means "this check could not be performed" here, so a failure to establish scope
reads differently from a clean tree and from a real hit.

Every run now prints how many files each root contributed. Pass or fail alone
cannot tell a clean tree from a tree that was never looked at, and this scan has
now been narrowed once; the number is what makes the next narrowing visible.

The file is deliberately left unformatted. Every line ruff format would change
is one it would have changed before this commit, none of them in the code added
here, and ruff check passes identically before and after.

feat(i18n-foundation): a Canadian tax rate answers by province, or does not answer

Canada does not have one sales tax rate. Five per cent is the federal GST, and
it is the whole answer in Alberta, half the answer in British Columbia, and
wrong in Ontario, where a single harmonised thirteen per cent replaces it. The
tax table had nowhere to say which province a row applied in, so every Canadian
project priced at five.

Tax configurations now carry an ISO 3166-2 subdivision, and the resolver
composes the rate from the layers that actually apply: a harmonised rate that
replaces the federal one, a provincial rate that stacks on it, or a compounding
rate charged on the federal inclusive base. The response names each layer and
the base it is charged on, so a quantity surveyor can see how thirteen or
14.975 was arrived at instead of being handed a total to trust.

The decision worth recording is what happens when the province is not known. It
returns no number at all. A plausible rate is the worst kind of wrong, because
five per cent in Toronto looks exactly like a correct answer and will be
carried into a tender. Zero is worse still, because it reads as a deliberate
exemption rather than as missing information. So an unanswered question stays
visibly unanswered, and it does so under three distinct statuses: the project
never named a province, the province was named but has no row, or the rows
disagree about which one is the default. Those are three different problems
with three different fixes, and the caller can tell them apart.

Refusals are 409 rather than 422. The request was fine. The configuration is
what needs changing.

Enforcement is part of this rather than a convention to remember. A subdivision
that does not belong to the country, a subnational combination with no
subdivision, and a national combination that carries one are all refused on
write, by the seed loader, by the API, and by a check constraint in the
database. A rate that is not a number is refused on the same path: the column
stores rates as text, so an unparseable rate used to be accepted quietly and
then raise on a read of the province it belonged to.

Canada's five per cent federal row is unchanged. It is correct, and it is what
Alberta and the three territories are supposed to answer.

Two things here are worth naming rather than leaving to be discovered. The
shared module files carry work in flight from another author that cannot be
split out by file, specifically the ambiguous default status and the Romanian
VAT rows. And the boot repair that labels the shipped rows with the subdivision
they apply in is not in this commit, because the repair registry it registers
against is not on main yet. Until that lands, an install that has not been
reseeded answers subdivision unknown for Ontario, which is the safe half of
this design working as intended rather than a wrong rate.

fix(brazil-sinapi): restore the accents the Portuguese pack file lost

says Relatorios where Portuguese says Relatórios and Orcamento where it says
Orçamento. Nothing has ever read the file, which is why nobody noticed. The

feature rather than a bonus attached to it, and it lands alone so it can be

and the 11 that stop changing anything are exactly the ones that had been

feat(partner-pack): load the vocabulary the packs already ship

Twelve partner packs ship thirteen locale files carrying the words their
market actually uses, and every one of those files was dead on disk. Nothing
in the frontend had ever called GET /api/v1/partner-pack/locale/{code}, not
once anywhere in the source tree. That single missing call is the whole
defect. usePartnerPackLocale was not discarding regional vocabulary, it had
none to discard, so the hook normalising the region away and the endpoint
having no caller turn out to be one fault seen from two ends rather than two
faults.

normalizePackLocale keeps its behaviour exactly. A pack that names a region
the interface does not ship has to inherit the base language, so fr-CA must
still resolve to fr, and breaking that would hand a Denver user British
English. The fix needs both codes true at the same time instead: fetch with
the pack's own code, which is the only thing the endpoint answers to, and
merge into the language the app actually renders. Collapse the two either way
and the feature stays dead, once with a 404 and once by writing strings into
a bundle nothing reads.

Three further defects came out of measuring this rather than reading it. The
overlay was bound only at activation, so india-cpwd's Hindi file and
batimatech-ca's second file could never load at all. resetPackLocale awaited
a locale that already ships inside the main bundle, so the await returned
immediately and deactivating a pack left its words on screen until a full
reload. And applying a pack does not reload the app, so switching from one
pack to another merged the new vocabulary on top of the old and kept every
key the outgoing pack defined and the incoming one did not. A fourteenth
locale file is named by a manifest but absent from the pack that names it,
which the loader treats as a pack with no vocabulary rather than an error.

common.loading comes out of the eight pack files that shipped it, across
seven packs. The entire difference was three full stops against a single
ellipsis character, which is typography rather than regional vocabulary, and
at 179 render sites it was by a wide margin the most widely shown key in the
set. A pack locale file is there to say that a British project calls it a
Coordination Centre.

What this actually moves, counted rather than claimed. 1346 keys ship across
the thirteen files, 485 of them name a key the app still renders, and 110
change any text on screen. 27 replace generic English with regional English,
so a uk-jct user reads Coordination Centre where the sidebar had said
Coordination Hub. The other 83 replace one already localised wording with the
pack's preferred one, so a Quebec user reads Avenants in place of Ordres de
modification, having been reading French all along rather than English. None
of the 110 replace an English fallback with the user's own language. That is
worth stating plainly because it is the claim this feature invites and the
one that would sell it hardest. The expectation going in was that some would
and the count is zero, because every pack key that renders already had a
translation behind it.

fix(validation): eleven rules convicted the headers above the rows they judge

A section header aggregates its children. It carries no unit, no rate and
no classification code because those live on the leaf rows underneath it,
and eleven error severity rules asked every row for a code anyway, so
every header in the tree was convicted of missing something it cannot
hold. On a deep bill that is most of the findings.

The demo counts move and only one of them moves to zero, which is the
part to read before believing the demos are clean. residential-saopaulo
goes from 63 to 57, commercial-london from 19 to 10, commercial-denver
from 17 to 0. Denver was purely the header defect. The 57 and the 10 that
remain are leaf rows that genuinely carry no SINAPI and no NRM code, and
the rules are right about them: that is data debt in two demo templates,
not a rule that missed, and it is a separate question from this one. What
this change does clear is every header, on all three: measured across the
whole registry, no error rule now convicts a section row in any of them.

Eleven of the nineteen, not nineteen. The other eight judge something a
header genuinely has, so narrowing them would trade a false positive for
a false negative, and a rule that stopped firing is indistinguishable
from a rule that passed. A header still has to have a title and an
ordinal nothing else shares. A negative quantity is wrong on any row. A
header whose stored total contradicts its own zeroes is corrupt. A stray
currency on a header splits the bill just as a stray currency on a leaf
does. And the three valid-code rules skip a row that carries no code at
all, so they never convicted a header for being a header; they only judge
a code someone chose to put there, and narrowing them would go blind to a
malformed one. Each of those eight now carries a test with a payload that
proves it still fires on a section row, and a second test proving it says
nothing about a well formed one, because "we deliberately did not narrow
this" belongs in an assertion rather than in a comment.

The eleventh was already half fixed and that is the more useful finding.
bc3.code_required had grown its own guard inline, reading the row's type
field and skipping sections. The shared helper detects a header two ways,
by that field and by the parent_id graph, because the seed and
spreadsheet import paths never stamp a type. So the hand rolled copy was
correct on the payload the BOQ router builds and convicted every header
on the two paths that do not stamp one, while passing any test written
against the explicit branch. Both branches are exercised for all eleven
now, and that second test is what caught this.

The registry wide test is a property rather than a list. A list of the
rules that had this defect can only catch the next one after somebody
remembers to add it, so instead it asks every registered rule whether it
convicts a header that is correct in every way a header can be, and the
answer has to be no. A new standard's code_required rule fails it on the
day it is written without anyone touching this file. It carries a load
control, since a registry that came back empty would answer the question
with silence and silence reads as a pass here, and a negative control
that runs the same sweep against a deliberately broken header and
requires it to find one.

The helper's docstring named the wrong field. It said the explicit branch
reads metadata.type; the code reads a top level type, which boq/router.py
computes per row before handing the payload to the engine. Anyone writing
a section row from that docstring would have stamped a field nothing
reads.

One consequence worth knowing, because it belongs to the detector rather
than to the rules. A header is not recognised by having children: the
router and the spreadsheet importer both call a row a header when it has
no unit, no quantity and no rate, so a row of that shape is skipped even
when nothing hangs beneath it. The thirteen rules already on this helper
have always drawn the line there, and the eleven now agree with them
rather than disagreeing. Change any one of the three and the row is a leaf
again and is still judged. The test table asserts both halves, because
"skips headers" is one careless edit away from "skips whatever is cheap
to skip".

The blast radius recorded on the previous commit is unchanged, and I
re-measured rather than assumed. Those twenty rows were all priced leaves
with no classification, so they were never the false positive this fixes:
six of seven packs still take such a bill from 1.000 to 0.024, one error
per line. This narrows what the rules look at, not what they conclude.

fix(i18n-scripts): a one key edit stops rewriting every line of the file

Twelve scripts that edit locale files read them with Path.read_text and write
them back with Path.write_text. Neither call passes a newline argument, and on
this platform the pair converts every LF in the file to CRLF. All 43 locale
files under frontend/src/app/locales are LF on disk and LF in the committed
blob, so each of these scripts turns a one key insert into a whole file rewrite.

Measured by running a copy of backfill_nav_project_files.py in a throwaway tree
against a nine line locale file. As committed it produced ten added lines and
nine removed for one new key, and the file came out CRLF. With the fix it
produces one added line and none removed, and the endings are untouched.
Against a CRLF fixture both versions produce identical bytes, which is why this
was never visible to anyone whose locale files were CRLF.

The reason it has been invisible here too is core.autocrlf, which converts the
damage back to LF on the way into the index. Nothing wrong has been committed:
zero of the 43 frontend locale blobs and zero of the 28 backend locale blobs
carry CRLF. The cost falls on anyone with autocrlf off or on Linux, who gets a
whole file diff instead of a one line one, and a whole file diff is also where
a lost invisible character would hide.

add_users_i18n.py is in this commit although the census that found the other
eleven excluded it. That census keyed on the extension the write names, and
this one writes backend/locales/*.json rather than .ts, so it was excluded by
the instrument rather than because it is safe. It carries the same defect in
the other idiom, open(path, "w") with no newline, and json.dump emits \n. Round
tripping de.json, ru.json and en.json through it with the fix gives bytes
identical to the committed blob for all three; without it none of the three
match. Expect 25 of the 28 files to change on disk the first time it runs and
none of them to change in git diff.

This is not a judgement call about style. scripts/i18n_new_locale.py:170
already carries the correct idiom with a comment explaining it: "Read
preserving line endings. Path.read_text has no newline= and would translate
CRLF to LF, which turns a one-key edit into a whole-file diff." Every one of
these twelve is a deviation from a convention this repository had already
written down and explained.

Eight of the twelve build a new line with a literal \n. Those now take the
ending the file already uses, so an insert into a CRLF file no longer mixes
endings. patch_nav_v3_modules_insert.py needed one line more than the others:
its anchor regex ends with \s*$, which stops after a \r but before the \n, so
on a CRLF file the insertion point sat inside the pair.

before and after and refused to write any file whose count had changed. That is

linted: the CI backend job runs ruff with working-directory set to backend, so

36 removed lines inside a rewrite of all twelve files. ruff check --select
F,E9 reports the same three findings before and after, two unused imports and
one unused local, none of them introduced here.

On method, the first census of this population said nineteen scripts and
twenty three writes and both numbers were wrong. It resolved variable names
transitively and pulled in two writes to files that are not locales. It was
caught by verifying two files by hand against its own output. The count that
survived that check, sixteen scripts of which eleven tracked, is what this

fix(cases): the face cast takes the vocabulary it is actually keyed by

caseFaces.ts deals a photo for each case out of a map called ROLE_CAST. The
name says role. The keys are company types. The module was copied from the
marketing site before the two case vocabularies were split into firms and
people, and it kept the old vocabulary's name along with a header comment
describing the world before the split, so the comment did not merely go stale,
it instructed the reader to do the wrong thing.

The parameter was readonly string[], so passing a case's roles into a lookup
keyed by company types compiled and ran. The two vocabularies intersect in
exactly one id, project-manager, which is a firm on one axis and a person on
the other. So that call returned a portrait for one id and null for the other
fourteen: fourteen cases lose a photo, one keeps it, and nothing anywhere
says so. A partial success is the worst shape available here, because the
function looks like it works and the missing faces read as missing data.

What is worth naming is that the single overlap is luck rather than a defect
in the entry that overlaps. Four company ids are person-shaped words, and each
has a counterpart on the role axis naming the same work: cost-consultant
against quantity-surveyor, designer against design-lead, bim-consultant
against bim-coordinator, project-manager against project-manager. Only the
last pair happened to choose the same word. Had either axis picked
differently the intersection would be larger or empty with no change to how
well either list was written, and the size of that intersection is what
decides whether this bug fails loudly or quietly.

So the fix is to make the type carry the meaning rather than to rewrite the
comment. caseFaceFor and CaseFaceInput now take the company-type union, and
CaseRole is an alias of CompanyType instead of a hand-duplicated eight-member
union that had drifted out of the dictionary's sight. The compiler now refuses
the role array outright. The comment is corrected to say what the field holds
today and to record that it changed, because the next reader needs to know the
old shape existed.

The narrowing found three call sites in the tests before it could find one in
production, and all three were deliberately out-of-vocabulary values that the
old signature had never checked: two feeding an unknown id to assert the first
castable entry wins, one asserting an unknown company type resolves to nothing
rather than to a minted 404 path. They now route through a single named
constant whose comment says the double cast marks a negative control rather
than a shortcut around an inconvenient type. The runtime branch still has to
hold, because both id schemes arrive as plain strings from the server and from
localStorage. The sibling checks on companyThumbFor and companySceneFor are
left uncast on purpose, since those functions genuinely do take a string.

The new gate uses the overlap as its own assertion. Fed the role list,
fourteen of fifteen resolve to nothing and project-manager resolves to a
portrait, and that surviving hit is asserted explicitly, because a test
claiming the role list resolves to nothing would be quietly false. The two
vocabularies are also asserted not equal as sets, so the file cannot end up
comparing something to itself, and the cast map is asserted to be keyed by the
company ids, so nobody can add a role id to fill an apparent gap.

test(procurement): prove a buyer can reach the bill position picker

BillPositionPicker shipped on 20 August with a thorough test and no caller.
It was wired into the purchase order form three days later. For those three
days the component was written, covered and mounted by nothing, its test was
green the whole time, and the coverage number counted it. That is the failure
mode worth naming: a test that mounts a component itself cannot fail because
nothing in the application mounts the component, so the one thing it can never
tell you is whether a user can get there.

ProcurementPage had no test at all, which is why nothing noticed. This adds
the first one, and it starts where a buyer starts rather than where the
component starts. It renders the page with a project selected, presses the
New Purchase Order button that is actually on screen, and requires the picker
to arrive in the form. Then it follows the value the rest of the way: the
position chosen on line one has to appear as items[0].boq_position_id in the
body posted to /v1/procurement/, because a control a user can reach that drops
what they picked on the way to the server is not meaningfully wired either.

Three of the six tests exist to stop the other three from being decorative.
The picker is required to be absent on the landing page, so arriving at it has
to be the click doing the work. It is required to be absent when the project
has no cost spine, which is the case the component deliberately renders
nothing for: that test opens the identical form and finds no picker, which is
the only thing ruling out an assertion that merely tracks whether the modal is
open. And an unattributed line is required to omit boq_position_id entirely
rather than send it as null, asserted against the serialised body, since that
is a distinction the form makes on purpose and exactly the kind a later tidy
up removes without noticing.

The assertions key on the per line accessible name, Bill position for line 1,
which only the picker renders and only from inside the per line map. The bare
label would have been weaker, because the picker gives that same text to its
own search box as a placeholder, and a match on it could not tell a mounted
control apart from its own internals.

The empty spine assertion was confirmed by inverting it and watching it fail
on the right line while the other five stayed green, which is what separates a
failure caused by the picker being absent from one caused by the harness
collapsing.

Two notes for whoever writes the next page level test here. The active project
has to come from the project context store, because the shared test setup
mocks useParams to return an empty object and a route parameter is silently
ignored. And mocking the request verbs in shared/lib/api covers both the page
and the picker's own cost spine client, since they go through the same module.

No new translation keys. Every string asserted on already ships in all
42 locale files.

universe. The old figure was not wrong about its eleven. It was a measurement of

fix(bim-hub): every PDF sheet export has failed to link its document

For as long as this code has existed, generating PDF sheets for a converted
model has left nothing in the documents hub, and the only trace was a warning
reading "PDF sheets to Document linkage failed". An operator reading that
concludes the export hit a problem. The export was fine. The row was built with
a created_by keyword, Document has no such column, and the declarative
constructor raised TypeError before a byte reached the database. Not refused,
never attempted. The wording blamed the operation for something the code did.

That grammar is the more useful finding than the keyword. Seven blocks in this
module swallow a database write, and four of them share it: warning level, the
exception interpolated into the message, phrasing that attributes the failure
outward. One carries a comment saying validation is advisory and never fatal,
which is true of the policy and false of the effect. A defect inside any of
them is reported as the operation having trouble, which is why this one lasted
from the commit that introduced it until now.

The keyword was never a column on Document in any revision. It belongs to three
other classes in that same models file and to BIMModel in this very module,
whose created_by is the GUID the discarded cast was building. So nothing dropped
a column and walked away from its readers; the name is simply ambient, defined
in 86 model files across the backend, and it was picked up from a neighbour. The
same wrong keyword is commemorated in a comment a hundred and seventy lines
below in this router, where it bit the upload path once already. Twice in one
file is a pattern.

Its guard exercises the worker rather than reading the call site, because a test
that reads the call site would have agreed with this defect for its whole life:
the call was self-consistent and named a neighbouring model's field. Only the
converter binary is stubbed. The construction, the insert and the commit are
real, through the session the worker opens for itself, and the project is
committed on the application engine and removed afterwards, with the teardown
asserting the cascade took the row rather than assuming it. Against the fixed
code three tests pass; with the keyword and the old handler put back, all three
fail.

A syntactic guard covers the class rather than the instance, reading the
router's Document constructions out of the AST and checking them against the
mapper both ways. Every keyword has to be a field the model has, and every field
the model cannot default has to be supplied. The second half is the one that
decides whether this fix works at all: a constructor that accepts a keyword is
not a database that accepts a row, this block has never executed its insert
once, and it cannot be executed on a machine without a converter installed. Had
Document carried a non-nullable column with no default that the block does not
pass, the fix would have moved the failure from wrong log and no PDF to right
log and still no PDF, with every test green either way. The required set is
computed from the mapper and asserted non-empty before anything is concluded
from it, so a model that later defaults everything makes the guard fail rather
than go quiet. The same check across the backend covers 1355 constructions in
623 mapped classes and finds one more hit, a dataclass of the same name
shadowing an ORM class inside a function body, recorded here as the false
positive it is.

The other half of this change is the August cross-link fix on the upload path,
which the record carried as shipped without a test. It has one. "The fix commit
added no test" and "the fix has no test" are different statements, and only the
first can be answered by walking a source directory's history and counting test
files inside each commit, because a test-only follow-up lands in neither place.
Six days separated the two, which is exactly the window in which an item gets
written down and then quietly closed by somebody who never saw the item.

So rather than taking that guard's word for itself, it was run against the code
from before the fix, since a test written by reading a fix usually asserts what
the fix does rather than what the defect did. This one does not. With the
savepoint reverted, three of its four tests fail, and the two cross-link
failures die where the fix's own message predicted, blaming a transaction twenty
lines below the row that actually broke. One test is added there, because every
existing one injects the failure by patching and so only says what would happen
if an insert failed. A 300-character filename overflows the varchar behind
Document.name and is refused on the cross-link and on nothing else, with the
model row and the stored file already committed. That is the difference between
a savepoint being defensive and being load-bearing.

Both handlers narrow from except Exception to except SQLAlchemyError. On the
upload path that turns a defect in the block into a failed request. In the
background worker it cannot, because the worker has nobody to raise at and its
whole body sits under a catch-all, so what narrowing buys there is a traceback
naming the line instead of a warning naming the database. That is written next
to it, because a comment claiming more than the code does is worse than none.

Both guards in tests/modules/bim_hub ran in no lane a person reads. The string
bim_hub appears in no workflow in this repository, tests/modules is named five
times in the PostgreSQL lane and never for that directory, and the tenant
isolation job selects on a marker these files do not carry and on a keyword
chain in which no word matches any of their node ids. They now have a named step
there, running the whole files rather than a selection, since selecting is what
went wrong in the first place. It needs a database and takes about three minutes
locally, nearly all of it cluster boot and per-test template clones. The step is
not described as blocking and is not: main carries three protection rules,
deletion, non-fast-forward and linear history, and no required status checks at
all, so nothing in that workflow stops a push today. What the step buys is that
the guard runs where somebody looks instead of nightly where nobody does, and
that the list is already right the day required checks are turned on. The unit
guard needs no step of its own, matching a glob an existing one already runs,
which is remeasured here from 528 to 532 passed with no skips.

One thing is written down for the next person rather than for this change. A
mocked flush that merely raises does not set the session's rollback-only flag,
because only a real database failure does. A transaction-isolation test built on
one passes identically before and after the fix it claims to guard. It is not a
weak test, it is a test of nothing, and it looks like a strong one because the
code really does contain the isolation being asserted. That now sits at the top
of the isolation test, together with the only proof that a test of this kind
works, which is running it against the code from before the fix and watching it
go red. Running it is also what caught a symptom test here passing against the
live defect: it matched the phrase the repaired code uses while the defect's own
message said something else, so it now asserts on log level instead. A level is
a property of the system, a phrase is a property of whoever typed it.

test(ci): the lane map now says which question it answers

This file classifies test trees by reading the workflow files, and it was read
as saying which trees are protected. Those are different questions and it only
ever answered the first. Its header says so at length, in a paragraph written
for exactly this misunderstanding, and somebody working in this repository
made the mistake anyway, quoted a class called PUSH_FULL back as evidence that
a tree was gated, and had to be corrected from the repository ruleset. A caveat
in a docstring loses to a label in the output, because the label is what gets
quoted and the header is what nobody opens.

So the caveat moved into the vocabulary. The classes are named for what they
report, DECLARED_FULL through DECLARED_NOWHERE, and every value they carry now
begins "workflow declares". A reader who never opens the header still cannot
turn one of these into a claim about enforcement, because the string that
reaches an assertion message says what it is a statement about.

What is enforced is recorded next to them. main is protected by three rules,
deletion, non-fast-forward and linear history, and carries no required status
checks at all, measured against the ruleset on 2026-08-26. So no job in any of
these workflows stops a push, whatever their own comments say about themselves,
and several of them do say it. One of those comments pointed at the old class
name and has been repointed here.

The pin is a frozen set rather than a live query on purpose. A guard that asks
GitHub is a guard about network conditions: it fails in an offline clone, fails
without a token, and fails differently in CI than on a laptop, and a test that
red-flags a missing token teaches people to ignore it.

That leaves a limit worth stating rather than papering over. Branch protection
lives in the repository settings and leaves no artefact in the tree, so turning
required checks on changes nothing here and no test can notice. This file
cannot go red on the event itself. What the single new assertion does is
narrower and still worth having: the moment somebody records that a check has
become required, it fails and sends them back to re-read the map, because a
tree declared as a whole run in a workflow nobody requires is in a different
position from the same tree in a workflow that is now required, and these
labels cannot tell those apart. Whoever changes the setting is the right person
to be asked, and the map going stale silently is the failure this file exists
to prevent in the first place.

Verified by putting one check name into the pin, which fails that assertion
alone and leaves the other fifteen green, so the guard discriminates rather
than merely running. Sixteen passed with the pin as it stands.

precedes the Korean one, so a reordering is caught even by a string nobody
thought to sample. A third records that the two predicates really do overlap,
so that if the overlap ever disappears the comments claiming the order matters
are corrected rather than left standing.

The two controls that asserted Hangul falls through to the widest face were

which remain genuinely uncarried. Those two need embedded faces rather than a
referenced pack and are a separate decision.

test(calendar): the two country registries are held together by an assertion

The working week table and the holiday function table are meant to hold the
same countries, and that has been the stated reason for turning work away.
Spain and France were declined on it. Until now the rule existed only as a
sentence in a docstring, which said the two registries held exactly nineteen
countries. Both held twenty. A sentence cannot fail, so it had been wrong
about its own count for a while and nobody could have known.

The next country to arrive in one table and not the other would have made it
wrong about the identity too, and quietly. Both parametrized tests in this
file walk the working week table, so a new entry adds cases that pass, and an
entry whose week matches the default additionally hits a skip. A green suite
was never going to report it.

There is an assertion now. It compares the two registries against each other
in both directions and names the direction the difference falls in, so a
country present in one and absent from the other is reported with the registry
that holds it. It takes both tables as arguments rather than reading the module
globals, which is what lets the control feed it a pair that really differs.

The control is parametrized over both directions and asserts the result is
exactly the one expected line, so a comparison that reported the wrong
direction, or reported both, fails rather than passing for looking busy. Its
country is ZZ, which ISO 3166-1 leaves user assigned, and the control asserts
ZZ is absent from both registries before using it so it cannot pass by
colliding with something real.

Deliberately not a roster. Comparing against a hardcoded list of the countries
that happen to be there today would need the same manual update the stale count
needed, and would break on the first legitimate new arrival, which is the
failure repeating itself one layer down. Registry against registry pairs up a
twenty first country with nothing to edit.

The docstring now states the invariant instead of a number, keeps Spain and
France and the reason they were declined, and points at the assertion by name.
The count is gone rather than refreshed.

One thing the docstring says on purpose, because the strictness could be read
as a claim it does not make. An unpaired row is not necessarily harmful: a row
whose working week matches the default changes no computed answer at all, and
the row that bites is one whose week differs from it. Strict pairing is
asserted anyway, because pairing is what the rest of the file leans on when it
declines to add a country. The test enforces a coupling, not a prediction of
harm.

fix(schedule): a holiday the engine cannot read is refused, not dropped

A calendar exception the CPM engine could not parse was discarded by a bare
except and the day was then scheduled as working. Nothing downstream could tell
that day from one nobody had marked, so a user could mark a holiday, have the
request accepted, and watch the system work the day.

The write schema refuses it now, beside the work_days check that already refuses
the sibling field in the same JSON object. Surfacing it later would be worse: by
the time anything surfaced, the schedule would already have been computed with
the holiday missing and the user would already have looked at wrong dates.

The refusal is narrow, and that is the part that took the work. An entry is
normalised before it is validated, so surrounding whitespace is stripped and
accepted, an ISO datetime is reduced to its date, and the basic YYYYMMDD form
keeps working because it already did and refusing it would have been a
regression. A date pasted from a spreadsheet arrives with a trailing space and
names one day as plainly as the trimmed form does. What stays refused is
01/05/2026 and anything like it, because day-first and month-first read as two
different days and a guess would put a wrong holiday into a schedule that looks
right. The error names the offending value and lists the accepted forms, since
a bare "invalid date" teaches a spreadsheet user nothing.

Rows already stored are not reached by a write-time check. Nothing revalidates
them, so the engine now logs the value it dropped instead of passing silently.
That does not repair the row, it makes the row findable, which is the difference
between a defect and a mystery. A bare string in the slot warns once rather than
once per character.

Normalising at the write also settles a second reader without touching it.
progress_math._is_working compares d.isoformat() against stored strings and
never parses them, so an untidy but valid entry matches no date there by a
different mechanism and with the same silent outcome. Storing one canonical
spelling fixes that path too. That half is a read of the code rather than a
measurement, and it is worth saying so plainly.

A second silent miss turned up while fixing the first, and it needed no
malformed string at all. datetime subclasses date, so a datetime entry was
stored unchanged, and a datetime never compares equal to the date the engine
tests membership against. It was dropped as quietly as bad text. It is narrowed
to its date now.

Tests lead with the control, because a suite where every case raises looks
identical to a suite where every case is correctly refused. One readable holiday
moves a real finish from day 7 to day 8 first, and every other case is measured
against that. Checked against the previous parse rather than assumed: five of
the eight accepted spellings did not count before this change, and three already
did, which is what makes those three regression guards rather than new
behaviour.

fix(a11y): attributes that never translated, and controls with no name at all

Two different defects land together because they share a cause rather than a
symptom. Neither is a missing key, so no gate this repository owns could see
either of them.

The first is a single stale attribute. The chat panel named its dialog with an
aria-label fed from state seeded by t() inside a useState initialiser. That
initialiser runs on the first render and never again, so the accessible name
kept whatever language the panel opened in while every visible string around it
translated. A reader who switched language got a panel that announced itself in
English, fluently and confidently, which is worse for someone using a screen
reader than no name at all, because nothing on screen shows the mismatch. The
title is now held as null while the conversation is unnamed and derived during
render with t in the dependency list, so a conversation the user renamed keeps
the words they typed and only the unnamed default follows the language.

The second is 27 icon only controls that had no accessible name in any
language, plus 45 attributes that never went through translation at all. A
control with no name is not a translation gap, it is a control that does not
exist for anyone who cannot see the icon. The untranslated attributes are
invisible to the key gates by construction: check_i18n_orphan_keys.py asks
whether a key is answered by the locale files, and a string that never became a
key is never asked about, while tsc, eslint and the build all pass because the
strings are valid TypeScript.

Most of the naming needed no new key. A common namespace already carried close,
clear_search, remove, next_page, previous_page, cancel, zoom_in, zoom_out and
dismiss, each present in every locale file, so 21 of the 27 controls and 13 of
the 45 attributes are reuse rather than new debt. Reuse also settled a casing
question on its own, since common.move_up already reads "Move up".

This commit looks like it breaks the rule that wiring and keys land together,
and it does not. That rule exists because wiring without keys renders the
English defaultValue in every language and no gate can tell. Here the order ran
the other way: the 34 keys this wiring calls landed first, inside other
people's commits, while the locale files were being worked by a translation
queue, and the wiring follows them. Keys nobody calls yet are inert, and
check_i18n_orphan_keys.py confirms it at exit 0. The forbidden order never
occurred, so there was never a red intermediate state to avoid.

Fifteen of the files touched here had no i18n wiring at all, including the
shared SideDrawer, Breadcrumb and PartnerLogoBadge. Those get useTranslation
for the first time, which is why the change is wider than the attribute count
suggests.

The product and company names stay in English deliberately. OpenConstructionERP
and DataDrivenConstruction read the same in every language, and they are
recorded in the new gate's allowlist with that reason, so the next sweep knows
they were considered rather than missed.

The ratchet gate ships in the same commit because it cannot be separated from
the fixes. Its baseline records the accessibility debt that remains, and that
baseline describes the tree these fixes produce; landing it on a tree without
them would report 45 defects it has already recorded as repaired. Each of its
three checks asks a question about one item rather than carrying a list of
known sites, because a detector built from a list of 45 reports green the moment
something adds a 46th. It skips the locale files on purpose: those are data
rather than components, so a translated value containing angle brackets could
only ever read as a false positive, and they are rewritten constantly enough
that a gate reacting to them would be a gate people learn to ignore. Its
negative control runs ahead of it in CI, since a detector that stops firing
reports a clean tree and the tree then looks like it got better. Writing that control found two silent defects in the gate itself:
a backward scan for the owning tag that walked past any element whose earlier
attribute contained an arrow function, which found 1 of 257 literal
placeholders, and an apostrophe inside an ordinary code comment read as the
start of a string literal, which hid one seeded hook while still reporting an
identical one four lines above it.

Deliberately left as recorded debt: the placeholders whose split between real
prose and sample values is a judgement per string, the seeded values that feed
toasts rather than attributes, and the pdf-takeoff count label. That last one is
persisted as measurement data, so it is a question about records that already
exist rather than a display bug, and it should not be answered inside an
accessibility change.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(a11y): the nine saved view icons say which picture they are

The icon picker in the save view dialog offered nine buttons whose only content
was the icon itself. A screen reader announced all nine as "button", so the
choice was not merely hard to make without sight, it was not presentable at all.
This is the last entry in the accessibility baseline's unnamed controls check,
and the baseline shrinks by exactly that one line.

Each option now carries its own name. Here the picture is the label, so the name
has to describe what is drawn rather than what choosing it accomplishes.

The nine names are local keys rather than reuse from the common namespace, which
is the opposite of the decision the previous change made and is deliberate.
Reuse worked there because close, cancel and clear search are action names with
one correct rendering wherever they appear. These nine are picture names, and
they only work as a set: what makes them useful is that each is distinct from
the other eight, which is a property of the group and not of any one of them.
Borrowing layers from the plan room and chart from the reporting namespace would
scatter one visual row across several features and let each drift when somebody
edits it for an unrelated reason, with this row nowhere in front of them.
common.pin already exists and is declined for the same reason, since eight local
names and one borrowed one is worse than nine local ones.

The group is a group and not a radio group, though the semantics argue for one.
Exactly one icon can be chosen, which is single select, and the honest role for
that is radiogroup. That role carries a keyboard contract: a reader told this is
a radiogroup presses the arrow keys and expects the selection to move. Claiming
it without implementing roving focus would announce a promise the widget does
not keep, which is worse than the unnamed buttons it replaces, and it is exactly
the defect class this work exists to close. role="group" accepts a name and
promises nothing about the keyboard, so the visible Icon caption becomes the
group's accessible name through an id generated by useId rather than a literal
that would collide if the dialog were ever rendered twice.

The names are translated rather than left to fall back to English, because
wiring whose keys are missing renders the English default everywhere and no gate
reports it. Thirty locales carry them here. Twelve do not, and the reason is
worth stating: German, French, Russian, Japanese, Chinese, Spanish, Portuguese,
Italian, Dutch, Polish, Turkish and Arabic currently hold several hundred lines
each of a separate translation pass still in flight, and committing those files
here would take work that is not this change's to take. The nine names are
already written into them on disk and will land with that pass. Until then those
twelve show the English default, which is correct English rather than a raw key,
because every call carries one. en-US is deliberately untouched: it is an
overlay of about 1580 keys rather than a full locale, and none of these nine
words differ between US and UK English.

One property has to hold that no gate checks: the nine must stay distinct from
one another after translation, since the name is now the only thing separating
one button from the next. Layout and Layers are the pair most likely to collapse
together, and a translator working key by key cannot see that they are adjacent,
so the constraint is written where the options are defined. All nine were
verified pairwise distinct in all 42 locales on disk, the twelve held back
included.

Worth recording because it limits what the gates can promise here. The call
takes its key from a variable, which is a shape the computed key scan reports as
not checked, alongside 439 other call sites. Nothing verifies these nine keys
resolve, so that was verified directly instead: all nine are answered by en.ts
and each default matches its English value exactly. The defaultValue on every
call is what keeps a renamed key degrading into correct English rather than a
raw key leaking into the interface.

fix(schedule): the CPM endpoint refuses the calendar it cannot read

The engine has two entrances and only one of them was guarded. A work
calendar reaches the CPM engine through a schedule's metadata, which has been
checked since the exception dates were fixed, and through the CPM endpoint's
own request body, which was not checked at all. The request body does not
touch the schedule's stored metadata on its way through, so the check on that
field never saw it.

That mattered more here than an unguarded field usually does, because the
endpoint persists what it computes. An override naming a weekday the engine
cannot count, or an exception date it cannot read, produced wrong dates and
wrote them onto every activity, and the response said success. Refusing at the
write is the last point where the writer is still present to be told.

Since the exception fix landed, that door was unguarded but no longer silent:
the engine logged each dropped exception, so the wrong answer left a trace even
though nothing stopped it. The log line was carrying this entrance on its own
in the interval, which is worth knowing for anyone reading those warnings in
older logs.

Both halves of the override are checked, not just the one that prompted this.
Weekdays go through the same range check that has always refused the
Sunday-is-7 mistake, and it has never covered this entrance either. Guarding
the exception dates and leaving the week definition open would ship a door that
refuses a bad holiday and accepts a week running to eight days, which is a
strange thing to leave for the next reader, and it is the same shape of defect
as the one being fixed: a check named for its container, covering one way in.

The rules now live in one function that takes the source path as an argument,
so both entrances share them and a third joins by calling it rather than by
growing a second copy. The messages are unchanged for the metadata door.

Scope, stated because it is easy to read this as more than it is. This is a
write-side fix. It covers new writes and updates that carry metadata, and
nothing else. A PATCH that omits metadata never re-runs the check, so every row
already stored keeps its bad string until something rewrites it. No data is
cleaned by this commit.

The per-activity path needs no guard because it cannot carry a raw calendar at
all. Activities reference a calendar through calendar_id as a foreign key, so
that entrance is closed structurally rather than by validation, which is worth
recording so nobody goes looking for a third door there.

Tests are parametrized over the entrances rather than written twice, so a door
added later has an obvious place to join and inherits every case. The refusals
carry a negative control aimed at the new door specifically: the request model
as it stood before is kept as a fixture, and every value now refused is
asserted to have been accepted by it. Verified by stripping the new validator
off that door alone and re-running, which turns nineteen cases red, all of them
the request-body parametrization and none of them the metadata one. A suite
that passed for both doors while only one was guarded would have shown nothing.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(costs): a market switch is a write, so it stops accepting a read permission

POST /base-market/{base_region}/{market_token} reads like a load but it writes.
On one request it overwrites the region's resource price rows from the market
CSV, and that overwrite deliberately includes rows a user saved by hand, so
choosing a market discards other people's saved price work. It then reprices
every work item, stamps the market currency onto every cost item in the region,
and swaps the work item text into the market's language.

The endpoint was gated on costs.read, which is viewer level, and the comment
above it described the operation as a viewer level action. That comment is
plausibly why this sat unnoticed, so it has been replaced with one that says
what the endpoint actually rewrites.

The rows are shared. oe_costs_item carries no tenant column and is named in the
never policy list in app.core.rls_setup, which exists so that reference data is
never tenant filtered. What one caller writes is what every tenant reads next.
Gating the switch on costs.update means an editor has to ask for it rather than
anyone who can open the page.

load-cwicr keeps its viewer level gate on purpose. It only ever populates a
region that was empty, it returns early once the region has rows, and it sits in
the first run path, so raising it would lock a viewer out of the setup step they
are in the middle of. Both endpoints now carry a comment explaining why they
differ, because side by side they otherwise look like an oversight.

The tests pin the invariant a permission gate can establish. A caller holding
only costs.read is refused, and the shared rows are read back afterwards to
prove the refusal landed before the write rather than after part of it. A second
test checks that an editor is not refused, since tightening this to admin only
would lock estimators out of their own job and nothing else would catch that.

fix(i18n): the coverage audit stops calling an overlay a hole

A regional variant carries only the words that differ from its base language.
en-US, es-MX, es-CL, es-CO and pt-BR resolve through en, es and pt, so a key
they do not declare is answered there, in the reader's own language. The
coverage audit did not know that. It globbed the locale directory and measured
every file it found against en.ts, so it reported the one genuine overlay we
own as tens of thousands of keys short and printed RED beside it. That line is
an instruction to destroy the overlay, because the cheapest way to make it go
away is to paste a full copy of English into en-US.ts. The orphan guard learned
this the hard way once already, when the same miscount turned a 1499 key file
into 25280 errors.

The rule comes from check_i18n_orphan_keys.py and is imported, not restated.
Two definitions of which file answers a variant would drift, and the drift is
silent because each copy reads correctly on its own. That guard now exposes
base_of under a public name, and its parameter is annotated for what it really
needs, membership of a set of locale stems.

A base language that parses to zero keys is refused rather than used. An empty
base answers nothing, so every variant riding on it would go quietly back to
being measured against English and the report would print the same false
numbers with nothing on the page saying why. The keys are still found by a line
regex rather than by parsing TypeScript, deliberately, so counts stay
comparable with earlier runs of the same tool.

The report gained a basis block naming the commit and a digest of the locale
bytes the run actually read. Several people edit those files at once here, so a
count is an instant and not a settled state, and a reader a week later needs to
be able to tell whether it still applies. Words a variant repeats from its base
are now counted apart from its own untranslated bleed, because they are not
work for that file: if the repeated word is still English, the base is the one
bleeding and the base is what has to be fixed.

No locale file changed.

fix(schedule-advanced): the calendar stores holidays in one spelling

The calendar write schemas constrained work_days and left holidays open. The
same model that refused a week running to eight days accepted a holiday
written 01/05/2026, stored it as sent, and handed it to three readers that
matched it in none of them, so the day was worked as ordinary and nothing was
logged. That is the same shape as the defect fixed one commit ago: a model
that looks guarded because the field beside it is.

A correct parser for this already existed. offset_calendar_from_work_days
validates every holiday, raises a message that names the entry and the format
it wants, and has a test pinning that 25/12/2026 is refused. It had no
production callers at all. That is worse than having no validator, because
anyone auditing this sees a tested guard and moves on, and the green test was
describing a function nothing ran.

On reusing it rather than writing a second parser, since the diff does not
show what it looks like it shows. The function builds a whole calendar object,
so calling it from a field validator would mean constructing and discarding an
engine calendar to check a list of strings. The parsing is extracted instead,
and the extraction delegates the per-entry decision to the parser in core that
the CPM exception dates already use. There is one parser. There are two
messages, because the field the writer has to correct is called holidays in
one place and exceptions in the other, and a message that names the wrong
field is worse than a general one.

That delegation widens what the engine factory accepts, deliberately. It took
YYYY-MM-DD and nothing else, while the CPM door accepted an exported
YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS, so the same date in the same schedule was valid through
one entrance and refused through the other. They now accept the same set, and
the agreement is asserted rather than assumed. Locale day and month orders stay
refused through both, because reading 01/05/2026 correctly means guessing
whether the writer meant the first of May or the fifth of January.

Untidy input is repaired rather than turned away. A date pasted from a
spreadsheet or written by an export is accepted and stored canonically. Only a
value naming no single day is refused, and an empty entry counts as one:
holidays carrying a blank string is a mistake worth reporting at the write,
where the writer is still present, rather than dropping it quietly.

Storing the canonical form is the point of doing this at the write. The readers
downstream compare ISO strings without parsing them, so two spellings of one
holiday are two holidays to them and neither matches the day being tested.

Scope, because this is easy to read as more than it is. New writes and patches
that carry holidays are covered. Rows already stored keep their strings until
something rewrites them, and no data is cleaned here. Every writer in the tree,
the seeder included, passes an empty list, so nothing we ship is refused by
this; that was checked rather than assumed.

The refusals carry a negative control per door: the field as it stood before is
kept as a fixture and every value now refused is asserted to have been stored
verbatim by it. The agreement between the two doors is guarded by a corpus that
is asserted to contain both accepted and refused spellings, so two parsers that
both said yes to everything could not pass it by agreeing vacuously.

fix(fx): a converted amount is rounded to the currency it is denominated in

The FX service rounded every converted amount to two decimal places with a
quantum that never looked at the target currency. That is not a display choice,
it is the value that gets stored and handed on. A Kuwaiti dinar lost its third
digit, which is a real fils that a real payment can carry, and a yen or a forint
gained two decimals the currency has no way to settle. The identical hardcoded
quantum had already been found and removed from MoneyValue.convert, and this was
the second conversion path still carrying it.

The fix gives app.core.money two small functions, minor_units and money_quantum,
and makes every backend place that rounds an amount ask them instead of keeping
its own table. There are four such places: the conversion in app.core.money, the
FX service, the unit price analysis in price_breakdown, and the e-invoice
document resolver. The document resolver keeps its own list of codes it has
deliberately decided, the forint and the rupiah among them, and asks the registry
for everything it has not, so the document count is the value count capped at
what EN 16931 permits rather than a second opinion about the same currency.

decompose_movement now takes the reporting currency, because a movement
attribution has to round in the units the report is written in and there is no
default for that worth having.

The registry follows ISO 4217 with two deliberate exceptions, the Hungarian
forint and the Indonesian rupiah, whose subunits stopped circulating long ago and
which no payment, invoice or ledger in those countries writes with decimals. The
reasoning, and which of the three layers governs which question, is written out
above minor_units, so that the next reader who arrives here from a display bug
finds out that the screen is the one layer that does not read this file.

The new test compares the resolvers against each other rather than against a list
of currencies, sweeping the whole registry, so a currency added tomorrow is
covered without anybody editing a test and two resolvers that start to disagree
fail on the first run. The per currency decisions stay pinned where they are
made, in the e-invoice rules test and the ISO minor unit test, because recording
a decision and detecting drift are different jobs.

test(pdf): the Chinese control went quiet when the Korean rung arrived

Fourteen tests in this file assert that a generator prints Chinese as boxes
once the face ladder can no longer reach a Chinese face. That is the control
proving the Chinese rendering comes from our wiring rather than from something
reportlab does on its own. The fixture threw the switch by turning off the
Chinese rung alone.

Adding the Korean rung made that half a switch. Han encodes in EUC-KR, so the
Korean pack answers coverage for Chinese text too, and with only the Chinese
rung disabled the ladder simply carried on to the Korean one and drew the
document. Five of the fourteen stopped discriminating and reported it, and the
other nine kept passing for a reason unrelated to what they were checking. The
comment in the ladder about the two packs overlapping was already there and
said the order was load bearing; what it missed is that ordering only settles
the question while both rungs exist, and the control exists precisely to remove
one of them.

The fixture now turns off both. That is not a tidier way of writing half of it,
it is the whole switch: the scenario the control describes in its own docstring
is a reportlab build that cannot supply the Adobe packs, and both packs come
from the same CID mechanism, so a build that lacks one lacks the other. One
pack off and the other on was never a state the product could be in, which is
why the control could sit in that state and look fine.

No production behaviour changes here. This is a test regaining the ability to
fail.

feat(pdf): Thai and Devanagari print correctly rather than merely visibly

Both scripts printed as boxes in every generated PDF. Neither has an Adobe CID
pack, so unlike Chinese and Korean they could not be added by referencing
something reportlab already carries metrics for. Each needed a real face in the
repository: Noto Sans Thai at 73 KB and Noto Sans Devanagari at 276 KB, both
under the SIL Open Font License 1.1, committed whole with their licence texts
beside them.

A face alone would have been the wrong fix, and worse than none. Thai stacks a
tone mark above an upper vowel, and the glyph that belongs above a vowel is not
the glyph that belongs above a bare consonant, so without shaping the font
draws the consonant-height mark and the two collide into a blot. Devanagari
stores the i-matra after its consonant and draws it before, so without shaping
the vowel sits on the wrong side of the letter and reads as a different
syllable. Boxes read as missing text and get reported. Both of these read as
text and do not.

So the substance here is uharfbuzz rather than the fonts. It is declared in the
backend manifest and reportlab picks it up by import. Prebuilt abi3 wheels
exist for all three targets we build and for the Debian based Docker image, so
no platform compiles it. Installing it changes nothing on its own: shaping is
opt in on both reportlab paths and defaults off, which was measured rather than
assumed, with the PDF suite giving an identical 443 passed before and after.

Shaping reaches the page through Paragraph and not through the canvas.
pdf_style_for_text now turns it on for the clone it already makes, so a
generator that already routes its styles through that function gets correct
Thai and Devanagari without changing a line. The canvas is a trap and the
module says so: drawString takes a shaping argument, and without rlbidi
installed reportlab selects a definition of its shaping entry point that
discards that argument and returns the text unshaped, with no warning and no
error. pdf_shaping_for_text exists for canvas callers and carries the warning,
and a test pins the trap so it fails if the canvas path ever starts working.

The two faces sit at the bottom of the ladder, and unlike the Korean rung the
reason is not overlap. Neither script shares a codepoint with Han or Hangul.
The hazard is that both faces carry a full Latin alphabet, so each is a face
that draws "Concrete C25/30" perfectly well and would capture ordinary Latin
strings if anything above it stopped answering first. Their position is what
keeps a German invoice out of a Thai face, and it is asserted directly rather
than through its consequences.

The tests measure shaping rather than presence, which is the distinction a
future reader needs, because a page renders either way. Five Thai stacks are
asserted to be substituted by the shaper and five controls, the same
consonants and vowels with the tone removed, are asserted to come back
untouched. Either half alone is satisfiable by something uninteresting: a
shaper that rewrote everything passes the first and a shaper that did nothing
passes the second. One test renders the same text twice through Paragraph and
compares content streams, because a shaped string is not yet a shaped document.

The two faces live in a subdirectory of their own, and that is load bearing.
The guard that checks every shipped font has resolvable licence text picks
between several licences in one directory by longest shared filename prefix,
and LICENSE_DEJAVU shares no prefix with DejaVuSans; it resolved only by being
the sole candidate there. Dropping two more licence files beside it left every
font in that folder unattributable, DejaVu included. One directory per vendor
keeps each family's licence the unambiguous answer and leaves DejaVu as it was.

On the licensing, NOTICE gains three entries. Neither Noto face declares a
Reserved Font Name, which was checked in the binaries rather than assumed: OFL
clause 3 restricts only names specified as such after the copyright statement,
and neither specifies any. The restraint on renaming rests on trademark
instead, since the metadata states Noto is a trademark of Google Inc. and the
OFL grants no trademark rights. The third entry is HarfBuzz, and it is the one
worth reading. uharfbuzz declares Apache-2.0 and means it, but the HarfBuzz
statically linked into its extension module is under the separate "Old MIT"
licence, the wheel ships no copy of that text, and the compiled binary carries
no copyright string at all. We redistribute that object code in every installer
and in the Docker image, so the notice Old MIT requires in all copies would
otherwise appear in none of them. Both licences are compatible with AGPL-3.0.

Known limitation, stated rather than papered over. Neither face carries U+00B2
or U+00B3, so a string mixing Thai with a squared or cubed unit falls back to
the widest face and boxes the Thai. No backend locale string does this today,
0 of 385, but user data can.

fix(schedule): one stored holiday now means one day to every reader

Four different normalisations of the same stored column. One reader truncated
each entry to ten characters, one passed it through whole, one truncated it
again somewhere else, and the only parser that actually validated had no
production callers at all. The write door being open is how a bad holiday got
in. Four readers disagreeing about what it meant is why nobody could tell what
the system believed once it was there.

Three of them could not report, and that is the part worth naming. A truncation
cannot fail, so there is no error branch and nothing is ever logged. That is
the same blindness as a swallowed exception arriving by a different route, and
it is worse, because a swallowed exception at least has a place where someone
could put a log line. An operation with no failure mode has nowhere to put one.
A holiday written 01/05/2026 matched no date in any of them, the day was worked
as ordinary, and the system was silent about all of it.

They now share one function. It returns the canonical spelling for every entry
that names a day and warns, naming the calendar and the entry, about every one
that does not.

It drops rather than refuses, and the asymmetry with the write side is
deliberate. The write schemas now turn away a value naming no single day, so
anything malformed arriving at a read was stored before those guards existed.
Failing the read would turn an old row into an error on a path nobody asked to
change, and would hide the very calendar an operator needs to see in order to
fix it. Empty entries are dropped without a warning, which preserves what the
previous code did on purpose: a blank carries no date to misread, and warning
about it would write a line on every reschedule for the life of the row.

This also closes a disagreement that the exception fix opened. Before it, all
three readers worked a holiday written with a leading space, uniformly and
silently. After it, the CPM engine took the day off and the other two did not,
so one stored value produced two different schedules depending on which reader
looked at it. Making the correct reader lenient again would have been the wrong
repair. Normalising on the way in and reading one way on the way out is the one
that leaves every reader agreeing.

The progress engine's date parser is fixed in the same pass because it is the
same confusion. datetime subclasses date, so a lone isinstance check against
date returned a datetime unnarrowed, and the calendar then compared
2026-05-01T09:30:00 against a set of YYYY-MM-DD holidays, matched nothing, and
reported a holiday as a working day. Nothing reaches it that way today: the
activity date columns are strings. It is two lines and a test rather than a
fix with a story, and the reason to spend them is that the day one of those
columns becomes a real date column, every holiday would quietly stop being a
holiday and nothing anywhere would fail. It has a tripwire now instead of a
comment.

Tests assert two different properties, because they are different. That the
readers agree, which is what makes one stored value mean one thing, asserted as
agreement between them rather than as three separate right answers, so a fourth
reader that is wrong in the same way as the others still fails. And that an
unreadable entry is reported, with a negative control confirming a readable
calendar logs nothing, since a reader that warned about everything would
otherwise pass every assertion in the file.

fix(bim-hub): a conversion failure record belongs to the upload that hit it

The DDC failure context lived in a module-level dict and the router reads
it back afterwards to build model.error_message and model.metadata_.
Uploads are not serialised: process_ifc_file runs through
asyncio.to_thread, so two users convert at the same time on one thread
pool and whichever conversion failed last owned the record. One user's
stderr tail, which carries the file path and file name of their upload,
could be reported on another user's model.

The record now lives in a context variable the caller binds around its
own conversion. asyncio.to_thread copies the caller's context into the
worker thread, so the worker fills in the same record object and the
router takes its copy while the scope is still open. Propagation only
goes one way, which is why the record is a dict mutated in place rather
than a value rebound in the thread. With no scope open the context is
logged and dropped, because there is nowhere to put it that another
conversion could not read.

The comment claiming module-level state was fine because conversions are
serialised per upload is gone. Nothing serialised them, and that sentence
is what explained the defect away.

The new test runs two conversions that each record a failure, held at a
barrier so both writes land before either read, and makes each one read
back its own. Against the shared dict one of the two comes back with the
other one's file path.

test(schedule): an agreement between the two calendars must prove both sides answered

Two registries answer which days a country works, and both substitute silently
for a country they do not carry. get_work_calendar returns the DEFAULT
Monday-Friday calendar, core.calendar reads its own default week, and neither
says it has done so. That makes a difference between them trustworthy and an
agreement not, because a difference is a positive result that something had to
compute, while an agreement is the absence of a computed difference, and an
absence has two causes. The systems agree, or nothing was measured.

The new gate sorts every country either registry knows into comparable,
unmeasured and absent, and keeps the third state visible. Resolution is proved
by identity against the DEFAULT object and never by reading a label, because
the fallback is a complete and confident calendar whose label looks like an
answer. An earlier pass at this measurement read the label and reported Nigeria
as a genuine difference when nothing had been measured at all.

Five countries are unmeasured today. BG, JP and NG hold a week in core.calendar
and get DEFAULT from the planning table, and ES and FR are the reverse. That
count comes from asking the resolver rather than differencing the two tables,
which matters because get_work_calendar tries a calendar key before it consults
the country map, so UK resolves through the key path despite being absent from
that map. Differencing the tables gives six, and one of the six is wrong.

The five are recorded as a ratchet rather than asserted to be zero. A gate that
lands red today and stays red until five countries are sourced is not a gate,
it is a build people learn to route around. So one test fails when a country
joins the unmeasured set, and a second fails when a recorded country is given
its missing entry and the baseline is not shrunk, which means the ratchet can
only tighten. The population it walks is derived from both registries, so a
country added to either side is covered without anyone editing the gate.

Four controls guard the gate's own premises. No country may be mapped to
DEFAULT explicitly, because identity stops proving anything the moment one is.
Calendar labels must stay distinct, because a duplicate label is how a
substituted calendar passes for a resolved one on sight. A synthetic code,
asserted absent from both registries first, runs in all three directions. And a
positive control asserts that at least one country is comparable, without which
everything else here would still pass if the classifier were broken to answer
unmeasured for everything.

One note for whoever reads this beside test_work_calendar_rest_days_do_not_conflict.py.
That gate asks whether a misplaced rest day can exist, and it correctly skips
countries whose week is Monday-Friday, since a Monday-Friday fallback cannot
put their weekend on the wrong days. All five unmeasured countries are
Monday-Friday on the side that has them, so they sit exactly inside that skip.
Two correct gates, each doing its own job, and the gap between them is where
this lived.

fix(license): the AGPL text ships where we say it does

We license the platform under AGPL-3.0-or-later and say so in the package
metadata, the README, NOTICE, the desktop installer and the About page, but
the licence text itself was in none of the places those pointed at. It was
not in the tree, not in the built wheel and not in the container image. The
root LICENSE file held a short notice instead, which is the worse of the two
failures because it looks like the licence it stands in for.

The verbatim text from the FSF now sits at the root LICENSE, and a byte
identical copy at backend/LICENSE. The second copy is not decoration. PEP 639
resolves license-files against the project root, and for this build that root
is backend, which cannot reach one level up, so the wheel had nothing to
carry. With license-files declared, a freshly built 15.9.1 wheel writes
License-File: LICENSE into METADATA and puts the text at
dist-info/licenses/LICENSE, checked on the artefact rather than on the
config. Both container targets install that same wheel and also receive
backend/LICENSE through the source copy, so the image carries it twice.

The root .dockerignore line that excluded LICENSE is now anchored to the repo
root so it cannot reach down and drop backend/LICENSE from the build context.
Real Docker anchors its patterns there anyway, but the gitignore grammar our
dockerignore test models it with does not, and leaving the two to disagree
about a licence file is not worth the ambiguity.

The notice that used to occupy LICENSE moves to COPYRIGHT with its substance
untouched, and it now opens by saying plainly that it is not the licence. A
new test keeps the two licence copies identical and keeps a summary from ever
taking that place again. The About page already told users the full text
ships with the source, so that line is left exactly as it was, and it is now
true.
