fix(classification): one country, one standard, whatever the spelling

A project region of PL resolved to DIN 276 and PL_WARSAW to MasterFormat.
Same country, two standards, decided by whether a city happened to be
appended. Seventeen of the forty-eight shipped catalogue rows answered
differently for their bare country code than for their own region id.

There was a city-suffix net in the resolver and it could not fire for the
cases that needed it. It only ran when the whole region string missed the
lookup, and a catalogue region id never missed: the derivation loop had
already inserted every id with a standard taken from the country table,
which for a country that hung off a macro-region cluster rather than the
table itself meant the MasterFormat default. So the net covered invented
regions and skipped every real one.

Six tables carried an opinion about which standard a place reads, and they
had drifted apart. The match pipeline held a country table of twenty-seven
and a fallback region table of eleven, and derived a third of a hundred and
thirty-five entries at import. The validation rules held one of five. The
shipped catalogues declared a standard on thirty-three of forty-eight rows.
The BOQ rule-set builder keyed its own by raw region. Australia, India and
South Africa read NRM in one and MasterFormat in another. Brazil, Morocco
and Tunisia disagreed the other way.

They are one table now, in app/core/classification_registry.py, keyed by
ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 and nothing else. Every region string is reduced to a
country once, before any lookup, so PL and PL_WARSAW reach the same answer
by construction rather than because both are listed. A catalogue region id
resolves through the country_iso the catalogue declares, which is why
SV_STOCKHOLM is Sweden, ZH_CHINA is China and VI_HANOI is Vietnam. The
catalogue field is derived from the registry instead of stored, so it can
no longer hold an opinion of its own.

Resolution stays total, because it runs on the BOQ section-path render
path where an exception costs the page, but it is no longer silent. Every
answer carries the country it matched and whether it matched at all, a
blank region logs at info because that is the ProjectCreate default, and a
region that was filled in and still resolved to nothing logs at warning
naming the region. Silently falling through to DIN 276 is how a wrong
standard used to reach a user with no signal anywhere.

Where the copies disagreed the merge was mechanical rather than inventive.
The deliberate per-country heuristic wins first, then the standard the
shipped catalogue declares, then the cluster the country hung off. That
keeps Australia, India and South Africa on the Commonwealth NRM lineage
and moves Brazil to SINAPI, which its catalogue had been declaring all
along. Morocco and Tunisia move from DIN 276 to MasterFormat for the same
reason. Ghana, Uganda, Tanzania, Senegal, Ivory Coast, Cameroon and Angola
had no entry at all and were reaching the DIN 276 default in silence.

The test is an invariant rather than a roster. It is driven from the
registry and from the shipped catalogues, so a country added tomorrow is
covered without anyone remembering a case, and it asserts equality and
disjointness between the sources directly. A structural check refuses a
second country-to-standard table anywhere in the backend, and a negative
control removes the normaliser and requires the invariant to go red, so a
suite that passed for some other reason would be caught.

Rule packs stay a table of their own because a country reads one
classification standard but can pull several packs. What they share now is
the normaliser, which is the part that was wrong: a project keyed to
DE_MUNICH used to pick up no regional rule pack at all.

feat(i18n): ask real i18next what a non-English reader actually sees

Principle 2 says i18n everywhere and is nominally a blocker, and nothing was
checking it. Two measurements showed why. Rewriting 30,964 t() calls into bare
literals left the suite 91 of 91 green, because the harness mock returns
defaultValue verbatim and almost every call site passes one, so the rendered DOM
is byte identical whether translation works or not. Corrupting all 38,895 German
values with placeholders preserved turned exactly one assertion red, in a file
nothing runs before merge. The only two tests that raise real i18next both swap a
three key fixture in for the dictionary, on purpose and with a sound reason,
which leaves the shipped dictionary on the far end of no real t() call anywhere
in this repo.

The new guard builds a real i18next instance with the application's own init
options, hands it every bundle under src/app/locales as read by the TypeScript
compiler, and asks it to render. It asserts two properties of the answer and
never judges the wording. An offered locale may not render blank where English
renders text, and an offered locale may not come back mostly English. Comparing
each value against English and grading it was considered and rejected, because
thousands of strings are identical on purpose and a guard with a large false
positive population gets switched off within a week, which is worse than nothing
since it also looks like coverage.

Nothing in it is a written down list of keys or locales. Keys come from en.ts,
locales from the directory intersected with SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES, and a regional
variant's base is derived from its own code, so overlays such as es-MX and pt-BR
inherit rather than reading as thousands of holes. Two controls run over the real
tree on every pass and prove the fallback chain is live before any count is
trusted, because English reported as German would otherwise look like a perfectly
good number.

The ceiling is 15 percent, measured rather than guessed. The 39 offered non
English locales span 1.76 percent for Ukrainian to 6.00 percent for Dutch, so a
locale has to more than double its English content to trip it, while one shipped
as a copy of en.ts scores 100. The table prints on every run so the evidence to
tighten it is always to hand.

The self test runs first in CI and fails if the detectors stay quiet on a locale
copied from English or on a blanked value, so a green run means something. The
guard was also shown to fail on a copy of the tree. Blanking one German value
named that key and that locale and exited 1, and replacing fr.ts with the English
dictionary named fr at 100 percent and exited 1.

It found 25 real cells, declared in the new baseline as debt that may only
shrink. Eight clash profile strings are empty in Bulgarian, Italian and Romanian,
and the first fragment of the login headline is empty in Kyrgyz. No locale file
was edited here.

fix(schedule): a stored calendar that is not a calendar stops the read

The previous commit gave every reader of a stored calendar one convention, and
made an entry that names no day get dropped with a warning rather than silently
truncated. It applied that same leniency to a column that is not a list at all,
and that was the wrong call. Dropping one bad entry loses one day. Dropping the
column loses every holiday in it, and the caller cannot tell the difference,
because a schedule computed from no holidays looks exactly like a schedule
computed from a calendar that happened to have none. A log line is not visible
to whoever reads the finish date, and these dates are planned against.

The two cases only look like the same decision at different scales. They have
different populations, and that is what actually settles it. A malformed entry
has a legitimate history: it was storable until the write guards landed two
commits ago, so refusing it now would turn an old row into a failed read and
hide the very calendar an operator needs to see. A non-list has no such
history. The column is JSON with nullable=False, default=list and a [] server
default, and every write path in the tree goes through a schema typed as a
list, so no version of this code could ever have produced one. Reaching that
branch means the row was written around the application, and degrading quietly
is the wrong answer to data nothing we ship can create.

Worth correcting the record on what the old code did here, because the case for
this change was originally made on the idea that a crash was being traded for a
log line. That is not what happened. None of the old readers failed on a bare
string. A generator over one walks it character by character, so ten junk
entries silently replaced the calendar and nothing was logged anywhere. Only a
value that could not be iterated at all, a number, ever raised. So this is a
new refusal rather than a reinstated one, which makes it a stronger change than
it first appeared and not a revert.

None keeps reading as an empty calendar. The column cannot be NULL, and where a
caller passes None it means there is no calendar rather than one that cannot be
read.

The commitment validator needed a second fix for the guard to mean anything on
its own path. Its ORM branch called list() on the column before handing it over,
which turned a bare string into ten characters, so the whole-column case was
unreachable by that route and one corrupt row produced ten separate warnings
instead of one refusal. A guard is worth nothing if the reader flattens the
column before the guard can see it.

Tests cover the refusal, that it names both the calendar and what was found
instead of a list, that it survives the trip through a reader rather than only
holding when called directly, and that the ORM branch no longer flattens. The
control for the last pair asserts a normal stored list still reads through that
branch, since both would pass against a branch that had simply been broken. One
test pins what the old form really did to a bare string, so the correction above
stays in the record rather than resting on the commit message.

fix(desktop): the shaper the installers promised was never in them

Thai and Devanagari shaping landed with uharfbuzz declared in the backend
manifest. That covers the wheel and the Docker image, both of which install
from pyproject.toml, and it covers nothing on the desktop channel. The sidecar
build installs from requirements-desktop.lock and then runs pip install -e .
with --no-deps, so a name absent from that lock is absent from all four
installers no matter what the manifest says. uharfbuzz was absent from it. The
lock is a uv compile output that predates the dependency, so nothing had gone
wrong, the file was simply never regenerated.

What those installers would have shipped is the bad half of this feature. Both
Noto faces are bundled in the sidecar and register fine, the ladder still picks
them for Thai and Devanagari, and reportlab then reports every face as
unshapable because its optional import of uharfbuzz found nothing. Our own
font_needs_shaping answers False on that, by design, so nothing raises and
nothing logs. The pages come out with a Thai tone mark drawn at consonant
height on top of the vowel already sitting there. That is a wrong glyph rather
than a missing one, the failure that reads as text and never gets reported.

The pin is added by hand rather than by recompiling. uharfbuzz declares no
dependencies of its own, so for this entry a hand insertion and a regen produce
the same two lines, and the guard file's own header records that a no-op regen
on 2026-08-17 moved 37 pins and three major versions. One of the three was
reportlab 4 to 5, which is worth knowing now that shaping rides on it. The lock
still pins reportlab 4.5.1 while the tree runs 5.0.1, and 4.5.1 was checked to
carry the same shaping API and to produce the same substitution.

PyInstaller needs nothing here, which was the first suspicion and it was wrong.
6.21.0 follows the try/except import at the top of reportlab.pdfbase.ttfonts,
collects the extension module unaided, and the frozen binary substitutes the
Thai tone to its raised alternate exactly as an ordinary process does. That was
measured by building a sidecar with the pinned packer and running it against
the committed face, rather than reasoned from the spec, and it is why no
hiddenimports entry appears alongside this.

The guard test gains the name and loses a sentence that was never true of it.
_REQUIRED_BASE_DEPS described its members as dependencies imported by
application code, and every existing one is. uharfbuzz is imported by reportlab
on our behalf and never by us, which is exactly why nothing that scans our own
imports could have caught this, and why the entry has to be kept by hand.
Removing the pin now fails that test by name.

fix(i18n): the render guard cannot be red for work that went well

Three things the first commit got wrong, none of them in what the guard
measures.

The lane installed typescript and i18next in two separate npm calls. An install
of a named spec rebuilds the tree it is pointed at rather than adding to it, so
the second one can leave the first one's package gone, and the parse guard would
then fail for a reason that has nothing to do with locales. There was no
precedent for that sequence anywhere in this workflow. Both specs are now named
in one call, which cannot get into that state.

Both chain controls took the first candidate locale and then reported a failure
if that one happened to offer nothing to measure. A regional overlay filled in
until it declares every key its base declares is ordinary finished work, and it
would have turned the whole lane red for being finished. es-MX and pt-BR are
already close to that, at around 38,000 keys each against the 35,411 in en.ts.
The controls now walk the offered locales until one can actually be measured and
speak up only when none of them can, which really is a run that proves nothing.

A blank cell is counted as blank and not also weighed as English, while the
denominator stays the whole of en.ts, so a locale's English share is understated
by however many cells are blank. That is 8 at the most today and it only matters
if a locale went blank at scale, where the blank finding fires first and louder.
Said in a comment rather than left for a reader to work out.

Both negative controls were re-run against the changed code on a scratchpad copy
of the locale directory. Blanking one German value still names that key and that
locale and exits 1, replacing fr.ts with the English dictionary still names fr at
100 percent and exits 1, and the clean copy still exits 0. The self test is 7 of
7 and the guard takes 31 seconds over 43 bundles.

fix(pdf): four documents stop printing a long cell over the column beside it

The payment application, the meeting minutes, the meeting export route and the
punch list give their tables explicit column widths, so they always fitted the
page and their geometry never looked wrong. They also handed reportlab bare
strings, and a bare cell is drawn with canvas.drawString at the column's left
edge and simply allowed to run on. The width decides where the grid line goes
and has no say over where the ink stops.

So an architect's practice name was drawn 35pt into the certification date
beside it. An action item written as a sentence went 268pt into the owner
column, and the owner went 64pt into the due date. An attendee's company went
109pt into the status column. A punch item's assignee went 25pt over the Due
Date label, and the trade beside it, being the last column, went 95pt off the
sheet. A site address in the meeting information table went 228pt off the sheet.
Nothing raised, nothing was logged, and a text extractor still returned every
field in the right order, which is what kept it quiet: the file reads complete
and the page is not.

Cells become Paragraphs, so a value longer than its column wraps inside it. The
column widths are untouched; these tables were always the width they meant to
be. Documents that already fitted are drawn at exactly the coordinates they were
drawn at before.

A table command cannot reach a flowable cell, so the FONTNAME, FONTSIZE,
TEXTCOLOR and ALIGN commands these tables carried had to move onto the paragraph
styles, and pdf_table_paragraph_rows grew a style_for hook to place them per
column and per row. The commands themselves are deleted rather than left behind
describing a layout nothing obeys, which is how the one appearance defect here
had survived: the continuation sheet's header row asked for white bold text
through a TEXTCOLOR and a FONTNAME command, its cells were already Paragraphs,
and so it had been drawn in regular black on a #1f2937 fill since the day it was
written. It is white and bold now, which costs two of its labels one more line
of wrap and shifts the rows under them.

check that its English output was byte identical to the builder before the face
wiring. A Paragraph reaches the same coordinates through different operators, so

carries, and the file preview pane on /files renders CommentThread for

Nothing in this product runs alembic upgrade: the schema moves at boot through
the heal and create_all, neither of which executes a revision body, and the head
stamp then records the database as current. So a backfill, a rename or a
de-duplication runs only where an operator runs alembic by hand, and every

fix(pdf): six table headings stop being drawn in the colour of the fill behind them

A TableStyle command cannot reach a cell that holds a flowable. Six tables
across four modules filled their header row dark and then asked for white text
through a TEXTCOLOR command, so they got the fill and not the colour and the
row rendered in whatever its paragraph style happened to carry. On the bill of
quantities that style was #1a1a2e and the fill was #1a1a2e, the same colour, so
"Pos.", "Description" and "Unit" were not low contrast, they were absent. The
three money columns beside them came out #333333 on the same near black.

The same shape had shipped in the section summary of the large BOQ builder, in
the step table and the appendix of the methodology export, in the record list
of the report exporter, and on the sales contract, where the parties table, the
instalments table and the move-in checklist drew their headings #374151 on a
#1f2937 fill. A signed contract whose Name, Role, Email and Milestone headings
cannot be read.

Nothing we run could see any of it. The characters are all present and in the
right order, so extract_text returns them and every assertion written against
extracted text passes on a page whose heading is not there. Ruff and the type
checker see a valid command list. The only witness is the rendered page.

So the header colour moves onto the header's own paragraph style, which is
where a flowable reads it from, and the commands that were describing a row
nothing draws are deleted rather than left behind. Sizes are untouched. Those
same style blocks carried a FONTSIZE the header could not obey either, and
honouring it as well would have resized the right hand headings and moved the
tables without making anything more readable, so the paragraph styles keep the
sizes these rows already rendered at.

The gate that catches this reads the page rather than the style. For every run
of text it finds the filled rectangle drawn under it, and where that rectangle
is dark it requires the text to contrast against it at the WCAG AA ratio. There
is no list of headings and no list of tables in it, so a table added tomorrow
with the same mistake fails on arrival. Both halves of the instrument are read
out of the content stream, the ink and the fill, because a gate that takes the
background from the source is only checking the source against itself. Cell
contents are drawn inside their own transform, so it composes the CTM; without
that every run reports its position within its cell and no rectangle is ever
found under anything.

It was watched red before any of this was fixed: five documents failing on 29
runs, from contrast 1.00 where the colour equalled its background to 1.42 on
the contract. Two controls hold it honest, one that builds the defect on
purpose and requires the reader to report it and then go quiet once the colour
is white, and one that requires pale text on a pale fill to be ignored, since
this is not a general contrast gate and burying the invisible heading under
every muted caption would help nobody.

It runs in CI (PostgreSQL), last in the backend-postgres job, together with the
column overflow checks from the previous commit. Both were sitting in
tests/unit, which that workflow's own comment records as running in no lane
that blocks a merge. It carries the not-cancelled condition the locale guards
above it use, so a failure earlier in the job cannot leave the pages unread.

One test changed meaning and it is worth naming. The methodology export had a
check that its English output was byte identical to the builder before the face
wiring, and recolouring a header changes those bytes on purpose. It compares
placement and embedded faces now, both of which a recolouring leaves alone, and
asserts the bytes do differ, which pins that the fix is still there.

Two things found and deliberately not done here. property_dev/regulatory.py
builds its cells as plain strings, so its own header is white as intended, but
that also means those cells cannot wrap and it belongs to the overflow defect
rather than this one. And document_templates._kv_table_style names FONTNAME and
TEXTCOLOR over Paragraph cells that already carry the same appearance, so the
commands are inert but nothing is drawn wrongly.

feat(migrations): the boot-path data repair registry, and its gate in a blocking lane

Nothing in this product runs alembic upgrade. The schema moves at boot through
the heal and create_all, neither of which executes a revision body, and the head
stamp then records the database as current. So a revision whose upgrade()
backfills, renames or de-duplicates rows never runs on an ordinary install,
while every signal we have reports success. That is how a de-brand left
trademarked rows in customer databases for eleven months.

This adds the place those rewrites are written instead. app.core.data_repairs
holds the registry, the ledger table that records what ran, and the contract a
repair is held to; each module owns its own repairs.py and registers there. Two
of them arrive with it. One is superseded by date rather than wrong: a national
VAT rate that was correct until a reform and wrong after it, so the repair
closes the old row's window and inserts the new rate beside it rather than
editing a rate that historical invoices still have to resolve against. The other
was always wrong: shipped tax rows seeded without the subdivision they apply in,
which is an incomplete row rather than a value that used to be right, so it is
filled in place and the rate itself is never touched. The registry knows the
difference and checks it, instead of trusting each repair to have got it right.

The gate that reads all this is already on main and could not do its job. It
scans app/**/repairs.py for registrations and resolves every "registry=" line a
revision declares against them, and both registering files were uncommitted, so
it found nothing to resolve against. It failed safe and said so rather than
passing vacuously, which is the only reason this was visible at all.

That failure is the part worth recording. Run the gate against a working tree
and it passed, because the tree held the uncommitted files. Run it against a
pristine export of the very same commit, which is what a clean clone and CI both
get, and it exited one. A check that reads files can only be trusted against the
committed tree, and the difference between the two is invisible from the disk
where the work was done.

So the CI step comes back in the same commit, as the comment above it has been
asking. It is in the structural job of Repo hygiene, which is a lane this
project treats as a gate, and it now has both halves it needs.

The boot wiring that calls the registry on startup is deliberately not here.
One of the two repairs reaches its implementation through a module that is still
uncommitted, so registering it is inert but running it would not be, and the
wiring lands with that file rather than ahead of it.

fix(meetings): a long action item splits across the page instead of failing the export

Wrapping the cells moved this failure rather than removing it. A value too long
for its column used to be drawn on a single line straight off the paper, which
lost the text silently. Once the cell wraps, the row grows instead, and a row
taller than the frame is something reportlab refuses outright: the export
answered 500 on a document that had been rendering, which is louder but no more
correct.

Almost no field can reach that. A punch list trade and category are
String(100), a meeting location and title are String(500). MeetingActionItem
description is Text with no cap at all, and it is drawn in a narrow column on
both the minutes and the export route, so it is the one place where a person
typing a long paragraph takes the document down.

The two documents ran out of frame at different lengths, about 2900 characters
on the minutes and about 2200 on the route, because the route's table is 9pt on
11pt leading against the minutes' 8pt on 10pt and its description column is
narrower. Two geometries is the reason a length cap would have been the wrong
fix: any single number is wrong for one of the two, and it leaves the worst
available shape, the same meeting rendering its minutes and failing its export.
A cap also destroys text somebody typed, and the obligation in a meeting action
is usually in its last sentence.

So the row is allowed to split across the page break, on both tables, and every
character is kept.

There is no length ceiling left to state. Measured on both paths after the
change: 3500 characters gives 2 and 3 pages, 14000 gives 6 and 7, 70000 gives
24 and 32, and 280000 characters renders 95 and 126 pages with nothing raised.
What replaces the ceiling is time, and it does not grow linearly. Up to 70000
characters both documents build in under eight seconds; 280000 takes three
minutes on the minutes and four and a half on the route. The field is still
uncapped, so that remains worth a decision, but it is a slow response rather
than a lost document or a 500.

Both tests were watched failing first, with the LayoutError, on the lengths
above the old ceilings.

feat(i18n): the Romanian VAT reform reaches an install that was seeded before it

Romania raised its standard VAT from 19 to 21 percent on 1 August 2025 and
replaced both reduced rates with a single 11 percent band. The seed file has
been correct for a while, and that changes nothing for anyone: the tax table is
seeded only when it is empty, so every database created before the reform still
carries one open Romanian row at the old rate and no reduced rate at all.

The repair closes rather than rewrites. The 19 percent row is given the
effective_to the reform gives it and the 21 percent row is inserted beside it,
so an estimate or an invoice priced before the reform still resolves at the rate
it was priced at. Rewriting the rate in place would have changed the value of
documents already issued, silently, and there would have been nothing left to
compare against afterwards.

It also refuses to make an install worse. The resolver answers a country-wide
question by finding exactly one row in force flagged as the default, and returns
nothing at all when the rows do not name one. An install carrying an operator's
own unflagged Romanian row would skip the standard-rate step, still receive the
reduced band, and end up with two rows and no default, which turns a database
that was quietly pricing at its own rate into one that cannot price. So both
steps are planned first, the planned result is put through the resolver, and
nothing is written unless the country still answers with a rate afterwards. A
repair that cannot improve an install leaves it alone; one that would break it
must.

The registry this registers into went in without its implementation, which left
a registration on main naming a revision that was not on main and reaching an
implementation file that was not there either. Nothing called it, so nothing
broke, and that is the whole problem with it: it was a trap armed for whoever
next touched the boot path rather than a fault anybody would trip over. The
revision and the implementation land here, ahead of the wiring in the same
commit, which is the order that never leaves that gap open.

The wiring is the other half. app.state carries the verdict, health reports it
beside the schema heal and degrades on it, the ledger model is imported before
create_all so its table is built, and the pass runs after the head stamp and
before the module loader. init-db runs the same registry so it leaves a database
where a first boot would have left it. Every repair is idempotent by contract,
so the ledger is never consulted to decide whether to skip one: a ledger allowed
to answer "already done" is what the alembic stamp is, and that is the defect
this whole path exists because of.

Tests for both halves, including the ones covering the repair added here rather
than left behind with it. Ninety pass. The migration graph has one head.

fix(migrations): the repair registry gate asks its question in both directions

The gate resolved every revision's registry= declaration against the
registrations it could find, and never asked the reverse: does the revision a
registration names actually exist. Only one half was there, which is how a
registration naming a revision that was not on the tree sat on main with every
gate green. Nothing downstream would have caught it later either. The runner
deliberately never consults the migration tree, so the registration is the only
place that revision is written down and nothing reads it back. An absent one is
not a failure waiting to happen, it is a claim nobody checks.

Three outcomes rather than two, because the field permits more than it first
looked like. A non-empty revision that is not in backend/alembic/versions
fails. An empty one does not: DataRepair documents the field as the revision
"or empty when the repair has no revision behind it", so an empty value is a
repair that never had a schema half, and failing it would be this gate
contradicting the contract it exists to guard. A revision that is not a literal
does not fail either, because this reading cannot see it, and unreadable must
never be reported as broken. The summary prints all four counts so a reader can
tell which case they are in instead of inferring it from an exit code.

No threshold of its own. The registry floor already refuses a read that comes
back empty, so by the time the reverse check runs the registrations are known
to have been read, and that is what stops a clean answer here from meaning
nothing. A second floor over three registrations would have been noise.

Proved by mutation on an isolated copy of the tree rather than asserted. The
copy answers exactly as the real tree does, 339 revisions and three
registrations all resolving. Pointing one registration at a revision that does
not exist fails the gate and names the repair id. Emptying that same revision
passes and counts it as naming none. Making it non-literal passes and counts it
as unreadable. The copy was restored byte for byte afterwards, and the shared
tree was never touched.

On the live tree: 339 revisions scanned, 29 rewrite pre-existing rows, three
registrations, all three naming a revision that exists.

fix(property-dev): a contract is written in the currency it is denominated in

Every contract, receipt and certificate the property module issues goes
through one renderer, and that renderer took a locale and no currency at
all. It quantised to a Decimal("0.01") literal, so a forint document was
issued carrying fillér that left circulation in 1999, and a Kuwaiti dinar
receipt was issued a fils short of what the payment actually settled. A
literal cannot know its currency, which is the shape this bug has taken
three times before on other paths.

It now asks app.core.money.minor_units, the one table in the platform that
records a currency's subdivision, and the trailing "00" is written only
where there is a subunit for it to mean, so a forint no longer ends on a
dangling decimal separator. The ten call sites all had the currency in
scope already. The instalments row takes the payment schedule's code
rather than the contract's, because that is the code printed in the column
beside it and the two are allowed to differ. A record that carries no
currency passes the blank through and takes the registry's own two-decimal
default rather than a guess made in the renderer.

The rounding step also moves from the decimal context default to
ROUND_HALF_UP, which is what every other money path in the platform uses.
That changes nothing except an amount sitting exactly on the half at one
digit more than the currency carries: 1.005 EUR now reads 1.01 where it
read 1.00. Everything else in EUR, USD and GBP is byte for byte what it
was.

Three test comments described the old behaviour and were bringing readers
back to a settled question. The resolver census said four places decide a
digit count when this renderer was an uncounted fifth; the invoice test
called HUF and IDR an open question when both are settled at zero with the
reasoning recorded in two places; and the property PDF test named the old
locale-only signature.

turned comma makes the letters oʻ and gʻ, which are letters of the alphabet and

fix(install): the docker branch writes the secrets it will not start without

Docker is the first branch both installers try, so the one line command at the
top of the documentation was the one command that could not work for anyone who
had Docker. It downloaded docker-compose.quickstart.yml and ran compose against
it with no .env anywhere. That file reads POSTGRES_PASSWORD and JWT_SECRET with
the fail fast form, deliberately, so compose stopped on an interpolation error
and started nothing. Neither script mentioned either name.

Both now write the two into a .env beside the compose file before anything is
started, using the recipe the README already publishes for that platform so the
script and the page cannot drift. On Linux and macOS that is openssl, base64 of
24 bytes for the password and hex of 32 for the JWT secret, falling back to
/dev/urandom through od where openssl is missing. Windows has no openssl, so the
bytes come from System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator, the OS
generator, as 64 hex characters, which is 256 bits.

The password stays base64 on purpose. It emits "/" about four times in ten and
that is harmless, because a connection URL splits its authority at the last "@"
and a slash before it changes nothing. What would be fatal is an "@", and base64
cannot produce one. 24 bytes rather than some other count because 24 divides by
three, so there is no padding character to reason about either.

The check is per key rather than per file. A .env carrying one of the two is
easy to arrive at, since the recipe in the README is two separate lines, and a
test for the file alone would leave those people exactly as broken as before. A
key that is already there is never rewritten, because the password in it is the
one PostgreSQL initialised its data directory with and replacing it would lock
someone out of their own database. A file that does not end in a newline gets
one first, so the new key lands on a line of its own.

Second thing, found while fixing the first and just as fatal to the same
command. The base compose file builds the app from source, and the install
directory holds no source, only the compose file, so even with the secrets in
place compose would have gone looking for a Dockerfile that is not there. The
published image override now comes down beside it as docker-compose.override.yml,
which is the name compose merges on its own, so the app is pulled instead of
built and every later "docker compose" typed in that directory, including the
ones the installer prints, still means the stack that was installed. Pulling is
spelled out ahead of up for the reason the quickstart-image make target spells
it out: a service carrying both an image and a build section leaves the choice
to compose otherwise.

Docker is not installed on the machine this was written on, so the compose
behaviour above is read from the compose files, the Makefile and the entrypoint
rather than observed. What was run: bash -n and the PowerShell parser over both
files, and the secret writing helpers lifted out and exercised on their own
against an absent .env, a complete one, one holding only the password, one
holding neither key but other lines, and one with no closing newline. The
installers themselves were not run end to end.

left and where the row carries no subdivision. An operator who set one of these

fix(docker): the guard asks for the host instead of guessing where it ends

The previous commit stopped truncating the URL at the first "/" and started
counting "@" over the rest, less any query string. That closed the reported
case and left the same hole one character over: a password holding "?" cut the
text at "oe:pa" again, counted zero, and passed, while make_url reads that URL
with host "ss@postgres" exactly as it reads the slash one. Counting also
refused two URLs nobody should be refused for, an "@" inside a query string and
an "@" inside a database name.

Both come from the same mistake, which is inventing a second parse and hoping
it agrees with the first. So take the parse the reader downstream takes: user
info ends at the first "@", the host runs from there to the next "/", and an
"@" still sitting in that host is the damage itself, because a host may not
contain one. Anything past the first "/" is not the host and is no longer
examined, which is why the query string and the database name stop mattering
without a rule of their own.

Measured against make_url on nine URLs, and the two agree on all nine: ordinary
password, base64 password holding a slash, literal "@", slash then "@",
question mark then "@", "@" in the query, "@" in the database name, an IPv6
host, and a URL with no user info at all.

The messages said "more than one '@'", which described the counting that is
gone, so they name the host now. That is the assertion the guard's test reads,
so the two tests naming it move with the message, and the file gains the "?"
case and the two past-the-host cases. Eleven pass.

fix(variations): a promoted order inherits what the request was approved on

Converting an approved variation request built the order from the payload
alone, and every field of that payload carries a schema default, so a caller
that named only a currency landed an order with no title and a value of zero.
That is exactly what the variations page sends, so every order a user promoted
through the interface lost the figures the request had been approved on, and
its mirrored change order was priced off the same emptiness.

The promotion now fills in the title, the cost impact, the schedule days and
the currency from the request for anything the caller did not name. It reads
model_fields_set rather than the values themselves, so an order deliberately
agreed at nil cost, or retitled on promotion, still gets exactly what was
asked for.

VariationOrderUpdate now carries affected_contract_id as well. Completing an
order that names a contract is what moves the contract sum, and until now that
link could only be set at creation, where nothing in the interface sets it, so
an order raised this way could never reach a contract at all. An order stops
being editable once it completes or is voided, so the link cannot be rewritten
underneath a posted amount.

nothing is invented. Naming the contract stays a human decision, it is only
possible now.

fix(change-intelligence): a converted variation is one change, not two

Promoting a variation request creates the variation order and a change order
that mirrors it, so every conversion leaves two rows carrying the same agreed
money. The committed impact gather and the run rate curve each read both
families and summed them, so a converted variation counted twice: the in force
order in the approved bucket and its draft mirror in the pending one. That
inflated the cumulative curve and the intake rate on every conversion, and the
committed impact too once somebody approved the mirror.

The mirror is now recognised by the link the promotion stamps on it and left
out, but only while its variation order is itself counted. A voided variation
carries nothing, so its mirror is the only surviving record of that change and
still counts. A change order nobody promoted is not a mirror and counts as it
always did.

The link is read from the change order rather than from the variation order's
reference_change_order_id, because that column also holds a change order a
variation merely refers to, and the demo data anchors one. This is the same
link the contracts money subscriber keys its posting identity on, so the two
readers agree on what a mirror is.

fix(i18n-foundation): a tax rate added to the seed file reaches the databases seeded before it

The tax seeder fills oe_i18n_tax_config only while the table is empty, so a
rate added to tax_configurations.json in a later release never reaches an
install that was already seeded. The file has grown from seventy rows to
eighty-one and eight of the additions are Canadian provincial rates, so a
Canadian firm on an install seeded before v15.5.0 has had three of the ten
shipped sub-national rates and gets subdivision_unknown for the rest, for the
life of that install. romania_vat_2025 was one hand-written instance of this
for one country.

The registry gets a third nature for it. always_wrong fills a value in place
and superseded closes one window and opens another beside it, but a row that
is absent is neither, so never_delivered says what this one does: it only ever
inserts, and verify_additive_shape holds it to that by refusing a pass that
edited a row, deleted one, or added a second copy of a rate line already on
file.

The hard part is not the insert, it is the claim in the name. An absent row
looks identical whether it never arrived or was deleted on purpose, and
restoring a rate somebody removed would be worse than the defect, because it
would come back on every boot and nothing inside the product would stop it.
Two things settle it. The seeder is all or nothing, so every shipped row on an
install carries one created_at and that timestamp says which seed file the
install was built from; a database seeded before a rate shipped provably never
received it. And every delivery is written to oe_data_repair_delivery in the
same transaction as the row, so from the first boot onward the question is
answered by a record rather than by inference and a delivered rate that is then
deleted stays deleted. Both residual gaps are misses rather than resurrections:
an install whose seeded rows are all gone cannot be dated and is given nothing,
and a fresh install of an old build reads as too young and is skipped.

Delivery is per rate line and only into a jurisdiction that holds nothing in
force. The population this serves is the one whose provinces have had no rate
for a year, so some of them typed one in under their own tax code, and handing
them ours as well would charge a province twice or leave a country with two
country-wide rates and no way to say which is the standard one. A collision is
logged and not recorded, so the line is still owed if it is ever cleared.

Only tax rates get this. Fifty-nine seed functions across forty-two files carry
the same early return and five of them seed shipped reference data, but the
safety argument rests on a row having a stable identity, and a starter cost
item or a country row is edited and renamed in normal use, so absent does not
mean there what it means for a tax line. Nova Scotia is left alone for a
related reason: the old install already holds its fifteen per cent row, so the
fourteen per cent one is a rate that changed rather than one never delivered,
and that needs a superseded repair that closes the old window.

Also carries the registration for tax_federal_scope. Its module landed in
8bf1e1c0a without it, so that repair has been present and never run since.

fix(costs): the snapshot restore button can finally say what happened

Restoring a pre-built vector snapshot could not report success, in two separate
ways, and both of them told the user the opposite of what the server had done.

The request ran on the default 45 second client budget. That call downloads
roughly 1.1 GB on a 600 second budget of its own and then hands the file to
Qdrant with an 1800 second restore timeout, and neither half looks at whether
the browser is still listening, so the abort was certain and the failure it got
reported as was not real. Five minutes of longRunning would only have made the
same lie less frequent, so the api wrapper grew a third position, an explicit
timeoutMs derived from the two numbers the handler is allowed to spend. A test
reads those two numbers back out of the handler, so the client cannot quietly
fall behind a server that is later given more time. When the browser does give
up, both callers now say the restore is still running rather than that it
failed. Neither can offer anywhere to check, and that is deliberate: the vector
status and region endpoints both read the cost_items collection while a restore
writes cwicr_<region>, so pointing the existing index poll at this would report
failure for every restore that actually worked.

The second half is a field name. The restore endpoint answers with
vectors_count and carries no indexed field at all, while the neighbouring
GitHub loader answers with indexed. Both callers read indexed, so the modules
page announced that the backend had indexed zero vectors at the end of a
restore of fifty thousand of them, and the setup page reported one. TypeScript
could not see it because the field was declared optional. Reading a restore
body is now one function the two pages share, since the last time they each did
it privately they disagreed.

The v3 catalogue registry gets a guard rather than a fix. Its flat GitHub LFS
paths really are dead, a HEAD answers 404 where the HuggingFace path for the
same region answers 302, but nothing installs from them: the override applied
at import rewrites every published region to the HuggingFace layout, and the
two rows that keep a legacy path are not offered for install. The one way to
turn that into a real defect is to mark such a row available, so a test now
refuses exactly that.

fix(variations): the promotion route commits the amount it was authorised for

Converting an approved request checks the high-value approval gate against the
figure the caller named, or the request's estimate when they named none, and
then built the order from the caller's field regardless. A conversion that
named no figure was therefore authorised against the estimate and committed as
zero. The variations page sends a currency and nothing else, which made that
the normal case: every order promoted through the interface was created worth
nothing, and the change order mirroring it was priced off the same nothing. The
gate was the only part of the route reading the right number, and it spent it
refusing promotions that were about to commit no money at all.

The order now takes the amount the gate was applied to, so the two cannot drift
apart again, and the schedule days fall back to the request's estimate as well.
Both figures are nullable on the request body the route accepts, though not on
VariationOrderCreate, which is untouched. Nil is a real answer for each of
them: a variation can be agreed at no cost, or add no time, and reading that as
"said nothing" would substitute the estimate for a figure somebody deliberately
negotiated. An empty title or currency is not an answer in the same sense, so
those keep the fallback the route already had.

The route can also name the contract the order amends. A request has no
contract of its own so there is nothing to carry forward, but the promotion is
the moment somebody knows which contract the money lands on, and no path
through the interface could say so until now.

The service-level fallback added earlier does not fire here, because the route
names every field itself. Nothing in the tree reached this route at all, so the
tests that come with this drive the handler directly, including one that reads
the authorised figure and the committed figure off the same amount.

fix(i18n-foundation): Nova Scotia bills the rate it actually charges

The province cut its harmonised rate from 15 percent to 14 on 2025-04-01 and
the shipped seed file carries both windows, but the seeder only ever fills an
empty table, so a database seeded before v15.5.0 holds the 15 percent row and
nothing was ever going to replace it. The reconciler added last week cannot:
it asks whether the jurisdiction holds a rate in force, sees that it does, and
declines, which is right, because handing over the 14 percent row beside an
open 15 percent one leaves two rates each replacing the federal one in the same
province and the resolver raises rather than answers. So the province kept
resolving at 15 percent for the life of the install while health reported a
clean boot the whole time.

This is the repair that closes the open window and inserts the rate that
replaced it, registered as tax_window_supersede and shaped like the Romanian
one: the old row is closed on the date the file gives it rather than rewritten,
so an estimate or an invoice priced before the cut still resolves at 15 percent.

It is general rather than one more country, and the reason is a measurement. No
gate in the tree fires when a window is added to an existing rate line. The
reconciler's coverage test pins a set of country and tax code pairs, so a second
window leaves both its count and its digest untouched, which is exactly how this
cut reached new installs, skipped every old one and went a year without a red
test. So the population is derived from the seed file, every line it ships more
than one window of, and pinned in a unit test, which makes the mechanism general
without letting the set of rows it rewrites on customer data grow unread. Today
that set is one line, so the difference from a Nova Scotia specific repair is
nil on any database in the field.

A window is closed only when the row is the one the seeder wrote, on the rate,
the start date, the default flag and a subdivision that is either the shipped
one or empty. Empty is the unlabelled shape an install carries until the
subdivision repair reaches it, so the predicate does not depend on registry
order, while a row somebody moved to a different province is refused rather than
closed underneath them. The planned table is then run through the resolver and
nothing is written to a rate line whose jurisdiction would come out of it
without an answer, which is reachable: the installs this serves are the ones
most likely to have typed the correct rate in by hand, and the resolver raises
on that shape rather than returning an unresolved answer, so the guard treats a
raise as no answer instead of letting it out into the runner.

Measured on the pre v15.5.0 cohort rebuilt from the seed file that release
shipped. Nova Scotia resolves at 15 percent with the repairs that shipped before
this one and at 14 percent after it, on 2025-03-31 it still resolves at 15, and
Ontario does not move. Every guard was checked by removing it and watching a
named test go red.

fix(schema-heal): say so when a NOT NULL is dropped on the way in

The heal enforces NOT NULL on a column it is adding only when a default exists
to backfill the rows already in the table. Without one it adds the column
nullable, which is the right call, because the alternative fails outright on a
populated table and turns a divergence into a failed boot. What was wrong is
that it happened in silence. The column went in, the heal counted it as a
success, and no log line, no health field and no gate recorded that the models
and the database had just been left disagreeing about that column, for the life
of the install, since no revision body ever runs to tighten it later.

So the decision is now announced, naming the table and the column and saying
plainly that nothing on the boot path will finish the job. The warning already
in that function is a different case, it fires when the database refuses a
DEFAULT rather than when the models never offered one, which is why this needed
a line of its own rather than a wider condition on that one.

The behaviour is deliberately unchanged. Adding the NOT NULL instead would fail
on any table already holding a violating row, which is a much worse trade than
a divergence that is at least now visible.

Both halves are pinned. Removing the warning turns the announcement test red,
and making it fire unconditionally turns both control tests red, which is the
half that matters, because a line that named every added column would satisfy a
test for a warning appearing and be useless in a real boot log. The controls
are a NOT NULL the heal can carry, which must stay silent, and a column the
models call optional, which is agreement rather than divergence.

The limit is written into the test file rather than left to be discovered. The
line fires on the boot that adds the column and not on the boots after it, so
an install that took the divergence on an earlier release says nothing about it
now. Answering whether a database matches the models today is a standing
question about the schema and needs a standing signal, which this is not.

fix(health): the stale stamp is a fact, the diverged schema is the fault

The product never runs alembic upgrade. Schema moves through create_all and the
boot heal, so the recorded revision falls behind on a normal, correct upgrade
the moment a release adds any revision at all, and alembic_head_matches has been
degrading the status on exactly that. Every upgraded install has therefore been
reporting degraded for the rest of its life over a stamp, with no schema problem
of any kind behind it.

An aggregate signal with a permanently active cause is not a signal. That is not
an argument from first principles, it already happened here: with status pinned
to degraded by a stale stamp, frontend/dist was wiped and the app began serving
500 on /, and status did not change by a single character. The only field that
told the truth was frontend_dist_present flipping beside it. So the monitor has
to hang on the cause.

The stamp stays published, because the release lane and any external monitor
still need to see it, and it stops degrading anything. What degrades instead is
the question somebody actually wants answered, whether the schema still matches
the models, and that needed a field because nothing anywhere reported it. The
heal enforces a NOT NULL on a column it is adding only when a default exists to
backfill the rows already in the table. Without one it adds the column nullable,
finishes without raising, and leaves the constraint permanently absent, since no
revision body runs to tighten it later. Until now that install answered healthy
with schema_heal_failed false while the models and the database disagreed.

schema_matches_models follows the shape the two fields beside it already use:
true they agree, false they do not, null nobody asked, which is where a
deployment whose database is not PostgreSQL stays for its whole life. Only a
determinable false degrades. Which columns diverge is not published, because the
endpoint is unauthenticated and a list of internal names maps the deployment for
an anonymous caller; the names go to the boot log and to app.state, the same
rule the failing heal statement and the failed repair ids already follow.

The check asks the standing question rather than reading what this boot did. A
column added nullable three releases ago is exactly as diverged as one added a
minute ago, and the heal's own warning is silent on every boot after the one
that makes the decision. It reports nullability only, which is a floor rather
than the finished job, and the reason is written where the next person will
look: nullability cannot disagree for reasons of spelling, and comparing a model
type against a reflected one can, so type divergence needs its own work before
it can be trusted to degrade anything.

Written as one catalog query rather than an inspector call per table. The
obvious form cost 5.0 seconds against 626 tables, measured, which is far too
much to spend on every boot for a diagnostic; the same answer in one round trip
takes 0.19 seconds, which is 2 percent of the heal it follows.

The release lane needs no change and that was measured rather than assumed. It
reads schema_heal_failed and alembic_head_matches by value, never reads status,
and pins no key set, so removing the stamp's authority and adding a field leaves
its cohort logic correct as written.

Every guard has an ablation behind it. Putting the stamp's degrade back turns
the differential stamp test red, removing the divergence degrade turns the
divergence test red, publishing the column names turns the disclosure test red,
and deleting the boot wiring turns the source test red. That last one exists
because every other test here sets app.state by hand and all of them would stay
green if nothing on the boot path ever wrote the field.

fix(catalog): the local catalogue is looked for where an install keeps it

The resolver for the locally generated catalogue CSVs counted five parent
directories up from its own file. That reaches the repo root in a source
checkout and the virtualenv's Lib in a pip or desktop install, where no data
directory has ever existed. Measured on the installed venv in this tree, the old
expression produced .venv-run/Lib/data/catalog/regions, so every install looked
in a place nothing has ever written to. Unlike the packs defect this mirrors
nobody complained, because the lookup falls through to a GitHub download, so an
online host kept working and only an offline or air-gapped one got nothing.

The location is now derived rather than counted. The depth comes from the
module's own dotted name, three candidates are tried, beside the app package,
one level above it and under the working directory, and each has to actually
hold a catalogue CSV before it is accepted. The second half of the old tuple was
wrong for its own reason: Path.cwd() was evaluated once at import, so a process
that changed directory afterwards kept answering for the directory it no longer
ran in. Resolution happens per call now.

The bytes are deliberately not shipped, and that is a decision rather than an
omission. The tree carries 39.1 MB of catalogue CSV across sixteen files, 7.7 MB
deflated, but size is the secondary argument. desktop/pyinstaller.spec has
recorded since it was written that data/catalog stays out of the installer
because bundling it is a licensing decision and not a packaging one, and NOTICE
records the licensing basis of the largest base in it as PENDING. That base
accounts for 29.5 MB, 75 percent of the payload, and a wheel or a signed
installer cannot be taken back, so it stays out until the basis is written down.
Nothing changes in backend/pyproject.toml or desktop/pyinstaller.spec, so the
wheel and spec parity gate is untouched by design.

What the fix buys with no bytes shipped. The directory beside the app package
becomes somewhere a container image or a distributor can populate and be found,
the source checkout keeps the behaviour it already had, and the silent
degradation becomes a stated one. The fallback now says which of the two
situations it is in before reaching for the network, no catalogue directory at
all or one that does not carry this region, and the failure names the
directories it searched instead of only the download that failed.

The new test drives a synthetic installed layout as well as a checkout, because
a check that only ever runs in the source tree is what let this survive. Every
assertion was mutated and confirmed to go red, and the depth case records which
single-level errors its window absorbs rather than claiming to catch them all.

fix(geo-hub): the basemap upstream stopped being keyless and said so in the pixels

The tiles came from a keyless CARTO raster. It is not keyless any more. There
was no release, no notice and no failing check, because the refusal is not in
the response: it still answers 200, with a valid PNG, of the correct
geography, and prints API KEY REQUIRED diagonally across it. Status checks,
byte length checks and image decode checks all stayed green. The founder found
it by looking at the screen.

The interactive maps now read vector tiles from OpenFreeMap and draw the
streets in the browser. OpenFreeMap serves OpenStreetMap data under ODbL,
keyless and quota free, with no clause against proxying, and the whole stack
is self hostable, which is the property that decided it: an operator who
outgrows the public endpoint repoints one constant instead of shopping for a
vendor. Raw OpenStreetMap tiles stay off the table whatever they return, since
the OSMF tile usage policy forbids proxying and app use.

The style is vendored rather than fetched and rewritten at boot. A style names
the URLs the browser goes on to request, the vector source, the relief raster,
the glyph template and the sprite base, and a style that keeps even one
upstream host still renders, so the leak would never show on screen. Vendoring
puts every one of them in the diff, and the vendoring script refuses to write
a file with an external reference left in it.

Two surfaces cannot consume vector data at all, the img card thumbnail and the
Cesium globe imagery provider. Those read public domain Natural Earth shaded
relief, proxied straight through. This is a real downgrade in detail: a
project card and the 3D globe now show terrain rather than streets. It is
taken deliberately, because no keyless raster street basemap survives and a
coarse honest tile beats a detailed one with a watermark across it. Both
surfaces clamp to the zoom that source actually has.

The browser still talks only to our own origin. Ad and privacy blockers block
public tile hosts by name and leave maps blank, so every tile, glyph and
sprite goes through the backend. The raster path deliberately moved from
/tiles/ to /basemap/. The old responses carry Cache-Control immutable for a
week, an immutable entry is never revalidated, and a browser holding a
watermarked tile would keep painting it no matter what the server returns.
A new path is the only way to retire it. The old path is kept for XYZ clients
such as QGIS.

Attribution is one exported constant instead of three pasted copies, and the
raster surfaces carry a separate one. Crediting OpenStreetMap for relief tiles
that contain no OpenStreetMap data would be the same defect mirrored.

The new gate asserts which hosts we are allowed to proxy and why, with the

fix(norm-expansion): creating a norm no longer serializes an unloaded collection

the flush has just made persistent is unloaded rather than empty, and the router
reads it from a synchronous NormResponse.model_validate, where the selectin
loader tries to emit its SELECT outside the async greenlet. That surfaced as

about. Posting a material leaves only the back reference unloaded and the
response model never reads it, build-assembly already refreshes the two
attributes it serializes, and every other path reaches the norm through a select
that fires the loader. Only create_norm had it.

while the API appeared to accept null. The database is right, a null
productivity coefficient has nothing to mean because the expansion math
multiplies it, so there is no migration here and the alembic heads are
unchanged. NormUpdate types every field optional purely to mark it absent, and
model_dump with exclude_unset cannot tell an omitted field from one sent as
null, so an explicit null reached setattr and failed the flush with an integrity
error. The schema now refuses an explicit null across the whole model, which

rejection says which part failed - spec.field, spec.filters[1].op - together
with the value it refused and the vocabulary that path would have accepted.

is how you ask for them on purpose. And a code already owned by a built-in
formula is refused, because the formula wins the lookup and the spec would
have been stored and never consulted.

Custom rows live in the same table as the built-ins and stay apart from them
structurally rather than by anyone remembering: the starter pack upserts by

fix(bi-dashboards): a KPI cannot be deleted out from under its readers, and a report says what it means

Two threads from issue #441. They are one commit because they met in one file:
kpi_spec.py carries both the filter-value check and the null-group key, and
splitting a single file by hunk in a tree a dozen sessions are writing to buys
tidier history at a real risk of committing half an edit.

The custom KPI half. Deleting a KPI checked whether widgets or alert rules
still named it, and a report definition naming it was not counted, so deleting
one broke every report built on it. The referrer scan now reads the alert
expression and the report query spec as well, and the guard asks any() over the
whole result rather than naming two kinds, so a referrer kind added later is
refused by default instead of silently ignored. The exception message was built
from the same two counts and would have said "referenced by 0 widget(s) and 0
alert rule(s)" for a report-only referrer, which is the shape of message that
teaches people the guard is broken; it now names only what is actually holding
the KPI. KPIValue rows are deliberately not referrers: they record what the KPI
measured while it existed, they stay true after the definition goes, and
counting them would make every KPI ever computed with persist=True permanently
undeletable.

The filter value check accepted anything for a text or uuid or bool field and
type-checked only numbers, and isinstance(True, int) is true in Python, so a
four-character JSON payload gave you a KPI that read zero forever and said
nothing. bool is now tested before the numeric acceptance, and the check runs
on each member of an "in" list as well as on a scalar, because a list was a way
round the check its scalar sibling already got. One correction to how this was
first described: a bad uuid does not fail at the driver. GUID is a VARCHAR(36)
decorator that passes any string through, so it is valid SQL matching nothing,
which is the same silent zero by a different road, and uuids are now normalised
to canonical spelling for the same reason.

Delete also did no project access check at all. It takes a required user id
now, not an optional one, so no caller can forget it, and the order is lookup,
not-found, access, is-system, referrers. That order is the point: without it an
outsider was told the KPI is in use and handed widget ids from a project they
had just been refused.

The report half. Three writers each formatted cells their own way, so the same
run read differently depending on which button you pressed. They share one
table now. The CSV was printing Python dict literals into cells verbatim, the
literal string the reporter pasted into the issue, and it was also the fallback
for any unknown output format, so it was the default path rather than an edge.
XLSX was appending raw column keys as headings.

fix(desktop): a link with an ampersand in it stops being two commands

On Windows the OS opener runs cmd /c start "" <target>, and Rust puts quotes
around an argument only when it holds a space or a tab. A target with neither,
https://example.invalid/&calc, therefore reached the command line bare, and
cmd read the ampersand as a separator: everything after it ran as a program.

The scheme check in open_external_url does not stop that, because the string
really does begin with https://. Its docstring said the opposite in as many
words, that a stray or crafted href can never launch an arbitrary local program
through the opener, and a comment asserting a safety property the code does not
have is worse than no comment, because it answers the question for the next
reader who thinks to ask it. That sentence is corrected here too: the scheme
test bounds what the opener is asked to open, and says nothing about how the
string survives the shell on the way there.

The target is quoted now, in spawn_os_opener, which is the one place that
builds the command line and is shared by all three callers, rather than in the
three of them separately. Quoting neutralises the separators and the escape
character, so the only characters left that matter are the ones that break out
of the quoting itself: a double quote and a line break. Those are refused.
Nothing else is, and in particular the ampersand is not: it is ordinary inside
a query string, and a fix that refused it would have broken far more links than
it protected. Percent signs stay too, with the reason written down, since every
encoded character in a URL is spelled with one.

The quoting is written with raw_arg because Rust's own escaping would turn the
quotes into backslash-quote for a program that parses its command line the C
way, and cmd does not.

Four tests, and one of them exists because the other three would not have
caught this. A predicate that refuses quotes and line breaks is easy to test
and would go on passing if the quoting itself came off tomorrow, which is the
whole defect. So the command-line pieces are built by a small pure function and
the test asserts the text actually written onto the line, spelled out in full
rather than rebuilt with the same format! the implementation uses, because an
assertion that cannot disagree with the code it checks is not checking it.
Proved by taking the quoting back off: exactly that test fails, 49 pass, and
the three predicate tests stay green, which is the evidence they were not
enough on their own.

How reachable this is today, stated plainly rather than talked up. Tauri
classifies the app page as a remote origin, because the launcher navigates to
http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ and is_local_url matches only the tauri protocol
origin or a URL relative to the app url, so the four app commands are already
rejected from the application UI and only splash.html can reach the opener.
That is a narrow door and it is ours. But it is narrow by an accident of URL
matching rather than by anything written down, and the desktop remote-server
work in issue #444 turns exactly this into the question of what a page we do
not control may ask the shell to do. A latent primitive behind a comment
claiming it cannot exist is not a thing to leave for later.

50 launcher tests pass. rustfmt deviations on the file stay at the six that
were already there, none of them here; clippy reports nothing in these lines.

implement it, that they intend to run a pilot and adapt the platform to their own
market with an AI assistant, and asked whether there is anything that gets an
assistant up to speed here. There was not. This is that file, DEVELOPING.md, and

The reason it has to exist at all is that the working notes this project runs on

who clones gets none of the conventions, none of the rules and none of the
procedures. Everything a newcomer needs was either in a developer's head or in a
file that does not ship.

It says which document wins when two disagree, and it points at the tree rather
than at itself, because a file that claims to be authoritative about a tree it
cannot see is how documentation rots. The worked example is real: CONTRIBUTING.md
said the Python line length was 100 and pyproject.toml says 120, and ruff reads
the second, so a reader who trusted the prose would have reformatted correct code.

grounds. CONTRIBUTING.md opened with a fork and clone quickstart, a branch naming
scheme and a pull request checklist, so the file a first time contributor reads
first walked them straight into work that would be turned away, and a bot would
have asked them to sign a contributor licence agreement for a merge that was never
going to happen. Both files now say the same thing in the same place: issues,

they cannot propose. It keeps the thank you and now leads with the briefing and

directory, a locale key that falls back silently with every gate green, two

ci: three things nothing was checking, and the Python nothing was linting

The Python outside backend/ was ungated. CI runs ruff from inside backend/ because
that is where the configuration lives, so scripts/ and tools/ were neither linted
nor format checked by anything, 116 files of it. Running ruff from the repository
root does not fix that, it makes it worse in a quiet way: there is no config at
the root, so ruff finds none, silently falls back to its default line length of
88, and reports violations against a standard this project does not use. The gate
names the config explicitly. It went in at 267 lint errors and 85 files that
wanted reformatting, and comes out at zero and zero.

That normalisation would have been undone on the next commit anyone made. The
ruff hooks in .pre-commit-config.yaml run with no config, so from the root they
would reformat scripts/ back to 88 columns. Naming the config on the existing
hooks is not the fix either, and this was measured rather than assumed: from the
root, `ruff format --check --config backend/pyproject.toml` reports 19 of the
demo pack tables as needing reformatting, because an explicit config resolves its
exclude patterns differently from a discovered one, and those tables are hand laid
out one BOQ position per line. So the hooks are split by path. Backend keeps
discovery and behaves exactly as before, scripts and tools get the config named.

A module directory with no manifest.py is invisible to the loader. Not an error,
not a warning, a bare continue: the module is absent from the registry and from
GET /api/v1/modules, its router is never mounted so every endpoint in it answers
404, and its models are never seen by Alembic autogenerate. Every other way a
module can be wrong is loud. This is the one case where a module that is missing
and a module that was never written look identical, and there is no diagnostic to
grep for. check_module_manifests.py now fails on it. Three directories carry no
manifest on purpose, einvoice, measurement and price_breakdown, which are shared
libraries imported by name rather than mounted, and they are allowlisted with a
reason each. The gate rechecks the reason rather than trusting it, so an
allowlisted directory that grows a router or a table fails.

That recheck is worth a line of its own. The first version of it keyed on the
filenames router.py and models.py, and two of the three libraries keep their data
in model.py, singular. The tables half could therefore never have fired. Right
answer, wrong mechanism, green forever. It finds routers by filename now, which is
how the loader finds them, and tables by content.

countryPortraits.generated.ts is generated, imported at compile time by
caseFaces.ts, and npm run build runs no codegen ahead of tsc, so the file has to
be committed and has to agree with the asset folder. Its generator carried a
--check flag from the day it was written and no workflow ever called it. Two
failures rather than one: art dropped into the folder without regenerating leaves
the manifest stale, so the picture ships and the feature cannot see it, and a
manifest that never reached git fails compilation in whatever clone tries first.

make typecheck ran npm run typecheck, which is tsc --noEmit and stops there. The
gate this project treats as authoritative is npm run build, which is tsc followed
by a bundle, and reading a green --noEmit as a green build is how three broken
HEADs shipped recently. It runs the build now. The mypy half is untouched.

The three new steps go into the job named "Whole-tree structural guards". The
workflow is called "Repo hygiene" and the job is not, and a required check or a
condition written against the workflow name matches nothing and stays silent
about it, which has misled people here repeatedly.

Every gate was run in both directions before landing rather than only in the
direction that passes: a planted defect for each, a non-zero exit that names it,
then a restore verified by sha256 and a clean exit.

The workflow and the two new scripts have to travel together. A step whose script
is not in the tree dies on exit 2 and takes the job red, which this file's own
header records happening twice before.

ci: the guard on the ruff lane now counts both halves, because they can empty separately

The step that proves the ruff lane is reading something counted only the lint
half. The two halves have separate exclude lists and this repository already
sets one of them, [tool.ruff.format] exclude in backend/pyproject.toml for the
demo pack data tables, so a format only exclude is the realistic way this drifts
and it is the quietest of the lot. With every file excluded from formatting,
ruff format --check exits 0 printing nothing at all, not even the stderr warning
the other empty cases produce, while ruff check goes on reporting normally, so
the lane looks alive while the formatting step opens no files. The old guard
passed on exactly that.

Measured on 0.15.20 rather than reasoned about, because the three ways a scope
can empty out do not behave alike. A path that does not exist is already loud,
check exits 1 and format exits 2. A path that exists and holds no Python exits 0
from both with a warning on stderr, and check even prints all checks passed. A
path whose files are all excluded by config is identical to that, in both the
plain exclude and the force-exclude form. So a typo was never the risk here. A
widened .gitignore pattern is, and .gitignore line 394 already empties part of
this scope by that mechanism today.

Proven in all three directions by pulling the step's shell body verbatim out of
the parsed YAML and running it under the same shell the runner uses. A good
scope reports 116 and 116 and exits 0. A scope with no Python reports zero and
zero and exits 1 naming the lint half. A format only exclude reports 116 and
zero and exits 1 naming the formatting half, and that is the case that would
have shipped green.

The floor stays at zero rather than a number near today's 116. A count that has
to be edited whenever a file is added is a ratchet somebody eventually raises
without reading, and there is a second reason that only showed up while this was
being written: the same command reported 130 files at one point and 116 minutes
later, because a dozen sessions are writing to this tree. A floor pinned near
today's count would go red on tree movement alone. Both counts are echoed so a
partial collapse is still visible to a human reading the log.

One thing worth knowing that reads backwards when you need it: a path named on
the command line bypasses exclude unless force-exclude is set. The gate names
scripts and tools, so an exclude pattern matching those two directories
themselves would be ignored and the lane would keep reading. Only patterns
matching files inside them apply during the walk.
