fix(bi-dashboards): an alert threshold has to be a number, and it is checked when the rule is written

The same hole as the one closed in the KPI spec in 401c84b6a, one module
over. An alert rule compares a measured KPI against a threshold somebody
typed, and the coercion in front of that comparison fell back to
Decimal("0") only when a value failed to parse. NaN, sNaN and Infinity all
parse, in any case and in their short forms, so none of them ever met the
fallback. What they met was the comparison. An ordering comparison against
NaN raises out of the evaluator once a cycle for as long as the rule
exists, neq against NaN is true whatever the measurement so the rule fires
on every evaluation, and an infinity is simply larger or smaller than
everything. A boolean took the other route, because Decimal(str(True)) does
raise, and the fallback turned true into zero, which is a threshold
somebody could have meant, so nothing about the stored rule said it had
been rewritten.

Expressions are validated now in create_alert, next to where a custom KPI
spec is validated, and the router answers a refusal with 422 naming the
path into the tree that was refused. The walk also refuses an empty and,
which evaluates to True and fires every cycle, a kpi leaf with no code,
whose empty code resolves to a zero computation that is then compared
against the threshold, and a field source outside the one the evaluator can
actually read.

_coerce_decimal keeps its name and loses its fallback. It returns None for
a value it cannot read, because zero is a threshold somebody may genuinely
mean and a value that could not be read must not arrive at the comparison
wearing one. The two sides it serves are not symmetric. The threshold is
written by a person and can be refused while they are still looking at what
they wrote. The measured side arrives from a KPI or an ORM column at
evaluation time, so the only place to catch it is the comparison, and there
it raises rather than answering False. False looks like the safe answer and
is not, because under a not it inverts and a rule nobody can evaluate would
fire every cycle. The raise is caught per rule in evaluate_alert and again
in evaluate_alerts, so one unevaluatable rule fails closed and the loop
carries on. Two things stop being answered wrongly as a result. A NULL
project column used to become Decimal("0"), so a rule reading
project.budget below a hundred fired on a project with no budget recorded.
And a boolean comparison folded both sides onto zero, so True equalled
False.

Validation closes the way in, it does not sweep the rows that came in
before it, and there is no migration here for them.

docs(licensing): say what the LGPL libraries in our binaries oblige us to do

We ship LGPL code in every artefact and until now the notice for it was
partly right and partly not there at all. This writes the position down
and puts the licence texts where they travel with the code.

What was measured, on the published 16.0.0 release rather than on the
tree. The Linux sidecar inside the AppImage carries the psycopg2
extension with fifteen native libraries beside it, and the OpenCV
extension with fifteen more, five of which are FFmpeg. It carries 365
dist-info directories and neither psycopg2's nor OpenCV's is among them,
so the code arrived in the installers and the licence did not. The
AppImage itself carries about a hundred and seventy shared objects
including GTK 3 and WebKitGTK, with seventeen Debian copyright files
that cover neither of those two. The Python package and the container
image are in a different position and were already fine, because pip
installs each library's own licence beside it.

So three texts are now committed under backend/app/core/licenses, the
route that already carries the HarfBuzz text and that the same
measurement found reaching the sidecar. LGPL-3.0 for psycopg2, LGPL-2.1
for FFmpeg and the Linux desktop stack, and GPL-3.0 because LGPL-3.0 is
written as additional permissions on top of it and asks for both; the
AGPL text we ship for our own code is a different licence and does not
stand in for it.

NOTICE gains a section that answers the three things LGPL actually asks
of a distributor, per artefact: telling the recipient the library is
there and giving them its text, giving them the source, and leaving them
able to run their own build of the library instead. It carries an offer
of source that names an address rather than gesturing at upstream, and
it says that the same components on the same terms are in the community
edition and the commercial one, because there is no separate build. A
second new section says what the AppImage contains, which nothing in the
file mentioned before. The FFmpeg entry used to say the codecs ship as a
separate dynamically loaded library so nothing is missing. That is true
of the wheel and the container and false of the frozen desktop build,
and it now says which is which. The same entry now names the OpenSSL
inside the Linux OpenCV wheel as 1.1.1k, which predates the Apache
relicence, so the Apache text committed for the OpenSSL 3 and 4 copies
is not the licence of that one.

COMMERCIAL-LICENSE.md gains 4b, next to the PyMuPDF section, saying that
a commercial licensee gets the identical binaries with the identical
libraries, that deploying obliges them to nothing, and what changes if
they redistribute. THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md explains why its generated
table shows Apache-2.0 for OpenCV while the wheel carries LGPL codecs.

Whether a frozen single file bundle satisfies LGPL-3.0 section 4 by way
of a public build specification and a pinned lock is the one question
here that is a matter of law rather than a fact about the build. NOTICE
says what we do and says plainly that the question is with counsel,
rather than asserting an answer.

aborts on the first entry it cannot find. Two 16.2.0 commits added

feat(boq): own every file we ship to read and write GAEB

The repository carried three schema files published by GAEB and two
conformance files published by BVBS, 8,070 lines of the first and 105 KB of
the second, all verbatim. They were test-only and never reached PyPI, since
the release builds a wheel and no sdist, but they sat in a public repository
and in every source tarball GitHub generates for a tag.

The specification they come from is copyrighted. The title page of the GAEB
DA XML 3.3 Fachdokumentation reads "(c) 2023 by DIN Deutsches Institut fuer
Normung e. V.". The schema files and the conformance files can both be
downloaded from the publishers without payment or registration, which is
worth knowing, but free to download is not free to redistribute, and no
grant of a redistribution right appears on the download pages, in the site
imprint, in the Fachdokumentation, or inside the files, which carry no
notice at all. Where the terms are silent the conservative reading is that
nothing was granted, so we stop shipping them.

Nothing about GAEB support is dropped. A reader and a writer do not need the
publisher's file, they need the element model, and that is published for
implementers to use. What replaces the deleted files:

A profile schema of our own, in backend/app/modules/boq/gaeb_profile/, one
file per exchange phase. It is written from the documented element model and
from our own reader and writer rather than by editing anyone's copy, it
covers only the subset this product supports, and it uses type names of our
choosing. It ships with the product, so a customer can validate our output
against a schema we can answer for.

Two conformance fixtures of our own, generated by
backend/scripts/generate_gaeb_conformance_fixtures.py, which also carries
the reasoning and the arithmetic. They keep every shape the deleted files
were pinning, because a fixture that avoids the hard cases stops testing the
bugs it was written for: four Indexpositionen distinguished only by
RNoIndex, an embedded base64 graphic in a Langtext, a three-part OZ mask,
Bedarfspositionen with no price, an X84 whose items carry UP and IT but no
Qty at all, and a markup whose percentage applies to a partial base. The
money is round on purpose: 27 items summing to 1,915,000.00, a markup of
85,000.00, a declared total of 2,000,000.00.

The conformance claim now rests on the publisher's schema rather than on
ours. Validating our own writer against our own schema proves less than it
looks, since a mistake present in both would pass, so the tests that make
the conformance claim fetch the published schema at test time and skip when
no copy is available. That is use, not redistribution. CI sets
OCE_GAEB_FETCH_XSD so they run there; a developer can point GAEB_XSD_DIR at
a local copy instead; and a test that cannot reach the publisher skips
rather than fails, because an unreachable web server says nothing about our
exporter.

One belief died in the process. The tests used to adapt the 3.2 schema into
a 3.3 oracle by rewriting its namespace and widening two enumerations,
because a comment said GAEB does not publish the 3.3 schema as a free
download and ships it to members. That is not true and has not been: the
3.3 schema packages are listed on the public downloads page. The whole
adaptation is gone, and both our exports and both new fixtures validate
against the real 3.3 schema unmodified.

docs/standards/GAEB.md states what our implementation is built from, what we
assert about conformance, and what we do not, which is any kind of
certification. NOTICE carries the short version.

docs(costs): correct how seeding interacts with the zero quantity defect

The previous commit described the component quantity defect as reproducible by
importing the assemblies template, seeding prices and repricing. That sequence
does not reproduce it, and the message and the guide both said it would.

Seeding reads the price already recorded on each component under unit_rate, and
freshly written recipes carry none, so it produces a sheet of zeros. A resource
priced below half a cent counts as unpriced, and an item on which nothing priced
is left alone rather than zeroed, so a reprice straight after a seed changes
nothing and reports the items unpriced.

The defect itself is real and is unchanged: a missing quantity is read as zero
rather than as absent, so every line prices at zero cost and still counts as
priced. It bites on the first run after the prices are real, which is the first
run anyone is inclined to believe. The documents now say that, and the seeding
step says what a seeded sheet actually contains.

feat(rebar-schedule): a bending schedule arrives as a file and leaves as steel

Adds oe_rebar_schedule, an importer and exporter for the ABS reinforcement
data interchange format described by the BVBS guideline "Datenaustausch von
Bewehrungsdaten", interface description version 3.1 of May 2021. It reads the
BF2D, BF3D, BFWE, BFMA, BFGT and BFAU super-groups, keeps each record's exact
source line, and re-exports the bytes the bending shop received rather than
our reading of them, because the format's checksum covers exact characters and
a line rebuilt from parsed columns is a different record.

The codec is written from the published specification. Its tests are built
from the guideline's own worked examples, each of which reproduces its printed
checksum, together with data constructed here to break one rule at a time. Two
places where the guideline disagrees with itself are recorded in the test data
rather than smoothed over: the lattice girder example whose printed checksum
does not satisfy the rule the same document states, and the spacer example
whose header omits two fields its own applicability table requires.

fix(costs): a component with no quantity is not a component priced at zero

Repricing read a recipe component's quantity through a helper that returns zero
for an absent key. A component carrying no quantity therefore contributed a
line cost of nothing, counted as a priced line, and left the work item counted
as fully priced. The rate was then overwritten with 0.00 and every figure in
the response agreed the run had gone well: coverage complete, no missing
resources, nothing to look at.

That is the worst way for a costing tool to be wrong. A rate of zero that
announces itself as fully priced is indistinguishable from a measurement, and
the person who finds out is whoever bid on it.

A quantity is now read by a function that answers None when the component
carries none, and a component with no usable quantity stops the item being
repriced at all. Blank, unparseable, negative and non-finite values answer None
too, since a NaN can arrive from a parquet column with nulls. An explicit zero
is a real quantity and is kept.

Three outcomes now leave an item's rate alone rather than publish a number that
cannot be trusted, and each is reported separately rather than folded into one
count. No line priced at all is items_unpriced, which is what it always was. A
component with no usable quantity is items_unreadable, which is a different
statement: we know the prices and cannot read the recipe, rather than knowing
the recipe and not the prices. A fully priced recipe that computes to nothing
while the item already carries a rate is items_zero_total, because whatever the
cause, replacing a real rate with 0.00 and calling the run a success is the
worse of the two available mistakes. Only an item whose rate was actually
recomputed counts towards coverage.

The stored breakdown now adds up to the rate it explains. Costs were
accumulated over every component type and published under three, so a
subcontractor line was inside the rate and absent from its explanation: one
shipped roofing recipe reprices to 442.10 and stored a breakdown showing 17.10.
Anything outside the three named buckets lands in other_cost, which is derived
from the total rather than re-summed so rounding cannot leave the buckets short,

ci(migrations): ask about the graph in the commit, not the one on this disk

The head check read the versions directory on disk. In CI the working directory
is the checked out ref, so it worked there and only there. In a working tree
shared by several sessions it answers about a tree that exists on one machine
and nowhere else, and it does that most confidently in the case where it is
most wrong.

That case happened. A revision was committed declaring a parent that is a
finished file sitting untracked in this tree. The author ran this script first
and it reported one head, which was true of the disk. In the commit the same
graph held a parent that did not exist and therefore two heads, alembic upgrade
refused to run at all, and every install built from that commit could not
migrate. CI caught it, because CI is the reader that sees the ref, and by then
it was pushed.

The committed content is read from the index with git ls-files and git cat-file.
The index already is HEAD's blobs with staged changes applied, so no temp
directory is written, no history is needed, and nothing is created under the
versions directory where every other session would read it as a revision.

Work here goes in as git commit --only with explicit paths, which builds its
tree from HEAD plus the working-tree content of those paths and never stages
anything. A check that only read the index would therefore be silent about the
very file being committed, which is the original failure wearing a hat, so
--committing takes the paths and lays their working-tree content over the index
base. Run that way against the untracked revision, the check goes red and says
exactly what committing it as it stands would do.

Both graphs are still computed. When they agree the output is one line. When
they differ the difference is stated as the finding, naming the revisions on
each side and the ones whose parentage changed, and the committed graph decides
the exit code. A disk that is broken while the commit is sound is reported as a
warning that says so in those words, because the obvious repair otherwise is to
edit a revision that is already correct and already pushed.

One thing the self-test found about itself. The floor that catches a scan which
never saw the migration tree was one of the structural faults, and every
in-memory fixture holds three or four revisions, so every fixture tripped it.
Every assertion of the shape "this sound graph reports no fault" was therefore
true of a graph that was reporting one, and the assertions the rewrite most
needed were the ones the floor had made vacuous. The floor is a fact about the
scan rather than about the graph and now sits on its own, where a committed
scan that reads too little exits non-zero saying it concluded nothing rather
than passing.

fix(desktop): open links without handing them to a shell

Opening a link on Windows ran cmd /c start "" "<target>", so the address became
part of a command line that cmd.exe then re-parsed. Quoting held off the command
separators, but cmd expands %NAME% inside quotes as readily as outside, so a
link could carry a variable reference that cmd substituted on the way past.
Measured on Windows 11, with the exact command line the old code produced:
%USERNAME% became the account name and %CD% became the full path of the working
directory, both sent to whatever host the link named. That is the local username
and the local filesystem layout disclosed to a third party, and the user sees a
page load.

It mattered more than it used to because the application window can now invoke
the link command. Until then every link came from one of our own string
literals. Now a value carried in a project can reach it.

Sanitising was the wrong instinct and two plausible rules were tried and
rejected on measurement. Refusing a percent followed by two hex digits fails
because %CD% is a real variable and C and D are both hex digits, so the rule has
to refuse it and then also refuses every legitimately encoded character.
Refusing names that std::env::var resolves fails because cmd expands dynamic
pseudo-variables that are not in the environment block at all: CD, DATE, TIME,
RANDOM and ERRORLEVEL all expand while the environment reports them absent. Six
of seven names measured expanded and one of them was in the environment. An
undefined name survives literally, so a test written with an obvious name
returns a green that means nothing. Enumerating what a shell does to a string is
a list, not a fix.

So the command line is gone. ShellExecuteW takes the target as one argument and
no shell parses it, which closes quoting, separators and percent expansion at
once rather than one at a time. The call runs on its own thread with COM
initialised, because the shell may delegate an open to a shell extension that
requires an apartment and a Tauri command runs on whatever thread Tauri chose;
a dedicated thread makes the pairing with CoUninitialize exact and leaves no
apartment behind on a worker something else reuses. The caller waits the same
400ms the child poll used to get, so a refusal is still reported and a slow
shell still cannot freeze the window.

Reporting improves as a side effect. The old code spawned a child and inferred
from an early exit. ShellExecuteW answers synchronously, so a missing file
association is now reported as one instead of read as success.

This closes the %VAR% disclosure on Windows. It was reported when the access
control list work made the link command reachable from the application page, and
this is the commit that answers it. There is no remaining path from a link to a
shell on any platform.

macOS and Linux are untouched. They never had a shell in this path: both pass
the target to the opener as an argument already.

The Cargo.lock is unchanged. windows-sys was already a direct dependency of this
crate for the Win32 message box on the startup failure path, and cargo records
versions and dependency edges rather than features, so asking for Win32_UI_Shell
and Win32_System_Com adds no package and moves no pin. Verified with --locked
and by hashing the file either side.

Three tests that pinned the cmd.exe quoting contract are gone with the contract,
and two take their place. The replacement asserts the exact wide string handed
to lpFile against one built from the literal, for an ampersand, a double quote,
a CRLF, percent-encoded text and %CD%, %USERNAME%, %RANDOM%, %TIME% and %DATE%
together, all of which must now arrive unmodified. The other refuses an interior
null, which is the one character that still has to be refused because it
truncates what the shell sees. %CD% is a case rather than only a sentence, since
it is the name that defeats both of the rules above and the next person to look
at this will reach for the first of them.

docstring said so. That is a publisher's authored test data reproduced in full,

rather than silent: the BVBS imprint states that reproduction, editing,
distribution and any form of exploitation beyond the limits of copyright need

without the example.

test(desktop): fail the build if the link opener starts a process

The shell is gone from the Windows link opener, and the only thing keeping it
gone was that the three helpers doing the quoting had been deleted. That is
less protection than it looks. The compiler refuses calls to functions that no
longer exist and has nothing whatever to say about a fresh Command::new("cmd")
written under a fourth name, and a guard keyed to a helper stops protecting the
moment somebody adds a second caller.

So the gate asks a property of the path rather than the absence of three names.
Does anything in the Windows link-opening path construct a process at all, and
does anything anywhere in the crate start a program that re-parses what it is
given. The first question is scoped to the Windows arms of open_with_os_default,
shell_target and shell_execute. The second covers every Rust file in the crate,
which matters because the remote server work is adding one.

A scan cannot report its own empty scope, so the gate asserts it found the
opener before concluding anything about what it did not find there. If one of
those functions is renamed, split or moved, the gate fails saying it can no
longer find the path instead of passing on having read nothing. That check
earned its place immediately: writing the false-positive control for the macOS
and Linux arms found that #[cfg(not(target_os = "windows"))] contains the string
target_os = "windows", so matching the substring collected the arm meaning the
exact opposite. Both arms share a name and the negated one is written second, so
it displaced the arm under inspection while the gate went on reporting that it
had found three functions. not(...) is now stripped before the attribute is
read, bodies are returned as a list of pairs rather than a mapping so two arms
under one name are both scanned, and a round asserts the arm inspected in
main.rs is the one that calls shell_target rather than the one that spawns.

The general rule behind that is in the docstring because it keeps coming back. A
proof that plants a defect has to check the defect actually landed, or its
silence is indistinguishable from its success. The proof for the opener change
first reported finding zero sites to plant, because main.rs is a CRLF file and
the planted literals were not; had it asserted only that the tests went red it
would have said nothing at all while looking like it ran.

Six rounds, none of which touch main.rs, since that file belongs to the remote
server work now. Three go through the gate end to end with a probe file that is
created and removed: a shell started under a name the gate has never heard of
fails, a process that is not a shell inside the opener path fails, and the same
words in comments stay green, which is what stops the gate being switched off by
whoever has to write the sentence explaining it. Three drive the detectors
directly for the cases that could only be expressed by editing main.rs. The
source tree hashes identical before and after every round.

The container's LV member put the position's internal unit into <QU> verbatim,
so a lump sum left as "lsum" and a piece as "pcs". Neither is a GAEB unit code.
The other writer in the platform translates through a lexicon before it emits
<QU>; this one did not, so the one file the module exists to hand to somebody
else carried a vocabulary only we understand.

What a consumer sees. Before, <QU>lsum</QU> and <QU>pcs</QU>, which a reader
working from the GAEB lexicon cannot resolve and will either reject or read as
an unknown label. After, <QU>psch</QU> and <QU>Stk</QU>, which are the codes for
a lump sum and a piece. Units that were already codes, m3 and kg and m2, are
unchanged, which is why the existing round-trip tests never saw this: every unit
they used mapped to itself.

The mapping now lives in boq/units.py as GAEB_UNIT_CODES rather than inside the
other writer, because two writers were translating the same direction and only
one had a table. The inverse map in importers/gaeb_xml.py already claimed to be
the single source of truth for the round trip and had no partner on this side.
The exporter in boq/router.py still carries its own copy; that one is left for
the commit that changes the exporter, so this change stays readable.

Round-trip is preserved rather than traded away, and there is a test for it:
"lsum" leaves as "psch" and the platform importer maps "psch" back to "lsum", so
the container keeps the lossless property the module is built around.

Two smaller things fixed on the same line. The unit was capped at 20 characters
where our own X8x profile schemas allow 10, so a long locale label could exceed
what we ourselves say is valid; it is capped at 10 now. And an empty unit used
to emit an empty <QU/> element, which is now omitted, since the schema makes the
element optional and an empty one states nothing.

The new tests assert against the format's vocabulary rather than an expected
string, and that vocabulary is written out in the test rather than imported from
the table the writer uses, so the test cannot be satisfied by whatever the table
happens to say. Verified against the previous writer: with the old behaviour
restored in memory the emitted codes are lsum and pcs and both assertions fail,

fix(boq): a stated unit retires the claim that the file stated none

A GAEB import records the source's own QU in metadata gaeb_unit_original,
writing the empty string when the file said nothing, which an X84 item always
does because it cannot carry a unit at all. The importer then guesses a unit so
the row can be stored, and that empty key is what marks the stored unit as ours
rather than the file's.

The key was carrying two claims at once: what the source said, and whether the
current value is still our guess. Those agree at import and come apart the
moment somebody edits the row. An estimator who corrects an invented lsum to m3
has stated a unit, and the row went on asserting that nobody had. Every reader
of that claim then acted on it, the GAEB export among them, so the export
discarded a unit a person had deliberately supplied, on exactly the rows
somebody cared enough to fix. Worse than the fabrication it was meant to fix,
and pointed at the users doing the right thing.

A real change to the unit now retires the claim.

The claim is dropped, not rewritten. It says this unit came from our fallback
because the file could not state one, and once a person types m3 that is not
superseded, it is false. Storing the new unit under the same key would keep a
slot alive that reads as provenance and no longer is, for the next reader to
interpret or the next writer to fill in. Absence is the honest form of having no
claim, and it already means the right thing everywhere downstream: no key means
this is not a row we guessed for, which is exactly true once a human has spoken.

Only a real change counts, compared case-insensitively. Re-submitting the same
unit is not a person stating anything. It is a grid echoing a form back, a bulk
update touching every row, an import re-running over an unedited export. If
those cleared the claim the provenance would evaporate on any workflow that
rewrites rows wholesale, and it would do it invisibly. There is a test that
submits the identical unit and asserts the claim survives, because that is the
case a later refactor breaks without noticing.

One function needed changing. update_position is the only place a unit reaches
the database on an edit: bulk_update_positions loads each row and delegates to
it per row to keep the downstream invariants firing, the import round trip
reaches it through _prepared_row_to_update, and the repository has no unit
writes at all.

The test that earns its place most is the one where the patch carries its own
metadata. The grid sends the whole blob back on an edit, still holding the empty
original, so a rule that only read stored metadata would let the client's stale
copy win and lose the correction precisely where a human is most likely to make
it. The new metadata is consulted first for that reason.

Eight tests, including one end to end: import an X84, correct one position by
hand, export X83, and confirm the corrected row carries m3 while its untouched
neighbour still carries no unit at all.

ci(prompts): hold open the assumption an Article 5 measurement was built on

A sweep for prohibited AI practices came back clean across the platform. That
result does not rest on anybody's judgement, it rests on one property of the
code: every instruction we send to a model is a literal somebody can open and
read. Read the constants and you have read what we ask a model to do. The sweep
was only meaningful because that was true.

Nothing makes it stay true. The day a prompt is assembled from a database row,
a settings record, a request body or an uploaded file, the source stops
answering the question, and a customer could ask for an inference we have never
shipped through a pipeline we did ship, with no change of ours to find. The
measurement would not become wrong, it would become unanswerable, and the
person quoting it a year from now would have no way to tell the difference.

So this guards the property rather than the conclusion. If it goes red the
honest response is to redo the measurement, not to widen the guard.

It is deliberately not a clean bill, because the property is already not
universal and hiding that would be the worst version of this file. Seven call
sites are recorded with the reading behind each. Six are places the scan cannot
follow and a person did: a helper that appends a language line to a constant, a
closure invoked from one place with a module constant, a role that picks between
three constants. One is genuinely runtime, the custom-agent runner, where the
text is written by the agent's own creator and read back only for them. Somebody
asking "where else can instruction text come from" now has one list to read
instead of a codebase.

Three things about how it is built are worth knowing before trusting it.

It resolves an argument by hops rather than by whole-program dataflow: one hop
through the enclosing function, one through a private helper's callers in the
same file, then module constants and imports. Imports are collected from
anywhere in a file, not just the top, because this codebase defers imports into
function bodies on purpose and reading only the top left most real prompt
constants looking unresolvable.

A slot it cannot resolve fails exactly like a violation and says it concluded
nothing, and so does an interpreter too old to parse the syntax the backend
uses. A scan that skipped what it could not read would be quietest about the
newest code, which is the code most likely to have just changed.

The self-test carries red fixtures as well as green, and it earns them: three
mutations were run against it, one per mechanism, and each was caught by the
fixture aimed at it. One of those mechanisms is a bug this scan had. A bound
method's self is not among the call's positional arguments, so the parameter
index was one too far, and the scan cleared a real call site by reading the
payload sitting next to the instruction. It reported that with full confidence.
That is the failure mode worth designing against here: not a guard that misses,
a guard that inspects the wrong thing and passes.

Not wired into any lane yet. It reads every file under backend/app to decide
which ones to parse, which is a few seconds alone and much longer when the tree
is busy, so where it belongs is a call about everybody's commit loop rather than
about this file. Run it as python scripts/check_prompt_provenance.py, and with
--self-test to check the scanner before believing the scan.

docs(privacy): the transfer section describes what the software actually does

Section 2 said no personal data left the EEA except under standard contractual
clauses put in place by DDC. Neither half held. The clauses half could not: the
AI features run on a key the operator supplies, so the account and the
agreement are between the operator and the provider, and DDC is not a party to
that relationship and cannot conclude clauses inside it. On a self-hosted
install DDC is not involved at all.

The absolute half did not hold either, and that is the part the old sentence
got wrong quietly. The application makes outbound requests beyond the AI
providers, and some leave the EEA. Setting a project address sends that address
to the public OpenStreetMap Nominatim service by default, which is user content
and not merely a request. Weather features send coordinates to Open-Meteo or
OpenWeatherMap. Cost-base files, encoder weights and vector snapshots are
fetched from GitHub and Hugging Face, which carry no project content but do
disclose the requesting server's address like any HTTP request. None of that
was covered by the old sentence and none of it was disclosed anywhere else.

So section 2 now lists the outbound requests the software makes, says which
are optional and how to switch them off, and states where the geocoder can be
pointed at a self-hosted mirror. It states facts about the software and leaves
the legal characterisation to Chapter V, which it cites without paraphrasing
what it requires of a reader. The replaced sentence is called out in the
section rather than swapped silently, because a privacy document that changes
a material claim without saying so is worse than one that admits it changed.

Section 5 listed six AI providers where the product offers eighteen. The twelve
missing were every provider outside an adequacy decision except DeepSeek, which
is the opposite of a harmless omission. The list is now complete and carries
the endpoint host for each, taken from the endpoint constants rather than from
memory, so a reader can see where content would go before enabling anything.

assertion about adequacy would have done as well. The lead-in says plainly that
listing a provider is not a recommendation and implies no assessment of it.

which left the one path that transmits a third party's voice invisible: phone
log and voice capture send the recording to OpenAI. The note ends by putting
the question to the person about to upload rather than instructing them.

acknowledgement is now actually consulted, and ai/router.py advisor_chat, whose

matches nothing. Both read as a reviewed exception from outside and only the

fix(norm-expansion): match a material by name before scoring it

A material was priced by the lexical matcher alone, so a name that is present
in the catalogue verbatim could still be answered by a different row that
merely scored well. An exact tier now runs first: the name and every catalogue
description are folded to a comparison key, and a row is accepted only when
the keys are equal, with the tie broken on unit, then region, then price
freshness, then code. Candidates are loaded by three widening passes and the
key comparison decides all of them, so a wider scan never loosens a match.
Only an exact identity is returned without review; everything else stays a
scored proposal with needs_review set. The key keeps Unicode letters rather
than ASCII, so a Cyrillic or CJK name is compared on its own words instead of
on whatever digits it happens to carry, and a decimal separator between digits
leaves a character behind in the key instead of vanishing, so a 1,2 mm sheet
and a 12 mm sheet cannot become the same key while a comma and a point still
agree. Two limits remain pinned as failing tests: a row reachable only by its
localized description, and a punctuation-only material name that the lexical
tier still scores.

One boundary is worth stating because it is easy to read this change as
wider than it is. The tokenizer emits Cyrillic and CJK tokens, and that is
proven and independent of any environment. Whether those tokens then reach
rows whose stored text differs only in case depends on the database, because
PostgreSQL folds case through the database ctype and under the C locale that
is ASCII only. The cluster the desktop build creates is pinned to C on
purpose, for a documented reason, so on that cluster this tier can only match
a non-Latin row whose stored case already equals the folded token. That is not
a regression, since before this change there was no exact tier at all and the
miss falls through to the scored matcher exactly as it did, but it does mean
the tier is not yet doing for non-Latin catalogues what it does for Latin
ones. Fixing that properly is a platform change and is not this one.

feat(compliance): modules declare what they do with inference

The first question a regulator or a buyer asks is which of the things you ship
performs inference, and on what. Until now that could only be answered by a
person reading every module and forming an opinion, which is how a sweep of
this platform's AI surface finished without having opened the module that
posts call audio to a speech to text provider. A module can now answer for
itself, and a scanner checks the answers against the code, because a register
nobody checks drifts and this one gets quoted outside the project.

The vocabulary is closed rather than free text, because two hundred modules
and an open string become four spellings of the same word within a quarter.
The default is absent rather than none, and that difference is the point of
the field: absent means nobody has looked at this module, none means somebody
looked and there is nothing there. Defaulting to none would turn every module
that has never been read into a module asserting it performs no inference,
producing a register that reads as complete while being populated by silence,
which is worse than one that is visibly empty because an empty register is not
quoted and a wrong one is. A module may declare more than once, since one
answer per module is the wrong shape for at least one endpoint here, where the
catalogue matcher runs a predefined string rule in one mode and a learned
encoder in another with the mode chosen by a request parameter.

An incomplete declaration is collected rather than raised. A manifest that
raises is skipped by the loader, which would take the whole module off the air
and answer every one of its endpoints with a 404 over a missing sentence, so a
paper problem would become an outage. A role outside the vocabulary does raise,
because that is a wrong statement rather than an incomplete one and it raises
in the manifest that wrote it, one line from its author.

The scanner is scoped by what a module actually reaches rather than by its
name, because a gate keyed on names passes the speech to text module in
silence, that module having a filing sounding name, and flags a pure rule
engine that sounds like inference. Every import under backend/app is read with
ast and resolved into a graph, and the walk stops at another module's boundary,
because following every edge puts 56 modules in scope and most of that is one
module calling another's public function that happens to run a model inside;
the producer carries the obligation. A second textual pass runs alongside it
for the shape no import graph can find, a model constructed in place, and
reports separately.

The scanner is wired into the structural hygiene job, where it REPORTS AND
DOES NOT BLOCK ON FINDINGS. Measured on the tree as this lands: 193 module
directories scanned, 31 reach an inference primitive on their own account, 7
declare it, 24 declare nothing, none declare the opposite. Article 50 is not
satisfied by this commit and the gate says so in its own output every run,
which is the honest state to land in; making it fail today would paint every
lane red over a gap that predates the register. It does still block on a
broken or stale scan, a file that will not parse or a primitive whose name has
left the tree, and that second case is the one worth having, because a renamed
primitive makes every module stop reaching it and the instrument would read
green while blind.

Two manifest sentences were wrong and are corrected here. One claimed a write
tool was gated on manager rights when the check is owner or admin or any team
member with no role filter, which widens the stated exposure rather than
narrowing it. The other claimed no attribute chain in an evaluator that has
six, all of them naming literal attributes, so the substance held but the
sentence would not have survived the first grep an auditor ran.

fix(procurement): hold the purchase order still while deciding to remove it

Removing a purchase order counted the records that depend on it and then
deleted, with nothing holding the row still in between. Three of the four
kinds of dependent are CASCADE or SET NULL, so a goods receipt or a retainage
release created in that window was counted as absent and then destroyed by the
delete that followed. Nothing logged it. The operator saw a purchase order
removed cleanly and the receipt was simply gone.

The row is now locked before anything is asked about it. The lock goes in the
one shared guard, so a fourth removal door cannot be added later that counts
without locking, and also at the top of the delete and cancel paths, because
both read the status trail before the guard runs and would otherwise decide on
a pre-lock snapshot. Cancelling is the case where that matters most: the prior
status chooses which compensating event fires, so a stale read releases a
budget commitment twice or not at all.

Three of the four kinds then serialise without the insert path cooperating,
because the database does it. A row carrying a foreign key to the purchase
order takes a share lock on its parent as it is inserted, which conflicts with
the lock the removal holds, so a concurrent goods receipt, retainage release or
material requisition either waits or committed early enough to be counted.

Payable invoices are the exception and the reason the lock is also taken when
one is raised. An invoice carries no foreign key to the purchase order; the
link is a stamp in a metadata column filtered in Python, so nothing in the
schema makes that insert wait. Those two paths serialise by agreeing to, which
means a second way of raising an invoice against a purchase order has to take
the lock as well. That is written where the next person will read it.

The new tests assert that the lock is taken and that it precedes everything the
decision rests on. They prove ordering and not serialisation: the stub has no
database and the call is inert on SQLite. That limit is recorded beside them so
a green run is not mistaken for evidence the lock works.

warehouse were described in a way that made them all look equivalent. They are
not. Most of the keys involved are permissive, so a row created between the
count and the delete is destroyed silently, and exactly three are RESTRICT, so
the same race ends with the database refusing the delete instead. Which of
those two a guard is standing on decides whether it is load-bearing, and the
header now names the three and their behaviour rather than leaving a reader to
find out by deleting something.

One claim beside the vendor count was simply false: it said the four tables
listed there were the four carrying a vendor id. There is a fifth. Corrected.

Two relations are deliberately not counted and now say so where the counting
happens. A vendor scorecard is derived rather than recorded, rebuilt from the
orders, receipts and invoices, so blocking on one would make a vendor that was
never traded with permanently undeletable to protect a cached figure. Stock
movements are the harder case and the note is honest about the trade: they are
destroyed with their item or warehouse, and counting them would make anything
ever stocked undeletable, which would contradict the rule that an emptied
balance does not block. The alternative for a location whose history matters is
to deactivate it rather than delete it, and that is now written down.

The stock movement model also stopped calling itself immutable. It is
append-only, which is a different claim and the true one: a correction is a new
movement in the opposite direction rather than an edit of the wrong row. A row
described as immutable while sitting on a cascading foreign key invites a
reader to believe something the schema does not do.

migration.

feat(construction-control): refuse to delete a record something still points at

Site records could be deleted while other records still referred to them, which
left a non-conformance report pointing at an inspection that no longer existed.
Deletion now goes through two separate questions. One asks whether the record's
own status permits it, so a closed or void inspection stays put. The other asks
whether anything else is holding it, and names what, so the refusal tells the
operator which report to deal with rather than only that the answer is no.

Keeping those two apart matters more than it looks. A status lock and a holder
lock both produce a refusal, and a test that only checks for a refusal cannot
tell which one fired. The test covering the held case now reopens the
inspection first, which is the real re-inspection workflow rather than a
contrivance, so the status lock is genuinely out of the way and the holder
branch is the only thing left that can refuse. It asserts the reopen succeeded
before it asserts anything about the delete, because if reopening ever stops
working the status lock would refuse anyway and the test would quietly go back
to passing for the wrong reason.

That test was checked by breaking the guard rather than by watching it pass.
With the reference count forced to zero the inspection is deleted, 204, while a
live report points at it, and the test fails naming exactly that. The negative
control, a reopened inspection with nothing holding it, still deletes cleanly
under the same sabotage, so the check discriminates rather than simply objecting.

The count's tolerance for a missing module is narrower than it was. Only the
absence of the non-conformance module itself returns zero; any other missing
import propagates instead of being reported as no holders, which would have let
evidence be deleted because something unrelated failed to import.

fix(calendars): repair the working weeks that were written on the wrong axis

Saudi Arabia was stored as a week containing 0, on a column read with
isoweekday, which answers 1 through 7 and never 0. So one day of the week
matched nothing and the country counted a four day week. The week of 4 January
2026 came back as four working days where it should be five, and nothing
reported a problem, because a shorter week is a perfectly ordinary answer.

The repair targets the impossible value rather than the country. A 0 in that
column cannot be a preference somebody chose, since it selects no day that
exists, so any week carrying one is wrong from the row alone without knowing
who wrote it. It rewrites 0 to 7 in place, keeps the order, and does not
duplicate a 7 the row already has. A booleanFalse is declined rather than
promoted to Sunday, because that is a different defect and guessing would
invent a working day out of a value that never meant one.

Checked by building the tempting wrong rule instead of an obviously broken one.
A repair keyed on the week being four days long gets Saudi Arabia exactly right
and passes five of the six tests, including the headline one. The test that
catches it is the one that gives a row a deliberate four day Monday to Thursday
week and demands it survive untouched. Without that test the suite would have
signed off on a repair that eats a customer's configuration on every boot.

Separately, countries whose calendars shipped after an install was seeded never
received them, so six countries resolved through the fallback instead of their
own week. Four of them are on a Sunday to Thursday week, so the fallback was
answering with confident and wrong dates rather than declining. That is now
reconciled for installs that predate each calendar, and declined for a fresh
install, for one that already holds the calendar, for one seeded afterwards and
missing it on purpose, and for one whose seed cannot be dated.

The set of countries that shipped in the first release is frozen as what it is,
closed history, so a country added to the seed file without a ship date fails
loudly instead of silently becoming an anchor nobody is ever given.

Neither of these could be delivered as a migration. Schema moves at boot through
additive revisions, so a revision whose body rewrites rows never runs on an
existing install while the version table records it as applied. The revision
that would have fixed the axis now points at the repair that actually does.

Two functions claimed the lazy import made construction control degrade
gracefully when the non-conformance module is disabled. Neither had a guard.
With that module gone they raise, and they should: the gate override creates
the report first and writes its id into the override's audit metadata, so a
silent fallback would issue an acceptance certificate over open items with
nothing recording why.

The module already decided this twice, in the two places where degrading is
right, and both carry a real guard rather than a promise. The open-report count
falls back to zero on a read, and the seeder returns an optional and writes the
trade out. Reads and seeding degrade; a live write something downstream depends
on does not. The manifest says the same by putting the module in depends and
keeping a separate optional list for the three that really are optional.

The old premise could not happen anyway, since that module is core and the
loader refuses to disable a core module. What can happen is the module missing
from disk, because nothing enforces declared dependencies at startup, so the
docstrings describe that instead.

report can be counted rather than that none exists, and why zero is still
right: it is a read-only count feeding a delete guard, and raising would turn
every delete in the module into a 500 the moment the module went missing, which
fails closed in the wrong direction. That trade holds only while the write path
refuses to degrade, so the two docstrings now point at each other.

fix(cases): a case nobody could validate was published as validated

Running the case rules is guarded, because a broken rule must not stop somebody
saving their work. The guard returned an empty list. An empty list is also what
a case gets when it has been checked and nothing is wrong, so one value carried
two meanings and no caller could tell them apart.

The caller that mattered was the publish gate. It asks for the blocking
findings, gets none, and shares the case with the team. So the path taken when
validation could not run at all was identical to the path taken when validation
ran and found the case clean, and the case went out carrying a claim that
nobody had checked. Validation is not optional in this product, and an engine
that cannot run is a reason to withhold publication rather than to grant it.

The failure now produces a finding instead of a silence. It is an ERROR, so the
publish gate stops on it exactly as it stops on a case with no steps, and it is
DIAGNOSTIC, because what it records is that the infrastructure failed and not
that anything is wrong with the case. It deliberately does not set the engine
error flag: that flag marks rows which are reported alongside a verdict without
changing it, and this row is the verdict.

Both halves of the original requirement survive. A private draft still saves,
because losing an author's work over an outage they did not cause is the worse
failure of the two. Sharing is refused, because sharing is the claim.

No new column. The only stored state that amounts to a claim is the shared
flag, so declining to set it is the whole of "do not record this as checked",
and there is nothing further to persist. Worth saying because a migration in
this product does not reach installations that already exist, so a fix needing
one would not have been the same fix.

Three tests. The first makes the engine throw and was written before the change
and watched to fail on the empty list. The second is its negative control, a
case that validates clean and must still be publishable, without which a change
that always blocked would have passed the first test. The third drives the
publish gate itself and holds both halves at once: the draft saves, the share
raises, and the refusal names the finding.

engine errors, so a single rule that throws is also invisible, which is the
smaller version of what this commit fixes.

feat(module-builder): the server checks that a module was reviewed, not just that the wizard showed it

Installing a generated module writes Python to disk and loads it into the running
server. That is allowed because a person reads every generated file first. Until
now the server could not tell a reviewed spec from an unreviewed one: preview and
install took the identical request body, so an install carried no evidence that a
preview had ever happened, and the review step was enforced by the screen rather
than by the API.

Preview now returns a short-lived token signed over the spec digest, the user and
the issue time, and install refuses a spec that does not arrive with a matching
one. A digest the caller computes would prove nothing, since any caller can
compute one without asking to see anything; only something the server issued shows
the server was asked. Binding the digest is what stops a spec being edited after
the reading, and binding the user is what stops one person's review authorising
another person's install. It signs rather than stores, so there is no table, no
migration and no cleanup job.

The wizard now installs the spec the review step rendered instead of whatever the
form holds, so what lands on disk is what was read.

A spec also records who wrote it. The draft endpoint stamps it after the model
call, where the code that actually called the model can vouch for it, and whatever
the model puts in that field is overwritten. Editing a drafted spec does not clear
the mark, because a model still wrote the first version.

Confirmation stays human. Only the check that a human was given something to read
moves from the client to the server.

test: stop source-reading assertions from passing on the wrong region

Some rules can only be checked by reading a source file as text. That a
component references the shared credit constant rather than pasting the string
is a claim about how the file is written, and importing a value cannot answer
it. The failure mode of those scans is not an error, it is a confident wrong
answer, and two shapes produce it.

A slice whose end marker is missing gets minus one from indexOf, and slicing to
minus one runs to the end of the file, so the assertion examines whichever
declaration happens to sit last and reports on it under the name of the one it
meant. That happened here: one half of a map credits check overran that way and
failed while saying nothing true, and its sibling overran identically and
stayed green purely because nothing was declared below it. Adding one export
under that line would have been enough to make it lie while still passing. The
other shape is an empty population, where a walk that collects no files makes
an assertion that the offender list is empty true for free.

The shared helper added here puts a floor under both. It refuses a region whose
markers it cannot find rather than returning whatever the arithmetic produced,
and the tests that walk the disk state a minimum population in their own file.
The page title suite is moved onto it as the first caller.

feat(ci): the guard now catches the commoner half of the same silence

The alpha-drop guard looked for one shape: a real colour token given a modifier
it cannot take, bg-oe-blue-subtle/60. The two commits before this one repaired
190 classes of a different shape it could not see at all, a name that resolves
to nothing, bg-surface-muted, where the theme defines surface as primary,
secondary, tertiary and elevated and there is no muted. Same silence, and the
larger population, because it takes no cleverness to write. Only a plausible
word.

Dropping the alpha requirement opens a false-positive source the alpha form
structurally could not have, because every candidate no longer has to carry a
modifier. Every one of them turns out to have the same cause, a string that is
not a class list: stroke-width and border-color are attribute names, and to-do
and to-ako are English and Croatian prose in the locale bundles, caught because
to- is the gradient utility and also a word.

Two filters answer it, neither a list of words to ignore. The first is shape, a
class list is lowercase and is not a sentence. The second is the compiler:
every survivor is compiled and only those producing no rule at all are
reported, which is what makes a legitimate class unreportable rather than
merely unreported. The shape filter was chosen by measuring candidates against
the two known populations rather than by taste: one that read a string as a
class list was rejected for losing real hits, taking oe-blue-subtle from 173 to
65, and the one kept holds full recall while leaving about 1% noise, on the
grounds that a reporting gate should not buy silence by dropping findings that
are real.

The selftest now writes six classes that look alike in source and demands three
findings and three not, including text-sm/6, a real utility whose token is not
a colour, and to-do. It earned that: it caught a double-count in the new half
before that half had ever run on the tree, where the two halves numbered a
multi-line template literal from different points so the deduplication key
never matched.

Still reporting, still not blocking on findings, and still blocking on being
broken or stale, which is the part that matters. Every count in both files now
names the commit it was taken at. The dead-name half read 769 classes in 156
files at acd3bad9c and reads 579 in 124 today; the difference of 190 is exactly
what the two repair commits removed. A figure with no commit against it is one
a reader cannot tell apart from a wrong one, and the previous version of these
comments had four such figures in it.
