fix(ui): a projects list that answers with an object blanks the whole app

The header's project picker asks for a list and trusts what comes back. When the
projects endpoint answered 200 with a well-formed JSON object instead of an
array, the picker called filter on it, the call threw "is not a function", and
the browser was left holding an empty document. Measured against a running
instance: zero characters of text, no app shell, no children under the root
node, and an uncaught TypeError on the page. Not a fallback, not a recovery
card, nothing at all.

Nothing in the code was in a position to notice. The type argument on apiGet is
a compile-time claim about a body that arrives exactly as the server sent it, so
it reads as checked while checking nothing, and the ?? [] beside the call
answers for null and undefined while saying nothing about a value of the wrong
type. Two readers of that body were exposed rather than one. The render path
filtered it, and the effect that clears a selection whose project no longer
exists called some on it behind a check that only asked whether the value was
falsy. An object passes that check, so guarding the render alone would have
moved the same throw one line down into the effect, where React still carries it
to a boundary and the screen still goes blank.

What turned a broken dropdown into a blank document is that there was nothing
above it to catch anything. AppLayout, which is the sidebar and the header, was
mounted outside the only error boundary in the shell, so every crash originating
in the application chrome was uncatchable by construction, and the promise of a
recovery card instead of a white screen held for pages only. The chrome was
hoisted there deliberately, because when the layout lived inside each route
element the router tore the whole thing down and rebuilt it on every navigation,
and that reasoning still stands. So the chrome stays hoisted and gains a
boundary of its own wrapped around it, placed under the auth gate so a signed
out visitor still gets the login redirect rather than a recovery card.

The two boundaries nest rather than compete. React hands a throw to the nearest
boundary below it, so a page crash still stops at the inner one that is keyed by
pathname, with the sidebar and header alive and the next navigation clearing it,
and only an error the chrome itself raised reaches the outer one. That outer one
has no key and no surviving navigation to escape through, so its recovery button
reloads the document rather than clearing a flag and rebuilding the same shell
from the same cache that just crashed it.

One more way the recovery UI could have failed to appear. The boundary reads
sessionStorage while deciding whether a stale chunk error deserves an automatic
reload, and reading that property throws outright in a browser configured to
block site data, or inside a sandboxed frame. A throw from componentDidCatch is
raised again to the parent boundary, and above the outermost boundary there is
no parent, which is the blank document again by a second route. It is wrapped
now, and a failure there skips the reload and renders the card.

Carried in the same file, a separate fix. The online status dot on the header
avatar had its animate-ping ring painting past the right edge of the window,
because the avatar sits flush against that edge at desktop widths and the ring
scales to twice its box. That pushed the document wider than the viewport and
produced a real repeating horizontal scroll. The ring is clipped to the badge
now.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(cases): a rule that crashed is shown to the author instead of dropped

evaluate_case ended its filter with "and not result.is_engine_error". That is
the right idiom for a list that feeds a gate and the wrong one here, because
this single list is also everything the author of a case is ever shown. A case
where one rule crashed came back looking exactly like a case where every rule
ran and found nothing, and the check that failed was the one worth reading
about.

The rows are carried through now. They keep the INFO severity the engine gives
them, so they tell the author a check did not run without changing the publish
verdict, which is what the flag has always meant. Their message is restated in
words a case author can use, because no locale carries a string for an engine
failure and the reader falls back to it, and they render under a key of their
own rather than the crashed rule's, whose translation describes a check that
ran and found something.

CaseFinding carries is_engine_error, so the response says which kind of row it
is instead of leaving the reader to work it out from English prose.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(serve): a frontend bundle that went missing answers 404 and says which

The SPA fallback ended in a FileResponse on an index.html that was checked
once, at mount time. When the dist went away under a running server, a
redeploy wiping the build directory or a volume that unmounts after boot,
that raised and the stack turned it into a bare 500 in plain text. The
operator was told the server had crashed when the server was fine and a
directory was not, and went reading application logs for a filesystem
problem. Measured before the fix, with the dist removed under a running
client: /boq, /favicon.svg and /logo.svg all 500.

The two root static handlers had the same shape and the same answer, since
they close over paths checked in the same place. /assets was worse than it
looked. StaticFiles stats its directory once and raises if it is gone, and
that check runs on the first request rather than at construction, so the same
deployment answered 404 or 500 depending on whether anything had warmed the
mount. A probe that happened to ask in the lucky order reported the honest
number.

All of them answer 404 now, with a body that names the deployment problem
instead of only denying the path, and one error line per process rather than
one per page load. The assets mount logs and falls through to the 404 its own
lookup already produces, rather than losing the check entirely.

A server that never found a bundle already answered 404 and already said so
at startup, but the 404 was the bare Not Found that reads as a mistyped URL,
so it now says the deployment shipped without a UI and the API is still up.
The startup warning names both directories it looked in, because an empty
wheel and an unbuilt checkout are different problems with different answers.
Server-side paths stay in the log and out of the response body.

Resolution was tightened to match what the server needs. It gated on exists,
FileResponse needs a regular file, so a directory named index.html passed the
lookup and then 500'd on the first request.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(labor-rates): creating a template with no on-cost components crashed the request

Creating a labor rate template through the API failed with a server error
whenever the template had no on-cost components attached, which is the common
case for a brand new template. The template was never saved, the request just
died after passing validation, and the caller had no way to tell why.

The service built the component list by appending to it inside a loop over the
incoming components. When there were none, that loop never ran, so the
collection on the new template stayed untouched in memory. The save itself
worked, but reading the components back immediately afterward to build the
response tried to load them from the database inside a part of the request
handling that is not allowed to wait on the database, and that is what actually
broke. Templates with components attached happened to avoid this because the
loop touched the collection along the way, which is why the bug only showed up
on the minimal case.

The fix builds the component list once, up front, so it is always set on the
template in memory whether it is empty or not, and the response no longer needs
to go back to the database for something it already has.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(client-errors): a page navigating away while reporting an error crashed the reporter

The endpoint the frontend uses to report its own errors was itself failing
whenever the browser closed the connection before finishing sending its report,
which happens routinely because the reporter fires and forgets right as the
page navigates away. Every error caught this way was silently lost, and it
showed up in the server logs as an unrelated internal error rather than as what
it was, so the backend logs were quietly understating how often the frontend
was actually failing.

The handler read the request body without accounting for the connection
dropping mid read. When that happened it raised rather than returning, and
nothing caught it, so it surfaced as a server error even though the server had
done nothing wrong.

The fix treats a dropped connection the same way the endpoint already treats a
malformed report: accepted and discarded, since nobody is listening for the
response either way and there is nothing left to log.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(search): every result read zero percent, because nothing ever scored one

The score on a search hit was not lost on its way to the screen, it was never
computed. The helper that builds a hit declares rank_score with a default of
zero, and every one of the roughly fifteen branches that calls it omitted the
argument, so the default was the only value the field ever held. The response
schema declares score with a floor of zero, which makes zero perfectly valid,
so nothing along the way had grounds to complain. The client then rendered
exactly what it was given, which is why the display code was the wrong place
to look.

It was every result rather than some because the vector track is not running on
a stock install. Its packages are an optional extra, the collection search
catches the import failure at debug level and returns nothing, so the lexical
track was the only track and it scored everything zero.

Hits are now scored on how well they actually match: where the phrase landed,
since a title beats a body, how many of the query terms appear, and how much of
the matched field the phrase covers. The floor is twenty percent rather than
zero, because every row reaching the scorer has already matched, and a hit
found on something the reader cannot see in the visible text, an ordinal or a
code, is still a match and should not read as none. The recency ordering inside
the underlying queries is untouched, so it survives as the tie break between
equally scored hits.

The fused rank score is deliberately not what gets shown. Fusion orders results
well and its raw values sit around 0.016, so normalising them to fill the scale
would make a single character typed against a long description render as a
perfect match. Ranking keeps doing the job it is good at and the number now
reports the hit's own match quality, which is what a reader takes a percentage
to mean.

Two other surfaces were printing the same zeros and are corrected by this with
no edit of their own: the chat panel's semantic search results, and the
retrieval context handed to the model by the project advisor, which had been
stating a zero score on every hit it passed along.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(auth): the second sign-in screen offered a demo account nobody ever seeded

The newer sign-in screen listed a demo manager by a name that exists in no
seeder anywhere in the tree. The seeder writes one name for that account, the
older sign-in screen agreed with it, and this one did not, so a visitor reading
the newer screen was told about a person the installation had never created.
The screen is routed and reachable, so this was not dead code.

Both screens hold their own hand-typed list of demo accounts rather than
reading one. That is the mechanism, and it is worth being plain that this
change does not remove it. There is nothing to single source against for the
password, because the installer generates one per installation rather than
storing a literal, and the email list is duplicated on purpose for a circular
import reason that is documented where it happens. So what changes is that each
end now names the other in a comment: the seeder says which screens mirror the
names it writes, and each screen says where the names come from. The next
person renaming a seeded account has something telling them there are two other
places to look, which is exactly what was missing when this drifted.

The seeded password is untouched, deliberately. Making the literal on a screen
true by changing what the installation actually creates would fix the
disagreement in the wrong direction.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(e2e): repair four smoke specs that could not fail

The error boundary spec never ran at all. Its locator comma joined plain CSS
with the text= and :has-text() engines inside one CSS string, which Playwright
rejects while parsing, so the file raised a selector error before it reached an
assertion. It also named the React error boundary while injecting a 500, which
is a different mechanism entirely. It is now two tests, one per mechanism. The
first breaks the projects list with a 500 and measures that the page swaps the
list for a recovery card rather than going blank, that the card carries exactly
one action, and that clicking that action really re asks the backend, counting
only the page's own request and not the header switcher's copy of the same
endpoint. The second serves a 200 whose body is not the array the callers are
typed for and measures that a throw during render leaves the application shell
standing with a fallback inside it. That second test fails today and the
failure is the finding, not a flake. AppLayout is mounted outside the only
ErrorBoundary, so the header project switcher's filter over that list throws
where nothing can catch it and the entire page goes white.

Settings died on a strict mode violation, an .or() chain resolving to two
elements. Naming the element it meant, rather than taking the first of two,
turned up why there were two. The tab strip carrying the test id the old spec
reached for is the mobile one and is display none at the viewport these tests
run at, and the heading is screen reader only, so neither was the honest
signal. Both tests now key off the tab panel, which is unique and present at
every viewport. The tab walk iterates the desktop strip only, asserts a floor
on how many tabs it found instead of skipping itself when it found none, and
checks after every click that the panel is still mounted and is now labelled by
the tab just clicked.

The dashboard widget test claimed three selectors and rested on one. Two of
them matched nothing anywhere in the source and the third was a Customize
button found by English or German text, with .first() choosing between it and
Customise branding. Every selector is now anchored to a test id that exists,
and the test opens Customize and checks that the panel lists a row for widgets
the grid itself rendered, with a floor on the row count, so panel and page
cannot drift apart in silence.

The mobile spec was tagged for phones and ran everywhere, because the tag
selected it into the phone project without deselecting it from the desktop
ones, and a test named for an iPhone SE viewport also measured a 1280 by 720
window where it means nothing. Both halves of that filter now come from one
constant so they cannot drift. The overflow test names the widest offending
element in its failure message rather than only the number of pixels. The
sidebar test measures geometry instead of visibility, because the drawer is
moved off screen by a transform and keeps a full size box, so nothing was ever
hidden, and it then clicks the burger and waits for the drawer to arrive on
screen, which is the part that fails if the button is wired to nothing.

The phone project could not have run any of that. It spread a device descriptor
whose default browser is WebKit, so despite its name it launched WebKit and
failed to start on any machine with Chromium only. That stayed invisible while
the desktop project was picking the same specs up anyway. Now that they are
filtered out of it, this project is the only place they run, so it launches
Chromium explicitly and keeps the phone metrics the specs assert against.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(fx): a project with no currency policy was filed as an error on every visit

The currencies screen asks the server for the project's currency policy the
moment it opens. The endpoint exists, it is reached at the path the client
uses, and the 404 it answers with is correct. A project with no currency policy
is the ordinary state rather than an error, and stays that way until somebody
sets one, which the screen already said in as many words by rendering the empty
state as an invitation to set one. Nothing about the request or the route was
wrong, and nothing was missing behind it.

What was wrong is what the client did with the answer. The shared request layer
files every non-success response into the bug report buffer, keeps it in local
storage and posts it to the client error sink, so an expected empty state was
recorded as a warning every time an operator opened the page. On a fresh install
that means the demo project the application selects by default produces an error
report before the operator has done anything at all. The buffer already carries a
list of handled responses that must not be recorded, written for exactly this
shape of problem after a user log came back with fifty identical handled 404s in
it, and the currency policy read simply was not on that list.

The entry that keeps it off is deliberately narrow. It matches the policy read at
the policies prefix followed by a project id and nothing after it, so it does not
match the validation report that lives one level deeper under the same prefix.
That endpoint answers with a 200 and an empty report when there is no policy, so
a 404 from it would be a routing fault and has to stay visible. An entry left
unanchored would have swallowed that too, and the failure mode of over
suppression is silence, which is the same symptom as the thing working. A test
covers the anchoring in both directions, and a second one keeps a 500 on the
policy path recorded.

This stayed invisible because everything an operator can see was correct. The
page rendered, the empty state was worded properly, no toast appeared and no
error boundary caught anything. The only trace was a line the browser itself
prints for any non-success response, which no application code can suppress, and
an entry in a log nobody reads until the day they file a bug and find it full of
noise.

The policy tab had the opposite fault and is fixed with it. It treated any failed
load as proof that no policy was configured, so a server error or a dropped
connection would have told the operator that nothing was broken and invited them
to create a policy that may already exist. Only a 404 renders the empty state
now, and anything else renders the error with a retry.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(boq): a row nobody had typed into counted as a position and reached exports

"Add Position" in the editor creates the row on the server straight away and
opens its description cell for typing. That is the behaviour the author built
and it is right: the create handler posts an empty description with a zero
quantity and a zero rate, and the grid puts the cursor in the new row. So a
bill legitimately holds rows carrying nothing yet, and the product's job is not
to stop making them but to stop treating them as priced lines.

Two things were wrong with such a row. It was counted, so a blank line inflated
the position tally on the bill's card in the listing and again in its detail.
And it reached every export, so a delivered bill could carry a line with no
description, no quantity and no money against it, which is a defect the
recipient sees before we do.

The test for emptiness is a description and a quantity, because those are the
first things an estimator types and either of them makes the row real. Section
headers are excluded from it and stay subject to the existing section test on
their own: a header carries no quantity by definition, so without that guard
every seeded header would read as empty and the exports would lose their
structure entirely. A row that passes the test provably carries no money, since
a total is always quantity times rate, so leaving it out of an export cannot
change what that export sums to.

The listing count subtracts the blank rows in Python rather than in SQL. The
quantity column is a string, so "0", "0.00" and the empty string are three
spellings of one zero and no portable comparison catches all of them. The query
narrows to the rows that could possibly be empty, which is a small set even on
a bill of thousands of priced lines, and Python decides each candidate.

Exports read a separate structured payload that applies the same narrowing, so
the editor endpoint keeps returning every row including the one the user has
just created and is about to type into. The client-side Excel and PDF exports
apply the same rule, so a file downloaded from the browser matches one
downloaded from the API. The GAEB panel now previews the count the file will
actually contain rather than promising a position the export then drops.

fix(boq): the demo seeder wrote a bill status nothing could produce or leave

The status column is a plain string, so the database constrains it not at all.
The only constraint anywhere is the pattern on the update schema, which permits
draft, final and archived, and the only writers that meet it are the ones going
through the API. The seeders write the column directly and are therefore the
one class of writer that is never checked.

That is how a state nothing can reach came to ship. The demo seeder wrote
"approved" for its budget-level estimate. Nothing in the API produces that
word: the single act that approves a bill is the lock endpoint, and it records
who approved it and when while setting the status to final. Nothing consumes it
either, so a demo bill sat in a state with no transition into it and none out
of it. Meanwhile archived, which the schema permits and a patch can reach, was
written by nobody.

The seed now writes final, which is what approving a bill actually produces and
what the lock endpoint would have written had a person clicked it. The pattern
on the schema is unchanged, because it was already right; what it gained is a
description and an example, so the state set is legible from the generated API
documentation rather than only from a regular expression, and the next person
adding a writer can see what the words mean before choosing one.

The test reaches the writers the schema cannot. It scans the source for every
constructor that sets a status literal, asserts each one is a member of the
permitted set and that the update schema would accept it, and separately checks
that the lock and unlock transitions in the router write permitted states with
final among them. It carries a load control as well, asserting that the scan
found the demo seeder at all, because a scan that quietly matches nothing
passes for the same reason a clean tree does.

What it deliberately does not assert is that every permitted status is
reachable. Archived is written by no seeder and by no transition, only by a
direct patch, and whether that is a gap or the intended design is a question
about the product rather than something a test should decide on its own.

fix(geo-hub): an image declaring an implausible surface answered 500, not 413

Uploading a raster overlay whose header declares something like thirty thousand
by thirty thousand pixels produced an unexplained server error. The request was
understood perfectly and the refusal was deliberate, which is the part the
answer failed to say.

Pillow reads the declared width and height off the header without allocating
anything, so a few dozen bytes are enough to trip its own decompression-bomb
guard. What it raises for that is DecompressionBombError, and that does not
inherit from ValueError, which was the only failure the overlay upload knew how
to handle. So the exception travelled past the handler, past everything between
the rasteriser and the client, and surfaced as a 500 on a request the server
had already decided to reject.

The dimension reader now translates the bomb guard into an exception of its
own, deliberately not a subclass of ValueError so that folding the two together
is not possible by accident: they deserve different answers. Bytes we cannot
recognise as an image stay a 422, and an image we recognise and refuse to
decode is a 413 that says so in terms of pixels. The reader stays free of any
web framework, so the status mapping lives in the service where the other
upload refusals already are, next to the signature check that answers 415.

The documents module already handled the same Pillow behaviour this way for
photo uploads, so this is the overlay path catching up with an idiom the code
base had rather than a new one.

The test builds a structurally valid PNG whose header declares the oversized
surface and whose pixel data is a stub, because the guard fires off the header
and never reaches a decode. It asserts the status and that the message names
pixels, so an answer that merely stops being a 500 without explaining itself
would still fail.

fix(dashboard): the sites panel sent every site's coordinates to a weather host regardless of the opt-in

The forecast widget is opt-in, and the project list and the project detail page
both honour that. The sites panel on the dashboard did not: it rendered a
forecast for every located site on every load, whatever the setting said.

That is not a presentation preference being ignored. Each cell's forecast is a
request the browser makes directly to a public weather service, naming that
site's latitude and longitude, so rendering one for somebody who never turned
the widget on discloses where their sites are to a third party on their behalf.
The panel now reads the same store the other two surfaces read. The cities,
their counts and their links do not depend on the forecast and are unchanged,
so the panel keeps working with the widget off.

The widget itself also stopped being honest when the network said no. A refusal
left it rendering an empty card still headed with a forecast title and footed
with a refresh note, which names data it does not have. It now renders nothing
at all, which is what a decoration that has no content should do, and it
remembers the refusal under a much shorter lifetime than a forecast so a
dashboard full of sites stops asking a host that has just turned it away
instead of repeating the burst on every load. Ten minutes for a refusal against
an hour for a forecast: one describes the network right now, the other
describes the weather.

Recorded in the component for whoever audits outbound traffic next: this call
is made by the browser and no operator switch stops it. The environment
variable that disables geocoding gates the server-side address geocoder and
never reaches this component. The daily diary module already calls the same
host from the server, which is where this belongs too, the same move the update
checker made when it stopped calling a code host from the browser.

fix(cases): a check that crashed was shown to the author as advice about their case

The backend already says which kind of row it is sending. Each finding carries
is_engine_error, so a remark the product wants to make about a case and a rule
that fell over while looking at it arrive distinguishable. The editor was not
reading that flag, so both went into one list headed "Worth a look", with the
crash wearing the same severity badge as everything else.

Read that way, an outage reads as an opinion. Someone whose case triggered a
broken rule was told, in the register the product uses for advice, that there
was something worth looking at, and the thing worth looking at was our own
failure to look. The two rows also compete: a real remark sitting next to a
crash is quietly downgraded, because the reader has no way to tell that one of
them is about their work and the other is not.

They are now two cards. What could not be checked goes above the remarks, not
below them, because how much of the review actually ran decides how much the
rest of it is worth and that is not a footnote. It is deliberately styled as a
gap rather than a verdict, dashed and grey and without a severity, because none
of it blocks saving or sharing the case, and dressing a row that blocks nothing
as a blocker is its own way of misleading the author. The text says plainly
that the case was never looked at on that point and that they can carry on.

Three strings, in every locale the guard requires, in this commit rather than a
later one.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(site-inventory): stock items and locations could not be deleted at all, and the refusal was English prose

The register listed items and locations and offered no way to remove either.
The endpoints have been there the whole time, so the gap was the control, not
the capability, and the workaround was editing a row into meaninglessness and
leaving it in the list.

Adding the button is the small half. Both deletes are refused with a 409 when
anything still points at the row, and that refusal exists for a reason worth
restating: a movement's item_id cascades, so deleting an item takes its whole
ledger with it, and both of a movement's location columns are SET NULL, so
deleting a location turns a record of where material went into a record of
nowhere. Without the refusal each delete reports success while destroying the
history it was recording.

The refusal reaches the browser as one English sentence the server composed.
It is prose in detail, with no holder list in it, so there is nothing to read
out and nothing to translate, and a Spanish or Japanese reader would have been
shown an English explanation of why their click did nothing. So the page asks
first instead of clicking and catching. A guard counts what holds the row,
from the same rows the server counts: movements by item_id for an item, and
for a location the movements whose source or destination leg is it, plus the
items defaulting to it and the balances still standing there. One probe answers
both of a delete control's questions, what would be destroyed if this went
ahead and, when nothing would be, why this row is the removable one.

That makes the whole sentence local. Counts come back as numbers and the page
builds the explanation through i18n with plural forms, so the reader is told in
their own language which records hold the row and how many, before anything is
destroyed rather than after it is refused. A row nothing holds is deleted with
a plain confirmation naming what is about to go.

The guard is unit tested against the shapes that matter: nothing holding, one
kind holding, several kinds holding at once, and the plural boundary between
one and many, which is the case a language with more than two forms gets wrong
first.

Twenty two strings, in every locale the guard requires, in this commit.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(auth): during an outage the sign-in screen told people their password was wrong

Both sign-in screens sorted a failed attempt into two boxes. Either fetch threw,
which meant no answer at all and produced "unable to connect", or the response
came back not ok, which was read as the server having checked the credentials
and rejected them.

A proxy in front of us breaks that in the worst direction. A 502 is a response,
so fetch resolves, so the throw never happens and the outage lands in the second
box. The user is told their email or password is wrong. It is not: nothing ever
reached the part of the system that could have an opinion about it. This was
live for twenty four hours while the site was down, and the advice it gave was
to doubt a password that was correct, which sends people to a reset flow that
was equally unreachable.

Status now decides. Anything from 500 up says the server did not answer and
the details were never checked, which is both true and actionable, since the
useful thing to do is wait rather than change anything. Below 500 keeps the
existing credentials wording, because 401 and 422 really are answers about what
was sent. The split is one small pure function with the reasoning written down
next to it, called by both screens so they cannot drift apart again, and it is
tested across the boundary pair and every status either screen can actually
receive.

The end to end spec that claimed to cover this could not. It signed in as a
seeded demo account with a deliberately wrong password, and in any install with
demo seeding on those accounts are routed past the password check on purpose,
so the sign-in under test succeeded by design. It then asserted the browser had
not navigated yet, which is true for free whenever anything is slow and can only
fail when the system is fast. It now uses an account the server does not know,
which no shortcut exempts, and waits for the refusal to appear on screen rather
than for time to pass, so a sign-in that wrongly succeeded produces no error to
wait for and fails.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(norm-expansion): a nameless material priced at full confidence, and a negative labour rate answered 500

Three residuals under the same endpoint, all reachable through POST
/build-assembly, all measured rather than reasoned about.

A material whose name reduces to an empty comparison key went straight to the
lexical matcher, and the lexical matcher does not refuse it. Measured against a
single "Sand - washed" row at m3, both "- - -" and "-" resolved at confidence
1.0, because token_set_ratio treats the query's token set, a lone hyphen, as a
subset of the candidate's. The confidence floor cannot catch this: the score is
not low, it is perfect. So sand's rate landed on a nameless material and read
as a settled price. The guard belongs next to the exact tier's own, before
either tier is offered the name, and that is where it now is.

The exact tier queried the primary description and nothing else, in all three
of its candidate passes. A catalogue row carrying the norm's product name under
descriptions['es'] was therefore found only when its English description
happened to share a distinctive token. When it did not, the exact tier reported
no match, the material fell through to the fuzzy tier, and a different product
priced the line while the right row sat in the same table. That is the class of
wrong answer this module exists to remove, so the token passes now search the
localized names as well. The comparison in Python still decides every match, so
the scan widened and what counts as a match did not. One limit is written down
where it bites: the JSON column is serialised with non-ASCII escaped, so an
accented localized name is not reachable by any spelling of the word and
degrades to the existing accent-insensitive window rather than to a wrong
answer.

The third is not a matching bug. base_wage is gt=0 on create, but an on-cost
component's value is unbounded and the build-up does not refuse negatives, so a
labour template could compute to exactly zero and report priced with confidence
1, or compute below zero and crash. The crash is the part worth naming: a
component unit cost carries ge=0, so building a negative rate raised a
validation error inside service code rather than during request parsing, where
the router does not catch it, and the endpoint answered 500 on a request that
was well formed. Both doors into the hourly rate, the explicit one and the
template, now refuse a non-positive result and return the line unpriced with a
reason, which is what an unusable rate is.

The two tests that documented the first two as expected failures are now
ordinary tests, the placeholder one parametrized across five shapes of
punctuation-only name. Two new tests cover the zero and the negative template.
One new expected failure is added rather than hidden: a placeholder that does
carry a comparison key is still priced, which is a narrower gap than the one
closed here and is left standing where it can be seen.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(desktop): nothing had ever run Tauri's real URL matcher against the grant every link depends on

Every command the desktop application page invokes is refused unless an ACL
entry resolves for it, and the whole of what stands between the page and that
refusal is one string in capabilities/app-window.json, http://127.0.0.1:*. The
user-visible shape of getting it wrong is that every outbound link in the
product does nothing when clicked.

Whether that string covers http://127.0.0.1:49512/boq is not a question about
anything we wrote. It is a question about Tauri's URL pattern parser, which
substitutes a wildcard for a pathname that is absent or bare, which is why a
pattern carrying no path still covers every route. Our Python gate answers it
by reimplementing a subset of that rule. A reimplementation can agree today and
part company on the next upgrade, and it would part company silently, so the
load-bearing fact under the fix was the one thing nothing measured.

The first test asks the real type. It parses the capability the bundle ships
and drives tauri::utils::acl::RemoteUrlPattern over the default port, an
arbitrary port, a deep route with a query and a fragment, and then over a
public host and a private network address, which must not be covered: this
capability hands the operating system opener to whatever origin it names, so
widening is as much a defect as narrowing. Both ports are asserted because the
launcher picks between them at runtime, and a gate that only ever tried the
default would call a second copy of the app with dead links fixed.

Proven to bite rather than assumed to. Narrowing the pattern to the default
port makes it fail on port 49512 and names the reason; the capability file is
tracked by include_str!, so cargo rebuilds on the edit. That plant also
confirmed the pathname rule independently, since the no-path pattern kept
matching / and /boq and only the port assertion broke.

The second test resolves capability identifiers through the permission file to
real command names and asserts the two link-opening commands are reachable.
This overlaps what the Python gate already checks and is kept anyway, for one
reason worth stating rather than pretending it is novel coverage: it puts the
question in the cargo lane, so a Rust-only change cannot pass without it. No
dependency is added, both types are already in the graph.

Suite goes from 78 to 80 passing.

Recorded for whoever audits the grant next, because counting from the wrong
place gives the wrong answer twice over. The six commands the application page
invokes come from two sources: four from the frontend's desktop bridge, and two
from a script the Rust side evaluates into the window. Grepping the frontend
alone finds four and concludes the capability over-grants by two.

Left alone deliberately: in remote-server mode the window is navigated to an
organisation's own server, no pattern covers that origin, and every external
link there is refused and toasts. This test asserts that non-loopback hosts are
not covered, so it documents the behaviour rather than hiding it. Granting the
operating system opener to an origin somebody typed in is a product decision,
not a test's to make.

fix(i18n): the guard against unanswerable keys never read the form half the calls use

A key called with a default that no locale file answers renders its English
words in every language, and no other gate we own can see it. There is no
translated value to compare against, so the leak guard passes, the type check
passes and the build passes. That is the whole reason this guard exists.

It read one spelling of the call. i18next takes a default two ways,
t(key, {defaultValue: "text"}) and t(key, "text"), and the regex matched only
the object form. The docstring did claim the bare form was out of scope, but
on the grounds that a key with no default at all is loud and reports itself by
putting a raw key on screen. That is true, and it is about a different thing.
The positional form does carry a default and is exactly as silent as the
object form, so the exclusion was reasoned for one case and applied to
another. The blind spot was an accident wearing the clothes of a decision.

There was a second half to it, in the file level skip. The reader moved on
from any file that did not contain the string defaultValue, so even after the
pattern learned the positional form it would still never have been offered a
file that uses only that form. Both halves had to go, and a fix to either one
alone would have measured as an improvement while changing almost nothing.

Widened, the guard sees 1120 keys that are called only positionally, and 20 of
them are answered by no locale that needs them. Those 20 predate this change
and nobody is part way through translating them, so they are recorded in
scripts/i18n_orphan_baseline.json, which is the file that exists for exactly
this and which may only shrink. Recording them is deliberate. Translating them
in the same commit would bury a structural change inside a locale diff, and
narrowing the guard back would restore the blind spot in order to keep a count
tidy. The ratchet still bites: any new key, and any baselined key that loses
further locales, still fails.

The claim under all of this is about the i18next build we actually ship, not
about the documentation, so it is tested against the running instance rather
than asserted. Five cases, the load bearing one being that the two forms
return the identical string for a key no locale answers. If a future upgrade
makes the positional argument mean something other than a default, that test
fails and this guard gets revisited, which is the correct order of events.

Counting note for whoever audits the number next, because the obvious probe
gives an answer roughly five times too large. Five of the 43 locale files are
regional overlays, en-US, es-MX, es-CL, es-CO and pt-BR, and they carry only
the words that differ from the language they refine. A key absent from an
overlay is answered by its base and is not a gap. A probe that counts files
rather than resolving through the base reports 111 where the truth is 20.

fix(tests): the retainage cascade test switched off the cascade it was checking

test_retainage_release_cascades_on_po_delete deletes a purchase order and
asserts that its retainage release log goes with it. It failed, and the
failure looked like a missing constraint. It was not one. The database
catalog reports confdeltype 'c' on the release table, the constraint
definition reads ON DELETE CASCADE, and the model and the migration that
created the table both declare ondelete CASCADE. All three layers agree,
and the constraint name is 62 characters, comfortably inside the identifier
limit.

The fault was in the fixture. It opened the session with disable_fks=True,
which sets session_replication_role to replica. PostgreSQL implements a
foreign key cascade as an internal referential integrity trigger, so
switching triggers off switches the cascade off with them. A control run
settles it: with enforcement live the delete leaves zero release rows
behind, with enforcement off it leaves one.

The flag was not needed in the first place. oe_procurement_po declares no
outgoing foreign keys at all, so its project_id and created_by columns are
plain identifier columns and the synthetic values these tests use have
nothing to satisfy. The fixture docstring claimed the opposite and the
module docstring repeated it, so both are rewritten to say what is actually
true and to record why enforcement has to stay on here.

Only this one test noticed, because PurchaseOrder carries no ORM
relationship to PORetainageRelease. Its items and goods receipts are
cascaded by SQLAlchemy in Python, while the release log depends entirely on
the database doing the work.

fix(tests): the dormant rule check read one call shape and accused the other

CI (PostgreSQL) failed on 2dc37e47d with one failure out of 857. The check
said the variations module requests a validation rule set that nothing
registers into, which would mean variation bills are validated by an empty set
and every report comes back clean without running. That is a serious thing to
be told and it is not what is happening.

The check reads the sources with ast and collected only the second positional
argument of rule_registry.register, on the stated grounds that the positional
form was the whole signature. variations/validators.py passes the set by
keyword, rule_sets=[VARIATIONS_RULE_SET], two lines below the constant it
names, and the package exposes the on_startup hook that runs the registration.
So the rules are registered and the check could not see the line that
registers them.

Measured across the tree rather than guessed: of forty seven register calls,
forty two are positional and five pass rule_sets by keyword, in
authority_submission, rebar_schedule, validation/router.py and variations.
Only variations showed, because the other modules also register positionally
somewhere and one visible call was enough to clear the name. So the blind spot
was four modules wide and one module deep, and it surfaced now only because
variations registers by keyword and by no other route.

The reader now takes the argument in either shape. It still resolves only a
literal or a constant declared in the same file and still refuses to guess at
anything else, because every name it wrongly counts as registered is a dormant
rule set it would wave through.

Proved in both directions before and after. A set declared and never
registered is still condemned, a set registered without an on_startup hook is
still condemned, a keyword argument whose value cannot be resolved is still
condemned, and both call shapes with a hook present are accepted. Two tests
were added that hold the reader against both shapes written out by hand,
rather than against the tree, which can stop using the keyword form without
anybody noticing.

The lane runs this file with OE_TEST_DB=pg, and the whole directory silently
skips without it. Eleven skipped and exit zero reads exactly like eleven
passed, which is worth knowing before trusting a local run of this suite.

feat(labor-rates): ship a starter rate library so the picker is not empty

Fifty three modules carry a seed.py and labor rates was not one of them, so a
fresh install opened its template picker on nothing. The cost lands one screen
away rather than on the page itself: the norm expansion build panel prices
labour from a rate template, its own norms are seeded, and with no rate to
pick it answers "No labour-rate templates yet. Create one on the Labour Rates
page first.", which is a dead end on the screen that turns a production norm
into a priced assembly.

covers the currencies the demo portfolio is priced in. Each is hand authored
in its own currency rather than converted from one base, and the on-costs name
the kind of charge rather than any agreement or employer. They are generic
starting points an estimator is expected to tune per project and region.

templates are owner scoped, and a row with no owner is readable by an admin
alone: the collection endpoint drops the owner filter for the admin role, and
the single-template loader answers 404 on a null owner for everybody else. So
the platform-wide seed that waste factors and production norms use would fill
the page for the one persona least likely to build a rate and leave it empty
for the estimator. The library is seeded against the estimator demo account
instead, which the admin accounts see regardless because their view is
unscoped, and it falls back to the demo admin where no estimator account
exists. It is wired after the demo users are committed rather than from the
module startup hook, because that hook runs before any user exists and would
leave the first boot, the one that matters, unseeded.

the build-up arithmetic without a database, which catches a component kind the
math would otherwise read as a flat amount without complaining. The seeder
itself is run against the real tables, twice, so a field the schema does not
carry fails here rather than inside the fail-soft try/except at boot, where it
would log a warning and leave the page exactly as empty as before.

fix(gates): the head import check followed imported names but not module aliases

check_head_imports.py resolved every intra-app "from a.b import name" against
the committed text of a.b, which is the shape that once shipped a router
importing a function nobody had committed. A symbol is not always imported
under its own name, though. "import app.core.events as ev" and "from app.core
import events" both bind a module, and the symbol is reached afterwards as an
attribute, so the import statement alone says nothing about whether that symbol
exists. The check read import statements only, so a commit could alias a
module, call something the module does not carry, and still be told its imports
were fine. It fails later than a missing import, on the first request that
reaches the line, which is how this one reached production as a 500 rather than
as a boot failure.

Reproduced on a throwaway commit before anything was changed here. A router
that aliases app.core.events and calls ev.record_activity, sitting next to one
from-import that does resolve, and the old check reported that its one imported
name resolved and exited 0.

So the check now follows every local name that holds an app module and asks
each attribute loaded through such a name of that module's own text. Three
things keep it quiet where the text cannot answer. Dunder attributes such as
__path__ are put there by the interpreter. A name bound to two different
modules in one file is dropped rather than guessed at, which the tree really
does in app/core/validation/rules. A name that a parameter or a local also
binds is dropped for the same reason, since nothing here says which of the two
a use meant.

Measured over HEAD before the fix: 18368 import statements under backend/app,
of which 5 alias an app module, 7 import one plainly and 183 bind a submodule
through a from-import, so 188 module bindings in all. No defect of this shape
lives in the tree today, so this is regression proofing rather than a catch.
The check now resolves 1281 attributes on top of the 15158 imported names it
resolved before, and that second number is unchanged, which is what says the
name half was extended rather than rewritten.

The script gains a self-test that runs on every invocation, the way its sibling
check_migration_heads.py does, because the tree it is pointed at is almost
always clean and the branch that matters would otherwise never be seen to run.
It also takes --selftest to run only that. Fixtures are built in memory and
nothing is written to disk.

One shape stays uncovered and is worth naming. A plain "import app.core.x"
followed by "app.core.x.foo" is reached through a dotted chain rather than
through a single name, and following that needs different machinery for 7
statements and one attribute use in the whole tree, which is a dunder anyway.

fix(labor-rates): an empty base wage was sent as zero and came back a raw 422

The base hourly wage normalises to '0' when the field is left blank. That is
right for the live build-up preview, because the compute endpoint accepts a
wage of zero, and wrong for saving a template, because create and update both
refuse one outright. Nothing stopped the blank field from reaching them, so a

template, save changes, and save as new. A translated line under them says a
base wage above zero is what saving needs. Zero is refused as well as blank,
for the reason the server refuses it: a template that builds up to nothing
prices labour hours at nothing while every consumer reads it as a finished
rate.

The predicate reads the field through the same normaliser the request uses, so
it judges the string that would be sent rather than the raw text. The
normaliser itself is left alone, because the preview, the on-cost values and
the crew rates all go through it and zero is a real figure in each of them.

The new string is added to every locale rather than English alone. A key
answered by no locale file renders its English default in all forty-two
languages, and no gate we own can see it.

did not answer, which is not literally what happened to it, but it points at

fix(migrations): alembic upgrade head never asked the server its version

The PostgreSQL 16 floor was checked when the application started and nowhere
else. An operator who deploys the wheel and runs migrations before ever
booting it takes a different path, and on a blank server that path does not
walk the revision chain at all: env.py builds the entire current schema
through create_all and stamps head. So the command most likely to meet a
freshly provisioned cluster was also the one that created every table on it
without once asking what the server was, which is exactly the failure the
startup check exists to prevent, arriving much later as a broken query
somewhere unrelated.

The rule now lives in one place. postgres_version grows a _resolve_version
holding all of it, which source is authoritative, when the banner may stand
in for the number and what the minimum is, plus a synchronous entry point
that runs the same two statements over the engine migrations actually use.
env.py calls it right after create_engine, before the fresh database probe
and before the version table DDL, and only when the dialect is PostgreSQL so
a SQLite install is untouched. Offline mode is deliberately left alone,
because alembic upgrade head --sql renders statements for a database it never
connects to and there is no server to ask.

Stamp and downgrade go through run_migrations_online too, so they are gated
as well. That is intended. Recording head on a server below the floor writes
down a claim about a schema that server cannot hold.

fix(search): a result found by one column was named by another, or not at all

Both searches match a row on one set of columns and then build the row's title
from a narrower set. Where the two sets differ, a record that carries only the
column outside the title comes back unnamed. Every column involved is NOT NULL
so nothing ever crashed, but an empty string is legal in all of them, and a
blank title is a perfectly valid response as far as the schema is concerned.

The contact case was closed on its own in 0a02a5efd. It was not the only one.
In core global search, eight of the nine types were affected: documents, tasks,
RFIs, meetings and NCRs could return a genuinely blank line, and positions,
cost items and inspections shipped their composite separator with nothing
beside it, so a position with no ordinal read as " - Concrete C30/37". The fix
is a rule rather than a patch per type. Every column the WHERE clause can match
on is now also a candidate for the title, so whatever the searcher typed comes
back inside the label they are given, which is the string their eye is looking
for. Composite titles join only the halves that carry a value, and a row that
answers none of its columns falls back to its type and a short id rather than
to a full UUID, which names nothing to a reader.

The same hole was on the unified search, which is the one the command palette
actually calls, and there it read worse. VectorHit.title already falls through
to the snippet and then to the row's raw id, so a BOQ position found by its
ordinal, a risk found by its register code and a submittal found by its spec
section all arrived as a bare UUID, measured against the shipped code before
this change. A requirement found by its notes arrived as a single dot, because
its title is entity and attribute joined and both may be blank. A cost item
found by its code read as the code, a dash and nothing. Four collections gain
the missing fallback and one gains a helper for the pair.

Nothing changes on the frontend. The command palette passes the title straight
through to the row label with no handling of its own, so the fix reaches it,
and no new user-facing string is introduced: the last resort uses the record
type the response already carries, which is a machine token rather than prose,
so there is nothing to translate.

Nineteen tests. Eleven cover core global search against the real schema, nine
of them red before this change, and eight cover the unified search, four of
them proved red by running the same rows against the committed copy of the
service. Each one asserts the title carries the token that was searched for,
because a title of " - " or of a raw id is truthy and would satisfy a check
that only asked for a non-empty string. The negative controls pin the other
direction: a named document is still named by its name, a titled risk by its
title, a numbered position still reads number then description, and a
requirement still reads entity dot attribute.

test(packs): the rule set gate could pass without having read a pack

The check that no pack advertises a rule set the engine does not register had a
control on one side only. It proves the registry it measured was actually
loaded, because an under-loaded registry answers "not registered" for
everything, and it proved nothing about the other half. Every assertion that
walks the packs builds its list by globbing the packs directory and reading each

or renaming the field would each leave the walk empty, and "no pack advertises a

advertised sets before anything is concluded from their contents, as floors
rather than exact counts, because a test that pins the numbers of the day it was

the two readers to agree per pack and per field. The regular expression
describes one way of writing the declaration; write it from a constant instead
and the reader returns nothing for that pack, which is indistinguishable from a
pack that advertises nothing. That is the same blind spot that once let a rule
set ship with full translations and never execute, and the repair is the same,

into the China manifest, one of the seven removed in August, fails the
reachability assertion and names the pack and the slug. Rewriting the uk-jct
declaration to read from a module constant fails the agreement assertion and
says what the manifest declares against what the reader saw.

days stale. The China pack advertises one rule set, gbt50500, and it resolves to

manifests, thirteen rule sets are advertised and thirteen resolve. Eight
advertised against one delivered was accurate on 23 August, was corrected on the

run nothing and engine identifiers that do.

fix(bi-dashboards): a breakdown per estimate read back as a column of uuids

A custom KPI grouped by boq_id is how you ask for a number per bid, and it
is the only way to ask, because the id is what the database can group by.
What came back was keyed by uuids. The name was reachable by setting
label_field to boq_name, but only by an author who already knew that field
existed, and the point of a whitelist is that nobody should have to.

The catalog now declares which field names which id, boq_id by boq_name,
and a spec that groups by an id and asks for no label is stored with that
name filled in. Filled in when the definition is created rather than while
it computes, so a definition that already exists keeps the shape it was
created with, and the author can read back what they got and change it.
The form reads the same declaration, so the picker shows what will be
stored instead of offering to leave a column of ids alone while the server
names them anyway. The parity check that keeps the catalog and its bindings
honest now also refuses a declared name that is missing or numeric, which
is the same condition that makes it offerable in the picker.

The drill-down was the surface where this actually showed. Every custom
KPI lands in the synthesised-record path, since a spec has no registered
record provider, and that path put the uuid in the record's key with the
name buried inside its value. The name is a field of the record now, so it
reaches every reader of the drill-down rather than one drawer.

A name can also be blank. boq_name is NOT NULL and still arrives empty:
BOQCreate checks min_length before the HTML sanitiser runs, so a bid named
with a script tag is accepted and stored as an empty string. An empty
label renders as nothing at all and the row reads as a bug rather than as
an estimate nobody named, so a blank one takes the same reserved key an
absent group takes, and the consumer says what it says. The screen was not
one of those consumers, and printed the reserved key at the reader where
the report writers had been mapping it all along. It says it there with the
key every other screen already uses for a field with nothing in it, so no
locale had to be told a second wording of a sentence it can already say.

ci(desktop): compile the Rust crate on every platform we ship, not only at tag time

Nothing in the repository ran cargo outside desktop-release.yml, and that
workflow runs on a version tag. The first compiler to see a change on macOS or
Linux was therefore the one building a public release, which finds a compile
error after the docker image has been pushed and before the release is created.
Most of the crate is platform gated, so a developer on Windows compiles none of
the other arms locally and neither does anything else.

This adds a lane that runs cargo check on Windows, macOS and Linux for pushes to
main that touch the desktop directory. It packages nothing, signs nothing and
uploads nothing. Check rather than build because it still runs the build script,
expands the context macro and type checks every arm the target selects, which is
the whole class of error we are exposed to, and it finishes in a few minutes
instead of the two hours the release matrix allows.

Two paths have to be stood in for before the compiler gets anywhere. The
frontend bundle is what frontendDist points at and the context macro panics
rather than degrades when it is missing, and the server sidecar is resolved from
externalBin per target triple and is a PyInstaller artifact that is not
committed, so it is absent on a fresh checkout everywhere including Windows.
Both are created empty for the compiler and neither is shipped.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(e2e): fail a run in which a configured Playwright project did not execute

The main Playwright config declares five projects and nothing checked that they
all still run. The two ways of contributing nothing look completely different
from outside. A project whose browser is not installed is loud, every one of its
tests dies with "browserType.launch: Executable doesn't exist" and the run exits
1. A project whose grep matches no spec is silent. Asking for chromium and
rtl-arabic over a file carrying neither @rtl nor @i18n prints "Running 2 tests
using 2 workers" and a chromium-only summary, names rtl-arabic nowhere and exits
0. Nothing there separates a project that passed from one that never ran, and
that is the case worth catching, because the green summary is then reporting
coverage we do not have.

A reporter now reads the resolved config and the suite about to run, and asks
two questions of every project the run asked for. Did it select at least one
test, and is its browser on disk. The project list comes from the config rather
than from a list written out here, so a sixth project is covered the moment it
is declared. The reporter escalates the run to failed and never demotes a run
that had already failed on its own.

Working out what a run asked for has to come from the command line, and both
obvious alternatives were measured and rejected. config.projects is not filtered
by --project, a run pinned to chromium still reports all five, and config.grep
keeps its match-everything default even after --grep was passed. Either would
have produced a gate that silently never fired. A run narrowed by a grep, a
shard or an explicit file reports what it excluded but does not fail, because
whoever typed the filter knows what it leaves out. An unnarrowed run is a claim
about the whole suite, and there a dead project is a defect.

The decision logic sits in its own module with no Playwright import so the tests
beside it stay cheap to run. Importing @playwright/test from a vitest worker
exceeds that worker's startup budget, and vitest reports the timeout as "Test
Files no tests", which is the same did-not-run-reads-as-nothing-wrong shape this
reporter exists to remove.

CI runs only the half that travels between machines. Whether a project selects a
test is a property of the config and is true everywhere alike. Whether its
browser is on disk is a property of one machine, and a runner that installs no
browsers would condemn all five projects while saying nothing about the config.
That half belongs to whoever is about to run the tests, and it runs by default
for them.

The registry-wide sweep in test_validation_rules_skip_section_rows read
rule_registry from its own process, and that object is filled by import side
effects. Run this file alone the registry held 125 rules, with the module
validators imported 165, and in two sessions where an earlier test had already
built a FastAPI app 251 and 297. So the sweep asked its question of a population
up to 172 rules wider or narrower depending on what happened to run first, and
two sessions of the same kind did not even agree with each other. A rule that
convicts a well formed section header would have been caught in one order and
missed in another on the same tree, and both verdicts would have been equally

in an interpreter of its own that loads a stated set and nothing else: the
built-in rules, every validators.py under app/modules, and every register_*_rules

either at import or from its on_startup hook, and importing alone leaves

convicts a well formed header, while the in process registry those same runs
carried was 125, 251, 125 and 125.

the embedded text, and finally from the row id. That last rung is the one
thing a result may never be, an identifier, because both consumers of the
unified search render this string as the row label and it names nothing to the
person reading it. Two unnamed rows next to each other are also
indistinguishable, which is the part that makes the list useless rather than

failing that, the id, and that guard is narrower than the problem in two ways.
It only sees an empty title, so a title of spaces went to the screen as
spaces, and it cannot see a title that is itself the id, which is truthy and
walks straight past the fallback. Measured on the compiled module, the three
rows that arrive with nothing to say rendered as a UUID, a UUID and three
spaces. They now fall back the same way the backend does. Only an exact match
against the id counts as the fallback shape, so a title that merely quotes an
id is still treated as a title someone wrote, and the wording comes from the
caller rather than the helper, which keeps the helper pure and keeps the
string in the locale file under global_search.unnamed_hit.

sends, so the backend rung covers it, and stopping at that one consumer is why
the modal was missed the first time round.

Thirteen tests. Six exercise the title chain with no database at all, four of
them red before this change, and seven cover the frontend helper. Each asserts
the label against the identifier rather than merely requiring one, because a
UUID is a non-empty string and would satisfy a check that only asked for a
truthy title. The negative controls pin the other direction: a stored title
still wins, a text snippet still beats the last resort, and a real title
survives untouched.

fix(property-dev): stop adding contract values that are not the same money

The sales kanban summed every buyer's contract value into one column total
with no currency check at all, and the development P&L took the first buyer
who carried a currency as the development currency, then dropped every buyer
who disagreed with it. So a development selling in euros and dollars showed a
column total that is money in no currency, and contracted revenue could come
back as zero when the lead who happened to be first had signed in a different
one. The same gate also dropped deposits held and deposits forfeited, so the
fix covers those rather than leaving half the function on the old rule.

Amounts are now bucketed per ISO code, converted to a base currency through
the project's own fx_rates, and anything with no rate is reported under its
own code instead of being folded in. That is the pattern variations, change
orders and BOQ already use, and the helpers are ports of theirs. The base is
the development's currency, else the parent project's, else the single
currency the rows agree on, else nothing, and nothing means every non blank
bucket is unconverted rather than silently blended.

Existing fields keep their names and types and every new field has a default,
so no frontend change is needed. Two meanings did change and are worth
knowing: the P&L currency was the first buyer's stamp on a blended figure and
is now the currency the scalars are actually in, and mixed_currency was "some
buyer differs from the first" and is now "more than one distinct currency is
present".

The standard rate in GB and DE became a dated history a few commits ago. The

this same repository already carried the start date, which makes this the same

GB reduced is now two periods. Domestic fuel and power was zero rated until the
Finance Act 1993 removed that from 1 April 1994 and taxed it at 8 percent, and
the Finance Act 1997 cut it to 5 percent from 1 September 1997. The seed's
single 1997 row is a claim about everything before it and that claim was wrong,
so a GB reduced contract signed between April 1994 and August 1997 was priced at
5 percent and now prices at 8. That is a changed number, not only a changed
field. Signed before 1 April 1994 it is now refused: there was no reduced rate
to charge and the supplies were zero rated.

fix(a11y): six clickable table rows announced themselves as buttons and orphaned their cells

A tr carrying role="button" overrides the implicit row role, and an ARIA cell
requires an owning row. Every td underneath was therefore orphaned and the
column headers associated with nothing, so a screen reader user got a flat
button with no way to tell which column a value belonged to. Removing the role
restores row and cell, keeps the element focusable, keeps the Enter and Space
handler working, and keeps the accessible name, because row supports a name and
the aria-label still applies. The only thing lost is the word "button" in the
announcement, which is one word against an entire table's structure.

The fuller answer for a genuinely interactive table is the grid pattern with
gridcell, or a real control inside the first cell. Both are larger changes than
this defect justifies and neither is needed to make these six correct, so they
were considered and deliberately not taken here.

The pattern was deliberate and well intentioned rather than careless. Somebody
reached for the role that describes what the row does instead of what it is, and
all six also wired up tabIndex and the keyboard handler, which is more care than
the 787 other rows that did neither. Five of the six also carry an aria-label;
the cost spine row never had one, so there is no name to preserve there and it
keeps only its focus and keyboard behaviour.

Nothing selected these rows by their button role. All 825 test and spec files
were scanned for getByRole('button') and [role="button"] against these six
accessible names and testids, and the count was zero. The audit log test reaches
its row through getByTestId, which is unaffected.

This surfaced from a Playwright accessibility snapshot rather than from the spec,
which matters because the spec and the page were both just claims. The snapshot
exposes the same tree assistive technology reads, and the ARIA specification says
independently that a cell needs a row, so two sources agreed and neither was a
party to the dispute. The specs were left targeting the row role rather than
retargeted to the button role, since a test that passes by asserting the broken
shape actively defends the bug.

Two of the four skip sites in the property development suite were hiding
something that works and something that is broken. Neither would ever have
surfaced from a lane that reported them as covered.

fix(tests): two suites had been red on main, one against a real change and one against correct data

anything a person watches. Both are in the test rather than in the product, but
they are opposite kinds of wrong and only one of them is a stale test.

inherit English by default. That was the right shape for the fix. One test

it was before it broke.

under the bundled licence directory out of NOTICE and asserts each names a file
that exists. Its pattern allowed a dot anywhere in the name, which a filename
may legitimately contain, but NOTICE is prose and two of those paths end a
sentence. The full stop was read as part of the filename, so the check reported

correctly named, and told whoever read it to either restore the file or stop
claiming the attribution ships. Both instructions were wrong. The pattern now
requires the last character to be one a filename can end on.

a full stop attached and four more were never reached at all. The number
written in that comment had been describing the reader rather than the notice,

dependency that stops bundling somebody else's object code should be able to
drop its entry without failing this. That choice has a cost and the comment now
says so: the assertion catches the section being deleted and would not catch it
being gutted.

against the real notice rather than a fixture: it extracts all seven paths, all
seven resolve to files on disk, and a path naming something absent is still

ci: a failing advisory step was hiding whether the frontend still builds

The Playwright project verification sat between Lint and Type check, and it is
currently red for a real reason: every configured project selects zero tests.
Because a failing step aborts the job, everything after it was reported as
skipped on all three runners. Type check, Build and the unit tests. So while
that check was red, npm run build had not executed in CI at all, on any
platform, and the one gate the frontend actually answers to was reporting
nothing while the summary looked like it was covered.

This is worth stating plainly because it inverts what the run appeared to say.
Three jobs showing failure looked like three signals. It was one signal
repeated, plus twelve verdicts nobody got.

The step now runs last. Nothing is weakened. It executes on every push exactly
as before, it fails the job on exactly the same defect, and the zero-selection
problem it is reporting is untouched and still needs fixing on its own. What
changes is that it no longer decides whether the compiler gets to speak.

It carries `!cancelled()` rather than `always()` so that it still reports when
an earlier step has failed, which is the entire point of the move, while not
continuing to run after a cancellation or a superseding push. That is also the
form the rest of this file already uses.

The general rule, since this will happen again: order the steps so the most
load-bearing gate reports first and the cheapest advisory reports last. A red
that hides four other verdicts tells you less than the four verdicts would
have, and it does it while looking like more information rather than less.

Checked by parsing the workflow and printing the resulting step list with each
condition rather than by reading the diff. That is not ceremony: the first
version of this edit silently swallowed the macOS unit test step, which would
have dropped test coverage on that runner while every remaining step still
looked correct in the diff. The parse is what caught it.
