test(i18n): a lock on the call-site discipline that is the only thing keeping sixteen catalogues honest

Labelled as a regression lock rather than a bug fix, because that is what it is
and the docstring says so. No locale a client can send today survives
normalisation and reaches a catalogue that answers English. The context path is
clamped twice, once by the middleware matching against a table that holds base
codes only and once by the setter storing the resolved code rather than the one
it was handed. The document path strips explicitly, reducing both the
client-controlled query parameter and the raw header before matching.

The defect underneath is real even though nothing triggers it. Sixteen lookups
across eight modules still resolve by exact match and answer English for a
regional code. Twelve have no production caller at all. The other four are the
reason a lock earns its keep: they sit on live export paths and are safe only
because every route reaching them passes through a wrapper first. The catalogue
does not defend itself, its callers defend it, and one new call site forwarding
a raw locale parameter into a label lookup makes it live with nothing else
changing. That call-site discipline is the thing being locked, and it is
invisible in the catalogue it protects.

The gate prints its population on the axis that can actually narrow, and that
axis is catalogues reached rather than languages. Languages cannot narrow it:
every probe asks the same base-versus-regional pairs of every lookup, so that
count is fixed by the code. What can silently shrink is how many modules the
probe imported and interrogated, so the report carries modules scanned, probe
executed, lookups asked, and import failures by name, and a baseline naming a
module the probe never reached goes red rather than quiet.

Two measurements of the same thing disagree, and both are recorded here on
purpose rather than one replacing the other. An earlier commit message put it
at 33 of 41 in-memory catalogues converged on stripping with two holding out,
arrived at by reading them. This puts it at 16 lookups across 8 modules out of
39 catalogues probed with 233 lookups, arrived at by importing each module,
finding its public lookups and calling each twice with a base and a regional
code, counting only pairs whose answers would differ if it stripped. The second
is re-runnable and the first is not, which is the argument for it, and it is
also the reason the next person should re-run rather than inherit either
number.

Four times during construction this lock called a known defect clean, and each
was found only by going after how it could be lying rather than by confirming
it worked. An ownership filter that skipped every function in a file-loaded
module. An argument filler that could not reach one table and was comparing two
identical fallbacks. A duck-type requiring an attribute the very catalogue it
exists for did not have. And a run under the wrong interpreter that reported a
healthy file as a syntax error, which is now a guard that raises instead of
skipping, because a skipped module is a silently narrowed denominator and
writing a baseline that way would have recorded a smaller set and turned the
next correct run into a pile of false regressions.

It was proved red against the real thing rather than a fixture: all three
catalogues from the commit that fixed them, taken from the parent revision,
flagged before and clean after. Both directions, since a lock that flagged
everything would pass the first half and be worthless. One of its own tests
asserted a phrase was absent, which passes unconditionally the moment the
phrase stops being emitted, so that branch was fired deliberately and then
pinned by a test of its own.

The three files land together because the dependency is three-way: the test
imports the script and the script loads the baseline. A baseline arriving
without its script does not fail as a red gate, it raises out of the loader
before any verdict exists, and a crash reads nothing like a failure in a log.

test(property_dev): check the router only calls methods the service actually has

PropertyDevService is assembled twice over. Most methods sit in the class body,
forty-one more are module-level _svc_* functions attached at import time with a
trailing type: ignore[attr-defined]. That ignore is the reason this test exists.
It silences the checker at the definition site, not at the call sites, so a route
calling a method nobody attached type-checks clean, imports clean, starts clean,
and raises AttributeError the first time a request reaches that one endpoint.

The test resolves bindings rather than spellings. The obvious version, collecting
every svc.X( in the router and looking X up on the class, was written first and
reported five failures, all of them false: cohort_retention, time_to_close,
lead_source_attribution, conversion_funnel and broker_performance belong to
AnalyticsService, which the dashboard routes construct locally under a variable
that happens to also be called svc. Two classes, one variable name. So this walks
each function and places every receiver it can, parameters by their annotation
and locals by their constructor, and attributes a call to the service only when
the binding says so. Receivers it places on another type are counted and named in
the failure message rather than dropped, because a classifier that discards what
it cannot categorise is quoting a denominator it does not have.

Proved red three ways before committing, not just green on the tree. Deleting the
get_broker attachment fails it, which is the shipping accident. Renaming a call to
a name nobody attached fails it, which is the typo. Renaming an AnalyticsService
call does not fail it, which is the false positive the first version produced and
is worth keeping as a control rather than a comment.

Today it passes over 199 resolved call sites and 157 distinct names, and carries a
floor so a refactor that stops routes taking the service as a dependency fails
loudly instead of going green over an empty set.

fix(gates): give the locale resolution lock a verdict when its baseline is gone

The lock reads scripts/locale_resolution_baseline.json. If that file was missing
or malformed it raised whatever the loader happened to raise, so the failure
arrived as a traceback rather than as an answer. Red, so not the worst outcome
available, but every other data-backed gate under scripts/ has a defined result
for a missing data file and this one did not.

Found by sweeping the other direction. The question was whether any gate in the
tree fails OPEN on absent data - catches the error, returns an empty set, and
reports OK over nothing. None does. All four loaders that swallow a missing file
fail strict instead: check_i18n_plural_forms and check_i18n_script_mixing empty
their suppression sets so every finding becomes unsuppressed, check_no_brand_tokens
empties its allowlist the same way, and check_i18n_leak_baseline checks its
pending-review ceiling on both sides, so a vanished file gives zero against a
floor and trips the lower branch. A two-sided ratchet cannot be silenced by
deleting its data, which is the pattern worth copying. check_seed_diacritics
already prints its denominator and guards the zero-scanned case explicitly.

So the sweep found the hazard did not repeat, and that the one gate answering a
missing file with a traceback was this one.

A missing baseline is deliberately not treated as an empty baseline. Empty is
also red, which makes the two look interchangeable from the exit code, but they
are red about different things: an empty baseline reports the sixteen known and
accepted lookups as fresh regressions and sends a reader hunting a change nobody
made. A gate whose reds cannot be trusted gets switched off, and then there is no
gate. The two failures now say which one happened and why the file should have
been there:

  ERROR: scripts/locale_resolution_baseline.json is missing, so this lock cannot
  say anything about anything. It ships in the same commit as this script; if you
  are seeing this, the two were separated.

Two tests assert on stderr and on the exit code, because a gate that printed
something is not the claim. Both were proved red by neutering the handler so the
original error escapes again, then restored and re-hashed. Fifteen tests pass and
the gate itself still reports 39 catalogues over 233 lookups against a 16-entry
baseline.

fix(costs): writes landed in one vector store while every reader opened another

Two halves of one defect, and they are in the same commit because the first
is only honest once the second is fixed.

The cost database card offers two install routes that fill different
collections. Generating an index fills cost_items, which is what rate
suggestion, classification and anomaly checks search. Restoring a published
snapshot fills the per-language v3 catalogue collections, which is what
element matching searches. Neither route populates the other. The card
described both with one number taken from an endpoint that can only see the
first, so restoring a snapshot left the tiles reading 0% over an install where
matching worked, and generating an index turned them green over an install
where matching returned nothing. The card already knew the two were different
in one place: the error path of the per-region loader carries a comment saying
so, added when somebody noticed that polling the cost_items count would report
failure for every successful restore. The summary tiles were never revisited.

The card now reads both stores and shows both numbers, side by side rather
than folded into one ready flag, because a single boolean over two independent
stores is how this happened. The catalogue signal is existence-and-non-empty,
which is a state and not a proportion, so it renders as a count next to a
percentage rather than being dressed up as a matching percentage. Inventing a
denominator to make two tiles look symmetrical would have been the same class
of mistake in a new place.

An unreachable catalogue server reads as unknown rather than as zero
installed. The backend derives every row's status from a single probe and
falls all rows back to available when that probe fails, so a bare count would
say zero for "nothing is installed" and zero for "we could not ask" in the
same word.

The failure direction is deliberately the opposite of the defect. If the
catalogue endpoint errors outright the tile reads unknown rather than zero
installed, and a LanceDB-only install, where matching does not exist at all,
reads the same way. The bug being fixed here was a surface reporting a
confident number it had not earned; the replacement declines to report rather
than guessing, in every case where it cannot speak for the store it names.

The success toast keeps its count and gains its scope. "N items indexed" was
true and was read as "matching is ready now", so the sentence naming which
features it actually powers now follows it. The count is untouched.

The second half is why the first was still not trustworthy. Four call sites
resolved the location of the CWICR v3 store and no two were written from the
same rule: the ranker consulted cwicr_qdrant_url alone and otherwise opened an
embedded store, the snapshot loader consulted it strictly in one function and
leniently in another, and the router helper added a fallback to qdrant_url.
That is not two things that drifted from a common origin, so there is no
commit where they split. It is four independent readings of the same pair of
settings.

The fallback was there to save a configuration step, on the reasoning that in
single-server dev both settings point at the same instance. They do not.
qdrant_url is defaulted to http://localhost:6333 and cwicr_qdrant_url is not
defaulted at all, so a lenient resolution can never fall through and a strict
one always does, and the two cannot agree until a human sets the CWICR
setting. Bring up a local Qdrant, change nothing, install a catalogue, and the
install writes to the server while the ranker reads embedded. The install
reports success and matching finds nothing, with no misconfiguration required.

Nobody is relying on that fallback, because it has never produced a working
system. With only QDRANT_URL set the restore writes to that server while the
ranker opens the embedded store, so there is no configuration in which the
fallback makes matching work. It only makes the write land somewhere the read
never looks. Removing it therefore does not break a working install, it makes
an already broken one say why.

So there is now one resolution and every caller goes through it. The reader
did not change behaviour, and no default was touched: lending the reader the
writer's fallback would have swung every unconfigured install off its embedded
store onto a port that is usually nothing, which is the same non-None default
causing the problem from the other side.

The refusal happens before the download rather than after it. The restore
handler could spend ten minutes pulling 1.1 GB and only then discover it had
nowhere to put it, so the target is resolved first and the message names both
settings and both concrete values. Two error strings that told operators to
set QDRANT_URL or CWICR_QDRANT_URL no longer offer the first, because it is
not a remedy.

Both halves are pinned, and each was checked by breaking it. The frontend test
drives the two stores in opposite directions, because one that moved them
together would have passed before this change as happily as after it; putting
the old reading back turned four of its five red. The backend test asserts
that the target a restore writes to and the target the ranker reads from
resolve from the same settings object, read through the router's own helper
rather than recomputed, so it crosses the boundary the bug crossed. It needed
two separate injections to prove, because it has two axes: restoring the
lenient fallback turns the three strictness assertions red and leaves the
invariant green, while letting the router resolve on its own again turns all
seven invariant cases red. Every settings object in that table is built with
_env_file=None, without which pydantic loads backend/.env and a developer
machine that sets CWICR_QDRANT_URL makes the whole file pass by describing the
machine rather than the product.

Worth recording why a defect on the default path survived this long: this
machine carries CWICR_QDRANT_URL in backend/.env, and so, presumably, does
every machine the feature was built on. Nobody working on it was ever in the
default configuration, which is the configuration every new user starts in.

The measurement that established all of this nearly went the other way, and
the failure is worth writing down because it points at retracting a true
finding rather than at inventing a false one. The first probe built
Settings(**kw) directly and reported that the resolvers agreed in all five
cases. pydantic-settings loads env_file even for a hand-constructed object, so
each case silently received this machine's CWICR_QDRANT_URL and the divergence
disappeared. A probe that invents a defect gets caught the moment somebody
looks at it; one that erases a defect you had already established leaves
everyone relieved, and it arrives wearing the authority of a measurement over
a static reading. What caught it was that the new instrument disagreed with a
conclusion already supported by seven independent sources, and a disagreement
between two sources is itself the finding. Constructing a config object does
not isolate you from ambient config; something has to be passed to switch the
ambient source off, and here that was _env_file=None.

One thing found and deliberately not fixed here. In the same restore handler
the collection is created through the general vector client, which resolves on
qdrant_url, while the snapshot is uploaded to the CWICR target. Where the two
settings differ that creates an empty collection on one server and uploads to
another. It is the same family and it wants the same treatment, but it is a
behaviour change in a handler this commit already changes, so it is written
down rather than folded in.

fix(property_dev): the global admin role no longer crosses a tenant boundary

The module answered two ways about the same question. One ownership helper
documented that a global admin does not reach another tenant's data and
implemented exactly that, while sibling helpers returned early for anyone
holding the admin role. Which answer a request got depended on which door it
came through, so the guarantee written in one docstring was not the
guarantee the module actually offered.

Ownership is now strict everywhere a caller reaches one named object. The
gates that resolve a plot, a lead, a broker, a buyer, a document, a house
type catalogue entry and a custom document template all compare the stored
owner against the caller and collapse a mismatch to 404, as the development
gate already did. Same tenant access is unaffected, because the owner id
still matches. Three copies of the same check in the buyer portal were
folded into one helper, since three copies of an authorization check are
three chances to fix two of them.

Two things here are deliberate rather than oversights. A lead that carries
no development is still reachable, because those are top of funnel inbound
webhook rows that belong to nobody and carry no project scoped data; only
the admin branch was removed from that condition, and the pass through for
an absent development stays. The bulk sales operations console keeps its
admin branch, because it decides how wide a batch runs rather than whether
one named object may be reached, and whether that batch should span tenants
is a product decision rather than a defect. It is recorded in the test
allowlist with that reasoning instead of being changed quietly.

The custom document template endpoints also stopped creating rows with no
owning project. Every ownership gate on those endpoints passes a row whose
project is unset, so a row created without one sat outside the boundary the
rest of this change draws. Every role now needs a project to upload or save
a template, which is the rule the other roles already followed.

What this does NOT change, stated so nobody has to re-derive it from the
diff. An admin gets no cross tenant reach on a named object, and that rule
does not bind how wide a listing runs. Eleven functions still branch on the
admin role and every one of them decides the width of a list, a dashboard
rollup or a batch rather than reach on one object: the development, lead,
reservation and template listings, five dashboard aggregates, the helper
that resolves the id set a listing is scoped to, and the sales operations
batch console. An admin still sees every development in the list. Narrowing
that may well be right, but it is a product decision with visible
consequences for the admin console, and making it silently as a side effect
of an authorization fix would be the wrong way to reach it. Each one is
recorded in the test allowlist with its reason, so changing the answer later
means editing a line that states the old answer.

The test discovers what it guards from the route table rather than from a
naming convention. This matters more than the fix. The first version of
this test enumerated helpers by their shared name prefix, and it would have
passed while missing the gate that does the real work, because the broker
helper matching that prefix is reached by no route at all and the live
broker gate is named differently. A scope written as a name is blind to the
sibling doing the work and it counts dead code as covered.

The population is every registered route and every verb, reads included,
because an admin reading one named object across the boundary is the same
crossing as writing it. Discovery narrows by nothing but wiring. The two
detectors do still read spelling, matching the admin literal and the owner
and tenant id fields, and both are deliberately broad so that residue costs
a false alarm rather than a silent pass. Exemptions are keyed to routes, so
renaming a handler breaks the stale entry test loudly instead of quietly
granting an amnesty. That same shape
of mistake has now been found four times in this codebase in a single day,
wearing a different coat each time: a scope written as a key name blind to
sibling keys, then blind to sibling jurisdictions under one key, then blind
to a sibling key at the same level, and now a function name prefix blind to
the gate actually wired up. The lesson is worth more written down than the
fix is. Ask what stands between a request and the data, not what it is
called.

Reading the assembled route table turned up the same trap one level down.
Iterating the router's own route list silently dropped all nine buyer
portal routes, because the included router sits behind a wrapper object
rather than being spliced in. The walk now descends by shape, so a rename
of that internal attribute cannot quietly shrink the population either.

fix(property-dev): repeating a cancel or an expire answered 200 and fired the event twice

Repeating any of these returned 200 and published a second lifecycle event for
one state change. The FSM helper returns early when the target status equals the
current one, and it returns from itself rather than from its caller, so the
repeat fell straight through to the status write, the plot release and
publish_detached. A downstream subscriber therefore saw one reservation
cancelled, or expired, twice. That is the kind of duplicate that is hard to
trace back, because from the outside the second request looks successful.

Where the codebase answers this question at all it answers 409. Of the 46
cancel, archive, close, void and revoke service functions across the module
service files, 8 raise a conflict mentioning "already" and 2 return quietly,
with the remaining 36 not answering either way. Property development is already
on the conflict side in its own cancel_buyer, which checks the terminal states
explicitly and raises before touching anything. So this is not a convention
argument across the platform, it is one module disagreeing with itself, and the
fix is to make the reservation, contract and expiry paths do what the buyer path
beside them already does.

The guard is deliberately at the three call sites rather than inside the shared
helper. That helper has 22 call sites, and several of them are PATCH handlers
where a client re-submitting the record's current status has to stay idempotent.
Removing the early return there would have turned every no-op update into a
conflict, which is a much larger and worse change than the one this fixes.

Expire was held back from the first version of this fix on the belief that it
was different, because it has a scheduled caller and answering 409 to a cron job
would turn a quiet idempotent sweep into a recurring error. That belief was
wrong, and it was wrong in a way worth writing down: it reasoned from the shape
of the caller rather than from what the caller selects. A scheduled caller is
only a hazard if it can reach the state in question. It cannot, for two
independent reasons. find_expired filters on status equal to active, so an
already-expired reservation is never in the batch's result set. And the loop
around expire_reservation already catches HTTPException and skips the row, with
a comment saying a transition conflict is a normal skip rather than an abort.
Since the transition helper raises 409, that except clause was already written
against exactly the conflict this adds. The guard does not change what the batch
does, it makes the code do what the batch already assumed it did.

Only the repeat needed a guard in each case. The other terminal states were
already rejected, because cancelled is not in the permitted set for converted,
expired, refunded or registered, and expired is not in the permitted set for
converted, cancelled or refunded, so those went through the existing check.
Keeping the guards that narrow matters. A broader expire guard, on status not
equal to active, would have rewritten the detail string on a path that
tests/modules/property_dev/test_r8_security.py:632 already asserts is an
invalid transition, breaking a file this change has no other reason to touch.
That was found by grepping the test tree for the route, not by reasoning about
what might exist, and reasoning would not have found it.

Four tests, none of which displaced an existing one, because none of these
behaviours was pinned before. Three pin the repeat at 200 then 409. The fourth
pins that the batch is undisturbed, which nothing tested before: a sweep run
with an already-expired reservation sitting beside an overdue one still expires
the overdue row, still answers 200, and does not expire the finished one a
second time. Note what that fourth test does and does not show. The guard is
never reached from the batch path, because the status filter excludes the
finished row before the loop sees it, so it demonstrates that the sweep is
unaffected rather than that the except clause catches the new conflict.

All three endpoints were also exercised directly, because a service raising a
conflict and an endpoint answering one are two different claims. Each returns
200 then 409, so nothing in the router layer flattens it on the way out.

fix(async): a cancelled gather sub-task was not a BaseException to the guard that filtered it

asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) captures a cancelled
sub-task's CancelledError exactly like it captures an ordinary
exception, but CancelledError has been a BaseException rather than
an Exception since Python 3.8. isinstance(x, Exception) does not
narrow that, so a cancelled sub-task walked straight through every
guard written against Exception and reached code that assumed a
normal result.

Swept every asyncio.gather call in backend/app and backend/tests: 37
call sites in 26 files, 10 pass return_exceptions explicitly (3 with
False, exempt - gather raises immediately with no per-item filtering
to get wrong), 7 with True. Of those seven, three were already
correct (takeoff/router.py, both sites in
tests/integration/test_boq_cycle_stress.py, all isinstance(x,
BaseException)) and are untouched. Also swept asyncio.wait (zero
uses), asyncio.TaskGroup (zero uses), Task.exception() (one use,
core/events.py, already correct) and except BaseException (two uses,
both deliberate and unrelated to task cancellation) - nothing further
to fix there.

Three real occurrences fixed, three different repairs because the
right answer depends on what a cancelled item means at that site, not
on matching the pattern:

* costs/qdrant_adapter.py cross_language_search - the seed instance.
  isinstance(res, Exception) let a cancelled collection's
  CancelledError reach merged.extend(res), raising TypeError on a
  non-iterable at the merge, nowhere near the cancellation that caused
  it. One collection failing or being cancelled has a legitimate
  default here - skip it, the others still contribute - so the fix is
  the same substitution the site already made for ordinary failures,
  widened from Exception to BaseException.

* project_intelligence/collector.py collect_project_state - the same
  shape, 14 unpacking lines. A cancelled collector has a domain
  default too: an empty BOQState (etc.) is a real answer, so
  substitution is correct here as well.

* clash_ai_triage/service.py triage_batch - a different repair. Every
  genuine per-clash failure is already caught and logged inside the
  batch's own worker helper, so the only things that can reach the
  per-outcome loop are ClashTriageUnavailable (already handled) or a
  cancelled worker's CancelledError. A cancelled triage is not a
  domain default the way an empty state is - it is an infrastructure
  interruption - so this site propagates it instead of substituting
  one. This site is also a third variant of the bug class in its own
  right: its guard named a narrow exception subtype
  (ClashTriageUnavailable) rather than Exception or BaseException, so
  a cancelled worker satisfied neither branch and simply vanished from
  the merged output with no log and no raise - indistinguishable from
  a clash that was merely skipped.

notifications/notification_worker.py stop_scheduler discards its
gather result entirely and is left alone - verified nothing calls
.cancel() on those tasks and nothing reads the discarded result, so
no wrong data can flow from it - but the reasoning rests on two
absences that could go stale silently, so a comment now names the
condition that would make it unsafe.

Each of the three fixes has its own test, and each is proven against
the actual pre-fix code rather than a synthetic reproduction: a
collector's CancelledError instance literally arriving in place of the
domain object, a batch that does not raise CancelledError when a
worker is cancelled, and the original TypeError: 'CancelledError'
object is not iterable that started this sweep.

ci: main never finished a run because every push cancelled the one before

ci.yml fires on every push to main and we work straight in main without PRs, so
cancel-in-progress: true meant each push killed its predecessor. Of the last 30
ci.yml runs on main, 28 were cancelled, 19 of the last 20 in a row.

The cost is not a wrong answer, it is no answer. A cancelled run has no
conclusion, nothing goes red, and the silence is indistinguishable from health.
It cost most of a day chasing whether a frontend step still runs after a step
reorder, a question that was never blocked on the ordering.

The pooled number hides this and is the one a reasonable person reaches for
first. Across all workflows on main the same window reads 24 success and 3
cancelled. Split by workflow, ci.yml is 28 of 30 cancelled while the other six
are healthy, because they either set no cancel-in-progress or do not fire on
push. Pooling across populations under different policies reports the majority's
health as everyone's, and it does it here as a false negative, which is the kind
that tells you to stop looking.

Measured and left alone deliberately, so nobody re-derives it. The other four
workflows carrying cancel-in-progress: true are not starved, and the reason is
structural rather than statistical, so it will still hold when these run counts
have turned over:

  e2e-cross-os      schedule + workflow_dispatch, no push   30 runs,  3 cancelled
  homepage-loops    workflow_dispatch only                   2 runs,  0 cancelled
  module-captures   workflow_dispatch only                   2 runs,  0 cancelled
  desktop-check     push to main, path-filtered              1 run,   0 cancelled
  ci                push to main                            30 runs, 28 cancelled

Three of the four have no push trigger at all, so their runs cannot collide.
Only ci.yml has both a trigger that fires constantly on main and a cancellation
rate to match. release-signing.yml already sets cancel-in-progress: false with a
comment saying why, so this directory already decides concurrency per workflow
rather than as a blanket policy.

One fact with a short shelf life, recorded here and going into CLAUDE.md beside
the paragraph on which lanes are authoritative: the lanes we treat as
authoritative, CI (PostgreSQL) and Repo hygiene, are 5 of 5 green in the same
window, and the starved lane is CI, which is not on that list. Nothing chose
that. Had CI been on it we would have been acting on blanks for weeks.

How to know this worked. Not that a run completes, because an uncontested run
always completed and a quiet period proves nothing. The property is two runs on
different SHAs both reaching a non-cancelled conclusion. Push twice to main in
quick succession and read:

  gh run list --workflow ci.yml --branch main --limit 5 --json headSha,status,conclusion

The first run must still reach a conclusion while the second is in flight. A
verification described in prose is a verification nobody performs, so the
command is here rather than the description.

fix(tax): a reduced tier was answering for a standard rate that had not started

The seed resolver picks the country-wide row flagged is_default, and when no
row in force carries the flag it promotes a lone unflagged row instead. That
fallback is right for a table written before the flag existed. It is wrong for
a table whose standard rate is on file with a window that has not started yet,
because what is in force on an earlier date is then a reduced tier that runs
alongside the standard rate rather than before it.

Six of the forty-one countries in the shipped seed are that second case, and
between them they misquoted every date before their standard rate begins.
Germany answered 7 % for 1990, Finland 14 % for 2015, Britain 0 % for 1990,
Ireland 13.5 % for 2005, Italy 10 % for 2000 and Russia 10 % for 2010, each
with resolved true and a number a caller would put on an invoice. This is
live rather than latent: the resolve endpoint takes an on_date and its own
service docstring promises that a past date reads the rate in force then.

Every one of those is a real published tier of the country that answered it,
on file with a real start date, returned through the branch that exists to be
right. The drift gate would have stayed green at 23 compared keys while all
six countries misquoted every past date they were asked about.

Romania decides the shape of the fix. It has a genuine two-row history of one
tax, 19 % closed on 2025-07-31 and 21 % open from the next day, so a question
about 2020 meets a single unflagged row that really is the standard rate of
that year. Refusing whenever nothing is flagged would have broken it. The test
is therefore the end of one window against the start of the next: a rate that
still has no effective_to on the day the standard rate begins is a parallel
tier, and one that ends where the standard rate begins is its predecessor.
That needs no tax code and no naming convention, so a country that renamed its
tax between periods still reads as a succession.

The legacy path is preserved deliberately and the code comment says which case
it preserves: a country with no default row anywhere still answers from its
single row, because that is most of the fixtures in this repo and every
install seeded before the flag existed. Only a country that has a standard
rate on file and is being asked about a date outside its window now refuses.

The refusal is a new status, default_rate_not_in_force, and it fails towards
no answer rather than towards a number. It is not in RESOLVED_STATUSES, so
combined_rate_pct is null and resolved is false, and a client that has never
heard of the status reads those two fields and shows no rate. It is mirrored
in schemas.py as well, because that Literal is what the response model
validates against and a status added on one side only would turn a repaired
country into a failed request.

The one client we ship needed its own state rather than the existing conflict
copy. That copy tells the reader to flag one of the rows already on file as
the default, which here would flag a reduced tier as the standard rate and
make the wrong number permanent; the new copy says the standard rate of that
period is missing and asks for it to be added. The panel's tone table is
keyed on the classification, so the new state was a compile error there until
it was given one, which is the one place in that feature where the vocabulary
is actually enforced rather than only described.

Britain moves as well as the six. Forty of its country-date pairs already
refused as default_rate_ambiguous, because two unflagged tiers are in force
there together, and they now refuse as this instead. That is the more accurate
of the two and the copy change matters more there than the status does: the
old advice would have had somebody mark the zero-rate row as Britain's
standard rate.

Proved red before it was trusted. The test names the six countries and asserts
Romania in the same run, and that pairing is what separates the fix from a
blanket refusal. It also sweeps the whole file rather than the six: 81 shipped
rate rows, 41 countries, 158 probe dates taken from every window boundary and
the day either side of it, 6478 country-date pairs, and it asserts the set of
countries that ever refuse rather than a count, so a seventh arriving is a
finding either way.

One note went into the property development yaml rather than the code. The
Russian reduced class is absent from that table on purpose, and the seed does
carry it, dated 2004-01-01 - which is exactly the day the Russian standard
rate moved from 20 % to 18 %, a suspicious day for the reduced rate to share
when the 10 % class is older than that and the two changes are unrelated. No
source consulted gave a day for it, so none was written in its place and the
doubt is stated where a reader will meet it.

The forty-two locale files each show three more lines changed than the two
this adds. Those are the costs keys from d5726f38c, already committed and
sitting at a different position in this worktree, so they read as removed and
re-added. Net new content in every one of those files is the two keys above
and nothing else.

Two counts landed beside the checks that produce them, in this file and in the
drift gate, because a verdict without its denominator is what let this sit: a
resolver reported fine over however many rows the last reader happened to
look at.

fix(costs): snapshot restore left an empty collection on a server nobody reads

Restoring a CWICR snapshot could create the collection on one Qdrant and upload
the vectors to another. Wherever CWICR_QDRANT_URL and QDRANT_URL point at
different hosts, the operator was left with an empty cwicr_<lang>_v3 on the
general server, a vectors_count read back from that empty collection, and a
success message describing a restore the ranker cannot see.

The handler took its client from app.core.vector._get_qdrant, which resolves on
qdrant_url, and then uploaded through the CWICR path, which resolves on
cwicr_qdrant_url. That is the defect fixed in d5726f38c, in the one call site
that still resolved twice. It now takes its client from
qdrant_adapter._get_client, so every operation in the handler talks to the store
the ranker opens and the resolution happens once.

The availability probe moved with it rather than being dropped. The old one
called get_collections on the general server, which is a real reachability check
aimed at the wrong host: it passed while the CWICR target was down and refused
while it was fine. It is also the only thing standing between an unreachable
server and a 1.1 GB download that can only fail once it has finished, so
deleting it as redundant would have quietly restored that wait. The two second
connect timeout it used to carry is deliberately not carried over, because the
client is shared with the ranker and a two second ceiling on a real search over
a large collection is a bug rather than a safeguard. The reasoning sits beside
the code, since that is the edit a future reader is most likely to undo.

Also adds the backend half of the lock on the BOQ editor readiness gate. That
gate was investigated and found correct, which is worth recording because the
opposite was reported and believed for a while: the page also hosts element
matching, so judging the gate by what the page is about gives the wrong answer.
The tests pin that the three gated actions reach vector_search and that
vector_search reads cost_items, so repointing either half fails here instead of
silently decoupling the gate from what it gates. The frontend half is
deliberately absent and the docstring records what it would have to assert.

On evidence, because the two kinds here are not equal. The driven tests were
proved red by repointing vector_search at cwicr_en_v3. The two AST tests were
not, because proving them that way means injecting a fault into a 5,816 line
service other work is live in, to demonstrate something a shared file is a poor
place to demonstrate. They were shown to discriminate instead, across 91 service
methods and 62 catalogue side functions, and the counts are in the file. That is
weaker than a red run and stronger than nothing, so it is stated rather than
glossed, as are the two assertions in the resolver tests that pin the positive
path and stayed green under both injections.

i18n(boq): six locales went back to calling the bill a BOQ

The keys added in bb1a57717 this morning were translated from the English
source, and the English source calls a bill of quantities a BOQ. Six locales
do not. German has the Leistungsverzeichnis, French the DQE, Italian the
computo metrico, and Chinese, Japanese and Korean each have a settled word of
their own, so on the validation page and in the matching wizard those readers
met the loan word on five keys while every neighbouring screen used the trade
term. Korean was worse than the rest: validation.subtitle read the bill as
물량 내역서, which is a second name for the object the file already calls
내역서, and Japanese named it 数量拾い, which is the takeoff and not the bill.

Twenty four strings, five keys, six locales. The wizard now names the Excel
source the way each locale's own tab does, Excel-LV, DQE Excel, computo
metrico Excel, Excel 工程量清单, Excel 内訳書, Excel 내역서. The two subtitles

the bridge and because French, Italian and Chinese already gloss that same
key. Agreement moved with the noun: the German LV is neuter, the French DQE
masculine and invariable, the Italian computo metrico takes its preposition,
and the Korean particles are the open syllable forms 를 and 가.

The interesting part is not the wording, it is the twelve days. The gate that
catches this, localesNameTheBillTheWayTheTradeDoes, has stood since 17.08 and
went red this morning without anyone noticing, because every run on main was
being cancelled by the next push. A gate nobody reads is a gate nobody has.

putting it back: 7 failed of 62 before, 62 passed after.

Locales outside the gate carry the same five keys and were left alone, since

chore(hygiene): the agent notes were kept out of git by a per-clone exclude and nothing else

Constraint 9 says an internal document goes in .gitignore and in the
check_repo_hygiene.py denylist. For .claude/ neither had been done. The only
thing holding it back was .git/info/exclude, which is per-clone and is not
carried by a clone, so in a fresh checkout there was no ignore rule and no
gate pattern, and the hygiene gate passed clean while blind to the whole
class. .claude/ holds pypi-api-token.txt, token.txt and _pat.txt next to the
notes, so the cost of that gap was never only a leaked document.

The two halves close different windows and neither substitutes for the other.
.gitignore stops the file being added. The denylist catches one that is
already tracked, which .gitignore cannot do, because .gitignore has no opinion
about a path git already follows. Both are here, and each was proved
separately rather than proved once and assumed twice:

  .gitignore half. git check-ignore -v .claude/CLAUDE.md previously answered
  .git/info/exclude:9 and now answers .gitignore:139, so the rule travels with
  the repository instead of living in one working copy.

  denylist half. Seeded a scratch index from HEAD via GIT_INDEX_FILE, staged
  .claude/CLAUDE.md into it with add -f, and ran the gate against that index:
  exit 1, naming the file. The real index was never touched, which matters
  with several agents working in this tree, since any pathless add here takes
  somebody else's work with it.

marketing-site/CLAUDE.md gets no .gitignore line. /marketing-site/ already
ignores that whole tree, 0 files tracked, and a redundant pattern is noise
that reads like coverage. It is in the denylist only, which is the half that
still applies if one is ever force-added.

Nothing under .claude/ is tracked today, so the blanket pattern changes
nothing that exists. If we ever want to ship part of it, .claude/skills/ being
the plausible one, this needs a negation rather than a wider net. Recorded
here because the wide pattern is the quiet one, and quiet is what makes it
hard to notice later.

playwright.config.ts ignored '**/runner/**', meaning the tests/e2e/runner/
directory. Playwright matches testIgnore against the absolute path of each file
and the match is not anchored at the start, so the pattern also matched any
checkout living under a directory called runner. GitHub checks out into
/home/runner/work/... on Linux and /Users/runner/work/... on macOS, so the
pattern ignored every spec in the repository: all five projects selected zero
tests and the "Verify every Playwright project still selects tests" step failed
on both. Windows runners use D:\a\..., so the same commit was green there.

The four directory patterns are now anchored with tests/e2e/, which is the
directory they were always about. node_modules keeps its bare form because it
is genuinely meant to match at any depth.

Reproduced before fixing, on Windows, by extracting the tree at this commit into
a path whose parent directory is named runner: all five projects reported zero
selected tests, byte for byte the CI output. The same tree in the same place
with only this change selects 12 files and 103 tests, which is what the working
copy selects at its ordinary path. No other config in the directory declares
testIgnore, so the defect had no radius beyond this file.

The failure could not be found by reading the config, because the pattern is
correct about the repository and wrong only about the machine.

DELETE /developments/{dev_id} is guarded by two independent walls, and when
the owning project belongs to an editor no role satisfies both. The
permission maps to MANAGER, so the editor who owns the project is refused
403. The ownership check is strict, only project.owner_id passes it, so the
manager and the admin who do hold the permission are refused 404. Measured
through HTTP against all three seeded roles: 403, 404, 404, and afterwards
the owner can still read the record it cannot remove.

Why nothing caught this. Every delete test in the package is a denial test.
test_r8_member_denied_delete_plot asserts the status is in (403, 404), which
is satisfied just as well by a world where the operation is impossible for
everyone. Asserting that a request is refused cannot detect that all
requests are refused. Nobody wrote the positive half, so the module has a
thorough set of tests that would stay green if every delete route in it
stopped working.

The collision was in fact already written down twice, from two directions,
and never joined up. test_security.py:235 explains that it probes with GET
rather than DELETE because the RBAC gate "fires first and would mask the
IDOR with 403". test_inventory_map.py:118 explains that its fixture role
"MUST be manager (not editor)" so the permission gate "passes BEFORE the
IDOR check". Each author needed only to get past the obstacle, so each
routed around it and neither reported it.

All three roles are asserted on purpose, in denial-first order. A test that
checked only the owner would pass against a repair that simply let the
global admin bypass ownership, and that direction is barred: strict
ownership here is deliberate and closes the cross-tenant IDOR (deferred
#66). The manager and admin cells are the control that keeps the repair
honest, so this fails both when nobody can delete and when the wrong party
can. Confirmed red for the right reason: both control cells pass, and the
failure is the owner's cell with "Missing permission: property_dev.delete".

i18n(uz): typewriter apostrophes where Uzbek Latin wants its own two marks

Uzbek Latin has two marks and neither is the ASCII apostrophe. Oʻ and gʻ are
letters of the alphabet and carry a turned comma, U+02BB. The tutuq belgisi
that marks a glottal stop is a different character, U+02BC, and it is what
maʼlumot and taʼminlaydi need. A plain ' is neither, so oʻzgartirish and
o'zgartirish are not the same word on the page, and the file was carrying both
spellings side by side.

Twenty nine values, sixty five marks. The letter in front decides which mark
goes in: o, O and g take the turned comma, a takes the modifier apostrophe.
Dimension notation is untouched, an apostrophe after a digit means feet and
the guard already exempts it.

Worth writing down how the count was found, because the report that started
this named seven keys and there were twenty nine. The seven were the tail of
the assertion's array as the runner printed it, not the finding. Running the
test's own predicate, value differs from English and carries a non-dimension
apostrophe, across the whole file is what gives the real set, and it reaches
site_inventory, auth, costs, bi and cases as well as the people and
procurement keys that were visible.

uz is commented out of the offered languages, so nobody is reading this today.
That is a reason to keep the file correct rather than a reason to skip it: the
list is one line away from being uncommented and the orthography would ship
wrong the day it is.

fix(auth): one source for the weak-secret rules, and a jti on every token

The denylist of known-weak JWT secrets and its minimum length existed twice,
in backend/app/config.py and in backend/app/main.py, each maintained by hand.
The premise for collapsing them was that they agree today and would drift
silently later. They had already drifted. The copy in main.py was missing
three of the strings the other rejected, and it measured length in UTF-8
bytes where the other measured characters, so the two gave opposite answers
on any non-ASCII secret. Nothing compared them, so nothing reported it. That
is the class of defect here: a constant kept in two places is invisible while
the copies agree and silent when they stop.

config.py is now the only place either rule is stated, exposed as
jwt_secret_is_known_weak and jwt_secret_is_too_short, and main.py imports
them. The length rule keeps both measures and takes the stricter answer, so
the collapse cannot quietly loosen anything: a byte-only rule would have
admitted a twenty-character secret. The startup block in main.py keeps its
control flow and its messages. Worth recording while it is measured: those
non-development branches were already unreachable, because the config check
is a pydantic model validator and raises while Settings is being constructed,
long before startup code looks at the secret.

scripts/check_secret_denylist_single_source.py refuses a second copy of
either rule, reading the AST rather than the text, and runs as a pre-commit
hook and as a repo hygiene guard. Proved red by adding a third mirror, which
it named on both counts, and green again once that was removed.

Separately, every issued token now carries a jti. Nothing reads it yet. It is
here because a token with no identifier cannot be named by a revocation list,
which makes revoking a single session inexpressible rather than merely
unbuilt; the only lever today is rotating the signing secret, which ends
every session at once. The change is additive: no decode path requires the
claim, and a token minted without one still validates. That last part has its
own test, because shipping it wrong would end every live session with the
very change meant to save us from doing that.

The storage, key id and rotation questions a real revocation list needs are
written up for a decision rather than answered here.

fix(costs): v3 status described one server while naming a collection on another

GET /vector/v3-status/ built its answer out of two stores. The collection name
came from country_to_collection, which is CWICR naming, but engine, connected
and the collection probe itself all came from the general vector store. Those
are not the same place: on a default install the ranker opens the embedded
CWICR store while the general store resolves to http://localhost:6333. So a
catalogue that was installed and matching perfectly well could be reported
disconnected or missing, and the reverse was equally available.

This is the same defect as d5726f38c and e0ec5d179, and the last call site that
had it. The handler now resolves once through resolve_cwicr_target and probes
through qdrant_adapter._get_client, so every field describes the store the
ranker opens. connected moved with the client rather than being left behind:
a field that answers for a different server than the rest of the payload is
worse than no field.

Two gates that stood in front of the probe went with it, because repointing the
client alone would have left them answering first. The connected check returned
disconnected before looking at anything, using the general store's verdict. The
non_qdrant band gated the probe on VECTOR_BACKEND, so a LanceDB install was told
the v3 layout did not apply while its CWICR collections sat there working. The
CWICR store is a Qdrant by construction, server or embedded, so VECTOR_BACKEND
says nothing about it and that band could only ever suppress a real answer.

The second defect was a confident answer produced without looking. When
get_collection raised, the handler set the band to ready. Failing to read a
collection was reported with the one word that means go ahead. There are now
three outcomes where there were two: present and counted, absent from a store
that answered, and could not look, the last carrying a reason. Unreadable is
deliberately distinct from missing, because they are different facts and a
caller should be able to act on them differently.

The reason names the failure class and never the resolved location. This
endpoint answers anonymous callers, which the IDOR tests in
tests/modules/test_costs_security.py pin as public by design, so the URL or
on-disk path of the store is not ours to hand out. The detail goes to the log,
where an operator can see the address anyway.

Nine tests, eight proved red against the old handler. They do not mock a client
and read the payload back, because that proves the handler can format a
response, not that it asked the right server. They set the two stores to
disagree, general unreachable and CWICR holding the collection, and assert the
answer follows the CWICR one, with the general store's client and status
function both booby-trapped so that touching either fails the test. The ninth,
that the failure reason does not leak the store location, was green before and
after: the old code also emitted a generic string, so it pins a property rather
than a fix.

Also corrects the docstring that said the match-elements page uses this to draw
a ready and missing banner. It does not, and no reader exists: the page's
readiness UI is QdrantHealthCard, which consults Qdrant directly, and
CataloguesPanelCard, which reads /catalogues-v3/. fetchVectorReadiness is
exported and never called, and the match-vector-readiness query key that two
components invalidate is registered by no query. That sentence was read as
evidence of a user-visible symptom while this fix was being scoped, which is
what a stale docstring costs, so it is replaced by what is actually true rather
than deleted.

test(i18n): the bill gate watched the abbreviation and let a second name walk past

The gate held each converted locale to one name for the bill, and it did that
by hunting the loan word. Which means it never looked at the two ways a locale
can still name the object twice without ever writing BOQ. Italian said "Carica
un Bill of Quantities .xlsx" on the upload label, which is the same English
moved from three letters to three words. Japanese called the bill 見積表 on
that label while calling it 内訳書 everywhere else. Korean called it 수량 명세서,
one syllable from the 물량 명세서 the rival list already carried, and did so in
fifteen places. All three files were green.

So the gate gains a fourth check, the loan word spelled out, and two rival
patterns. ENGLISH_NAME is deliberately a separate constant rather than a wider
BARE, because one of the existing checks reads BARE as "how often does this
file still say the abbreviation" and a ratio counting two different defects
answers neither question. It runs through the same explained() escape hatches,
so a locale that glosses its own term with the English one in brackets is still
fine.

The two rivals are scoped narrowly, because both words have honest work
elsewhere. Japanese needs 見積 for the estimate in about a hundred places and
only 見積表 is banned. Korean needs 명세서 for the payslip, the bill of
materials and the progress claim, so only the 수량 pairing goes, and the
self-tests pin 급여 명세서 and 자재명세서 as untouched.

Eighteen values changed: one Italian, two Japanese, fifteen Korean. The Korean
number is worth saying out loud, because it turns what reads like a one-label
typo into a conversion pass across notifications, the command palette, the
copilot, design options, the estimate basis and the project health card. It
was safe to do as a substitution rather than a rewrite for one reason worth
recording: 명세서 and 내역서 end in the same syllable, so every particle behind
the term carries over untouched and no agreement had to move.

Proved red on each of the three separately, one at a time, each failing
exactly its own locale and check: it on the English name, ja and ko on the
rival. 62 tests before, 70 after.

looks like.

which a commented line does not. deploy/docker/.env.example is left alone
deliberately, because compose interpolation may expect the key present and
that is not a guess worth making blind.

Also names, in main.py rather than only in a commit message, that the
non-development branches of the startup secret check cannot be reached. The
config validator is a pydantic model validator and raises during Settings
construction, long before that function runs. Dead code describing a
protection that lives somewhere else reads exactly like the protection, so
the next reader would otherwise restore the symmetry and believe the block is

included. Undersold by one copy, it sent a reader looking for an uncovered

docs(ci): the message for f4aab5fa2, which committed under another subject

f4aab5fa2 carries a 64 line change to .github/workflows/ci-postgres.yml under
the subject "chore(hygiene): the runtime upload directories had the ignore half
and not the gate half". That subject belongs to 0e2fe041f, which is a different
change by somebody else and is intact. Nothing was lost and no content is in the
wrong commit, but f4aab5fa2's message describes work it does not contain, and
two commits now share one subject.

Why it happened, because it can happen to anyone working in this tree. This
repository has a .git/hooks/commit-msg hook, so `git commit -F file` does not
use the file directly: git copies the message to .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG, runs the
hook against that path, and reads the result back. That path is one file per
clone, not one per process. Two commits running at the same second share it, and
the second writer wins the read. The hook printed OK both times because the
message it checked was well formed; it just was not mine. Anything that commits
here concurrently should read back `git log -1 --format=%s` and confirm its own
subject before believing the commit went out as written.

This commit is empty and exists to put the real message in the history where it
can be found. It is safe to drop if the branch gets tidied before it is pushed.
The message f4aab5fa2 should have carried:

  ci: nineteen test steps a run reported skipped instead of a verdict

  A step with no if: carries an implicit success(), so the first red step in a
  job turns every step below it into skipped. Skipped reads as not applicable
  when what it means is never asked. Counted off the parsed YAML rather than a
  grep for "- name:", which misses unnamed steps and multi-line blocks, the
  named steps carrying no condition were 22 in backend-postgres, 9 in
  access-control, 5 in upgrade-from-previous-release and 3 in frontend-tests.

  The cost is measured rather than argued. Run 33247219691 on 2026-08-29 failed
  at the first test step of backend-postgres. The eleven guarded steps after it
  ran and passed, the nineteen unguarded steps after those reported skipped, and
  the five guarded steps after those ran and passed. One job, one run, one
  failure, and the only thing separating the block that answered from the block
  that stayed silent was the condition. Six consecutive failing runs carry the
  identical shape, so this was eating nineteen verdicts a run for two days.

  Every step that returns a verdict about the tree now carries
  if: !cancelled() && steps.install.outcome == 'success'. That is 29 steps.
  access-control and frontend-tests had no step ids at all, so their install
  steps get id: install for the condition to name. The single bare !cancelled()
  is the frontend existence check, which is a file test over the checkout and
  does not need npm ci, so it should still answer when the install is what
  failed. Not always() anywhere: it also runs the step when the whole run is
  cancelled, which is a different behaviour and was corrected once already in
  6a5af0b34.

  Two exemptions, both deliberate and both written into the file. The
  environment steps at the top of each job are not verdicts about anything, and
  running them after one of them has failed reports a screenful of errors that
  all name the wrong cause, which is the reason the install step already gave
  for existing. And upgrade-from-previous-release keeps no conditions at all,
  because its steps are one chain rather than a list of independent checks:
  running the verifier against a database the aging step never built would not
  recover a lost verdict, it would manufacture a second red naming the wrong
  cause.

  What is not proven is that the newly guarded steps execute, which needs a run.
  What is proven is the mechanism, and it comes from run history rather than
  from a local model of how GitHub evaluates a condition.

fix(property-dev): split the delete permission that was guarding two different things

A development whose project belongs to an editor could be deleted by nobody.
Two independent walls guarded the route and no role satisfied both at once.
The permission mapped to MANAGER, so the editor who owned the project was
refused 403. The ownership check is strict, only project.owner_id passes and
the global admin role does not, so the manager and the admin who did hold the
permission were refused 404. Measured through HTTP across all three seeded
roles: 403, 404, 404, and afterwards the owner could still read the record it
could not remove.

Nothing caught it because every delete test in the package is a denial test.
test_r8_member_denied_delete_plot asserts the status is in (403, 404), which
is satisfied just as well by a world where the operation is impossible for
everyone. Asserting that a request is refused cannot detect that all requests
are refused. The module had a thorough set of tests that would have stayed
green if every delete route in it stopped working.

The collision was already written down twice, from two directions, and never
joined up. test_security.py:235 explains that it probes with GET rather than
DELETE because the RBAC gate "fires first and would mask the IDOR with 403".
test_inventory_map.py:118 explains that its fixture role "MUST be manager (not
editor)" so the permission gate "passes BEFORE the IDOR check". Each author
needed only to get past the obstacle, so each routed around it.

The cause is not the level, it is the sharing. property_dev.delete gated 24
routes. Measured over router.py by AST rather than by grep: on 19 of them the
handler also calls a _verify_owner_via_* helper, on the other 5 the permission
is the only wall there is. No single level is correct for both halves. At
MANAGER the 19 are unusable whenever the owning project belongs to an editor.
At EDITOR the 5 would lose their only protection, and brokers, commission
agreements, document templates and the house type catalogue would be deletable
by any editor in the system.

So there are now two permissions. property_dev.delete stays at MANAGER where
it is the only wall. property_dev.owner_scoped_delete maps to EDITOR and is
used by the 17 plain DELETE routes where ownership is already verified in the
handler. It is deliberately not called delete_own or delete_self, which would
read as a weaker variant of the first and invite exactly the merge that caused
this. The name says the wall is a different wall.

The two bulk inventory routes keep property_dev.delete on purpose, because the
MANAGER level there is a stated intention rather than an accident, and the
docstring now records what that costs instead of leaving it silent: on a
development owned by an editor those two endpoints stay unreachable by
everyone. Widening them is a sales-floor policy decision for whoever owns that
convention.

Nothing about ownership is weakened anywhere. The change is additive: one new
permission, 17 routes repointed, no helper touched, no admin path opened. That
matters because strict ownership is what closes the cross-tenant IDOR
(deferred #66), and the repair that would have been easiest, letting the admin
through, is the one that would have reopened it.

The split creates a new hazard exactly where it closes the old one, so it
ships with a gate. There is now an EDITOR-level permission that is safe only
because every route carrying it also calls an owner helper. The first route
that takes the permission and forgets the helper is a hole any editor can walk
through, and it would not look like a bug from outside: the request arrives,
passes its permission check, and is served. Review would have to notice an
absent line. So an AST test asserts the pairing for every route. It was proved
red rather than merely observed green: stripping the owner helper from
delete_development fails it and names that route, renaming the permission
trips its floor instead of passing over an empty set, and the tree as it
stands passes.

The accompanying test asserts all three roles in denial-first order. A test
that checked only the owner would pass against a repair that simply let the
global admin bypass ownership, so the manager and admin cells are the control
that keeps the repair honest: it fails both when nobody can delete and when
the wrong party can.

What this does not fix, since the same shape is wider than this permission.
Across the module 180 routes sit behind an owner-strict helper, and 41 of
them, spanning 20 other permissions, still require MANAGER+ and therefore
carry the identical dead spot for projects owned by an editor. Confirmed
through HTTP on delete_lead, which answers the same 403, 404, 404. Several of
those 41 are deliberate, so they do not all want the same answer and none of
them is changed here.

This is the backend half only, and on its own a user cannot see it. The UI
gates its delete buttons on a hardcoded role list that consults no permission
at all and excludes editor, so today the button is shown to exactly the roles
the ownership wall rejects and hidden from the only role that now passes. That
half is being done separately and this change is not complete without it.

The preceding commit, 16b600803, carries the three-role test on its own and
is red on purpose: it documents the dead spot before the repair exists. The
two are pushed together, so no workflow run sees the red state, and the cost
is confined to a bisect landing exactly on that one commit. That is a price
accepted deliberately rather than an oversight.

test(i18n): a locale can name the bill twice without ever writing the loan word

The bill gate holds six locales to a name chosen for them, and it cannot grow
past those six without somebody deciding what the rest should say. Deciding
that is inventing terminology rather than restoring it, so the gate has stayed
at six while the same disease sat unwatched in the languages nobody here can
adjudicate.

This gate asks a question that needs no such decision. Every locale already
answers what the object is called: the label its own module catalogue puts in
the navigation. So the check is not whether the name is right, it is whether
the file uses the same name twice. No terminology is chosen for any language,
and it covers every locale rather than six.

It finds twenty one divergences across eighteen locales on three keys.
Seventeen of them are on validation.subtitle, where a pass today put the key
into twenty five files: Czech says vykaz vymer while its catalogue says
Rozpocet, Dutch says hoeveelhedenstaat against Raming, Polish przedmiar robot
against Kosztorys, and so on through Arabic, Bengali, Danish, Greek, Persian,
Hindi, Indonesian, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Mongolian, Norwegian, Portuguese, Thai and
Urdu. Kyrgyz manages three names for one object across three keys, and one of
the three is the bill of materials rather than the bill of quantities.

None of them is corrected here, on purpose. In several the catalogue label
looks like the wrong half of the pair rather than the right one: vykaz vymer
and hoeveelhedenstaat are the settled trade terms while the labels they
contradict read closer to budget. Which of the two moves is a question for a
native speaker. So the baseline records the floor with the locale named and
the second name written out, and it may only shrink: a new divergence goes
red, and so does a fixed one, because a fixed locale has to leave the list.

Three things keep it from being a gate that quietly stops asking. The
population is asserted, so a narrowed question fails instead of passing. Every
locale must carry the catalogue label, because a locale missing it is
unmeasured rather than consistent. And the six short forms borrowed from the
sibling gate, LV for German and computo metrico for Italian, are each pinned
to still match their own catalogue label, so a locale that renames the object
in the navigation cannot leave a stale short form behind.

The key list is deliberately three. Most keys that name the bill in English do
not name it in translation, they say it or drop the noun: of the 880 English
values that say BOQ or bill of quantities, containment would call 23679 of
35977 translated values a divergence, which measures sentence shape and not
naming.

Proved red on each of the three failure paths separately, one at a time, each
one failing exactly one test: a nineteenth locale acquiring a second name, a
baselined locale getting fixed and having to leave the list, and a short form
outliving the label it is short for.

test(costs): separate the upload size mechanism from the size we chose

test_upload_rejects_oversize_payload asserted both at once and had been red
since June because of it. It sent 26 MB against a hard-coded expectation of a
25 MB cap, so when 4c6077812 lifted the cap to 100 MB the payload became
legitimately acceptable: it passed the size gate and died further down the pipe
in the CSV reader, whose default field size limit of 131072 bytes cannot hold a
single 26 MB field. The suite then reported a parser error for a size defect,
in a file nobody was working on, for twelve weeks.

The gate was never broken. _validate_cost_upload at router.py:3826 raises 413
above the cap and import_cost_file calls it at :4058, before parsing. One
number had gone stale, and the visible error named the wrong culprit.

Split in two. The mechanism test patches _MAX_COST_UPLOAD_BYTES down to a
kilobyte and posts a kilobyte and change, so it tests that oversize is refused
whatever we set the limit to, and it runs instantly instead of pushing a hundred
megabytes through the stack to compare two integers. The policy test is one
comparison against one number, and it is the check that did not exist: lifting
the cap was deliberate, that commit is called "Lift user-facing limits across
uploads, pagination and bulk ops", but nothing recorded what the limit was, so
the change landed silently. A behaviour test written THROUGH the value could not
do that job and hid the absence of one that could.

The cap stays 100 MB. Reversing a deliberate decision because a test lagged
behind it would be the wrong way round, and whether 100 MB is the right ceiling
for a catalogue upload is a product question rather than an engineering one; it
is written up with the numbers and the history in docs/strategy.

Proved by moving the constant one byte. The policy test goes red and names the
number, "assert 104857601 == ((100 * 1024) * 1024)", while the mechanism test
stays green, which is the whole point of the separation. Constant restored
byte-for-byte and re-hashed afterwards. Eleven tests in the module pass.

Not fixed here, and deliberately so: a 26 MB single-field CSV is now refused by
the parser rather than by the size gate, and the message it produces talks about
file format. Raising csv.field_size_limit would silence that and is the wrong
move, since it would make such a payload parse instead of being rejected.

test(change): the ownership chain's verbs are checked against the writers now

Two services reconstruct who held a change record and when, and both select
activity rows on the same two verbs, each declaring them as its own private
constant. Both say in a comment that those constants are kept in sync with the
write side, and core/audit_log.py makes the same claim from the other end:
"it must match on both the write and the read side". Three claims and no
mechanism.

The failure mode is silent and it lands in the feature that can least afford
it. A writer that stops emitting one of these verbs makes the select match
fewer rows - no exception, no empty-result branch, no log line. The chain comes
back shorter and the provability score comes back lower, and both look exactly
like a record that genuinely was never handed off. A claims-evidence module
that cannot tell "no hand-off happened" from "the verb was renamed" is
producing a claim its own history cannot support.

The two halves of the claim are checked differently because they are not the
same shape. The hand-off verb has a real source of truth: ACTION_OWNERSHIP_HANDOFF
in core is what log_ownership_handoff writes, and the readers merely copy it,
so that half is an equality against core plus an equality between the two
readers. The status verb has no constant anywhere in the platform - it is a
bare literal at 43 write sites across 23 files - so that half is checked per
module, against the three services whose records the chain actually resolves.

Counts beside the verdict. 2 readers, both checked rather than one; 3 writer
modules; 2 verbs; 3 definitions of the hand-off constant where there should be
one; 43 hand-written occurrences of the status verb and zero constants for it.
That last pair is the finding as much as the gate is.

The limit is written into the file rather than left to be discovered. A verb
renamed at every write site in one module fails here; a verb renamed at one of
that module's several sites does not. Per-module is the granularity at which
the damage appears, one change family quietly losing its status segments while
the others keep theirs.

Proved red three times before it was trusted, each probe landing on its own
assertion, each perturbation restored in a finally with the bytes compared
afterwards:

  a reader's private copy of the hand-off verb drifts from core
    -> the equality against core AND the agreement between readers, both
  moc stops writing the status verb
    -> the per-module status check, for moc only, the other two still green
  variations stops calling log_ownership_handoff
    -> the per-module hand-off check, for variations only

That last one matters more than it looks. build_ownership_chain_for
synthesizes a single open segment when it finds no hand-off rows, so a family
that stopped recording them does not return an empty chain that somebody would
question - it returns a plausible chain of exactly one holder.

denominator came from man_hours_total on each incident, and it initialised to
Decimal("200000") when that was absent, which is the same constant as the OSHA
normaliser in the numerator. The two cancel, so the rate came back numerically

plausible small number does not, and the reader here is a safety manager acting

No writer is invented. Where exposure hours come from is a product decision,
not something to settle inside a formula, and deriving them from timesheets or
adjacent tables would bury the question under a number that looks computed. The

fix(ui): a physical padding pair loses one side under rtl

The stylesheet mirrors every physical side utility into a rule that writes
BOTH sides, so [dir='rtl'] .pl-10 sets padding-left to 0 and padding-right to
2.5rem. Two such utilities on one element therefore do not compose under rtl:
the later rule wins outright and the other side is simply gone. A search field
written as pl-10 pr-3 computes 37.5px/11.25px in ltr and 0/37.5px in rtl. An
element pinned with left-0 right-0 takes left from both rules and gets no
right at all, so it collapses to zero width.

Replacing each pair with its logical equivalent removes the mechanism instead
of working around it. ps-10 and pe-3 compile to padding-inline-start and
padding-inline-end, which the browser flips by direction on its own, so they
need no mirror rule and cannot collide with one. Nothing in the config blocks
them: there is no corePlugins block, and the utilities generate natively once
something in the sources actually uses them.

Measured on computed values in both directions for all eight shapes that occur
here. Ltr is identical before and after, and every rtl case that read zero on
one side now reads the mirror of its ltr value. Arabic, Farsi and Hebrew ship
and the app sets dir on the document element, so these were live rather than
latent.

Thirty nine sites in thirty one files, located through the syntax tree rather
than by line number, because line numbers move while others edit the tree and
a scan for quotes loses its place at the first apostrophe in a comment. Each
file was rewritten only when the number of attributes changed matched the
number of sites reported for it, per pair.
