fix(frontend): the conflict gate lost every rule that followed a comment

The parser builds a selector prelude by accumulating characters up to the
opening brace, and it never dropped CSS comments, so a comment sitting in front
of a rule was glued onto it. A section banner in index.css turned the prelude
for oeMsgIn into text beginning with a slash rather than an at sign, so it
failed the test for an at-rule, was filed as an ordinary selector, and never
registered its keyframes. Every animate class that used them was then reported
as resolving to nothing.

Only the generated sheet was affected, because minification has already removed
the comments, so the two sheet sources disagreed by four sites while both
sheets in fact held the same rules. That is the worst possible shape for this
particular bucket. It was made loud on purpose so that it would be believed,
and a loud bucket that lies is worse than a quiet one.

The fault was not limited to keyframes. Seventy rules in index.css sit directly
after a comment, so ordinary utilities were being dropped from the table the
same way, which is a silent false negative for the mechanism the gate exists to
find.

Comments are stripped by slicing rather than by accumulating characters. The
same file has already been rewritten once for being quadratic on a multi
megabyte sheet, and appending character by character would have put that back.

Both sources now report the same five problems against the same sheet contents.

fix(email): a console transport nobody chose reported every send as delivered

EMAIL_BACKEND defaults to console, and the console transport answered every
send with a successful DeliveryResult. A deployment whose operator never set
the variable therefore wrote password resets, tender invitations and document
emails to its log and told everyone involved that the mail had gone out. There
was no failure log, no error to the caller and no counter that moved, so
afterwards nobody could even name who had not received their message. One
install ran that way for ten days.

diagnose_email_config could not catch it. Its first check needs an SMTP_*
variable to be present before it will report anything, and this shape has none
of them, so it returned None both for a server that was configured wrongly and
for a server that was not configured at all.

The thing that separates those two is not the value of email_backend, which
reads console either way, but whether a human supplied it. pydantic records
that in model_fields_set, and console_delivery_expected now asks it. An
operator who wrote EMAIL_BACKEND=console keeps exactly the behaviour they had,
which is what air-gapped installs and compliance freezes rely on; a deployment
that wrote nothing gets a failed delivery result instead of a false success,
and the same finding at boot rather than on the first send hours later.

Development is exempt, so a fresh checkout still runs with no configuration and
reaches the end of its boot log without an ERROR line. Where email_backend is
smtp with an empty host the resolver already fell back to console, and that
falls into the same net: delivery was asked for and did not happen.

Four consumers change behaviour outside development, all of them corrections.
The Property Development document mailer now raises 502 instead of returning a
false sent, the tendering draft to issued transition stops firing on a console
fallback, the reporting recipient counter goes to zero, and the compatibility
wrapper send_email returns False.

ci(frontend): the macOS test step went red on a heap it never set

Red before this, run 33282669278, job Frontend CI (macos-latest): 678 test files
and 7818 tests passed, nothing failed, and the step still exited 1. The job log
carries the reason on line 3661, "FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation
failed - JavaScript heap out of memory", with the last GC reported at 2063 MB.
One vitest fork died and vitest surfaced it as an unhandled "Worker exited
unexpectedly", which is not a test result and does not appear as one.

2063 MB is not a limit anyone chose. It is V8's default old-space, and that
default scales with machine memory: roughly 4 GB on the 16 GB x64 runners and
roughly 2 GB on this 7 GB arm64 one. So an unset NODE_OPTIONS is not one setting
shared by three runners, it is a different ceiling on each, invisible in the
file, and it is the whole reason ubuntu and windows run this identical command
green. Both factors of the peak were left to the machine: the fork count follows
the core count and the heap follows the RAM.

Pins both, so the worst case is arithmetic rather than discovered. At most 2
workers times 3072 MB is 6 GB, inside the 7 GB the runner has. 3072 rather than
4096 for that reason: two forks at 4096 is 8 GB and would put the ceiling back
above the machine, while 3072 still gives the fork that died half again as much
as the 2063 MB it died at.

What was verified locally, on Windows against the same vitest 4.1.9: the CLI
accepts --maxWorkers, the default pool is forks, and --exclude adds globs rather
than replacing the configured ones. The edited workflow parses, and the three
neighbouring steps are asserted unchanged - Type check and Build keep their
deliberate 9216 and their macOS skip, and the non-macOS Run tests keeps no
NODE_OPTIONS at all.

What cannot be verified without a run on the runner, stated plainly rather than
implied: whether the OOM is actually gone, and whether maxWorkers=2 lowers the
fork count or merely fixes it where it already sat. The runner's core count is
not printed in the job log, so the second is untested either way. The machine is
macOS and this one is not, so the first honest test of this change is the first
run of it.

The step is fixed rather than removed on purpose. macOS skips Type check and
Build deliberately, for the reasons written on those steps, but it still runs
lint and the unit tests to keep the OS-specific path, CRLF and runtime signal.
Deleting the step would trade that signal away to silence a symptom that has
nothing to do with it.

Worth recording what the standing red cost while it stood. It was present in
three consecutive runs, and in two of them it was carrying genuine test failures
at the same time, twelve at 20:27 and three at 20:48, gone by 00:10. A reader
who dismissed the red as the known macOS one would have dismissed fifteen real
failures with it in a single evening.

test(e2e): the config gate answers a different question than the one people read it as

check_playwright_config_selection.mjs asks whether every configuration selects at
least one spec, and it is green. Nobody had asked the inverse, whether every spec
is selected by some configuration. Same relation, two sides, and green on one
side says nothing about the other. Measured at 667d5e0ec and identical at the two
commits before it: 107 tracked specs under frontend, 37 selected by at least one
of 21 projects, 70 selected by none.

Most of those 70 are not defects, and no gate can be built by listing the innocent
ones, because a hand written list is a denominator somebody has to remember. So
this asserts only what the repository already states about itself. testMatch is a
positive selector and says nothing about the files it omits, but testIgnore fires
only on a file the configuration had already reached and matched, so removing one
is a decision about that specific file. playwright.config.ts writes its decision
out in words: 'tests/e2e/*.spec.ts' is ignored because those specs "are invoked
via their dedicated configs at the repo root". Resolving that pattern against the
commit gives a denominator of 11 that grows on its own when a spec is added next
to them. Six of the 11 hold. Five do not. compliance, folder-permissions,
markup-persistence, share-link and team-strip are excluded by the main harness on
the stated grounds that something else runs them, and nothing else runs them; no
configuration has ever named any of the five at any point in the history of the
config files. The step lands red on that, and it should, because the exclusion is
currently telling a reader something untrue.

The remaining 65 are printed as a census with names and do not affect the exit
code. 64 of them sit under frontend/e2e, and they are one fact rather than 64.
tests/e2e has a sweeping harness, so a spec added there runs by default;
frontend/e2e has none, and the four configurations aimed at it name their files
one at a time. The exception proves it, since the one subdirectory there that
does have a sweeping config, e2e/propdev, contributes nothing to the census at
all. A count only ratchet over the census was considered and rejected: it goes
green when one spec is orphaned and another deleted in the same change, which is
a number nothing recounts.

Population comes from git ls-tree at a resolved commit printed beside the verdict,
not from the disk and not from the index, because a count taken off a working copy
carrying unpushed commits is a correct number about a tree nobody else has. The
red control runs before every real count and plants three shapes: an orphan that
must be found, a spec ignored by one config and run by another that must pass, and
an exclusion of a file no config reaches that must stay out of the denominator, so
the gate cannot inflate its own population. It can be made to refuse on demand with
--prove-control, which hands it a matcher that ignores nothing and requires it to
complain. Selection is not reimplemented here. The four helpers it needs are now
exported from the sibling script, which grew an entry guard so it still runs
standalone, and the two halves therefore resolve paths through one implementation
rather than two that can drift apart.

Wired as the last step of the job Frontend CI, after the sibling, so a failure
skips nothing behind it.

test(agents): one tool name is registered by two modules and nothing says so

ToolRegistry.register overwrites by name and returns None, so two modules
registering the same tool name is not an error, not a warning, and not visible
in the registry afterwards. The only difference it makes is which copy every
agent gets, and that is decided by the order of the register_ calls in
on_startup, which is written down nowhere as an interface.

search_costs is registered twice today, by boq_drafter and again by
rate_benchmarker. on_startup runs the drafter first, so the benchmarker's copy
is the live one for every agent, the drafter included. The two implementations
are the same lookup and differ only in the observation each hands back to the
LLM when the cost database is unreachable, so what the defect buys today is a
drafter run being told the rate could not be benchmarked while it is drafting a
BOQ. It stays that small only until somebody edits one of the copies.

The collision already misleads a reader in the tree. register_cost_classifier
carries a docstring saying search_costs "is registered by
boq_drafter.register_boq_drafter into the same global registry", which is true
of the call and false of the result: that registration is the one discarded.

Pinned rather than repaired. Repairing means deleting one of two live
implementations or merging them behind a single message, and the two error
texts are each right for their own agent, so the choice belongs to the module
owner rather than to a test.

Two mechanics decide whether any of this is measurable. Registration happens
inside on_startup rather than at import, so a probe that only imports the agent
packages reports an empty registry and would report that as a finding. And an
overwrite leaves nothing behind, so it has to be recorded as it happens rather
than looked for afterwards, which is what the fixture's recording wrapper does.

The second check is that TOOL_PERMISSIONS never prices a tool nothing
registers. It asserts in one direction only. The comment above that map says a
read-only tool is meant to ride DEFAULT_TOOL_PERMISSION with no entry, so a
missing name proves nothing and is not checked. An entry resolving to no tool
does prove something: it was written to hold a permission onto a specific tool,
a rename detaches it in silence, and the comment explaining the arrangement
goes on describing something that stopped happening.

Registering modules are discovered by reading the source for registration
sites rather than listed, so a third module registering into the same global
registry is measured from the day it does. Naming the two we have today would
be the same defect this file is about.

Counts beside the verdict. 2 modules register tools, 16 registrations produce
15 tools, and the one that goes missing is the collision. 9 tools are priced in
TOOL_PERMISSIONS and 6 ride the fallback, all 6 read-only and so unmapped by
the documented design rather than by omission.

On the proof. Both checks pass on the tree as it stands, and an assertion only
ever seen passing is not known to be able to fail, so three tests hand each one
a planted input it has to reject. Those are permanent, not scaffolding.

The collision check was also driven red against the real tree, by emptying the
pin and changing nothing else: with the pin it passes, without it, it fails
naming search_costs and both defining modules. No production file was touched
to get that, which is deliberate. The earlier version of this proof perturbed
two agent modules and restored them in a finally, then exceeded its timeout,
was moved to the background and killed before the finally ran, leaving both
files wrong in a shared tree for around twenty minutes. Worse, the next run of
the same probe read the already-broken files as its baseline and wrote them
back, reporting a byte-for-byte restore of the damage. A probe that writes to a
tree other people are working in cannot rely on its own cleanup.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(ui): a field icon stays on the left when the field flips to the right

An icon inside a search or filter field is pinned with a physical side while
the field reserves room for it with logical padding. Under a right to left
locale the padding moves to the other edge and the icon does not follow, so it
lands on top of the text at the far end of the field.

The mirror block in index.css only covers left-0, left-3, left-4 and their
right hand counterparts, so the sites written with left-2, left-2.5, right-2
and right-2.5 never flipped at all. Measured in a browser on computed values,
those icons sat 374 to 376 pixels away from the 30 pixels of padding reserved
for them in a 400 pixel field. They now sit at the same offset they have in a
left to right locale.

The missing values are deliberately not added to the mirror block. Writing a
mirror for left-2.5 would fix these four sites by extending the mechanism that
produces the defect, and the mechanism is what makes two physical utilities on
one element impossible to compose. The logical utility needs no mirror because
the browser resolves it against the direction itself.

The nineteen broken sites are the fix. The remaining twenty three already
flipped, through the mirror, and are converted with them so that no container
is left with logical padding and a physical icon. That half migrated state is
what produced this defect in the first place. Both directions were measured for
all eight tokens and the left to right rendering is byte identical to what it
was, so nothing was traded for the right to left result.

This frees no mirror rules. Every class involved still has other users, so the
block cannot shrink yet.

fix(frontend): the conflict gate generated a stylesheet with no utilities in it

tailwind.config.js is transpiled ESM, so require hands back a wrapper holding
__esModule and default rather than the config. The gate spread that wrapper and
replaced content on it, producing a config with no theme and no plugins. The
builder does not treat such a config as a real one and falls back to searching
for a config file starting at the current directory, which is where the second
symptom came from: run from the frontend directory it found the real config and
emitted 4984 rules, run from anywhere else it found none and emitted 190, of
which every single one came from the hand-written part of the entry sheet.

So the gate answered 3 problems or 23 on one unchanged tree depending only on
where it was invoked from. The 23 were not conflicts, they were every animate
class in the tree reported as resolving to nothing, animate-spin at 366 sites
among them. All of those classes exist. A gate whose verdict depends on the
caller's working directory cannot be believed in either direction, and the
louder direction is the more dangerous one because it looks like diligence.

Unwrapping the module fixes both symptoms. The three directories that used to
disagree now return an identical 3955 rules, 34 animations and 3 problems.

The guard meant to refuse an incomplete sheet did not fire, because it asks
whether fewer than a hundred rules parsed and a hundred and ninety had. Counting
rules cannot distinguish a generated sheet from the entry sheet those rules were
copied out of. What separates them is whether the classes the tree actually uses
came back, so the gate now measures that and reports it beside the verdict: 3963
classes fed to the generator, 3159 of them resolved, eighty percent. Under the
broken config not one core utility was generated at all, so the same number
would have been near zero.

Reporting the size of the input is the part worth keeping. A gate that reads a
generated stylesheet and prints only its verdict makes an empty sheet and a
complete one look the same, and an empty one makes every class look broken while
making every conflict look absent.

fix(frontend): the conflict gate could fail a tree with nothing wrong with it

The guard added with the coverage report refused a sheet covering less than a
quarter of the classes fed to it. That number was picked by looking at what this
tree measures today, eighty percent, and halving it twice. It is the wrong shape
of threshold: it guards against a generator that produced nothing, but it is set
close enough to the healthy value that ordinary drift reaches it.

A large share of classes legitimately resolve to no rule and always will. Icon
and grid library names, our own oe- prefixes, arbitrary values and plain typos
are all in the eighty percent's complement, and that complement grows by itself
whenever a module arrives carrying a library that stamps its own class names.
Nothing about that is a broken stylesheet, but at a floor of a quarter it would
eventually read as one.

Failing that way is worse than the failure being guarded against. A gate that
goes red on a healthy tree gets read as noise, and then it is ignored on the day
it is right.

The real catch for this defect is not the coverage number at all. It is the
check on the generated config, which refuses a config carrying no theme, fires
deterministically, and cannot false-positive, because a config either was
unwrapped or was not. Coverage is only a backstop behind that, so it now sits an
order of magnitude below the healthy value rather than beside it. The broken
config generated no core utilities whatsoever, so the case it exists to catch
lands near zero and is nowhere near five percent.

fix(frontend): the conflict gate called a working animation dead

CataloguesPanelCard declares @keyframes catalogues-progress in an inline <style>
element on the line directly below the animate-[catalogues-progress_...] that
uses it. The gate reported it as an animation resolving to no keyframes, which
is a defect the component does not have. No stylesheet can hold that rule,
generated or built: it lives in a JS chunk and is injected when the component
mounts, so reading a sheet and concluding nobody defined the keyframe is
reasoning from an input that structurally cannot contain the answer.

The gate now collects @keyframes names from source as well and skips an
arbitrary animation whose name is among them. Collected tree-wide rather than
per file on purpose, because the claim being tested is that nobody defined the
keyframe, and a definition anywhere refutes it.

It reports the size of that scan beside the verdict, for the same reason the
coverage line exists. This scan is the only thing standing between the gate and
its previous behaviour, so a scan that silently matched nothing would put the
invented defects straight back, and a zero in that column says so at a glance.

The completeness guard no longer asks whether the sheet was generated here. It

element then reverts to its base style, and the base style is shadow-md. For a

fix(signing): a session recorded the capability it required, never the one it got

provider_capability on a signing session is what the caller requires of the
signature: qualified_electronic, advanced_electronic, simple_electronic or
digital_certificate. Nothing recorded what was actually delivered. Core ships a
single provider, which performs no cryptography and reports simple_electronic,
and get_provider falls back to it for any capability no adapter has claimed.
There are no adapters anywhere in the tree, so every session of every tier
resolved to it. The row then carried the requirement, the contract panel
rendered the requirement, and nothing beside it said the requirement had not
been met. The evidence was in fact written down, in
metadata.provider_initiation, where it names the provider as null and the mode
as manual_attestation, and nothing read it.

Sessions are not refused. Refusing would break existing sessions on upgrade and
is a separate product question. delivered_capability is taken from the resolved
provider's own capability wherever the status is derived, and is carried on the
session response, the contract signing payload and the manifest, which is the
closest thing this module has to a legal record. The panel renders it beside
the requirement as its own labelled field.

The column is nullable and is deliberately not backfilled. Every row that
exists today was derived before it existed, and copying the requirement into it
would manufacture exactly the claim this removes, while making every test agree
with itself. Null reads as not recorded, end to end, and there is a test that
fails if anyone later fills it in from the requirement.

test_get_provider_defaults_to_null_provider_for_unknown_capability passed
qualified_electronic, a known, documented, pattern-validated tier. The name
said that a typo must not crash; the body blessed the highest legal tier being
downgraded in silence, which is how this shipped. It now passes a genuinely
unknown capability, and the known-tier case has a test of its own asserting
that the difference is recorded and visible rather than raised.

fix(signing): the signing page still showed the required tier alone

A signing session carries two separate facts. provider_capability is what the
caller requires of the signature, and delivered_capability is what the resolved
provider actually delivers. Core ships one provider, which performs no
cryptography and delivers simple_electronic, and the registry falls back to it
for every capability no adapter has claimed. There are no adapters in the tree,
so a session requiring a qualified electronic signature resolves to it and gets
the weakest tier there is.

2fea854a1 recorded that difference on the row, returned it from the API and put
it on the contract signing panel. It did not reach the signing module's own
page, which is the screen a user opens to look at signing sessions. There are
exactly two frontend surfaces that render a session's capability and only one of
them was changed, so the register itself kept rendering the requirement as a
bare badge with nothing beside it. Its SigningSession type did not carry the
field at all, so the value was being dropped on arrival rather than shown and
ignored.

The row now states the requirement and, when the resolved provider delivered
something else, flags what it delivered beside it, following the same idiom as
the stale badge next to it: a field is stated, a discrepancy is flagged. The
title carries the pair labelled so two capability names side by side are never
ambiguous. Expanding the row states both as labelled fields, always, whether or
not they agree, which is what the contract panel already does. Null renders as
not recorded and never borrows the requirement, since a session written before
the column existed has nothing recorded and saying otherwise is the claim being
removed.

No new locale keys. signing.field_capability, signing.field_delivered_capability
and signing.capability_not_recorded already exist in every locale that has them,
and the capability labels were already there.

The tests assert the two values render as different strings rather than merely
that the delivered one is present. A later delivered-or-required fallback
anywhere between the API and the badge would make the two agree, which reads as
correct everywhere except in an assertion that the two differ. They are scoped
to the session row, because the capability filter in the toolbar renders every
tier as an option carrying the same label, and a document-wide count of those
labels measures the wrong population.

fix(db): an abandoned transaction held its locks until the connection closed

The only bound this tree had on a wedged lock was lock_timeout, and that sits
on the far side of the problem. It makes each victim of an abandoned
transaction give up faster while the transaction itself stays open and waits
for the next victim, and statement_timeout does not cover a lock wait at all.
The setting that removes the culprit is idle_in_transaction_session_timeout,
and no application connection carried it. The only place it existed was the
test conftest, which sets it on the test database with ALTER DATABASE and so
says nothing about a real install.

create_engine_from_settings now sends it as an asyncpg startup parameter on
every connection the app opens, so it travels in the connection packet, costs
no round trip, and cannot be missed by a code path that forgot to issue a SET.
The value comes from the new database_idle_in_transaction_timeout setting, 300
seconds by default, 0 to disable. PostgreSQL only counts a session that is
idle inside a transaction, so a long query is active and never touched and
slow migrations or big imports are not at risk.

The two lock_timeout calls in the app stay where they are. Both bound DDL
(postgres_migrator heal, RLS provisioning), which is the shape that really
does queue behind an idle reader, so they are not the useless ones.

The test proves the bound on a live server rather than in the configuration:
three connections idle for the same 3.5 seconds on budgets of 2s, 120s and
none at all, and pg_stat_activity afterwards shows only the 2s backend gone.

fix(jobs): a killed worker held its locks with nothing to end the transaction

Background job dispatch builds its own engine instead of using the application
factory, so the bound on abandoned transactions added in f6d5fecba never
reached it. A worker killed mid-dispatch left its transaction open and holding
every lock it took until the connection closed, which is the exact case the
setting exists for and the one most likely to happen, since that path is where
work gets abandoned.

Routing dispatch through create_engine_from_settings to pick the parameter up
was measured and rejected. The factory returns AsyncAdaptedQueuePool with 24
connections plus 10 overflow, pre-ping and a 1800s recycle, while dispatch
needs NullPool: every dispatch gets a fresh event loop, and a pooled asyncpg
connection opened on one loop and reused from the next raises "attached to a
different loop" from the second dispatch onward. The factory also takes its URL
from settings.database_url rather than the bound engine the caller passed,
which would move a dispatch to a different database than the one its session
factory chose. Five test call sites rely on exactly that indirection.

So the parameter is set on the dispatch engine directly, from a separate
database_jobs_idle_in_transaction_timeout, and the two configuration paths stay
two on purpose. Comments on both sides say so, because the duplication looks
like something worth consolidating and is not.

The jobs default is an hour rather than the 300 seconds a request gets. A job
handler holds a transaction open while it parses a large file, runs a clash
pass or calls an external service, and the server counts all of that as idle in
transaction because the client has stopped talking; the request-side value
would be an unmeasured deadline on legitimate work. 3600 is not measured
either. It is an order of magnitude chosen so a legitimate handler is not cut
while a wedged worker does not sit on its locks for a day. We have no
measurement of real background handler idle time, and this number should be
revisited when we do.

The tests ask the server what a dispatch connection actually got, on a budget
no default supplies, and assert the engine still pools nothing, which is the
regression that would follow from consolidating the two paths.

fix(auth): a password change closed the front door and left the rest open

`password_changed_at` is the only session kill switch this product has. A token
whose `iat` predates it is refused, so changing a password ends a stolen session
on the next request. It was enforced in exactly one of the six places a token is
accepted, the HTTP bearer resolver, because that is where it was written inline
instead of into the check every door shares.

Refresh was the wider gap. UserService.refresh_tokens verified the signature,
the `type` claim and `is_active` and never looked at the watermark, so a refresh
token minted before the change still minted a new access token, and that token's
`iat` is the present moment, so it passed the very check meant to stop it. That
does not weaken the kill switch, it cancels it: a refresh token lives thirty
days against the access token's hour, so whoever held one kept the account for a
month after the victim changed their password.

The sockets were the quieter gap. Every entry point that is not the HTTP bearer
resolver authenticates through verify_user_exists_and_active, which loaded the
user, checked `is_active` and stopped, so a live socket outlived the password
change that closed every HTTP call beside it.

The rule now lives in one function and is called from the three places that load
a user, the HTTP resolver, the shared helper and the refresh endpoint. The inline
copy is gone, so no second statement of it is left to drift.
verify_user_exists_and_active takes `issued_at` keyword-only with no default, so
an entry point that has not decided fails to start rather than failing to protect
somebody. Passing the argument is not by itself the enforcement, which is worth
saying because it was accepted as required here for a while before the body read
it, and all four callers looked correct throughout.

The watermark works to whole-second precision by construction. `iat` is seconds
since the epoch by RFC 7519 and the comparison truncates to match, so a
credential minted inside the same second as the change survives it until
per-session revocation lands. Widening the comparison is not the fix: the fresh
pair that change-password itself returns carries an `iat` inside that same second
and would be refused, logging the user out of the session just created.
Revocation by session id asks whether a session is alive rather than when its
token was minted, so it does not consult the clock at all.

Every assertion in the test carries a positive control, because both defects
present as a refusal and a test that only asserts the refusal passes against a
build where refresh is broken for everyone and the socket never opens at all.
Each door is therefore first shown open for the very token that is about to be
refused. The test also waits for the next whole second between the login and the
change: registering, logging in and changing a password fit inside a few hundred
milliseconds, so whether they straddled a second boundary was decided by when the
run happened to start, and the same code went green or red on consecutive runs.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(auth): a session could only be ended by ending all of them

Revoking one session was not unimplemented, it was inexpressible. Every token
carried a `jti` and nothing ever read it, so an issued credential had a name
and no record behind it, and there was nowhere to write down that one session
should stop being honoured. The only lever was rotating the signing secret,
which ends every session of every user at once, or changing a password, which
ends every session of one user. Neither can sign out the laptop left in a hotel
and leave the phone alone.

Tokens now carry a `sid` naming a row in `oe_users_session`, and the access
token and refresh token minted together carry the same one, so refusing the row
refuses the pair and every pair rotated out of it. Two self-service routes use
it: list your own sessions, and end one of them. The write is scoped by the
owner taken from the caller's own token, so quoting somebody else's session id
answers exactly as a session id that does not exist.

The count of places that mint a pair was the part most worth measuring rather
than remembering. Read from memory it was three, and it is five: login, demo
login, desktop bootstrap, refresh and change-password. A missed one is not a
cosmetic gap, it is a session that authenticates perfectly and can never be
signed out, and each site looks correct on its own. All five now go through one
helper that opens the row and mints the pair together, and a test parses the
whole application package to assert that no sixth site appears elsewhere later.
The formula of the revocation test cannot see that, because it exercises login
alone and stays green while every other endpoint leaks unrevocable sessions.

Revocation sets `revoked_at` and never deletes the row, because a token whose
session cannot be found is honoured rather than refused, so deleting would undo
a revocation instead of enforcing it. That fail-open choice is written out
beside the check with the three ways a row can go missing: a failed insert at
login cannot produce one because the row is flushed before any token exists,
pruning cannot reach one because it may only touch rows past `expires_at`, and
what remains is restoring from a backup, where failing closed would sign out
everybody at the worst possible moment. The horizon is pushed out on every
refresh so pruning stays behind live credentials.

A token that names a row which is gone is adopted into a fresh session rather
than left as it was. Without that the update would match nothing, the new pair
would carry the same orphan name, and the session would be unrevocable for
good, which is worse than the case fail-open was chosen to avoid. Tokens minted
before this existed carry no `sid` and are treated the same way, so no deploy
and no restore signs anyone out, and the next refresh is when they become
revocable again. That one has a test of its own, because honouring such a token
is indistinguishable in the code from having forgotten the case, and every
other token in the file carries a `sid`, so nothing else would notice somebody
tightening the check later.

`verify_user_exists_and_active` takes `session_id` keyword-only with no
default, so a new entry point that has not decided fails to start. That
argument buys nothing on its own and the docstring says so, because the
neighbouring `issued_at` was required at every call site before the body read
it and every caller looked correct throughout.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(auth): the deliberate fail-open looked exactly like an ordinary success

`reject_revoked_session` honours a token whose session has no row on file, and
the reasoning for that sits beside the check: the one remaining way to get an
orphaned session is restoring the database from a backup taken before the
session began, and failing closed there would sign out the whole platform at
the moment it can least afford it.

The check read `revoked_at` alone, which cannot express that decision. That
column is NULL both for a live session and for a row that is not there, so the
two cases collapsed into one branch and the exception became indistinguishable
in the code from the ordinary success it is an exception to. Nothing was wrong
at runtime and nothing was measurable either.

Selecting `sid` alongside it separates them, and the missing-row branch now
says so. The frequency of that line is the only thing that tells its three
causes apart. A restore produces a burst across every live token that decays as
sessions refresh, a pruning predicate that reaches unexpired rows produces a
flat rate that never decays, and isolated events mean the login-time flush has
stopped refusing a failed insert. Without the line all three look like silence,
which is also what a healthy system looks like.

The test asserts both halves, because the branch is unfalsifiable with only
one. Removing the log line leaves the request answering 200 and fails the run
on the trace assertion alone, which is the state this commit is measured
against.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(auth): the line that watches for a lost session could fill the disk by itself

`reject_revoked_session` writes a warning when a token names a session that is
not on file. The line is there to be counted: a restore from a backup arrives
as a burst of sessions that stops growing, a pruning predicate reaching
unexpired rows arrives as sessions that keep appearing, and isolated ones mean
the flush at login has stopped refusing a failed insert.

The count that carries all of that is of distinct sessions, not of lines, and
the line was written on every request. One of the three causes never decays, so
in exactly the scenario the warning exists to expose, every affected token
writes a line for the rest of its life. A log that grows without bound is a way
for this diagnostic to take down the host it is diagnosing, and a disk filled by
a log is not hypothetical here.

A session is now reported the first time it is seen missing and stays quiet
after that. The registry of reported sessions is capped, because a restore
would otherwise grow it by one entry per live token, and a session falling out
of the cap may be reported once more later, so the cap degrades into a rate
limit rather than into silence. Sessions asking most often are the ones kept
quietest.

The test asserts the second request with the same session is still honoured and
no longer logged. Bypassing the check leaves the request answering 200 and fails
the run on the repeat assertion alone.

fix(i18n): twenty Uzbek strings were typed with a keyboard apostrophe

Uzbek writes two marks that a keyboard does not offer. The letters o' and g'
carry U+02BB, and the glottal stop after any other letter is U+02BC. A plain
ASCII quote is neither, and in Latin Uzbek it reads the way a missing accent
reads in French: understood, and visibly the work of somebody who does not
write the language.

All twenty came in with the document appearance panel in e1ea67e51, which is
also where common.center and common.right were added. The mark to use was
taken from the corpus rather than from memory: across the rest of uz.ts U+02BB
follows o, O, g or G in all but a dozen of its 28767 positions, and U+02BC
follows every other letter. A digit before the mark is left alone, because that is the
feet and inches notation carried over from the English source, and correcting
it would break an example the English deliberately shares.

Only values that differ from their English source were touched. Most of uz.ts
is still English interim text while the remaining batches are translated, and
English prose carries straight apostrophes legitimately, so a blanket pass
would have corrupted the untranslated part of the file.

fix(core): a settings save landing in the same clock tick was never seen

The document appearance and the app branding each keep a process-local cache of
their parsed settings file, and each decided whether that cache was still good
by comparing modification times. That assumes two different contents get two
different timestamps. Windows does not give that: two writes in the same clock
tick get a byte-for-byte identical st_mtime_ns, measured at 139 collisions in
200 consecutive pairs on a developer machine. The file changes, the recorded
time does not, and the cache keeps answering with the previous values until a
later save happens to land in a different tick.

For appearance the damage outlives the render. The PUT endpoint reads the
stored values, merges the admin's fields over them and writes the result back,
so a stale read is written to disk and quietly reverts whatever the shadowed
save had changed.

The stamp is now modification time and size together, and every writer drops
its own entry instead of trusting the clock to have noticed. The size term is
what a second process gets, since a worker rendering an export never sees the
API process make that call.

The tests force the timestamp collision with os.utime rather than racing for
it, so they fail on every platform. Raced, this showed up only on the Windows
shard, which runs with continue-on-error and cannot fail a build, so the store
was guarded by a lane that reports without blocking. The branding store had no
test of its own at all, which is how the same cache shipped twice.

feat(packs): a Hungarian bill had no item order of its own to be read against

Hungary resolved to DIN 276, which was the Central European default rather
than a statement about Hungary. A Hungarian bill is not written against a
cost group hierarchy at all. It is written against a sectoral item order:
a seventeen chapter code for building works, a per project item number for
infrastructure, and every priced line split into a material half and a fee
half, because the two are contracted, taxed and reported separately.

So the country pack brings the item order with it. Four rules under the
hungary rule set check that a priced line carries a code, that the code
names a chapter that exists, that the two halves add up to the rate, and
that no item number is used twice, with messages in all four validation
locales. The registry now answers tetelrend for HU, and the two project
screens that name standards were taught the word.

The reading side is a workbook profile rather than a separate importer.
An xlsx is a zip, and the four kilobytes a detector sees name a worksheet
part and nothing else, so the shape cannot be identified before the file
is open. The profile is asked inside the Excel importer once openpyxl has
the workbook, and returns nothing for anything it does not recognise, so
every other spreadsheet keeps the generic reader and its error messages.
It reads both shapes of the two files it was written for: a chapter sheet
does not repeat the whole code on every line, so the code of a row is the
running composition of the segments above it, and a heading carries the
totals of what is beneath it rather than a price.

The pack deliberately does not declare a Hungarian interface. There is no
hu locale file, and a pack that declares one it cannot ship promises a
Hungarian UI and delivers English with no signal that it did. Both that
limit and the chapter list are asserted, the chapter list in all three of
the places it is written down.

fix(i18n): a find and replace on the German umlauts left 99 words that are not words

German writes an umlaut either as the letter or as the ASCII digraph standing
in for it, ue for u-umlaut and so on. The German locale had drifted into
carrying both, fuer four times beside 1761 spellings of the same word with the
umlaut, and at some point someone fixed that with a mechanical replacement.

The digraph is not a marker. It is two ordinary letters, and it sits inside
perfectly normal German words that were never folded: Steuer, Quelle, neue,
bauen, zuerst, aktuell, manuell, Mauerwerk, Feuer, dauerhaft, genau, grau,
trauen, and Konto followed by einstellungen. The pass ate those too. What
shipped was Qülle for Quelle, Steür for Steuer, zürst for zuerst, baün for
bauen, aktüll for aktuell, Maürwerk, Feürwiderstand, Kontöinstellungen. 99
occurrences of 43 words that no German reader can parse, in the UI of a DIN
276 and GAEB country.

Nothing could have caught it. The key is present, the placeholder count is
unchanged, the file parses, the build is green and every coverage check counts
a string that is there. It needs a German reader looking at the page.

Also restored the 78 folds in the frontend locale and the 89 in the backend
validation messages, which is what invited the replacement in the first place.

Repaired with an explicit word list, not a rule. Substitution runs on the value
side of the colon only and skips every placeholder span, which is not
decoration: all 31 occurrences of gross in the German locale are i18n keys,
payportal.gross and certified_payroll.col.gross among them, and folding those
to the sz-ligature would have renamed 31 keys and broken every lookup at
runtime with every gate still green.

Left alone, with reasons, because they are not defects: Masse is mass and the
sz spelling is dimensions, both used correctly here, one prices a steel profile
by weight; in Massen means in bulk; Geschoss with sz is current Austrian
orthography; Dauer, Steuer, Vertrauen, Teuerung and Mauerarbeiten never had an
umlaut to begin with.

Verified by the invariants rather than by reading the diff: the key set, the
placeholder multiset, the line count and the line endings are identical before
and after, the backend file still parses to its 335 messages, and both
detectors report zero. Only spellings moved.

fix(i18n): four locales shipped sentences with every diacritic stripped

Found by the guard added here, which named two Swedish words and so pointed at
the sentences holding them. The Swedish read "En driftsattningskontroll utan
ett overenskommet godkannandevarde ar ett grael i vantan" with every a-umlaut,
o-umlaut and a-ring gone. Nothing renders wrong, nothing fails to parse, and a
Swedish reader sees text that is not Swedish.

Measured across all 43 locale files: 2208 strings in 10 of them, ro 876, cs
461, sv 440, fr 291, it 67, no 42, tr 13, fi 7, pl 7, hr 4. Mostly the howto
and cases prefixes, plus small clusters in finance, geo_hub, defects_liability
and interface_management that hit four to six languages identically and so came
from single bulk-translation commits. They were born this way: git log -S on the
accented spelling returns nothing for any of them, so there is nothing to
restore from history and each has to be written.

Repaired 33: the whole of Finnish, Croatian, Polish and Turkish, which leaves
those four with none, plus the two Swedish sentences the guard named.

Checked by a reachability walk rather than by eye, because a reword hides
perfectly in a diff of a 40 000 line locale file. Every character of the
replacement has to be reachable from the original by identity, by adding a
diacritic, or by collapsing one of the digraphs ae, oe, ue, aa and ss. That
last rule is what makes grael to gral-with-umlaut and fastslaa to
fastsla-with-ring legal, and it needs backtracking rather than a greedy scan:
in grael the bare a matches the accented a on its own and only everything after
it failing reveals the digraph. The checker was red-proved on five rewords
first, among them skrev ner to skrev ned and yok. to yok!, which it rejects.

What that walk checks is that nothing but diacritics was added. Whether the
diacritics added are the right ones rests on reading alone. There is no second
pair of eyes on these 33 strings, and the walk cannot be one: a word it passes
through unchanged is a word it never examined.

The guard, check_locale_umlaut_folding.py, is for the other half of the same
damage and is described in its own docstring: a word must not appear in one
locale file both with an umlaut and in its folded spelling. It reads the value
side of the colon only, since folding a key renames it, and it covers the
backend validation messages as well as the frontend locales. Four exceptions
carry written reasons: German Masse against the sz spelling for dimensions, the
same pair in the plural, Geschoss against the Austrian orthography, and Finnish
haen, "I fetch", against the pronoun han.

Remaining after this: 2176 strings in ro, cs, sv, fr, it and no. The count fell
by 32 rather than 33 because one of the 33 was never in the detector's
population to begin with. The guard reached it by naming a single word, while
the detector asks for three stripped words in one string and found only two in
this one. The three that did not count, mal, ar and fran, each have a bare twin
somewhere else in the same file, and a word only counts when every other
spelling of it in that file carries its diacritic. Which is worth saying
plainly: a file's own stripped strings supply the bare twins that disqualify
words in its other stripped strings, so the per-language numbers above are a
report and not an upper bound, and this Swedish string is one measured example
of a miss. Relaxing that rule is not the fix, it returns 2886 for German and
3713 for Spanish, both of which are correct files.

The rest is translation work and not a pass anyone can run: a mechanical
restore is exactly the mistake that produced the German non-words in 6a33a1982.

the right order, and not the language. The Romanian reads "Aceasta
inregistreaza plata ca o intrare imuabila in registru si inchide factura", the
French "Arreter le decompte final et liberer la retenue de garantie". 2176 are

parses, the build is green, and every coverage check counts a string that is

This repairs nothing. Repair is translation work, and a mechanical restore is
exactly what produced the German non-words in 6a33a1982. It holds the line
instead, in the shape this repo already uses for declared debt: the 2176 are
recorded per locale and per key beside the script, and a key entering that set

The detection lives in the committed script rather than in whatever produced

none was stripped. A word only counts as evidence when the file spells it with
its accent everywhere else, which is what holds the false positive rate at zero
on correct files, and it is equally why the detector under-reports worst where
the damage is heaviest. The Swedish soft-landings string is 32 words of fully
stripped Swedish that it does not report, because mal, ar and fran each have a
bare twin elsewhere in sv.ts. Relaxing that rule is not the fix: it returns

more words to evidence and uncovers damage the detector could not see before.

which is the walkthrough text an estimator reads to learn a workflow, so this
was the part of the product most likely to be read slowly by a French speaker
and the part least able to survive being unreadable.

The text read "Arreter le decompte final et liberer la retenue de garantie" and

green: the keys are present, the placeholders match, the file parses, the build
passes and coverage counts every one of them.

Restoring them is not mechanical and cannot be, which is the whole point of
doing it by hand. French bare "a" is the verb "has" and accented it is the
preposition "to". Bare "ou" is "or" and accented it is "where". Bare "du" is

with a circumflex it is "safe". All four pairs occur in these strings in both

while "le moment ou l'argent est depense" takes the accent, and "un site plus
sur" means a safer site. A replace cannot tell them apart.

fix(i18n): restore the Czech diacritics the detector could not see

The Czech bundle was reported clean last week, and it was not. The detector
disqualifies a word when the same file spells it bare somewhere else, so a file
whose damage is widespread feeds itself the evidence that hides it: ninety three
Czech strings, most of the module guide, sat under that rule. This puts the
marks back on all of them, and on three Romanian case steps that were under it
for the same reason.

Two measurements found them, and they answer different questions. The first asks
how surprising a bare string is against its own locale's accent density. If a
file marks a fraction p of its long words, a bare string of n of them has
probability (1-p)^n, so the length at which fewer than half a false report is
expected across the file is n >= log(alpha/candidates)/log(1-p). Czech sits at
p 0.59 and lands at eleven words. English lands near p 0, so the threshold goes
to infinity and English excludes itself, which is the property that makes the
rule safe to run everywhere without a hand kept list of which languages carry
accents.

The second is the same question asked per word rather than per string, because a
presence test cannot see prose that kept one accent by accident. Line 5669 was
stripped Czech with a single surviving mark on one word. Under Binomial(n, p) a
string with k marks is reported when the whole file is expected to yield fewer
than alpha of them, which at k=0 is exactly the first rule, so the second
contains the first. That is what surfaced the what family, howto.boq.what and
its neighbours, all stripped with one mark left standing.

Both were then run again after each batch, because repairing a string removes
the bare twins that were disqualifying words in the strings still to come. Fifty
became sixteen more, which became twenty seven more, which became zero.

Every replacement went through the same two checks as the Romanian work. The
walk requires each character of the new string to be reachable from the shipped
one by identity, by taking a diacritic or by collapsing a digraph, so a reword
cannot pass as a repair. The cross check looks each repaired word up by its
accent stripped skeleton against what the file already spells elsewhere. Nothing
mismatched.

Six words could not be reached by marks alone and are recorded as exceptions
with the evidence, all of it from cs.ts itself. trizit becomes tridit with a
hook, because the file spells that word properly once and its relatives twelve
times and never spells trizeni at all. sdiletelny becomes sdilitelny, which the
file spells correctly elsewhere. viteziovi becomes vitezovi in two more places,
the same stray letter already recorded twice. prirazte becomes priradte with a
hook on the d, against forty five correct spellings. meridici becomes merici,
against two.

Two words are left exactly as they shipped and are worth naming. stavili would
have to become staveli to make sense, and staveli is not stavili with a mark on
it, so the walk refuses and the sentence keeps a word that is odd rather than
gaining one that was invented. sprav becomes sprav with an accent, a genitive
plural the file uses elsewhere, even though spravy would read better; the letters
decide, not the reading.

Three locales the density work flagged are not damaged and were dismissed on
evidence. Turkish looks stripped only because the dotless i has no canonical
decomposition, so every word marked with it counts as bare and the file scores

snippets, which are code. The long French projects.intro_more sits at 0.108
against a file average of 0.250 and is correctly accented throughout, which is

A Czech user deleting rows was asked "Jsou vy sure vy want na smazat 5 vybrano
polozky? Tento akce nelze byt undone." That is not a translation. Something ran
word by word over the English, wrote a Czech word where it had one and left the
English word where it did not, and the result reads as nonsense in the places
that matter most: the confirm dialogs, the tour, the pipeline help, the module
developer guide. This translates 102 of them properly.

Nothing we own could see this. The bundle parses, the placeholders match, the
key exists in every locale, the script is Latin either way, and no gate asks
whether the sentence is in the right language. It surfaced by accident, while
sampling candidates for the diacritics work, which is the uncomfortable part.

Finding the rest took three tries and the first two were wrong in instructive
ways. Counting English words the translation reused, against the English source
for the same key, returned 15 868 strings, because GAEB, BIM, Alembic, manifest
and router are words every locale keeps. Letting the locale set decide which
those are, a word most locales repeat for a key is that key's vocabulary rather
than this locale's failure, cut it to 4 010, but Dutch and French still filled
the list: consultant, dossier, feedback and roadmap are theirs as much as ours,
and overlap alone cannot tell a shared noun from an abandoned sentence.

Grammar can. A translation borrows nouns and never function words, so the marker
set is English function words only. Two things had to be excluded before that
worked. Placeholders are stripped first, because {{shown}} is a variable name and
was the single loudest thing in the first run, and a marker refuses to match
inside a hyphenated compound, because what-if is a term every locale keeps and
was the second loudest.

The last trap was assuming a marker is a marker everywhere. It is not: need is
Estonian, find and have and give are Danish, taken is Dutch, just is Estonian and
Swedish, compare is Spanish, Portuguese, French and Italian, same is Polish and
Croatian, will is German, once and quite are Spanish, and most is Czech, Polish,
Croatian and Russian for bridge. Dropping a marker globally to protect one
language blinds the tool in all the others, so each collision is now recorded
against the language that owns it. That is what the last three Czech reports are,
all of them the word bridge, all correct, none touched.

The replacements go in through a sibling of the diacritics applier. The walk that
proves only marks moved is exactly the wrong check here and would reject every
one of these, but everything else it does still matters and is kept: the value is
spliced in place so line and CRLF counts cannot move, the key must already exist,
the placeholder list must come back identical and in the same order, the escaped
quote count must match, and the replacement is re-scanned so a half-finished fix
cannot be written. Six of the strings had no English source at all, the pipeline
node help among them, and were read back from what the machine pass had left.

The same batch of keys got the same treatment in other languages. Croatian is at

fix(i18n): the requirements import sample was translated into a row that will not import

The requirements import panel shows a sample row under the paste box, and the
line above it names the seven fields: entity, attribute, constraint_type, value,
unit, category, priority. A user reads that sample to learn the format and
copies its shape. Five of the seven are free text and translating them is right.
Two are closed vocabularies the importer matches literally, and 36 of the 42
locale files had translated them.

Every one of the 36 had translated the priority, so the German sample read
"wand | dicke | min | 200 | mm | tragwerk | muss". RequirementCreate validates
priority against a pattern built from PRIORITY_ORDER, so that row raises a
ValidationError and never lands. Checked against the real schema rather than by
reading it: must, should and may are accepted, muss, obligatorio and the rest
are not.

Ten had also translated the operator, and that one is quieter and worse. The
Russian sample said min and max as mup and makc, the Greek as elach and meg, and
an operator outside OPERATORS does not fail. The parser appends a warning and
substitutes equals, so a minimum thickness of 200 silently becomes a requirement
that the thickness be exactly 200. Nobody reads the warning line on a row they
believe they copied correctly.

Only the constraint_type and priority fields are touched, and they are taken
from the English row because the operator is fixed by what the sample means: a
thickness has a minimum, a u-value has a maximum. Every locale keeps its own
entity, attribute, value, unit and category, decimal comma included, since the

feat(i18n): the diacritic ratchet was counting the damage as its own alibi

The locale diacritic gate treats a bare word as evidence only when the file
never writes that skeleton bare anywhere else. That condition is what keeps it
precise, and it is also an alibi the damage writes for itself. A file
translated in bulk with its marks deleted supplies exactly the bare twins that
disqualify the words which would have convicted it, so the wider the damage
spreads the better it hides. The Italian locale shipped 689 stripped words
while this gate reported nothing at all, and the gate's own docstring has
called that the honest limit since the day it was written.

Reading that limit was not enough, because a green lane that cannot see the
defect still reads as consent. The gate now runs a second, independent rule
beside the first. Every key is filed under a top level namespace and the damage
arrives per namespace, in whatever block a bulk pass touched, so for each
namespace the dictionary is every other namespace. A word counts as evidence
when the rest of the file spells that skeleton only ever accented, only ever
one way, and at least three times. The damaged strings never get to vote on
their own spelling, which is precisely what the first rule lets them do.

Run against each locale as it stood at the commit before its repair, the first
rule reports 1 string of the French damage where the second reports 86, and on
Romanian and Czech the first reports nothing at all where the second reports
112 and 248. The Swedish goes the other way, 442 against 290, which is why the
Swedish was the damage that got noticed first. Both are heuristics, both are
ratchets, and the run fails if either gains a string.

Neither rule sees damage spread evenly over a whole file, and that is written
into the docstring rather than glossed. Both need the damage to be local: the
first needs a clean twin somewhere in the file, the second needs a clean
namespace. The Italian scores zero on both at the commit before its repair
while shipping those 689 words, because that pass touched every namespace at
once and left no half of the file clean enough to be the dictionary. What
actually found the Italian was a third method, asking the language instead of
the file through a closed list of forms that do not exist unaccented. That one
needs a hand checked word list and a homograph guard per language, since meta,
unita and sara are all real Italian words, so it is named in the docstring as
the gap to close rather than half built here.

Placeholders and markup are now removed before either rule reads a value. Their
names are ASCII by construction and were being counted as ordinary words: the
Danish about text reads "<star>Stjernemarkér projektet</star>", where the tag
name star is not a bare spelling of står, and counting it as one both invented
a hit and, worse, disqualified the real word everywhere else in that file.
Removing them turned up three genuinely stripped Swedish strings the first rule
had not been able to see.

The verdict line now prints the population it was drawn from, 1666197 keys in
43 locale files, because a green line that names no denominator is how a
narrowed run passes for a clean one. Current findings are banked as declared
debt, 3 strings for the first rule and 353 across 14 locales for the second.
Those 353 are real, the Czech alone accounting for 158, and repairing them is a
separate job per language. What this change buys is that the number cannot go
up again without the lane saying so.

Found while sweeping for something else. A word that carries a mark on the
wrong letter is invisible to both diacritic rules, so I scanned every locale

my own instrument talking to itself, and one thing was real.

In ar, da, it and no the takeoff formats string reads "PDF drawings" followed
by the three characters a-circumflex, euro sign, right double quote. That is
what an em dash becomes when its UTF-8 bytes E2 80 94 are handed to something
that decodes one byte at a time as CP1252. The value stays valid TypeScript,
parses, quotes and renders without complaint, and it is simply the wrong text.
Same key in all four, one translation batch, while twelve other locales carry
the correct character for that key and the English source has had it all along.

Nothing we run could see it. Both diacritic rules ask whether a word lost a
mark and this text gained characters. The homoglyph rule asks about Cyrillic
against Latin and all three of these are Latin. The folding rule asks whether
one word is spelled two ways and the corrupted spelling occurs once. The leak
baseline asks whether a value equals the English one and a corrupted
translation equals nothing. The parse gate asks whether the file is valid and
it is.

The test is the definition of the corruption rather than a guess at it: a
candidate has to encode back to CP1252 as a lead byte in C2 to F4 followed by
the right number of continuation bytes in 80 to BF, and then decode as UTF-8.

circumflex and tilde letters across fr, pt, pt-BR, ro and vi, in Ambito,
Ancora, Age and Am, and every one of them puts an ordinary letter after the
lead, which is not a continuation byte. The rule passes over all 108. It has no
baseline and no declared debt because the count is zero and any hit is new.

fix(projects): the project total joined its estimates together instead of adding them

Reported from a live installation running three estimates on one project. The
screen showed the currency code followed by NaN, and it had done so on 14.0.0,
14.6.0, 16.0.0 and 16.4.0, which is not a regression but something that has
always been there.

Money crosses the wire as a decimal string. That part is deliberate and right:
a Decimal rendered verbatim survives a 126 million total that a float would
round, and both BOQResponse and PositionResponse carry a field serialiser that
does it. The defect is at the consumer, and it starts with a type. This page
declared grand_total, quantity, unit_rate and total as number, so the compiler
did not catch the mismatch, it enforced it. Both of the following type-checked
cleanly for as long as the file has existed.

The first is the reported one. Summing with += over a string concatenates, so
two estimates produce "0126150861.5085944498.86", which formats to NaN. One
estimate hides it, because 0 + "2264760.32" coerces and looks correct, so the
fault only appears from the second estimate onward.

The second was found while fixing the first and is worse, because nothing looks
broken. The project health panel counted unpriced positions with
!pos.unit_rate || pos.unit_rate === 0. The rate of an unpriced position is the
string "0", which is the column default. A non-empty string is truthy so the
first test is false, and the types differ so the second is false too. The
counter therefore stayed at zero however many positions had no rate, and the
"every position is priced" check went green on a project where not one position
was priced. A green check with no measurement behind it is worse than a red one,
because it ends the conversation.

Both now go through toNum from the shared money module, which already exists and
whose own docstring describes this exact class of bug. The types say what the
wire says, so a future += will not compile.

One place that looks like the same defect is not, and was traced rather than
patched. The BOQ editor filters for unpriced positions with the same spelling,
!p.unit_rate || p.unit_rate === 0, but it reads boq.positions, which comes back
through normalizePositions at the fetch boundary and is already coerced. The
editor's number type is honest after normalisation. The projects page reaches
the same endpoint by its own path and normalises nothing, which is the whole
difference between the two.

The test asserts on behaviour rather than on how the sum is written, which the
reporter asked for and gave the reason for: they had been patching their own
shipped bundle by matching the minified text, a later build renamed the
variables, the patch reported "pattern not found" and carried on, and the bug
was quietly back while their tooling said it was fixed. Both cases fail in both
directions. The sum is required to be a finite number AND to equal the right
total, because the concatenated string is a perfectly good string and only the
second assertion knows it is wrong. The unpriced case pins the priced spellings
too, so a helper that answered true every time would not pass.

Closes #448

fix(migrations): four revisions created tables the boot heal had already built

Reported from an installation carried across 12.8.0, 14.0.0, 14.6.0, 16.0.0 and
16.4.0, stamped at v3258 while head was v3284. Every attempt at
`alembic upgrade head` died on the same table and the stamp never moved, so it
sat twenty-six revisions behind for two months.

The mechanism is worth stating precisely, because the damage is much larger than
the one table. The boot path builds the schema with create_all before anything
reads alembic_version, which is deliberate: the baseline revision is a no-op and
the quickstart entrypoint never runs alembic, so without create_all a fresh
volume comes up with no tables at all. The consequence is that on every install
this application has ever started, every table in the model metadata exists by
the time an operator runs alembic by hand. An unguarded op.create_table then
raises DuplicateTable, and because PostgreSQL runs DDL inside a transaction the
failure rolls back the entire run rather than the one revision. So a single
unguarded create_table does not cost you that revision, it costs you every
revision behind it, including the data backfills inside them, and it does so
again on every subsequent attempt.

This turned out to be four revisions rather than a design problem. 169 of the
173 revisions that create tables already ask an inspector first, so the house
pattern was there and nearly universal. Three of the four that missed it are
consecutive, v3259 to v3261, which is exactly where the report came from, and
the fourth is v100 from the 1.0 baseline.

The first count taken here was wrong and in the direction that would have caused
pointless churn. Grepping said 116 of 182 were guarded, which would have meant
66 files to repair. That number came from comparing a recursive grep over the
directory, which matched compiled .pyc files, against a glob over .py files: two
different populations, so the set difference was meaningless. Reading it with an
AST gives 173 revisions that actually call op.create_table, nine fewer than the
grep because the text also appears in docstrings, and 169 of them guarded.

Each table is guarded on its own rather than the whole upgrade returning early
when the first one is present, because a boot that failed midway leaves some
tables built and some not, and an early return would leave that database
permanently short of the rest.

The rewrite was mechanical, so it was proved rather than reviewed by eye. Every
op.create_table and op.create_index call in the four files was dumped as an AST
node before and after, and the two lists are identical; the only permitted
difference is that the statements now sit inside an If. A rewrite that dropped a
column, reordered an index or altered a constraint would have failed that check
even though the file would still import.

The gate is the part that matters more than the four fixes. A convention that
98 percent of a population already follows is one nobody notices breaking, and
this one broke three times in a row without anything going red. The new check
parses every revision, counts how many create tables, and requires each of them
to consult the database first. It prints the population beside the verdict, so
"0 problems" cannot be confused with a glob that stopped matching. It is green
at 173 of 173 and goes red when a guard is removed from any one of them, which
was tested rather than assumed. It runs on pre-commit and in Repo hygiene.

Closes #449

feat(bi): a custom KPI can break down by a key inside classification

classification is the only place a BOQ position records what KIND of work it is,
and an estimator's own vocabulary lives there: labour, material, equipment,
subcontract, indirect. The KPI spec catalogue did not offer it, so the nearest
reachable field was source, which answers a different question entirely, how the
row was entered. That column defaults to manual and every ordinary create path in
the tree writes it literally, only the CAD and AI import paths write anything
else. So on an installation where the BOQs were typed or imported from a
workbook, a breakdown by source renders one bar and still looks like a working
cost analysis. A KPI that reads a plausible number for the wrong reason is harder
to catch than one that reads zero, which is why this is worth more than the
missing field it looks like.

The column is JSON, so there is no finite list of names to whitelist. The keys
are din276 or masterformat or nrm or whatever the estimator's workbook calls its
cost types, and a catalogue that had to know them in advance would need editing
before a deployment could read its own data. So the catalogue declares the COLUMN
and the spec supplies the key. That makes the key the one name in a spec that is
not already a key in a table in the module, so it is bounded by a pattern rather
than by a lookup: a letter, then up to 63 letters, digits or underscores, one
level, no nesting.

Safety here does not rest on the pattern. The key reaches the database as a bound
parameter through classification[key].as_string(), never spliced into SQL text,
and there is a test that compiles the expression and asserts the key is absent
from the compiled string and present in the parameters. The pattern is there to
give the author an error at validation time instead of an empty breakdown at
compute time.

The two ways of getting a path wrong now say different things. Asking for
description.tipo says description is not a JSON column, asking for
classification.ti-po says ti-po is not a usable key. Neither mistake is visible
in the list of allowed names, since the column is in it and the path is not, so
the message is the only thing that tells the author which one they made.

The parity check between the catalogue and the binder was widened to cover the
JSON columns, and that widening matters more here than for plain fields. A JSON
column declared and not bound would pass validation, because validation reads the
catalogue, so the definition would be accepted and stored and the failure would
arrive at compute time on a KPI already sitting on somebody's dashboard.

The bare column is deliberately not offered as a groupable field. Grouping by a
whole JSON object is not a breakdown anybody wants, so the API serves it under
json_path_fields with an example of the shape instead, which is what a picker
needs to build the control.

Closes #451

a project with four estimates reports four buildings, and a sum over its lines
reports one building per line. So there is now a project entity, with one row per
building, and area is offered there and deliberately nowhere else. It carries
contract_value and budget_estimate for the same reason, plus the text fields a
breakdown needs, so a portfolio KPI can be keyed by project type or phase.

price_as_of lives on the cost catalogue, which has no project column anywhere, so
it cannot be an entity in an engine where every reading can be narrowed to the
project the dashboard is showing. The usage ledger does have one, and it is
written on the ordinary position-create path whenever a position is created with
a cost-item link, so the entity is the join of the two: cost_item_usage. It is
offered as an age in days rather than as a date, which matters more than it
sounds. A stored definition outlives the day it was written, and "older than 90
days" keeps asking the question it was saved with where "before 2026-06-01"
quietly stops being that question. That needed a small dialect-aware construct,
days_since, because PostgreSQL subtracts dates and SQLite has no date type; both
now count whole days, where the obvious SQLite spelling would have carried the
elapsed fraction of today and disagreed with PostgreSQL on every row.

Markup rows are exposed, markup money is not, and that is the part of the request
deliberately left out. percentage and fixed_amount are the rates as the estimator
entered them, which answers what margin an estimate carries and how many carry
none. What a line ADDS to a total depends on the compounding order, on whether it
applies to the direct cost or cumulatively, and on whether a section-scoped line
overrides a bill-wide one. That cascade is the BOQ service's, and a second copy of
it written as SQL here would be a second answer to the same question that drifts
from the first. So markups_total and direct_cost_total are not offered.

Two things found while doing it, both about the guards rather than the fields.

Every one of the new numeric fields sits over a nullable text column, and
numeric_value reads NULL as 0 on PostgreSQL. Without a declared nullable_source
the compute path has nothing to exclude on, so min of a portfolio where one
project records an area and thirteen do not comes back 0, and avg divides one
building by fourteen. The test for this walks the bound expression down to the
columns it is built from rather than listing the fields, so an entity added later
is covered without anybody remembering. Written the obvious way that walk matched
nothing, because it yields ORM attributes and not columns, and every test built on
it passed by looking at an empty list. There is now a control test asserting the
walk actually reaches the column, and the invariant was checked by removing a
nullable_source and watching it name the field.

The parity check between catalogue and binders could not report the failure it
exists to catch. Declaring an entity and binding it are two edits in two places,
and an entry with no binder raises KeyError out of the binder dict, which is not
the ImportError the check caught, so the test died with a traceback naming a dict
instead of failing with the name of the entity left half-added. It now reports it.

What still will not work, said plainly rather than left to be discovered: cost per
m2 is a ratio across two entities and there is no ratio aggregation. Both halves
are now readable and the tile that divides one by the other is not expressible
yet.

Also corrects a claim about `source` shipped in the previous commit. It said the
column is manual for 257 of 258 rows on a real installation, which is a number
this tree cannot support. The mechanism can be: the column defaults to manual and
every ordinary create path writes it literally, only the CAD and AI import paths
write anything else.

Closes #452
