fix(desktop): a startup that died before any of our code ran was reported as our server failing

The screenshot attached to the Windows start failure report had never been
opened. It shows the packaged sidecar dying inside the bundler's own loader,
unable to unpack one of its bundled libraries into the temporary folder, which
happens before the bundled interpreter exists and therefore before a single line
of ours runs. The launcher labelled that death, like every death before the
server reports ready, as the server stage. So the one artefact a person can send
us named the wrong half of the program, and the database step was left with its
spinner still turning because the splash only ever back fills a step to active
or done and never to failed.

The launcher now recognises an unpack failure, attributes it to the sidecar
rather than to the server, resets the database step to pending rather than
leaving it running forever, and replaces the loader's own wording with something
a person can act on, which is the temporary folder, the antivirus and the free
space rather than a return code.

The test asserts the stage, and it is red with the old value on the reporter's
exact text, with the reason written into the assertion rather than into a
comment: no server code runs before the payload is unpacked.

The gate added yesterday, which starts the shipped sidecar and waits for it to
answer, could never have caught this. It runs on a machine where unpacking
succeeds. That is worth saying plainly because the gate was added in response to
this same report, and it closes a real hole, just not this one.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(install): the Windows installer asked whether a name resolved, not whether a usable Python exists

The script probed the bare name python and read its version out of a banner. Its
POSIX sibling has always tried a list of candidates. Those are different
questions and they disagree in both directions. The name can resolve to an
unrelated virtual environment that happens to be first on the path, and a
perfectly good interpreter can be present under a name that probe never tries,
which is the common case on Windows because the official installer leaves the
path option unchecked by default and always installs the launcher.

Each candidate is now run and asked its own version through the interpreter
rather than through a printed banner, so the verdict comes from the process that
would actually be used. The launcher forms are tried first for the reason above.
The search happens once and is remembered, because the answer is needed twice
and every probe starts a process.

The failure message matters as much as the detection. Nothing found and found
but too old take the same path and give the same advice, but the second one adds
a line naming what it found, because a bare statement that Python 3.12 or newer
is required reads as you have no Python to somebody whose python answers when
they type it.

The originally reported symptom was milder than first described and is corrected
here rather than left standing. The line about the version requirement is
unreachable from the automatic path, which is guarded by the same test. What a
person actually saw was the script announcing that neither Docker nor Python was
found and going off to fetch a package manager, with a working interpreter
sitting behind the launcher the whole time.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(desktop): the guard against multiprocessing re-execution sat in the one file we do not freeze

On macOS the sidecar served a cold start and then died on a restart over its
own data, which on a user's machine is the app working the first time it is
opened and stopping at "Starting the application server" the second. Measured
in run 33834902654: the process printed

    openconstructionerp: error: argument command: invalid choice:
    'from multiprocessing.resource_tracker import main;main(18)'

and went down with Abort trap: 6 without ever answering /api/health.

In a frozen build sys.executable is our own binary, so when the standard
library starts one of its helper processes it re-executes us. There are two
such command lines and they need different handling. A spawned child arrives
as "--multiprocessing-fork ..." because spawn.get_command_line has a
sys.frozen branch, and multiprocessing.freeze_support answers it. The resource
tracker has no such branch: resource_tracker.py always builds the interpreter
form, so the frozen binary is handed a "-c" line that only an interpreter can
answer, and ours went straight into argparse.

freeze_support was called, correctly, and had been for a long time. It was
called in backend/app/__main__.py, and desktop/pyinstaller.spec freezes
backend/app/cli.py. So the guard was right in every detail and absent from
every artifact we have ever shipped. It had never been seen to fail because it
had never been seen to run.

cli.py now answers both forms before it builds its parser, gated on sys.frozen
because outside a frozen build the standard library re-executes the real
interpreter and never reaches us. The flags that may precede -c are whatever
subprocess._args_from_interpreter_flags derives from the parent's sys.flags,
and a frozen build commonly carries no_site, so checking for a bare -c would
have passed on a runner and failed on a laptop.

Two of the new tests are the ones that would have caught this. They read the
entry script out of the spec rather than naming it, and they assert that the
file PyInstaller actually freezes carries the guard and reaches it before the
parser. Against the previous commit both fail. The rest cover the argument
scan and the dispatcher, which are the parts provable without a runner.

The release workflow gains a step that asserts the same thing directly, and it
is separate on purpose. The serve step found this defect only because the
encoder happened to download on that run: the cold start passed because the
download failed and nothing reached multiprocessing, and the restart failed
because it succeeded. A green serve step alone is therefore settled by luck
with a model host. The new step needs no network, no database and no port, and
it runs on all three platforms. The serve step now also prints whether the leg
it just ran loaded the encoder, so a green log says which path it took.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test(install): the two scripts a stranger runs first were exercised by nothing

scripts/install.ps1 and scripts/install.sh are the first things anyone runs,
before any of the rest of this product exists on their machine, and until now
neither was touched by anything in the repository. There were no PowerShell
tests anywhere in the tree, and none of the twenty workflows invoked either
script by any name. The two files with the largest blast radius for a new user
were the two with no coverage at all.

The harness dot-sources the shipped install.ps1 with its Main block removed and
drives the detection branch with candidate lists it controls, so the cases run
against the real file rather than a copy of it. Twenty-two of them. The ones
worth naming are the pair where the name and the interpreter disagree: a
candidate spelled 3.12 that reports 3.11 is rejected, and a candidate spelled
3.9 that reports 3.12 is accepted. That is the defect in the shape it actually
takes, and asking the name instead of the interpreter is what shipped.

The lane reports, it does not block, and the header says so rather than leaving
a reader to assume otherwise. The main-protection ruleset carries deletion,
non_fast_forward and required_linear_history and no required status checks, so
a red run here stops no push and no tag. What it buys is a failing check on the
commit that broke the script. That is worth having: the same kind of lane, one
nothing could block on either, caught a macOS defect earlier today that would
otherwise have gone out inside an installer.

cancel-in-progress is off on main deliberately. A cancelled run carries no
conclusion, so a lane that cancels itself on every push goes quiet without ever
going red, and that silence cannot be told apart from health. We have already
paid for that lesson once.

install.sh is deliberately not in the paths. There is no harness for it yet, and
a run that proves nothing about the file that changed is worse than no run. It
was read and has no equivalent defect: it asks the interpreter, and it builds
the virtual environment with the candidate it picked.

the draft in local state and wrote it only on Save draft or on Issue minutes.

fix(desktop): every installed copy signed its tokens with the key that is in the repository

The frozen sidecar is started by the CLI, and the CLI sets APP_ENV to
development and JWT_SECRET to the bundled literal, neither of them with a
branch for a frozen build. The function that exists to stop a zero-config
deployment from keeping that literal, _ensure_persistent_jwt_secret, returned on
its first line for anything calling itself development. So it never ran inside
an installed copy of the desktop app, and every copy signed with the same
secret. That secret is in _JWT_KNOWN_WEAK_SECRETS, and the comment above that
set already says why it is there: anyone who can read the public source can
forge admin tokens against a deployment that kept it.

The artifact says so itself. The health body from the macOS sidecar in run
33834902654 carries "env":"development", which is what sent me looking.

This is the second thing to come out of the same root as the multiprocessing
fix earlier today. backend/app/__main__.py documents itself as the PyInstaller
entry point and carries the frozen-only branch that sets APP_ENV to production,
and desktop/pyinstaller.spec freezes backend/app/cli.py. Everything conditional
that file holds has been dead in every artifact we ever shipped.

The environment is deliberately left as development and only the secret is
fixed. Promoting the frozen build to production would fix this too, but the
census of what else changes says it would disable the passwordless demo sign-in
and flip the takeoff privacy badge from "never leaves your computer" to
"processed on your server", which on a desktop is the less true of the two. It
would refuse to start nowhere, but neither of those is a trade worth taking for
a secret we can fix directly. desktop_mode() is the predicate because it answers
for both signals a shipped build carries, sys.frozen and OE_DESKTOP.

Existing installs will find themselves signed out once, on the launch that
provisions the secret. That is the correct outcome and worth stating plainly:
the sessions being invalidated are the ones signed with a key anybody could
have minted.

Five tests. Two of them fail on the previous commit with the defect written out
in full, assert 'openestimate-local-dev-key' != 'openestimate-local-dev-key'.
The other three are controls that pass either way on purpose: a source checkout
in development still boots on the bundled default with no ceremony, the desktop
secret survives a restart rather than signing everyone out on every launch, and
a secret the operator chose is never overwritten. The thirty-five tests already
guarding this area pass in both directions.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(vector): startup built the embedding model three times at once and macOS did not survive it

get_embedder is a lazy singleton that takes seconds to build and is reachable
from several threads at once. It checked whether the instance was None and then
built one, with nothing in between, so every thread that arrived during the
build started its own. They all assigned to the same global, so every copy but
the last was discarded after being paid for in full.

The startup path did not merely allow that, it guaranteed it. init_pool submits
one warm-up job per worker, all in the same instant, and the comment above them
said the parent had already loaded the model via maybe_preload_in_process. That
function runs only under OE_VECTOR_PRELOAD=1, which is off by default and is not
set in the desktop build, so on a default startup those jobs were the first
callers and there were min(4, cpu_count()) of them.

Measured on macos-latest in desktop-release run 33841183277, the restart leg:
three "Loaded sentence-transformers model" lines 138 ms apart, then SIGSEGV.
Three is min(4, cpu_count()) on that runner. "Embedding pool initialised" never
appears in the log, which puts the death inside init_pool between submitting the
warm-up jobs and reporting the pool up. The cold start in the same run loaded the
model once and served fine, including the pool encoding on three threads
afterwards, so concurrent inference on one model is not the problem and
concurrent construction of three is.

Two changes, and the second is not cosmetic. get_embedder now serialises the
build behind a lock, with the instance check repeated inside so the steady state
stays lock-free. init_pool loads the model in its own thread before it submits
anything, which is what its comment already claimed happened. The lock alone
would still leave the build happening in whichever worker thread won the race,
and loading it in the caller keeps it on the thread that has always done the
rest of startup. It costs no extra work: the warm-up jobs called get_embedder
anyway, and get_embedder honours the download lock, so a deployment with no
encoder installed and downloads off gets the same fast nothing-to-load it gets
today.

Five tests. Four of them fail on the previous commit with the defect written out
as a number: six models built for one singleton, twelve attempts for a load that
cannot succeed, and the pool's own event order coming back as job, job, job with
no load before it. The fifth is the control and passes either way on purpose,
because the process pool's workers each hold their own model and warming the
parent there would load one the parent has no use for.

What this does not prove is that the crash is gone. It proves the race is gone.
Neither the segfault nor the memory ceiling that may be behind it reproduces off
that runner, so the macOS gate is the only thing that can answer, and the gate
now prints the load counts for both legs instead of only the one that succeeded.
In the failing run the numbers existed only for the healthy leg and had to be
read out of a 200 line tail.

The same unguarded-singleton shape exists on the LanceDB and Qdrant clients in
the same file. Neither is reachable from the warm-up stampede and neither is
this bug, so both are left alone.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(i18n): Uzbek was shipping to users while no test could see it

i18n-fallbacks.ts aggregates every per-locale resource so tests can iterate the
locales without repeating forty imports. A locale missing from it is offered no
less, it is simply invisible to every test that reads the object, and the file's
own docstring records that this is how Kyrgyz, Greek and Ukrainian each went
unchecked while shipping.

The same docstring named uz as a deliberate exception, absent because it was
commented out of SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES, and told whoever uncommented it to add the
import in the same commit. It was uncommented, in the commit that closed the
last English bands in uz.ts on 2026-09-01. The import was not added. So the
paragraph explaining the exception became the reason nobody looked: it read as
current, and it had been false for three days.

Measured now rather than remembered, because the counts here have gone stale
four times: 44 locale files on disk, 42 entries in SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES, 41
imports in the aggregator. Cross-checking the two lists in both directions
leaves exactly three names. en-US is offered and not aggregated on purpose, an
overrides-only overlay of about 1.6k keys that would be compared against a 35k
key file. mn is aggregated and not offered on purpose, so the Mongolian file
keeps its coverage while it waits for a native-speaker pass. uz is the third and
is the defect.

A comment recording a rule cannot enforce it, so the fix is not only the import.
everyOfferedLanguageIsInTheFallbackAggregator.test.ts compares the two lists as
exact set differences in both directions and names each exception in a constant
next to the reason for it. Exact differences rather than counts on purpose: a
count starts passing again the moment two mistakes cancel out.

Three tests, all passing. The reverse, removing the import again and watching
them go red, was attempted and gave no verdict: the vitest worker timed out
under a concurrent build on this machine and the run reported "no tests", which
is silence rather than a failure. It is worth saying plainly rather than
implying a proof I do not have. What is measured, by grep against the two files
themselves, is that uz is present in one list and absent from the other on the
previous commit.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

ci(desktop): the serve gate could not say what the restart dies of

The previous round answered one question and closed it. The encoder was being
built three times at once on a restart, the singleton is guarded now, and the
counters this step prints went to one load on both legs. The restart still
segfaults. So the crash is not construction concurrency, and continuing to edit
the embedder is editing the wrong file.

The step cannot currently produce the evidence that would settle it. A process
that dies of SIGSEGV writes nothing to its own stdout about why, so the 200 line
tail this step prints is by construction incapable of carrying the cause. macOS
does write it, to a separate report naming the faulting thread and the library
it died in, and nothing was reading that. It is read now, from both the user and
the system report directories, with a wait because the reporter is asynchronous
and the file is usually not on disk yet when the shell notices the process is
gone.

Second, a third leg. It differs from the failing one in exactly one thing: the
embedding worker pool is off, which is a knob the module already documents and
already honours at zero. It runs whether or not the leg before it passed,
because a leg that only runs when everything is green answers a question nobody
is asking, and it is printed rather than asserted so a setting nobody ships with
cannot turn a release gate red. Serves with the pool off and dies with it on,
and the fault is in the pool or in what it warms. Dies either way, and the pool
is innocent.

Third, the machine between the legs. This step's own comment records that
killing serve does not stop the embedded PostgreSQL it started, and the second
leg deliberately reuses the directory, so that leg is not a user relaunching the
application. It is a second instance opening a data directory whose postmaster
belongs to a process that no longer exists. If that is the difference, it shows
up in the process list and the memory figures now printed between them, and the
gate is testing something harsher than the case it is named after.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(email): the plain text part kept the link label and threw the link away

The plain text alternative of every outgoing message is derived from the HTML
body by stripping tags with a regex over angle brackets. An anchor is a tag, so
the whole element went and only the anchor text stayed. Someone reading the
password reset in plain text got the words "Reset password", no URL anywhere in
the message, and no way to reset a password. Rendered through the real template
and the real conversion, the string http did not occur in the body at all.

Nine distinct bodies reach that conversion and seven of them emit an anchor: the
five shared templates in core/email/templates.py, the notification dispatcher
and the tender invitation. The document cover note and the progress report carry
no link and are unaffected. Three of the seven are reachable from a live call
site today, and the password reset is the worst of them, because there the link
is not an optional call to action, it is the entire message.

The conversion now runs on html.parser rather than a regex, in a new module
core/email/html_text.py. A regex over a tag pattern also ends the tag at the
first closing bracket even when that bracket sits inside a quoted attribute, so
an anchor carrying a title with a greater-than sign in it used to render as
attribute debris with the URL gone. It decoded only the handful of entities
somebody remembered to list. The parser knows where an attribute ends and
resolves character references itself, so a query string written as an escaped
ampersand reaches the recipient as the character they have to type.

The same choice was already made for the inbound direction in
modules/inbound_email/eml_parser.py. That extractor is deliberately not shared:
core has to keep working when an optional module is not installed, and the two
contracts differ, since the inbound one rebuilds line structure for a recovered
body while this one has to stay the single flowed paragraph the MIME part has
always been.

Links are written the way plain text mail writes them, the label followed by the
target in angle brackets. An anchor whose text already is the destination prints
once, an anchor pointing at a fragment or at a script scheme prints its label
alone, and stylesheet and script content no longer leaks into the body.

Twenty tests, no database and no network, the end to end one reading the decoded
text/plain part back out of what the transport was handed. Putting the original
bytes back turns thirteen of them red, and the file was restored from its own
saved bytes and hash checked afterwards.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(schedule): an activity's planned cost was accepted and thrown away

The Activity model has carried cost_planned and cost_actual since the 4D work,
along with percent_complete_type, remaining_duration, budgeted_units and
installed_units. None of the six appeared in ActivityCreate, ActivityUpdate or
ActivityResponse, and both request schemas declare extra="ignore", so a client
that posted a planned cost got back 200 and an activity with no cost on it.
The earned value rollup then summed cost_planned over rows that were all null,
reported a budget at completion of zero and has_cost_data false, and every
figure derived from it was wrong with nothing anywhere reporting an error. The
interchange import and export have read and written all six fields all along,
so the CRUD API was the odd one out rather than the model being incomplete.

Adding the fields to the schemas alone would not have been enough. Two places
build these objects with explicit keyword arguments, create_activity in the
service and _activity_to_response in the router, and both would have gone on
returning nulls, so both now pass the six through. The money fields follow the
work order pair in the same file: Decimal in, plain decimal string out, bounded
and refused when not finite, and nullable here because the columns are. The two
unit quantities take the same wire shape and the same lower bound as the typed
progress request, which is the other writer of those columns.
percent_complete_type gets the pattern its neighbours have, so this route can no
longer write a value the progress engine would refuse.

extra="ignore" stays. The frontend types both the create and the update helper
as Partial<Activity> over the response shape, which carries id and schedule_id
among others, so forbidding extras would turn a call that is legal under the
app's own typing into a 422. It was never the defect either, only what made the
defect quiet, and the quiet is gone now that the fields exist. Tightening it is
a decision for the whole module, not a side effect of this fix.

The generic PATCH writes these as raw columns, exactly as it already does for
progress_pct. Deriving a percent from installed units and recomputing the
remaining duration stays with the typed progress endpoint, which is where the
warnings come from.

Tests cover a create that sends a planned cost and reads it back, the same
through a patch, and an earned value summary over a schedule built through the
API whose budget at completion is three thousand rather than zero. Two controls
pass either way on purpose: the rollup arithmetic given rows directly, which
never saw this defect, and an uncosted schedule, which must still report that
it has no cost data.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(changeorders): a corrected variation order left its mirror posting the old amount

When a variation order is promoted, a change order is created that mirrors it.
Correcting the amount on the order after that point did nothing to the mirror,
and approving the mirror posted the superseded figure to the project budget and
to the payload the contracts subscriber reads. Measured on the commit before
this one: an order corrected from 7200 down to 6800 approved at 7200. The same
7200 was shown at submission, which is the number an approver signs against.

The refusal a user meets when they try to reprice a mirror directly tells them
to change the amount on the variation order and let the mirror follow. Nothing
made it follow, so the message sent people down a path that did not work, which
is worse than no message at all.

The mirror now resolves its amount from the variation order at the two moments
that decide money, submission and approval, rather than keeping a copy that
something has to remember to push to. Reading rather than subscribing, because
an update to a variation order publishes no event to subscribe to, and because
a value resolved from its source cannot drift between the figure an approver is
shown and the figure that posts. The approval chain funnels back through the
same call, so a chained approval resolves too.

A mirror that has already been approved is left alone. An order corrected after
its mirror has posted is a new commercial decision and needs a new variation,
not a silent rewrite of money that has already moved. An approval on a stale
mirror is not refused: it posts the corrected number and records the
substitution, in the audit metadata, in the log line and on the approved event,
so it is auditable rather than quiet. Refusing would have been a second thing to
explain to somebody who had already done what the product told them to do.

One related hole is closed with it. The guard that held the amount against a
direct patch did not cover the line items, and every line item write recalculates
the cost impact from the sum of the lines, so a mirror that refused an amount of
9999 still arrived at 9999 through a single line for 9999. Adding, changing and
deleting a line on a mirror are all refused now.

Ten tests. Eight of them go red on the previous commit, and the two money rows
among those carry the defect itself. Two controls pass on both sides, which is
what separates a plumbing fix from a change in the arithmetic: a standalone
change order is still priced by its own lines, and a mirror whose variation
order was deleted keeps the only figure left to it.

The file is named in the PostgreSQL lane beside the double-post guard rather
than left to be run by hand. That lane names its integration files one at a

fix(vector): a frozen build sent its encoder to Metal and did not survive it

one, and on any Apple Silicon machine it chooses Metal. The log of the run this
was found in says so in as many words: no device provided, using mps. Nobody
decided that. It is what happens when the argument is left out.

The round before this one removed a genuine defect, three copies of the model
being built at once, and the macOS restart went on segfaulting afterwards, which
said plainly that construction concurrency was not the cause. So this round
measured instead of guessing. A third leg was added to the serve check that
differs from the failing one in exactly one thing, the embedding worker pool
turned off, and it runs whether or not the leg before it passed.

The three answers, from desktop-release run 33851623420 on macos-latest. The
restart serves with the pool disabled and dies with it enabled, which puts the
fault in the pool or in what the pool warms rather than in the load. The encoder
loads exactly once and successfully, and the process then raises SIGSEGV before
the pool reports itself initialised, with the multiprocessing resource tracker
complaining about a leaked semaphore as the last thing written. And the machine
between the two legs holds no leftover process and three and a half gigabytes of
free memory, which retires the other theory on the table, that the second leg
was really a second instance opening a data directory whose postmaster belonged
to a dead process.

What the pool does immediately after the load is run several encode calls at
once against the one model object. A frozen bundle dispatching concurrent
inference to Metal is a combination we neither test nor need, and it is worth
nothing here: this is a 384 dimensional sentence encoder embedding short
strings, and a desktop workspace is not the machine anyone chose for throughput.

So the device is named now. A frozen build and the desktop sidecar get the CPU,
a server install is still left to choose its own accelerator, and
OE_VECTOR_DEVICE overrides both, so somebody who wants Metal on their own
desktop build can have it and so the decision can be measured from both sides
rather than only asserted. The loaded line says which device it used, and the
pipeline step prints it, because not printing it is why the last round needed a
round of its own.

Six tests, and the one that matters most reads what the constructor was actually
handed. Resolving the right string and then failing to pass it would leave the
defect exactly where it was while every other assertion here stayed green. Two
of the six are controls: a server install must still be left alone, and it must
be handed no device argument at all rather than an explicit null, which some
versions of the library read as a request rather than as silence.

can, and only the macOS leg of the pipeline will say.

fix(install): asking for the latest version did not undo an older pin

and neither had any way to remove one. That file outlives the run that wrote it
and is read on every compose invocation in its directory, so the first install
decided the version for every install after it. Somebody who once ran the
one-liner with a version and later ran the documented default one to upgrade
pulled the version they pinned. The pull succeeded, the containers came up, and
the script told them the installation was complete. Nothing anywhere reported a
problem, which is the shape of defect that survives longest, and it lands on
this release, since this is the release those people are trying to reach.

Writing a pin and never clearing one is not half a feature. It is a feature
that reverses meaning on the second run: the first time, latest means latest,
and every time after, latest means whatever was asked for once. So asking for
latest now removes a pin as well as declining to write one, and says so, since
a version quietly changing under somebody is what got us here.

pinned once and read the value back would have passed against the broken
script. Both the two functions and the branch that chooses between them are
sliced out of the shipped file rather than restated, and the reason is the same

passed against a call site that had gone back to never clearing. Restoring the
old call site fails the run. They also cover what must not move, the database

somebody out of data PostgreSQL has already written.

attempt spends before sleeping, so against a socket that accepts and never
replies a person waits about two minutes and is told sixty seconds. The comment

healthy install from it. The Windows script rejects those same bytes. Two
installers disagreeing about one response is the finding rather than the

well before seed_i18n_data. On a fresh data directory that means they meet an

nothing else is coming, so that install really does need somebody to add the
rows by hand, and it gets the only notice it will ever have.

cohort now asserts the warning it has to keep, so the two situations are told
apart rather than quietened together.

fix(finance): an invoice total was written for reading and then read back as a number

Issue #466 arrived as the total field blanking out at a thousand, and the
blank field is the smaller half of it. The total is auto filled, and since
07bfdec42 on 18 August it was auto filled through fmtFixed, which writes the
reader's separators. A number input refuses any value carrying one, so from a
thousand upwards the box came up empty. The same grouped string is what the
form read back when it built the request, and parseFloat stops at the first
character it cannot use, so nine thousand left the browser as nine. For a
reader whose decimal mark is a comma the same call dropped the cents off every
invoice at any size, with no thousand needed.

Nothing was stored wrong, and that is the rest of the story. create_invoice
replaced whatever total arrived with subtotal plus tax on every write, so the
database stayed right while the client had been sending a truncated figure for
weeks and nothing anywhere reported it. Silently correcting a number a person
typed is how a defect like this stays invisible, so the service now keeps a
total the caller asserts and refuses one that does not add up. The tolerance is
two cents, the same figure invoice capture already holds a scanned document to,
so an invoice that passes review cannot be refused when it is booked. Line
items are weighed the same way against the subtotal they are lines of, at a
cent per line for the rounding that accumulates. Invoice capture is exempted
from the line sum and says so in one place: its lines are what a reader could
make out of a scan while the net comes from the document's own header, and a
line that went unread must not strand an invoice whose journal entry is already
posted.

On the input side the choice was between formatting only while the field is not
focused and never grouping an editable value at all. It is the second. A number
input sanitises every value it is handed, not only the ones handed to it while

fix(validation): a run that finished between two ticks of the clock reported that it took no time

Durations were measured with time.monotonic. On Windows that clock is backed by
the interrupt timer and advances about every 15.625 ms, so a validation pass
over a few hundred rules already held in memory routinely started and finished
between two identical readings. The subtraction then gave exactly zero, the
report stored a duration of 0 and the page printed "Duration: 0.0ms" as though
the run had been measured and found instant. What rules out a genuinely instant
run is the spread of the values that were stored, 0, 15, 16, 31, 32, 47, 93,
110, 140, 141 and 1578, every one a whole number of ticks with nothing in
between, and nine of twenty five sitting at zero.

Measured on a Windows machine, monotonic advertises a resolution of 15.625 ms
and 995 of 1000 short operations read as 0.0 ms through it. perf_counter
advertises 0.0001 ms and none of the same 1000 read as zero, so the four places
in validation that difference two readings into a duration now use it. Linux has
a nanosecond monotonic and cannot provoke any of this, which is why it survived,
so the new test freezes the coarse clock instead of trusting the platform and
fails against the old code everywhere.

The display keeps its zero rather than hiding it. The backend rounds to two
decimals, so the smallest non-zero duration it can send is 0.01 ms, and one
decimal printed that as the same "0.0" an untimed run produces; short durations
now carry the two decimals that are actually on the wire. A zero is rare after
this and it means something, usually that the report predates the fix. Reports
already stored keep the zeros they were measured with, since no change to the
clock can reach a number written down months ago.

fix(projects): four sidebar modules asked for a column their table never had

The module presence probe decides whether to dim a sidebar entry by asking
each module's table whether the active project has a row in it. Four of the
fifty seven entries asked a question the schema cannot answer. The equipment
fleet, the service ticket and the portal access rule tables carry no
project_id at all, and oe_bim_asset_register was never a table, because the

those probes raised, the caller swallowed the error and returned False, so
Equipment, Service, Portal and Assets were reported as empty for every project
on every install no matter how much data they held. Absent and broken read the
same to the user.

The cost was not only wrong dimming. Every sweep sent four statements that
were certain to fail, and each failure also forces a rollback to clear the
aborted transaction, so an uncached sweep cost sixty one round trips instead
of fifty seven. In one reporter's launcher log covering seventy eight days
this produced ninety one thousand nine hundred and forty eight server side
errors, and the error and statement lines together were forty five percent of
a fifty two megabyte log.

Equipment and the portal user list are company wide registers with no project
column, so they take the company scope that the subcontractor directory and
the contacts book already use. Service tickets reach a project through their
contract, and that link is nullable because a service contract exists before
it is struck against a delivery project, so service takes the hybrid scope
that CRM uses. Assets now probes tracked BIM elements through their model.

Issue 228 fixed three entries of exactly this shape one table at a time, which
is why four more survived it. The new test asserts the property instead: it
builds the canonical schema from the ORM metadata and runs every registered
probe against it, so a module added later cannot reintroduce this quietly. It
also guards its own population, because a collapsed model import would
otherwise leave nothing to check and read as agreement.

The project header clipped its right edge in German and Russian, and the
clipped part could not be scrolled to. A bare fractional grid track is
minmax(auto, Nfr), and that auto minimum resolves to min-content, so where two
of them share a row the longer language walks one past its share and the row
grows past the viewport. Measured at a 1440 viewport, German resolved the
header template to 462.953px 955.328px and documentElement.scrollWidth reached
1704 with maxScrollLeft 0. Every arbitrary track list in the tree was searched
and the eighteen carrying two or more bare fractional tracks now use
minmax(0, Nfr). One of them, in the HSE five whys panel, also separated its
tracks with commas rather than underscores, which reaches the stylesheet as
invalid CSS, so the browser had been dropping the declaration and collapsing
that row to a single column.

Relative timestamps stayed English everywhere. date-fns does not read the
ambient language, it defaults to en-US, so formatDistanceToNow without a locale
returns a perfectly valid English string in all forty two languages and nothing
goes red. The count of English phrases was identical in German, Russian,
Chinese, Arabic and Japanese, which is the signature of a missing locale rather
than a missing translation. There is now one place that answers which date-fns
locale a reader reads in, and every call site that prints words asks it. Three
were the dashboard, the projects list and the shared date component; the other
two, the drawing upload label and the accommodation calendar month and weekday
headers, turned up by widening the search rather than in the browser pass.
date-fns publishes no locale for Filipino, Kyrgyz or Urdu, so those three still
fall back to English, and that gap is named in code and asserted in both
directions rather than left to happen quietly.

Nineteen German strings under match had their diacritics stripped in a single
batch. The correct spelling appears hundreds of times elsewhere in the same
file, so this was one bad batch and not an encoding fault. Repaired from a list
of the eight words rather than by pattern, because Umfang and Unterzeilen sit
under the same prefix and really do begin with a bare capital U.

The layout guard asserts on the class string, not on computed style. jsdom has
no layout engine and does not compile Tailwind, so a computed-style assertion
there would pass without ever measuring anything. It proves in the same run

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

feat(postcalc): answer what a production norm predicted against what the job spent

The write side of this shipped in 844f652c1 and nothing read it. Applying an
assembly built from a production norm put norm_id and work_key into the
position's metadata, which is enough to record a fact and not enough to answer a
question about it, so the estimate against outturn comparison the feature exists
for could not be run at all.

The identity is now a column on oe_boq_position, backfilled in v3320 from the
metadata of the bills priced in between. There is no foreign key to the norm
library on purpose. A norm can be edited or deleted after a bill was priced from
it, and provenance that has to be resolved through a mutable row is not
provenance, so the id and the human readable work key are both copied and the key
survives the deletion of the row it names.

Deriving the column from the metadata happens at every writer, not just the
single create. A line is also written by duplicating one, by duplicating a bill
into a revision, by restoring a snapshot and by the bulk create the importers go
through, and each of those builds the row field by field. Before this a copy
carried the identity in its metadata against a null column, which nothing would
have noticed, because the read side coalesces column then metadata and answers
correctly either way. It would have shown up much later as a group by returning a
fraction of the work in the shape of the whole of it, on exactly the bills that
have been revised most, which are the ones anybody wants an outturn comparison
for.

The read side is a new endpoint under postcalc, one row per norm, carrying what
the bill predicted, what the library says today, what was installed, what was
spent and the productivity factor between them. It reuses the position actuals
report for the measured half rather than reading timesheets again.

Four limits are deliberate and visible in the response. A norm with nothing
recorded against it returns a named status rather than a zero, so no progress and
no actuals never read as perfect productivity. A norm used by several positions
sums the numerator and the denominator across all of them instead of averaging
per line factors, which is the difference between a rate and the mean of rates.
The two baselines are reported apart, the bill one immutable and the library one
live and absent when the norm was deleted. Positions in one group that are not in
one unit have no denominator to share, so the per unit figures collapse and the
row says so instead of adding metres to square metres.

fix(system): a converter status check named the operator's own home directory

Three routes answer without credentials on purpose and described the machine
while doing it. The converter version check returned installed_path, the
converter listing returned path and buried the same folder in health_message
prose, and the install progress poll carried both a path and a message quoting
the install location back, for the three minutes a finished record lingers. On
a default install those paths sit under the operator's home directory, so what
went to anyone who could reach the port was the home directory layout and the
operating system account name of whoever runs the server.

Two shapes were available: require authentication, or keep the routes open and
stop them describing the disk. Took the second. What these endpoints are for
survives without the path. A caller asking whether a converter is installed is
answered by installed, and one asking whether a newer build exists is answered
by comparing two SHAs, and neither needs to be told where anything lives. The
BIM page also asks for the listing before anyone has signed in, so gating it
would have broken a working screen to fix a field. An authenticated caller
still gets the path, because the Settings panel and the BIM banner both print
it and an operator repairing a broken install needs the folder name, so this is
a redaction and not a deletion.

No auth dependency was added anywhere. OptionalUserPayload never refuses, it
resolves to None for a caller with no usable token and costs an anonymous
request neither a header nor a database read. Measured over the whole route
table on both sides of the change: 5619 routes, 266 of them reachable without
credentials, the same 266 either way, none added and none removed.

The redaction runs on a copy, which is why the helper is shared rather than
written inline three times. Two of these answers come out of a cache held for
hours and handed to every later reader, so emptying the cached dict for one
anonymous request would have emptied it for the operator who asked next. One
canonical body is cached and each response is redacted on its way out.

The listing carries a docstring saying no authentication is required because it
is a public status check. That is still true and was never the question. It
authorises the route being reachable and says nothing about what may travel in
the body.

The test asserts the absence of a host path, found by walking every string in
the response and asking whether it names a place on this machine, rather than
the presence of any particular new field. A test written around the new shape
would have stayed green against a regression that put the path back somewhere
else, and this one disclosure already wore three different field names. Five of
its eight cases fail against the previous code and all eight pass now; the
three that pass either way are the ones pinning that a signed in operator is

fix(embedded-pg): a Windows path over MAX_PATH was reported as a corrupted install

Windows caps a fully qualified path at 259 characters for programs that do not
declare long-path support, and the bundled PostgreSQL binaries do not declare
it, so the machine-wide LongPathsEnabled switch does nothing for them. An
install deep enough to push its own support files past that cap cannot open
them, and initdb reports them as missing with a hint that the installation may
be corrupt. Measured on a 16.8.0 install from PyPI: the support directory was
257 characters, postgres.bki under it 270, the file present and readable by any
long-path-aware tool. Our own message on top of that sent the reader to pip
install --force-reinstall, which downloads 84 MB into the same directory to fail
the same way.

The bring-up now measures both directories before it runs initdb and refuses
with the path, its length, the limit and the fix. The limit is not 260. initdb
is not given -L, it derives its support directory from where its own executable
sits, and it opens names below that directory, so what has to fit is the
directory, a separator and the deepest name underneath. Those depths are walked
out of the shipped tree, 63 characters for the installation and 52 for the data
directory, and a test re-derives the first from the installed tree so a
PostgreSQL bump that ships something deeper goes red there rather than widening
the gap in silence.

Only while the cluster still has to be created. A PG_VERSION already on disk is
proof the paths were once short enough to work, and refusing to open a database
that opened yesterday would be worse than the bug being fixed, so that case is
logged and let through. doctor runs the same measurement with no such gate, for
the user who reinstalled somewhere deeper under a data directory that stayed
put. Nothing changes away from Windows, and a boot that fails for any other
reason still reports exactly what it reported before.

ci(full-suite): a nightly nobody could read was the same as no nightly at all

This is the only lane that runs tests/integration and tests/modules, 268 files
between them, and measured over its last 40 runs on main it completed 40 times,
failed 40 times, succeeded never and was cancelled never. Not one of those runs
came from a push, because the workflow has never had a push trigger. So the two
trees had gone about a month without a green and every red looked exactly like
the red before it, which is a slower way of not testing them at all.

The obvious repair is a push trigger and it was measured and rejected. On run
33951533720 exactly 20 of the 34 test jobs started in the first second and the
21st only three minutes later, which puts the concurrency ceiling at 20 jobs.
main takes 25 to 50 pushes a day and ci.yml already fans out to about 20 jobs
per push, so 34 more per push would queue CI (PostgreSQL) behind this workflow.
Runner minutes are not the constraint, the repository is public, slots are.

The reason that actually decides it is the state of the tree. The failures are
real and unrelated to each other, an unexpected keyword argument, several plain
assertion mismatches, a permission denial, an asyncpg session state error, so
any lane pointed at this tree today is born red and stays red until those are
fixed one at a time. Folding the tree into ci-postgres.yml would have turned the
one lane we trust permanently red on the first push, spending working signal to
expose broken signal, and a second red lane on push would just be a second lane
nobody reads. So it stays nightly and the nightly gets teeth instead.

The gate job now writes every job's verdict into the run summary and raises an
error annotation naming the failing jobs, so one glance says how many are red
and whether the set moved since the night before, where before that cost 34 log
downloads. It counts cancelled, skipped and still running as no verdict rather
than folding them into pass or fail, since an absent answer is the failure mode
this repository keeps paying for. It also now waits on the cross-OS pair, not
the shards alone: a run whose Windows or macOS job was red used to publish the
Backend Full Suite check green, and that check is what a person actually reads.

The header says what the lane covers, what it does not, and how to tell it from
ci-postgres.yml, which runs a different tree on a different trigger. It records
that a check name is a job name, that the gate's name is a strict prefix of all
32 shard names, and that the workflow name is not a check name at all. It also
names the condition for adding a push job later and why no subset of the current
matrix can be that job: pytest-split partitions by test count and is pathless,
so a handful of shards is a random sample of the whole tree, not integration
coverage. Finally it date stamps the max_locks_per_transaction note, whose
symptom is gone as of this run even though the setting should stay.

fix(deps): pin fflate off a version that can hang on a malformed archive

The open advisories on main are ordered by severity, and that ordering points
at the wrong one. Every high is build tooling that never reaches a user:
fast-uri under ajv under workbox-build, browserslist under babel and under
autoprefixer, postcss-selector-parser under tailwind and postcss-nested. All
of them resolve dev only. The one that actually ships is the moderate. fflate
arrives through jspdf, and three product files import jspdf to build PDF
exports, so it lands in the bundle a user downloads.

fflate 0.8.0 through 0.8.2 can loop forever inside unzipSync when a crafted
archive declares the ZIP64 sentinel compressed size and omits the extra field
that has to accompany it (CVE-2026-45820). Our three call sites only hand
jspdf data the app generated itself and none of them reads archive bytes, so
the practical exposure is low, but the fixed version is a straight swap and
there is no reason to keep carrying it.

This pins four packages rather than one. jspdf asks for fflate ^0.8.1 and
@types/three asks for ~0.8.2, so 0.8.3 satisfies both declared ranges and
nothing has to change at the call sites. The three build-only advisories come
along because regenerating the lockfile resolves them in the same pass and
splitting that apart would be error prone for no gain. npm audit on the
committed lockfile reported four findings before this and reports none after.

The app version literals are left out on purpose. A 16.8.1 bump is in flight
across the other version files and both of these carry it, so it belongs in
that commit rather than this one.

ci(hygiene): a commit could import a module only its author's disk had

A tracked Python file that imports a module existing only as an untracked
file passes everything on the machine it was written on. The gates read the
commit and the build reads the disk, and the two agree right up until one
file is committed without its neighbour, at which point the backend stops
starting on the first machine that reads the commit instead of the disk.

scripts/check_untracked_imports.py parses every tracked Python file under
backend/, resolves intra-project imports through the AST and refuses when
the defining file is untracked or absent. Three sites were live in the tree
this morning, in app/main.py, app/modules/takeoff/router.py and
app/modules/postcalc/service.py, across two modules. All three resolve now
because their authors committed the modules, which is luck rather than a
gate.

Getting the false-positive rate to zero took three rules, each of them
forced by a false positive rather than guessed. A top-level name counts as
intra-project only when backend/<name>/__init__.py exists, without which
51 of the first 54 findings were alembic, a namespace directory that loses
to the installed distribution at runtime. A bare except Exception makes an
import optional only when the try body is nothing but imports, without
which the guarded startup blocks in app/main.py exempted the very file
carrying the defect. Directories with no __init__.py are namespace portions
that import fine and have no file to track, so they are not findings.

Over 4780 tracked files, 40629 import statements and 17353 intra-project
imports, the tree comes back clean.

Two limits worth stating rather than discovering later. The check reads
backend/ only, over the roots app, openconstructionerp, scripts and tests,
so repo-root scripts/, packs/*/src/ and the frontend are outside its
population. And it reports without blocking, because main-protection
carries no required status checks. The pre-commit entry is inert until
somebody runs pre-commit install in their clone.

fix(embedded-pg): every start replayed the whole postgres log instead of the lines it wrote

pixeltable-pgserver hands pg_ctl the cluster log with -l, which opens it for
append, and logs the whole of that file whenever the start fails or times out.
Nothing truncates or rotates it, so the tenth start replayed nine earlier ones
and the hundredth replayed ninety-nine. The desktop launcher pumps this
process's output into its own log, so opening the application showed the user
every FATAL line their installation had ever produced, stamped with the moment
it was re-read rather than the moment it happened. One reported log had reached
384744 lines across 97 launches, with a June block of 138 lines repeated
identically in every run from mid June onward. Counting errors in a log like
that measures how long the installation has existed, not what is currently
wrong with it, which is how this was misread twice before anyone looked at the
two clocks on each line.

A filter on the pixeltable_pgserver logger now records how far the log had
already grown before a start appends to it, and replaces exactly that inherited
prefix in an oversized record with one line naming how many lines were dropped
and where they still live. The file on disk is left alone, so a user asked to
send their log in still has the whole history. Arming happens after the last
step that can shrink the file and before the first that can grow it, because a
stale baseline would cut a start's own opening lines instead.

The launcher failure screen now quotes only what this start wrote. A pg_ctl
that dies before the postmaster writes anything leaves the last lines of the
file belonging to a run months earlier, and that screen presented them under
today's failure as today's cause. It is the only surface a user whose window
will not paint can read, so the same misreading is worse there than in the log.

The inherited prefix is read through the same newline normalisation the
library's Path.read_text() applies. Without it the binary read and the text read
are two spellings of the same lines on Windows, they never compare equal, the
prefix is never found, and the cap degrades silently to a plain length trim on
precisely the platform this fault was reported from. There is a test for it,
because an assertion on the size of the output passes either way.

fix(i18n): a regional locale never downloaded the language it falls back to

fallbackLng has mapped es-MX to es and then en for a long time, but that map
only names a bundle, it does not fetch one. loadLocaleResource imported the
chunk for the code it was handed and nothing else, so a Mexican reader's lookup
walked es-MX, then an es bucket that was never loaded, then landed on English.
Around 2700 cases.* keys that es.ts carries and es-MX.ts does not were rendering
in English while a complete Spanish translation sat in a chunk nobody asked for.
es-CL, es-CO and pt-BR were all in the same position. en-US was unaffected only
because its base is the English bundle that ships in the main chunk, which is
also why the one variant with a test was the one variant that worked.

The loader now derives the base from the code instead of carrying a branch per
locale, so the next regional variant is chained by existing code rather than by
somebody remembering to copy a line. Both chunks are awaited together, because
initialLocaleReady is what main.tsx waits on before mounting and a base still in
flight would paint the first frame in English for exactly the keys this fixes.
Each chunk keeps its own error handling, so a failed base fetch still leaves the
reader the variant's own strings.

The direction is a fallback and never a replacement. The two bundles go into
separate per-language buckets and i18next reads the variant first, so every key
es-MX defines keeps winning and only the ones it omits come from es. That is the
point of the variants: they exist for the wording Mexican practice does not share
with Spain, and quietly overwriting it would be a regression nothing on screen
would reveal.

The new test probes the store after calling the real loader, which the existing
en-US test could not do because it hand-adds both bundles and then asserts
resolution order, and resolution order was never the broken part. It also checks
both directions, so a chain wired backwards fails rather than passing quietly.

Cost is that a reader on a regional variant now downloads two locale chunks
instead of one.

fix(api): the first visit to the API reference built the whole schema and froze the app

The OpenAPI document was cached, but only by whoever asked for it first. On the
16.8.0 stand that first request took 140.97s by the server's own slow-request
log, over 2922 paths and 3601 component schemas, and it is built on the event
loop, so the process answered nothing at all for those two and a half minutes.
Every later request came back in 0.53s to 2.38s from the cache, so generating
the document outweighed serialising the 6.75 MB body by roughly 235 to 1, and
the fix belongs at generation rather than at the response.

The schema is now built during the startup lifespan, after the module loader
and the alias mounts that follow it, which are the last routers this process
ever gains. Priming any earlier would cache a document written before ~190
module routers existed, and a schema missing most of the API is worse than a
slow one.

It is not awaited. Starlette accepts no requests until the startup handler
returns, so waiting there would have moved the stall off the first docs
visitor and onto every user of the app, health checks included. It runs on a
worker thread instead, which does not make the build free, since this is
CPU-bound Python holding the GIL, but does make it interruptible: requests are
served throughout rather than not at all. A visitor arriving mid build waits on
the same lock instead of starting a second copy of it.

The override that stamps the DDC markers into info{} checked only whether the
cache was populated, which quietly dropped the invalidation FastAPI does on its
own route counter. Modules mount routers during startup and enable_module
mounts one at runtime, so a module an operator switched on never appeared in
the documentation until the next restart. It rebuilds when the route table
moves now, and the markers survive the rebuild.

Swagger UI itself was loaded from cdn.jsdelivr.net and its favicon from a
second host, so the page rendered as an empty shell on any install without
outbound internet. A self-hosted VPS is the premise here rather than an edge
case, so the two files ship in the wheel, pinned to swagger-ui-dist 5.32.15:
1.74 MB on disk, about 438 KB of the archive once deflated, and nothing added
to dependencies. The docs route is registered by hand to point at them, through
the same get_swagger_ui_html with the same arguments and the same add_route
FastAPI used, so it still carries none of the app-level dependencies.

/api/redoc keeps the stock route and is still blank without a network. That is
another megabyte of vendored bundle for the page the boot banner does not
advertise, so it is recorded beside the assets rather than done here.

test(rbac): fixtures asked for a rank below the verb the test then uses

Seven integration tests in the nightly full suite have been answering 403 with
a "Missing permission" detail. Not one of them is a product defect. Every one
is a fixture handing its caller a role that cannot do what the test goes on to
ask for, and every permission ladder they run into is deliberate. Nothing here
lowers a permission to make a test pass.

Four files share one cause. Each module registers <module>.create at editor and
<module>.delete a rank above it, at manager. Commit c16705d77 fixed a real
order dependency in the tenant isolation fixtures: they had registered the
owning tenant through the public endpoint and counted on it becoming an admin,
which only the very first account on a fresh install gets, so on a shared
database exactly one module won that slot and the rest got a viewer. It
promoted the owner explicitly instead, and chose editor so the caller would
pass verify_project_access on the ownership branch a real tenant uses rather
than on the admin bypass. That reasoning still holds. What it missed is that
these same files also exercise the delete verb, which sits one rank higher, so
test_delete_session, test_delete_visit, test_checklist_and_defective_notice and
test_expiring_soon_widget_and_delete in both source_data and credentials have
been refused ever since. Before that commit they passed only when their module
happened to win the admin slot, so this is a rank that was never really chosen.

The owner is now promoted to manager, the lowest rank that covers every verb
these files use. Manager is not admin, so both the project access check and the
permission check stay real comparisons instead of short circuits, and the
attacker tenant stays editor so the isolation probe still reaches the isolation
check rather than being turned away by a role check first. The helper is
renamed to _promote_to_role because it no longer only makes editors.

The compliance one is a contract change rather than a drift, and it is worth
saying plainly. v5.9.0 put the rule builder write verbs behind
compliance.rule.create and compliance.rule.delete at manager on 2026-05-30, on
the argument that a saved DSL rule runs against project data and a read-only
viewer must not be able to register one. The natural-language helpers were left
open because they have no side effects. The test's synthetic auth payload
carries a subject and a tenant and no role at all, so it was never going to
satisfy that gate. It now names the permission it needs, as an explicit list
rather than a claimed role, so the check does not depend on which modules
happened to populate the shared registry first. The tests that only reach the
ungated helpers still send a caller holding nothing, which is what proves those
endpoints stay open to any signed-in user.

The module routes smoke file still carried the pre-c16705d77 scaffold that
registers a user and assumes it becomes an admin, which c16705d77 itself
flagged as copied across more files and worth retiring. That is also why its
project fixture had been quietly falling through to its listing fallback:
projects.create is an editor verb too. It promotes to editor now, activates the
account so the admin-approve registration mode cannot turn login into a generic
wrong-password error, and asserts the login instead of sending an empty bearer
token when it fails.

Measured locally rather than read off the nightly. On the unmodified tree,
test_credentials_api.py with test_compliance_nl_api.py gave 2 failed, 14
passed, and test_signing_api.py with test_module_routes_smoke.py gave 1 failed,
16 passed, each failing on exactly the credentials.delete,
compliance.rule.create and signing.delete details the nightly reported. All six
files together now give 53 passed, including every cross-project isolation
probe.

The finance one is the exception and it is worth naming. It passes on this
machine whichever order the files run in, because the local cluster hands its
user enough rights, and it fails only where the nightly puts it, on a database
another module has already registered into. That order dependency is the defect
rather than a reason to doubt the 403, which has one cause, a caller below
editor. Pinning the role removes the dependency in either environment.

fix(projects): project cards showed a country-scale terrain patch instead of the site

The card variant painted one static raster tile of shaded relief at zoom 6,
which is the deepest zoom that source has and carries no streets at any zoom.
It looked like a map, so nothing caught it: the request was a 200, the PNG
decoded, and the geography was correct. A construction user opening the
project list wants streets, roads and building footprints, and got landform.

The card stays an image, because the grid renders about twelve cards at once
and twelve live GL contexts streaming vector tiles is why that page never
reached network idle. Instead the new streetThumbnail module renders the
vendored vector style once into an offscreen MapLibre instance, reads the
canvas as a data URL and destroys the context. Renders are serialised through
a module level queue, so there is one transient context at a time even for a
full grid, and results are cached in memory and in session storage on a key
made of rounded coordinates, zoom, pixel size and the effective pixel ratio.

Zoom 15, about three metres per pixel, so a 480 pixel card spans roughly one
and a half kilometres. Measured through a real GL context rather than assumed:
six European cities returned 95 to 235 road segments and 12 to 46 building
footprints each at that zoom, against zero buildings and zero street names at
the retired zoom 6. Deliberately no tighter, because a card's coordinates
often come from geocoding a city and country string, which answers with a
centroid, and zoom 16 or beyond would frame an arbitrary downtown block with
no way for a reader to tell the pin is approximate.

The relief tile is now the fallback rather than the only picture. It is what
the card shows until the snapshot arrives, what it keeps if the snapshot never
arrives, and what it drops back to if a snapshot fails to decode, so a browser
without WebGL still gets a picture rather than an empty box. Every failure
path resolves null instead of throwing, and after two consecutive failures the
module stops trying for the rest of the session rather than spending the
timeout once per card.

Attribution follows the picture. The card previously rendered no credit at
all, so this closes a gap rather than swapping one credit for another: a
vector snapshot is a produced work over ODbL data and carries the OpenStreetMap
and tile provider credit, while the relief fallback carries the Natural Earth
courtesy credit. TILE_ATTRIBUTION_TEXT is derived from the existing

fix(build): backend ignore rules never reached the wheel build

The repo-root .gitignore carried 43 lines anchored at backend/. Git honours
them, so the files they name are untracked and invisible in git status, and
that is why nobody noticed the build disagreed. Hatchling takes its project
root from pyproject.toml, which here is backend/, and its VCS exclusion walks
up from there for the nearest .gitignore, then matches every pattern in it
against paths relative to backend/. A line reading
backend/app/scripts/demo_seed_issues.md was looked for at
backend/backend/app/scripts/demo_seed_issues.md, so all 43 were inert.

Four paths had files on disk and rode into the wheel: an internal defect log
with BLOCKER and BUG entries, two seed_demo_v2 scripts, and 495 entries of a
stale frontend bundle nothing reads, about 11 percent of the archive. Repo
hygiene passed on that wheel because it matches names and none of those four
names was on its denylist. Tag-driven releases are unaffected, they build on
clean runners and the published 16.8.0 carries none of it. The exposed path is
a local twine upload, and make build-wheel also emits an sdist, which has no
exclude list protecting it at all.

The rules move to backend/.gitignore, each anchored with a leading slash so it
means what backend/... meant before, bound to that directory rather than
matched at every depth. Measured over 86395 candidate paths, git ignores
exactly the same 81345 before and after. The wheel goes from 4698 entries to
4200, removing those four and nothing else, and from 96.6 to 85.8 MiB.

Repo hygiene gains the structural question rather than four more names: does
the archive hold a file git does not track. Archive paths map back to repo
paths through the build's own packages and force-include map, read from
pyproject, so a new force-include cannot quietly escape it, and an unmapped
prefix is reported rather than skipped. Untracked build outputs are allowed by
an explicit list with the reason written next to each. It reads sdists too.
Running it on the as-built wheel names 507 files, on a clean-room build none.

Also asserts the wheel fits under PyPI's 100 MiB per-file limit, budgeted at
95 MiB with the arithmetic beside the number. Nothing checked this before, and
the limit is enforced at upload, after the tag is public.

fix(boq): a position answered a different norm depending on which endpoint you asked

Issue #457 shipped in v16.8.1 with the write side done and the headline read
side not. A position was turned into a PositionResponse by two builders, one in
the service and one in the router, and only the service one set norm_id and
norm_work_key. So GET /boqs/{boq_id} returned the provenance and
GET /positions/{position_id} returned null for the same row, with the value
sitting in the column.

The two builders had drifted on six fields, in both directions. The service one
alone set risk_dispersion, price_basis, norm_id and norm_work_key. The router
one alone set cost_item_id and version, so the whole bill read reported the
optimistic concurrency token as 0 on every row, and the two of them read a word
shaped confidence differently, 0.0 against 0.9. Patching one copy would have
left three ways to disagree instead of two, so there is now one builder,
boq.service.build_position_response, and it is the union of what the pair used
to set. The router keeps its own name for it as a thin delegate because that
name reads at its thirteen call sites.

Also corrects a claim that was measured to be false and had spread to three
places: the migration header, the copy helper docstring and the copies test.
The read side does not coalesce column then metadata. The copy path does, in
_norm_provenance_of_copy, which is why a duplicated line keeps its norm, while
both readers of the provenance take the column and only the column. A row that
predates the column reads back null and is repaired only by being copied or by
the backfill in the migration.

perf(boot): the first person to open the app after a restart paid for the route table

FastAPI builds a route's dependant tree, its response field and its operation id
the first time a request reaches route matching, for every route the router
holds, at once and on the event loop. With 190 module routers mounted that
measured 32.1s here against 0.04s for the second request, and it fell on
whichever request arrived first, which is not necessarily an expensive one. GET
/ is a static index.html that touches no database and no dependency and it paid
the same 32s a health check did. Everything else queued behind it: a health
check issued alongside that first request answered 33.9s later, five times the
12s probe deadline the desktop launcher gives each poll, so the splash screen
sat in front of a backend that was alive, listening and reported unreachable.

The work is not avoidable, so it moves to the end of the startup lifespan.
Uvicorn binds the listening socket only after the lifespan returns, so there a
client either cannot connect yet, which every launcher already handles and the
boot log narrates a step at a time, or connects to a process that answers. The
warm-up is a synthetic ASGI request rather than a call into FastAPI internals,
aimed at a path that matches nothing: matching stops at the first route that
matches, so replaying a plausible request would have left every later router
cold, which is the same defect moved somewhere harder to see.

The OpenAPI document is no longer built at boot. It takes 73.0s once the route
table is warm, 118.2s before that change and 133.9s on a first run, for 2923
paths, and a worker thread is not the same as out of the way: with the prime
opted back in and nothing else running, the first request after the port opened
took 64.6s, then 2.3s, then 2.2s, before latency settled at 0.15s. Its only
consumers are /api/docs, /api/redoc and /api/openapi.json and none of them is on
the startup path, so every launch spent a minute of a core, in the window where
somebody is watching a splash screen, filling a cache that install would never
read. Whoever opens those pages now pays the build there, cached and locked
exactly as before, which is what this deployment did until the prime was added.
OE_PRIME_OPENAPI_SCHEMA=1 brings the old behaviour back for an operator serving
the reference pages to other people.

Measured on one Windows machine, warm data directory, cold process, no demo
seed. Before: port accepted at 110.6s, the first /api/health answered 59.3s
later at 169.9s, the first page took 58.7s and arrived at 169.8s, and the
process stayed slow until the background build finished at 229s. After: port
accepted at 143.6s with the route table already built, the first /api/health
took 1.5s, the first page 1.4s, and everything after that 25 to 60ms.

Whether the route state is deferred at all depends on the installed FastAPI, and
both behaviours sit inside the pinned range. 0.136.3 builds it when the route is
registered; 0.141.1, which is what runs here, defers it. The test measures the
installed behaviour rather than trusting a version, and skips with a message
naming the version where the defect cannot exist, so a suite run against the
older release says so instead of passing quietly.

0b6914d9b staged the working copy of backend/app/main.py, and that copy already

after the default class", which is false. The other said the fixed height was
there so the map would not collapse to zero, which was the intent and was being
defeated by the first. Both are corrected rather than deleted, because the next

fix(desktop): the one call that starts the database said nothing while it ran

A Windows install was killed by our own launcher while it was working. The
database was replaying its write-ahead log, reported ready at 377 seconds and
the app server came up at 381, but the launcher gives up on a backend that has
written nothing for 240 and that is where it stopped.

The quiet timer is refreshed by any line the sidecar writes, and there was no
line to refresh it with. pgserver.get_server() is a single call that can run for
the whole length of a replay. It does report what it is doing, but every one of
those reports is a logging call at INFO level, and the embedded cluster is
brought up before the application configures logging, so they go to
logging.lastResort, which passes WARNING and above and drops everything else.
From the launcher the call is simply silent. The recovery heartbeat that exists
for exactly this problem did not help, because it only runs once get_server has
raised, and here it had not raised yet.

So the heartbeat now wraps the call instead of only following it. A ticker
thread reports every fifteen seconds while the call is outstanding, saying how
long it has been waiting, how much of the boot budget is left, and which of the
two phases it can actually observe on disk: a live postmaster owns the data
directory and has not finished starting, or none does and this is still initdb
or the launch itself. No percentage, because nothing here knows one. The call
does not move off the calling thread, since pgserver shells out to pg_ctl and
initdb from there and moving it would risk turning a slow start into a failure.

Raising the timeout was the other option and it is the wrong one. The silence
was as long as the replay, not as long as some number we could pick, so a
slower machine would land in the same place against whatever we raised it to.

A start that genuinely never finishes is still given up on. The ticker stops at
the shared boot deadline, 600 seconds by default, so silence returns there, the
launcher's quiet timer fires 240 seconds later, and both sit well inside the
1200 second ceiling the launcher enforces separately.
