fix(boot): every silent phase of startup now says which one it is

The database bring-up was not the only phase that goes quiet before the port
opens, and fixing only that one would have left the same shape everywhere else.
Building the route table takes 32.1s on a quiet machine and 58.6s under load and
writes a single line when it finishes. The module load, the migrations and
first-run seeding are built the same way. Until the socket is bound the only
evidence a boot is working is what this process writes, and the launcher gives
up on a sidecar that has written nothing for four minutes.

None of those phases is near four minutes today, so this is not a fix for a
failure that is happening. It is the general form of one that did happen: a
phase nobody has measured lately is a phase nobody knows the silence of, and the
limit is the same for all of them. So the requirement is that no phase of a
working boot is silent for longer than the interval, rather than that the phases
measured so far happen to be short enough.

A reporter thread now runs for the whole startup lifespan and names the phase it
is in every fifteen seconds, the same interval the database bring-up uses. It
takes the name from the section headers the boot log already prints, so the
heartbeat and the log can never name different steps. The route-table header was
written inline rather than through that helper, which would have had the
heartbeat reporting the previous phase throughout the longest silent step of the
boot, so it goes through the helper now and a test holds it there.

A thread and not a task on the event loop. The route-table build does not yield
while it runs, which is the measurement that moved it here in the first place: a
health check issued alongside it answered 33.9s later. Anything scheduled on the
loop would be starved during exactly the phase that most needs reporting.

A wedged boot still dies. The budget is per phase rather than per boot, so a
boot that keeps reaching new phases is waited for however long it takes, while a
phase still running after ten minutes stops being vouched for and the launcher's
own four minute rule takes over, well inside the twenty minute ceiling. That
number is four times the whole quiet-machine boot.

This adds output and no work. There is no new step before the port opens and the
time to bind is unchanged.

fix(projects): the height guard mocked a promise as undefined and threw

The card case of theMapShellCarriesOneHeight failed on all three runners
while the other four passed, and the difference between them is that the
card variant is the only one that renders a street snapshot. Its effect
calls renderStreetThumbnail and chains .then onto the result. The mock was a
bare vi.fn(), which returns undefined, so the effect threw a TypeError during
render and the case failed before it could assert anything about a height at
all. The defect the file guards was never in question; the file simply could
not reach the question in one of its five cases.

convenient one. Null is what a real render answers when it cannot produce a
snapshot, so the card stays on its fallback image, which is the state whose
height this file was written to measure.

compiler has nothing to say. A bare vi.fn() satisfies every type in sight,
only the caller knows the value has to be thenable, and the gap therefore
surfaces as a runtime error inside an effect in one case out of five rather
than as anything a build would report.

fix(desktop): showing a file in its folder failed silently behind an ACL

An in-app report captured "Command plugin:shell|open not allowed by ACL"
as the last error of a session. The file manager's "show in folder" button
called the shell plugin's open command, and the desktop capability never
granted that plugin, so every click was refused. Nothing told the user:
the click did nothing and the error went only to the console.

Granting the plugin would have been the one-line fix, and the wrong one.
That command runs whatever the page hands it, with an argument the page
chooses, which is far more than a button that opens a folder needs.

Instead the desktop gets a command of its own, reveal_path_in_os. It
resolves the path, refuses anything outside this installation's data
folder, and opens the folder that holds the file. The rule that decides
what may be opened is a plain function so it can be tested against real
directories on disk rather than invented paths: a file inside resolves to
its parent, a folder resolves to itself, the root resolves to itself, and
a sibling whose name merely starts with the workspace's name is rejected,
which is the case a string prefix gets wrong and a path comparison gets
right.

On the frontend the button now reports both outcomes it can have. A
refusal or a failure raises a toast that names the path and offers to
copy it, so a user who cannot be taken to the file can still get there
by hand. The shell plugin import is gone from the file manager.

The capability description was also corrected; it counted four commands
and there are seven.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(desktop): clear the unpacked copies that forced stops leave behind, and stop forcing them

The Windows sidecar is a one-file bundle, so every start unpacks the whole
program, embedded PostgreSQL included, into a fresh _MEI directory, and only a
bootloader that exits normally removes it again. The launcher ends every stop it
cannot complete cleanly by killing the process tree, and a killed bootloader
removes nothing. The launcher log attached to issue 462 names 84 such
directories over two and a half months, fifteen of its stops ended in the forced
stop, and it had already recorded "No space left on device" eleven days before
the bootloader began failing to decompress numpy and OpenCV, which is where the
report starts. Nothing told the user what was filling the drive.

Three changes, in the order they run.

The bundle now unpacks into %LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenConstructionERP\extract on
Windows rather than into the system temporary folder. _MEI is PyInstaller's
prefix for every program built with it, so in the shared folder a sweep would be
judging other vendors' directories; in a folder we created, every _MEI directory
is ours by construction. Measured with a probe built by PyInstaller 6.21.0, the
version the release workflow pins: the bootloader expands the environment
variable, creates the missing parent chain itself, and removes the _MEI
directory on a clean exit. POSIX keeps the system folder, because that
bootloader takes the string literally and a fixed path would be shared by every
user on the machine. A test reads the spec and fails if the two copies of the
path stop matching.

Before starting the sidecar, the launcher sweeps that folder. A directory goes
only when it is a directory, is named like an extraction, was last written more
than an hour ago, and holds no executable, library or extension module that some
process still has open, which is asked with an exclusive open of each such file.
The same log shows why that last guard is the whole point: a postmaster went on
serving out of _MEI195482 after the directory had lost files under it, failing
on timezonesets 470 times and leaving a crash recovery for every start after.
Removal takes the probed files first, so a holder that appears between the probe
and the removal stops it on the file it holds with everything else still there.
The sweep does not run at all while the embedded cluster's pidfile names a live
process, is bounded to ninety seconds, and never runs on POSIX, where nothing
about an open file can be read off the filesystem. It also measures the free
space on that drive and refuses to start with a message naming the folder and
both numbers when there is less than 512 MB, which is below what the compressed
archive alone occupies; a drive that is merely tight is logged and started
anyway. The bootloader failure that 16.8.1 learned to recognise now carries that
measurement too, so the user is told whether they are looking at a full disk or
at antivirus rather than being handed both.

And the stop that caused the debris is no longer forced so early. The backend
stops its cluster through pg_ctl -w stop, which waits pg_ctl's default of sixty
seconds for the fast shutdown; the launcher used to give the whole backend ten
seconds before killing the tree, so any checkpoint that took longer produced the
write-ahead-log replay it was meant to avoid and an orphaned extraction. It now
waits seventy, polled at 100 ms, so a small cluster still costs a fraction of a
second and the full wait is only ever paid where the alternative is minutes of
replay. A test pins the launcher's wait above the backend's budget.

Starting the sidecar moved off the setup thread, since setup runs before the
event loop paints and a sweep can take a minute, and the spawn now happens under
the same lock the exit path takes, so a window closed during the sweep either
finds the child and stops it or is seen before anything is started.

The splash learns the sweep's sentence in all 38 of its languages, and its
sidecar label reads "Starting the backend" everywhere, which is what the
launcher reports once the sweep is done.

Refs #462

fix(cases): compose-case-layers drifted on every non-Windows checkout

--check composed each playbook in memory and compared it against the
file on disk with strict string equality. The emit step forced every
line ending to CRLF, and the comparison read the disk file with no
normalisation, so the check only ever passed where the working tree
itself carried CRLF.

The committed playbooks are LF: the git blob for each of the eleven
frontend/src/features/cases/data/*.playbook.ts files under
f01-progress-payment has no CR before any newline, and .gitattributes
sets no eol rule for them. A Windows checkout re-adds the CR on
checkout (core.autocrlf), which is why the check passed there and
nowhere else. Checked out on a runner that does not do that
conversion, the composed CRLF text differs from the LF file on every
line, which is what failed on both macos-latest and ubuntu-latest in
CI run 34024347397 (commit 2b261caa8) for all eleven playbooks in the
family.

Fix, verified on an isolated worktree at that commit so the numbers
are not read off a tree with other agents' unrelated edits in it:

- Stop forcing CRLF in the composer output; join with a plain newline,
  matching what is actually committed.
- Normalise the disk side of both the --check comparison and the
  rebuild's change detection (CRLF to LF) before comparing, so the
  check is a content check on any checkout, Windows included, rather
  than one that only balances by accident on one platform.

Hashed the composer's output against the raw git blob with
--no-filters (bypassing this clone's own autocrlf, which would
otherwise quietly re-normalise the comparison and hide the bug). The
unfixed composer's output differs from the blob on all eleven
playbooks; the fixed composer's output is byte-identical to the blob
on all eleven. No playbook file needed regenerating: the shipped data
was already correct and only the check's own comparison was wrong.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

ci(i18n): catch a locale value that loses the accents it used to carry

Ten Czech module names reached main written bare, Rizeni projektu where
the file spells that word Řízení projektu 46 times elsewhere, and every
gate we run stayed green. This is the rule that would have stopped them.

Why the existing one could not. check_locale_stripped_diacritics.py
judges a bare word by what the rest of the file spells, which leaves two
holes. It needs several words in a value before it will speak, so Ukoly
and Schuzky are invisible however plainly wrong they are. And its
cross-namespace rule wants the spellings outside the namespace it is
judging to agree, so damage spread across two namespaces supplies its own
bare form as a second opinion and switches the rule off for exactly the
strings it exists to catch. Both holes were open at once here. The proof
is what happened when the ten were restored: the lane went red on the
repair, naming a help text that had been bare for months, because taking
the damage away took away the second opinion with it.

The new rule asks a question the file cannot answer about itself. Same
key, two commits, no thresholds: if the letters are unchanged and the
combining marks are fewer than the value that key carried a commit
earlier, the accents were removed. Breadth of damage cannot defeat it,
because the evidence is the key's own history rather than its neighbours.

Every commit in the window is read against its own parent, not the two
ends of the window against each other. That is the whole design and it is
not a detail: those ten accents were added after 16.8.3 and removed
before 16.9.0, so the two ends of that window agree and an endpoint
comparison reports nothing at all. Damage that arrives and departs inside
one release is still damage while it is there. A loss a later commit
repaired is not reported, so the rule guards the release rather than
grading history, and the window starts at the most recent tag so it
resets when the next one is cut.

It lives in the commit-history job because it is the second guard that
needs full history, which is what that job's checkout is for. The header
count moves 74 to 76 and its own guard agrees.

Verified before it went in: the selftest covers nine values and a diff,
including a repair and a substituted word, which must both stay silent,
and the Cyrillic short i, which is a combining mark like any other. Run
over v16.8.3 to the commit that shipped the defect it reports all ten and
exits 1. Run over the repaired tree it reports none. It prints how many
changed key lines it read against how many it saw, so a narrowed
population cannot pass itself off as a clean one.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

ci(i18n): the diacritic ratchet read a file no commit contains

hu.ts sits in the locales directory, is in no commit, and is loaded by
nothing, since it is not in SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES. The ratchet read it
anyway and reported 52 stripped strings in it, on every local run, while
CI read a checkout and never saw one of them. So the same script gave two
different answers depending on where it ran, and the local answer was
always red.

That is worse than noise. It cost real time today: the one finding that
mattered, a Czech help text with its accents removed, was printed under
those 52 and read as more of the same. A guard whose local verdict cannot
agree with its CI verdict teaches people to skim it, and a skimmed guard
is not a guard.

Files git does not track are now skipped and named in one line, so the
skip is visible rather than silent. A file that gets committed comes back
under the rule automatically, which is the right moment for it to start
counting.

The baseline is deliberately not re-banked here, though the run says it
could be: the cross-namespace rule now observes 19 where the baseline
records 35. Banking that from this working copy would record a state no
commit has, because the tree holds other people's repairs that are not
committed yet, and CI would then read those strings as new and go red.
The coverage floor was banked from a dirty tree twice this week and that
is exactly what happened. It should be banked from a clean checkout, by
whoever lands the repairs.

feat(bug-report): require a description before a report can be filed

The GitHub issue body carried the template's own placeholder, an HTML
comment reading "describe what you were doing". A comment renders as
nothing on GitHub, so a reporter who pressed submit without editing it
filed an issue that looked deliberately blank, and only learned it was
useless a day later when we wrote back to ask what they had clicked.
The fault was ours rather than theirs: the menu opened GitHub with the
placeholder already in the body, and the only submit control in the
flow belonged to GitHub, where we can disable nothing.

So the guard sits on our side of the hand-off. The menu now asks what
happened in a field of its own, and the two channels that transmit a
written report stay disabled until it is answered, with the minimum
stated above the field rather than discovered on the way out. The web
form and the log download are deliberately not gated, because neither
files a written report and downloading the log is usually the step
before writing one.

The popover becomes a dialog rather than a menu. A textarea is not a
valid child of role="menu" and a screen reader in menu mode cannot
reach it to type, so the role had to change with the field.

Nothing is prefilled, which is the mechanism rather than the result:
the prompt is a placeholder attribute, so an untouched field is empty
and empty cannot be filed. The reporter's own words lead the body, so
the size guard, which keeps the head and trims the tail, is never what
drops them. That text is not passed through the anonymiser, because it
rewrites "invoice 1234567 failed" as "invoice [ID] failed" and would
eat the detail the report exists to carry; the diagnostic half is
still anonymised at capture.

Refs #468

chore(deps): move to PDF.js 6 and i18next 26

Two major bumps written from scratch against the upstream changelogs
rather than taken from anyone's branch: pdfjs-dist 4.10.38 to 6.1.200
and i18next 24.2.3 to 26.4.2, with react-i18next 15.7.4 to 17.0.13
alongside it because 17 is the release that speaks i18next 26.

PDF.js needed real work rather than a version string. Since 5 the
library fetches WebAssembly decoders for JBIG2 and JPEG 2000 images and
an ICC profile for CMYK colour from paths the host has to supply, and a
viewer that does not supply them renders a blank page for precisely the
scanned drawings a takeoff receives most often. Five viewers configured
the worker independently, so all five were one edit away from that. They
now go through a single binding in shared/lib/pdfjs, which is the only
place that loads the library, and a Vite plugin publishes the decoders
under assets/pdfjs/<version>/ while the dev server streams the same
paths out of node_modules. The version segment is load bearing: those
files keep their names across releases and everything under /assets is
served immutable for a year, so without it a future bump would pair a
new worker with a decoder cached from the old one.

The binding takes the legacy build deliberately. The default build of 6
targets the newest browsers and reaches for Promise.withResolvers,
Promise.try, Float16Array and Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed with no
polyfills; legacy carries them and states its floor, which is what the
desktop WebView on an older macOS and a browser in a site office
actually are. It costs about 100 KB.

Two API removals are handled rather than guarded around.
PDFDocumentProxy.destroy is gone, the loading task owns the transport
now, so closePdf is the single spelling of teardown and no viewer can go
on calling a method that no longer exists behind optional chaining while
leaking the parsed document for the life of the tab. And page.render
takes the canvas itself instead of its 2D context.

fix(embedded-pg): the long path refusal quoted a limit that did not decide it

Three installs measured on one Windows host: a pginstall path of 213 characters
refused, 207 refused, and 211 warned and then booted through migration to
healthy. All three were over the same 195, so length did not separate them. What
separated them was PG_VERSION in the data directory, and nothing the user was
shown said so. A reader at 211 concludes the number is wrong, and a reader at 213
shortens to 207 and gets the same refusal for a reason they were never given.

The limit is not a constant. It is 259 minus a separator minus the longest name
below the folder being measured, so 195 for pginstall and 206 for the data
directory. That part was right. The branch was right too, though not for the
reason written next to it: the comment said an existing cluster proves the paths
were once short enough, which is evidence about the data directory while the same
gate also lets through a problem measured on the install directory that a deeper
reinstall can have changed. What actually licenses it is that the deep names are
needed to create the cluster, since initdb derives its support directory from its
own executable and scans the timezone tree, and a postmaster attaching to a
cluster that exists opens neither.

So the fix is the message, not the rule. Refusing the 211 machine would break an
install measured as working to make the arithmetic look tidy. The shared
paragraph now says what needs the room instead of calling the number a maximum
the code itself overrides, the two branches say which outcome they are taking and
why, and the checklist line names creating the database. One piece of advice was
useless as well: with both directories too long the user was told to move the
install, and got a second refusal with a different number once they had; the
message now names the data directory too.

The tests over this all pinned one path 62 characters over the limit, where every
branch looks alike, so they would have passed whichever input the branch read.
Replaced with a matrix that moves each input one step, at the limit and one over,
with and without a cluster, plus the three field lengths held to one answer per
cluster state. Checked against a mutant carrying the old wording: the new test
fails and all 27 older ones pass.

fix(desktop): the silence limit was counting a phase in which nothing can speak

The launcher gives up on a backend that has said nothing for four minutes, and
the clock behind that limit started the moment the sidecar was spawned rather
than the moment it first wrote something. On Windows the sidecar is a one-file
bundle, so every launch unpacks the whole program, embedded PostgreSQL
included, before a line of our own code runs, and the bootloader writes nothing
while it does that. An unpack has been measured at 302 seconds on a published
build against a limit of 240, so a slow or nearly full drive was enough to have
a start that was working perfectly abandoned before it had begun, and then
reported to the user as a backend that had stopped responding.

Silence is only evidence about a process that has spoken, so the clock now
starts at the first line and there is nothing to measure before that. This is
not the limit moved to a bigger number, it is a measurement with no input yet
being left unmade. Nothing that was guarding anything is lost, because a bundle
that cannot unpack writes to stderr and exits, and the termination handler
reports that at once and by name, which is what a full drive already looked
like in the field. The twenty minute ceiling still bounds the whole start, so
an unpack that never finishes is still given up on, and it is now told apart
from a slow backend in the log and in the message the user sees, since the two
have different causes and different remedies.

The decision moved into startup_give_up, which is pure and takes the two facts
the wait actually has, so the three ways a start can end are written down as
data in the tests instead of being reproduced by waiting minutes in front of a
real backend.

fix(tax): Russia charges 22 percent VAT from 2026-01-01

The standard rate rose from 20 to 22 on 1 January 2026 and the seed file still
shipped a single open window at 20 dated from 2019-01-01, so every Russian
document dated in 2026 has been priced two points low for eight months.

The 20 percent window is closed at 2025-12-31 and a 22 percent window is added
beside it. The old rate is not edited in place. That would leave one open
window running from 2019 and silently re-price every Russian document back to
2019 at 22 on its next read, which is the failure the date windows exist to
prevent.

Both windows keep is_default true. That is the Israeli shape rather than the
Romanian one, and here it is a constraint rather than a preference: the NDS_RED
reduced row is open ended from 2004-01-01, so it is in force alongside every
standard window. Unflagging the closed row the way Romania unflags its 19
percent one would leave two unflagged country-wide rows in force for every date
from 2019 to 2025, which _country_wide_standard cannot choose between and
_is_earlier_period cannot rescue because that path needs exactly one row in
force. Russia would answer default_rate_not_in_force, no rate at all, for six
years of documents. Because the flag does not move, tax_window_supersede
carries already-seeded installs forward with no new code, so RU/NDS joins its
pinned population instead of getting a repair module of its own.

The reduced rate did not change. NDS_RED stays at 10 percent, open ended, and a
test asserts that it did not move rather than leaving it unexamined.

test_tax_tables_do_not_drift named the rest of the edit set rather than leaving

the RU stack in boq/markup_templates.py. On that last one only the percentage
on the tax line moved. The step order, the apply_to and the overhead, profit
and contingency figures are untouched.

Display only, named here so a later reader does not mistake them for the

fix(release): the signed manifest named its assets without checking their bytes

Two runs of Release Signing share one release by design, and `gh release
upload --clobber` replaces an asset in place. On v17.0.2 the dispatched run
wrote and signed a SHA256SUMS over the SBOMs it had just attached, the
workflow_run run regenerated both SBOMs and clobbered them at 06:49:51, and
for the 63 seconds until the second manifest landed at 06:50:54 the release
served a manifest stating the wrong hash for two of its own twelve assets.
Every check was green throughout, because the confirmation asks whether each
asset is named in the manifest and never whether the hash beside the name is
the hash of the published bytes. A run that dies between those two uploads
does not close the window at all, and the confirmation runs on `always()`, so
it would have reported full coverage over a release that was permanently
wrong.

Both generators stamp the moment they ran into the document they emit, so the
same tag inventoried twice produces two files that differ. Two fields carry
the whole difference and only two, the components and dependencies came back
byte identical across both runs. The timestamp is the obvious one.
serialNumber is the one that hides: it is a fresh UUID per generation and two
UUIDs are the same length, so the v17.0.2 pair were both 174222 bytes with the
same 141 components and still hashed apart. Both are now derived from the
release rather than from the clock, the timestamp from the tag's own commit
date and the serial from a UUIDv5 over the release and the filename.
Normalising the two recorded generations of each SBOM makes them byte
identical, which is a measurement rather than a claim. With that in place the
second run regenerates a file the release already carries and no longer
clobbers it, so the delete before upload that killed the dispatched run on
v15.6.0 is not spent on a file whose bytes did not move.

Reproducibility alone would not protect an asset that genuinely changed, so
the confirmation now compares every entry in the published manifest against
the digest GitHub reports for that asset. It needs no download. It prints how
many entries it compared next to its verdict and refuses when that number is
zero, because an empty comparison finds no mismatch and would otherwise print
the same words as a manifest that checked out.

The pinning is inline rather than a script under scripts/, because the SBOM
job checks out the tag and a script added to main today does not exist in the
tree of a tag cut before today. It rewrites the emitted JSON rather than
passing a generator flag, because neither generator is pinned in the install
step above it.

fix(i18n-foundation): India's shipped 2026 festivals were not on their tithis

Six of the sixteen dates in India's 2026 calendar are lunisolar, and all six
were wrong. Holi and Diwali also contradicted the curated _HINDU_HOLIDAYS
table that app.core.calendar serves, so the same calendar answered
differently depending on which source a caller reached.

The dates were not merely off by a day. Every Hindu festival is fixed to a
tithi, the interval in which the Moon to Sun elongation advances 12 degrees,
and each seeded date fell on a tithi that cannot carry its festival. Holi is
Phalguna Purnima, a full moon, and 17 March 2026 is Krishna Chaturdashi, two
days before a new moon and 14 days from the nearest full moon. Diwali is
Kartik Amavasya, a new moon, and 10 November 2026 is Shukla Dwitiya. The
seed was also inconsistent with itself: it placed Maha Shivaratri, which is
the day before a new moon, seven days before Holi, which is a full moon, and
that gap is fifteen or sixteen days in every year there has ever been.

The corrected dates were computed from the lunar and solar longitudes rather
than copied from the table, so the table is corroborated rather than assumed.
Maha Shivaratri 15 February, Ram Navami 26 March, Dussehra 20 October,
Diwali 8 November and Guru Nanak Jayanti 24 November each follow from the
defining tithi covering the hour of observance on exactly that day. Holi is
the one that needs the convention as well as the arithmetic: Purnima runs
from 2 March 17:58 to 3 March 17:10 IST, but Bhadra covers the whole of the
2 March evening and clears only at 05:30 on 3 March, which puts Holika Dahan
on 3 March and Holi on 4 March, the curated table's value.

The seven fixed and Islamic and Christian dates in the same calendar were
checked and are all correct, so this is a lunisolar defect and not a bad
calendar.

feat(einvoice-clearance): the regime registry had nowhere to say when an obligation starts

The registry could describe what a country does to an invoice and not whether it
does it to this taxpayer yet. Thirteen fields, and not one of them could hold a
date, a phase, a threshold or a scope, so nothing we ship could tell an operator
when their obligation begins. The two halves of that obligation commonly start
years apart, and a mandate usually arrives in waves keyed to turnover rather than
all at once, which is why one date would not have been enough either.

Commencement is now a tuple of phases, one per obligation and wave, each naming
the source it was read from and the date it was read. Those two are required
arguments rather than defaulted ones, because a date a business plans around that
nobody can trace back to the authority that set it cannot be rechecked and cannot
be aged. legal_status separates a date in force from one enacted but future and
from one only announced, which is the difference between answering "not yet" and
answering "no". An entry level scope says who the regime covers today.

The taxonomy also had three classes and no way to describe a country that does
two of them at once, which several do. regime keeps naming the act that decides
what a successful submission means, additional_regimes names the others, and
regime_class reads hybrid when there is more than one. It is derived and not a
fourth member of REGIMES on purpose: the terminal state of a submission is
decided by the act it was made under, and hybrid would leave that undecidable.

Mexico's cancellation deadline is the fiscal year of issue, which the old comment
correctly called a calendar and then stored as a count of days anyway. It now
declares its basis. Brazil's note claimed 24 hours was the shortest window and
therefore the safe one to warn on; states depart from the federal figure in both
directions, so that rationale was false on its own terms and the field can hold
neither a sub-day window nor a per state one.

All of it is additive. Every existing entry reads as it did with the new fields
absent, and the meta endpoint keeps every key it carried.

We ship holiday dates twice, once computed in app/core/calendar.py and once
stated as data in work_calendars.json, and nothing put the two side by side.
That is how Japan's Sports Day shipped hardcoded to 14 October while the seed
carried the correct second Monday, and how India's seeded festivals came to

regardless of which side is wrong, because at most one of them can be right and
both are reachable.

and each difference is recorded with its exact date set, a reason, and which
side is authoritative. Recording the set rather than exempting the country makes

way, and it also fails if somebody fixes an existing difference, so the table
cannot quietly describe a tree that has moved on.

The seventeen countries with no engine function are named in the output rather
than skipped in silence, with their seeded date counts, because a gate whose
denominator is invisible can be satisfied by narrowing it. Floors on the seeded
and bound populations stop that too.

fix(i18n): name sorts ignored the language the reader picked

Sorting text is language dependent and JavaScript's defaults are not. A bare
localeCompare(b) with no locale argument sorts in the runtime's default locale,
which a browser takes from the browser and the OS, not from the language picker
in this app. So a reader who chose Swedish while running an English browser got
English collation on Swedish names. German files Aerger under A; Swedish and
Danish file it after Z; Czech sorts ch as one letter after h; Turkish has its
own i. One comparator that knows none of that gets some of them wrong by
construction.

Adds shared/lib/collator.ts as the single answer to "in what order does this
reader expect names", built on one cached Intl.Collator per locale rather than
a fresh one per comparison, and routes 31 call sites in 28 product files
through it: the project and estimate lists, assemblies, the cost catalogue and
its variants, documents, resources and the schedule resource picker, global
search, playbooks and their step targets, takeoff groups and the DWG takeoff
page, broker and buyer names, analytics, approval routes, the BIM property
search, the inbox, the markup aggregator, the property development compliance
and pricing pages, retrieval, tax rate resolution, the clearance registration
form, and the alphabetical mode in How It Works, which sorts labels that are
already translated. numeric collation comes with it, so Block 2 now precedes
Block 10.

Not every localeCompare is a defect and the count of them is not the count of
defects. Dates held as ISO strings, ids, codes and currency tags are sorted
with the same call and are correct that way, so they are out of the gate's
population by construction. countries.ts is left ordering by the English name
because that is what it documents and what its picker shows.

The gate prints its population beside its verdict and was driven red in both
directions before being kept: red when a converted sort is reverted, and red
when its own input goes empty. Its first version was green because the
classifier read only the property access, so it could not see
typeLabel(a).localeCompare(typeLabel(b)); widening it to name shaped function
calls immediately found a real buyer name sort that had been missed.

The 31 conversions are symmetric with 31 removed bare localeCompare calls, file
by file, so nothing was routed through the collator that was not taken off the
old path.

fix(i18n): the week started on Monday for readers whose week does not

Four surfaces drew a week and each answered the first day of it on its own.
Three of them answered Monday unconditionally, so the accommodation calendar,
the daily diary and the resource planner rendered one grid for all 42 offered
languages. The fourth, field reports, did read the real value out of Intl and
then threw most of it away: it collapsed the answer to firstDay === 7 ? 0 : 1,
which is right for the 40 languages that start on Monday or Sunday and wrong
for the two that do not. Arabic and Persian start the working week on
Saturday and got Monday, and the region map underneath that branch listed
Arabic as Sunday, a third answer for one language that nothing could reach
because it only ran on engines without weekInfo.

shared/lib/weekStart.ts is now the one place that answers it, in the same
sense and for the same reason as intlLocale.ts next to it: a leaf module that
imports nothing, so the shipped function can be run on its own, with the two
current-language wrappers at the bottom the only part that needs i18next and
React.

Two numbering conventions meet in this problem and mixing them is how the
defect returns, so each has a name and the conversion is an exported function
rather than an inline ternary at a call site. CLDR and Intl number Monday 1
through Sunday 7 and never use 0; getDay and date-fns number Sunday 0 through
Saturday 6. weekStartFor speaks CLDR because that is what the data source
speaks, and weekStartsOnFor converts at the boundary.

weekInfo is read in both of its spellings, as a property and as getWeekInfo(),
because it shipped as one and was respecified as the other. Reading only the
one this Node happens to have would send every other engine down the fallback
and answer Monday for the whole world without a word.

The fallback table is exported so the test can assert it agrees with ICU for
every offered language rather than sitting there as a statement of intent
nobody re-reads. That check is what makes the table a checked copy instead of
a fourth answer, and it is the assertion that would have caught the Arabic row.

fix(i18n): a decimal comma was read four different ways outside the BOQ grid

A European estimator types 48,60 and 1.234,56; an American types 48.60 and
1,234.56; both have to land on the same stored number. The BOQ grid has known
this for years and runs every typed cell through one strict parser. Nothing
else did. The same typed string arrives on every costing surface, and those
surfaces each answered it their own way: parseFloat, which reads 1,5 as 1 and
throws the half away without a word; a bare Number, which returns NaN and then
meets a || 0 that turns the reader's number into zero; replace(',', '.'),
which is right for 48,60 and wrong for 1.234,56 because String.replace with a
string pattern swaps only the first match; and in some places no parse at all,
with the raw string posted straight into a Decimal field.

None of those fail loudly. Each produces a finite, plausible, wrong number,
which is the worst way for a cost figure to be wrong, and it happened in the
languages most of our markets write in.

So parseDecimal moves up to shared/lib as the one grammar for the whole
product and 24 surfaces are routed through it: the CVR cost heads, the
withholding tax gross, allowance drawdowns, waste factors, the price index,
labour rates, the cost model, equipment work orders and damage reports, the
takeoff calibration dialog, the payment application portal, project settings,
the payment clock, change intelligence apportionment, the MoC cost impact, the
scenario dialog and the batch value bar. Fields become text inputs with
inputMode="decimal" so the mobile keypad is still the numeric one, because a
number input drops the comma keystroke before any code can see it.

Two things the parser now does that it did not:

It folds the non-Latin digits our own formatter emits. Intl.NumberFormat takes
the numbering system from the locale, so bn renders 1234.56 with Bengali
digits and fa with extended Arabic-Indic ones, U+066B for the decimal point
and U+066C for the group separator. Copying a figure off the screen and
pasting it back is a real path, and the parser used to reject a number the
product itself had written a moment earlier. The fold is deliberately limited
to arab, arabext and beng, the systems our formatter can produce, so the
accepted set stays known.

And the round trip is now a test rather than an assumption. Display and entry
are mirrors and only display was ever checked. A locale whose formatter writes
1.234,56 and whose parser reads 1.234 is not a formatting bug or a parsing
bug, it is the pair being wrong together, and neither half alone can see it.
The locale list is read from SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES rather than written out, so
the next language we ship is covered on the day it ships. 1000 is excluded on
purpose and asserted separately: a dot-grouping locale writes it 1.000, which
is also how a person writes one point zero zero zero, and that collision
cannot be resolved from the string alone.

fix(variations): a pill named the linked record and then opened the register

fix(variations): three payloads the screen sent dropped fields the API accepts

The variations workspace is where a change is priced, agreed and promoted, and
at three of its boundaries the screen sent a smaller payload than the endpoint
behind it reads. Each one is silent: the request succeeds, the record comes
back, and the field nobody filled is simply absent afterwards.

Seeding a bill. createVariationRequestBOQ was called with no argument at all,
so the endpoint that seeds a variation bill from named contract lines and
estimating positions was reachable only over the API. Every bill opened from
the product itself started empty and carried no provenance, which is the one
thing a variation bill is later argued about. A source picker now collects it.

Approving a request. The approve route takes the amount that was agreed and
the reason for it, and the screen posted only a shared notes box, so the
agreed value fell back to the requested one. That is exactly the inheritance
the agreed-value column was added to stop. The decision panel that collects
the amount now builds the payload, and the EoT decision keeps the plain notes
box it always had, which is why that state stays where it is.

Promoting to an order. convertVRToVO takes the contract the order amends and
nothing set it, so an order promoted through this screen reached no contract
and never posted against one. The promote card asks for it.

Behind that, submission now keeps the bill and not only its total.
v3317_variation_agreed_value froze which bill was in front of the approver and
at what figure. A total is the right thing to agree against and the wrong
thing to defend a price with: the bill goes on being revised after submission,
which is how a variation gets negotiated, and once it moves nothing can say
which lines at which quantities the frozen figure was made of. The BOQ module
already keeps point in time copies for its own version history, so submission
writes one and the request names it.

The column is nullable with no backfill and carries no foreign key, for the
same reason submitted_boq_id carries none. A request submitted before this has
no copy of its bill and nothing can reconstruct one; a request with no bill has
nothing to copy. Both read back NULL and mean it. The snapshot is deleted with
its bill, and the request's record of what was submitted must not block that
delete or be nulled by it in a way the request cannot tell from never having
had a bill: the id stays and the reader that follows it learns the bill is
gone. The ADD COLUMN is guarded the way this tree guards create_table, because
the boot path runs create_all before an operator can run alembic by hand, and
an unguarded add raises DuplicateColumn that rolls back every later revision
with it.

chore(deps): move PDF.js to 6.2.108 for the advisory on 6.1

GitHub reports one high severity advisory against pdfjs-dist on the default
branch and 6.2.108 is the first release past it. Written here rather than
taken from the bot's branch, as every dependency change in this tree is.

The version is the whole change, and the reason it needs a commit message at
all is the thing that could have gone wrong silently. The build plugin that
copies the JBIG2 and JPEG2000 decoders and the ICC profiles out of the package
reads the version from node_modules and then does `if (!existsSync(dir))
continue` over the wasm and iccs directories. A release that moved those under
build/ or legacy/ would trip that guard, emit zero files, log nothing and fail
no test, and the first anybody would hear of it is a scanned drawing that will
not render for a user.

So it was checked at the artefact rather than at the manifest. In 6.2.108 wasm,
iccs, cmaps and standard_fonts are all still at the package root, and a full
frontend build puts dist/assets/pdfjs/6.2.108/ on disk carrying eleven wasm
files including jbig2.wasm and its no-wasm fallback, and the ICC profile. The
comment in pypi-publish.yml that names the version those guards were verified
against is moved on with it, because a dated claim that nobody re-dates is how
the next move gets missed.

fix(ui): four surfaces pushed the whole page sideways on a phone

A row that cannot fit has to be told what to do about it, and four of ours
were not, so at a 390px viewport the page itself scrolled horizontally rather
than the thing that was too wide.

The tab strip is one nowrap row, so a register with many tabs dragged the page
with it: finance reached 909px of page scroll with eight tabs and change
intelligence reached 1672px with sixteen. It scrolls itself now. Only the
underline variant is scoped, because the pill and segmented variants lay out
differently and were not measured.

The page header's action cluster carried shrink-0, which is right while the
buttons share a row with the subtitle and also meant the box was never
narrowed to its container, so its own flex-wrap could never fire. Seven action
buttons laid out in one 668px line. A max-width cap lets the wrap happen and
is inert whenever the row already fits.

The contacts grid had no grid-template-columns below the sm breakpoint, so the
implicit single track was auto-sized and took the cards' min-content instead
of the container: 704.719px of track inside a 360px column. grid-cols-1
resolves to minmax(0, 1fr), which caps the track and lets the truncating
fields inside each card do their job. This is the one that looks cosmetic and
is not.

The geo hub header is a single nowrap row whose picker cluster alone is 811px.
It wraps now, and the pickers stack onto extra rows instead of running off the
side.

Every one of these is inert at desktop widths by construction: wrapping and
scrolling engage only when the row cannot fit, and the width cap only binds
when something is already too wide.

What is not in this commit, said plainly rather than left to be discovered:
the smoke test that asserts no horizontal scroll measures exactly one page,
the dashboard, so none of these four was ever in its population. Widening that
test needs a browser run against a live app, which is a separate change with a
separate verdict.

fix(hse): incident-keyed mutators skipped the project check

Six routes in hse_advanced enforced the caller's role and nothing about which
project the row belonged to. Investigations and the slim corrective actions
carry no project_id of their own, they hang off a safety incident, and only
the read routes resolved the owning project through that link. Row level
security is a no-op here, so verify_project_access is the only boundary
between projects and its absence was the whole hole: any authenticated editor
could overwrite an investigation of a project it cannot otherwise see, a
manager could complete or abandon it, and both creates would file a record
against a foreign project's incident, each addressed by UUID alone.

The mutators now resolve the project the way their read siblings already do,
through the module's own _guard_project helper, and they do it before the
service call so an immutability or FSM conflict cannot confirm that a foreign
row exists. The incident lookup moved out of investigation_project_id into
HSEAdvancedService.incident_project_id so the corrective actions can share it.

The new integration suite drives all six routes across two tenants and carries
an owner-side control for each, run by a plain manager on a project it owns.
Without those controls a mistyped prefix would answer 404 to every probe and
the suite would read as a pass.

docs(ci): the concurrency note claimed main gets a verdict again

The note under the concurrency group explains why cancel-in-progress is not
an unconditional true, and reads as though the fix closed the problem. It did
not close it. Remeasured today, 8 of the last 20 runs of this workflow on main
were cancelled.

The setting is doing exactly what it says. It governs the run that is already
executing, and it says nothing about the run waiting behind that one. A
concurrency group holds at most one pending run, so a third push evicts the
pending one, and with a dozen commits landing in an hour that is most of them.
The evidence is that the cancelled runs carry zero jobs and a run_started_at
equal to their created_at, which is what eviction from the queue looks like
rather than a stop mid-flight.

What is guaranteed is therefore narrower than the note implied: the newest
push gets a verdict once the pushes stop, not every push. That is enough for
how we actually read this workflow, on a settled head before a tag, and it is
not enough for anyone reading a per-commit result. The remedy, if it is ever
needed, is the sha in the group rather than a change to the line below, and
the note says so along with what that costs, because the previous version of
this comment sent a reader to the wrong line.

fix(estimate-basis): the freshest price base was picked by string order

BOQ.base_date is free text because a quantity surveyor states a price
base in whatever precision the pricing carries: a day, a month, a
quarter or a year. The basis of estimate picked the project's price base
with SELECT max(base_date), which ranks the strings, and those strings
do not sort in the order their dates run. "Q" is above every digit, so
"2026-Q1" outranked "2026-12-01", while "2026-01" sorted below both. A
project whose bills mix shapes quoted whichever bill was spelt luckiest,
and the value goes into a document the client reads as "prices are
current as of".

Both readers, the seeded basis in seed.py and the derived pricing base
date in the service, now rank the bills through latest_base_date in
app.modules.boq.base_date. It reads each stated value into the day it
falls on, the same reading the tax point already uses, picks the bill
whose day is latest and returns that bill's text as the estimator wrote
it. The boq_id narrowing in the service is kept. The ranking itself is
already asserted in the unit test for the helper; the new PG test adds
that the real query, against a real database, returns the December bill
over the quarter label, the November month over a quarter and a year,
and None when no bill states a basis at all.

feat(variations): a traced line could not say whether it adds, removes or changes its source

Issue #435. The trace on a line of a variation's bill recorded where the line
came from, the schedule-of-values line it affects or the estimating position it
was priced from, and nothing about what the variation does to that source. A
line citing contract line 020 at 30 m3 could be extra quantity of the same
item, a re-measure down from 40, or the whole item omitted, and the three price
differently: an omission is money coming off the contract. That distinction is
what makes an omission price correctly, and the bill had no column for it.

Each trace row now carries a change kind, one of added, removed or modified,
stated by the estimator on both writers, the seeding of a bill from named
sources and the trace PUT, and reset to added when a trace is cleared. It is
never inferred from the sign of the quantity, because a negative quantity is
consistent with an omission and with a typing error and only a person knows
which. A line with no trace row is added scope, and the column's server
default is added for the same reason, so a row that predates it reads the same
way as no row rather than as a claim nobody made.

The bill view splits the direct cost by kind, three subtotals and their sum as
the net, valued line by line with the same helper the bill's own totals use so
the three add up to the bill's direct cost rather than to a figure beside it.

A third validation rule, variations.change_kind_matches_numbers, reports a
removed line carrying a positive quantity, an added line carrying a negative
one, and a removed or modified line that names no contract line to remove or
modify. It is a warning, like its two siblings, and it corrects nothing: the
contradiction is a person's statement disagreeing with a person's figures. The
messages ship in the four locales of the validation bundle.

Migration v3322_variation_trace_change_kind adds the column, inspector guarded

beside a price_base that really is USD, with nothing on the row or on the

currency disagrees with the matrix's. A plot's money is read in its own
stamp, else the development's, else the project's, which is the fallback the
module already declares for a blank currency. A blank on either side is not a
mismatch, so a development with no currency anywhere is priced exactly as
before. The detail names the matrix, both currencies and the plots concerned,

whose currency disagrees with its account: a write that would mis-stamp money
is refused, not labelled. The stock cost fix (1365566e4, v3304) labelled
instead, and the difference is what the number is. A stock average is rolled
forward from receipts that cannot be refused, because the goods are on the
shelf, so the honest move there was to label the average and withdraw it

BOQService.update_position re-derives unit_rate as the sum of quantity times
unit_rate over the resource rows whenever an edit changes them. That is right

The AI estimator stores rows whose quantity is factor times the position
quantity, its fallback stores allowance rows whose quantity is the position
quantity itself, and positions booked before the estimator read the catalogue
norm hold the position quantity on every row. All of them price correctly at
apply time, because the rate is written from the chosen candidate, and the

factor_estimated, or an estimator-booked position whose rows hold factor times
the position quantity means the sum is not a unit rate, so the stored rate
stands. The position is stamped with the reason and the rate it kept, gets a
boq_quality warning marker in the shape the duplicate-content check uses, and
a new rule, boq.resources.unit_rate_not_rederived, carries the stamp and the
estimator's own flags into the validation report. Nothing is repaired: the rows
are left as they were for a person to review. A buildup that can price the
line, which is the shape a re-derivation writes back, still re-derives exactly
as before, and a trusted edit clears a stale stamp.

The pure predicates live in a new module so the service, the rule and the
review path that follows read one definition of an untrusted buildup. The
rule's message keys follow in the validation message files; until they land
the bundle renders its humanised fallback and logs the exact key.

fix(property-dev): two brokers without a tenant could share a licence number

The brokers table has carried uq_oe_property_dev_broker_tenant_license on
(tenant_id, license_number) since brokers shipped, and it reads as if a licence
number were unique per tenant. tenant_id is nullable and SQL treats every NULL
as distinct from every other, so two brokers with no tenant and the same
licence never collided. Single-tenant installs, which is the default and every
demo, keep tenant_id NULL on every broker, so there the licence number was
unique on paper only. test_broker_license_uniqueness, which registers without a
tenant, got 201 for the duplicate and has been red since the constraint was
written.

Three parts, one rule. The service now looks the licence up in the caller's
tenant cohort before inserting and answers 409 when it is taken, and it also
maps the unique violation from a concurrent insert to the same 409 instead of a
500. The model declares a partial unique index on license_number WHERE
tenant_id IS NULL, so a fresh volume gets it from create_all; the constraint
keeps covering brokers that have a tenant. The lookup helper returns the oldest
match instead of raising on several, because installs that predate the index
may hold duplicates already.

Migration v3323_broker_license_unique_without_tenant adds the same index to a database managed by
alembic. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX cannot be NOT VALID: over existing duplicates it
fails and rolls back the whole upgrade run, so the revision first asks whether
the NULL-tenant cohort already shares a licence number. If it does, the index is
not created and the duplicates are written to the migration log, one licence
per line with the broker ids that hold it. Nothing is merged or deleted, each of
those brokers carries agreements and accruals of its own and which one to keep
is not a decision a migration should take. Such an install stays protected on
the write path by the 409, and the guarded upgrade can be re-run once the
operator has resolved the rows. Note that the boot-time index heal skips
partial indexes, so an embedded install that stamps alembic instead of running
it relies on the service check alone; that check is the enforcement, the index
is the backstop.

fix(validation): an outlier rate was a fixed number in no currency

boq_quality.unrealistic_rate compared every unit rate against 100,000 and
every total against 10,000,000, and boq_quality.rate_vs_benchmark compared a
rate per m2 against 10,000 and per m3 against 50,000. None of the four figures
named a currency, so they were euros on a German bill and rupiah on an
Indonesian one. A unit rate of 100,000 is a fortune in EUR and about six euros
in IDR, which is why the two rules fired on every line of every Indonesian,
Vietnamese, Korean or Hungarian bill and never on a real outlier in a strong
currency below the same nominal figure. The median-based unit_rate_in_range
rule was already correct and is untouched.

The thresholds are now written once in a reference currency and scaled into
the bill's currency when the rule runs. The reference is EUR because the rate
register in app.modules.fx is quoted against EUR in every layer (the ECB feed,
the bundled seed and the resolved rate map), so one lookup and no rebase
reaches any bill currency, and because EUR is what the figures were written
in: a EUR bill keeps exactly the thresholds it always had. Scaling goes
through the FX bridge the assemblies module already uses, so the project's
own typed exchange rates win over the register, the register degrades from
the applicable rate set to the seed, and every row records which source and
which rate priced it.

When no source can price the bill's currency, or the bill names none, the
rules no longer judge those positions against the reference. They emit one
row per currency in the shape the engine gives a rule it could not execute:
INFO, DIAGNOSTIC, is_engine_error, saying in words how many positions were
not assessed and why. Every consumer already keeps such rows out of the
findings and the score, so the report neither claims a pass it did not check
nor charges the bill for a rate table it does not control. A row carrying no
money still passes in any currency. Amounts in messages are formatted with
the currency's own minor units, so a rupiah threshold shows no decimals.

The currency is read from the position first, then the bill header the
estimate audit supplies, then the project record the shared payload builder
carries, then the run metadata. The not-assessed messages and suggestions
are added to the en, de, es and ru validation message catalogues under both

fix(validation): a 1 percent broker commission was flagged as 100 percent

PropDevBrokerCommissionRateWithinBounds checks that a percent agreement's rate
sits between 0.1 and 15 percent. It tried to accept two notations at once,
2.5 and 0.025 for the same rate, by reading any value up to 1 as a fraction.
So an agreement at 1 percent became a rate of 1, that is 100 percent, and
failed; 0.5 percent became 50 percent and failed too.

Nothing else in the module stores that field as a fraction. The agreement
schema caps pct at 0 to 100 and the ladder tier pct the same, the accrual
divides by 100 (compute_commission_amount), Broker.default_commission_pct is
Numeric(5,2) capped at 100 and the UI prints it through fmtPercent, and this
rule is the only rule in the property_dev set that reads a percent at all.
So 0.025 in this field means 0.025 percent, a data entry error the rule
exists to catch, not a notation to be tolerated. The rule now reads pct as
the percentage it is and checks 0.1 <= pct <= 15. A new test pins 1 percent
and 0.5 percent as passing and 0.025 as the one agreement flagged.

This is what turned test_rule_commission_passes_with_valid_percent red. The
rule validates every agreement scoped to the development or broker-wide, the
test suite shares one PostgreSQL cluster per session, and the broker test
module leaves a broker-wide agreement at 1 percent behind. Run alone the test
was green; run after that module it failed on an agreement it never created,
and the failure was the rule's, not the test's.

fix(api): build the OpenAPI document on a worker thread so health keeps answering

Found by the fresh-install test of the 17.0.2 wheel. The first request for
/api/openapi.json, which is what opening /api/docs or /api/redoc sends,
took 52.5s on an idle 16.9.0 install and 113.6s and 139.7s on two 17.0.2
installs, and while it ran the process answered nothing else: a GET
/api/health issued during one of those builds came back after 71.5s,
exactly when the build ended, against 0.05s at any other time. The health
endpoint is what the desktop shell polls to decide whether a backend is
alive, so one visitor opening the API reference could make the shell
conclude the backend had hung.

The cause is the route FastAPI registers for openapi_url in setup(): an
async handler that calls app.openapi() inline, so the whole build runs on
the event loop. The startup prime is off by default for good reasons
recorded next to it, which leaves this request as the place the build
happens, and it happened on the loop.

create_app now swaps that route, in place so it keeps its position ahead of
the frontend catch-all, for a handler that runs the build and the 6.75 MB
serialisation on a worker thread and returns the same bytes FastAPI would
have sent, root_path servers included. _custom_openapi keeps its cache and
its lock, so concurrent first callers still share one build and every
later request is served from the cache in about a second. A thread does
not escape the GIL: the loop is slowed while a build runs, not stopped,
and a request queued behind the build no longer waits for its end. The
build is logged with its duration and path count when it happens.

Measured on this stand with the tree served from a fresh --no-demo data
directory: the first document request took 172.2s to build 2927 paths, and
GET /api/health polled once a second throughout answered all 74 times with
200, median 0.81s, p90 1.04s, worst 3.96s, against 0.05s to 0.10s with no
build running. Before the change the same poll got one answer, after the
build ended.

Tests use a small FastAPI app whose build blocks on an event: the route is
replaced in place and only where openapi_url exists, the body is byte
identical to FastAPI's own JSONResponse, a root_path is added to servers
exactly as FastAPI does without touching the cached document, the build
runs on a thread other than the loop's, and health is answered while the
build is still running, with FastAPI's default route kept as the control
case that waits for the build to end.

i18n(uz): eighteen values wrote the Latin marks as plain ASCII quotes

Uzbek Latin uses two marks and neither of them is the ASCII quote. U+02BB, the
turned comma, rides on o and g to make the separate letters oʻ and gʻ, and
U+02BC is the tutuq belgisi, the glottal stop that follows any other letter.
Eighteen values written when the Uzbek case terms moved out of Cyrillic used
the ASCII quote for both jobs. uzLocaleResolves asserts exactly this, so
Frontend CI was red on all three platforms with one failing test out of 8365.

The rule was read out of the file rather than asserted from what I believe
about Uzbek. After o the file already writes the turned comma 26606 times and
after g 3553, while after a, e, s, t, b, d, r, n and q it writes the
apostrophe, so this change is the file agreeing with itself. Every spelling it
produced already occurred elsewhere in the file before the edit, most of them
dozens or hundreds of times, which is the check that a per-character rule
cannot pass by accident.

one is not.

fix(installer): an upgrade refused to proceed over a file the uninstall left behind

A reporter could not upgrade to 17.0.2 on one of their three Windows
machines. The installer said the previous version could not be removed;
uninstalling from Settings first and then running the installer worked, and
two identical laptops upgraded without trouble.

The template treated two different outcomes as one failure. It ran the
uninstaller already on disk, then aborted if that uninstaller returned a
non-zero code or if the program file was still in the install directory
afterwards. The second arm is wrong: the install that follows overwrites that
file anyway, and a file still held at the moment of deletion, by an indexer or
a scanner, is exactly the sort of thing that differs between one machine and
two others. The abort now fires only when the uninstaller itself failed.

The message it showed said nothing anyone could act on. It now names what
happened, the exit code from the old uninstaller or the fact that it never
started, the path of the file that survived when one did, and the step that
works, which is to remove the application from Settings first. The first
sentence is unchanged so the bundler's translations still apply; the detail
that follows is English only, because that string lives in the bundler's
language files and the template cannot reach it.

Two smaller faults in the same block. A failure to launch the uninstaller
fabricated an exit code of 2 for a process that never ran, which would have
put an invented number in the new message. And the branch that migrates from
an older WiX built install ignored which of the two options the user had
selected. It now honours the selection, with a guard for passive mode: the
page handler is called directly there, before the dialog exists, so the radio
state reads as zero and an unattended migration would silently stop removing
the old package.

check_nsis_template_drift.py now reconstructs three edits rather than one,
each checked against the text the earlier edits produced. It was already a
step in Repo hygiene, which reports without blocking, so it also runs in the
Windows leg of Desktop Release, where a red check withholds an artefact
instead of only colouring a square.

The template is not compiler verified here, no NSIS toolchain is available.
The evidence is that the file still reconstructs byte for byte from upstream
tauri-cli v2.11.4 plus exactly these three edits, that the conditional count
moves by three and closes by three, and that all 86 Handlebars expressions
survive.

fix(desktop): the macOS build asked for a runtime it had no identity to satisfy

On macOS the bundled PostgreSQL would not initialise. initdb aborted and dyld
said libpq.5.dylib and the process loading it have different Team IDs, on a
machine where neither file has a Team ID at all. Clearing the quarantine
attribute changed nothing, which is the clue: this is library validation, not
Gatekeeper.

The cause is one truthy string. The spec set codesign_identity to "-",
meaning ad-hoc, and PyInstaller reads that field as "did the caller name a real
Developer ID". Its sign_binary uses the empty case to mean ad-hoc and the
non-empty case to add --options=runtime, so "-" turned the hardened runtime on
for every Mach-O collected into the archive while the spec passed no
entitlements at all. The hardened runtime enables library validation, library
validation accepts only a library carrying the process's own Team ID, and an
ad-hoc binary has none, so the load is refused. None is what actually produces
the plain ad-hoc signature the old comment claimed "-" was producing.

It wore two faces, which is why it took this long. Until 14.7.0 Tauri put the
runtime back on the outer wrapper too and the app died earlier, on its own
Python framework. From 14.7.0 the wrapper is healthy, because two later signing
passes reach it and neither adds the runtime any more. Nothing reaches the
members: by then they are bytes inside a file rather than files on disk. So
14.7.0 through 17.1.0 start, and fail in the child processes instead.

The existing signature census was green on the broken build and would have
stayed green on any fix that kept the flag. It asks whether the members agree
with the wrapper, and on that artifact all 76 of them did agree, all having no
Team ID. The new --fail-on-hardened-adhoc asks the question that separates
them: a binary carrying the runtime flag and no Team ID is a binary that cannot
load its own neighbours. It runs on the wrapper and on every member, and a
member whose signature cannot be walked fails rather than passing quietly.

Both gates are proved on the same stubbed archive, one exiting 0 and the other
1, so the pair records that the old one was green on the build that broke. The
flag detection itself is proved on five real Mach-O files taken from the
shipped wheel, poisoned and clean.

Reported against 17.1.0 on macOS 26, Apple Silicon, from the official DMG with
a matching SHA-256.

removes what a killed run leaves behind. Both are right and neither helps the
person the change was made for. Their leftovers were written by earlier

fix(scripts): the route gate read App.tsx and missed the routes a module builds

On 9 September the whole regional BOQ exchange feature answered 404 on the public
origin. The hub and twenty country screens were built, bundled and served by the
app, and the edge never learned they existed: one hostname carries the marketing
site and the app, and the proxy decides between them from a single allowlist of
top-level path segments. A route the list does not carry never reaches the app,
so it falls into the static site and comes back as its 404. Nothing goes red and
the application log has no record of the request at all.

There was already a gate for this and it had been run that same day. It read
Route elements out of App.tsx and nothing else, so it saw three of the
twenty four missing segments. The second collector, in check_case_routes.py, did
read module manifests, but through a regular expression that matches a quoted
literal, and the regional module builds its paths from a template over a table of
markets. Two collectors, both incomplete, disagreeing silently.

So there is one collector now, scripts/app_routes.py, and both gates import it.
It is Python rather than Node because the job that will run it is ubuntu with no
node installed. It scans TypeScript with a small state machine that separates
code from strings, comments, regular expressions and template literals and tracks
bracket nesting, so a path in a comment or a translation value is not a route and
the enclosing map call can be found. It resolves exactly one computed shape, a
template path over a property of the map parameter, where the array is a const of
object literals in the same file or one imported relatively. Everything else
becomes an unresolved record carrying file, line, expression and reason, and every
consumer fails on a non-empty list rather than quietly shortening its answer. It
also cross-checks the manifests on disk against the module registry in both
directions, so a third source of routes cannot appear without saying so.

One divergence between the two consumers stays, and it is a decision about shared
metadata rather than a second collector. check_case_routes drops the routes of
modules that ship disabled, because a case step really does dead-end for a reader
who has not switched the module on. The allowlist gate keeps them, because
enablement is client side and the proxy answers before the app is ever asked.
Both are commented where they happen.

The gate compares against a committed mirror of the proxy's side, since the runner
has no access to the host. The mirror is extracted from a real Caddyfile and
stamped with its digest, never generated from the route table, and --write-mirror
refuses to install one the current routes contradict. --caddyfile compares against
a live file and --compare-mirror is the deploy-time check that the mirror has not
gone stale.

Proved on the file that failed. The pre-fix Caddyfile gives exit 1 and names all
twenty four segments, the live one gives exit 0 with 200 against 200, and the
control that says those two numbers are measured independently is the pre-fix run
reporting 176 against 200 with zero allowlist-only segments in both. Four
mutations of the collector each turn its self-test red, including one that does
not shorten the answer but corrupts it: switching off regular-expression
detection makes an apostrophe inside a regex swallow its own array entry, and the
self-test reports six unresolved with a wrong reason instead of five.

Runs in repo hygiene, structural job, and as a pre-commit hook, which is where the
answer is cheapest: it reads the tree and the mirror, no network, under a second.

ci: the sidecar timeout killed a build in which every check had passed

The 17.2.0 desktop release produced no installers. The macOS sidecar leg ran
75 minutes and 26 seconds against a cap of 75, so it was cancelled two steps
from the end, after the frontend had built, PyInstaller had run and all eight
checks on the frozen binary had passed. Copy and upload were skipped, the
bundling job had nothing to download and skipped itself, and the job that reads
the assets back off the release failed because there were none. Everything the
run existed to verify had already succeeded.

The cap was 75 because macOS took 25.6 to 34.4 minutes when it was measured,
over v14.3.0 to v14.5.0. It does not any more. Across the last twelve runs that
leg took 18.8, 37.9, 51.2, 52.6, 55.2, 57.7, 60.1, 63.2, 66.6, 68.3, 68.3 and
75.4 minutes, nine of them over fifty.

The spread matters more than the average, and it is the reason this is a cap
change rather than a performance fix. The same commit builds the frontend on
macOS in 18 minutes on one runner and 60 on another. Linux and Windows are
steady at 30 and 37 and never came close. So the macOS number is not tracking
anything about the code, and a cap set near its middle fires on which runner
the job landed on. 120 is what build-tauri already uses and sits above every
run in that sample, which keeps the property the cap exists for: a job that
reaches it is stuck, not unlucky, and a hung PyInstaller still cannot cost six
hours across three legs.

There is a real inefficiency behind this and it is written into the comment
rather than fixed here, because it changes the shape of the pipeline. All three
legs build the same frontend from the same commit and get the same bytes, and
on macOS that build is most of the job. Building it once and handing it to the
three would remove the variance from two of them.

fix(cases): four countries told the reader to invoice against an approval they never get

The progress payment family composes eleven country pages from one spine. The
spine's invoice step says the pay document is raised against an approved
valuation, and that is true of the arc it was written for, where somebody
certifies the month and the invoice follows. Three of the eleven layers never
surface the certify step at all, and a fourth surfaces it after the claim has
already been served.

So the neutral page said to issue the interim application against the approved
interim valuation, then its very next step said to put the approved figure next
to the figure you asked for, which is the approval arriving afterwards. Germany
said to raise the Abschlagsrechnung against the approved Aufmass and then, in
the same paragraph, to take that Aufmass jointly with the client's site
supervision, which is the opposite of it having been approved first. New Zealand
said to issue the payment claim against the approved progress valuation, and the
whole point of the Construction Contracts Act is that a payee serves a claim
without anybody approving anything.

No gate in that pipeline can see this. The composer checks that two slots in one
sentence do not resolve to the same word, that no two countries override the same
step, and that every slot has a value. It cannot know whether the sentence is
true of the arc the layer surfaces, and its own header says so: the gates remove
the failures a reader would not catch, they do not remove the reader.

Australia already carries the one override the design allows on that step, so the
remedy is the one the composer prescribes for exactly this: widen the sentence
with a slot rather than let a second country keep a copy of it. payAgainst says
what the pay document is raised against, an approved valuation where the arc has
one and the measure behind the claim where it does not. Seven countries compose
the sentence they already had, word for word.

The invoice reason was rewritten too, because it argued from approval as well.
It now says a pay document the other side cannot check against the measure
behind it comes back, which is true in both arcs and is the actual reason.

The certify step had a second defect, found while reading the same page. It said
the payment clock runs from the approval. Spain's clock step, two steps later,
anchors the clock on the day the client receives the invoice, and Ley 3/2004 is
what makes that the right answer. The same sentence was wrong the same way in
Brazil, Hungary, Mexico, Russia, Saudi Arabia and South Africa, each of which
records a different clock start of its own. It now names that start rather than
the approval.

20 keys are newly reworded and their translations are stale until the next pass.
The English is right today and it was not before.

fix(desktop): the old uninstaller can no longer freeze the upgrade

ExecWait on the old NSIS uninstaller blocked the installer indefinitely
when that uninstaller's own process-stop hooks hung. Every release from
v11.7.1 to v15.8.0 shipped hooks that called nsExec without /TIMEOUT,
and on a machine where PowerShell never returns (antivirus, PowerToys,
wedged WMI) the upgrade stopped dead with no way out but the task
manager.

since v16.1.0, but anyone who explicitly chose to uninstall still hit
the hang. Now ExecWait is replaced with nsExec /TIMEOUT=300000 (five
minutes). If the old uninstaller times out, nsExec terminates it and the
upgrade continues: NSIS_HOOK_PREINSTALL stops anything left running, and
the install overwrites the files.
