fix: version-aware onboarding, locale reset on update, boot progress

On update, localStorage flags from the previous session (oe_lang_explicit,
i18nextLng) silently override browser locale detection, so a user who
previously tested in Russian gets Russian after the update even though
their browser is German.

Root cause: both flags persist across updates with no per-user scope and
no version awareness. The onboarding completed flag is a boolean that
never re-triggers regardless of version.

Changes:

- Store oe_onboarding_completed_version alongside the completion flag.
  On dashboard load, if the major.minor changed, show an UpdateWelcome
  dialog offering to re-run setup or continue.

- The "Re-run setup" path clears oe_lang_explicit so browser detection
  kicks in, resets the server onboarding flag via a new DELETE endpoint,
  and navigates to the wizard.

- Settings "restart onboarding" now also resets the server flag and
  clears oe_lang_explicit, fixing the case where a fresh-browser user
  could not re-enter the wizard because the server still said completed.

- All five bare i18n.changeLanguage calls in the onboarding wizard
  replaced with the async changeLanguage wrapper that pre-loads the
  locale chunk before switching, preventing an English flash.

- Backend DELETE /v1/users/me/onboarding/complete/ endpoint added.

- Boot progress: _set_boot_phase now emits STAGE:migrate:progress
  markers so the desktop splash screen shows which startup phase is
  active instead of appearing frozen. The heartbeat thread also emits
  these markers every 15 seconds. migrate:done emitted before server
  start.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix: always verify onboarding state against server, not stale localStorage

WebView2 on Windows preserves localStorage across uninstall/reinstall,
so a fresh install inherits oe_onboarding_completed=true from the
previous one and the user never sees the setup wizard. The previous
logic trusted localStorage as a fast-path and returned early without
checking the server, which meant a reinstalled app skipped onboarding
entirely.

Now the dashboard always waits for the server response before deciding.
If the server says not completed, stale localStorage flags are cleared
and the user is redirected to onboarding with a clean slate, including
clearing oe_lang_explicit so browser locale detection works correctly.
The server is authoritative, localStorage is a cache.

fix: let upgrade continue when old uninstaller fails

When the old uninstaller exits with a non-zero code (other than user
cancellation), the installer now asks the user whether to continue
instead of aborting outright. The install writes over every file in
INSTDIR and NSIS_HOOK_PREINSTALL stops running processes, so continuing
is safe and strictly better than leaving the user stuck between a broken
uninstaller and an installer that refuses to proceed.

The specific case that triggered this was exit code -1 on a machine
where the old uninstaller's PowerShell hook (pre-v15.9, no /TIMEOUT)
failed under antivirus policy. The installer's error dialog told the
user to go to Windows Settings and remove the app manually, which works
but is not the experience we want for an upgrade.

user to add an exclusion, instead of three opaque retries and a generic

should fix this" instead of timing out.

pre-flight check failures in cli.py all now emit STAGE:<id>:fail so the
desktop launcher checklist shows the actual cause.

Fatal short-circuit: when _pre_initialize_cluster detects a condition no
retry can fix (disk full, binary blocked) it sets _fatal_detail and boot()
exits immediately instead of burning three retry attempts on a doomed start.

Tray restart: right-click menu now carries "Restart application" between
"Open in browser" and Quit, calling app.restart(). A user whose database
disconnected can restart without finding the task manager.

test: gate subscriptions to events nothing publishes

The event bus matches subscribers to publishers by exact string and nothing
checked that the two sides agree. A handler subscribed to a name no module
publishes imports fine, registers fine, passes its own unit tests and never
runs, with no log line and no failing assertion anywhere. The only symptom is
a feature that quietly does not happen.

The new gate scans the backend tree and fails in both directions. A new
subscription to an unpublished name fails and names the site. A seam that gets
repaired without its allowlist line being deleted also fails, so the list can
never outlive the bug it describes.

Thirty one such subscriptions are in the tree today. They are listed with the
site and the nearest published name rather than as a bare count, because the
list is a work item and every entry removed is one handler that starts working.
Nothing is renamed here on purpose. Several of these handlers write contract
value or create records and have never executed against real data, so turning
thirty one of them on in one commit would be a behaviour change wearing the
clothes of a rename. One seam per commit, each with a test that asserts the
handler's effect.

Three of the thirty one were found by this scan and were not known before,
including snapshot.refreshed, whose constant is declared twice in the
dashboards module, subscribed once and published nowhere, while the module
docstring describes the refresh cascade as if it runs. Two names previously
believed dead turned out to be live: they are published through an attribute
reference rather than a bare name, which an earlier sweep could not resolve.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test: pin the drift between the backend and wizard module registries

The onboarding presets module says in a comment that it mirrors the module
catalogue the wizard renders, and the test file said the backend list was
authoritative so a client catalogue drifting behind the server would still
leave the whole platform visible. Measured, the drift runs the other way and
nothing was watching it. The wizard carries 157 keys, the backend carries 93,
and all 64 of the difference are modules the backend has never heard of. In
the reverse direction the count is zero, so the backend is a strict subset.

The new test parses the wizard catalogue on every run rather than mirroring
the key list, because a mirrored copy would be a third registry and a gate
whose expectation drifts with the thing it guards cannot fail. It fails in
both directions: a module added to the wizard and forgotten on the backend
grows the gap past the allowlist, and a key that reaches the backend without
its allowlist line being deleted shrinks it below. Both were verified by
breaking them on purpose and reading the failure.

The 64 keys are named rather than counted. A bare allowance of 64 differences
passes just as happily when someone adds one key and deletes another, and it
never tells a reader which modules are affected.

Nothing is added to the registry here, and the allowlist says why. modules_for
writes an explicit False for every key it knows that a profile omits, while
the sidebar's isModuleEnabled is fail-open and shows anything it has no
preference for. Those 64 modules are therefore visible today precisely because
the backend stays silent about them, and naming them in a narrow profile would
hide working screens. Which profiles should carry which of them is a product
decision rather than a mechanical one.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

test: pin document references the database does not enforce

Twenty eight columns across twenty one modules hold a document id that no
foreign key constrains. Six other document columns do carry one, so this is a
choice made repeatedly rather than a convention the codebase lacks, and the
reason given in the comments is portability across PostgreSQL and SQLite.

What makes the set worth pinning is the delete path. Deleting a document looks
up the row, records an activity entry, deletes, and unlinks the file. It never
asks whether anything still points at the id, and no reference check exists
anywhere in the module. It then publishes a deleted event detached, and exactly
three subscribers listen for that name: the module's own handler, the search
indexer and the file reference purger. None of the three owns any of the twenty
eight columns.

One consumer is handled, and how it is handled is the strongest evidence the
gap is real. Takeoff has its blobs preserved by a direct call placed inline in
the delete path, and the comment there explains why it is not driven off the
event: the publish is detached, so a subscriber would race the unlink and lose
nondeterministically, passing on a developer's box and failing on a loaded one.
That reasoning applies to the other twenty seven referrers equally. They just
have nobody calling for them. Meanwhile the confirmation the user sees is not
even a dialog, it is a strip inside the table row reading Delete, Yes, No, with
no room to say what would break.

This does not fix it. A reference count spanning these tables and a warning
that names the referrers is scoped work, and how hard to block a delete is a
product decision. What this does is stop the set growing quietly and give that
work a census to start from. It fails in both directions: a new unconstrained
reference fails and is named, and a pin that outlives its column fails too.

The population is asserted beside the verdict because an earlier draft of the
scan compiled its pattern without multiline matching, so the anchor only
matched at the start of each file and the census came back empty. Zero findings
look exactly like a clean tree.

The regex helper read a capture group straight off the match array and mapped
another one over the results, and under strict indexed access both are string

was run afterwards looked for a blank line rather than for the doubled return,
so it reported the file clean. Every blob in the three commits was rescanned
for the same shape and this was the only one.

fix: bound the memory a cost database import holds at once

A report from a small virtual server described the process dying while loading
a country cost pack, with no traceback and nothing in the log. That signature
is the Linux out of memory killer. It sends SIGKILL, so Python never reaches an
except clause and never prints anything, and because the import runs on a
worker thread inside the API process the kill takes the whole server down
rather than failing the one request that asked for it.

The load into PostgreSQL was already chunked. The caller was not. It appended
every work item of a region to a single list and handed the whole list over at
the end, so peak memory scaled with the region rather than with the chunk. For
a large region that is tens of thousands of tuples, each carrying the
serialised JSON of its own resource breakdown, alive at the same moment as the
resource dictionary they were serialised from and the two lookup tables built
beside it. The parquet reader above them had already been narrowed to the
columns actually used for the same reason, which left this as the remaining
peak.

The rows now go over in bounded slices while the loop runs, so peak memory is a
function of the slice size rather than of the region. The second effect matters
more on the machine this came from. The staging table is dropped on commit and
the insert is idempotent on code and region, so every slice is a complete
transaction, and an import that is killed part way through now resumes from
where it stopped instead of starting the region over.

until the one in front of it was cleared.

variable before the column is declared, and 48 of them build at least one table
or index name from a loop variable or a module constant, so a probe that

beside the verdict. Two columns that the chain creates and no model declares

fix: page every vector reindex and report the ones that stop short

Nine places in the tree reindex a vector collection. Six reach it through a
factory that already walked the table in pages. Two are hand written copies
that read the whole table into one list first, and they happen to sit on the
two highest cardinality tables in the product. The ninth runs at startup and is
capped already.

Neither copy could simply move onto the factory, because each carries a
permission gate and a filter the factory knows nothing about, one by bill and
one by model. So the walk was lifted out of the factory instead and both
endpoints now enter through the same door, with their gates still ahead of any
read.

The walk has five properties and the docstring numbers them, because a reindex
that builds its own loop has to re-derive all five and the one it forgets fails
quietly. It orders by primary key, appending that to any ordering the caller
asked for, since an offset into an undefined ordering is not a position. It
pages. It flushes before releasing, because expunging first detaches instances
with work still pending and throws that work away. It releases, because a
session holds every entity it handed out until the transaction ends, so paging
without releasing bounds nothing at all. And it reports.

The page is 500 rows and the ceiling is 100 000. A ceiling is right on this
path in a way it was not for reads that merely buffered, because every row here
goes through the embedding model inside the request, so a pass without one is
unbounded work on an open connection. The numbers come from measuring the per
row footprint of each indexed model: the heaviest holds about 29.7 KiB per row,
which put 100 000 buffered rows at roughly 2.9 GiB held at once, against a
documented floor of 3 GB with PostgreSQL running beside it.

One measurement lesson is worth keeping. The first instance of a mapped class
pays for instrumenting that class, so whichever model was measured first read
about 2.7 times heavier than it is. Three runs hours apart agreed to the
decimal, which is a reminder that a repeatable number and a correct one are
different things.

A pass is only called truncated after the walk reads one row past the ceiling,
so a collection that ends exactly on it is reported as complete, which it was.
The response carries how far it got and what the limit was, next to the counts
it already returned.

The reindex docstring was also corrected to describe what the code does. The
delete before an index is by id on both backends rather than a wipe, which is
the reason purging per page and purging once are equivalent, and a caller that
starts paging would have to revisit this if that ever changed.

fix: stop a bill of quantities accepting a tax rate it cannot keep

Both write schemas for a bill advertised a tax rate, with a description and a
worked example showing that 0.19 means 19 percent. The model has no such
column. Create builds its row from a named list of fields, so the rate was
dropped and the caller got a 201. Update passes whatever was set to a Core
update against the mapped class, which refuses an unknown column while
compiling the statement, so that path raised and the caller got an opaque 500.
One field, two write paths, and it was lost differently on each.

Nothing sends it. The frontend declares three fields for creating a bill and
has no bill level patch except two that set a status. No internal caller, no
seed, no country pack and no raw statement names the column outside the
migration that created it. The only tests that mentioned it built their own
object, multiplied the rate themselves and asserted the result, so the field
looked covered while never reaching the service at all.

So it is refused rather than stored, and the refusal names the markup row where
consumption tax actually lives. Storing it was not really available: the test
that records which columns the chain creates and the models do not already
explains that tax belongs to a markup row, and the editor page says the same
thing, that the tax markup is the single source of truth. A second place to put
a tax rate is how the two come to disagree.

The upper and lower bounds are gone along with the example, because a schema
that still says a value must be between zero and one goes on implying that some
value would be accepted.

One detail the refusal alone does not cover. Responses still carry the field as
null for wire compatibility, so a client that reads a bill, changes its status
and sends the whole object back is sending an explicit null. An explicit null
counts as set, so it would have survived into the update and produced the same
500 for the one caller the field is kept for. The update schema therefore also
drops it from the dumped payload, which was measured to leave the published
validation schema untouched rather than assumed.

The tests fail in both directions: fifteen fail if the guard is removed, and
the two that prove an ordinary caller still gets through fail if the guard
fires on null. One of them puts a 19 percent tax markup on a direct cost of a
hundred and requires a grand total of 119 through the real calculation, so the
suite cannot pass against a build where tax does not work at all.

The neighbouring column the chain also creates without a model was checked and
deliberately left alone. It has no input surface, so nothing can be sent and
nothing is lost, and a test already records that whether a project may override
its pack's measurement system is an open design question rather than a bug.

fix: tighten the healed column the revision was only backfilling

A database that got its tables from the boot heal rather than from the
migration chain ends up with detail_params nullable and without a default,
because the model gives it a callable default and the heal can only render a
default that has a literal spelling. The sibling column next to it carries an
empty string, which does have one, and lands NOT NULL. Two columns added in
the same edit, arriving in two different shapes.

The revision already knew about that and repaired half of it. It filled the
NULL rows, which is what the reading code needs, and left the column
declaration alone, which is what the health endpoint reads. So the rows were
fine and the schema still disagreed with the model, and such an installation
reported schema_matches_models false for the rest of its life. Found on the
local database, which has been answering degraded over this one column while
every row in it was already populated.

A standing false alarm is worth more attention than it looks. Its cost is not
the noise, it is that an operator learns to read a degraded status as normal,
and the next divergence arrives into a signal nobody trusts any more.

The two statements are unconditional on purpose. On the migration path they do
nothing, because add_column has already supplied both properties there, and
writing them under a second guard would leave two paths whose agreement
nothing checks. That is the shape of the original defect, so the fix should
not reproduce it one level down. They also have to follow the backfill rather
than precede it, since tightening a column that still holds a NULL aborts the
upgrade on exactly the databases this revision exists to repair, and on no
others, which is the kind of ordering bug that passes every test written
against an empty table.

The tests run the revision against a recording double and check which
statements reach which path. Three deliberately broken versions were tried
against them, the tightening removed, the tightening moved inside the guard a
healed database skips, and the tightening placed before the backfill. All
three were caught, each failing a different subset, and the revision was
restored byte for byte afterwards.

difference is not obvious. The version check compares each file against the

fix: let a reassigned approval be decided by the person holding it

Two places worked out who is entitled to decide a step and they disagreed.
Reassignment wrote the stand-in onto the instance, sent them a notice saying
the approval was now theirs to decide, and refused the original approver with
a 403. The advance check then asked whether the step's named approver was
among those who had approved, which is a question about the original person.
The stand-in therefore approved, got a 200 and the instance back, the step did
not move, and the one person who could have moved it was locked out. The
instance waited with nothing red anywhere, no error code, and a screen that
looked correct. An active delegation went the same way.

Entitlement is resolved once per request now and both the refusal and the
advance read that one answer, so the two cannot drift apart again.

Fixing the deadlock opened a worse hole, and closing it is most of this
change. Once a stand-in's approval can clear a step, handing over a step that
wants three approvals lets one person spend a quorum the route author asked
for. Reassignment now refuses a step that needs more than one approval and
says how many it wants. The count comes from the same function the dry run
already shows the route author, rather than from a fourth place that works out
how many people can decide something, since a second opinion on that question
is what caused all of this. The refusal is raised before anything is written,
so a refused reassignment leaves the instance exactly as it was.

Two more things follow from having one answer instead of several. Escalation
no longer climbs to somebody who is already holding the step through a
delegation, which used to burn a rung of the ladder, write the de-duplication
record and leave the first real authority above unaware for another sweep. And
the person named as holding a step is now worked out in one place for the API
and for the breach reminder, which could previously name two different people,
the reminder reaching whoever actually sits on the step and the interface
naming an approver who is away.

What is deliberately not here: whether escalation is a chase or a hand-off.
The product currently says both. The reassignment notice says the approval is
yours to decide and it is, while the escalation notice says the same thing and
links the recipient to an approval they are refused on. That is a decision
about what escalation means rather than a defect to repair, and the two
answers lead to different code, so it is left alone and written down.

test: run the funding revision's statements against a real PostgreSQL

The four tests already there prove which statements the revision emits on
which path. They run upgrade against a recorder, so they say nothing about
whether a server accepts the result, and nothing else in the suite does
either: the unit schema is built from create_all rather than from alembic, so
no test anywhere runs this revision. The two statements added to it yesterday
would have reached every installation having never been executed once, and a
rejection would have shown up as a failed upgrade on somebody's database
instead of here.

The new test executes them. It takes the SQL from the recorder rather than
retyping it, so a change to the revision changes what is run and a paraphrase
cannot drift away from the real thing. The table is temporary and deliberately
carries the real table's name, since the temporary schema comes first in the
search path and the revision's unqualified SQL then resolves to it. That is
worth doing carefully, so the test refuses to execute anything until it has
confirmed the name resolves into the temporary schema, which is the difference
between running against a scratch table and quietly altering the real one.

It then checks the shape rather than the catalog alone. The column has to come
out not null with a default, the default has to actually apply to a row that
omits the column, and an explicit null has to be refused. A default recorded
in the catalog that never applies would be the same false alarm in a new
place.

Writing it turned up the trap it now documents. Asking information_schema for
a column by table_name matches every schema at once, so with both the real
table and the temporary one present the query came back with two rows and the
first run failed. It asks pg_attribute by regclass instead, which resolves
through the search path to the one table the statements just altered.

fix: repair the funding obligation parameter column where the product can reach it

Commit 26b46badd added SET DEFAULT and SET NOT NULL to
v41_funding_obligation_detail and claimed that closed the permanent
schema_matches_models=false a healed install reports over
oe_funding_obligation.detail_params. It does not. The reason is written in the
gate that flagged the revision afterwards: the product never runs alembic
upgrade. It moves the schema at boot through the heal and then stamps head, so
a revision body runs only where an operator runs it by hand. Every statement
that commit added is correct, and none of them arrives anywhere the defect
actually lives. The tests written alongside it proved the statements were
emitted and later that PostgreSQL accepts them, which is true and is not the
same as the column being fixed on anybody's database.

The column is repaired in two directions here, because one without the other
leaves the work undone.

Backwards, app/modules/funding/repairs.py registers
funding_obligation_detail_params_not_null with the data repair registry, which
runs on every boot after the heal and records each run in
oe_data_repair_ledger. It calls the existing tighten_not_null helper with the
literal the revision declares, so the two build paths cannot end up disagreeing
about the value. This follows the requirements module, which had the same
defect for the same reason, with one difference worth naming: there a NULL
reached model_validate and the read raised, whereas FundingObligationResponse
carries a before validator that coerces None to an empty dict. No read is
broken today. What is broken is the column declaration, which makes the install
answer degraded for good over a column whose rows are by then all populated,
and the missing default, which makes an insert that omits the column behave
differently on a healed database than on a migrated one.

Forwards, the model declares server_default on detail_params. Without it the
repair would be permanent employment rather than a repair: the heal renders a
column default into DDL only when the model gives it one it can spell,
default=dict is a callable with no spelling, so every newly healed install
would keep arriving in the broken shape and the repair would keep cleaning up
after it. The default is spelled as a plain string rather than as a text
construct because the heal quotes a string default and compiles an expression
inside a bare except that falls back to emitting no default at all. Both
spellings produce the same DDL and only one of them has a silent way to produce
nothing.

Three tests. The repair is run against the real table, put into the broken
shape first and rolled back, so what is exercised is the table the repair
names. One of them runs it twice, because tighten_not_null decides by asking
whether a default is present rather than by comparing its text, and every other
caller is a varchar whose default reads back as ''::character varying while
this one is json and reads back as '{}'::json. A comparison written against the
varchar spelling would re-issue the ALTERs and write a ledger row on every boot
forever, which is the same class of false signal this commit exists to remove.

attribute that is merely present has been true before while the DDL still came

fix: read the pid file the test reaper was only counting

The suite removes abandoned embedded PostgreSQL data dirs at conftest import,
and skipped any dir that still had a postmaster.pid on the reasoning that a pid
file means somebody is serving out of that directory. That reasoning covers a
live session and a session whose postmaster is still up, and both of those do
have a live postmaster. It misses the third case, which is the one that piles
up: a force-killed postmaster leaves its pid file behind and nothing ever comes
back to remove it, so the directory is excluded from reaping for good.

The warning made this hard to see rather than easy. It reported those dirs as
clusters still running and said their number was a leak this function could not
fix, which reads as a diagnosis and was in fact a description of the bug. On
this machine eleven dirs were being held out of reach by pid files naming
processes that had not existed for days. After this change the same directory
listing is down to two, one of which is the cluster the probe had just started.

The pid file is now read rather than counted, and the liveness question goes to
embedded_pg._pidfile_owner_is_live, which the product's own boot and shutdown
paths use. Reusing it matters for what it does with doubt: it answers yes when
it cannot tell, and it treats a pid that is alive but belongs to something else
as gone, which is the distinction a bare liveness check gets wrong on Windows
often enough to matter. A dir is removed only on a definite no, and the
existing minimum-age check still applies on top, so the original bias is
intact. Erring towards keeping a directory costs disk, erring the other way
deletes a database somebody is serving out of.

The two reasons for keeping a dir are counted and reported apart. A live
postmaster is a cluster this machine never shut down; an unreadable pid file is
a dir nothing can currently judge, which is what a machine that lost power
leaves behind. Reporting the second as the first would describe a half-written
file as a running database, and telling somebody what is actually holding their
disk is the entire job of that warning.

Three tests. One states the leak directly, one holds the unreadable file to
keeping its dir and to being named as its own case, and one pins that the
question reaches the product function about the directory the pid file is in
rather than the cluster root, since the relpaths allow either and handing over
the wrong one reads no pid and then looks exactly like caution.

The guard excludes a key that appears literally at a call site, because such a
suffix belongs to the name rather than to a plural, and without that exclusion
it would report every key with an unlucky ending. It found those names with a
regex over the frontend source that had no idea what a comment is.

A comment in the test that forbids choosing a plural in JavaScript writes the
anti-pattern out in full, naming connectors.just_imported_one beside
connectors.just_imported_many so a reader can see what not to do. Those two
names went into the excluded set, both forms of a real counted key dropped out
of every locale at once, and the guard reported 37 rows of a hole that is not
there. It has been red on main since that test landed yesterday, which is also
how long it has been unable to report anything new.

Every one of the 37 was checked against the locale file it named before this
was written. All 50 of the individual form claims are present, so the whole
output was one comment.

Comments are blanked before either scan now, including the one that builds the
counted population, which never misfired but is fed from the same text and
would demand forms for a family that only an example mentions. Measured over
the real tree the change removes exactly five names from the literal set, the
two above and three that prose writes as t('key') or t('literal'), and adds
none. The counted set does not move at all.

The way the scan errs is the point of it. Blanking too little leaves the noise
being removed here, which is loud and visible. Blanking too much drops a real
call site, the family leaves the counted population, and the guard falls silent
about a key that genuinely lacks a form, which looks exactly like a guard with
nothing to report. So string contents are never touched, only comment spans
are, and a quote the scanner misreads can at worst let a comment survive.

Eleven tests, arranged as opposed pairs for that reason. Against a bare
line-comment strip the pair that matters goes red: a URL sharing a line with a
call loses the call, and both sets come back without it. The first version of
that test put the two on separate lines and passed over the very implementation
it exists to reject, which is worth saying because the weaker version looked

test: pin the three sentences an approval refusal can answer with

Deciding a step can be refused with 403 from two places and with three
different sentences, because one of them picks between two of them on whether
the instance currently names a stand-in. Only the status code was asserted
anywhere, and a status code cannot tell those apart.

The distinction is the whole value of the message. Named means the route
itself picked somebody else, so the reader's next move is to ask whoever wrote
the route. Assigned means the step has been handed to a stand-in, so the next
move is to ask the person now holding it, and one of the people who will read
that sentence is the approver the route did name, who could decide this step
yesterday. Swapping the two arms of that conditional sends every reader to the
wrong place and nothing in the suite would have noticed, because both arms
answer 403.

The third sentence comes from the role branch, which is only reached when no
user is entitled at all, and it is the one that stops somebody holding the
decide permission from clearing a gate the route pinned to a higher role. The
pinned cases never reach it.

Four tests. Three assert whole strings rather than substrings, since "Not the"
would pass for either of the first two, which is the confusion being guarded
against. The fourth asserts the three are distinct, because if two of them
were ever made identical the other three would still pass while the reader
lost the distinction.

Writing the reassignment case turned up the guard in front of it: a hand-off
is refused unless the person receiving it can reach the route's project, so a
freshly created user fails at a different check and never reaches the sentence
under test. The stand-in is the project owner for that reason, and the comment
beside it says so, since the test would otherwise look like it was making an
arbitrary choice.

Five list endpoints that returned a bare array now return a page with the
count behind it. Four hang off one funding application, its draws, its
accounts, its dated obligations and the costs allocated to it, and each of
those grows for as long as the grant is live. The fifth is the procurement
rollup of what has been ordered against each BOQ position.

page. The two are equal on a short register and that is the trap: an envelope
whose total is the length of its own items looks correct on every project
small enough to fit in one page and starts lying on the first one that does
not. Every test here builds more rows than the page it asks for, so a total
echoing the page cannot pass.

Two endpoints in the funding module deliberately keep answering with
everything. The application detail response embeds all four child lists at
once, and the obligation calendar crosses applications, because a calendar
missing next week is not a calendar. Giving the unpaged reads a default limit
would have cut both down to a page without a single caller asking for one.

The procurement rollup was in a different state. It had never returned a

method sat on MaterialRequisitionService while the route called it on

error.

this module carries as Decimal end to end. The fold from cost line to bill
position happens in Python too, several cost lines can name one position, so
the number of rows the caller sees is not known until they are folded; the
page and the total come off one sorted list rather than out of two queries
that could drift. An order against a cost line that names no position keeps
its own row rather than being dropped, since that is real committed money, and
the field carries an id of one kind or the other, which is why it is text and
why a test now pins it instead of only the schema saying so.

wrapper built the URL with the whole query string interpolated as one suffix,
so the route collapsed to a shape no entry in check_page_envelope_consumers
could match, and the endpoint would have been correct, enveloped, read and
unguardable at the same time. It now writes its own question mark the way

the entry is recorded. The four funding routes stay out of that file on
purpose: the interface POSTs to them and reads the detail response, so an
entry would report no call sites and pass without reading anything, which that
file bans three times over.

The response type is the shared Page rather than a fourth local copy of the
same four fields, which is also the only spelling the guard reads as migrated.

Sixteen tests across the two modules.

fix(server): keep accepting connections on Windows after a client resets

On Windows uvicorn runs on asyncio's proactor loop, and CPython closes the
listening socket for good when one accept fails. A single client that gives
up while it waits in the listen backlog is enough (WinError 64). The process
stays alive, the port refuses every new connection, and in the desktop app
that looks like a frozen window until the app is restarted. We reproduced it
on a test server that was slow for a minute: it logged the accept failure and
never answered again.

The server now runs on the selector loop on Windows, which logs a failed
accept and keeps the listener open. Linux and macOS keep uvicorn's default.
The backend has no asyncio subprocesses, and the test suite already runs on
this loop on Windows. A new test replays the reset with real sockets and
shows the proactor loop going deaf and the selector loop serving the next
client.

Co-Authored-By: DataDrivenConstruction <info@datadrivenconstruction.io>

fix(server): stay on the proactor loop and re-post an accept a reset client broke

fd21a4327 moved the Windows server to asyncio's selector loop so that one client
resetting in the listen backlog could no longer close the listening socket. That
traded a loud failure for a silent one. On Windows the selector transport pops a
buffer before send() and drops it when send() raises BlockingIOError, and there is
no sendmsg path to fall back on. asyncpg's executemany goes through exactly that
write: a batch of 346 UPDATE statements applied 313 of them and reported success.
A server that stops answering is bad, a server that quietly skips writes to the
database is worse.

The server is back on the proactor loop, with a proactor whose accept re-posts
AcceptEx when the pending one fails because the client went away (WinError 64,
1236, 10053, 10054) and the listener is still open. The future the loop waits on
then simply resolves with the next client, so the stock "Accept failed on a
socket, close the listener" path is never reached. Any other error, a closed
listener or a cancellation still goes through unchanged, and a listener that
fails a hundred accepts in a row is treated as broken.

The single accept is a copy of the stdlib one without its helper task. That task
only existed to close the unused socket on cancellation, and when the accept
failed it was left holding the error, so asyncio logged "Task exception was never
retrieved" for every reset client and the socket leaked. A done callback now
closes the socket on every outcome but success.

The tests replay one and five reset clients with real sockets and require that
the next two clients are served, the listener stays open and nothing reaches the
exception handler. The stock proactor stays as the control that proves the
reproduction still reproduces.

fix(boq): a price edit reprices its own line and no longer loads the bill

Two things behind the report that the BoQ froze when a price was entered.

A price edit could reprice other lines of the project. A unit_rate edit on a
line with resources rescales that line's resource rates (OC-21), and the
shared resource propagation of #133 then read the rescaled rates as a person
redefining the resource. When the edited line was the oldest carrier of a
resource code, every other line in the project sharing that code was rewritten
to the new rate. Paste, fill down, the bulk rate factor, the audit fix, restore
and the AI match accept all send a bare unit_rate, so the grid's locked rate
cell was no protection. On the demo bill one typed number rewrote 299 other
lines, and at 2,080 lines the request did not finish. Propagation now looks only
at what the client sent in its resource list, compared by amount rather than by
text, and carries only what was stored for those fields. The editor coerces
"100.0000" to 100.0 when it sends the resources back, and a text comparison had
read every untouched rate beside an edited quantity as a new master rate.

When a real resource edit does propagate, only the lines that may carry the code
are read, as plain rows narrowed in SQL, and they are written in one pass with
one boq.positions.resource_propagated event instead of an ORM load of the whole
project and an event per line. The writes stay single-row UPDATEs because an
asyncpg executemany goes through the selector transport the Windows tests run
on, which dropped 33 of 346 rows without an error. The activity log splits the
event back into one entry per bill it touched, so a bill whose lines were
repriced from another bill still shows them in its own feed, and the event is
listed in the notification catalogue so webhooks can subscribe to it.

Every single-line PATCH also loaded the whole bill, positions and markups, three
or four times: the ownership guard, the lock guard, the activity log and the
duplicate check each fetched the BOQ object to read one column. They read that
column now.

fix(payment-clock): run the statutory clock on the sum that had to be paid

Statutory interest and the paid in full check both measured against the sum
applied for. That is the wrong figure wherever the payer answered in time. A
payer who served a payment notice for a lower sum within the statutory window
and then paid exactly that sum was still told the difference was overdue and
still accruing interest, which is the opposite of what the statute says.

The figure is now decided in the order the statutes put it. A payment notice
served in time states the notified sum. Failing that, a payee's own default
payment notice does, in the regimes where silence lets it. Failing both, the
sum applied for stands, and under a regime whose silence concedes the claim
the finding says so, because there the applied sum became the notified sum by
operation of the statute rather than by anybody agreeing to it. A pay less
notice served in time and stating the basis for it lowers whichever figure
applies without displacing the notified sum, which is a distinction that loses
adjudications when it is blurred. A notice served late is left out, and so is
one written in another currency, because converting it needs a rate and a date
that the record does not carry.

Three groups of regimes change. In all forty four, a valid notice now sets the
figure interest runs on. In the eleven whose silence concedes the claim the
finding now names that concession instead of reporting the applied sum as if
nobody had considered it. And in the eighteen that set no deadline for a
payment notice at all, a recorded notice now counts for something, where
before it was ignored for missing a deadline that does not exist.

Every finding names the figure it used and where that figure came from, so a
reader can see which document the clock was measured against.

feat(contracts): retain at the country's ladder from the day the contract is signed

The regional packs have declared a retention policy per country for a long
time, and the engine applies one only from a RetentionSchedule row. Nothing
ever wrote that row, so the two never met. A United States contract retained
its opening rate to the end of the job while the pack beside it said the rate
halves at half complete, which is the worst of both, because the pack reads as
though it were in force. On a 100,000 contract billed to sixty per cent that is
6,000 held where the ladder says 5,500.

The ladder is written at signing, in the draft to active transition, for the
same reason the contract value is frozen there. What a signed contract
withholds cannot then be rewritten by a later correction to a pack or by
somebody changing the project's country. It goes into the same metadata dict as
the compliance audit, because a second assignment would have dropped that audit
with nothing to say so.

It is written only when the pack's opening rate is the rate the parties agreed,
and equality is the test in both directions. A ladder opening below the agreed
rate would release money early and one opening above it would withhold more than
was agreed, and neither is ours to decide. Where the two agree, the parties took
the country's standard opening rate, so the country's standard step down comes
with it, and from there the ladder can only reduce what is held. Every refusal
is recorded on the contract as retention_policy_seed with a reason, so a
contract that was not given a ladder says why rather than looking the same as
one that was never considered.

What that promises to somebody who has configured nothing is less than it
sounds, and it is worth stating plainly. The seeding needs a country on the
project and a pack that declares tiers for it. A project with no country, or a
country whose pack is silent, is stamped pack_silent and keeps the flat rate it
had, which is every instance that has not set a country up. A cost plus or time
and materials contract is skipped by type, and a contract that already has a
policy somebody wrote is never overwritten.

Three validation rules come with it. pay_application.retention_above_cap blocks
a claim whose retention has passed a cap the contract's policy states, and where
no cap is stated but the country limits retainage by state law it says so as
information instead. That notice names its own remedy: it reports that the
project carries no subdivision code, so no state could be resolved and no
statutory cap was checked, and it tells the reader to write the state's limit
into the policy as a cap. A notice that cannot be acted on is noise, and this
one stops appearing the day somebody adds the field. The error branch waits on a
cap being written, which today happens through the API and not by itself.
contracts.retention_policy_single warns when a contract carries more than one
schedule, which is legal in the table and ambiguous in the money.

The last change is in the engine and is smaller to read than it is to rely on.
policy_from_rule promised in its docstring that an unreadable retention ladder
is refused as a ValueError, and three callers hold it to that, one of them by
declining to write the row. It kept the promise for a bad rate and broke it for
a rule whose tiers are not a list at all, where it reached .get on a string and
raised AttributeError straight past every guard. Both shapes now raise
ValueError, the docstring says that this is load bearing rather than tidy and
names the callers, and the existing parametrised refusal test grew five cases
rather than gaining a sibling, so there is one gate for the promise instead of
two that can drift apart.

fix(contracts): show the retention the payment applications certified

The schedule-of-values tracker worked retention out for itself, the contract's
flat rate applied to everything billed, while every claim line it walked was
already carrying retention_to_date, the figure that was certified and printed
on the payment application. The two agree only while a contract retains at one
rate for the whole job. On a laddered contract they do not: at sixty per cent
of a 100,000 contract the certificate says 5,500 held and the tracker said
6,000, and a user with both screens open has no way to tell which is the job's
retention.

The tracker now reads the figure rather than recomputing it. Per contract line
it takes the latest counted claim's retention_to_date, in billing order, and
never a sum, because a to-date figure already contains the ones before it and
adding two of them would have counted the first period twice. The payment
application has always read it this way, preferring the line's own figure and
computing only when there is none, so this is the tracker catching up with the
document rather than a new convention.

Where no claim recorded a figure the old computation stands. That is cost plus
and time and materials claims, where the retention engine is never asked for a
per-line share, and rows written before these columns existed. No figure is
not a figure of zero, and reading the absence as zero would have reported a
laddered contract as retaining nothing at all. Paid work is treated the same
way from the latest paid claim, because leaving that one on the flat rate
would have made the panel disagree with itself in the next column.

Ties break on the claim id. claim_number has no unique constraint and defaults
to empty, so two claims closing on the same day and created together can match
on all three parts of the billing-order key. The generator never produces that
pair, and the point is not which claim wins but that the same one wins every
time: a figure that flips with whatever order the database returned is worse
than one that is merely wrong.

One behaviour change on contracts that have no ladder at all, which is most of
them. The figure the engine recorded comes from its cent allocation across the
lines, while the old code applied the rate to each line's billed value
independently. The totals match and an individual line can differ by one cent
in either direction. The recorded figure is the better answer, because it is
what the payment application printed and what the payer is holding, but it is
a change, and a line on a live contract that moves by a cent moved for this
reason.

That paragraph says most contracts because the population turned out to be
much wider than I had it. I recorded that retention_to_date is written only on
the laddered branch, which would have made this a change to contracts that
have a ladder and to nothing else. It is written by contract type: every
lump-sum and unit-price claim records a figure and only cost plus and time and
materials do not. What corrected it was the end to end test, which failed on
its second assertion with a figure where it expected none, so the reason the
sentence above is right is that the test contradicted me, not that I measured
before writing it.

The repository now hands back the claim beside each line instead of just its
status, and is renamed lines_with_claim_for_contract to say so, since the
rollup needs the billing order and that is three of the claim's own columns.
The private _claim_status attribute the two functions used to pass between
themselves is gone with it: one writer, one reader, both rewritten here, and
keeping it would have left the line carrying a tag duplicating a field the
caller now has in its hand.

perf(db): index the owner columns a page load actually filters on

An audit of every ownership-style column in the schema found 624 of them,
223 without an index usable for a filter on the column alone. Most of that
is noise. 200 of the 223 are filtered by no query anywhere in the codebase,
and an index for a query nobody runs only costs writes. Narrowing to the
columns that are both unindexed and actually filtered left 22, and
narrowing again to the ones a user waits on left the seven indexes here.

Two of them are felt when a page opens. oe_bim_quantity_map carried no
index of any kind while the quantity rules page lists it at mount with a
limit of 500. The contacts scope clause is tenant_id = ? OR created_by = ?,
and PostgreSQL will only combine an OR of two equality tests into a
BitmapOr when it has an index for each side, so the missing half turned the
whole clause into a sequential scan on a table the code itself describes as
holding a few thousand rows. The other four sit behind a tab, a panel or a
toggle, which is still someone waiting.

Worth stating because it is the usual trap here: a foreign key does not
create an index in PostgreSQL. Two of these columns are foreign keys that
looked covered and were not.

The model declaration and the migration are both needed and serve
populations that do not overlap. create_all builds the schema for every
fresh install and skips a table that already exists, so a running install
gets these only by walking v43 to v44, and a new one gets them only from
the models. The migration's index list was generated from Base.metadata
after the model change rather than written by hand, and checked to match
in both directions so the two halves cannot disagree about a column.

Also corrects the _tenant_scope docstring, which asserted that both
branches of that OR were indexed while created_by was not, and says why
both have to stay indexed.

docs(alembic): mark v44 as one that must be run, not merely stamped

The previous commit left the impression that an install already running
would pick these indexes up from the migration. It will not, and neither
half of that change reaches it.

create_all decides table by table. It skips a table that already exists,
so it never adds an index to one, which means the model declaration is
skipped along with the table. Measured rather than assumed: create a table
without an index, then run create_all again from fresh metadata declaring
the same table with index=True, and the index does not arrive, while the
same metadata against a blank database does create it.

The deploy is create_all plus alembic stamp head and never alembic
upgrade, so the stamp marks this revision applied without executing it.
That is documented in env-config, in the release procedure, in
alembic_version_table, and in the single-head test, and nothing heals it
at boot.

So an existing database gets these seven indexes only when someone runs
the revision against it by hand. Four revisions already carry that marker
for the same reason, v3237 and v3245 through v3247, and this one now
carries it in the same words. Both halves stay as they are: a fresh
install gets the schema from create_all and the model declaration is the
only half it will ever see.

No schema change here, docstring only.

pointing at it survive and bill against nothing at all.

The contract screen has always known this and enables line editing only while
the contract is a draft. The server did not. update_line and delete_line
loaded the line, never looked at its contract, and would rewrite or remove a
line on an active, suspended, completed or terminated contract for anybody
calling the route directly. A guard that lives only in the client is a guard
against the client.

Both now refuse with 409 and the refusal names the remedy, which is a change
order, because a refusal that only says no gets worked around by editing the
row some other way. Draft is the only editable status: suspended is signed
work that has stopped, not work that has not yet been agreed. Deleting a line
that is not there stays a silent no-op rather than becoming a 404, so a
retried delete is still not an error, and the guard is reached only for a line
that exists, which is the only case that can destroy anything.

Creating a line on a signed contract is a related hole and is deliberately not
closed here. Nothing already certified is restated by an addition, and the
right remedy is probably that the change order is what adds the line, which is
a larger question than this guard and wants deciding rather than assuming.

The test lands with the fix rather than ahead of it, so it carries no marker.
Two of its three cases were red before this change. The third, a draft
contract still editing and deleting its lines freely, passed before and has to
keep passing, because that is the reason the write exists at all.

fix(contracts): put money no schedule line carries on the certificate that bills it

A payment application is assembled from claim lines, so money an earlier
claim billed that no schedule of values line carries never reached column D,
while line 7 still carried that month's certificate. Line 8 then subtracted a
certificate the columns had never added. Line 8 is floored at zero, so
however large that gap was the document reported the same thing, nothing due,
and the defect could not be sized from the certificate it produced.

The sheet now carries a row for that money, appended before the column is
allocated to cents so it is rounded with the rest of it rather than after.
Two different things land on that row and the label has to be true of both. A
contract may have had no schedule to bill against at all, or it had one and
the claim outran it, and the remainder that could not be placed on a line is
the same money in the same position. So the row says what the money is, that
no schedule of values line carries it, rather than what the contract lacks.

The retention half is the same blind spot one layer down. Column I on a
certified claim is reconciled to the retention that claim froze, and that
figure is measured on the schedule alone. Putting the new row in front of the
snapshot let it draw a share of a total that never counted the month it
stands for, so line 5 understated by exactly the retention held on that
month, and line 8 paid it out. Only the schedule rows go to the snapshot now,
and the new row keeps the column I it was built with.

Both halves are needed and neither should ship alone. With the column on its
own these certificates stop calling for nothing and start calling for more
than is owed, which is the worse of the two errors: a short payment is
corrected next month, an overpayment has to be recovered.

The residual is floored per claim rather than on the total. The two forms
return the same number on every row that exists today, because a claim's
gross is held equal to the sum of its lines by a recompute that runs on every
line write. That recompute is being removed so a claim billed from cost keeps
its basis when somebody adds a line by hand, and after that a claim whose
gross falls below its own lines contributes a negative term. Flooring the
total would let that cancel a real remainder from another claim, understating
column D and overstating line 8 with nothing going red anywhere.

mark that passes is a failure. The stored material mark stays; that one is
still failing and is not this. The new regression test asserts the two halves
of column I by where each comes from, since the column total cannot disagree
with line 5, and asserts that the face closes rather than asserting a
literal.

fix(contracts): record what a claim's gross is made of, so a hand-typed line cannot overwrite recorded cost

A cost-plus or time and materials claim bills a gross worked out from the
recorded cost of work, and has no schedule of values behind it. The retention
roll-up re-read that gross back off the claim's lines whenever the claim had
any, which is right for a claim whose gross is the sum of its lines and wrong
for this one. Type a single breakdown row against a fifty thousand cost claim
and the claim became worth that row. The presence of lines was standing in for
the basis of the gross, and the two stopped agreeing the moment anybody added
a line to a cost claim by hand.

The claim now records the basis instead of leaving it to be inferred.
ProgressClaim.gross_basis is "cost" for a claim generated from actual costs,
"lines" for one whose gross is the sum of its own period values, and NULL for
every claim written before the column existed. NULL means not recorded, not
"lines", so an old claim keeps exactly the behaviour it had. The basis cannot
be reconstructed after the fact either way: by the time anyone looks, a cost
claim that was already overwritten from its lines is indistinguishable from a
line claim that always said that. The column is declared on the model and not
only in the revision, because a running install adds model declared columns on
boot and never runs the upgrade, so a column that exists only in a revision is
a live failure on the API rather than a migration to catch up on later.

Both writers that make a gross out of lines now say so. The generator records
the basis from the branch it took rather than from the contract type, and the
populate commit records "lines" because that is what it has just made the
claim, including on a cost-plus contract that also carries a schedule of
values, which nothing prevents. A claim left recording a cost basis after a
populate is this defect inside out: a claim genuinely made of lines, frozen at
whatever the populate put there, refusing every later edit to its own rows.
Adding one line by hand is the opposite case and leaves the basis alone,
because a breakdown row is not a decision to rebuild the claim from the
schedule.

Until now a claim's gross always equalled the sum of its lines whenever it had
lines, held there by the recompute this change removes, and two readers leaned
on that. The totals rule asserted the equality outright and would have failed
every legitimate cost claim carrying a partial breakdown, so it is widened
rather than duplicated: a cost claim is held to the weaker statement that its
breakdown cannot ask for more than the claim does, and a claim of any other
basis is still held to exact equality. The residual behind the certificate's
out of schedule row floors each claim at zero rather than netting the claims
off against each other, so it is already right when a gross sits below its own
lines; the two forms of it differ only in that case, which is the case this
change makes reachable.

A gross below its own lines is reported, not corrected upward. Correcting it
would be the same re-read of the gross from the lines that the basis exists to
stop, arriving under a different name, and it would move money on a document a
payer acts on. It is an error rather than a warning because a warning does not
hold the claim: between the warning being raised and somebody acting on it the
continuation sheet and the header are already saying two different things, and
the certificate goes out regardless.

In the same branch retention is now derived from the gross and the contract
rate rather than read back off the claim. Every generator that reaches this
path computes retention with that exact formula and that exact rate, so no
claim any current writer produces changes value, and the demo seed writes the
same formula at cent precision. What changes is the guarantee rather than the
numbers: a writer that set a gross and forgot the retention beside it would
have billed the whole gross with nothing held and said nothing about it, and
the error is in the direction of paying out too much. The ladder branch has
always restated retention in full, so the flat branch preserving it was the odd
one out rather than a decision anyone took.

Covered by a test that adds a line to a cost claim by hand and asserts the
gross survives it, one that populates a cost claim and asserts it becomes a
line claim that follows its rows afterwards, and one that holds a cost claim to
its breakdown in both directions: an understated breakdown raises nothing and
submits, an overstated one raises exactly this error and is refused at
submission.

fix(contracts): work line 7 out from figures that can see a month no schedule line carries

Line 7 of a payment application is what the claims before this one certified.
It was read from the previous claim's frozen cumulative, and that figure is
assembled from schedule lines, so a month billed with no line behind it is
missing from it and stays missing. On a cost-plus job billed from cost in
March and against the schedule in April and May, May's certificate read
27000 where the first two months had certified 72000.

That did not show until now because line 4 was wrong in the same direction
and by the same amount, and the two cancelled. 275aa80a6 corrected line 4 and
not line 7, so they stopped cancelling: May then called for 54000 against
9000 actually owed. Measured from both ends rather than argued. A worktree at
275aa80a6^ prints line 4 at 40000, line 7 at 27000 and line 8 at 9000, equal
to the claim; the same fixture after it prints 90000, 27000 and 54000. Line 7
is 27000 in both, so it was already wrong on its own, and what the previous
commit removed was the second error that had been hiding it.

previous_certificates now refuses the snapshot when an earlier claim billed
gross that no line of its own accounts for, and reconstructs instead. The two
are not the same quantity. A snapshot is one claim's cumulative to date,
assembled per schedule line. Reconstruction sums each claim's own gross less
its own retention, so the month with no lines is counted once, on the claim
that billed it. The snapshot is not a cheaper reconstruction, it is a lossier
one that agrees whenever every month has lines, which is the population it
was written against and tested on.

This is detection and containment rather than repair, and the distinction
matters for anyone reading it later. A claim can reach this state two ways.
It can have been billed from cost, with no schedule to bill against, which is
ordinary. Or its claim lines can have been destroyed: contract_line_id
carries ondelete CASCADE, confirmed on the deployed schema rather than in the
model, and deleting a schedule of values line takes every claim line that
billed against it, in every claim, in any status. The claim keeps its gross
and its retention, because those live on the claim and have one writer. What
it loses is the justification. By the time this code runs the rows are gone
and nothing downstream can tell a line that was never billed from a line
whose billing was deleted, so this cannot repair such a claim. What it does
is stop the certificate quietly printing a number built on the loss. The
guard that prevents the deletion is separate work and is not here.

Reconstruction is not the more mutable of the two, which was the reason to
hesitate. Every writer of gross_amount and retention_amount refuses a claim
that is not a draft, a release can only be billed onto a draft claim and
cannot be voided off a locked one, and the claim status map sends certified
only to paid and paid nowhere, so the door cannot reopen. Both branches read
values frozen at certification. Reconstruction simply reads all of the prior
claims where the snapshot reads only the last.

The part worth knowing for anything built on this later: the snapshot branch
is the only consumer that reads completed_stored_to_date and
retention_held_to_date, and that column pair has two writers with no shared
definition, the retention engine when a claim has lines and the certification
freeze when it does not. Reconstruction reads the claim's own billed figures,
which have one author. A reviewer will assume both branches read the same
storage, and they do not.

The condition is computed by the method that defines the quantity, not by a
second expression that means to say the same thing. That is deliberate and it
is the shape of the original defect: line 4 and line 7 answered one question
in two places and disagreed. A guard derived separately from the thing it
guards would have been the same bug with a longer fuse.

No widening of the old double count that reconstruction carries for claims
generated before the claim basis fix. The columns the snapshot branch reads
were added by v42_contracts_billing_depth, which is part of that same commit,
so a claim from before it has nothing frozen and was already being
reconstructed. This only redirects claims certified after it, and for those
reconstruction is exact. The one exception is a claim that existed before an
install upgraded, was never regenerated and was certified after, which holds
a frozen pair written by current code over a gross written by the old rule.

Measured rather than reasoned, on the deployed database: 41 contracts, 162
claims, 437 claim lines, and zero claims carrying gross with no lines, taken
with a partition control so the zero is a count and not a query that failed
quietly. The demo estate is zero as well. That zero counts the pattern and
not the damage, and it does not make the new path rare. The same signature
has two producers, claim lines destroyed underneath a claim and ordinary
cost billing with no schedule to bill against, and by the time this code
runs nothing can separate them. On a cost-plus or time and materials install
reconstruction is not an alarm, it is the normal path, from the second claim
of every such contract onward, and two tests here bill exactly that way and
read reconstructed. What the zero does say is narrower: no claim on the
deployed database changes its certificate the day this ships.

The fixture goes to three months permanently. Two months cannot express this:
April's line 7 reads March, which is lineless, and a lineless month's frozen
figures happen to cover the whole job. The divergence needs a prior claim
that HAD lines, so it starts in May. The test asserts the basis as well as the
amount, because 72000 read off the wrong basis would pass and break again at
a fourth month, which is how this arrived in the first place.

docs(contracts): correct what the retention snapshot says line 5 measures

fix(subcontractors): read the German exemption certificate on the payment date

The German pack says the construction tax exemption certificate counts on
the day of payment (valid_at: payment_date), and the claim rollup ignored
that and judged it at the claim's period end like every other certificate.
So a certificate valid on 31 March and expired on the day the money went in
May read as met, and the payment the law then taxes at 15% of the gross,
VAT included, went through without a word.

The rollup now reads valid_at from the pack. A certificate marked
payment_date is judged on each pay application's own payment day: covered,
or missing, expired or revoked on that day. The day is the UTC calendar day
on which the pay application was marked paid in the platform, since that is
the payment record it keeps; a bank value date is not recorded. A pay
application marked paid with no payment date is reported as not checkable.
Before payment there is no verdict, and the rollup says so instead of
calling it met: the certificate is read on the payment date, here is when
the one on file ends, or there is none that could cover a payment at all.
Only included pay applications are judged; earlier paid ones are not
re-read here.

A new rule in the pay application set words it. It warns and never blocks,
and it deducts nothing: the message names the withholding the law requires,
with the rate, whether the base includes VAT and the annual small-amount
limit taken from the shipped German scheme, and the suggestion says the
deduction is not made here. An unpaid pay application gets a note rather
than a warning unless nothing on file could cover it. The wording is in the
module's English, German and Russian bundles, and the claim panel shows a
chip for a certificate still waiting for its payment day.

This takes the exemption out of the period-end certificate rule, which is
an error and blocked submission. On a German claim an exemption that has
run out now warns instead of blocking, which is what the law asks: it
decides the tax on the payment, not whether the work may be billed.

A pack without payment-date certificates gets exactly what it got before.
A US claim's rollup, rule context and every rule result are compared byte
for byte against a snapshot written from the code before this change. The
API adds optional fields only, which are null for such packs.

fix(contracts): count retention outside the schedule once on G702 line 5

On a contract where the retention engine does the work, a month billed with
no schedule line behind it holds its own retention, and the continuation
sheet carries that money on a separate row. The engine compared what the
schedule requires against everything earlier claims had held, and that
included the lineless month. When a ladder had stopped retaining, the
lineless retention got ratcheted into the schedule's held figure and the
sheet printed it a second time on its own row. With a flat rate it came off
the next claim's accrual instead, so that claim under-accrued. The stored
net due also took line 7 from the whole job and the completed figure from
the schedule alone, which put it under line 8 by the lineless month's net.
Since a release could never reach that row, a final release left it held
for good.

The engine now looks only at the schedule. It leaves out the retention that
earlier claims held on money none of their lines carry, and that money's
share of the releases. The net due and the sheet add the money back into
both lines 4 and 5, so line 8 and the stored net due come from the same
calculation. A release is split pro rata between the schedule and the row,
according to what each has accrued, and it is recalculated at every claim,
so releasing everything clears both. The row's column I now comes from the
retention those claims actually stored, not from the current contract rate.
The floors stay, and the policy requirement is still measured on schedule
lines only.

Worked cases: 10% until half complete, then nothing, on 200,000. Month 3
now prints line 5 at 12,000 and pays 40,000, where it printed 14,000 and
paid 20,000. A final release of 12,000 clears line 5 to zero and pays
12,000. On a flat 10% the month after a lineless month accrues its full
6,000 and pays 54,000.

The earlier-claim residual is now summed per claim by an aggregate query.
It no longer loads every claim line on the contract.

fix(contracts): leave draft claims out of previous certificates

A draft has not left the contractor, so it certified nothing, and counting it
put work nobody had applied for into column D and G702 line 7. A certificate
built now leaves drafts out.

When a claim leaves draft, the claims it counted as previous are frozen onto it
(prior_claim_ids), and every later print reads only those, less any rejected
since. A claim issued before this change carries no such set and keeps counting
drafts, so certificates already out keep their figures. A metadata write
through the claim update path cannot change the frozen set.

Leaving drafts out opens one order of events that counting them had closed. If
a later claim goes out while an earlier one is still a draft, the later claim
bills that work, and the earlier one would then bill it again. Submitting such
a draft is now refused with 409 later_claim_already_issued. A later claim that
went out counting it, or a rejected later claim, does not block it. The other
order, where the earlier draft goes out first, was already caught:
pay_application.prior_matches_earlier_claims blocks the later claim until it
is generated again.

The first attempt (2c4d92790) turned nine certificate tests red. In every one
of them the earlier claim was a draft only because the fixture never submitted
it. The business case each test describes is that claim going out before the
next one is drawn, so the fixtures now submit it through transition_claim, the
same path that freezes the set. The two tests about an earlier claim
regenerated after a later one existed now send the later claim out first, so
billing order is still what they check and not the draft rule. The earlier
claim goes back through rejected to draft, the route the API offers. These
files also register the pay_application rules, because submitting now runs
that gate in them.

receipts put there.

A contract that a subcontract agreement carries is not a second commitment,

fix(costs): keep the loading session alive through a long cost base import

Loading a large regional base (Toronto, about 55 700 items) ended as failed
at 15% with "Can't reconnect until invalid transaction is rolled back" while
every item had in fact landed. The item count read at the start of
load_cwicr_region opened a transaction on the caller's session, and that
session then sat idle in transaction for the whole download and import,
which run on their own connection. PostgreSQL ended it once the engine's
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout ran out, the resource price seed failed
on the dead connection and was swallowed, and the caller's commit raised.
The price sheet for the base was silently never seeded.

The read transaction is now committed before the long part starts. A price
seed that still fails rolls the session back and is reported in the result
as resource_prices_error instead of only in the log.

One row PostgreSQL refuses, such as a NUL character in a description, used
to sink its whole flush and the import with it. A flush that hits a data
error is now split and retried down to the single row, which is skipped and
counted in the result as failed and failed_codes. Connection errors still
fail the import.

Both are pinned by PostgreSQL tests: a one-second idle budget with a slower
import reproduces the exact error, and a parquet with one NUL row loads the
other five.

fix(notifications): stop emailing deactivated users

owner of an overdue item by checking that the user row existed, not that it
was active, and the email dispatcher resolved a user id to an address the same
way. On the showcase one deactivated external account collected between 7 and
80 overdue notifications a day, and the only thing between those and an inbox
was the production transport being switched to noop.

The sweep now picks recipients among active, non-erased users only. A
deactivated owner falls through to the project managers, deactivated managers
are dropped from both the nudge and the escalation, and with nobody active
left the item is logged and nobody is notified. The dispatcher skips an
inactive or erased user, and EmailService.send refuses any address that
belongs to a deactivated account, next to the seeded-login refusal, so
invitations, reports and document mail follow the same rule. An address that
is nobody's account is still mailed, and a failed lookup sends anyway, so a
password reset never depends on it. Password reset already refused inactive
accounts, and self-registration in gated modes sends no mail, so no activation
flow is affected.

The sweep also published the email inside the same savepoint as the
escalation step. When escalation raised, the savepoint took the in-app row,
which is the dedupe record, with it while the email was already on its way,
so the next tick sent it again and the lifetime ceiling never counted it. The
email is now collected and published only after the nudge's own savepoint has
released, and escalation runs in a savepoint of its own. No separate daily
throttle is added: the existing ceiling of three nudges per item holds once
its record survives.

The rows are now claimed before anything is sent, with a conditional UPDATE

concurrent flush waits on those row locks until the first one commits and
then finds nothing left to claim. The PostgreSQL test holds the first flush

and has no per-app exception, so a signed installer alone does not help. The
sidecar unpacks about 490 exe, dll and pyd files at every start and 409 of them

sidecar is built from before PyInstaller seals it, the onefile sidecar right
after, the bundled converters, and through bundle.windows.signCommand the
launcher, the NSIS plugins, the uninstaller and the installer. Files already
signed by their own publisher keep their signature.

ARTIFACT_SIGNING_* secrets exist. Half a configuration fails the run, and only
version tags sign. docs/desktop/WINDOWS_SIGNING.md explains the setup.
